XCII Under Vine and Fig-Tree

THE VIRGINIANS

On the paneled wall of a certain American scholar—one who made his fame not by steel but by sentences—there hang two swords crossed in mute argument. One was drawn for a king, the other for a republic; both are now only bright shapes catching light in a quiet room. I have seen, too, in an English parlor, two portraits facing one another across a fireplace: a colonel in scarlet, a general in blue and buff. In that household they have long been called, with a family fondness that turns history into a nickname, “The Virginians.”

Their story survives because a woman saved it the way a careful housewife saves seed-corn and preserves fruit against winter. Madam Esmond—so she was styled ever after Castlewood in Virginia burned and she took refuge in Richmond—kept her sons’ letters as if each sheet were a cloth laid over something perishable. The earliest is a child’s scrawl with duty and love; the last came “from my beloved son” only hours before her own death. Between are pages stained with travel, with tears, with camp-smoke ground into the paper; one is pierced by a bullet, another blotched by blood so that half the inked words are swallowed up, like a voice drowned by a sudden roar. The letters themselves are often scanty—hints, not full pictures. So, bending over the yellowed folds, I have tried to hear the rooms they were written in, to catch the clink of glasses after a ball, the crackle of a fire by a bivouac, the hush of a sick-chamber, and to set down what the writers only half-said.

It was a summer morning in 1756, in the reign of King George the Second, when the Young Rachel, Virginian ship—Edward Franks, master—came up the Avon with the tide, returning, as she did yearly, from the Potomac. The river’s brackish breath mixed with the sweeter smell of tar and wet rope; the rigging spoke in small creaks and complaints as the ship steadied herself for Bristol. She moored in the stream as near to Trail’s wharf as might be, and Mr. Trail—part owner, factor, and a man who could look from his counting-house window and count his profit by the angle of a mast—took boat and came aboard.

He was large, grave, and neatly self-possessed, wearing his own hair and a demure face as if piety were part of his cargo. He shook Captain Franks’s hand and congratulated him upon a quick and fortunate passage, pausing to acknowledge Heaven’s mercies with the same air he used in balancing a ledger. But gratitude in Mr. Trail was a short prayer that led directly to business.

“Cargo? Passengers?” he asked.

Franks was a broad, easy fellow, with a sailor’s relish for a jest and a sailor’s bluntness in offering it.

“We have,” said he, “but yonder ugly negro boy, fetching the trunks, and a passenger who has had the state cabin to himself.”

Mr. Trail’s face fell, as if Providence had been stingy.

“Confound you, Franks, and your luck! The Duke William, in last week, brought fourteen—and she’s not half our tonnage.”

“And this passenger,” Franks went on, enjoying the pinch he gave, “who has had the whole cabin, don’t pay nothin’.”

Mr. Trail stared as if he had been told the ship had sailed without ballast.

“A passenger take the whole cabin and not pay? Gracious mercy, are you a fool, Captain Franks?”

“Ask the passenger himself—for here he comes.”

As the words were spoken, a young gentleman came up from below: nineteen, straight-limbed, handsome in that clear, fresh way youth has before it learns to guard its face. He carried a cloak and a sword under his arm. His clothes were deep mourning, which made his skin look the fairer and his eyes the more alive. Behind him, in black likewise, followed the boy called Gumbo, struggling with baggage.

“Gumbo, you idiot,” the young man cried, quick with impatience, “why don’t you fetch the baggage out of the cabin? Well, shipmate, our journey is ended. You will see all the little folks to-night you’ve been talking about. Give my love to Polly and Betty and little Tommy—not forgetting my duty to Mrs. Franks. Yesterday I thought the voyage would never be done, and now I am almost sorry it is over. That little berth in my cabin looks very comfortable now I am going to leave it.”

Mr. Trail scowled at this passenger who had cost him a cabin and brought him no coin. He was barely civil with his nod; but Franks, with the pride of a man introducing a friend, said:

“This here gentleman is Mr. Trail, sir, whose name you have a-heerd of.”

“It’s pretty well known in Bristol, sir,” Mr. Trail said, drawing himself up with a merchant’s majesty.

“And this,” Captain Franks continued, “is Mr. Warrington—Madam Esmond Warrington’s son, of Castlewood.”

The effect was as immediate as the change of wind in a sail. Mr. Trail’s hat flew off as though snatched by reverence; he bowed again and again, his face smoothing itself into cordiality.

“Gracious powers! Mr. Warrington! This is a delight indeed! What a crowning mercy that your voyage should have been so prosperous! You must have my boat to go ashore. Let me cordially and respectfully welcome you to England—let me shake your hand as the son of my benefactress and patroness, Mrs. Esmond Warrington, whose name is known and honoured on Bristol ’Change, I warrant you. Isn’t it, Franks?”

“There’s no sweeter tobacco comes from Virginia, and no better brand than the Three Castles,” said Franks, and brought out a great brass tobacco-box with the air of a man producing a family treasure. He lifted the lid; the scent sprang up—dark, warm, almost fruity, with that clean bitterness that sits at the back of the tongue like a promise. He packed a quid into his mouth as if he were stowing cargo. “You don’t know what a comfort it is, sir. You’ll take to it, bless you, as you grow older. Won’t he, Mr. Trail? I wish you had ten shiploads of it instead of one. You might have ten shiploads—I’ve told Madam Esmond so; I’ve rode over her plantation; she treats me like a lord when I go to the house; she don’t grudge me the best wine, nor keep me cooling my heels in the counting-room as some folks does”—and here he looked squarely at Mr. Trail—“She is a real born lady, she is; and might have a thousand hogsheads as easy as her hundreds, if there were but hands enough.”

Mr. Trail, who heard “hands” as a bell hears its own ringing, leaned in with eager softness.

“I have lately engaged in the Guinea trade, and could supply her ladyship with any number of healthy young negroes before next fall,” he said, as though offering a new kind of barrel or rope.

The young Virginian’s face tightened; a different cold entered his voice.

“We are averse to the purchase of negroes from Africa. My grandfather and my mother have always objected to it, and I do not like to think of selling or buying the poor wretches.”

Mr. Trail lifted his hands in a pious flutter.

“It is for their good, my dear young sir! for their temporal and their spiritual good! And we purchase the poor creatures only for their benefit; let me talk this matter over with you at my own house. I can introduce you to a happy home, a Christian family, and a British merchant’s honest fare. Can’t I, Captain Franks?”

“Can’t say,” growled Franks. “Never asked me to take bite or sup at your table. Asked me to psalm-singing once, and to hear Mr. Ward preach: don’t care for them sort of entertainments.”

Mr. Trail, pretending not to hear, lowered his tone into something meant for confidential wisdom.

“Business is business, my dear young sir, and ’tis only my duty—the duty of all of us—to cultivate the fruits of the earth in their season. As the heir of Lady Esmond’s estate—for I speak, I believe, to the heir of that great property?—”

The young gentleman bowed, but it was the bow of someone enduring, not receiving.

“I would urge upon you, at the very earliest moment, the propriety—the duty—of increasing the ample means with which Heaven has blessed you. As an honest factor, I could not do otherwise; as a prudent man, should I scruple to speak of what will tend to your profit and mine? No, my dear Mr. George.”

“My name is not George,” the young man said, turning his head sharply away. His eyes filled, in spite of himself, and a tear slid down as if grief had been waiting behind the talk of profits. “My name is Henry.”

“Gracious powers!” Mr. Trail gasped, struck at last by the mourning and the tears. “What do you mean, sir? Did you not say you were my lady’s heir? and is not George Esmond Warrington, Esq.—”

“Hold your tongue, you fool!” Captain Franks cried, and cuffed the merchant’s sleek side with a sailor’s hard hand. “Don’t you see the young gentleman a-swabbing his eyes, and note his black clothes?”

Mr. Trail recoiled, offended at being handled, yet still bewildered by the correction.

“What do you mean, Captain Franks, by laying your hand on your owners? Mr. George is the heir; I know the Colonel’s will well enough.”

“Mr. George is there,” said Franks, and jerked his thumb upward, toward the deck and the sky beyond.

“Where?” Mr. Trail cried, looking about him as if the dead might step from behind a coil of rope.

“Mr. George is there!” Franks repeated, pointing higher, past mast and rigging. “He is dead a year, sir, come next ninth of July. He would go out with General Braddock on that dreadful business to the Belle Riviere. He and a thousand more never came back again. Every man of ’em was murdered as he fell. You know the Indian way, Mr. Trail?” And with his hand he made, quick and dreadful, a circle round his head.

The deck seemed to hush for a moment, as if even the river had stopped its small lap against the hull. Franks’s voice, rough as it was, had the tremor of honest pity.

“Horrible, ain’t it? horrible! He was a fine young man—the very picture of this one; only his hair was black, which is now hanging in a bloody Indian wigwam. He was often on board the Young Rachel, and would have his chests of books broke open on deck before they was landed. A shy and silent young gent— not like this one, which was the merriest, wildest young fellow, full of songs and fun. He took on dreadful at the news; went to his bed; had that fever which lays so many of ’em by the heels along that swampy Potomac, but he’s got better on the voyage. The voyage makes every one better; and in course the young gentleman can’t be for ever a-crying after a brother who dies and leaves him a great fortune. Ever since we sighted Ireland he has been quite gay and happy, only he would go off at times, when he was most merry, saying, ‘I wish my dearest Georgy could enjoy this here sight along with me,’ and when you mentioned the t’other’s name, you see, he couldn’t stand it.”

And now the Captain’s own eyes brimmed; he turned his head away, ashamed, like a man caught praying.

Mr. Trail arranged his face into a proper sorrow, ready with condolences that would offend no customer; but Henry Warrington answered him curtly, declined the offered hospitality, and stayed in the merchant’s house only long enough to swallow a glass of wine and take up money he needed. If Mr. Trail’s wine was honest, it had no welcome in it; it went down like duty, not comfort.

With Captain Franks the parting was altogether different. There were warm grips of the hand, messages repeated, promises made; and as Henry left the ship, the little crew of the Young Rachel cheered him from the side until the sound scattered over the water.

He and his dead brother had pored over maps as boys pore over cookbooks—hungry with imagination, tasting places before they ever see them. They had traced a pilgrimage through England: Bristol, Bath, Salisbury, Winchester, Hexton—Home. They had named the great sights as if naming dishes on a grand table: London with its enormous churches; the Tower with its cold stories; Whitehall’s fatal window; parks and playhouses; Shakespeare’s resting-place by Avon among the Warwickshire pastures; the battlefields where loyalty had bled and failed. Yet there was one point more sacred than all—a house in Hampshire, old Castlewood, spoken of in Virginia as “home” with that affectionate wrongness the colonies still used for the mother country.

Henry traveled like a man drawn by a cord. He was young, and health made a kind of music in his blood; he had money; and he had grief that flared and dulled by turns like a coal on the hearth. The post-chaise took him through an English summer that seemed to him almost extravagant in its abundance. Where his Virginian journeys had been through swamp and pine solitude from one rough ordinary to another log-house, here every mile offered a new arrangement of comfort: hedgerows thick as walls, meadows shining, villages tucked like careful garnishes along the road. The inns were loud with life; the highroad itself was no deserted strip but a busy artery. Heavy wagons went by, bells chiming; post-coaches rattled with practiced haste; packhorses still threaded along with patient feet; a nobleman’s chaise-and-six flashed past with outriders; squires rolled ponderously; farmers jogged toward market; a parson bumped along on Dumpling with his wife on the pillion.

Through open windows came the clatter of dishes and the thick, nourishing smells that make a traveler suddenly aware of his own hunger: roasting meat, bread cooling, ale frothing, onions sweating in fat. In kitchens he glimpsed copper pans bright as shields and heard the music of work—knife on board, spoon on pot, the hiss when something met hot iron. Those sounds were not noise, but the ordered acoustics of a living place: wheels on gravel, a smith’s hammer, a child’s cry, a distant church bell measuring the day. Even the great elms had their own soft speech overhead.

At each stop, eyes followed him. The plump landlady, surrounded by china and punch-bowls and stout gilded bottles of strong waters and glittering rows of silver flagons, looked kindly after the young gentleman in black. The obsequious chamberlain bowed him upstairs to the Rose or the Dolphin. The chambermaid made her best curtsey for the fee that would sweeten her evening. Gumbo, down in the kitchen among the drinkers by the great fire, bragged in his rough way of his master’s splendid house in Virginia and the immense wealth to which he was heir; and the townsfolk listened, weighing the boy’s dark face against the strange boast, and then peering more curiously when Henry passed.

Henry barely gave Bath Abbey more than a passing glance, nor Salisbury Minster more than a moment’s wonder; not because they were small, but because his desire was larger than sight-seeing. Until he beheld Home, he felt as if he had no eyes for any other place.

At last the post-chaise drew up at the rustic inn on Castlewood Green—an inn his grandsire had spoken of so often that Henry knew it before he saw it. From an elm near the porch swung its sign: the Three Castles of the Esmond family. The same cognisance appeared over the gateway of Castlewood House, but there it was joined with the dark symbolism of death: a hatchment showing the arms and, now, an earl’s coronet.

That hatchment was for Francis, Lord Castlewood, newly laid in the chapel hard by; his son reigned in his stead. Henry had heard of Frank all his life—how wild he had been, how bravely he had fought under Marlborough, how he had married abroad and taken up the wrong religion, how loyalty in the family ran so strong that even when he wavered between Prince and King it was still called loyalty, only turned to a different star. He had returned to the Established Church upon his second marriage, had supported the King and the Minister of the hour, and for those services had died an English peer. So much for a life: a coronet painted on a board above a gate, and then the board itself weathering under English rain.

Colonel Esmond—Henry’s grandfather—had corresponded with his stepson briefly but affectionately, and loved him in memory; Madam Esmond had always spoken of him with a cool contempt. “Dull,” she said, “except when he drank too much wine—which was every day at dinner.” A fine tall animal, yes, good-looking; but she’d rather her boys took a different model. The boys themselves, brought up on their mother’s staunch Jacobite talk (respectful to the reigning Majesty, but firm that right was right), had never learned to reverence the dead lord very much.

Now Henry, heart beating as if it were knocking on the gate before he did, left the inn and walked toward the house where his grandsire’s youth had been spent. Castlewood Green sloped down to a river crossed by an old bridge of a single broad arch; beyond, the ground rose gently toward the house—grey, gabled, buttressed, backed by a darker wood that seemed to hold its breath.

At the wicket sat an old man on a stone bench before the great arched entrance. An old dog crouched at his feet, keeping, as dogs do, a small warm vigil over age. Above the sentry at the gate was an open casement with homely flowers in the window, and behind it good-humoured girls’ faces peeped out, curious. They watched the young gentleman in black and the ebony attendant in black following him; and Henry noticed, with a start that made his grief feel suddenly shared, that the man at the gate wore mourning too, and when the girls came out they had black ribbons.

To Henry’s surprise, the old man spoke to him at once, naming him as if he had been expected.

“You have had a nice ride to Hexton, Master Harry, and the sorrel carried you well.”

“I think you must be Lockwood,” Henry said, his voice trembling in spite of his effort to steady it. He held out his hand. He had heard of Lockwood a hundred times in Virginia—how he had followed the Colonel and the young Viscount through Marlborough’s wars forty years before, how he had been faithful as a hound and stubborn as a gatepost.

The veteran looked puzzled at the offered hand, as though affection were a language he could no longer translate cleanly. The old dog lifted its eyes, regarded Henry, and then tucked its head between its knees again, as if refusing to be hurried into friendship.

“I have heard of you often. How did you know my name?” Henry asked.

“They say I forget most things,” the old man answered, smiling; “but I ain’t so bad as that quite. Only this mornin’, when you went out, my darter says, ‘Father, do you know why you have a black coat on?’ ‘In course I know why I have a black coat,’ says I. ‘My lord is dead. They say ’twas a foul blow, and Master Frank is my lord now, and Master Harry’—why, what have you done since you’ve went out this morning? Why, you have a-grow’d taller and changed your hair—though I know—I know you.”

By this time one of the young women had tripped out from the porter’s lodge and dropped Henry a pretty curtsey. Her cheeks were wholesome, her eyes bright; she had the look of someone who knows every sound a house makes at night and can tell by a creak whether it is wind or a thief.

“Grandfather sometimes does not recollect very well,” she said, and tapped her head gently. “Your honour seems to have heard of Lockwood?”

“And you—have you never heard of Colonel Francis Esmond?”

“He was Captain and Major in Webb’s Foot,” Lockwood cried at once, memory flaring up like a match in dry straw, “and I was with him in two campaigns, sure enough. Wasn’t I, Ponto?” The old dog’s tail thumped once, as if the name of war were still a summons.

“The Colonel as married Viscountess Rachel, my late lord’s mother?” the girl said eagerly. “And went to live amongst the Indians? We have heard of him. Sure we have his picture in our gallery, and hisself painted it.”

“Went to live in Virginia,” Henry said, “and died there seven years ago—and I am his grandson.”

The girl’s face changed; astonishment loosened into warmth.

“Lord, your honour! Why, your honour’s skin’s as white as mine,” she cried—blurting the thought as simply as a country girl speaks of cream. Then she turned to the old man. “Grandfather, do you hear this? His honour is Colonel Esmond’s grandson that used to send you tobacco, and his honour have come all the way from Virginia.”

“To see you, Lockwood,” Henry said, and the words, meant kindly, came out with a thickness in his throat. “And the family. I only set foot on English ground yesterday, and my first visit is for home. I may see the house, though the family are from home?”

The girl—Molly, as it seemed by the ease with which Lockwood’s speech had named her—said she dared say Mrs. Barker would let his honour see the house. And Henry Warrington crossed the court as if his feet remembered what his life had never known, while Molly followed, and Gumbo behind them made her a profusion of bows and speeches, his voice fluttering and over-earnest in the new acoustics of England, where every word of his sounded like a foreign coin struck on a familiar table.

Colonel Esmond’s grandson stood a full while at the gate of Castlewood, and made that honest clatter upon the knocker which in Virginia would have brought half a house to the door with smiles and questions and a hand already reaching for a saddle-bag. Here, the old stone seemed to swallow sound. The only answer was the distant hush of rooms shut up, and—more plainly than any welcome—the thin tick of leisure within, as if time itself were a servant who need not hurry.

At last the door opened no more than was necessary; and John the footman, who had been playing cards with Thomas in a window-seat, appeared with the air of a man obliged to interrupt a serious business for a trifling one. To be told that the visitor was of the family altered nothing in John’s face. The family were away. In their absence, he cared little for their kin, and much for the game waiting at the sill.

Harry, heat in his cheeks from travel and hope, begged—begged again—until permission was grudgingly given to step into my lady’s sitting-room and the picture-room. There, sure enough, the past was hung as neatly as a pantry of preserves: his grandfather in periwig and breastplate, the very counterpart of the canvas at home in Virginia; and his grandmother as Lady Castlewood, in an earlier fashion, her neck bare in Charles the Second’s time, her fair hair falling in ringlets—ringlets which in Harry’s living memory had been snowy white. He looked till the old varnish seemed to breathe, and the painted silks rustled in his fancy; but the housekeeper, brisk with preparations and sharp with importance, drove him onward as one drives a boy from a larder when dinner is to be served for guests of consequence.

“My lord and my lady are expected this evening,” she said. “There is my lady the Countess, and my lord and his brother, and the young ladies, and the Baroness, who is to have the state bedchamber.”

“The Baroness?” Harry asked, catching at any thread of relation as a hungry man snatches at the smell of bread.

“Baroness Bernstein—the young ladies’ aunt,” said the woman, and her eyes were already elsewhere, counting linens, weighing candles, measuring courtesies.

In the hall, with the stubborn politeness of a stranger who will not be made invisible, Harry wrote his name on a leaf torn from his own pocket-book and laid it where it must be seen.

Henry Esmond Warrington, of Castlewood, in Virginia, arrived in England yesterday—staying at the Three Castles in the village.

The lackeys, scenting a possible “wail,” rose from their cards only to profit by him; and Gumbo, faithful as a shadow, left the bench at the gate where he had been talking with old Lockwood the porter. Lockwood took Harry’s guinea with a bewildered gratitude, as though the yellow piece were a foreign coin whose value lay in the giver’s hand rather than in the King’s head upon it.

Harry walked away from that house of his fathers with a dryness in his mouth that no ale could mend. In all those faces—servant, housekeeper, porter—little Polly’s was the only countenance that had held any unselfish light; and he would not own, even to himself, how the chill of it had struck him. They ought to have known him. Had any ridden up to Castlewood in Virginia—master at home or abroad—the stranger would have had a chair drawn near the hearth, and a plate set as if he had been expected. Yet here, in sight of his ancestors’ hall, he must go and ask a country alehouse for a dish of bacon and eggs.

At the Three Castles they gave him what he asked, and more than he asked, for hunger makes men bold in ordering. The bacon came from a hog salted hard enough to keep its virtue through winter; the eggs were fresh, with yolks deep as marigolds, and the fat in the pan carried a clean sweet smoke that rose and clung to his mourning coat as if to comfort it. He watched the hostess turn the rashers with a fork worn bright at the tines, and for a moment the homely sizzle steadied him—sound as much as savour; a small domestic music against the great silence of Castlewood. He ate. He could taste pepper and salt, could feel the crust of fried edge and the soft give of white; and yet every mouthful seemed paid for in something more than coin.

After dinner he went to the bridge and sat upon it, looking towards the old house, behind which the sun was sinking. The rooks came cawing home to the elms, and their harsh, communal talk made a canopy of sound above the river; beneath it, the water moved with a low, constant tongue. Hard by, a blacksmith’s forge clinked and rang—iron on iron—so steady that it might have been a heart at work.

In that mingling of evening noises—rook-calls, forge-clinks, bird-cries from the hedges—his fancy peopled the ford with what his mother and grandsire had told him: knights and huntsmen crossing where the shallows glittered; cavaliers of King Charles’s day; my Lord Castlewood, his grandmother’s first husband, riding out with hawk and hound. The past came as naturally as the smell of smoke in a kitchen: not a story told, but something you breathe.

Then, as always when he allowed himself tenderness, the recollection of his dear dead brother rose and smote him. The pang was so sharp it made him bow his head as if struck. All his pleasures and griefs had been shared with that companion until of late; and now, with the rooks talking above him and the forge chiming beside, he felt again the cruel newness of being alone.

It was then that two young men on horseback dashed over the bridge, cutting across the calm as a knife cuts through cloth. One, with an oath, called him a fool and bade him keep out of the way; the other—who might well have jostled him clean over the parapet—spurred on the instant he had passed, shouting to his fellow to come on. They were up the hill towards Castlewood before Harry had recovered from surprise and wrath.

A moment later came two servants in livery on horseback, scowling at him with that peculiar British question which sounds like a curse: Who are you to be here at all? And after them, heavy as an age, a coach-and-six rumbled onto the bridge, so weighty the horses seemed to sweat at the very idea of drawing it. Within were three ladies, a couple of maids, and an armed man perched behind. Three handsome pale faces looked out at Harry as the carriage passed; not one returned the salute he gave, for he recognized the family arms and would not forget himself. The armed man glared haughtily, as if his stare were itself a weapon.

Harry remained on the bridge and felt the river’s cool talk below him and the rooks’ rough talk above, and in that moment both sounded like a language that did not include him. He thought—half sick with longing—of Captain Franks, of the Rachel and her small tossing cabin. Even that cramped place at sea seemed cheerful beside this ancestral ground where he stood unclaimed.

Back at the inn the folk did not know the name of Warrington; they knew only titles. They told him that was my lady in the coach, with her stepdaughter, my Lady Maria, and her daughter, my Lady Fanny; that the young gentleman in the grey frock was Mr. William, and he with powder on the chestnut was my lord. It was my lord who had sworn loudest and called him a fool; it was Mr. William in the grey frock who had nearly ridden him into the ditch.

The landlord had shown Harry a bedchamber, but Harry had refused to have his portmanteaux unpacked. Surely—surely—the great house would send for him. One hour passed, then two, then three; and no footman came with a civil message, no groom with a led horse, no note with a seal. At last he was forced to have his trunks opened like a man who admits defeat, and to call for slippers and gown.

Just before dark—two hours after the first carriage—another chariot with four horses crossed the bridge. A stout high-coloured lady with very dark eyes looked hard at him as she passed. That was the Baroness Bernstein, said the landlady—my lord’s aunt; and Harry remembered how the first Lady Castlewood had come of a German family. Earl and Countess and Baroness, postillions, gentlemen and horses, all vanished behind the gate; and he, the grandson of the house, lay down at last in the inn with a cruel sense of neglect pressing on his young heart.

Sleep would not come. And presently from below rose a prodigious noise—cursing, giggling, a woman’s scream, a man’s shout—the bar’s rude revel. The inn’s sounds were the opposite of Castlewood’s silence: not exclusion, but invasion; not coldness, but too much heat. The very boards seemed to shake with it.

Then Gumbo’s voice sounded without, steady and pleading. “You cannot go in, sar—my master asleep, sar!” But a shrill voice, thick with drink and oaths—a voice Harry recognized from the bridge—cursed Gumbo as a stupid negro woolly-pate. Gumbo was thrust aside, and a flood of profanity poured into the room, followed by a young gentleman reeling as if the floor were a deck at sea.

“Beg your pardon, Cousin Warrington,” cried the young blasphemer, “are you asleep? Beg your pardon for riding you over on the bridge. Didn’t know you—course shouldn’t have done it—thought it was a lawyer with a writ—dressed in black, you know. Gad! thought it was Nathan come to nab me.” And Mr. William laughed, not merrily but as liquor laughs through a man.

“You do me great honour to mistake me for a sheriff’s officer, cousin,” Harry said with great gravity, sitting up in his tall nightcap.

“Gad! I thought it was Nathan, and was going to send you souse into the river. But I ask your pardon. You see I had been drinking at the Bell at Hexton, and the punch is good at the Bell at Hexton. Hullo! you, Davis! a bowl of punch; d’you hear?”

The very word punch brought with it a phantom scent—hot spirit, lemon-peel bruised on the rim, sugar melting into sting; the sort of drink that makes talk louder than truth. Harry’s stomach turned from it, not from delicacy but from weariness.

“I have had my share for to-night, cousin, and I should think you have,” Harry answered, still in that dignified tone which is sometimes only anger in full dress.

“You want me to go, Cousin What’s-your-name, I see,” Mr. William said, suddenly solemn, swaying his judgment as he swayed his body. “You want me to go, and they want me to come, and I didn’t want to come. I said, I’d see him hanged first,—that’s what I said. Why should I trouble myself to come down all alone of an evening, and look after a fellow I don’t care a pin for? Zackly what I said. Zackly what Castlewood said. Why the devil should he go down? Castlewood says, and so said my lady, but the Baroness would have you. It’s all the Baroness’s doing, and if she says a thing, it must be done; so you must just get up and come.”

He poured it out in a stream, words running into one another like spilt liquor, and he tacked about the room as he spoke, his boots thudding, his breath sour with spirits and citrus. Harry’s wrath, which had been cooling into melancholy, flared up afresh.

“I tell you what, cousin,” he cried, “I won’t move for the Countess, or for the Baroness, or for all the cousins in Castlewood!”

The landlord entered with the bowl of punch Mr. William had ordered—a steaming, amber-coloured thing that smelled of peel and heat. Harry, furious at the insult of it in his chamber, called to the host to turn the sot out.

“Sot, you little tobacconist! Sot, you Cherokee!” screamed Mr. William. “Jump out of bed, and I’ll drive my sword through your body. Why didn’t I do it to-day when I took you for a bailiff—a confounded pettifogging bum-bailiff!”

He went on screeching oaths and incoherencies until the landlord, the drawer, the hostler, and half the kitchen folk crowded in to lead him away as men lead away a bull that has got into a garden. After which Harry shut himself again behind his anger as behind canvas—closed his tent round him, as soldiers say—and at last, no doubt from sheer exhaustion, slept.

In the morning the landlord was obsequious, having now learned precisely who his guest was. Messengers had come from the castle in the night, it appeared, to fetch both young gentlemen home; and poor Mr. William had returned in a wheelbarrow, being not altogether unaccustomed to that mode of conveyance. The landlord swore Mr. William never remembered a thing next day; he was of a real kind nature; the men got crowns and half-crowns from him by saying he beat them overnight when he was in liquor. “He’s the devil when he’s tipsy,” the landlord said, “but when he’s sober he is the very kindest of young gentlemen.”

Meanwhile, within Castlewood’s walls—where last night’s candles had burned down upon old plate and family portraits—Harry’s name upon the paper had occasioned a little council. My Lord Castlewood supposed that must have been the young gentleman they had seen on the bridge; as they had not drowned him they must invite him. Let a man go down with the proper messages. Let a servant carry a note. Lady Fanny thought it would be more civil if one of the brothers went, considering the greeting they had given. My Lord Castlewood had not the slightest objection to his brother William going—yes, William should go.

Upon which William said, with a stronger expression, that he would be hanged if he would. Lady Maria thought the young man on the bridge was pretty enough. Castlewood was dreadfully dull; neither of her brothers did anything to make it amusing. He might be vulgar—no doubt he was vulgar—but let them see the American. Such was Lady Maria’s charitable curiosity.

Lady Castlewood, however, was for neither receiving nor refusing him, but for delaying. “Wait till your aunt comes, children; perhaps the Baroness won’t like to see the young man; at least, let us consult her before we ask him.” Thus hospitality remained in abeyance like a dish kept back because one is uncertain who will sit at table.

At length the equipage of the Baroness Bernstein appeared; and if there was any doubt about the Virginian stranger, there was no doubt about this wealthy kinswoman. The state-chamber had been prepared. The cook had arrived the day before with instructions to make a supper such as her ladyship liked—sustenance here being not merely nourishment but a kind of language, the family’s truest dialect of deference.

The oak dining-room shone with old plate; the table was set as if to reflect every candle back into the faces that coveted favour. Around the walls looked down their dead: the late Viscount, his father, his mother, his sister—two lovely pictures; a predecessor by Vandyck and his Viscountess; and there Colonel Esmond too, in red coat and cuirass, black periwig vast as a cloud—about whose grandson the living Esmonds showed such a moderate sympathy.

The feast was a good one and the Baroness enjoyed it. The Countess pressed dish after dish upon her; the butler filled her glass with champagne the moment it was empty; the young folk and their mother kept the conversation not by speaking but by listening—by that careful, flattering silence which is itself a kind of music. The Baroness was full of spirits and humour. She knew everybody in Europe, and about those everybodies she told the wickedest stories. The Countess, ordinarily demure and severe and a stickler for propriety, smiled at the worst; the girls laughed when their mother signalled; the boys roared with especial delight at their sisters’ confusion. They drank freely too; and after supper came a bowl of smoking punch, hot and sweet and treacherous, set down like a centerpiece of temptation.

Many and many a night, the Baroness said, she had drunk at that table by her father’s side. “That was his place,” she said, pointing to the chair the Countess now occupied. She saw none of the old plate in those days. It had been melted to pay gambling debts. She hoped—young gentlemen—that they did not play.

“Never, on my word,” said Castlewood.

“Never, ’pon honour,” said Will, winking at his brother.

The Baroness was glad to hear they were such good boys. Her face grew redder with punch, and she became more voluble—might have been thought coarse, but times were different, and critics especially favourable to those who might leave them money.

She spoke of the boys’ father, their grandfather, other men and women of the house; and then, lifting that arm which was still beautifully round and white, she pointed toward the portrait of the military gentleman in the cuirass.

“The only man of the family was that,” she said.

“The Virginian? What is he good for? I always thought he was good for nothing but to cultivate tobacco and my grandmother,” said my lord, laughing.

The Baroness struck her hand upon the table with such energy the glasses danced. “I say he was the best of you all. There never was one of the male Esmonds that had more brains than a goose, except him. He was not fit for this wicked, selfish old world of ours, and he was right to go and live out of it. Where would your father have been, young people, but for him?”

“Was he particularly kind to our papa?” Lady Maria asked.

“Old stories, my dear Maria!” cried the Countess hastily. “I am sure my dear Earl was very kind to him in giving him that great estate in Virginia.”

“Since his brother’s death, the lad who has been here to-day is heir to that. Mr. Draper told me so! Peste! I don’t know why my father gave up such a property,” said my lord.

“Who has been here to-day?” asked the Baroness, the punch and something else making her eyes shine.

“Harry Esmond Warrington, of Virginia,” my lord answered; “a lad whom Will nearly pitched into the river, and whom I pressed my lady the Countess to invite to stay here.”

“You mean that one of the Virginian boys has been to Castlewood, and has not been asked to stay here?”

“There is but one of them, my dear creature,” the Earl interposed. “The other, you know, has just been—”

“For shame, for shame!”

“Oh! it ain’t pleasant, I confess, to be se—”

“Do you mean that a grandson of Henry Esmond, the master of this house, has been here, and none of you have offered him hospitality?”

“Since we didn’t know it, and he is staying at the Castles?” Will put in.

“That he is staying at the Inn, and you are sitting there!” cried the old lady. “This is too bad—call somebody to me. Get me my hood—I’ll go to the boy myself. Come with me this instant, my Lord Castlewood.”

The young man rose, plainly in wrath. “Madame the Baroness of Bernstein,” he said, “your ladyship is welcome to go; but as for me, I don’t choose to have such words as ‘shameful’ applied to my conduct. I won’t go and fetch the young gentleman from Virginia, and I propose to sit here and finish this bowl of punch. Eugene! Don’t Eugene me, madam. I know her ladyship has a great deal of money, which you are desirous should remain in our amiable family. You want it more than I do. Cringe for it—I won’t.” And he sank back again.

The Baroness looked from one lowered head to another; then at my lord—without dislike this time. She leaned toward him and spoke rapidly in German: “I had unright when I said the Colonel was the only man of the family. Thou canst, if thou willest, Eugene.” My lord only bowed.

“If you do not wish an old woman to go out at this hour of the night,” the Baroness said aloud, “let William, at least, go and fetch his cousin.”

“The very thing I proposed,” said my lord.

“And so did we—and so did we!” cried the daughters.

“I am sure I only wanted the dear Baroness’s consent,” said their mother, “and shall be charmed for my part to welcome our young relative.”

“Will! Put on thy pattens and get a lantern, and go fetch the Virginian,” my lord said.

“And we will have another bowl of punch when he comes,” Will answered—already too far gone. And so he went forth upon his embassy, as Harry had seen, and ordered more punch, and failed miserably at civility.

Lady Castlewood, catching sight of young Harry by the river-side, must have seen a handsome and interesting youth; and very likely had reasons of her own for not desiring his presence. All mothers are not eager to encourage the visits of a nineteen-year-old in a house where there are virgins of twenty. If Harry’s acres had lain in Norfolk or Devon instead of Virginia, no doubt her welcome would have been warmer. People of fashion, when selfish, are at least frank in their selfishness; when cold-hearted, they seldom waste hypocrisy of affection.

Why should her ladyship put herself out for a friendless stranger? Because he was alone? Only a simpleton imagines so romantic a motive in such circles. Great folk are friendly to those who have plenty of friends. A poor lad from a distant country, with moderate means and those not yet in his own power, likely uncouth manners and provincial habits—was a Countess called upon to trouble herself? Allons donc. He was quite as well at the alehouse as at the castle.

This, no doubt, was her ladyship’s opinion; and her kinswoman, the Baroness Bernstein, who knew her perfectly, understood it too. The Baroness herself was a woman of the world; she could be selfish enough on occasion. She understood the deference shown her by mother, daughters, sons; and being a woman of humour, played upon it—amused herself with their greediness and their humiliations, with their artless respect for her money-box and their clinging attachment to her purse. They were not very rich. Lady Castlewood’s own money was settled on her children. The two elder had inherited little but flaxen heads from their German mother and a pedigree of prodigious distinction. Those who had money and those who had none were alike eager for the Baroness’s; in this matter the rich are as greedy as the poor.

So if Madam Bernstein struck the table and made glasses—and hearts—tremble, it was partly because champagne and punch warmed her blood, and partly because a generous impulse does sometimes rise with generous wine. She thought of the poor lad outside his own door and felt indignant—not because she imagined her relatives different from what they were, but because she could not help seeing, with a sudden clarity, the shameful smallness of their silence.

She was restless and resolute, extraordinarily active for her years. Long before the languid Castlewood ladies—home from London routs and balls—had quitted their feather-beds, and before jolly Will had slept off his various potations, the Baroness was up and pacing the green terraces that sparkled with morning dew. The dew lay twinkling also upon trim parterres and the crisp dark walls of box, under which marble fauns and dryads cooled themselves. A thousand birds sang; fountains plashed and glittered in rosy sunshine; and rooks cawed from the great wood. The estate’s morning soundscape—water, wings, leaf, distant hoof—was the true music of Castlewood, older than any harpsichord brought in for show, unpurchased, unbranded, and therefore honest. One could not help thinking how cheap and harsh the bar’s racket at the inn had been by comparison, and how much of a man’s peace depends on the noises he must live inside.

After half an hour’s pacing, the person for whom she waited came to her: young Harry Warrington, to whom she had despatched an early billet by one of the Lockwoods. The note was signed B. Bernstein, and told Mr. Esmond Warrington that his relatives at Castlewood—and among them a dear friend of his grandfather—were most anxious he should come to “Colonel Esmond’s house in England.”

Now, accordingly, he appeared beneath the old Gothic doorway and came down the steps from terrace to terrace, hat in hand, his fair hair blowing off a flushed cheek. He was clad in mourning; his slim figure moved with the modesty of youth that has not yet learned to swagger in sorrow. The Baroness, watching, was pleased—as a woman may be pleased when the living carries something of the dead she once knew.

He bowed low, a bow that would have done credit to Versailles. She held out her little hand, and when his palm closed over it she laid her other hand softly upon his ruffle, as if to feel by touch the truth of him. She looked kindly into his honest blushing face.

“I knew your grandfather very well, Harry,” she said. “So you came yesterday to see his picture, and they turned you away—though you know the house was his of right?”

Harry’s blush deepened. “The servants did not know me. A young gentleman came to me last night,” he said, “when I was peevish, and he, I fear, was tipsy. I spoke rudely to my cousin, and would ask his pardon. Your ladyship knows that in Virginia our manners towards strangers are different. I own I had expected another kind of welcome. Was it you, madam, who sent my cousin to me last night?”

“I sent him,” she said; “but you will find your cousins most friendly to you to-day. You must stay here. Lord Castlewood would have been with you this morning, only I was so eager to see you. There will be breakfast in an hour; and meantime you must talk to me. We will send to the Three Castles for your servant and your baggage. Give me your arm. Stop—I dropped my cane when you came. You shall be my cane.”

“My grandfather used to call us his crutches,” Harry said.

“You are like him,” she answered, her dark eyes softening, “though you are fair.”

When the last cannon of Queen Anne’s wars had cooled, and the last toasts to her memory had been drowned in new loyalties, Henry Esmond—who had carried a colonel’s commission and a gentleman’s conscience with equal stiffness—found himself pinched between what he had attempted and what the kingdom would forgive. He had played, however briefly, at the dangerous game of restoring a fallen family; and though the nation, with a practical appetite, chose another dynasty, some of those who had erred out of devotion—or vanity, or old habit—were advised to slip away from the three kingdoms until the heat of accusation abated.

Esmond went, not with the romantic air of an exile, but with the tired exactness of a man who had mismeasured a recipe and did not care to taste the result again. His friends, who understood how mild the new sovereign’s temper could be when properly approached, soon contrived his peace; and had he cared to return, the way lay open. But there were tangles at home—of family, of memory, of a private hurt that had steeped itself into his days like bitter bark left too long in a pot—and he chose instead the broad, slow-breathing country across the Atlantic, where an old grant from King Charles I. waited like an uncut loaf.

So he took possession of the Virginia estate that had belonged, in law and in story, to his line, and named his American house Castlewood, after the patrimonial home in Hampshire. Virginia, in those years, loved to model its manners on England as faithfully as it could manage with different air and different soil. The very sound of it tried to be English: the clop of horses along red roads, the church-bell’s sober tongue on Sunday, the creak of wharf-planks as hogsheads of tobacco rolled toward the river, the drawled salutations under great trees. Those who called themselves gentry held their heads above the Dutch traders to the north and the industrious dissenters farther up the coast. No people in the world seemed less republican than these planters who would, in another generation, be foremost in revolt.

The great estates were run after a patriarchal fashion: broad fields roughly coaxed into yield; smokehouses and dairies, stables and kitchens; and—under it all, like the steady undertone in a piece of music—labor compelled. There were purchased and assigned servants from Europe, and there were black servants born to bondage; and in that time the question of slavery had not yet been forced into the daylight of argument among such people. The land gave corn and meat; the woods gave game; the rivers, with their thick living swish and splash at dawn, gave fish that needed only net and hand. Ships came up to private wharves along the Potomac or the James, taking away tobacco heavy with the smell of its own cured leaf, and bringing back English goods—cloth and metalwork and china, spices and tea—so that the tables of Virginia, though fed by maize and pig and river, still held the taste of London and Bristol in their cupboards.

Hospitality was not merely a virtue but a habit, like salting meat for winter. A stranger did not go unfed from a gate. The gentry visited one another with an almost feudal certainty—arriving with servants and trunks, staying as long as the larder and conversation held, leaving behind the fading acoustics of laughter in the hall and the softer after-sounds of domestic work resuming its usual rhythm.

It was in this world that Esmond’s daughter and grandsons were born, and his wife died. The lady he had married was widow to his kinsman, the unlucky Viscount Castlewood, killed in a duel by Lord Mohun at the end of King William’s reign. Grief, in Esmond, did not explode; it settled, like lees at the bottom of a bottle, leaving the upper part clear enough for daily use but forever altered in taste. He was not unkind—indeed, to those around him he was gentle and considerate, even obsequious to the women of his family, whom he scarcely ever contradicted. Yet something in him had failed and never repaired: a bankruptcy of heart, as though the currency of his feelings had been called in and replaced with quieter coin. He submitted to life more than he enjoyed it, and was never in better spirits than when he spoke of laying it down.

After his wife’s death, his daughter took the management of him and of Castlewood with brisk capability. He surrendered both to her with a sort of grateful acquiescence. So long as he had his books and his quiet, he asked little more. When company came, he entertained handsomely—there was always a table fit to make a hungry man reverent, and always drink enough to persuade a guest that his host was the most genial of fellows. Esmond had a pleasant, sarcastical turn, and could season a story as neatly as a cook seasons stew—without overdoing it, so that the flavor came through. But when the guests went away, he was not sorry.

“My love,” he said once to his daughter, with that calm irony which was almost tenderness, “I shall not be sorry to go myself; and you, though the most affectionate of daughters, will console yourself after a while. Why should I, who am so old, be romantic? You may, who are still a young creature.”

He did not mean all he said, for the lady he addressed was a matter-of-fact little person, with very little romance in her nature. Her imagination, when it kindled, burned chiefly in one direction: lineage, precedence, the ordering of the world into ranks as carefully as she ordered her household stores. After fifteen years of good profit from Virginia soil and tobacco, she pressed him to build a mansion grander and more durable than the plain wooden house in which he had been content. Neighbors had raised handsome brick dwellings; she would not have Castlewood seem mean by comparison. Esmond, who cared neither for quarters nor quarterings, yielded with a shrug, and even helped her.

For he did possess antiquarian learning, and a painter’s skill besides. A century earlier, heraldry had been part of polite education; and during a visit to Europe, his daughter had hunted pedigrees with a hunger that had nothing to do with appetite and everything to do with pride. She returned to Virginia with documents and printed volumes from France and England, treating them as sacred receipts that proved, beyond doubt, the ingredients of her own importance. They satisfied her entirely that the Esmonds sprang from noble Norman warriors, and farther still—from native English royalty. Esmond, indulgent and amused, put brush to paper and painted two magnificent heraldic trees for her: on one side Charlemagne, in plate armour with imperial mantle and diadem; on the other Queen Boadicea, whom he insisted upon giving the light costume of an ancient British queen, with a prodigious gilded crown, a trifling fur mantle, and a symmetrical person tastefully marked with brilliant blue figures. From these two roots the family rose, in painted branches and gold-lettered names, until the stocks united somewhere in the thirteenth century in a fortunate Esmond who claimed both.

Of the Warrington family, into which she married, good Madam Rachel thought little. She wrote herself Esmond Warrington, but in the country she was Madam Esmond of Castlewood, and after her father’s death she would rule the domain accordingly. Indeed, she was sometimes so certain of her own grandeur that the colony’s assemblies at Jamestown were disturbed by quarrels for precedence—sharp words, and even a scuffle or two, preserved in her notes with indignation. King James II. and his son had once offered her father and grandfather the title of Marquis; he had burned and disowned the patent, but she behaved at times as though it lay still in some strong-box and needed only to be unfolded. She considered the English Esmonds of an inferior dignity to her own branch; and as for the colonial aristocracy, she made no scruple of asserting her superiority over the whole body.

Yet this same colony, for all its provincial jealousies, was as loyal in profession as any shire at home. Virginians boasted that Charles II. had been king in Virginia before he had been king in England. English king and English church were honored with equal steadiness; and the two young twins at Castlewood—bred on family pride as regularly as they were fed on hominy and bacon—were faithful little subjects of the crown.

When the boys’ grandfather died, their mother proclaimed in great state her eldest son George successor and heir of the estate. Harry, younger by half an hour, was always enjoined to respect his senior, and the whole household was instructed accordingly—black servants, of whom there was a large, noisy, contented family, and assigned servants from Europe, whose lot was made as bearable as it might be under the lady’s government. In all that busy little kingdom, there was scarcely a rebel save Mrs. Esmond’s faithful companion Madam Mountain, and Harry’s foster-mother, a devoted black woman who could never be brought to understand why her child should not be first when he was, as she swore, handsomer, stronger, and cleverer than his brother. In truth, there was scarcely any difference in beauty, strength, or stature between the twins. Their faces matched as closely as two loaves from the same batch, and when they lay in their beds with their heads swallowed by enormous ribboned nightcaps, only a nurse or mother could tell which was which—except for the color of their hair.

In temper, however, they were unlike. George, the elder, was peaceful, studious, and silent. Harry was warlike and noisy. Harry could learn quickly when he began, but was slow to begin; no threats of the ferule could force him into a lesson during an idle fit. George, by contrast, would sit and labor without complaint, and would even help his brother over a hard passage when Harry at last applied himself. Where George’s mind brightened in the library, Harry’s came alive in the stable-yard and the woods. He drilled the little negroes on the estate and caned them like a corporal, sparring with them in earnest boxing-matches; and if he was worsted, he bore no malice, only a hotter desire to win next time. George was sparing of blows and gentle with all about him, with a softness that could become stubbornness when he believed a thing unjust.

As was customary, each boy had a special little servant assigned to him. It became known through the house, and was told with different emphases in kitchen and parlor, that George once found his little black attendant asleep on his master’s bed. Instead of calling out or striking, George sat down beside the sleeping child and brushed the flies away with a feather fan. Old Gumbo, the boy’s father, came upon the scene and was horrified to see his young master performing such offices; Madam Esmond, hearing of it, was indignant at the “insolence” of a servant in such a place and ordered the young negro to the proper officer for a whipping.

George implored and entreated. He burst into passionate tears, and begged remission of the sentence. His mother was inflexible. The little culprit went off beseeching his young master not to cry. Then George, trembling with rebellion against what he conceived to be injustice, turned his anger on his mother. He declared the punishment a shame—a shame; he said he was master of the boy, and no one—no, not his mother—had a right to touch him. If correction were needed, let it fall on him; he and Harry had often endured it. But no one should lay a hand on his boy. And in his fury he shrieked out an oath—an ugly word from the mouth of the usually gentle child—which shocked his mother and his governor, who had never before heard such language from him. He vowed that when he came of age he would set young Gumbo free, and that very day he went down to the quarters, sought out the child, and gave him one of his own toys as if to salt a wound with kindness.

The young black “martyr,” as some called him in later telling, was in fact an impudent, lazy, saucy little personage, and would likely be none the worse for a whipping, as the old Colonel thought. Esmond acquiesced when his daughter insisted upon punishment, and laughed in his good-natured way when his indignant grandson flung at him, “You let mamma rule you in everything, grandpapa.”

“Why, so I do,” the old man answered easily. “Rachel, my love, the way in which I am petticoat-ridden is so evident that even this baby has found it out.”

“Then why don’t you stand up like a man?” cried little Harry, always ready to abet his brother in any fray.

Esmond looked queerly at that—his eyes narrowing as if some private sound had passed through him, like a distant drum heard in sleep. But he only said, “Because I like sitting down best, my dear. I am an old gentleman, and standing fatigues me.”

It was George, for all his quietness, who was his grandfather’s companion. There was a kind of apish drollery and humor in the boy that pleased the old man, and an early liking for some of Esmond’s own pursuits. George, demure in company, would grow animated in the library; his senses seemed to wake there as if books gave off a scent he could breathe. He knew volumes before he could well carry them, and read in them long before he could understand them—moving his lips over the lines with the seriousness of a priest over a prayer. Harry, in that same room, would sit gloomy and restless, as though the muffled hush of paper and leather oppressed him. But set him among saddles and bridles, among the clean animal heat of horses and the sharp tang of oiled tack; set him where the woods spoke in birdsong and wind, and where a river made its own music against the bank—and he was all life and appetite.

Once, when their grandfather’s ship was sailing for Europe, the boys were asked what present Captain Franks should bring back. George wavered between books and a fiddle. Harry declared instantly for a little gun. Their mother was hurt that her elder son should choose what she deemed low tastes, and she applauded the younger’s desire as more worthy of the name she guarded so jealously.

“Books, papa, I can fancy to be a good choice,” she said to her father, trying to keep her tone respectful while her pride bristled, “though I am sure you must have pretty nigh all the books in the world already. But I never can desire—I may be wrong, but I never can desire—that my son, and the grandson of the Marquis of Esmond, should be a fiddler.”

“Should be a fiddlestick, my dear,” the old Colonel answered. “Remember that Heaven’s ways are not ours, and that each creature born has a little kingdom of thought of his own, which it is a sin in us to invade. Suppose George loves music? You can no more stop him than you can order a rose not to smell sweet, or a bird not to sing.”

“A bird! A bird sings from nature; George did not come into the world with a fiddle in his hand,” Mrs. Warrington replied, tossing her head. “I am sure I hated the harpsichord when a chit at Kensington School, and only learned it to please my mamma. Say what you will, dear sir, I cannot believe that this fiddling is work for persons of fashion.”

“And King David who played the harp, my dear?”

“I wish my papa would read him more, and not speak about him in that way,” she said sharply; for in her ear, sacred words belonged to sermons and not to arguments about instruments.

“Nay, my dear, it was but by way of illustration,” he answered gently.

It was Esmond’s nature, as he himself had owned elsewhere, always to be led by a woman. With his wife dead, he coaxed, dandled, and spoiled his daughter; laughing at her caprices, but humoring them; making a jest of her prejudices, but letting them stand. He held that meddling could not change dispositions—only teach children hypocrisy by commanding them overmuch. So he let Rachel rule the outward order of Castlewood while he sat with his quiet, and with the inward knowledge that what mattered most in a life was untranslatable: no pedigree chart could express it, no title could carry it, no proud word could keep it from slipping away.

At length the time came when he was done with the affairs of this world. He laid them down almost as if glad to be rid of their burden. There was no need to begin a history with tolling bells, yet the colony would have its solemnities. Parson Broadbent of Jamestown preached a funeral discourse that caused listeners to wonder where such eloquence and Latin had been found. Perhaps Mr. Dempster knew—the boys’ Scotch tutor, who corrected the proofs of the oration, later printed, at the desire of his Excellency and many persons of honor, at Mr. Franklin’s press in Philadelphia.

No such sumptuous funeral had ever been seen in the country as that which Madam Esmond Warrington ordained for her father—pompous grief that the dead man himself would have been the first to smile at. The twins, almost smothered in black trains and hatbands, headed the procession. Behind them came my Lord Fairfax from Greenway Court; his Excellency the Governor of Virginia in his coach; the Randolphs, the Careys, the Harrisons, the Washingtons, and many more, for the whole county esteemed the departed gentleman—his goodness, his talents, his benevolence, and that unobtrusive urbanity which had made even his sarcasm feel like wit rather than wound.

News crossed the water to England, to the family of Colonel Esmond’s stepson, the Lord Castlewood of Hampshire. They offered to bear the charges of a marble slab to record the names and virtues of his lordship’s mother and her husband. In due time the monument was set up, displaying the arms and coronet of the Esmonds, supported by a chubby group of weeping cherubs, and inscribed with an epitaph which, for once, did not tell falsehoods.

Kind neighbours, civil speeches, a house filled to the rafters with what a country life counts riches—linen, plate, horses, orchards, a long cellar of bottles sleeping in dust, a library with the smell of calf and glue; a score of hands, black and white, ready at a clap; good health, two sons, and a cook who could coax comfort out of Indian corn and a stringy fowl—these seem, on paper, the very inventory of content. Madam Esmond Warrington, at Castlewood in Westmoreland County, had them all, and in her prayers morning and night she ticked each blessing as carefully as she ticked her household accounts.

Yet in the midst of plenty she moved like a small crowned creature for whom ease is not rest, but merely more territory to govern. The country gentry paid court, the lesser planters yielded to her opinions as they yielded to her physic, and at backgammon they let her win with that obedient smile which is only another form of tribute. Still, few envied “the little Princess Pocahontas,” as the neighbourhood called her half in jest, half in awe. She had been bred to command; to be crossed was to be affronted; and if a soul resisted her, she worried the point as a terrier worries a rat, until one or the other gave way. In church she spoke the public confession of human sin in a voice so clear and resolute that it sounded like an accusation against the congregation rather than humility before Heaven; and at home she seldom admitted to herself—never to others—that she could be wrong.

Her father, Colonel Esmond, in his old age had watched those imperious fits with a dry amusement that disconcerted her. She always felt his eye, and his humour—which she scarcely possessed—held her in check by making her, for once, uncertain. But the Colonel was gone, and with him the single presence she could not quite master; and Castlewood, left to her rule, stiffened beneath it.

She had long managed the estate; now she tightened every screw. She dismissed the English factor her father had trusted and chose another; she appointed a new overseer; she set men to building, improving, planting; she measured tobacco-fields with her own quick step; she imported a new tutor, as one imports a tool. Much as she loved the Colonel, there were maxims of his she would not continue. Had she not obeyed papa and mamma all her life, as a dutiful daughter? So must her children obey her, that their days might be long in the land. The princes she had borne were her first subjects.

Before long she laid aside her husband’s name, and in the country she would be Madam Esmond. The family pretensions were known; she had no objection to the Marquisate King James had once given her father and grandfather being spoken of with respect. Her father’s enormous magnanimity might make him resign titles to the younger branch—to her half-brother, Lord Castlewood, and his children—but she and her sons were of the elder blood, and were to be treated accordingly. Lord Fairfax alone, in all Virginia, might take precedence of her. She demanded the pas before lieutenant-governors’ ladies and judges’ wives; to a governor’s lady, as the sovereign’s representative, she would yield—formally, and no more. The family papers held, as in vinegar, accounts of battles she fought on such questions of ceremony; for etiquette, with her, was not silk and bowing, but a language of power, in which a single place at table could say “master” or “subject” without any man daring to translate it aloud.

Of the Warringtons in England—her husband’s people—she thought almost nothing. She had married a younger son of a Norfolk baronet to please her parents, when she was still a boarding-school chit, ready, she said, to jump overboard if papa ordered it. “And that is always the way with the Esmonds,” she would add, as if obedience were not duty but blood. Once a year, with great solemnity, she sent letters to the Warringtons and to her noble Esmond kin in Hampshire; but a judge’s lady, with whom Madam had quarrelled, returned to England, met Lady Warrington in London whilst Sir Miles attended Parliament, and repeated some of the Princess’s speeches about her English relatives. The tale went to my Lady Castlewood; and after that, the letters from Virginia were not answered. Madam Esmond’s surprise hardened into wrath; she left off writing, too, and carried the silence like a grievance pinned inside her stays.

So she fell out with neighbours, with kindred, and—most bitterly—with her sons. The first breach between the Queen and her Crown Prince came over the dismissal of Mr. Dempster, the lad’s tutor and the late Colonel’s secretary. During the Colonel’s life she had endured Dempster as one endures a thorn in a cushion; or rather, Dempster had hardly been able to endure her. She was jealous of books, as if the very smell of ink concealed a plot, and thought “bookworms” dangerous: subtle men, whispering principles into boys’ ears. She had heard—how does such a rumour ever die in a province?—that Dempster was a Jesuit in disguise. Out he went; and the poor dominie went to build a cabin in a clearing and make himself useful teaching, and doctoring, and living where he could among the sparse folk of the country. Master George vowed he would never forsake his old tutor, and kept his vow, trudging to him and from him as faithfully as some men go to their church. Harry, who loved fishing and a good horse better than declensions, had liked Dempster well enough, but not with that grave, hungry affection his brother gave.

Then came the money.

By an aunt’s death, and at his father’s demise, young George Warrington—heir of Castlewood—became entitled to six thousand pounds in England, of which Madam Esmond was one trustee, and a London lawyer the other. She could never be made to understand, in her bones, the difference between holding and owning. The sum, in her mind, was not a trust but a thing withheld from her by insolence; and when Mr. Draper, the lawyer, refused to send it across at her order, she burned with indignation.

“Is not all I have my sons’?” she cried. “Would I not cut myself into little pieces to serve them? With that six thousand pounds I would have bought Mr. Boulter’s land and negroes, and had a thousand a year out of it—ay, and made a handsome provision for my Harry.”

Mr. Washington of Mount Vernon—young then, and already with that steady way of looking at a question as if it were a field to be measured—could not convince her that Mr. Draper was right, and that trust is not possession. She wrote to London with a sharp pen, and, as some women season even their paper with pepper, called the lawyer an insolent pettifogger, and said he deserved punishment for doubting the honour of a mother and an Esmond.

When the matter was referred to George, and his mother demanded his declaration as if it were a confession in church, the boy sided—miserably, yet honestly—with Washington and Draper. He said he could not help himself; he did not want the money; he would gladly give it to his mother if he had power; but the trust was the trust, and the law the law.

Madam Esmond would hear none of it. Feelings were her reasons; tears her evidence; scorn her judgement. Here was Harry—dear Harry—left with a younger brother’s slender portion, and the wretches in London would not help him; and George, who inherited the Colonel’s estate, would not help him. “Mean at fourteen!” she cried, as if thrift or honour were meanness when they opposed her wish. Add long estrangement, bitter outbreaks, passionate appeals to Heaven, and the widow’s mind may be imagined: for when a person makes of affection a whip, every stroke seems to her an act of love.

That quarrel turned her into a saver for the younger son. The fine buildings the Colonel had begun at Castlewood were stopped short, like a story interrupted mid-sentence. Ships no longer came from New York freighted with Dutch bricks; no more carved cornice-work arrived; no more sashes and glass, no more carpets and costly upholstery from home. No more books were bought. The agent had orders to discontinue the wine. Madam Esmond regretted, with a sharp inward groan, the great coach she had ordered from England, and would ride in it only to church, sitting stiffly in silks, and crying across to the boys opposite her as the wheels ground the sandy road:

“Harry, Harry! I wish I had put by the money for thee, my poor portionless child—three hundred and eighty guineas of ready money to Messieurs Hatchett!”

“You will give me plenty while you live,” Harry answered gaily, “and George will give me plenty when you die.”

“Not unless he changes in spirit, my dear,” said Madam Esmond, with a grim glance at her eldest. “Not unless Heaven softens his heart and teaches him charity, for which I pray day and night; as Mountain knows; do you not, Mountain?”

Mrs. Mountain—Ensign Mountain’s widow, Madam Esmond’s companion and manager—sat the fourth in the coach on these Sundays: a plain-spoken woman with a mouth set like a door that would not be forced open by rank. She said, “Humph! I know you are always disturbing yourself and crying out about this legacy, and I don’t see that there is any need.”

“Oh no! no need!” cried the widow, rustling. “Of course I have no need to be disturbed, because my eldest born is a disobedient son and an unkind brother—because he has an estate, and my poor Harry, bless him, but a mess of pottage.”

George looked at her as if struck, until his eyes brimmed. “I wish you would bless me, too, O my mother!” he said, and broke into passionate weeping.

In a moment Harry’s arms were round his brother’s neck; he kissed him again and again, quick as a boy comforting a hurt dog. “Never mind, George. I know whether you are a good brother or not. Don’t mind what she says. She don’t mean it.”

“I do mean it, child!” cried the mother. “Would to Heaven—”

“HOLD YOUR TONGUE, I SAY!” Harry roared out. “It’s a shame to speak so to him, ma’am.”

“And so it is, Harry,” Mrs. Mountain said, catching his hand in approval. “You never said a truer word in your life.”

“Mrs. Mountain, do you dare to set my children against me?” Madam cried. “From this very day, madam—”

“Turn me and my child into the street? Do,” Mrs. Mountain returned. “That will be a fine revenge because the English lawyer won’t give you the boy’s money. Find another companion who will tell you black is white, and flatter you: it is not my way, madam. When shall I go? I shan’t be long a-packing. I did not bring much into Castlewood House, and I shall not take much out.”

“Hush! the bells are ringing for church, Mountain. Let us try, if you please, and compose ourselves,” said the widow; and she looked with eyes of extreme affection, certainly at one—perhaps at both—of her children.

The bells—iron tongues set swinging in the little belfry—threw their sound across the fields like a net. Their peal, clear and measured, rinsed the air of the coach’s quarrel for a moment, as if the very countryside took a long breath. Under that clean ringing, which belonged to old custom and not to any man’s temper, George kept his head down; and in church, while the minister’s voice rose and fell, Harry drew close and sat with his arm round his brother’s neck, steadying him as if warmth could be a language truer than words.

It was after such scenes—after years of them, so that affection and offence went round and round like the seasons—that Harry, now in England, found himself telling his tale in a wainscoted parlour where meals had been eaten “in ordinary” for two centuries. The room had the settled smell of old oak, beeswax, and the faint ghost of dinners long since vanished: roast meats, gravy, nut-brown ale; a sweetness of apples stored in a distant pantry; and, from the hearth, that honest reek of coal which London gentry pretended not to notice and country folk always did. Outside, the place had its own hush—no drum, no hammer, no city din; only the soft domestic acoustics of a great house: the click of knitting-needles; the faraway fall of a door; a footman’s step padded to be unheard; and, now and then, a carriage on gravel like a brief shower.

Madam Bernstein sat in a great chair beneath a brilliant Kneller, knitting as she listened, never tired of the boy’s voice. Her hostess and the young ladies of the house came more than once to ask if she would ride, or walk, or take tea, or play at cards; but she declined all, saying she found infinite amusement in Harry’s conversation. And whenever any of the Castlewood family were present she redoubled her caresses, insisted the lad speak close to her ear, and called out to the others, “Hush, my dears! I can’t hear our cousin speak.” They would withdraw, striving still to look pleased, as persons do who have learned that even kindness can be made a weapon.

“Are you my cousin, too?” Harry asked her at last, honest bewilderment in his face. “You seem kinder than my other cousins.”

They were sitting under the portraits of the race—men in armour and lace, women with heavy lids and jewelled throats, all looking down with that painted confidence which outlives the flesh. Over Madam Bernstein’s chair, the Kneller showed a young lady of three or four-and-twenty in the easy flowing dress of Queen Anne’s time: a hand on a cushion; auburn hair parted from a fair forehead and falling over pearly shoulders and a lovely neck. The painted lips almost smiled, as if she knew a secret the room could not hear.

“That picture is by Sir Godfrey,” Madam Bernstein said, her needles clicking like small castanets. “He thought himself the greatest painter in the world. But he was not so good as Lely, who painted your grandmother—my—my Lady Castlewood, Colonel Esmond’s wife; nor he so good as Sir Anthony Van Dyck, who painted your great-grandfather yonder—and who looks, Harry, a much finer gentleman than he was. Some of us are painted blacker than we are. Did you recognise your grandmother in that picture? She had the loveliest fair hair and shape of any woman of her time.”

“I fancied I knew the portrait from instinct, perhaps,” said Harry, “and a certain likeness to my mother.”

“Did Mrs. Warrington—I beg her pardon; I think she calls herself Madam, or my Lady Esmond now—?”

“They call my mother so in our province,” the boy answered.

“Did she never tell you,” Madam Bernstein asked, her voice low, “of another daughter her mother had in England, before she married your grandfather?”

“She never spoke of one.”

“Nor your grandfather?”

“Never. But in his picture-books, which he constantly made for us children, he used to draw a head very like that above your ladyship. That, and Viscount Francis, and King James the Third, he drew a score of times, I am sure.”

Madam Bernstein’s hands paused an instant, and the room’s small sounds seemed to grow louder in the pause—the fire’s faint snap; the distant clink of china; the house’s own breathing. “And the picture over me reminds you of no one, Harry?”

“No, indeed.”

“Ah! Here is a sermon!” she said, with a sigh, and began knitting again as if to brace herself with the familiar motion. “Harry, that was my face once—yes, it was—and then I was called Beatrix Esmond. And your mother is my half-sister, child, and she has never even mentioned my name!”

Harry Warrington told his kinswoman his plain tale of Castlewood—of rivers and rides and raw mornings in the tobacco-fields, of a house that was half manor and half village, of a mother who governed as if she had a crown tucked into her cap-strings. Madam Bernstein, bred where streets answered to bells and carriages, could scarce keep her city soul from shrinking at the notion of such country rule: days measured not by assemblies and visits, but by bread ovens, spinning-wheels, and the sickbed in a slave’s cabin. Yet Rachel Esmond—Madam Warrington to all Virginia—knew no other greatness, and wore her dominion as naturally as she wore her keys.

Nothing was done at Castlewood without the click of those keys and the brisk patter of her little shoes.
