If a pie was to be baked, her finger—small, quick, authoritative—must press the crimp into the edge; she would taste the custard for nutmeg and judge the fire by the smell of hickory on the air. She set the girls to their flax and wool, saw the kitchen-wenches scalding the great pans, peered into the dairy where cream thickened with a clean, sweet breath, and went herself to the still-room, that warm, herb-scented closet where pennyroyal and balm hung drying, where roses surrendered into waters, and where she compounded cordials and bitter draughts from a book of receipts as carefully kept as any prayer-book. Her medicine-chest was a legend: neighbours, hearing she had crossed the yard towards their door, would rather have borne a fever in peace than be seized upon by her resolute little hands and dosed into obedience.

In those days Virginia had few towns; each gentleman’s seat was a small polity, a cluster of cabins and barns and smokehouses about a great house, with the fields spreading like an empire. Rachel ruled Castlewood like a queen, and the neighbouring planters—some grand, many needy, most improvident—kept open gates and ragged liveries, turned away no traveller, hunted and drank and boasted of lineage, while their cellars emptied faster than their accounts could be made up. She was as hospitable as any and twice as thrifty; her table might be plentiful without being wasteful, and even her indulgences had order. Many a widower or bachelor would gladly have stepped into the place of father to her boys and master to her acres; but Rachel, who had been taught to think nobly of the Esmond blood, found no candidate equal to her idea of herself. The gossips swore she waited for a prince; and she, with grave composure, would hint that alliances had been offered to the Esmond family by persons as high as any duke.

Her chief lieutenant in this little kingdom was an Englishwoman, Fanny Parker—Mrs. Mountain now—who had stood by Rachel long ago, when they were girls at the Kensington Academy and the English pupils baited the American stranger for her proud little airs and her odd accent of the plantations. Fanny defended her then; they wrote to each other as “my Rachel” and “my Fanny,” married ensigns in the same regiment, and were knitted by that quick intimacy which youth makes and sorrow seals. Fanny’s husband died leaving debts and an infant, and Captain Franks, in one of his yearly passages, brought the widow over in the ship named the Young Rachel, as if Providence itself would not let the old friendship be stranded.

Castlewood had room enough to take in a whole new life, and Mrs. Mountain filled it with bustle and laughter. She played cards with the mistress, kept count of linen and candles, saw that strangers’ chambers were aired, and knew enough music to guide the elder boy’s fingers over a tune. She was brisk, rosy, and jolly-looking; more than one planter asked her to change Mountain for his own name. But she hugged that unlucky name close. One marriage was enough, she said: her poor Mountain had spent her little fortune and his own, and her last trinkets had gone to pay for his burial. While Rachel would keep her, she preferred a home without a husband to any that Virginia offered.

They quarrelled as regularly as they took chocolate in the morning, and made up with equal certainty. Their disputes were as domestic as bread-making: a heat, a rising, a knock-down, and then a softening. When either boy was ill, each vied in watching, brewing possets, warming bricks for cold feet, and sending a servant running for herbs. Mrs. Mountain’s cheerfulness in the Colonel’s last sickness had been dear to him; Rachel, who kept her dead husband’s memory like a relic, kept his friend’s friend too. Every year Captain Franks would ask, with a wink, whether Mrs. Mountain meant to go back to England in his ship; and every year she would say, No—one year more.

Suitors came, as suitors will to a youngish widow with broad acres. Rachel received their compliments as a queen receives embassies, and would sometimes ask, with an air of innocence that was not always innocent, whether it was she or her dependant they sought. If the gentleman persisted it was she, she would drop him her gravest curtsey and remind him the daughter of the Marquis of Esmond lived for her people and her sons, and did not propose to alter her state. Like that great Queen Elizabeth of whom she had heard tales, she liked to inspire awe and affection together. She accepted praise as her due, was kind or cruel as whim dictated, and her little foible was so well understood that wags practised upon it: Rattling Jack Firebrace lived for months at Castlewood on free quarters because he brought her verses—stolen, it was said, from other men’s pocket-books. Tom Humbold of Spotsylvania won a wager of hogsheads by persuading her to institute an order of knighthood, with Castlewood ribbons and ridiculous ceremonies, and she, delighted, played her part as if she had been born to dubbing.

George, the elder twin, watched these antics with a hot, silent indignation. Even as a child he revolted at the incense offered to his mother and tried, with sharp young wit, to prick the flatterers’ bubbles. Rachel, offended yet secretly pleased, would say gravely that the Esmonds were a jealous race and her boy took after his grandsire. George hated Jack Firebrace and Humbold and their crew; Harry, on the contrary, went fowling and fishing and cock-fighting with them, and took all the rough mirth of the country as naturally as he took corn-bread with bacon.

After the first tutor was dismissed, Rachel carried the boys to Williamsburg for such schooling as the place could give. There they heard the famous Mr. Whitfield, whose trumpet voice shook the drowsy colony where the established clergy—paid by the State, living on glebes, imported from England as one might import tools—were too often neither saints nor orators. Men fled from bailiffs and creditors and brought their stained cassocks across the sea in hope of a safe living. No wonder Whitfield’s thunder woke people whom mild Mr. Broadbent never stirred. Rachel and the boys were kindled alike. They sang hymns, they waited for the sacred “call” as if it might come like a sudden gust through the pines at night. Had Whitfield lingered, both lads might have worn black coats instead of epaulettes one day.

But Whitfield’s mission was to sweep the continent, not to nest in one little congregation. He went, leaving Rachel letters that she hoarded, and promising to send her a tutor who should teach not only “profane learning” but confirm them in a precious science.

In time such a “chosen vessel” arrived from England—young Mr. Ward, a handsome fellow with a voice like a market bell and a tongue that could run as readily as a mill-race. Morning and evening the hall rang with his exhortations. The very soundscape of Castlewood changed under him: where once you heard only the scrape of chairs, the clink of trenchers, the low talk of servants, and the outdoor chorus of birds beyond the windows, now there rose a ceaseless religious declamation, and beneath it the hum and shuffle of listeners. The house-servants—black faces and crisp heads—crept to doorways and crowded the porch windows; and when Ward gave out a hymn there burst such a rolling negro chorus as might have been heard across the Potomac—deep, antiphonal, swelling and falling like wind in a pinewood. It was strange music, at once homely and ominous: a new power taking possession of familiar rooms. In the Colonel’s time no such thing had been endured; he distrusted cassocks and said he would never have controversy with a clergyman except over backgammon. Yet the Colonel had been charitable where money was needed, and the easy parson who loved dice and boards would say charity covered other shortcomings.

Rachel drank Ward’s sermons as she drank her cordials—eagerly, credulously, sure they cured whatever ailed her. Women, a century before, had fewer defences against admiration; they were trained to believe, and belief, once kindled, could blaze. For weeks and months she never tired of Ward’s great glib voice and his commonplaces, and would summon neighbours to listen as she summoned them to dinner, ordering their conversions as she ordered their dishes. She was especially anxious to influence her young favourite, Mr. Washington; but that tall, handsome gentleman found, with a soldier’s punctuality, that particular business always called him away when the hour of Ward’s exercises drew near, and he would order his horse.

The twins grew quickly weary and then rebellious. Ward, for all his volume, was a bad scholar. George knew more Latin and Greek than his master and caught him in blunders and false quantities. Harry—bolder, permitted liberties denied to his elder—mimicked Ward’s way of chewing and talking until Mrs. Mountain laughed outright and even Rachel’s stern mouth twitched; little Fanny Mountain would crow as if it were a game. Rachel might have discovered Ward for a vulgar quack but for the very opposition that should have opened her eyes. Her sons’ contempt only hardened her will. What mattered profane learning, she cried, when he taught the one precious book? Rough manners proved Heaven did not choose its elect from the great and wealthy. It was wicked pride—the pride of all the Esmonds—that made them resist. They must pray to be corrected.

Ward, that evening, discoursed on Naaman the Syrian and the pride of Abana and Pharpar against Jordan—making himself, without shame, the keeper of the healing waters and the boys the conceited sufferers who must bathe in his stream or perish. George listened with a face too still, and something began in him—an inherited gift perhaps, a quiet, skilful sarcasm which, once used, can make a whole household miserable. He took up Ward’s pompous sayings and turned them into jokes; Ward chafed, and his great meals sat ill on him. Rachel grew angrier the more George’s small smiles set Harry laughing. Her authority was mocked, her officer scorned, her younger son “perverted,” she said, by the obstinate elder. She resolved on a desperate attempt to restore command.

The boys were fourteen. Harry, taller and forward, already had the look of a young man; George was delicate, childlike beside him, with a fine, pale face that could look proud and hurt at once. In those days the cane was a common argument: sergeants, schoolmasters, overseers used it as readily as speech. The boys had been “horsed” often enough by Mr. Dempster, their old Scotch tutor, in their grandfather’s time. But since the Colonel’s death the rod had been laid aside; the young gentlemen of Castlewood had tasted the sweetness of licence. Now Rachel, feeling her command slipping, took counsel with Ward, who could find chapter and verse for any severity he desired. He had begun with flattery—snug quarters are agreeable to a man with no estate—but the boys laughed at his compliments, despised his bad breeding, yawned at his sermons; and the more Rachel favoured him, the more they hated him.

Mrs. Mountain, who loved the lads—especially George, whom she thought unjustly treated—warned them in the pantry one day as she oversaw the slicing of ham and the setting out of a cold pie whose crust gave off a nutty, buttery smell. The kitchen noises—the thump of a cleaver, the hiss of a pot-lid—made a safer cover for speech than the echoing hall where Ward’s voice prowled like a watchdog.

“Ward is more obsequious than ever to your mamma,” she whispered, her nostrils flaring as if his flattery had an odour. “It turns my stomach, it does, to see him gobble. Be on your guard, my poor boys. Learn your lessons. Don’t anger him. Mischief will come—I know it will. Your mamma was talking about you to Mr. Washington t’other day when I stepped in.”

“I don’t like that Major Washington, you know I don’t,” she added, then checked herself as Harry began to protest. “Don’t say, ‘O Mounty!’ You always stand up for your friends. He is handsome and tall, and may be very good, but he is much too old a young man for me. Bless you, the wild oats your father sowed and my poor Mountain when they were ensigns in Kingsley’s would fill sacks full. Show me Mr. Washington’s wild oats—not a grain! I came in, and I’m sure they were speaking of you, for he said: ‘Discipline is discipline, and must be preserved. There can be but one command in a house, ma’am, and you must be mistress of yours.’”

“The very words he used to me,” Harry cried. “He told me he did not like to meddle, but mother was dangerously angry, he said, and begged me to obey Mr. Ward, and to press George to do so.”

“Let him manage his own house, not mine,” George said, haughtily; and the warning, instead of softening him, made him more stiff.

Next day the storm broke. In morning study words passed between George and Ward; the boy was insubordinate, and even Harry cried out and owned his brother wrong. Ward “kept his temper”—that is, he corked it down and promised it should burst later—and said he would speak to Madam Esmond. At dinner, when the meats had been carved and the room still held the savour of peppered gravy and roasted fowl, Ward requested her ladyship to remain. Temperately, he laid his complaint before her.

He called on Harry to confirm him, and poor Harry, trapped between truth and loyalty, admitted the dominie’s statements. George, standing under his grandfather’s portrait by the chimney, said stiffly that what Mr. Ward had reported was correct.

“To be tutor to such a pupil is absurd,” Ward began, and launched into one of his long speeches, thick with Scripture phrases. At each solemn citation George smiled—small, scornful—and made a faint pish of contempt. Ward ended by asking leave to retire.

“Not before you have punished this wicked and disobedient child,” Rachel said. Her anger had been gathering through Ward’s harangue, and it flared hottest at George’s demeanour.

“Punish?” George repeated, as if the word were in a foreign tongue.

“Yes, sir—punish! If means of love and entreaty fail, as they have with your proud heart, other means must bring you to obedience. I punish you now to guard you from greater punishment hereafter. The discipline of this family must be maintained. There can be but one command in a house, and I must be the mistress of mine. You will punish this refractory boy, Mr. Ward, as we have agreed; and if there is the least resistance, my overseer and servants shall lend you aid.”

She spoke with vehemence, seasoning her private wrath with sacred texts as if Heaven were her witness and ally in a domestic quarrel. This habit—dragging the thunder of Scripture into the narrow room of family—was a new language Rachel had learned under her impetuous guide; and if it gave her power, it also thinned something in her, like a sauce reduced too far until it turns bitter and catches at the throat.

In the midst of it George felt his own fault. He grew very white. “There can be but one command in the house,” he said slowly, “and you must be mistress—I know who said those words before you.” He swallowed. “And I know, mother, that I have acted wrongly to Mr. Ward.”

“He owns it! He asks pardon!” Harry cried, catching at hope as at a knife’s edge. “That’s right, George! That’s enough—isn’t it?”

“No, it is not enough!” Rachel answered, sharp as vinegar. “The disobedient boy must pay the penalty. When I was headstrong before my spirit was humbled, my mamma punished me, and I submitted. So must George. Do your duty, Mr. Ward.”

“Stop, mother—you don’t quite know what you are doing,” George said, his voice shaken.

“I know that he who spares the rod spoils the child,” Rachel replied, and George heard her as if from far off, pale and desperate.

On the mantelpiece beneath the Colonel’s portrait stood a china cup Rachel prized above any in her cupboard because her father had always drunk from it. It was part of the house’s memory—thin, bright porcelain that had crossed seas, held lips long dead, and still carried, if you lifted it close, a faint ghost of tea and smoke and old cedar. George’s hand went to it. A strange smile crossed his white face.

“Stay one minute. Don’t go away yet,” he cried as Rachel turned. “You—you are very fond of this cup, mother?” Harry stared, not understanding. “If I broke it, it could never be mended, could it? All the tinkers’ rivets would not make it whole again. My dear old grandpapa’s cup! I have been wrong. Mr. Ward, I ask pardon. I will try and amend.”

Rachel looked at him with indignation that was almost scorn. “I thought,” she said, “I thought an Esmond had been more of a man than to be afraid, and—”

She gave a little scream. Harry cried out and sprang forward, hands flung wide.

George lifted the cup, opened his fingers, and let it fall. It struck the marble slab below with a clean, cruel sound—porcelain shattering into bright fragments. The room seemed to hold its breath. Harry’s hands closed on nothing.

“It is too late, Hal,” George said quietly. “You will never mend that again—never. Now, mother, I am ready, as it is your wish. Will you come and see whether I am afraid? Mr. Ward, I am your servant. Your servant? Your slave! And the next time I meet Mr. Washington, madam, I will thank him for the advice he gave you.”

“I say, do your duty, sir!” Rachel cried, stamping her little foot. George bowed low to Ward and begged him to go first to the study.

“Stop! For God’s sake, mother, stop!” Harry pleaded. But passion boiled in Rachel like a pot left too long on a fierce fire; it had burned past listening. “You only abet him, sir!” she cried. “If I had to do it myself, it should be done!” And Harry, with wrath and sorrow set in his face, followed them out.

Rachel sank into a great chair near the door and stared at the cup’s broken pieces as if they were bones. The house had gone oddly silent: no hymn, no lesson, only the distant creak of a board, the far-off chirr of insects outside, the faint clatter from the kitchen where life, indifferent, went on with plates and knives. She inclined her head toward the carved mahogany door—one of the Colonel’s European purchases—listening as if her ear could catch and translate what her will had set in motion.

For a moment there was nothing. Then a loud outcry—raw, human—made her start as if struck.

In another instant Mr. Ward burst out, blood streaming from a great wound on his head; behind him came Harry with eyes aflame, brandishing a little couteau-de-chasse of his grandfather’s that had hung among the Colonel’s weapons on the library wall.

“I don’t care. I did it,” Harry said. “I couldn’t see this fellow strike my brother; and, as he lifted his hand, I flung the great ruler at him. I couldn’t help it. I won’t bear it; and if one lifts a hand to me or my brother, I’ll have his life,” he shouted, shaking the blade.

After the unlucky divine had ridden away from Castlewood—his books shut, his arguments left like cold ashes on the hearth—Madam Esmond and her eldest boy moved about one another with a careful peace, such as follows thunder. They did not speak again of the quarrel. Yet silence, like salt on a raw place, bit the more.

George bore it in his body. A fever came upon him with the first hard weather, and in the night, when the house lay muffled under snow and the pines outside stood listening, the child’s mind broke its tether. He would start up, eyes wide in the candle’s wavering light, and cry out in a voice that was not his own: “Broken! Broken! It never, never can be mended!” The words struck Madam Esmond with a terror more keen than any bodily danger, because they sounded like prophecy—like some old family hurt returning in a new tongue.

She watched him hour after hour, the bedcurtains breathing with his tossing, the chamber filled with the small, cruel noises of sickness: the rasp of breath, the clink of spoon against cup, the shifting of linen. Her closet of remedies—root and leaf and cordial, powders wrapped in paper, bottles that smelled of camphor, bitter bark, and steeped mint—failed her. She had always healed her people with those nostrums; she could set a servant’s ague right with a draught, or bring down a child’s heat with a cloth and a tea, and had long trusted the knowledge that women hand to women without writing it down. Now her simples were like words in a dead language: remembered, repeated, and powerless.

At last she took the only medicine left, which was humiliation. One day, while the snow lay crisp and bright and the air rang with the distant crack of trees in frost, little Mr. Dempster saw her at his own poor door, sitting her pony, cloak drawn tight, cheeks stung red. She had ridden through the weather to beg him.

“I shall bury my resentment, madam,” said he—small, stiff, and very pale with pride under his civility—“as your ladyship buried your pride. Please God, I may be time enough to help my dear young pupil!”

He packed his lancet and his little store of medicaments as carefully as if they were silver; called his one negro-boy; shut his lonely hut; and returned to Castlewood like a man going back into a household which had wounded him and still commanded him.

That night, and for some days following, it seemed likely that Harry would soon be heir of Castlewood. The fever mounted; the boy’s limbs burned; his speech wandered. Madam Esmond’s mind ran in circles, each turn bringing her again to the bedside, to the smell of vinegar and sweat, to the wick’s faint smoke, to the hush of the house that listens for a change in breathing. But Mr. Dempster, with the harsh mercy of his art, bled and dosed and watched with an attention that was almost tenderness. The heat broke. The intermittent attacks lessened. George returned by degrees, as one might hear a lost tune find its way back into the ear.

When the peril had passed, Dempster urged a change of air—“a voyage even to England,” he said—but Madam Esmond had quarreled with her children’s kin there, and now, with the contrition that comes when one has been forced to ask help, owned she had been too hasty. It was resolved instead that the lads should go north and east. So the two young gentlemen set out with Mr. Dempster for tutor, and two servants to attend them; and, leaving the quiet music of Castlewood—the mill’s steady groan, the frogs in the marsh, the kitchen’s morning stir—they took ship to New York and then journeyed up the Hudson to Albany.

They were received there by the first gentry of the province, and from thence passed into the French settlements, where their recommendations opened doors as readily as if gold had been laid upon the threshold. If the English colonies spoke one sort of sound—axes and carts, the long crack of whips, the hammering of new boards—these places had another music: fiddles in parlours, soft French voices that slid like cream, church bells that seemed to sweeten the air, and kitchens where the very pans spoke a language of their own. At tables where stews were tended with patience, where butter was beaten pale as winter sunlight, where herbs were lifted between fingers and breathed upon before they went into the pot, George listened and learned as if nourishment itself were a kind of history.

Harry, who was made for the open and noisy world, went where the sound was loudest. He camped with the Indians, took furs, and shot bears; slept under trees that creaked and sighed like old men; and came home from such excursions smelling of smoke, wet leather, and blood. George never cared for field-sports. His health remained delicate; his pleasure lay not in the crack of a gun, but in the minute attentions of a well-appointed room, the exact note of a violin, the way a sauce is thickened without haste, the name by which a Frenchwoman calls a particular bread.

He became a favourite with the French ladies, who were accustomed to see very few young English gentlemen speak their language with ease. George did more than speak: he wore it. He perfected his accent until, if he chose, he might pass for a Frenchman; he had the bel air, every person allowed. He danced the minuet with an elegance learned not only in the feet but in the ear, for a minuet is as much a pattern of sound as of motion. He learned the latest imported catches and songs, and played them beautifully on his violin; he would have sung them too, but his voice broke at that time and changed from treble to bass—an alteration which vexed him more than he pretended, for it made his own throat a stranger for a season.

And, to the envy of poor Harry—who was absent on a bear-hunt and could only hear the tale later—George had even an affair of honour with a young ensign of the regiment of Auvergne, the Chevalier de la Jabotière, whom he pinked in the shoulder. They afterwards swore an eternal friendship, as young men will, when a little blood has been paid for pride. Madame de Mouchy, the superintendent’s lady, said the mother was blest who had such a son, and wrote a complimentary letter to Madam Esmond upon Mr. George’s behaviour. Had Mr. Whitfield been there to read it, he would scarcely have been pleased with the widow’s elation at hearing of her son’s prowess.

When the lads returned at the end of ten delightful months, their mother was surprised at their growth and improvement. George especially had grown so as to come up to his younger-born brother. When their hair was powdered they might hardly be told apart; but powder was too cumbrous for country life, and commonly each wore his own: George his raven black, Harry his light locks tied with a ribbon.

The reader who has followed the first pages of the lads’ simple biography will have observed that Mr. George Esmond was of a jealous and suspicious disposition—most generous and gentle, incapable of an untruth; too magnanimous to revenge, and almost incapable of forgiving an injury. He had left home with no goodwill toward an honourable gentleman, whose name afterwards became one of the most famous in the world; and he returned not in the least altered in his opinion of his mother’s and grandfather’s friend.

Mr. Washington, though then but just of age, looked and felt much older. He always exhibited an extraordinary simplicity and gravity. He had managed his mother’s and his family’s affairs from a very early age, and was trusted by all his friends and the gentry of his county more than persons twice his senior.

Mrs. Mountain—Madam Esmond’s friend and companion, who dearly loved the two boys and her patroness in spite of many quarrels with the latter and daily threats of parting—was a droll letter-writer, and had written to the lads on their travels. She was of a jealous turn likewise; especially she had a great turn for match-making, and fancied everybody had a design to marry everybody else. There scarce came an unmarried man to Castlewood but Mountain imagined he had an eye towards the mistress of the mansion.

She was positive that odious Mr. Ward intended to make love to the widow, and pretty sure the latter liked him. She knew that Mr. Washington wanted to be married; was certain that such a shrewd young gentleman would look out for a rich wife; and as for differences of age, what matter that the Major—major was his rank in the militia—was fifteen years younger than Madam Esmond? Were they not used to such marriages in the family? Was not my lady her mother older than the Colonel when she married him—when she married him and was so jealous she would never let the poor Colonel out of her sight? The poor Colonel! after his wife, he had been henpecked by his little daughter. And she would take after her mother and marry again, be sure of that.

Madam, Mountain would say, was a little chit of a woman, not five feet in her highest headdress and shoes, and Mr. Washington a great tall man of six feet two. Great tall men always married little chits of women: therefore Mr. W. must be looking after the widow. What could be clearer?

She communicated these sage opinions to her boy—George—who begged her, for Heaven’s sake, to hold her tongue.

“This I can do,” Mountain said. “But I cannot keep my eyes always shut.” And she narrated a hundred circumstances from the young gentleman’s absence, which, to her mind, proved all.

Had Mountain imparted these suspicions to his brother? George asked sternly.

No. George was her boy; Harry was his mother’s boy. “She likes him best, and I like you best, George,” cries Mountain. “Besides, if I were to speak to him, he would tell your mother in a minute. Poor Harry can keep nothing quiet, and then there would be a pretty quarrel between Madam and me!”

“I beg you to keep this quiet, Mountain,” said Mr. George with great dignity; “or you and I shall quarrel too. Neither to me nor to any one else in the world must you mention such an absurd suspicion.”

Absurd! Why absurd? Mr. Washington was constantly with the widow. His name was forever in her mouth. She was never tired of pointing out his virtues and example to her sons. She consulted him on every question respecting her estate and its management. She never bought a horse or sold a barrel of tobacco without his opinion. There was a room at Castlewood regularly called Mr. Washington’s room.

“He actually leaves his clothes here and his portmanteau when he goes away. Ah, George, George! One day will come when he won’t go away,” groaned Mountain—who, of course, always returned to the subject of which she was forbidden to speak.

Meanwhile Mr. George adopted towards his mother’s favourite a frigid courtesy, at which the honest gentleman chafed but did not care to remonstrate; or a stinging sarcasm, which Washington would break through as he would burst through brambles on those hunting excursions where he and Harry Warrington rode so constantly together—hoofs drumming, dogs yelping, men shouting through the woods, a racket that shook the quiet. George, retreating to his tents, read mathematics and French and Latin, and sulked in his book-room more and more lonely, as if language itself were safer when it lay dead upon the page.

Harry was away from home with some sporting friends—his acquaintances, it is to be feared, not all as eligible as Mr. Washington—when the latter came to pay a visit at Castlewood. He was so peculiarly tender and kind to the mistress there, and received by her with such special cordiality, that George’s jealousy had well-nigh broken out in open rupture.

But the visit, it appeared, was one of adieu. Major Washington was going on a long and dangerous journey, quite to the western Virginia frontier and beyond it. The French had for some time been making inroads upon our territory. The government at home, as well as those of Virginia and Pennsylvania, were alarmed at this aggressive spirit of the Lords of Canada and Louisiana. Some settlers had already been driven from their holdings by Frenchmen in arms, and the governors of the British provinces were desirous to stop the incursions, or at least to protest against the invasion.

We chose to hold our colonies by a law convenient to its framers: that whoever possessed the coast had a right to all the territory inland as far as the Pacific; the charters laying down limits from north to south and leaving them free from east to west. The French, meanwhile, had their colonies to the north and south, and aimed at connecting them by the Mississippi and the St. Lawrence and the great intermediate lakes and waters westward of the British possessions. In 1748, though peace was signed in Europe, the colonial question remained unsettled—like a pot set off the fire too soon, the contents still seething where you cannot see them—until either party should be strong enough to urge it. In 1753 it came to an issue on the Ohio, where British and French settlers met.

There existed, to be sure, other people besides French and British who thought they had title to the soil—namely the native Indians. But the logicians of St. James’s and Versailles wisely chose to consider it a European question, eliminating the Red-man from argument, while employing his tomahawk as it served either litigant. The Ohio Company, having grants from Virginia of lands along that river, found themselves invaded by French military detachments, who roughly ejected the Britons. These applied to Mr. Dinwiddie, Lieutenant-Governor of Virginia, who determined upon sending an ambassador to the French commanding officer on the Ohio, demanding that the French should desist from their inroads upon his Majesty King George’s territories.

Young Mr. Washington jumped eagerly at the chance of distinction. He volunteered to leave home and his rural pursuits to carry the governor’s message. With a guide, an interpreter, and a few attendants, and following Indian tracks, in the fall of 1753 he made his way from Williamsburg almost to the shores of Lake Erie and found the French commander at Fort le Boeuf. The reply was brief: his orders were to hold the place and drive all the English from it. The French avowed their intention of taking possession of the Ohio. With this rough answer the messenger had to return through danger and difficulty—across lonely forest and frozen river, shaping his course by compass, camping at night in the snow by forest fires whose crackle was the only friendly speech.

Harry Warrington cursed his ill-fortune that he had been absent from home at a cock-fight when he might have had sport so much nobler; and on Major Washington’s return—after an expedition conducted with heroic energy and simplicity—the Major was a greater favourite than ever with the lady of Castlewood. She pointed him out as a model to both her sons.

“Ah, Harry!” she would say, “think of you with your cock-fighting and your racing-matches, and the Major away there in the wilderness, watching the French, and battling with the frozen rivers! Ah, George! learning may be a very good thing, but I wish my eldest son were doing something in the service of his country!”

“I desire no better than to go home and seek for employment, ma’am,” says George. “You surely will not have me serve under Mr. Washington, in his new regiment, or ask a commission from Mr. Dinwiddie?”

“An Esmond can only serve with the king’s commission,” says Madam. “And as for asking a favour from Mr. Lieutenant-Governor Dinwiddie, I would rather beg my bread.”

Mr. Washington at this time was raising such a regiment as, with the scanty pay and patronage of the Virginian government, he could gather, and proposed with these men-of-war—so the provincials called themselves in brave irony—to lay a more peremptory veto on French invaders than the solitary ambassador could. A small force under another officer, Colonel Trent, had already been despatched westward with orders to fortify themselves. The French troops, greatly outnumbering ours, came up with the English outposts at a place on the confines of Pennsylvania where the great city of Pittsburg now stands. A Virginian officer with forty men could not resist twenty times that number. He was suffered to draw back without molestation; and the French, taking possession of his fort, strengthened it and christened it by the name of the Canadian governor, Du Quesne.

Up to this time no actual blow of war had been struck. The troops were in presence—the guns loaded, but no one had yet cried “Fire.” It was strange that in a savage forest of Pennsylvania a young Virginian officer should fire a shot and wake a war to last for sixty years; to cover his own country and pass into Europe; to cost France her American colonies; to sever ours from us and create the great Western republic; to rage over the Old World when extinguished in the New; and of all the myriads engaged, to leave the prize of the greatest fame with him who struck the first blow. He little knew of the fate in store for him. A simple gentleman, anxious to serve his king and do his duty, he volunteered for the first service and executed it with admirable fidelity.

In the ensuing year he took command of the small body of provincial troops with which he marched to repel the French. He came up with their advanced guard and fired upon them, killing their leader. After this he had himself to fall back, and was compelled to capitulate to the superior French force. On the 4th of July, 1754, the Colonel marched out with his troops from the little fort where he had hastily entrenched himself—Fort Necessity—gave up the place to the conqueror, and took his way home. His command was over; his regiment disbanded after the fruitless, inglorious march and defeat.

Saddened and humbled, the young officer presented himself after a while to his old friends at Castlewood. There were no trumpets now in his step—only the quiet sound of boots on boards, the murmur of servants carrying dishes in and out, the house continuing in its domestic rites as if history were but another guest to be fed.

He was very young, and before he set forth on his first campaign he may have indulged in exaggerated hopes and spoken them. “I was angry when I parted from you,” he said to George Warrington, holding out his hand, which the other eagerly took. “You seemed to scorn me and my regiment, George. I thought you laughed at us, and your ridicule made me angry. I boasted too much of what we would do.”

“Nay, you have done your best, George,” said the other, who quite forgot his previous jealousy in his old comrade’s misfortune. “Everybody knows that a hundred and fifty starving men, with scarce a round of ammunition left, could not face five times their number perfectly armed; and everybody who knows Mr. Washington knows that he would do his duty. Harry and I saw the French in Canada last year. They obey but one will: in our provinces each governor has his own. They were royal troops the French sent against you—”

“Oh, but that some of ours were here!” cries Madam Esmond, tossing her head. “I promise you a few good English regiments would make the white-coats run.”

“You think nothing of the provincials; and I must say nothing now we have been so unlucky,” said the Colonel gloomily. “You made much of me when I was here before. Don’t you remember what victories you prophesied for me—how much I boasted myself very likely over your good wine? All those fine dreams are over now. ’Tis kind of your ladyship to receive a poor beaten fellow as you do.” And the young soldier hung down his head.

George Warrington, with his acute sensibility, was touched at the other’s emotion—at sorrow spoken plainly, without ornament. He was about to answer with something more friendly still, had not his mother, to whom the Colonel had been speaking, replied herself.

“Kind of us to receive you, Colonel Washington!” said the widow. “I never heard that when men were unhappy, our sex were less their friends.”

And she made the Colonel a very fine curtsey—so fine, so full of that old-fashioned grace which could seem like generosity and command in one motion—that straightway her son, who had been softened for a moment, felt the old jealousy leap up again, bitter as burned sugar on the tongue.

Surely no man ever stepped into a house with better credentials for a widow’s admiration than youth, courage, good looks, and a touch of calamity to make all the virtues shine the brighter. Madam Esmond had two sons of her own, and could have had twenty, and yet she claimed a right to extol her young soldier as though Providence had lodged him at Castlewood for her particular comfort.

Mr. Washington’s room was now more than ever Mr. Washington’s room. The very boards seemed to remember the weight of his boots; the curtains held a faint smell of saddle-leather and clean linen, and a whiff—whether from his own pomade or from the bay-rum a servant had splashed too liberally on his shaving-basin—haunted the place like a private signature. Madam Esmond spoke of him at breakfast, spoke of him at dinner, spoke of him when the preserves were brought in, and when the candles were snuffed. His name ran through her talk as steadily as the kitchen’s clock ticked through the stillness after supper.

At table she praised him in all companies; she cited him to her sons as the model of sterling worth, contrasting his sober, serviceable qualities with Harry’s love of pleasure (the wild boy!) and George’s bookish languor, his long spells of silence as he stared down at a page while the corn-cakes cooled on his plate. That kind of praise has a way of souring the mouth of the listener. George, who already held a jealous demon by the hand and coaxed it instead of striking it away, was not disposed to like Mr. Washington any better for his mother’s extravagant homage.

His humour turned saturnine. He made jokes too deep for his mother’s simple understanding; she sat bewildered at his sarcasms, and could not tell whether to laugh, rebuke, or pray for him. The household, which usually lived by sensible measures—ploughing, curing meat, laying in flour—found itself, even in its most domestic hours, being tugged by larger currents.

For public events were working their way toward Castlewood like a storm one hears days before it breaks. The quarrel between the French and English in North America, which had begun as a provincial bickering among distant forts and river-mouths, had swollen into a national contest. Reinforcements from France had arrived in Canada; English troops were expected in Virginia. Even letters came across the wilderness with the war in their very ink.

“Alas! my dear friend!” wrote Madame la Présidente de Mouchy from Quebec to George Warrington, her French phrases folding around English realities like pastry around a rough filling. “How contrary is destiny to us! I see you quitting the embrace of an adored mother to precipitate yourself in the arms of Bellona. I see you pass wounded after combats. I hesitate almost to wish victory to our lilies when I behold you ranged under the banners of the Leopard. There are enmities which the heart does not recognise—ours assuredly are at peace among the tumults. All here love and salute you, as well as Monsieur the Bear-hunter, your brother (that cold Hippolyte who preferred the chase to the soft conversation of our ladies!) Your friend, your enemy, the Chevalier de la Jabotière, burns to meet on the field of Mars his generous rival. M. Du Quesne spoke of you last night at supper. M. Du Quesne, my husband, send affectuous remembrances to their young friend, with which are ever joined those of your sincere Présidente de Mouchy.”

“The banner of the Leopard” was indeed flung out, and men rallied to it. It was resolved in London that the French should be wrested from all they had taken upon British dominion. Two regiments were raised and paid by the king in America, and a fleet with two more regiments was despatched from home under an experienced commander.

In February of 1755 Commodore Keppel, in the famous Centurion—Anson’s old ship that had circled the world—anchored in Hampton Roads, with two ships of war under his command and, on board, General Braddock, his staff, and a part of his troops. Mr. Braddock had been appointed by the Duke—by the Duke of Cumberland, called in those days The Duke as if England needed no other. He was not so great a prince as his party pretended, nor so black a monster as his enemies would paint, but he had power enough in his hand now, and the colonies were to feel its weight.

Transports followed speedily: stores, men, money—barrels and bolts and muskets; casks that smelled of tar and damp rope; crates of biscuit that would later taste of weevil and resignation. The General landed his troops at Alexandria on the Potomac and repaired to Annapolis in Maryland, where he ordered the governors of the different colonies to meet him in council, pressing each to call upon his province to help in the common cause.

The arrival of the General and his little army caused a mighty excitement through the provinces, and nowhere greater than at Castlewood. War, even at a distance, changed the daily music of the place. The farm had its accustomed sounds—the creak of a well-pulley, the soft thud of maize poured into bins, the knife’s steady percussion as it worked through salt pork, the hiss when lard met the hot iron in the kitchen—but now these were answered in the imagination by other noises: drums, fifes, the clank of bayonets, the shout of drill. In the evenings, when the wind carried up faintly the far-off rumour of wagons on the road, Harry would start as if it were the advance of glory itself.

Harry was off forthwith to see the troops under canvas at Alexandria. The sight of their ordered lines delighted him; the music of their fifes and drums went into his blood like strong drink. He came home talking not only of colours and officers, but of the very camp-smells: woodsmoke and wet wool, horse-sweat, gun-oil, and the sour tang of stale beer. He had speedily made acquaintance with the officers of both regiments; he longed to join the expedition upon which they were bound, and he was a welcome guest at their mess.

Madam Esmond was pleased that her sons should have an opportunity of enjoying the society of gentlemen of good fashion from England. She had no doubt the company was improving, that English gentlemen must be different from the horse-racing, cock-fighting Virginian squires with whom Master Harry would otherwise consort, and different too from the lawyers, pettifoggers, and toad-eaters at the lieutenant-governor’s table. Madam Esmond had a very keen eye for detecting flatterers in other folks’ houses; against the little knot of official people at Williamsburg she was especially satirical and had no patience with their etiquettes and squabbles for precedence.

As for the king’s officers, Mr. Harry and his elder brother both smiled at their mamma’s praises of the elegance and propriety of the gentlemen of the camp. If the good lady had but heard the songs they roared over punch, the coarse jests that flew about like sparks from a fire, if she had seen how many were carried away to lodgings with their fine faces turned to stupefied clay, she would scarce have recommended their society so warmly. Men and officers swaggered round the country, scaring peaceful farm and village folk with their riot. The General raved and stormed against his troops for their disorder; against the provincials for their traitorous niggardliness. His soldiers took possession as of a conquered land, scorned the provincials, insulted even the wives of their Indian allies who had come to join the English warriors and march against the French.

The General was compelled to forbid the Indian women his camp. Amazed and outraged, their husbands retired; and a few months later their services were lost to him, when their aid would have been most precious. Some stories against the gentlemen of the camp might have reached Madam Esmond, but she would have none of them. Soldiers would be soldiers, everybody knew; and those officers who came over to Castlewood on her son’s invitation were most polite gentlemen—so, indeed, they were in her drawing-room, where good linen lay on the tables and the servants moved in well-trained quiet.

She received them graciously and gave them the best sport the country afforded. And presently the General himself sent polite messages to the mistress of Castlewood. His father had served with hers under the glorious Marlborough, and Colonel Esmond’s name was still known and respected in England. With her ladyship’s permission, General Braddock would have the honour of waiting upon her at Castlewood and paying his respects to the daughter of so meritorious an officer.

If Madam Esmond had known the cause of Mr. Braddock’s politeness, perhaps his compliments would not have charmed her quite so much.

The Commander-in-Chief held levees at Alexandria, and among the gentry who paid him respect were our twins of Castlewood. They mounted their best nags, put on their last London suits, and with their two negro-boys in smart liveries behind them, rode in state to wait upon the great man. He was sulky and angry with the provincial gentry, and scarce took any notice of the young gentlemen—only asking casually of his aide-de-camp at dinner who the young Squire Gawkeys were in blue and gold and red waistcoats.

Mr. Dinwiddie, lieutenant-governor of Virginia, an agent from Pennsylvania, and a few more gentlemen happened to be dining with his Excellency.

“Oh!” says Mr. Dinwiddie, “those are the sons of the Princess Pocahontas;” upon which, with a tremendous oath, the General asked, “Who the deuce was she?”

Dinwiddie—who did not love Madam Esmond, having undergone a hundred pertnesses from the imperious little lady—now gave a disrespectful and ridiculous account of her, made merry with her pomposity and immense pretensions, and entertained General Braddock with anecdotes until his Excellency fell asleep.

When he awoke, Dinwiddie was gone, but the Philadelphia gentleman was still at table, deep in conversation with the officers present. The General took up the talk where it had been dropped, spoke of Madam Esmond in curt, disrespectful terms such as soldiers used freely in those days, and asked again what was the name of the old fool about whom Dinwiddie had been talking. Then he broke into expressions of contempt and wrath against the gentry and the country in general.

Mr. Franklin of Philadelphia repeated the widow’s name and took quite another view of her character. He seemed to know a great deal about her, her father, and her estate—as indeed he did about every man and subject that came under discussion. He explained to the General that Madam Esmond had beeves, horses, and stores in plenty which might prove very useful at the present juncture, and recommended him to conciliate her by all means. The General, who had already made up his mind that Mr. Franklin was shrewd and intelligent, graciously ordered an aide-de-camp to invite the two young men to the next day’s dinner.

When they appeared, his Excellency was very pleasant and good-natured; the gentlemen of the General’s family made much of them. George and Harry behaved as became persons of their name, with modesty and good-breeding. They returned home delighted with their entertainment, nor was their mother less pleased at the civilities shown to her boys.

In reply to Braddock’s message Madam Esmond penned a billet in her best style, acknowledging his politeness and begging his Excellency to fix the time when she might have the honour to receive him at Castlewood.

The arrival of the army and the approaching campaign became the staple of conversation in the household—at the very hours when other families thought of planting, pickling, salting, and baking. War insinuated itself into the kitchen as readily as into the parlour. While the cook beat eggs for a pudding, the talk was of battalions; while a ham was lowered into the smokehouse, Harry spoke of marches and sieges; while a servant skimmed the scum from a pot of broth, George sat silent, listening, as though even the bubbling had become a kind of drum.

To make the campaign was the dearest wish of Harry’s life. He dreamed only of war and battle. He was forever with the officers at Williamsburg. He scoured, cleaned, and polished all the guns and swords in the house until the metal caught candlelight like water. He renewed the amusements of his childhood and had the negroes under arms, drilling them with a seriousness that made the yard seem half a farm, half a parade-ground. The soundscape of Castlewood altered under his zeal: more stamping boots, more shouted commands, more clack of rammers against barrels; and yet in the midst of this the domestic music persisted—the rhythmic chop of herbs, the low murmur of women over bread, the soft sweep of broom on plank floors—steadier, older, like a language that would not consent to die.

Madam Esmond, who had a gallant spirit, knew the time was come when one of her boys must leave her and serve the king. She scarce dared to think on whom the lot should fall. She admired and respected the elder, but she loved the younger with all the passion of her heart.

Eager as Harry was, and with all his thoughts bent on that glorious scheme, he too scarcely dared to touch on the subject nearest his heart. Once or twice when he ventured on it with George, the latter’s countenance wore an ominous look. Harry had a feudal attachment for his elder brother; he worshipped him with extravagant regard, and in all things gave way to him as the chief. So Harry saw, to his infinite terror, that George too, in his grave way, was occupied with military matters.

George had the wars of Eugene and Marlborough down from the shelves—his grandfather’s military books—along with the most warlike of Plutarch’s lives. He and Dempster were practising with the foils again. The old Scotchman was an adept in the military art, though somewhat shy of saying where he learned it.

Madam Esmond made her two boys the bearers of the letter in reply to his Excellency’s message, and she accompanied her note with large and handsome presents for the General’s staff and the officers of the two royal regiments. The gifts were of the sort a plantation could make eloquent: hams cured to a deep rose and edged with fragrant fat; jars of preserved peaches glowing like late sunlight; sacks of meal ground fine as powder; bottles of cordial with spice warming the throat even in thought; and coffee and sugar laid out as though Castlewood meant to feed not only its friends but fortune itself. The servants moved these offerings with care, and the kitchen breathed out its own persuasive diplomacy—smoke, sweetness, salt, and the clean sharp scent of bay.

So much provision, so promptly and so gracefully given, caused the General more than once to thank Mr. Franklin for having brought this welcome ally into the camp.

“Would not one of the young gentlemen like to see the campaign?” the General asked. A friend of theirs—Mr. Washington, who had been unlucky in the affair of last year—had already promised to join him as aide-de-camp, and his Excellency would gladly take another young Virginian gentleman into his family.

Harry’s eyes brightened; his face flushed as if the words were a trumpet sounded into his veins. “He would like with all his heart to go!” he cried out.

George, looking hard at his younger brother, said one of them would be proud to attend his Excellency, whilst it would be the other’s duty to take care of their mother at home.

Harry allowed his senior to speak. His will was even yet obedient to George’s. However much he desired to go, he would not pronounce until George had declared himself. He longed so for the campaign that the wish itself made him timid, as if naming it might snatch it away.

On the ride home the brothers went for miles in silence, or strove to talk upon indifferent subjects—the condition of the roads, the quality of a horse’s shoeing, whether the spring would come early—each knowing what was passing in the other’s mind, and afraid to bring the awful question to an issue. The clop of hooves and the creak of leather were loud in that hush; even the birdsong seemed to pause and listen.

On their arrival they told their mother of General Braddock’s offer.

“I knew it must happen,” she said. “At such a crisis in the country our family must come forward. Have you—have you settled yet which of you is to leave me?” And she looked anxiously from one to the other, dreading to hear either name.

“The youngest ought to go, mother; of course I ought to go!” cried Harry, turning very red.

“Of course he ought,” said Mrs. Mountain, who was present.

“There! Mountain says so! I told you so!” cried Harry again, with a sidelong look at George, as if seeking the verdict he feared.

“The head of the family ought to go, mother,” said George sadly.

“No! no! you are ill, and have never recovered your fever. Ought he to go, Mountain?”

“You would make the best soldier, I know that, dearest Hal. You and George Washington are great friends, and could travel well together, and he does not care for me, nor I for him, however much he is admired in the family. But, you see, ’tis the law of Honour, my Harry.”

It was George who spoke then to his brother, and his voice had in it extraordinary kindness and tenderness—like a hand laid quietly on a wound.

“The grief I have had in this matter has been that I must refuse thee. I must go. Had Fate given you the benefit of that extra half-hour of life which I have had before you, it would have been your lot, and you would have claimed your right to go first—you know you would.”

“Yes, George,” said poor Harry, “I own I should.”

“You will stay at home, and take care of Castlewood and our mother. If anything happens to me, you are here to fill my place. I would like to give way, my dear, as you, I know, would lay down your life to serve me. But each of us must do his duty. What would our grandfather say if he were here?”

The mother looked proudly at her two sons. “My papa would say that his boys were gentlemen,” faltered Madam Esmond; and she left them, not choosing, perhaps, to show the emotion which was filling her heart.

It was speedily known among the servants that Mr. George was going on the campaign. Dinah, George’s foster-mother, was loud in lamentations at losing him, her cries rising and falling like a keening song that made the yard feel suddenly foreign. Phillis, Harry’s old nurse, was as noisy because Master George, as usual, was preferred over Master Harry. Sady, George’s servant, made preparations to follow his master, bragging incessantly of deeds he would do, speaking of French scalps and plunder as though boasting were the same as courage. Gumbo, Harry’s boy, pretended to whimper at being left behind, though at home he was anything but a fire-eater.

Yet of all in the house Mrs. Mountain was the most angry at George’s determination. She had no patience with him. He did not know what he was doing by leaving home. She begged, implored, insisted that he should alter his determination, and vowed that nothing but mischief would come from his departure.

George was surprised at the pertinacity of her opposition.

“I know, Mountain,” said he, “that Harry would be the better soldier; but after all, to go is my duty.”

“To stay is your duty!” says Mountain, stamping her foot so hard that the pewter on the sideboard gave a small answering rattle. “Why did not my mother own it when we talked of the matter just now?”

“Your mother!” says Mrs. Mountain, with a most gloomy, sardonic laugh. “Your mother, my poor child!”

“What is the meaning of that mournful countenance, Mountain?”

“It may be that your mother wishes you away, George!” Mountain continued, wagging her head. “It may be, my poor deluded boy, that you will find a father-in-law when you come back.”

“What in heaven do you mean?” cried George, the blood rushing into his face.

“Do you suppose I have no eyes, and cannot see what is going on? I tell you, child, that Colonel Washington wants a rich wife. When you are gone, he will ask your mother to marry him, and you will find him master here when you come back. That is why you ought not to go away, you poor, unhappy, simple boy! Don’t you see how fond she is of him? how much she makes of him? how she is always holding him up to you, to Harry, to everybody who comes here?”

“But he is going on the campaign too,” cried George.

“He is going on the marrying campaign, child!” insisted the widow.

“Nay; General Braddock himself told me that Mr. Washington had accepted the appointment of aide-de-camp.”

“An artifice! an artifice to blind you, my poor child!” cries Mountain. “He will be wounded and come back—you will see if he does not. I have proofs of what I say to you—proofs under his own hand—look here!”

And she took from her pocket a piece of paper in Mr. Washington’s well-known handwriting.

“How came you by this paper?” asked George, turning ghastly pale.

“I—I found it in the Major’s chamber!” says Mrs. Mountain, with a shamefaced look.

“You read the private letters of a guest staying in our house?” cried George. “For shame! I will not look at the paper!” And he flung it from him onto the fire before him.

“I could not help it, George; ’twas by chance, I give you my word, by the merest chance. You know Governor Dinwiddie is to have the Major’s room, and the state-room is got ready for Mr. Braddock, and we are expecting ever so much company, and I had to take the things which the Major leaves here—he treats the house just as if it was his own already—into his new room, and this half-sheet of paper fell out of his writing-book, and I just gave one look at it by the merest chance, and when I saw what it was it was my duty to read it.”

“Oh, you are a martyr to duty, Mountain!” George said grimly. “I dare say Mrs. Bluebeard thought it was her duty to look through the keyhole.”

“I never did lo

The day appointed for Madam Esmond’s entertainment to the General came in with a Virginia softness that seemed made to flatter hospitality, and to mock grief. Castlewood wore its best face. The broad house-front, with its covered gallery and white-pillared shade, stood as if newly washed by light; the windows were thrown wide; and from within there issued, not the thin perfume of idle finery, but the substantial incense of a great kitchen in full labour.

Madam Esmond, who commonly dressed with a reserved neatness, had this day armed herself in splendour; her silk made a faint, continual whisper as she moved, like dry leaves stirred in a still wood. If her heart shrank from the occasion, she would not have her guests guess it. To do honour to a man of war, she would have the house speak, in its own language, of loyalty and plenty. The sideboard shone; the glasses caught the sun; and past the parlour door, as she walked, she saw the domestic procession—negro servants, steady-footed and silent, bearing covered dishes, trenchers, jugs, and baskets. The very air was thick with culinary promises: the sharp sweetness of apple-toddy newly mixed in the great china bowl; the iron-and-fat fragrance that comes when meat has been turned and basted; the peppery breath of greens; a ghost of nutmeg from some custard or syllabub; and underneath all, the honest smoke of wood, the smell of bread-crust, and the clean wet scent of rinsed pewter.

The General’s new aide-de-camp was the first to arrive. He reined in at the steps; his servant took the bridle; another led the horses away to the well-known quarters. No young gentleman in the colony sat a saddle with more ease than Mr. Washington, nor carried his tall frame with more soldierly economy. Madam Esmond received him in the covered gallery itself, where the boards gave out a sober creak under their measured pacing, and where the soundscape of the estate—distant axe-strokes, a far-off call from the quarters, the soft fanning of pigeons in the eaves—made a kind of rural music that soothed, even while it reminded her of all that must soon be broken by drums and marching.

For a while, before the Major retired to rid himself of his riding-boots, he and his hostess walked there in talk. She had much to ask and much to say; she must hear, from his own mouth, confirmation of his appointment; and she must speak of her son’s approaching departure, though the words, for all their practised composure, tasted bitter as burnt sugar.

They descended the steps to the rough lawn and paced a little in the shade, where the leaves made that light, incessant rustle which country-bred people take for granted, until they are robbed of it; and Madam Esmond, who would have hated to live where wheels and hammers never ceased, listened almost greedily to every natural sound, as if laying up a store against the day when George and Harry should be hearing only orders, oaths, and the clank of arms.

Mr. Washington announced his Excellency’s speedy approach, and that Mr. Franklin of Pennsylvania was coming in the General’s coach.

“This Mr. Franklin,” Madam Esmond said, with a little tightening of her mouth, “was a common printer’s boy, I have heard. A pretty pass things are coming to, when such persons ride in the coach of the Commander-in-Chief.”

Mr. Washington, whose handsome gravity seldom altered, yet whose mind was liberal beyond his years, answered that a more shrewd and sensible gentleman never rode in coach nor walked on foot. A useful and meritorious man, he maintained; ingenious, too.

Madam Esmond thought him far too charitable to tradesmen; but the Major held his ground, and would not allow that worth must be measured by the cut of a coat or the ancestry of a name.

“I am glad, at least,” the widow said at last, drawing herself into her stateliest manner, as if the very stiffness of her back could keep the future at bay, “that, as my boy is going to make the campaign, he will not be with tradesmen, but with gentlemen—with gentlemen of honour and fashion.”

Mr. Washington had seen gentlemen of honour and fashion over their cups, and had observed, too, how the noise of their mirth—forced, loud, and idle—could sour a room more certainly than the smoke of bad tobacco. He wisely chose not to tell tales; and he only said that Harry and George, now they were coming into the world, must take their share of good and bad, and hear what both sorts had to say.

“To be with a veteran officer of the finest army in the world,” faltered Madam Esmond; “with gentlemen bred in the midst of the Court; with friends of his Royal Highness, the Duke—” She checked herself, as though names and titles were charms that might keep bullets off a son.

Her friend only inclined his head. He did not choose to let his countenance depart from its usual composure; yet a colour rose in him at her next words, and she, too, betrayed herself by a blush which, for all her breeding, would come.

“And with you, dear Colonel Washington, by whom my father always set such store,” she said. “You do not know how much he trusted in you. You will take care of my boy, sir, will you not? You are but five years older, yet I trust to you more than to his seniors. My father always told the children—I always bade them—to look up to Mr. Washington.”

“You know I would have done anything to win Colonel Esmond’s favour,” he replied; and then, in a tone that made the simple words carry a weight beyond their plainness, “Madam, how much would I not venture to merit his daughter’s?”

He bowed—not too ill—and she dropped one of the lowest curtsies in Virginia; her curtsey had long been esteemed unrivalled, and to see it now, with the colour in her cheek, was to be reminded how ceremony may serve as veil to feeling.

“Mr. Washington,” she said, “will always be sure of a mother’s affection, whilst he gives so much of his to her children.”

She gave him her hand, which he kissed with profound politeness; and leaning upon his arm, she re-entered the house. The parlour received them with its cool shade and its waiting plenty. On a side-table the apple-toddy stood, tawny and fragrant; the sliced fruit bobbed like golden boats; the spice rose warm and sweet; and the ladle clinked softly against china when a servant, rehearsing his duty, stirred it and withdrew again.

Here they were joined by George, who came to them accurately powdered and richly attired, saluting his parent and his friend alike with low respectful bows. His coat fitted to perfection; his ruffles were fine; his sword sat on him as if it had belonged there always; and the scent of his hair-powder mingled strangely with the kitchen odours—flour and roasting fat and peel—so that one might have thought him a confection dressed for war.

Yet, for all the politeness of his smile, he was by no means in good-humour with either of them. The lower part of his face performed civility; the upper part watched and burned. Madam Esmond continued to blush; Mr. Washington, as he shook George’s hand, looked somewhat red, and held his gravity with an effort. Nothing had been uttered that might not have been spoken before the most decent company; and yet the air was as if some sharp spice had been overscattered—pleasant in itself, but too much, too sudden, pricking the tongue.

The Colonel, to ease the moment, asked Mr. George if he had had good sport.

“No,” George answered curtly. “Have you?” And then, with a glance that was like the point of a knife, he looked at the picture of his father hanging in the parlour—Colonel Esmond, calm in paint, remote in death, and yet present enough to be appealed to.

Mr. Washington, not ordinarily a talkative man, straightway entered into a long description of the morning’s sport with the king’s officers: what woods they had ridden, how many birds they had shot, what game they had brought down. He described, too, Mr. Braddock’s heavy person and great boots as the General floundered through Virginian undergrowth; hunting, as they called it, with a pack of dogs gathered from various houses, with a pack of negroes barking as loud as the dogs, and actually shooting the deer when they came in sight. Mr. Washington gave it in sober mimicry—never insolent, never loud; but his very restraint made the scene comic.

“Great God, sir!” puffed Mr. Braddock in the story, “what would Sir Robert have said in Norfolk, to see a man hunting with a fowling-piece in his hand, and a pack of dogs actually laid on to a turkey!”

“Indeed, Colonel, you are vastly comical this afternoon!” cried Madam Esmond with a neat little laugh; but George listened, looking more glum than ever, as if each description of field-sport were an affront to his present humour.

“What Sir Robert is there at Norfolk?” she asked. “Is he one of the newly arrived army-gentlemen?”

“The General meant Norfolk at home, madam, not Norfolk in Virginia,” said Mr. Washington. “He had been speaking of Sir Robert Walpole, who lived in that county, and of the great hunts the old Minister kept there, and his palace and his pictures at Houghton.” And then, like a man who, however he strides forward, still hears the home-birds in his mind, he sighed: “I should like to see a good field and a good fox-chase at home better than any sight in the world.”

“Nevertheless, there is good sport here, as I was saying,” George put in, with a sneer.

“What sport?” asked Mr. Washington, looking at him.

“Why, sure you know, without looking at me so fiercely, and stamping your foot, as if you were going to charge me with the foils,” George rattled on. “Are you not the best sportsman of the country-side? Are there not all the fish of the field, and the beasts of the trees, and the fowls of the sea—no—the fish of the trees, and the beasts of the sea—and the—bah! You know what I mean. I mean shad, and salmon, and rock-fish, and roe-deer, and hogs, and buffaloes, and bisons, and elephants, for what I know. I’m no sportsman.”

“No, indeed,” said Mr. Washington, with a look of scarcely repressed scorn.

“Yes, I understand you,” George pursued, and now his voice took that thin sweetness which is sharper than bitterness. “I am a milksop. I have been bred at my mamma’s knee. Look at these pretty apron-strings, Colonel! Who would not like to be tied to them? See of what a charming colour they are! I remember when they were black—that was for my grandfather.”

“And who would not mourn for such a gentleman?” Mr. Washington said; and Madam Esmond, astonished, looked from one face to the other as if she had heard a dish crash in her pantry.

“And, indeed, I wish my grandfather were here,” George continued, “and would resurge, as he promises to do on his tombstone; and would bring my father, the Ensign, with him.”

At this moment Harry entered—freshly dressed in just such another suit as George wore: gold-corded frock, braided waistcoat, silver-hilted sword, and solitaire. The sight of him, so like and unlike his brother, was too much for their mother’s strained composure.

“Ah, Harry!” she cried, and burst into tears, and flew to her younger son.

“Oh, Harry, Harry!”

“What is it, mother?” Harry asked, taking her in his arms. “What is the matter, Colonel?”

“Upon my life, it would puzzle me to say,” answered Mr. Washington, biting his lip.

“A mere question, Hal, about pink ribbons,” George said airily, “which I think vastly becoming to our mother—as no doubt the Colonel does.”

“Sir, will you please to speak for yourself?” cried Mr. Washington, stepping forward with a suddenness, then sinking his voice again, as a man must in a lady’s room.

“He speaks too much for himself,” wept the widow.

“I protest I don’t any more know the source of these tears than the source of the Nile,” George said, with an insolence that wore a courtier’s mask. “And if the picture of my father were to begin to cry, I should almost as much wonder at the paternal tears. What have I uttered? An allusion to ribbons! Is there some poisoned pin in them, which has been struck into my mother’s heart by a guilty fiend of a London mantua-maker? I professed to wish to be led in these lovely reins all my life long,” and he turned a pirouette on his scarlet heels, his shoe-buckles flashing as they struck the floor.

“George Warrington! what devil’s dance are you dancing now?” Harry demanded. He loved his mother; he loved Mr. Washington; but, of all creatures, he loved and admired his brother George, and would have followed him into fire.

“My dear child, you do not understand dancing—you care not for the politer arts—you can get no more music out of a spinet than by pulling a dead hog by the ear,” George said. “By nature you were made for a man—a man of war. I do not mean a seventy-four, Colonel George, like that hulk which brought the hulking Mr. Braddock into our river. His Excellency, too, is a man of warlike turn, a follower of the sports of the field. I am a milksop, as I have had the honour to say.”

“You never showed it yet,” Harry broke out. “You beat that great Maryland man was twice your size.”

“Under compulsion, Harry. ’Tis tuptu, my lad, or else ’tis tuptomai, as thy breech well knew when we followed school,” George said, letting scraps of scholarship fall like coin. “But I am of a quiet turn, and would never lift my hand to pull a trigger—no, nor a nose, nor anything but a rose.”

As he spoke he took one of Madam Esmond’s bright pink apron ribbons between finger and thumb, and handled it with a teasing delicacy that made his mother wince as if he had touched a nerve.

“I hate sporting, which you and the Colonel love, and I want to shoot nothing alive—not a turkey, nor a titmouse, nor an ox, nor an ass, nor anything that has ears. Those curls of Mr. Washington’s are prettily powdered.”

Mr. Washington, offended by the first part and perplexed by the last, had taken a modest draught from the great china bowl of apple-toddy, as was the Virginian custom, the liquor smelling of orchard-cellars and autumn afternoons; and then, to cool himself without making a scene, he paced the balcony outside with a stiff propriety, listening, perhaps against his will, to the house’s noises—the clatter of a dish-lid, the far-off crackle of firewood, the steady hum of a place that kept its order through the hands of the enslaved.

Again almost reconciled with George by the mere need of holding the household together, Madam Esmond stood giving a hand to each of her sons. George, suddenly gentle in gesture if not in spirit, placed his disengaged hand upon Harry’s shoulder.

“I say one thing, George,” Harry began, flushing.

“Say twenty things, Don Enrico,” George returned, calling him by a name half-mocking, half-affectionate.

“If you are not fond of sporting and that,” Harry persisted, “and don’t care for killing game and hunting, being cleverer than me—why shouldst thou not stop at home and be quiet, and let me go out with Colonel George and Mr. Braddock? That’s what I say.”

Madam Esmond looked eagerly from the dark-haired to the fair-haired boy. She knew not from which she would rather part; and the fact that she must part from one of them at all made her heart feel like dough overworked—stretched, then torn.

“One of our family must go because honneur oblige,” George said, and his voice grew suddenly cold with a kind of fatalism dressed in wit. “And my name being number one, number one must go first.”

“Told you so,” said poor Harry, unable to hide his disappointment.

“One must stay,” George went on, “or who is to look after mother at home? We cannot afford to be both scalped by Indians, or fricasseed by French.”

“Fricasseed by French!” cried Harry, indignant and eager at once. “The best troops of the world! Englishmen! I should like to see them fricasseed by the French! What a mortal thrashing you will give them!” And he sighed to think he should not be present at the battue, thinking of war as boys think of it, with appetite and ignorance, as of a dish described rather than tasted.

George, as if to show how little he cared for such masculine talk, sat down to the harpsichord and began to play and sing, in a voice trained for drawing-rooms, “Malbrouk s’en va-t-en guerre, Mironton, mironton, mirontaine.” The tune, half nursery, half satire, went tinkling through the house like a spoon striking glass, and for a moment overlaid even the deeper kitchen-sounds. At the sound the gentleman from the balcony entered again.

“I am playing ‘God save the King,’ Colonel,” George said, looking over his shoulder, his fingers running in trills, “in compliment to the new expedition.”

“I never know whether thou art laughing or in earnest,” said Mr. Washington simply; “but surely methinks that is not the air.”

George crashed and fluttered among the keys with ever so many quavers; and the Colonel watched him, perhaps wondering that a gentleman of George’s condition could set himself so eagerly to an occupation which soldiers call effeminate, yet which in that house was part of gentility’s very grammar.

Then Mr. Washington took out his watch, saying his Excellency’s coach would be there almost immediately, and asking leave to retire to his apartment and put himself in fit condition to appear before her ladyship’s company.

“Colonel Washington knows the way to his room pretty well,” George called from the harpsichord, never offering to stir.

“Let me show the Colonel to his chamber!” cried Madam Esmond, in great wrath; and she sailed from the room, followed by the enraged and bewildered young officer. Her silk hissed; his spurs rang faintly; and the sound of their steps, retreating down the passage, seemed to beat time with George’s jangling music, as if the house itself were a drum.

Mr. Washington felt himself insulted—he could hardly say how. He was outraged and could not speak. His anger sat in him like something choking; and Harry, who could read the weather of a friend’s face, noticed his condition with alarm.

“For heaven’s sake, George, what does this all mean?” he asked when the two had gone. “Why shouldn’t he kiss her hand? I tell you it is nothing but common kindness.”

“Nothing but common kindness!” George shrieked out, and now the mask dropped, and jealousy showed its raw skin. “Look at that, Hal! Is that common kindness?”

He thrust into his brother’s hands a paper over which he had been brooding; only a fragment, yet plain enough. Harry read, his brows drawing together, as if the ink itself had a sting.

The paper began mid-thought: “… is older than myself, but I, again, am older than my years; and you know, dear brother, have ever been considered a sober person. All children are better for a father’s superintendence, and her two, I trust, will find in me a tender friend and guardian.”

“Friend and guardian! Curse him!” cried George, clenching his fists.
