Harry read on, the words falling like crumbs from a loaf one did not want to eat: “… The flattering offer which General Braddock hath made me, will, of course, oblige me to postpone this matter until after the campaign. When we have given the French a sufficient drubbing, I shall return to repose under my own vine and fig-tree.”

“He means Castlewood,” George burst out, shaking his fist toward the creepers sunning themselves upon the wall outside, as if the harmless leaves were accomplices. “These are his vines.”

Harry’s eyes went back to the fragment: “… Under my own vine and fig-tree; where I hope soon to present my dear brother to his new sister-in-law. She has a pretty Scripture name, which is…”—and there the document ended, the rest torn away like a word lost from a dying tongue, leaving only silence where certainty should have been.

“Which is Rachel,” George said bitterly, supplying what the broken paper implied. “Rachel is by no means weeping for her children, and has every desire to be comforted. Now, Harry! Let us upstairs at once, kneel down as becomes us, and say, ‘Dear papa, welcome to your house of Castlewood.’”

His Excellency the Commander-in-Chief set out to pay his visit to Madam Esmond with a bravery of show that became, as his attendants would have it, the foremost personage in all his Majesty’s colonies in North America. The dragoons clattered first—steel on leather, bits ringing, hooves drumming a hard measure that ran ahead of the coach like a proclamation. Williamsburg answered with its own noise: a loyal shouting that rose and fell in gusts, carried on the warm air, and in it the sharper cries of a chiefly negro crowd whose mirth and awe were both pressed into service for the day.

The General rode in his own heavy, emblazoned coach, which groaned as it took the rutted road, its springs complaining at every plunge. Captain Talmadge, Master of the Horse, kept at the door, and on horseback beside it, as though the vehicle itself were a great creature to be managed. In the front seat sat Major Danvers, and with him the little postmaster from Philadelphia, Mr. Franklin; a man who, though he had begun as a printer’s boy, had a bright, gathering mind, and a store of odd, useful knowledge that made even great gentlemen tolerate being taught.

“’Tis extraordinary,” the Commander-in-Chief observed, touching his hat with a grandeur that cost him nothing, “how a person of such humble origin should have got such a variety of learning, and such politeness of breeding too, Mr. Franklin!”

Mr. Franklin bowed as if he had been bred to bow before he could walk. He said it had been his occasional good fortune to fall among gentlemen like his Excellency, and he had taken advantage to study their honours’ manners and to fit himself, as far as a man might, to the company where Providence placed him. As for education, he could not boast it: his father had been in straitened circumstances, and in New England the advantages were small; yet he had gathered what he could, though it was nothing like what they had in England.

Mr. Braddock burst into laughter, the sound of it filling the coach more completely than his scarlet bulk did. “Education! There are gentlemen in the army, by George, who don’t know whether to spell bull with one b or two. I’ve heard the Duke of Marlborough was no penman. I didn’t serve under him—his Grace was before my time—but he thrashed the French soundly, scholar or no scholar.”

Mr. Franklin said mildly that he was aware of both those facts.

“Nor is my Duke a scholar,” Braddock went on, with that blunt affection for his own opinions which made them feel like blows; “aha, Mr. Postmaster, you have heard that too—I see by the wink in your eye!”

Mr. Franklin withdrew the offending wink with such speed that his face became instantly infant-innocent, his eyes wide and clear upon the General’s jolly, swearing countenance. “He is no scholar, sir,” he said, “but he is a match for any French general that ever swallowed the English for fricassee de crapaud. He saved the crown for the best of kings, the royal father of his Royal Highness—his Most Gracious Majesty King George.”

Off flew Mr. Franklin’s hat, and from the great buckled wig rose a halo of powder, white as flour sifted fine. He spoke of the Duke as the soldier’s best friend, the enemy of beggarly Scotch rebels and Romish Jesuits; and Braddock drank the praise as readily as he drank anything poured, his patriotism as hot as his oaths.

“You shall drink his health to-day, Postmaster,” said the General. “He is the best of masters, the best of friends, the best of sons to his royal old father—the best of gentlemen that ever wore an epaulet.”

“Epaulets are quite out of my way, sir,” Franklin said, laughing; “you know I live in a Quaker city.”

“Of course they are out of your way,” Braddock answered, satisfied to have every man filed into his place like a regiment on parade. “Every man to his business. You, and gentlemen of your class, to your books—welcome. We encourage you. We—to fight the enemy and govern the country. Hey, gentlemen? Lord! what roads you have in this colony, and how this confounded coach plunges! Who have we here, with the two negro boys in livery? He rides a good gelding.”

“It is Mr. Washington,” said the aide-de-camp.

“I would like him for a corporal of the Horse Grenadiers,” the General said, peering. “He has a good figure on a horse. He knows the country too, Mr. Franklin.”

“Yes, indeed.”

“And he is a monstrous genteel young man, considering the opportunities he has had. I should have thought he had the polish of Europe, by George I should.”

“He does his best,” Mr. Franklin said, looking up with that same mildness which, if it mocked, mocked without heat. Outside, the tall Virginian rode up, grave as a church door, followed by two neat negro grooms in smart livery-coats and velvet hunting-caps. The very sound of their horses—light, measured, well-shod—seemed cleaner than the coach’s struggling clank.

“Good day, Mr. Washington,” Braddock called out. “A pretty nag, sir. That was your first affair, last year?”

“That at Fort Necessity? Yes, sir,” Mr. Washington answered, saluting with composed exactness. “I began ill, sir, never having been in action until that unlucky day.”

“You were all raw levies, my good fellow. You should have seen our militia run from the Scotch and be cursed to them. You should have had some troops with you.”

“Your Excellency knows ’tis my passionate desire to see and serve with them,” said Mr. Washington; and though his voice stayed even, there was in it the hunger of a young man who had measured himself against misfortune and wished to be tried again by something better than chance.

“By George, we shall try and gratify you, sir,” Braddock swore, and the coach rolled on toward Castlewood, the dragoons’ hooves and the coach-wheels making a rough music over the country’s bones.

The progress of so great a personage could not be swift; and the road, like a stream gathering tributaries, drew in lesser guests bound for Madam Esmond’s table. None dared pass the General’s carriage; so behind it formed a procession—comical and dutiful in equal parts—raising a single long dust-cloud that hung in the warm air and muffled the sounds of the countryside.

First came Mr. Dinwiddie, the Lieutenant-Governor, with negro servants riding and running near; and with him Parson Broadbent, the jolly Williamsburg chaplain. After them, little Mr. Dempster, the young gentlemen’s schoolmaster, in a great Ramillies wig that made him look like a man dressed for a ceremony rather than a ride. Then Mr. Laws, the judge of the court, with Madam Laws perched behind him on a pillion, and their negro man riding a mule and carrying a box that held her ladyship’s cap, as carefully as if it were a crown.

Major Danvers and Mr. Franklin, spying this tail of dignities, laughed outright—though not so loud as to wake his Excellency, who, rocked by the coach’s violent lurching, had dropped asleep with the easy confidence of a man accustomed to be obeyed. Danvers bade the whole queer rearguard move on and leave the Commander-in-Chief and his dragoons to follow at their leisure.

At Castlewood there was room for all. There was meat and drink and the best tobacco for his Majesty’s soldiers; there was laughing for the negroes; and for their masters a welcome so full that it seemed to stand in the doorway before them, like a lit hearth in winter.

The house itself—broad-porched, familiar to the Virginia sun—did not glitter with any courtly magnificence; yet it had that older splendour which comes of plenty honestly ordered. From the kitchens drifted the steady breathing of labour: the low thump of a cleaver on a block; the hiss where fat met iron; the murmuring stir of spoons against pot-sides; the occasional sharp call in the negro women’s own speech, a cadence different from the English above-stairs, bearing meanings that did not all translate cleanly but that carried the work forward as surely as hands did. Outside, insects played their small incessant instruments in the dusk; within, the clink of glasses and the scrape of chairs began to gather like a second chorus. In such a place, sound itself made a kind of comfort—so long as it was living sound, and not the harsh, inhuman racket of some future world of wheels and engines that no one here could imagine yet.

The honest General required to be helped to most dishes at table, and more than once. He was forever holding out his glass for drink as if it were a duty for others to keep it from emptiness. Nathan’s sangaree he pronounced excellent, and had drunk largely of it before dinner. There was cider and ale, brandy, and plenty of good Bordeaux—some which Colonel Esmond himself had brought home to the colony, and which little Mr. Dempster declared, with learned satisfaction, was fit for pontifices’ feasts. He winked at Mr. Broadbent, and Broadbent returned the wink and nodded, drinking the wine without troubling himself over the Latin. Why should he? He had never made much of scholarship, but he could make a great deal of sport.

Parson Broadbent had the air of a man transplanted by accident into religion from some livelier soil: a guzzling, cock-fighting divine, with a history in the Fleet Prison and at Newmarket and Hockley-in-the-Hole, and sent at last to a Virginia living. He and young George had fought cocks together, taken roe, hauled in shad and salmon, slain wild geese and swans, pigeons and plovers, and destroyed myriads of canvas-backed ducks. Envious tongues said Broadbent was the midnight poacher on whom Mr. Washington once set his dogs, and whom he caned by the river-side at Mount Vernon; that the fellow escaped into a boat in the dark, but went about two Sundays after with the remains of a black eye and a new collar to his coat. Between Broadbent, the schoolmaster, and the wild abundance of Virginia, the Castlewood boys had professors enough. When they rode to get their reading with Mr. Dempster, it was easy to suspect that Harry sometimes stayed behind to take his European “accomplishments” from the other tutor—George going his own way, reading his own books, and telling no tales.

All the birds of the Virginia air and all the fish of the sea in season seemed gathered upon Madam Esmond’s board, and the ordering of it was no mere brute show of wealth. The gumbo was declared perfection—thickened and dark with patient simmering, the okra’s subtle silk binding the broth, the spices blooming in heat until they rose in steam that struck the nose first sweet, then sharp, then deep. Young Mr. George’s black servant had been found once behind a door with his head in a bowl of this delicious hotch-potch, and the late Colonel, grimly amused, christened the boy “Gumbo” on the spot; and thus a dish had become a name, and a name a yoke, in the careless custom of power. The shad were rich and fresh, laid in a dish with their fat shining and their smell of river and salt still living in them. The terrapins came stewed in a grave, savoury liquor, their flesh tender from slow coaxing rather than violence, worthy, as more than one swore, of London aldermen—worthy even, his Excellency deigned to say, of a Duke.

The negro-women had a genius for cookery, and in Castlewood kitchens there were adepts brought up under the keen eye of the late and present Madam Esmond. Certain dishes—especially the sweets and a flan—Madam Esmond prepared herself with neatness and dexterity. She carved several principal pieces too, the kindly cumbrous fashion of the day requiring the mistress to labour for her guests: pressing them with decent eagerness, watching who might be tempted to further enjoyment, knowing the hidden joints and yielding places of fowl and fish as if she had studied anatomy for charity. When she pushed up the laced lappets of her sleeves, she showed the prettiest round arms, small hands and wrists, as she wielded the knife with a practised confidence.

“I have kept for your Excellency the jowl of this salmon,” she whispered to Mr. Braddock. “I will take no denial. Mr. Franklin, you drink only water, sir, though our cellar has wholesome wine which gives no headaches. Mr. Justice, you love woodcock pie?”

“Because I know who makes the pastry,” said Mr. Laws, with a bow so low it might have swept crumbs from the table. “I often say to my wife, ‘My dear, I wish you had Madam Esmond’s hand.’”

“It is a very pretty hand; I am sure others would like it too,” said Mr. Franklin, and Mr. Esmond looked but half-pleased at the little gentleman.

“Such a hand for a light pie-crust,” the Judge continued, hastening back into safer admiration, “and my service to you, madam.”

She answered simply that she had lessons at home in England for her education, and certain dishes her mother had taught her to make, which her father and sons both liked. She was glad if they pleased her company. Then came more dishes, more urging, ten times more meat than the company could need, the old law of hospitality insisting on excess as a proof of heart.

Mr. Washington did not embark much in the general conversation. He sat with Mr. Talmadge and Major Danvers and the Postmaster, deep in talk of roads, rivers, conveyances, sumpter-horses, and an artillery train. On the table before him, bits of bread were laid at intervals—stations and distances—where he set his finger and spoke low and steady, while the others bent in. Yet even this small mapping had its fragility: a negro servant, changing the courses, brushed off the Potomac with a napkin and swept up the Ohio in a spoon, and the whole little campaign vanished as easily as crumbs.

At the end of dinner Parson Broadbent left his seat, went behind the Lieutenant-Governor’s chair, and said grace; then returned and resumed his knife and fork as if devotion were only another course. The sweets and puddings came—Madam Esmond’s careful triumphs—set out with such order and generosity that the eye could taste before the mouth. And then the table being cleared, Nathan, chief manager, laid a glass to every person and filled his mistress’s. Bowing, she said she drank but one toast, but knew how heartily all present would join her.

“His Majesty,” she called, bowing toward Mr. Braddock. The name was echoed loyally by aides-de-camp and colonial gentlemen alike. She drank, saluted them all with a composure that had cost her dear, and then withdrew, between a row of negro servants, making one of her handsomest curtsies at the door.

She had borne her part with admirable spirit, so gay and handsome, speaking with such cheerfulness and courage, that the few ladies present could not but congratulate her upon the elegance of the feast and her manner of presiding. But scarcely were they in the drawing-room when her artificial courage failed. She sank upon the sofa by Mrs. Laws’ side and burst into tears in the midst of a compliment.

“Ah, madam,” she said, “it may be an honour, as you say, to have the King’s representative in my house; and our family has received greater personages than Mr. Braddock. But he comes to take one of my sons away from me. Who knows whether my boy will return, or how? I dreamed of him last night—as wounded, and quite white, with blood streaming from his side. I would not be so ill-mannered as to let my grief be visible before the gentlemen; but you, my good Mrs. Justice—who has parted with children, and has a mother’s heart—would like me none the better if mine were very easy this evening.”

The ladies administered such consolations as seemed proper. Madam Esmond tried not to give way further, remembering she had still duties to perform before sinking into her own sadness.

“It will be time enough,” she said, wiping her eyes and forcing her voice back into steadiness, “to be sorry when they are gone. My boy must not see me following him with a wistful face, and have our parting made more dismal by my weakness. It is good that gentlemen of his rank and station should show themselves where their country calls them. That has always been the way of the Esmonds; and the same Power which graciously preserved my dear father through twenty great battles in the Queen’s time, I trust and pray, will watch over my son now his turn is come to do his duty.”

And now, instead of lamenting, she sat down with her female friends to a pool of cards and a dish of coffee—coffee dark and fragrant, its bitterness softened with sugar, the steam rising in little ghosts that carried comfort to the nose before it reached the tongue. In the neighbouring parlour the gentlemen still called their toasts and drank their wine, the laughter and loud talk swelling and sinking like surf against the walls. When one lady objected they had sat rather long, Madam Esmond answered that it would improve and amuse the boys to be with English gentlemen; such society was rare in a distant province; and though their conversation sometimes was free, she was sure men of fashion would have regard to youth and say nothing before her sons which young people should not hear.

It was evident the English gentlemen relished the good cheer. Whilst the ladies were yet at their cards, Nathan came in and whispered Mrs. Mountain. Mrs. Mountain at first cried out that she would give no more—the common Bordeaux they might have, and welcome, if they still wanted more—but she would not give any more of the Colonel’s.

It appeared the dozen bottles of particular claret had already been drunk up by the gentlemen, “besides ale, cider, Burgundy, Lisbon, and Madeira,” Mrs. Mountain said, counting the depleted riches with the dismay of a housekeeper who hears the pantry emptying itself.

But Madam Esmond would have no stint in the hospitality of the night. Mrs. Mountain was forced to bustle away with her keys to the sacred vault where the Colonel’s particular Bordeaux lay—surviving its master, who had long since gone underground. As they went, she asked whether any of the gentlemen had had too much. Nathan thought Mister Broadbent was tipsy—he always tipsy. Then he thought the General gentleman was tipsy. And he thought Master George was a lilly drunk.

“Master George!” cried Mrs. Mountain. “Why, he will sit for days without touching a drop.”

Nevertheless Nathan persisted: Master George was a lilly drunk. He was always filling his glass; he had talked; he had sung; he had cut jokes—especially against Mr. Washington—which made Mr. Washington quite red and angry, Nathan said.

“Well, well!” Mrs. Mountain cried, eagerness overcoming prudence. “It is right a gentleman should make himself merry in good company, and pass the bottle along with his friends.” And she trotted all the faster to the particular Bordeaux.

The tone of freedom—of something almost like impertinence—which young George Esmond had of late adopted toward Mr. Washington had deeply vexed and annoyed that gentleman. There was scarcely half a dozen years’ difference between him and the Castlewood twins; yet Washington had always been remarked for discretion and sobriety beyond his time, while the boys, long under their mother’s anxious tutelage, still carried about them the heedlessness of sheltered youth. They had looked up to their neighbour of Mount Vernon as guide, director, friend; indeed almost everyone did who came in contact with the simple, upright young man. Scrupulously grave and well-bred, he seemed in speaking with other folks to exact—if not by design, then by the mere weight of his nature—the same behaviour. Levity and jokes fell dead in his presence, as if embarrassed. He was slow to comprehend them; and when they did reach him, they had no place to rest.

Years afterward, Harry Warrington would write of him with a kind of awe: how Washington seemed always great; how to see him ride to hounds was like watching him charge an army; how if he fired a shot the bird must fall, and if he flung a net the largest fish must be in it; how his words were few but wise, grave, sober, strong, never idly spilled. Even George, for all his antipathy, respected and admired the man more than any other mortal.

Mr. Washington was the first to leave the jovial party doing so much honour to Castlewood’s wine. Young George, taking his mother’s place when she rose, had been free with glass and tongue. A score of little sayings—sharp-edged, half-laughing, half-stinging—had been aimed at their guest, and each one, because it came without cause, left Washington without reply. At length, angry beyond endurance, he rose and walked away through the open windows into the broad verandah that belonged to Castlewood as to all Virginian houses.

There the air met him—warm, smelling of crushed grass and distant river, and underneath it the kitchen’s faint savour of spice and smoke. Crickets kept their insistent tiny fiddling. The gentlemen’s laughter behind him was louder, coarser, threaded with the clink of glasses and the scrape of chairs. It was not merely loud; it was the wrong kind of loud—sound that trampled rather than accompanied. Washington strode up and down before the windows, as if his long body might walk off the heat in his blood.

Madam Esmond caught sight of him. The evening was warm, and perhaps her game was over; at any rate she gave up her cards to another lady and went out to her neighbour. He tried to compose his countenance; it was impossible he should explain to his hostess why and with whom he was angry.

“The gentlemen are long over their wine,” she said. “Gentlemen of the army are always fond of it.”

“If drinking makes good soldiers,” Mr. Washington answered, “some yonder are distinguishing themselves greatly, madam.”

“And I dare say the General is at the head of his troops?”

“No doubt, no doubt.” He received her remarks—playful or serious—with a peculiar softness and kindness that belonged to him with women, and with this woman in particular. “But the General is the General, and it is not for me to make remarks on his Excellency’s doings at table or elsewhere. I think very likely military gentlemen born and bred at home are different from us of the colonies. We have such a hot sun, that we need not wine to fire our blood as they do. And drinking toasts seems a point of honour with them. Talmadge—hiccupped to me—I should say, whispered to me just now, that an officer could no more refuse a toast than a challenge. He said it was after the greatest difficulty and dislike at first that he learned to drink. He has certainly overcome his difficulty with uncommon resolution.”

“What, I wonder, can you talk of for so many hours?” asked the lady.

“I don’t think I can tell you all we talk of, madam; I must not tell tales out of school. We talked of the war—of the force Mr. Contrecoeur has, and how we are to get at him. The General is for making the campaign in his coach, and makes light of it and the enemy. That we shall beat them, if we meet them, I trust there is no doubt.”

“How can there be?” she said, her father’s old Marlborough blood speaking through her confidence.

“Mr. Franklin—though he is only from New England—spoke great good sense, and would have spoken more if the English gentlemen would let him. But they reply invariably that we are only raw provincials, and don’t know what disciplined British troops can do. Had they not best hasten forward and make turnpike roads and have comfortable inns ready for his Excellency at the end of the day’s march? ‘There’s some sort of inns, I suppose,’ says Mr. Danvers, ‘not so comfortable as we have in England: we can’t expect that.’ ‘No, you can’t expect that,’ says Mr. Franklin, who seems a very shrewd and facetious person. He drinks his water, and seems to laugh at the Englishmen; though I doubt whether it is fair for a water-drinker to sit by and spy out the weaknesses of gentlemen over their wine.”

“And my boys? I hope they are prudent?” Madam Esmond asked, laying her hand on his arm. “Harry promised me; and when he gives his word, I can trust him for anything. George is always moderate. Why do you look so grave?”

General Braddock and the other gentlemen of consequence, being at last bestowed in the several chambers of Castlewood, the house settled into that post-feast hush when the very boards seem to sweat with heat and wine. In the boys’ room, however, the air was quick with indignation. Through the open casement came the night’s small rural choir—tree-frogs keeping time in the wet grass, a far whippoorwill calling as if it owned the dark, and, nearer, the steady breathing of the plantation: a cart-wheel creak, a bucket on a well-chain, the soft pad of bare feet where the servants moved like shadows. All those honest sounds—soothing in ordinary seasons—only sharpened the brothers’ sense that something monstrous had been spoken at their own table.

They would not bear such a marriage—no. Was the representative of the Marquises of Esmond to marry the younger son of a colonial family, a man bred to measuring acres like so much cloth upon a counter? Castlewood itself—Castlewood, and they at nineteen—handed over to the tender mercies of a stepfather of three-and-twenty! Harry, whose whole nature ran to ardour, was for bursting straight into his mother’s chamber that instant, where her black maids were even now taking from her throat and wrists the simple jewels she had worn in compliment to the feast, and protesting the match in language that would scorch. He would tell her they would ride home, live upon their little property there, and leave her forever, if this unnatural union came to pass.

George, pale by habit and proud by constitution, advocated another method; and as he unfolded it, his voice had that cold precision with which he would later recite Latin or a grievance.

“Our mother,” he said, “can’t marry a man with whom one or both of us has been out on the field—who has wounded us or killed us, or whom we have wounded or killed. We must have him out, Harry.”

Harry caught at the proposition as a starving man catches at bread. The logic—dark, childish, yet in their code unanswerable—seemed to him the very perfection of sagacity.

“No, George,” he breathed. “You are right. Mother can’t marry our murderer; she won’t be as bad as that. And if we pink him, he is done for. Cadit quaestio, as Mr. Dempster used to say. Shall I send my boy with a challenge to Colonel George now?”

“My dear Harry,” George returned, with a complacent recollection of Quebec and what he had there called an affair of honour, “you are not accustomed to affairs of this sort.”

“No,” Harry owned, with a sigh that was half envy, half worship.

“We can’t insult a gentleman in our own house,” George continued, with the majesty of one laying down law. “The laws of honour forbid such inhospitable treatment. But, sir, we can ride out with him—and as soon as the park gates are closed, we can tell him our mind.”

“That we can, by George!” cried Harry, grasping his brother’s hand. “And that we will, too. I say, Georgy—” Here his face reddened to the roots of his hair, and George, with a lift of his brow, required him to proceed.

“This is my turn, brother,” Harry pleaded. “If you go the campaign, I ought to have the other affair. Indeed, indeed, I ought.” It was promotion he begged—this chance to stand first, even for a moment, in the family’s quarrel.

“Again the head of the house must take the lead, my dear,” George said superbly. “If I fall, my Harry will avenge me. But I must fight George Washington, Hal; and ’tis best I should—for indeed I hate him the worst. Was it not he who counselled my mother to order that wretch, Ward, to lay hands on me?”

“Ah, George,” the more peaceable brother ventured, “you ought to forget and forgive.”

“Forgive? Never, sir, as long as I remember. You can’t order remembrance out of a man’s mind; and a wrong that was a wrong yesterday must be a wrong to-morrow. I never, of my knowledge, did one to any man, and I never will suffer one, if I can help it.” The old Bordeaux of their grandsire had set a flush in George’s ordinarily pale cheeks; and his words came fast, like a knife drawn and used without pause. “I think very ill of Mr. Ward, but I don’t think so badly of him as to suppose he will ever forgive thee that blow with the ruler. Colonel Washington is our enemy—mine especially. He has advised one wrong against me, and he meditates a greater. I tell you, brother, we must punish him.”

Harry, docile as ever before his elder, admired the rapid declamation and the high carriage, and prepared himself to follow where George led. Yet even in that hot room, with the night sounds ticking steadily outside like a clock of crickets, George found breath to issue injunctions: Harry must be civil to all guests while they remained under their mother’s roof on the morrow. The courtesy was to be a sheath for the blade.

Good manners and an aversion to carrying tales beyond the threshold forbid the naming of the first of Madam Esmond’s guests to sink beneath the weight of her hospitality; it is enough to say that in that century gentlemen took drunkenness as lightly as they took snuff. Let one imagine the descendants of Messrs. Talmadge and Danvers—then young aides-de-camp—reeling to their beds, supported by sympathetic negroes, and their vinous General, too stout a toper to be conquered by a half-dozen bottles of Bordeaux, conducted to his chamber by the young gentlemen of the house and soon sleeping the sleep Bacchus grants. The mistress of Castlewood watched all this without surprise or horror; and was up early to provide what the weather and the previous night required—cooling drinks for hot palates, carried by servants to the chambers where men moaned softly like sick children.

At breakfast, one English officer rallied Mr. Franklin, who took no wine and refused the morning’s cool draught of toddy. The young fellow said the disease was pleasant and the remedy delicious, and laughingly proposed to continue repeating them both. Colonel Washington—General Braddock’s new American aide—sat quite sober, serene, and watchful, as if the very clink of glasses were a kind of enemy. The British vowed they must take him in hand and teach him the ways of the English army; but the Virginian answered gravely that he did not care to learn that portion of the military education.

Madam Esmond, occupied with the great dinner and the great breakfast after it, had little leisure to watch her sons; but she saw at least that George was scrupulously polite to her favourite, Colonel Washington, as to all the others under her roof. The politeness was the thinner for being exact.

Before Mr. Braddock took leave, he asked a private audience of the lady of the house, and formally offered to take her son into his family. Arrangements were settled for George’s departure; and Madam Esmond—who had seen bottles do as much damage as bullets in her long life—showed no squeamish terrors about the bottle, though she had witnessed it as among the most certain dangers George would meet.

“Mr. Braddock is a perfect fine gentleman in the morning,” she said stoutly to her aide-de-camp, Mrs. Mountain; “and though my papa did not drink, ’tis certain that many of the best company in England do.”

The jolly General shook hands with George, bade him welcome, and ordered him to be in attendance at Frederick three days hence; shortly after which the expedition would set forth.

Then the great coach was called again; the General’s escort pranced round it; other guests and their servants went to horse. Madam Esmond attended his Excellency to the steps of the verandah; her sons followed and stood on each side the coach-door. The guard trumpeter blew a shrill blast that split the heavy air; the negroes shouted, “Huzzay, and God sabe de King,” as Mr. Braddock took leave and rolled away toward headquarters, the wheels grinding the gravel with that cheerful brutality of vehicles carrying men to war.

As the boys turned back up the steps, there stood the Colonel once more taking leave of their mother. No doubt she had recommended George to his namesake’s care; for Washington said, “With my life. You may depend on me,” as the lads returned to the porch. He was booted and ready to depart.

“Farewell, my dear Harry,” he said. “With you, George, ’tis no adieu. We shall meet in three days at the camp.”

Both young men were going toward danger, perhaps death; and the widow’s face, which could command a dining-room as if it were a battalion, softened and trembled now. Colonel Washington’s own expression was grave with those unspoken things which, in any language, refuse translation into common words—attachment, gratitude, regret.

George Warrington watched his mother’s emotion and interpreted it with a pang of malignant scorn. “Stay yet a moment, and console our mamma,” he said steadily, “only the time to get ourselves booted, and my brother and I will ride with you a little way, George.”

He had already ordered horses. The three young men were soon under way, negro grooms behind them. Mrs. Mountain, who knew she had made mischief between them and trembled for the issue, felt a vast relief that Mr. Washington was gone without open quarrel and, at least, without an open declaration of love to their mother.

No man could be more courteous than George Warrington upon the road. His neighbour and namesake, pleased and surprised at this altered behaviour, yielded to the softening influence of long friendship with the Esmond family, to the necessity of future fellowship, and to the tender adieux just exchanged at Castlewood. He was more than usually friendly. George, for his part, seemed gay and easy, his words falling smoothly as a knife falls smoothly into a ripe peach.

It was Harry who was melancholy now. He rode silent and wistful by his brother, keeping away from Colonel Washington, to whose side he had always pressed eagerly before. If the honest Colonel marked the change, he likely attributed it to Harry’s affection for George and his anxiety on the eve of their parting.

They spoke of the war, and of how the campaign must surely end. None of the three doubted success. Two thousand veteran British troops with their commander must overcome whatever force the French could bring, if only they moved in decent time. The ardent young Virginian soldier held an immense respect for the valour and tactics of regular troops. King George II had no more loyal subject than Mr. Braddock’s new aide-de-camp.

So they rode amicably until they reached a rude log-house called Benson’s, where, according to the custom of the country, the proprietor did not disdain to accept money for the hospitalities provided. A recruiting station was here; some officers and men of Halkett’s regiment assembled; and Colonel Washington supposed the lads would take leave of him at this point.

Their horses being baited, they entered the public room and found a rough meal laid out for such as were disposed to partake. Heat lay upon the place like a blanket. The room smelt of sun-baked pine, sweat-damp leather, horse, and spirits—molasses sweetness from the rum, sharp bite of raw whiskey, and the green bruised scent of mint where some hand had tried to make the drink seem civilized. A great bowl of toddy sat like a small brown pond in the centre, its surface pricked with bits of citrus peel, the sugar not wholly melted, the liquor breathing up a warm, heady steam. If there was any music, it was the clink of metal against wood, boots on planks, a fly’s persistent drone, and outside, the ceaseless rasp of summer insects—the acoustic country’s steady sermon against human quarrels.

George Warrington entered with a particularly lively air; poor Harry’s face was white and woebegone.

“One would think, Squire Harry, ’twas you who was going to leave home and fight the French and Indians, and not Mr. George,” said Benson, leaning in the doorway.

“I may be alarmed about danger to my brother,” Harry answered, forcing steadiness, “though I might bear my own share pretty well. ’Tis not my fault that I stay at home.”

“No, indeed, brother,” cried George, too quickly.

“Harry Warrington’s courage does not need any proof!” said Mr. Washington.

“You do the family honour by speaking so well of us, Colonel,” George returned, with a low bow. “I dare say we can hold our own, if need be.”

While he vaunted, Harry looked—truth to tell—by no means courageous. As his eyes met his brother’s, he read there an announcement that chilled him.

“You are not going to do it now?” he whispered.

“Yes, now,” George replied, very steadily.

“For God’s sake, let me have the turn. You are going on the campaign; you ought not to have everything—and there may be an explanation, George. We may be all wrong.”

“Psha—how can we? It must be done now. Don’t be alarmed. No names shall be mentioned—I shall easily find a subject.”

Under the porch sat two of Halkett’s officers, whom the Warringtons knew, with the Virginian toddy-bowl before them.

“What are you conspiring, gentlemen?” cried one. “Is it a drink?”

By the thickened cheer of their voices and the flushed skin at their temples, it was plain they had already been engaged in drinking that morning.

“The very thing, sir,” George said gaily. “Fresh glasses, Mr. Benson! What, no glasses? Then we must have at the bowl.”

“Many a good man has drunk from it,” said Benson; and the lads, one after another, bowing first to their military acquaintance, touched their lips to the rim. The liquor did not seem much diminished for their drinking, though George especially assumed a toper’s airs and declared it delicious after the ride. He called out to Colonel Washington, who was at the porch, to join his friends and drink.

The lad’s tone had an edge: it resembled the manner lately adopted by him which had so chafed Mr. Washington. The Colonel bowed and said he was not thirsty.

“Nay, the liquor is paid for,” George insisted; “never fear, Colonel.”

“I said I was not thirsty. I did not say the liquor was not paid for,” the Colonel answered, drumming with his foot.

“When the King’s health is proposed, an officer can hardly say no,” cried George. “I drink the health of his Majesty, gentlemen. Colonel Washington can drink it or leave it. The King!”

This was a point of military honour. Captain Grace and Mr. Waring, both of Halkett’s, drank “The King.” Harry Warrington drank “The King.” Colonel Washington, with eyes that seemed to harden and brighten at once, swallowed a slight draught from the bowl.

Then Captain Grace proposed “The Duke and the Army,” which toast likewise had no gainsaying. Colonel Washington had to swallow “The Duke and the Army.”

“You don’t seem to stomach the toast, Colonel,” George said.

“I tell you again, I don’t want to drink,” the Colonel replied. “It seems to me the Duke and the Army would be served all the better if their healths were not drunk so often.”

“You are not up to the ways of regular troops as yet,” Captain Grace said, thickly.

“May be not, sir.”

“A British officer,” continued Captain Grace, with great energy and doubtful articulation, “never neglects a toast of that sort, nor any other duty. A man who refuses to drink the health of the Duke—hang me, such a man should be tried by a court-martial!”

“What means this language to me? You are drunk, sir!” roared Colonel Washington, starting up and striking the table with his fist so that the bowl’s surface quivered and the scent of spirits rose in a fresh, aggressive wave.

“A cursed provincial officer say I’m drunk!” shrieked Grace. “Waring, do you hear that?”

“I heard it, sir!” George Warrington said promptly. “We all heard it. He entered at my invitation—the liquor called for was mine; the table was mine—and I am shocked to hear such monstrous language used at it as Colonel Washington has just employed towards my esteemed guest, Captain Waring.”

“Confound your impudence, you infernal young jackanapes!” bellowed Colonel Washington. “You dare insult me before British officers, and find fault with my language? For months past I have borne with such impudence from you, that if I had not loved your mother—yes, sir, and your good grandfather and your brother—I would—I would—”

His words failed him. He stood for a moment quivering, purple with wrath, speechless before his young enemy, while the tavern’s summer noises went on outside with cruel indifference—cicadas sawing, a horse stamping, a distant axe-blow in some clearing like the tick of fate.

“You would what, sir?” George asked very quietly. “If you did not love my grandfather, and my brother, and my mother. You are making her petticoat a plea for some conduct of yours—you would do what, sir, may I ask again?”

“I would put you across my knee and whip you, you snarling little puppy, that’s what I would do!” cried the Colonel, breath found again for fury.

“Because you have known us all our lives, and made our house your own, that is no reason you should insult either of us!” Harry burst out, starting up. “What you have said, George Washington, is an insult to me and my brother alike. You will ask pardon, sir!”

“Pardon?”

“Or give us the reparation that is due to gentlemen,” Harry insisted, his voice quivering as his hand clenched.

The stout Colonel’s heart smote him. To be at mortal quarrel with lads he had loved—boys whose voices he had heard break, whose heads he had patted, whose mother’s table had been his refuge—was misery. As Harry stood with fair hair and flushing cheeks, an immense tenderness filled Washington.

“I—I am bewildered,” he said. “My words, perhaps, were very hasty. What has been the meaning of George’s behaviour to me for months back? Only tell me, and perhaps—”

But the evil spirit was awake and victorious in young George Warrington. His black eyes shot scorn and hatred at the simple, guileless gentleman before him.

“You are shirking from the question, sir, as you did from the toast just now,” he said. “I am not a boy to suffer under your arrogance. You have publicly insulted me in a public place, and I demand a reparation.”

“In Heaven’s name—be it!” said Mr. Washington, and the grief in his face made the words heavy as iron.

“And you have insulted me,” Captain Grace began, reeling forward. “What was it he said? Confound the militia captain—colonel, what is he? You’ve insulted me! Oh, Waring! to think I should be insulted by a captain of militia!” Tears actually ran upon the noble Captain’s cheek at this harrowing thought.

“I insult you, you hog!” the Colonel yelled—humour being little in him, and rage making him blind to the ridiculousness of his adversary.

At that instant a fourth voice came in, brisk and affronted.

“Great powers, sir!” said Captain Waring. “Are three affairs not enough for you, and must I come into the quarrel too? You have a quarrel with these two young gentlemen.”

“Hasty words, sir!” poor Harry tried again.

“Hasty words, sir!” Waring echoed, indignant. “A gentleman tells another gentleman he will put him across his knees and whip him, and you call those hasty words? Let me tell you if any man were to say to me, ‘Charles Waring,’ or ‘Captain Waring, I’ll put you across my knees and whip you,’ I’d say, ‘I’ll drive my cheese-toaster through his body,’ if he were as big as Goliath I would. That’s one affair with young Mr. George Warrington. Mr. Harry, of course, as a young man of spirit, will stand by his brother. That’s two. Between Grace and the Colonel apology is impossible. And now—run me through the body!—you call an officer of my regiment—of Halkett’s, sir!—a hog before my face! Great heavens, sir! Mr. Washington, are you all like this in Virginia? Excuse me, I would use no offensive personality, as, by George, I will suffer none from any man! but, by Gad, Colonel, give me leave to tell you you are the most quarrelsome man I ever saw in my life. Call a disabled officer of my regiment—for he is disabled, ain’t you, Grace?—call him a hog before me! You withdraw it, sir—you withdraw it!”

“Is this some infernal conspiracy in which you are all leagued against me?” shouted the Colonel. “It would seem as if I was drunk, and not you, as you all are. I withdraw nothing. I apologise for nothing. By heavens! I will meet one or half a dozen of you in your turn, young or old, drunk or sober.”

“I do not wish to hear myself called more names,” George Warrington said evenly. “This affair can proceed, sir, without any further insult on your part. When will it please you to give me the meeting?”

“The sooner the better, sir!” said the Colonel, fuming.

“The sooner the better,” hiccupped Captain Grace, rising, swearing (as gentlemen then seasoned all speech), and reeling toward his sword by the door—only to fall as he reached it. From the floor he waved the weapon, knocked his own hat over his eyes, and cried again, “The sooner the better!”

“At any rate, this gentleman’s business will keep cool till to-morrow,” the militia Colonel said, turning to the other King’s officer. “You will hardly bring your man out to-day, Captain Waring?”

“I confess that neither his hand nor mine are particularly steady,” Waring said.

“Mine is!” George Warrington cried, glaring.

Washington, hot and savage still, answered with a sternness that tried to cover sorrow. “Be it so—with what weapon, sir?”

“Not with small-swords, Colonel. We can beat you with them. You know that from our old bouts. Pistols had better be the word.”

“As you please, George Warrington—and God forgive you, George! God pardon you, Harry! for bringing me into this quarrel,” said the Colonel, the sadness breaking through his anger like rain through smoke.

Harry hung his head; but George continued as calmly as if he were calling for salt at table.

“I, sir? It was not I who called names, who talked of a cane, who insulted a gentleman in a public place before gentlemen of the army. It is not the first time you have chosen to take me for a negro, and talked of the whip for me.”

The Colonel started back, turning very red, struck by remembrance as by a blow.

“Great heavens, George! is it that boyish quarrel you are still recalling?”

“Who made you the overseer of Castlewood?” George hissed, teeth grinding. “I am not your slave, George Washington, and I never will be. I hated you then, and I hate you now. And you have insulted me, and I am a gentleman, and so are you. Is that not enough?”

“Too much—only too much,” Washington said, with genuine grief. “Do you bear malice too, Harry? I had not thought this of thee!”

“I stand by my brother,” Harry replied, turning away from the Colonel’s look, and grasping George’s hand—an oath made without words.

The sadness did not leave Washington’s face. “Heaven be good to us! ’Tis all clear now,” he muttered to himself, as if speaking some private dialect of conscience which no other man could quite understand. Aloud, he said, “The time to write a few letters, and I am at your service, Mr. Warrington.”

“You have your own pistols at your saddle. I did not ride out with any; but will send Sady back for mine. That will give you time enough, Colonel Washington?”

“Plenty of time, sir.”

Each gentleman made the other a low bow. George put his arm through Harry’s, and they walked away together, their boots sounding on the boards with a dry finality that drowned, for a moment, even the insects outside.

The Virginian officer looked toward the two unlucky captains, now helpless with liquor. Captain Benson, master of the tavern, was propping the hat of one of them over his head with the rough tenderness of men who have seen too many foolish quarrels.

“It is not altogether their fault, Colonel,” Benson said, with a grim look of humour. “Jack Firebrace and Tom Humbold of Spotsylvania was here this morning, chanting horses with ’em. And Jack and Tom got ’em to play cards; and they didn’t win—the British Captains didn’t. And Jack and Tom challenged ’em to drink for the honour of Old England, and they didn’t win at that game neither, much. They are kind, free-handed fellows when they are sober, but they are a pretty pair of fools—they are.”

“Captain Benson,” said Colonel Washington, “you are an old frontier man, and an officer of ours, before you turned farmer and taverner. You will help me in this matter with yonder young gentlemen?”

“I’ll stand by and see fair play, Colonel. I won’t have no hand in it, beyond seeing fair play. Madam Esmond has helped me many a time—tended my poor wife in her lying-in, and doctored our Betty in the fever. You ain’t a-going to be very hard with them poor boys? Though I seen ’em both shoot: the fair one hunts well, as you know, but the old one’s a wonder at an ace of spades.”

Colonel George Warrington kept to his chamber of the tavern as if the very boards beneath his boots accused him. The place smelt of wet wool, pipe-ash, and yesterday’s ale, and through the thin wall he could hear—too clearly—the scrape of a chair, the dip of a quill, the low, set voice of his adversary dictating farewells.

In the other room Colonel Washington—General Braddock’s new aide-de-camp, with the same steady hand that could measure a road or lay a camp—thought proper to make his own dispositions. He wrote as a man writes who expects no indulgence from fate: five letters, each folded with care, sealed with his seal as if the wax might keep the world in order. One for his mother at Mount Vernon; one for his brother; one marked only with initials—M. C.; one to his Excellency Major-General Braddock; and the last, the tavern-keeper said, “for your mother, Madam Esmond,” which news, borne across a passage and into a young man’s already inflamed mind, fell like a coal into oil.

But in George Warrington’s room the tragedy was of another key—more boyish in its ornament, more fevered in its vanity. He had set his younger brother Harry to act as clerk and secretary. Harry’s hands shook so that the nib rasped, and his sobs kept time with the scratching. George dictated with a grandeur he borrowed from books, and with a bitterness he made entirely his own.

He framed it as a solemn farewell to their mother—he would not, he said, compromise her by naming any cause; he would speak of “the scheme which she had in view” with a satirical emphasis that made the phrase sound like a lash laid upon flesh.

“My dear, dear George, don’t say that!” Harry broke in, choking.

“‘As probably will be the case,’” George persisted, as if the very probability were a proof of his courage. “You know what a good shot Colonel George is, Harry. I am pretty fair myself, and ’tis probable that one or both of us will drop. —‘I scarcely suppose you will carry out the intentions you have at present in view.’”

Harry’s tears fell hot and salt, and the drops spotted the page. When he came to those words “in view,” he wrote, in vew; and the ink ran where his sleeve smeared it, and the salt water made a blurred little tide.

George peered over with sudden peevishness. “Why, child, what have you been writing, and who taught thee to spell?”

“I can’t think about spelling now, Georgy,” Harry whimpered. “I’m too miserable for that. I begin to think perhaps it’s all nonsense—perhaps Colonel George never—”

“Never meant to take possession of Castlewood?” George flamed, and every grievance he had been stewing like a too-strong sauce boiled over at once. “Never gave himself airs and patronised us there? Never advised my mother to have me flogged? Never intended to marry her? Never insulted me—and was insulted before the king’s officers? Never wrote to his brother to say we should be the better for his parental authority? The paper is there,” he cried, striking his breast-pocket, “and if anything happens to me, Harry Warrington, you will find it on my corse!”

Harry, driven past the point where tears are of any use, rubbed his fists into his eyes and made a mess of ink and salt and grief. “Write yourself, Georgy. I can’t write.”

So George pushed aside the blotted sheet, took a fresh one, and sat down with the air of a young man entering eternity by the gate of rhetoric. He made a will as he would have made a Latin exercise: longest words, grandest quotations, weightiest periods, the satire sharpened till it cut his own tongue. Yet there was tenderness in the bequests, as there is tenderness even in a hot-tempered boy when he thinks the world may be leaving him.

He desired that his negro boy, Sady, should be set free. He named his Horace, and a choice of his books; and—if possible—a suitable provision for his affectionate tutor, Mr. Dempster, who had taught him to scan verses and to speak of virtue with a Scotch precision that could not quite master Virginia heat. He left his silver fruit-knife, his music-books, and his harpsichord to little Fanny Mountain—small domestic relics, bright and intimate, like the scent that rises when an apple is pared cleanly and the peel curls away in one long ribbon.

He sealed the paper with the seal of arms his grandfather had worn, pressing down hard, as if to stamp the old world upon the new.

“The watch, of course, will be yours,” George said then, drawing out his grandfather’s gold watch and looking at it with a kind of wonder, as though time itself were an enemy he could not bring to the field. “Why, two hours and a-half are gone! ’Tis time Sady should be back with the pistols. Take the watch, Harry dear.”

“It’s no good!” Harry cried, and flung his arms round his brother. “If he fights you, I’ll fight him too. If he kills my Georgy—” and the boy’s mouth, in its misery, cast off more than one expression fit to send any recording angel flying.

Down below, the tavern was waking into its brutal holiday. The landlord—Captain Benson, in his old militia uniform, as if a coat could make a slaughter decent—came bustling with news and importance, smelling of stale spirits and damp leather.

He told them the Colonel was in the garden, walking up and down, waiting; and that the “Reg’lars was a’most sober, too, by this time,” which was offered as if sobriety were a fine polish for witnessing blood.

Benson’s had long been a rendezvous for the country’s rough sports—cock-fights, horse-matches, boxing and wrestling—and the very yard held the echoes of old hallooing, the crack of fists on bone, the coarse laughter that follows an eye gouged out. Today the air carried those memories like smoke clinging to rafters.

A plot near the Captain’s log-house had been enclosed with shingles and cleared for a kitchen-garden. The fence was new enough that the sap still showed pale at the cut ends, and within it cabbages sat in dull green patience, their leaves cupping last night’s dew. It was along that narrow strip of ordered earth that Colonel Washington paced, hands behind his back, head bowed, the sorrow on his handsome face as grave as any sermon.

Negro servants crowded at the palings, peering over. Their whispers and suppressed titters ran through the boards like mice. Sound ruled the place: the creak of porch-steps, a half-stifled snore from an officer rousing, the mutter of men trying to speak of death as if it were sport. Under the porch the British officers had bestirred themselves. Captain Waring walked almost steadily. Captain Grace lolled over the railing, eyes wide, unseeing, as if his gaze were fixed upon some floating point in a bottle.

Washington’s mind, for all its disciplined habit, moved in darker circles. There was no honourable way out in that country but the cruel customary one. He had been goaded into fury by a boy’s impertinence and had answered with insulting words. The boy had demanded reparation. Washington, who knew how long a grievance can sit in a young heart and sour, was shocked that Warrington’s jealousy and revenge had rankled so long—but the wrong had been his, and he had accepted the forfeit.

Then, from far off, came a sound that changed the air. A great hallooing and shouting rose from the road—such yelling as negroes love, noise for noise’s sake, and for the sheer joy of hearing the world answer them. Heads—woolly and powdered—turned at once. The shout grew louder; the clatter of hoofs came fast over the hard earth; and presently Mr. Sady burst into view on a foaming horse, riding as if he carried not pistols but a proclamation.

In the midst of the yard, with a flourish meant for drama and mischief alike, Sady fired a pistol. The crack snapped the morning, and the yard exploded in answering uproar. He fired the other—another sharp bite of sound. His horse, which had carried Harry on many a hunt, only tossed its head, accustomed to gunfire and to the sick delight men take in it.

Sady plunged into the courtyard amid a chaos of domestic life: fowls fluttering, turkeys scolding, horses kicking at flies and at one another, pigs shrieking as if they sensed that human violence always spills over into animal terror. Negroes crowded round him, bawling, laughing, slapping their thighs, the whole place an acoustic storm.

“Sady, sir, come here!” roared Master Harry.

“Sady, come here! Confound you!” shouted Master George, whose anger now found easy targets.

“Comin’, mas’r,” Sady said, and went right on talking, grinning, showing his teeth, savouring his own importance. He drew the pistols from the holster, snapped the locks with relish, and pointed one at a grunter that bolted squealing through the muck. He pointed down the road again, where the hoofbeats were returning like a refrain.

“Comin’, mas’r,” he repeated. “Everybody a-comin’.”

And indeed the gallop of other horses swelled upon the air. Into the yard clattered little Mr. Dempster, spurring his pony and digging at it as if he could kick knowledge into speed. Behind him rode a lady in a riding-habit upon Madam Esmond’s little horse—at first glance one might have thought it was Madam herself, but the figure was too stout, too full in the shoulders. As the horse’s grey flanks heaved and its bit foamed, recognition came: it was Mrs. Mountain, cheeks blown red by wind, skirts flecked with road-dust, riding as if she had no fear of broken bones.

“O Lor! O Golly! Hoop! Here dey come! Hurray!” rose a chorus from the yard.

Dr. Dempster and Mrs. Mountain flung themselves down from their horses, elbowed through the crowd, and rushed into the house, across the porch where the British officers sat in muzzy astonishment, down the steps, and into the garden, where George and Harry walked with their tall enemy stalking opposite. The cabbages stood between these lives and their possible ruin like innocent witnesses.

Almost before George could set his face into sternness and say, “What do you do here, madam?” Mrs. Mountain had thrown her arms round his neck.

“Oh, George, my darling! It’s a mistake! It’s a mistake, and is all my fault!”

“What’s a mistake?” George asked, drawing himself back with offended majesty, though her embrace had been warm and human as bread straight from an oven.

“What is it, Mounty?” Harry cried, shaking.

“That paper I took out of his portfolio—that paper I picked up, children, where the Colonel says he is going to marry a widow with two children. Who should it be but you, children, and who should it be but your mother?”

George’s face tightened. “Well?”

“Well, it’s—it’s not your mother. It’s that little widow Custis whom the Colonel is going to marry. He’d always take a rich one; I knew he would. It’s not Mrs. Rachel Warrington. He told Madam so to-day, just before he was going away, and that the marriage was to come off after the campaign. And—and your mother is furious, boys. And when Sady came for the pistols and told the whole house how you were going to fight, I told him to fire the pistols off, and I galloped after him, and I’ve nearly broken my poor old bones in coming to you.”

“I have a mind to break Mr. Sady’s,” George growled. “I specially enjoined the villain not to say a word.”

“Thank God he did, brother!” Harry said, and his voice cracked not with grief now but with relief so sharp it hurt. “Thank God he did!”

George, still angered by the humiliation of being dragged back from the brink, found a new indignity to clutch at. “What will Mr. Washington and those gentlemen think of my servant telling my mother at home that I was going to fight a duel?”

“You have shown your proofs before, George,” Harry said, respectful as ever in his love. “And thank Heaven, you are not going to fight our old friend—our grandfather’s old friend. For it was a mistake and there is no quarrel now, dear, is there? You were unkind to him under a wrong impression.”

“I certainly acted under a wrong impression,” George owned, unwillingly, “but—”

“George! George Washington!” Harry cried then, and sprang over the cabbage-garden towards the bowling-green where the Colonel paced. He ran with that heedless agility of youth, scattering the morning’s stillness with his breath and footfalls. Though the words did not reach us, we could see him with both hands out, the whole honest story tumbling from him in blunders and affection.

There was a custom then, now thinned out of manners like an old dialect forgotten: men could take each other in their arms without shame. When Harry had finished, Washington drew him close and held him to his heart. The Colonel’s voice faltered as he said, “Thank God, thank God for this!”

“Oh, George,” Harry answered, feeling in a rush how much he loved this friend, “how I wish I was going with you on the campaign!”

Washington pressed both the boy’s hands in a grasp that promised itself long life. Then, turning, he advanced towards the elder brother.

Harry, watching, perhaps expected the same embrace, that bodily sealing of renewed affection. But the air between the two Georges was not so easily sweetened. They joined hands, yet their salutation held itself stiffly, formal and stern on both sides, like two men tasting the same dish and finding it seasoned too sharply to enjoy.

“I find I have done you a wrong, Colonel Washington,” George Warrington said, “and must apologise—not for the error, but for much of my late behaviour which has resulted from it.”

“The error was mine! It was I who found that paper in your room, and showed it to George, and was jealous of you, Colonel. All women are jealous,” Mrs. Mountain cried, eager to shoulder blame as if she could carry it away like a basket.

“’Tis a pity you could not have kept your eyes off my paper, madam,” Washington said, and though his tone was controlled, it carried the edge of a man who has been made to pay for another’s curiosity. “You will permit me to say so. A great deal of mischief has come because I chose to keep a secret which concerned only myself and another person. For a long time George Warrington’s heart has been black with anger against me, and my feeling towards him has, I own, scarce been more friendly. All this pain might have been spared to both of us, had my private papers only been read by those for whom they were written.”

He checked himself, as if hearing in his own voice the beginnings of those “hasty words” he feared.

“I shall say no more now, lest my feelings again should betray me. Heaven bless thee, Harry! Farewell, George! And take a true friend’s advice, and try and be less ready to think evil of your friends. We shall meet again at the camp, and will keep our weapons for the enemy. Gentlemen! if you remember this scene to-morrow, you will know where to find me.”

He bowed very stately to the English officers on the porch—men still blinking as though wakened from drink into a different world—and then he left the abashed company, crossing the yard where the last echoes of Sady’s pistols still seemed to hang like bitter smoke among the squawking fowls and the frightened pigs, and he mounted and rode away swiftly, as if to outride both scandal and noise.

The brothers’ parting being once accomplished, George had taken his place in General Braddock’s household and on the line of march, and Harry was left at Castlewood to the duties of the quiet roof. He did them as he must; but there was no savour in them. The very passages of the old house had altered with George’s absence, as a kitchen seems when the chief hand is away and the accustomed fire burns without its master. Harry went by his brother’s empty chamber with his eyes averted, as a man passes a cold hearth. At table he sat where George had sat, and drank from the silver tankard that had so often rung against his brother’s teeth; and the bright metal gave back no warmth, only a thin, accusing glimmer.

Yet the household would not let the vacancy sit in silence. Madam Warrington, stiff as ever in her chair (she never deigned the mercy of a back), called “The King!” with a soldierly stoutness every day; and on Sundays, when Harry read the service and came to the prayer for travellers by land and water, her “We beseech Thee to hear us” had a weight that made even the old boards seem to listen. She spoke of George constantly, not with sighs, but with a kind of drilled cheerfulness, as if his return were a date already written in an almanack. She walked into his room with her head upright and her face composed; saw his linen laid straight, his books squared, his papers kept as though he might enter at any moment and touch them; and at meals she appealed, with a particular respect, to the old servants about what must be done “when Mr. George comes home.”

Mrs. Mountain could not keep from whimpering whenever his name was spoken; and little Fanny, prim at her sampler, pricked her finger oftener than the pattern required. Harry, who had been so quick of laughter, wore now a look as if he were perpetually startled by some sound half-heard. Madam, outwardly grave, was changed in smaller ways: she made blunders at piquet and backgammon beyond anything her pride would formerly have pardoned; and if the servants rose early, they found her already awake and dressed, as if sleep itself had become an enemy to be met standing. She had even prayed Mr. Dempster to return to residence at Castlewood; and the little Jacobite, with his sour mouth and faithful heart, came back under her roof. She was gentler now in assertion and reply, less haughty with any of the party; and she spoke often of her own father and his campaigns—how he had come out of them all with no very severe wounds to cripple him—and so, she said, she hoped and trusted would her eldest son.

George, for his part, wrote often; and when the army took the woods, he began a rough journal, sending it by such chances as offered. That packet, when it arrived, was treated like a loaf newly drawn from the oven: carried reverently, broken open with eager fingers, and made to feed the whole house. More than once on long July evenings Harry read it aloud in council, while Madam sat bolt upright at her tea-table, the scent of her strong bohea rising with the steam; while little Fanny stitched, the thread whispering through linen; while Mr. Dempster and Mrs. Mountain sat at their cards; while the old servants moved softly in the dusk and paused, as though the very air of the room were a thing to be handled with care. Outside, the summer had its own music—the far frogs in the marsh, the cicadas’ incessant rasp, the clap of a shutter now and then; and between those natural sounds, George’s words came with a sharpness that made him seem bodily present.

Hear Harry reading his brother’s page, the yellow paper crackling as he turned it:

“It must be owned the provinces act scurvily by his Majesty King George II., and his representative here is in a flame of fury. Virginia is bad enough, and poor Maryland not much better, but Pennsylvania worst of all. We pray them to send us troops from home to fight the French; we promise to maintain the troops when they come. We not only don’t keep our promise and make scarce any provision for our defenders, but our people insist upon the most exorbitant prices for their cattle and stores, and actually cheat the soldiers who are come to fight their battles. No wonder the General swears, and the troops are sulky. The delays have been endless. Owing to the failure of the several provinces to provide their promised stores and means of locomotion, weeks and months have elapsed, during which time, no doubt, the French have been strengthening themselves on our frontier and in the forts they have turned us out of. Though there never will be any love lost between me and Colonel Washington, it must be owned that your favourite (I am not jealous, Hal) is a brave man and a good officer. The family respect him very much, and the General is always asking his opinion. Indeed, he is almost the only man who has seen the Indians in their war-paint; and I own I think he was right in firing upon Mons. Jumonville last year.

“There is to be no more suite to that other quarrel at Benson’s Tavern than there was to the proposed battle between Colonel W. and a certain young gentleman who shall be nameless. Captain Waring wished to pursue it on coming into camp, and brought the message from Captain Grace, which your friend, who is as bold as Hector, was for taking up, and employed a brother aide-de-camp, Colonel Wingfield, on his side. But when Wingfield heard the circumstances of the quarrel, how it had arisen from Grace being drunk, and was fomented by Waring being tipsy, and how the two 44th gentlemen had chosen to insult a militia officer, he swore that Colonel Washington should not meet the 44th men; that he would carry the matter straightway to his Excellency, who would bring the two captains to a court-martial for brawling with the militia, and drunkenness, and indecent behaviour; and the captains were fain to put up their toasting-irons, and swallow their wrath. They were good-natured enough out of their cups, and ate their humble-pie with very good appetites at a reconciliation dinner which Colonel W. had with the 44th, and where he was as perfectly stupid and correct as Prince Prettyman need be. Hang him! He has no faults, and that’s why I dislike him. When he marries that widow—ah me! what a dreary life she will have of it.”

“I wonder at the taste of some men, and the effrontery of some women,” Madam said, setting down her teacup so that the china rang—small, clear, and commanding in the room’s hush.

“I wonder at any woman who has been married once, so forgetting herself as to marry again! Don’t you, Mountain?”

“Monstrous!” Mrs. Mountain answered, with a queer look that did not prevent her from drawing little Fanny closer.

Mr. Dempster kept his eyes on his glass of punch as if the amber surface held a battle-map. Harry’s mouth twitched, as though laughter and some other hidden thing strove together in him; but Madam, unmoved, said, “Go on, Harry. Continue with your brother’s journal. He writes well; but, ah—will he ever be able to write like my papa?”

Harry read on, the paper soft under his thumb:

“We keep the strictest order here in camp, and the orders against drunkenness and ill-behaviour on the part of the men are very severe. The roll of each company is called at morning, noon, and night, and a return of the absent and disorderly is given in by the officer to the commanding officer of the regiment, who has to see that they are properly punished. The men are punished, and the drummers are always at work. Oh, Harry, but it made one sick to see the first blood drawn from a great strong white back, and to hear the piteous yell of the poor fellow.”

“Oh, horrid!” Madam said. “I think I should have murdered Ward if he had flogged me. Thank Heaven he got off with only a crack of the ruler!”

Harry’s voice dipped as he came upon a sentence he did not care to carry, like a dish too highly seasoned for a child’s palate. “The Indians have just broken up their camp, and retired in dudgeon, because the young officers were for ever drinking with the squaws—and—and—hum—ha—”

He stopped; and little Fanny bent lower over her stitches, listening with the fierce attention of innocence.

“Pass over that about the odious tipsy creatures,” Madam commanded; and Harry, grateful for the order, lifted his tone again.

“Each regiment has Divine Service performed at the head of its colours every Sunday. The General does everything in the power of mortal man to prevent plundering, and to encourage the people round about to bring in provisions. He has declared soldiers shall be shot who dare to interrupt or molest the market-people. He has ordered the price of provisions to be raised a penny a pound, and has lent money out of his own pocket to provide the camp. Altogether, he is a strange compound, this General. He flogs his men without mercy, but he gives without stint. He swears most tremendous oaths in conversation, and tells stories which Mountain would be shocked to hear—”

“Why me?” cried Mrs. Mountain. “And what have I to do with the General’s silly stories?”

“Never mind the stories; and go on, Harry,” Madam said.

“—would be shocked to hear after dinner; but he never misses service. He adores his Great Duke, and has his name constantly on his lips. Our two regiments both served in Scotland, where I dare say Mr. Dempster knew the colour of their facings.”

“We saw the tails of their coats, as well as their facings,” growled the little Jacobite, and there was in his tone the old rasp of Culloden—an accent that carried a whole lost cause inside a few words, and made plain how a man’s native turn of speech can preserve what his rulers would gladly have him forget.

“Colonel Washington has had the fever very smartly, and has hardly been well enough to keep up with the march. Had he not better go home and be nursed by his widow? When either of us is ill, we are almost as good friends again as ever. But I feel somehow as if I can’t forgive him for having wronged him. Good Powers! How I have been hating him for these months past! Oh, Harry! I was in a fury at the tavern the other day, because Mountain came up so soon, and put an end to our difference. We ought to have burned a little gunpowder between us, and cleared the air. But though I don’t love him, as you do, I know he is a good soldier, a good officer, and a brave, honest man; and, at any rate, shall love him none the worse for not wanting to be our stepfather.”

“A stepfather, indeed!” cried Harry’s mother. “Why, jealousy and prejudice have perfectly maddened the poor child! Do you suppose the Marquis of Esmond’s daughter and heiress could not have found other stepfathers for her sons than a mere provincial surveyor? If there are any more such allusions in George’s journal, I beg you skip ’em, Harry, my dear. About this piece of folly and blundering there hath been quite talk enough already.”

Harry went on—glad, perhaps, to escape from that nettle of words into the safer brushwood of camp detail:

“’Tis a pretty sight to see a long line of redcoats threading through the woods or taking their ground after the march. The care against surprise is so great and constant, that we defy prowling Indians to come unawares upon us, and our advanced sentries and savages have on the contrary fallen in with the enemy and taken a scalp or two from them. They are such cruel villains, these French and their painted allies, that we do not think of showing them mercy. Only think, we found but yesterday a little boy scalped but yet alive in a lone house, where his parents had been attacked and murdered by the savage enemy, of whom—so great is his indignation at their cruelty—our General has offered a reward of five pounds for all the Indian scalps brought in.

“When our march is over, you should see our camp, and all the care bestowed on it. Our baggage and our General’s tents and guard are placed quite in the centre of the camp. We have outlying sentries by twos, by threes, by tens, by whole companies. At the least surprise, they are instructed to run in on the main body and rally round the tents and baggage, which are so arranged themselves as to be a strong fortification. Sady and I, you must know, are marching on foot now, and my horses are carrying baggage. The Pennsylvanians sent such rascally animals into camp that they speedily gave in. What good horses were left, ’twas our duty to give up; and Roxana has a couple of packs upon her back instead of her young master. She knows me right well, and whinnies when she sees me, and I walk by her side, and we have many a talk together on the march.

“July 4. To guard against surprises, we are all warned to pay especial attention to the beat of the drum; always halting when they hear the long roll beat, and marching at the beat of the long march. We are more on the alert regarding the enemy now. We have our advanced pickets doubled, and two sentries at every post. The men on the advanced pickets are constantly under arms, with fixed bayonets, all through the night, and relieved every two hours. The half that are relieved lie down by their arms, but are not suffered to leave their pickets. ’Tis evident that we are drawing very near to the enemy now. This packet goes out with the General’s to Colonel Dunbar’s camp, who is thirty miles behind us; and will be carried thence to Frederick, and thence to my honoured mother’s house at Castlewood, to whom I send my duty, with kindest remembrances, as to all friends there, and how much love I need not say to my dearest brother from his affectionate—

GEORGE E. WARRINGTON.”

The page ended; the room breathed again. Outside, the July heat lay over the land like a lid upon a pot, pressing down all scent and sound into a heavy closeness. For ten days thereafter no news came from the column pushing toward the Ohio. It was told and believed, in parlours and at tavern bars, that their slow labour through the forest must soon bring them up with the enemy; that the troops, led by consummate captains, were now seasoned to the wilderness and not to be surprised; that every precaution had been taken against ambuscade. It was always the outlying enemy, so the talk ran, who were discovered, pursued, destroyed by vigilant scouts and skirmishers. The last certain word was that the army had advanced beyond the ground of Mr. Washington’s former discomfiture, and in two days more must be within a day’s march of the French fort. Of taking it no fears were entertained. The numbers of French reinforcements from Montreal were known; and Mr. Braddock, with his veteran regiments from Britain and their colonial allies, was judged more than a match for any troops that could be gathered under the white flag.

So men spoke, as men will speak when they season danger with confidence, like over-salting a thin broth to persuade themselves it is rich. At Castlewood, too, at their family repasts, they kept their tone cheerful—never naming dread, never admitting uneasiness.
