Madam vowed George should have the best horse in Virginia or Carolina in place of Roxana; horses enough could be had for money, she said; it was only for the King’s service they were not forthcoming. Yet the house, for all its brave talk, could not sit still. They were forever on the trot from one neighbour’s to another, sniffing for news as a cook sniffs the air for a scent of burning. Reports ran with prodigious speed. When the noted border warrior called Colonel Jack offered himself and his huntsmen and the General declined his terms and his service, the defection of Jack and his men became the talk of thousands of tongues at once.

The very servants carried and scattered tidings. The house negroes, in their midnight gallops about the country in search of junketing or sweethearts, brought back scraps and shreds of intelligence from astonishing distances, and flung them abroad. They knew, and laughed, at the cheats practised on the army for horses, provisions, and the like—how bacon was salted too hard and sold too dear, how flour was cut with what it should never have met, how cattle were driven in lean and priced as fat; and there was in that laughter a sharp truth about power and words: the same bargain called “patriot thrift” in one mouth was “rascality” in another, and the name a man gave his act could change its moral weight like a spice altering a dish.

For three weeks after the army’s departure, the thousand reports were cheerful; and at supper the Castlewood news was still pleasant. But on the 10th of July a vast and sudden gloom spread over the province, as if a storm-cloud had fallen without wind. Terror and doubt seemed to settle on every face. The affrighted servants eyed their masters and withdrew, humming and whispering together. The fiddles ceased in the quarters; the song and laugh of those cheery black folk were hushed, and the night, which had been full of life, lay listening to itself. Right and left, everybody’s servants were on the gallop for tidings. The country taverns were thronged with horsemen, who drank and cursed and brawled at the bars, each bringing his gloomy tale, as though the land had but one dreadful story and could not decide which tongue must tell it.

The army had been surprised. The troops had fallen into an ambuscade and had been cut up almost to a man. The officers were picked off by French marksmen and savage allies. The General had been wounded and carried off the field in his sash. Four days afterward, the report grew worse: the General was dead—and scalped by a French Indian.

Ah, what a scream poor Mrs. Mountain gave when Gumbo brought that news from across the James River; and little Fanny sprang, crying, to her mother’s arms, her thread dangling like a broken line of prayer.

“Lord God Almighty, watch over us, and defend my boy!” Madam Warrington cried; and for once her pride gave way to nakedness of need, so that she sank on her knees and lifted her rigid hands to Heaven. The room’s sounds—the child’s sob, the mother’s gasp, the tea-spoon’s faint chink—seemed suddenly immense, as if the world had been emptied of all else.

The gentlemen were not at home when the rumour arrived; but within an hour or two they came in, each from his hunt for news. Mr. Dempster did not dare to look up and meet the widow’s agonised gaze. Harry Warrington was as pale as his mother. It might not be true about the manner of the General’s death—but he was dead. The army had been surprised by Indians, and had fled, and been killed without seeing the enemy. An express had arrived from Dunbar’s camp; fugitives were pouring in there.

Should he go and see? He must go and see.

He and stout little Dempster armed themselves and mounted, taking a couple of mounted servants with them. They followed the northward track which the expeditionary force had hewn out for itself; and at every mile that brought them nearer, the disaster of that fearful day seemed to magnify, as a sound swells when one walks toward its source. The land itself appeared to have changed its voice: fewer birds; the wind more restless in the leaves; the hoofbeats too loud on the hard road. It was as if Nature, which had sung so steadily through the summer nights at Castlewood, now held its breath and listened to the far-off cracking of muskets that still seemed to echo between the trees.

The day after the defeat, a number of the miserable fugitives from the fatal battle of the 9th July had reached Dunbar’s camp, fifty miles from the field. Thither poor Harry and his companions rode, stopping stragglers, asking news, giving money, getting from one and all the same dreadful reckoning: a thousand men slain; two-thirds of the officers down; all the General’s aides-de-camp hit.

Hit? But were they killed?

Those who fell never rose again, said the broken men. The tomahawk did its work upon them.

O brother, brother! All the fond memories of their youth—shared bread at the schoolroom table, the taste of apples stolen together and eaten breathless behind a hedge, the laughter that had rung along the river-bank, the romantic vows pledged in boyhood as though spoken in some private dialect only they two understood—came back upon Harry with pangs that no words could fully carry. Wounded men looked up and were softened by his grief. Rough women melted when they saw the woe written on the handsome young face. The hardy old tutor could scarcely look at him for tears, and grieved for him even more than for the dear pupil whom he believed lay dead under the savage knife.

With every mile Harry Warrington rode northward toward Pennsylvania, the tale of ruin swelled—like a pot left too long at the boil, each traveller lifting the lid and crying that the thing within was worse than any man had yet said. The King’s famous regiments, veterans who had marched to drums in Scotland and on the Continent, had broken in a wilderness where no parade-ground could be stamped; they had fled from an enemy half-unseen, and all their vaunted order had not saved them from a fire that came, not from a line of red coats, but from behind bark and leaf.

Men told it to Harry as they would tell a kitchen-boy how a grand feast was lost: first the confident laying-out of the work, then the sudden spoil. They spoke of the ford, the long string of troops threading through the green silence, of the first cracking shots ahead, and the cannon dragged forward as if iron might clear away invisible foes. Then—without trumpet or flag—the woods themselves seemed to spit flame. Behind every trunk, from every bush, a murderous fusillade; men dropping as if a scythe had gone through wheat. The commander—brave to the last—had his horse shot under him again and again, was wounded twice, and at last mortally, dying three days after. So ran the reports, each voice adding its own salt.

But not all of the General’s suite were dead. That rumour, at least, kept Harry’s heart in motion. An aide-de-camp—a Virginian gentleman—lay sick with fever and exhaustion at Dunbar’s camp. Which aide? Which gentleman? The very uncertainty drove Harry on as hunger drives a man toward the smell of bread.

He found a tent, and within it George Washington—stretched long, his skin hot and drawn, his eyes bright with illness. Yet sharper than fever, Mr. Washington said, was the pain of seeing Harry Warrington and having no comfort to give.

He did not tell everything—could not. His duty, for three days after the fight, had been to remain near the General. On the fatal ninth of July he had seen George Warrington ride forward with orders from the chief—and never return to the General’s side. When Braddock died, Washington, with a sick man’s stubbornness, had contrived to creep back upon the track to the field itself.

What lay there now was what battle leaves when it has been picked over. Corpses remained, stripped and horribly mutilated. One body he buried which he thought might be George’s. His illness, perhaps, had been fed by that search and the anguish of it—by crawling among the ruined, by turning faces with hands that shook, by the sickening knowledge that names and bodies, in such a place, slip from certainty.

“Ah, George! If you had loved him you would have found him dead or alive,” Harry cried; and the words came out like a knife. Nothing would satisfy him but that he too should go, and see with his own eyes.

With money he bought guides, and rode back. He forded the river at the very passage where the army had crossed, and went the length of the dreadful ground. No Indians haunted it now. The wilderness had quieted again, but it was not the quiet of peace. Birds of prey rose and settled, rose and settled; their wings made a low, steady clapping over the trees, and their cries cut through the air with a harshness that seemed to scrape the nerves. Even the insects had their terrible industry, and the wind, when it moved, moved through the leaves as through a church where some impure thing had happened.

Save for his grandfather lying very calm with a sweet smile upon his lip, Harry had never yet looked close upon the face of Death. Here death had no sweetness. The stench had its own weight, as if it pressed on the breast; it was thick, sour, and sickly, a heat-spoiled broth of blood and rot. The sight of mutilation made him turn away in shuddering loathing. What could the vacant woods tell him? What could those festering bodies under the trees give back—any syllable of his brother’s fate, any hint that could be translated into hope?

Desperation drove him toward the French fort—he would go unarmed, with a white flag. But his guides refused to advance.

“The French might maybe respect ye,” one said, “but the Injuns won’t. Keep your hair for your lady mother, my young gentleman. ’Tis enough she loses one son in this campaign.”

So Harry turned back to Dunbar’s—empty-handed, his quest profitless as a net pulled from a river after the fish have fled.

There it was his turn to be struck down. Fever took him as it takes a body already bruised by grief: quickly, heavily, with delirium close behind. He lay in a tent, on the very bed from which his friend had just risen convalescent. For days he did not know who watched him. Poor Dempster, who had tended him through more than one such malady, thought the widow must lose both her children. Yet at length the fever yielded enough for the boy to rally, to sit up, to be helped to horse.

Mr. Washington and Dempster escorted him home.

They came again to the gates of Castlewood, and though the fields stood green and the great house kept its accustomed look of plenty, the sight of it weighed like a cold stone in the heart. A servant had been sent ahead to announce them. First came Mrs. Mountain and her little daughter, with tears and embraces for Harry. She scarce gave Mr. Washington more than a nod. Then the child—little Fanny—made the young officer start and turn deadly pale by coming close with her hands behind her back and asking, with that cruel innocence children have, “Why have you not brought George back too?”

Harry did not hear; Mrs. Mountain’s sobs and caresses mercifully drowned the question before it could lodge.

Dempster was received with thanks.

“Whatever could be done, we know you would do, Mr. Dempster,” Mrs. Mountain said, giving him her hand. “Make a curtsey to Mr. Dempster, Fanny, and remember, child, to be grateful to all who have been friendly to our benefactors. Will it please you to take any refreshment before you ride, Colonel Washington?”

Mr. Washington had ridden enough, and counted on Castlewood’s shelter as naturally as on his own roof; yet he answered stiffly, as if every kindness must be measured.

“The time to feed my horse, and a glass of water for myself, and I will trouble Castlewood hospitality no further.”

“Sure, George, you have your room here, and my mother is above-stairs getting it ready!” Harry cried. “That poor horse of yours stumbled with you, and can’t go farther this evening.”

“Hush! Your mother won’t see him, child,” Mrs. Mountain whispered. “Not see George? Why, he is like a son of the house,” Harry said, bewildered.

“She had best not see him,” Mrs. Mountain answered. “I don’t meddle any more in family matters, child: but when the Colonel’s servant rode in, and said you were coming, Madam Esmond left this room—where she was sitting reading Drelincourt—and said she felt she could not see Mr. Washington. Will you go to her?”

Harry took his friend’s arm, begged the Colonel’s pardon for leaving him a little, and went up. He crossed the corridor with averted head, passing one door he could not bear to look at—the door of his brother’s room. But as he reached it, Madam Esmond came out and folded him to her heart, and led him in.

A settee stood by the bed. A book of psalms lay upon the coverlet, as if it had been left there only an hour ago. Everything in the room was as George had left it—his order, his quiet signs of habit, the very air holding something of him, like a pantry that keeps the scent of spice long after the lid is shut.

“My poor child!” she cried. “How thin thou art grown—how haggard you look! Never mind. A mother’s care will make thee well again. ’Twas nobly done to go and brave sickness and danger in search of your brother. Had others been as faithful, he might be here now. Never mind, my Harry; our hero will come back to us,—I know he is not dead. One so good, and so brave, and so gentle, and so clever as he was, I know is not lost to us altogether.”

The praise, lavish as it was, struck Harry oddly; perhaps because he remembered how, when George had been in the house, such words had not always come so readily. Yet he held his tongue, and only looked at her.

“Dry up thy tears, my dear! He will come back to us, I know he will come.”

Pressed for a reason, she said she had seen her father two nights running in a dream, and he had told her George was a prisoner among the Indians.

Grief had not prostrated her; it had kindled her into a hard brightness. Her eyes were eager, her face set, with something revengeful in its resolve. Harry, still weak, wondered at the strength—and the strange heat—of her.

Then he begged her to go down and welcome George Washington, who had brought him home. At once her excitement sharpened into pain.

She said she should shudder at touching his hand. She declared Mr. Washington had taken her son from her; she could not sleep under the same roof with him.

“He gave me his bed when I was ill, mother,” Harry pleaded; “and if our George is alive, how has George Washington a hand in his death? Ah! please God it be only as you say.”

“If your brother returns, as return he will, it will not be through Mr. Washington’s help,” Madam Esmond answered. “He neither defended George on the field, nor would he bring him out of it.”

“But he tended me most kindly,” Harry said, fighting for fairness. “He was yet ill when he gave up his bed to me, and was thinking only of his friend, when any other man would have thought only of himself.”

“A friend! A pretty friend!” she sneered. “Of all his Excellency’s aides-de-camp, my gentleman is the only one who comes back unwounded. The brave and noble fall, but he, to be sure, is unhurt. I confide my boy to him—the pride of my life—whom he will defend with his, forsooth! And he leaves my George in the forest, and brings me back himself! Oh, a pretty welcome I must give him!”

“No gentleman,” Harry cried, his weak voice gathering fire, “was ever refused shelter under my grandfather’s roof.”

“Oh no—no gentleman!” she echoed, her scorn thin and keen. “Let us go down, if you like, son, and pay our respects to this one. Will you please to give me your arm?”

She took the arm that could scarcely support itself, and walked down the broad stairs into the parlour where Colonel Washington sat. She made him a ceremonious curtsey and extended one small hand, which she allowed to rest in his for a moment—as if even that touch must be rationed.

“I wish that our meeting had been happier, Colonel Washington,” she said.

“You do not grieve more than I do that it is otherwise, madam,” he answered.

“I might have wished that the meeting had been spared,” she went on, “that I might not have kept you from friends whom you are naturally anxious to see,—that my boy’s indisposition had not detained you. Home and his good nurse Mountain, and his mother and our good Doctor Dempster, will soon restore him. ’Twas scarce necessary, Colonel, that you, who have so many affairs on your hands, military and domestic, should turn doctor too.”

“Harry was ill and weak,” the Colonel said, faltering, “and I thought it was my duty to ride by him.”

“You yourself, sir, have gone through the fatigues and dangers of the campaign in the most wonderful manner,” Madam Esmond replied, curtseying again and looking at him with those impenetrable black eyes.

“I wish to Heaven, madam, some one else had come back in my place!” he burst out.

“Nay, sir, you have ties which must render your life more than ever valuable and dear to you, and duties to which, I know, you must be anxious to betake yourself. In our present deplorable state of doubt and distress, Castlewood can be a welcome place to no stranger, much less to you, and so I know, sir, you will be for leaving us ere long. And you will pardon me if the state of my own spirits obliges me for the most part to keep my chamber. But my friends here will bear you company as long as you favour us, whilst I nurse my poor Harry upstairs. Mountain, you will have the cedar-room on the ground-floor ready for Mr. Washington, and anything in the house is at his command. Farewell, sir. Will you be pleased to present my compliments to your mother, who will be thankful to have her son safe and sound out of the war,—as also to my young friend Martha Custis, to whom and to whose children I wish every happiness. Come, my son!”

With another freezing curtsey she withdrew, her gaze fixed upon the Colonel as if she would pin blame to him by sheer force of looking. He stood dumb where she left him.

Though her belief in George’s safety sounded unshakeable, Castlewood could not help but be sad. She might forbid open mourning, but her heart wore black, whatever face she forced upon herself for the world. To look for her son was hoping against hope. No authentic account of his death had come, and no man appeared who could say he had seen George fall; yet hundreds had been struck down that day with no witnesses but the lurking enemy and comrades dying beside them.

A fortnight after the defeat—while Harry was absent on his fruitless search—George’s servant Sady reappeared at Castlewood, wounded and maimed. He could give no coherent account of the battle, only of his flight from the centre where he had been with the baggage. He had no news of his master since the morning of the action. For days Sady hid himself among the negro quarters, not daring to face Madam Esmond’s anger.

Neighbours whispered that the lady laboured under a delusion. Yet it held with such force that there were hours when Harry and the rest of the household nearly caught it, as one catches a tune that will not stop repeating. To her it seemed nothing strange that her father—out of another world—should promise her son’s life. In this world or the next, her family must be of consequence, she thought. Had not she, more than once, been visited with foreknowledge? No accident, no fever, no important illness had ever befallen her boys at a distance but she had felt it in advance. She could enumerate half a dozen instances—and her household, weary of contradiction, was obliged in part to confirm them—when she had known, by instinct, what had happened and what would follow.

No, George was not dead. George was a prisoner among the Indians. George would come back and rule over Castlewood—as surely as his Majesty would send a great force from home to wipe away the stain on British arms and drive the French out of the Americas.

As for Mr. Washington, she vowed she would never behold him of her own goodwill again. He had promised to protect George with his life. Why was her son gone and the Colonel alive? How dared he face a mother without her son? Some might plead he had to obey superior orders. Psha! A promise was a promise.

Do not tell her his coat and hat had shots through them. She had her answer ready, sharp as vinegar. Could she not go into the study and fire two shots through her paduasoy skirt—and would she be killed? She laughed at the notion; and her laugh, like the sound of a knife on bone, did not please those who heard it. Satire from a nature not given to humour is seldom sport; it lands where it means to land.

Thus, if Harry wished to meet his friend, he must do it in secret—at court-houses, taverns, places where the provincial gentry gathered; in little towns where men came for races and bargains and news. No man of spirit, she declared, could meet Mr. Washington after his base desertion. She was exceedingly excited when she heard the Colonel and her son had indeed met. What a heart must Harry have, to give his hand to one she called little better than George’s murderer!

“For shame!” she would cry, and then—without pausing—turn upon her own accusation. “How can he be George’s murderer, when I say my boy is not dead? He is not dead, because my instinct never deceived me: because, as sure as I see his picture now before me—only ’tis not near so noble or so good as he used to look—so surely two nights running did my papa appear to me in my dreams. You doubt about that, very likely? ’Tis because you never loved anybody sufficiently, my poor Harry; else you might have leave to see them in dreams.”

“I think I loved George, mother,” Harry cried once, stung. “I have often prayed that I might dream about him, and I don’t.”

“How you can talk, sir, of loving George,” she shot back, “and then—go and meet your Mr. Washington at horse-races—I can’t understand! Can you, Mountain?”

“We can’t understand many things in our neighbours’ characters,” Mrs. Mountain grumbled. “I can understand that our boy is unhappy, and that he does not get strength, and that he is doing no good here, in Castlewood, or moping at the taverns and court-houses with horse-coupers and idle company.”

And indeed the dependant spoke truth. There was grief in Castlewood, but there was disunion too, a cracking of bonds that had once held firm, like a well-made loaf that begins to stale and crumble at the slice.

“I cannot tell how it came,” Harry said later, when he told this history to his new-found English relative, Madame de Bernstein, “but since that fatal day of July, last year, and my return home, my mother never has been the same woman. She seemed to love none of us as she used. She was for ever praising George, and yet she did not seem as if she liked him much when he was with us. She hath plunged, more deeply than ever, into her books of devotion, out of which she only manages to extract grief and sadness, as I think. Such a gloom has fallen over our wretched Virginian house of Castlewood, that we all grew ill, and pale as ghosts, who inhabited it. Mountain told me, madam, that, for nights, my mother would not close her eyes. I have had her at my bedside, looking so ghastly, that I have started from my own sleep, fancying a ghost before me. By one means or other she has wrought herself into a state of excitement which if not delirium, is akin to it.

“I was again and again struck down by the fever, and all the Jesuits’ bark in America could not cure me. We have a tobacco-house and some land about the new town of Richmond, in our province, and went thither, as Williamsburg is no wholesomer than our own place; and there I mended a little, but still did not get quite well, and the physicians strongly counselled a sea-voyage. My mother, at one time, had thoughts of coming with me, but—” (and here the lad blushed and hung his head) “—we did not agree very well, though I know we loved each other very heartily, and ’twas determined that I should see the world for myself. So I took passage in our ship from the James River, and was landed at Bristol. And ’twas only on the 9th of July, this year, at sea, as had been agreed between me and Madam Esmond, that I put mourning on for my dear brother.”

So that little mistress of Virginian Castlewood—whom it is easy to respect, and not so easy to live beside—had the gift of making those around her uncomfortable; of quarrelling with the very people she loved best; of exercising jealousies and imperious humours until they were not sorry to escape. Here was money enough, friends enough, position enough, respect enough; a house stored with plenty—meat in the smokehouse, meal in the bin, tea in the caddy, the table set with silver—and yet poor Harry Warrington was glad to leave it all behind.

What good is a stalled ox for dinner every day, if content is not at table? Is it better to be loved and plagued by those you love, or to live with an easy indifference—following your fancies unmolested—and die without causing painful regret? When her boy was gone, Madam Esmond forgot the small tiffs and prickly exchanges; to hear her speak of her children, you would fancy both were perfect and had never vexed her for a moment.

With the boys removed, her sharp energies fell naturally upon Mrs. Mountain and the child, worrying and fretting them in turn. But women, perhaps, bear hard words more easily than men; forgive sooner, or dissemble anger better. Let us hope Madam Esmond’s dependants found their life tolerable; that they sometimes answered back, that if there were quarrels in the morning there were truces by night, and they could sit down again to cards and a dish of tea with something like peace.

Yet without the boys the great house of Castlewood was dreary to the widow. She left an overseer to manage the estate and paid it only occasional visits. In Richmond—growing daily into a prettier, busier little city—she enlarged and beautified her house, held company and card-assemblies, gathered preachers in plenty, and set up her small throne where the gentlefolks of the province might come and bow. Her domestic negroes, loving society as they do, were delighted to exchange Castlewood’s solitude for town life.

And there, for a time—while Harry Warrington’s story moves on across the sea—we leave the resolute little lady, with her dreams, her certainty, and the silence in her son’s room that no words, in any dialect, can truly translate.

When the young man began to tell his tale in the great house, the candles were already guttering in their sconces, and the night outside laid a cool hand upon the windows. From the avenue came the slow hiss of leaves in the wind, and farther off the faint, steady breath of the park—an owl’s single syllable, the answering bark of a dog, the soft hoof-stamp of horses in their stalls. Within, the air held that mingled scent which old rooms keep as their secret: beeswax from the polished tables, damp wool from cloaks shaken free of rain, a ghost of lavender in the linen, and—because the household had only lately left supper—roasted meat, nut-brown crust, and a wine’s last sweetness clinging in the warm.

Harry Warrington had no scholar’s art of oration; he did not spin his adventures as if he were selling them. Yet his voice was cordial, and it carried truth the way a well-made broth carries marrow—plain, nourishing, hard to resist. He spoke with the simplicity of a man who remembers by senses first: the tang of river-water on the tongue, the scorch of sun upon the neck, the smoke of a camp-fire caught in hair and coat, the bite of fear like pepper. It was enough.

Madam de Bernstein sat opposite him, her hands quiet in her lap. A woman who had long lived as if tenderness were a costly spice—used once, then locked away—found, to her own vexation, that the boy’s presence altered the climate of her mind. There were not many springs in the tract of her life; not many shaded places where one could stoop and drink. And now, as this friendly voice sounded in her ears, her heart beat with a strange ache, as though a door long barred had been opened and cold air rushed in.

She watched herself feel. Such a woman, trained to guard every motion of her soul as a housekeeper counts silver, could not help taking note of the quickened pulse, the heat rising to her cheeks when he leaned forward, the ridiculous happiness of simply hearing him say “my mother,” as if the words were a loaf broken and handed across a table. She doted on him—and, more than that, on the sensation of doting, so new that it seemed almost indecent.

“Wait,” whispered the dark mockery of Conscience within her. “Wait, Beatrix Esmond. You will weary. You always weary. When this fancy has passed, the boy may die, and you will not shed a tear. Or he will talk, and you will tire of his stories. Your lot is loneliness—lonely.”

Well, then—if life were a desert, there were still halting-places. For to-day there was shade and water. She would take what was given, and not poison it with tomorrow.

As he spoke of his mother, Madam de Bernstein smiled inwardly to hear, in his plain recounting, the old family lineaments—those moral features that outlast faces. Madam Esmond was jealous? Yes, Harry admitted with a blush that seemed to come from the same honest place as his words.

“She was fond of Colonel Washington?” Madam de Bernstein asked, her eyes narrowing with a curiosity that was half amusement, half old wound.

“She liked him,” Harry said carefully, as though measuring salt into a dish, “but only as a friend. I have heard her a hundred times vow she had no other feeling. And I”—here he hesitated, then gave the confession as a man hands over a debt—“I was once absurdly jealous of him myself.”

“Ah!” said Madam Beatrix, the syllable sharp with memory. “You will see that my half-sister will never forgive him. And you need not be surprised, sir, at women taking a fancy to men younger than themselves—for do not I dote upon you? and do not all these Castlewood people crevent with jealousy?”

However much jealousy may have pricked the Castlewood household, no open ill-will was permitted to show its face. Within two days in the ancestral house, Harry Warrington had become Cousin Harry upon every tongue. The very syllables were sweetened in the saying—by the young because youth is hospitable to novelty, by the middle-aged because civility is a craft, and by the old because kinship is a garment one can always bring out and shake fresh.

Especially when Madam de Bernstein was present, the Countess of Castlewood was all graciousness to her Virginian kinsman. She praised him lavishly before the Baroness, and in private found many opportunities—those delicate moments between the removal of a dish and the bringing of the next, or in the lull when music ended and chairs were drawn nearer—to express surprise and admiration.

“How charming the young Huron is!” she would say, her voice like sugared almonds. “How elegant his manners! And in such a distant province—how could the child have learned to be so polite?”

Madam de Bernstein received these remarks with a complacency as smooth as cream. It is a pleasing spectacle, to see ladies exchange compliments like flowers while their fingers feel for thorns. With what smiles they can strike; with what pretty phrases they can pour a drop of poison into a cup and hand it round as if it were cordial.

“You wonder, my dear Maria, that the boy should be so polite?” said Madame de Bernstein. “His mother was bred by two very perfect gentlefolks. Colonel Esmond had a grave courtesy, a grand manner, which I do not see among the gentlemen nowadays.”

“Eh, my dear,” returned the Countess, “we all of us praise our own time! My grandmamma used to declare there was nothing like Whitehall and Charles the Second.”

“My mother saw King James the Second’s court for a short while,” Madam de Bernstein persisted, “and though not court-educated—her father was a country clergyman—she was exquisitely well-bred. The Colonel, her second husband, had traveled, had learning, and had frequented the finest company in Europe. They could not go into their retreat and leave their manners behind them. The boy has them as his natural inheritance.”

“Nay, excuse me, my dear, for thinking you too partial,” the Countess said, still smiling as if she offered a dish for tasting. “She could not have been that perfection which filial fondness imagines. She left off liking her daughter—you have owned that she did—and I cannot fancy a complete woman who has a cold heart. No, no, my dear sister-in-law! Manners are requisite, no doubt—and for a country parson’s daughter your mamma was very well. I have seen many of the cloth who are very well. Mr. Sampson, our chaplain, is very well. Dr. Young is very well. Mr. Dodd is very well; but they have not the true air—as how should they? I protest, I beg pardon! I forgot my lord bishop, your ladyship’s first choice. But to be a complete woman one must have what you have, what I may say and bless Heaven for, I think I have—a good heart. Without the affections, all the world is vanity, my love! I only live, exist, eat, drink, rest, for my sweet, sweet children—for my wicked Willy, for my self-willed Fanny, dear naughty loves!”

As she spoke she kissed the bracelets on her arms, each bearing a miniature likeness, the enamel faces blinking in candlelight as if alive. Two Italian greyhounds—Mimi and Fanchon—trembling as if made of quicksilver, sprang into her lap and licked her hands, careful of her cheeks where rouge lay thick as a mask.

“Yes, Mimi! yes, Fanchon!” she cooed. “If they were to die—or you were to die—your poor mistress would die too! For nothing do I bless Heaven so much, though it puts me to excruciating torture very often, as for having endowed me with sensibility and a feeling heart!”

“You are full of feeling, dear Anna,” said the Baroness smoothly. “You are celebrated for your sensibility. You must give a little of it to our American nephew—cousin—I scarce know his relationship.”

“Nay,” replied the Countess, “I am here but as a guest in Castlewood now. The house is my Lord Castlewood’s, not mine—or his lordship’s whenever he shall choose to claim it. What can I do for the young Virginian that has not been done? He is charming. Are we even jealous of him, my dear? And though we see what a fancy the Baroness de Bernstein has taken for him, do your ladyship’s nephews and nieces—your real nephews and nieces—cry out? My poor children might be mortified, for indeed in a few hours the charming young man has made as much way as my poor things have been able to do in all their lives; but are they angry? Willy hath taken him out to ride. This morning, was not Maria playing the harpsichord whilst my Fanny taught him the minuet? ’Twas a charming young group, I assure you, and it brought tears into my eyes to look at the young creatures. Poor lad! We are as fond of him as you are, dear Baroness!”

Now, Madam de Bernstein—through her own ears, or through a servant’s careful listening—had heard a different music beneath that pretty speech.

The scene the Countess described had indeed taken place. In a room where the woodwork held the smell of varnish and old smoke, Lady Maria sat at the harpsichord. The instrument’s tone, bright and percussive, laid its little iron coins of sound upon the air; outside, the household went on—footmen murmuring in corridors, a distant clatter of a tray in the pantry, the faint tick of a clock like a patient tongue rehearsing time. Lady Fanny, flushed with the pleasure of being admired, was teaching Harry the steps of a minuet. He was earnest, as if the dance were another sort of drill; she laughed and corrected him, her slipper whispering against the floorboards as she turned.

Into this entered the Countess with her son William, who came in his boots from the kennel, bringing with him a gust of cold air and the sharper scents of leather, damp earth, and dogs.

“Bravi, bravi! Oh, charming!” cried my Lady, clapping her hands, nodding one of her best smiles toward Harry. And then—like the snap beneath a silk ribbon—she darted a look at Fanny which my Lady Fanny perfectly understood. Perhaps Lady Maria understood it too, for her fingers struck the keys with redoubled energy; the music grew louder, more insistent, as if it could drown what eyes were saying.

“Infernal young Choctaw!” muttered Mr. William, sour as ale left standing. “Is he teaching Fanny the war-dance? and is Fan going to try her tricks upon him now?”

That was what the Countess’s look asked: Are you going to try your tricks upon him now?

Fanny made Harry a curtsey, too low, too quick. He blushed like a boy caught stealing sugar, and both stopped dancing, disconcerted. Lady Maria rose from the harpsichord with a stiffness that made her silk rustle like dry leaves, and walked away.

“Nay, go on dancing, young people!” the Countess said at once, honey returning to her voice. “Don’t let me spoil sport. Let me play for you.”

She sat at the harpsichord and took over the tune herself. Her touch was practiced; the little notes rang as clean as knives tapped together.

“I—I don’t know how to dance,” Harry said, hanging his head, his blush deeper than any carmine in the room.

“And Fanny was teaching you? Go on teaching him, dearest Fanny!” said the Countess, with an encouragement that sounded oddly like command.

“Go on, do,” Mr. William added, the words dragged from him with a sidelong growl.

“I—I had rather not show off my awkwardness in company,” Harry said, and by the end of the sentence he had steadied himself, as a man does who has tasted mockery and decides not to swallow it. “When I know how to dance a minuet, be sure I will ask my cousin to walk one with me.”

“That will be very soon, dear Cousin Warrington, I am certain,” the Countess replied, her smile bright enough to blind.

“What game is she hunting now?” Mr. William asked himself, and could not answer; for though he knew the noises of hounds and horses and the honest uproar of a tavern, he could not always read the softer, more dangerous soundscape of a woman’s schemes—the hush before a word, the sudden sweetness of a tone, the way a name could be spoken like a net cast in water.

The Countess, fondly calling her daughter to her elbow, left the room with her. The harpsichord’s last notes died behind them; in the tapestried passage their footsteps were muffled, but not their voices.

No sooner were they away from company than my Lady’s blandness fell off as if it had been a cloak.

“You booby!” she began to her adored Fanny, her whisper fierce. “You double idiot! What are you going to do with the Huron? You don’t want to marry a creature like that and be a squaw in a wigwam?”

“Don’t, mamma!” gasped Lady Fanny; for her mother’s fingers were pinching her arm hard, leaving bruises that would flower by morning.

“I am sure our cousin is very well,” Fanny whimpered, half from pain, half from anger, “and you said so yourself.”

“Very well! Yes—and heir to a swamp, a negro, a log-cabin, and a barrel of tobacco!” The Countess’s contempt snapped like a crust cracking under a knife. “My Lady Frances Esmond, do you remember what your ladyship’s rank is, and what your name is, and who was your ladyship’s mother, when at three days’ acquaintance you commence dancing—a pretty dance indeed—with this brat out of Virginia?”

“Mr. Warrington is our cousin,” Fanny pleaded, clinging to the word as if kinship were protection.

“A creature come from nobody knows where is not your cousin! How do we know he is your cousin? He may be a valet who has taken his master’s portmanteau and run away in his postchaise.”

“But Madame de Bernstein says he is our cousin,” Fanny cried, “and he is the image of the Esmonds.”

“Madame de Bernstein has her likes and dislikes,” the Countess returned, each phrase clipped, like herbs chopped fine. “Takes up people and forgets people; and she chooses to profess a mighty fancy for this young man. Because she likes him to-day, is that any reason she should like him to-morrow? Before company, and in your aunt’s presence, your ladyship will be as civil as necessary; but in private, I forbid you to see him or encourage him.”

“I don’t care, madam, whether your ladyship forbids me or not!” Fanny burst out, the rebellion rising in her as quick as ferment.

“Very good, Fanny. Then I speak to my lord, and we return to Kensington. If I cannot bring you to reason, your brother will.”

At that point the passage swallowed the rest—either the voices fell, or the listener withdrew. It was only in after days that Madam de Bernstein told Harry part of what she had learned.

For the present, Harry saw only surfaces, and surfaces were smiling. His kinsfolk received him not unkindly. Lady Castlewood was perfectly civil. The young ladies were pleasant, pleased to be amused. My Lord Castlewood—cold, haughty, carved as if from pale stone—was not more reserved toward Harry than toward any of the rest of his household; his silence was distributed with justice. Mr. William was ready to drink with him, to ride with him, to go to races, to play cards; and that coarse, companionable noise—glasses clinking, boots on gravel, laughter too loud—seemed to Harry a sort of welcome, the way men show it when they will not show it softly.

When Harry proposed to go away, they pressed him, one and all, to stay. Madam de Bernstein said nothing of how such eagerness had its own hungers; she did not tell him what schemes he served, what plans he disturbed, whose temper he pricked raw by merely sitting at their table and taking their bread.

So he believed, in his honest way, that he was welcome because they were his blood. He never thought that enemies might share a decanter and offer the hand as if it were friendship; that one might drink from a cup offered with a smile and not taste, beneath the wine’s fruit and oak, the faint bitterness of design. He heard the house’s music—harpsichord, laughter, the domestic clatter of a great family at ease—and did not yet know how often such sound is arranged to cover silence, and how much can be said in England without any word at all.

The second day after Harry Warrington’s coming to Castlewood fell upon a Sunday; and Sunday, in that ancient house, had its own measured way of entering—less by any sudden hush than by a change in the very sounds and smells of the place. The kitchens roused earlier than common: the dull thump of a cleaver on a block, the iron whisper of spits turning, the soft, unhurried speech of women counting eggs and weighing flour by feel. From the court came the steady rasp of a groom’s currycomb, and, beyond the walls, the rooks rehearsed their morning clamor in the elms as if the day itself were a parish tune.

The chapel that belonged to the castle was likewise the village church. A door from the house opened straight into the great state pew where the family sat, raised above the honest benches below, so that the household might pass from corridor to consecration without once crossing the green. Harry, entering with the rest, drew in the scent particular to old churches—stone that had held damp through centuries, beeswax, and a faint ghost of winter smoke—mingled, oddly and homely, with the breakfasting air still clinging to coats and hair: a trace of toasted bread, a last pinch of nutmeg, the sour-sweet tang of ale.

Above, dusty banners drooped from the roof-beams like old stories half-forgotten; and Harry pleased himself with imagining they had once been carried by men of his blood in the Commonwealth wars, those loyal swords whose names were now as mute as the embroidery. Within the altar-rails lay, in marble, the Esmond of King James’s time—square-bearded, red-gowned, forever kneeling on a stone hassock before a great stone desk and book, under a shield of arms painted as if memory itself could be made to last by colour and Latin.

Madame de Bernstein, as a bishop’s widow, never failed attendance. She composed her devotions with a gravity that might have suited the marble ancestor; yet there was life enough in her, too, to observe all the human play of the morning with half an eye, as a housekeeper notes the temper of her servants even while she says her prayers.

The clergyman, Mr. Sampson, tall and high-coloured, read the service in a lively, agreeable voice, giving the Scriptures a point almost theatrical. The organ was touched by one of the young ladies; and the music might have flowed very well indeed, had it not been for an interruption from the servants’ pew—an eruption of laughter checked too late and too clumsily.

For Mr. Warrington’s lacquey Gumbo, hearing the psalm-tune given out, began to sing in a voice so loud and so sweet that heads turned as if pulled by a string. The very air in the church changed at once: the organ’s breath, the clerk’s dutiful droning, the parson’s cadence—all were suddenly made small beside that rich, ringing sound. Harry, who had heard field-songs carried over water in Virginia and hymns flung up in log-chapels, felt the thing in his chest like the stroke of a drum. The London footmen stared, offended out of all propriety; Mr. Sampson himself brought a handkerchief to his mouth. Pleased by the stir he made, Gumbo held on; what began as help turned almost into a solo, and the clerk’s voice was smothered.

The truth was, though Gumbo held the book along with pretty Molly, the porter’s daughter—who had been first to welcome the strangers—he sang by ear and memory, not by note or reading. The black letters before him were no more than marks; the tune was his own inheritance. There was, in that, something both triumphant and melancholy: a tongue of music alive in him while the printed words might as well have been in Greek.

The psalm ended at last; the church settled back into its accustomed noises—the faint creak of pews, a cough stifled in a hand, the rustle of a sleeve—and then came the sermon. Harry, accustomed in his mother’s company to more doctrinal thunder from ministers of a Calvinistic cast, expected a long exhortation; but Mr. Sampson’s was brisk, familiar, and strangely vivid, as though he addressed not saints and sinners in the abstract but neighbours whose faces he knew and whose appetites—of drink, sport, and mischief—he named without shrinking.

He told of an execution he had witnessed after Assizes: a horse-stealer, a man once of good character, with a wife and children who loved him, and the agony of his parting from them. Mr. Sampson painted it so that one might almost smell the crowd—sweat, damp wool, stale beer—and see the cart’s rough boards and the rope’s pale twist. He spoke not in a patchwork of Scripture phrases, but as one man of the world warning others who might be caught by the same slippery pleasures: drinking, card-playing, horse-racing, cock-fighting—the vices of the age, at which he was generously indignant.

He drew the poacher at midnight, the law’s eye watching, traps laid; he galloped the stolen horse over common and highway, from one county into another, with Retribution ever behind—closing, seizing, carrying the man before the justice, never unlocking the manacles until they dropped at the gallows-foot. And then—startlingly—he acted the scene. He leaned, as if to whisper to the criminal at the cart; he dropped his handkerchief so that it fell upon the clerk’s head like a cue in a play. Harry started as it fell. The parson had been in the pulpit more than twenty minutes, and Harry would gladly have heard him for an hour. It seemed to him five minutes, so keenly did the young divine command voice and picture.

The gentlefolks in the great pew were enlivened. Harry, glancing toward the servants, saw them attentive too—especially Gumbo, whose face bore an attitude of intense consternation at the sermon’s talk of traps and law and midnight watchers. But the smockfrocks below took the matter as they took weather: Gaffer Brown and Gammer Jones sat stolid; village lasses in red cloaks and broad hats remained rosy and unmoved.

When the service ended and the organ played them into sunshine, Sir Francis Esmond, temp. Jac. I., still knelt in marble, forever in the same posture, his stone prayer-book as unreadable as Gumbo’s printed page. My lord, before quitting his pew, nodded slightly to the pulpit as the divine’s wig and head rose above the cushion.

“Sampson has been strong to-day,” his lordship said. “He has assaulted the Philistines in great force.”

“Beautiful—beautiful!” Harry cried, his heart warmed by voice and scene.

“Bet five to four it was his Assize sermon,” said Mr. William. “He’s been over to Winton to preach, and to see those dogs.”

Mr. Sampson came out presently in cassock, nodding to the gentlemen who lingered. “Come up and tell us about those dogs,” William called; and the clergyman, laughing, signified assent.

They passed from the church by the gallery that joined it to the house—sacred and domestic stitched together by a covered walk, as if the family meant never to be quite out in the parish air. Mr. Sampson crossed the court to join them and was presented to Harry. He bowed profoundly and hoped Mr. Warrington would benefit by the virtuous example of his European kinsmen. He asked if Harry were related to Sir Miles Warrington of Norfolk—Sir Miles being Harry’s father’s elder brother—and opined it a pity Sir Miles had a son, since the estate was a pretty one and a baronetcy might have sat well upon Harry.

“Tell me about my uncle,” Harry cried.

“Tell us about those dogs!” William demanded in the same breath.

“Two more jolly dogs—two more drunken dogs, saving your presence, Mr. Warrington—than Sir Miles and his son I never saw,” said the chaplain. Sir Miles, he declared, could drink down any man in the county save his son and a few others. “The other dogs Mr. William is anxious about—Heaven hath made him a prey to dogs and all kinds of birds, like the Greeks in the Iliad—”

“I know that line in the Iliad,” Harry said, colouring. “I only know five more—but I know that one.”

His head fell a little as he thought, with an ache like homesickness, of his brother George, who knew the Iliad and the Odyssey and almost every book besides, as if learning were another sense in him.

“What on earth”—William named the place under the earth—“are you talking about now?” he demanded.

Mr. Sampson returned to the hounds, then slipped naturally, as men will, from dogs to horses. William was eager about the Six Year Old Plate at Huntingdon.

“Have you brought news, Parson?”

“The odds are five to four on Brilliant against the field,” the chaplain said gravely, “but mind you—Jason is a good horse.”

“Whose?” asked my lord.

“The Duke of Ancaster’s. By Cartouche out of Miss Langley.”

“Have you horse-races in Virginia, Mr. Warrington?” Mr. Sampson asked, eyes bright.

“Haven’t we!” Harry cried. “But oh—I long to see a good English race.”

“Do you—do you—bet a little?” the chaplain pursued, with a worldly innocence.

“I have done such a thing,” Harry answered, smiling.

“I’ll take Brilliant even against the field, for ponies with you, cousin!” William shouted.

“I’ll give or take three to one against Jason,” said Mr. Sampson.

“I don’t bet on horses I don’t know,” Harry replied, surprised to hear such traffic in odds so soon after that sermon of poachers and manacles.

“Hadn’t you better write home and ask your mother?” William sneered.

“My brother,” my lord said sharply, “our cousin Warrington is free to bet or not as he likes. Have a care, Harry. Will is an old file in spite of his smooth face; and as for Parson Sampson, I defy our ghostly enemy to get the better of him.”

“Him and all his works, my lord,” said Mr. Sampson, with a bow.

The allusion to his mother pricked Harry like a spur. “I’ll tell you what, cousin Will,” he said, “I manage my own affairs in my own way, without asking any lady to arrange them for me. I make my own bets upon my own judgment. But as I am your guest—and, no doubt, you mean to show me hospitality—I’ll take your bet. There. Done and done.”

“Done,” William said, looking askance. “It’s the regular odds in the paper, of course?”

“Well—no—it isn’t,” William muttered; then, forced, “The odds are five to four; you may have them, if you like.”

“Nay— a bet is a bet,” Harry returned. “And I take you too, Mr. Sampson.”

“Three to one against Jason. I lay it. Very good,” said the chaplain.

“Is it ponies too, Mr. Chaplain?” Harry asked, with an air as if he carried all Lombard Street in his pocket.

“No, no. Thirty to ten. It is enough for a poor priest to win.”

Here goes, Harry thought, a great slice out of my quarter’s hundred. Yet pride would not let him draw back. He had not begun the quarrel, but for the honour of Old Virginia he would not seem afraid.

When the bargains were made, William went away scowling toward the stables, where he liked to smoke with the grooms. The brisk parson went to pay his court to the ladies and to partake of the Sunday dinner that was preparing. Lord Castlewood and Harry remained together for a while.

Since Harry’s arrival, my lord had scarcely spoken with him. He was perfectly friendly in manner, yet so silent that he would sit at the head of his table and leave it without uttering a word, as if words were coin and he hoarded them. Now, in this pause between chapel and dinner, he spoke at last with an ease that was almost careless.

“I suppose yonder property of yours is a fine one by this time?” he asked.

“I reckon it’s almost as big as an English county,” Harry answered, “and the land’s as good too—for many things.” He would not have Virginia, nor his share in it, underrated.

“Indeed!” My lord’s look sharpened with surprise. “When it belonged to my father it did not yield much.”

“Pardon me, my lord. You know how it belonged to your father,” Harry cried with spirit. “It was because my grandfather did not choose to claim his right.”

“Of course—of course,” my lord said hastily.

“I mean,” Harry continued, “we of the Virginian house owe you nothing but our own—but our own, and the hospitality you are now showing me.”

“You are heartily welcome to both,” said my lord. “You were hurt by the betting just now?”

Harry hesitated, then spoke with the sudden plainness of his country. “Well—I am sort o’ hurt. Your welcome is different to our welcome, and that’s the fact. At home we’re glad to see a man, hold out a hand, and give him of our best. Here you take us in, give us beef and claret enough, to be sure—and don’t seem to care when we come, or when we go. That’s the remark I’ve been making since I’ve been here. I can’t help telling it out now it’s on my mind; and I think I’m a little easier now I’ve said it.”

As if to cover the heat in his cheeks, he knocked a billiard-ball across the table with a sharp click that echoed in the room, and then laughed, looking up at his elder kinsman.

“A la bonne heure!” my lord said. “We are cold to the stranger within and without our gates. We don’t take Mr. Harry Warrington into our arms and cry when we see our cousin. We don’t cry when he goes away—but do we pretend?”

“No,” Harry answered. “But you try to get the better of him in a bet.”

“Is there no such practice in Virginia? Do not sporting men there try to overreach one another? What was that story I heard you telling our aunt—of the British officers and Tom somebody of Spotsylvania?”

“That’s fair!” Harry cried. “It’s usual practice; a stranger must look out. I don’t mind the parson; if he wins, he may have it, and welcome. But a relation! To think my own blood cousin wants money out of me!”

“A Newmarket man would get the better of his father,” my lord replied. “My brother has been on the turf since he rode over to it from Cambridge. If you play at cards with him—and he will, if you let him—he will beat you if he can.”

“Well, I’m ready!” Harry cried. “I’ll play any game with him I know, or I’ll jump with him, or ride with him, or row with him, or wrestle with him, or shoot with him—there—now.”

Lord Castlewood was amused; he offered his hand. “Anything—but don’t fight with him,” he said.

“If I do, I’ll whip him—hanged if I don’t!” Harry burst out; and then, seeing my lord’s surprise and displeasure, he recollected himself as if a cold cloth had been laid upon his brow. “A hundred pardons, my lord,” he said, flushing deep. He seized his cousin’s hand. “I talked of ill manners, being angry and hurt. ’Tis doubly ill-mannered of me to show anger, and boast of prowess to my own host. It’s not the practice with us Americans to boast—believe me, it’s not.”

“You are the first I ever met,” said my lord, smiling. “I take you at your word. And I give you fair warning about the cards and betting—that is all, my boy.”

“Leave a Virginian alone,” Harry returned stoutly. “We are a match for most men—we are.”

My lord’s smile did not broaden. His eyebrows arched a moment, his grey eyes went down as if he listened to something within. “So you can bet fifty guineas and afford to lose them? So much the better for you. Those great Virginian estates yield a great revenue, do they?”

“More than sufficient for all of us—for ten times as many as we are now,” Harry said; and even as he spoke he suspected he was being sounded, as a man sounds a cask by tapping.

“And your mother makes her son and heir a handsome allowance?”

“As much as ever I choose to draw, my lord!” Harry answered quickly.

“Peste! I wish I had such a mother,” my lord said. “But I have only the advantage of a stepmother, and she draws me. There is the dinner-bell. Shall we go into the eating-room?”

Taking Harry’s arm, he led him in where the meal waited; and there the day’s piety, which had rung out in psalm and organ, took its second shape—meat and wine, the old sacrament of the table.

If the chapel had smelled of stone and wax, the dining-room was a warmer creed: roast beef giving up its fat in a fragrant sigh as the knife went through; gravy dark as polished walnut; bread with a crackling crust and a soft, steaming heart; claret breathing from decanters; and, beneath it all, the steady background of the house—fire ticking in the grate, plate set down and lifted, chairs shifting, voices weaving in and out like a reel.

Mr. Sampson proved the delight of the entertainment. Besides being chaplain to his lordship, he preached in London at the new chapel in Mayfair, endowed by my Lady Whittlesea; and he brought with him the choicest stories of clubs and coteries, the newest scandals—who had run away with whom—the last bon-mot of Mr. Selwyn, the wild bet of March and Rockingham; how the old King had quarrelled with Madame Walmoden; how a duke was suspected of a new love; who stood in favour at Carlton House with the Princess of Wales; and who had been hanged last Monday, and how well he behaved in the cart. He seasoned all with such plain terms and lively jokes as made Harry stare; fresh from the colonies, he was unused to these London elegances, where a man might preach damnation in the morning and laugh over vice at dinner as easily as he dipped bread into sauce.

The ladies laughed quite cheerfully. They did not play at being shocked; they had, like the house itself, their established measures of what was proper, and Mr. Sampson’s breezy worldliness sat upon those measures as naturally as pepper upon beef.

In due time the chapel bell clinked for afternoon service, summoning Mr. Sampson away for half an hour. There was no sermon then; he would be back before they were far into a bottle of Burgundy. Mr. Will called for a fresh one; the chaplain tossed off a glass and ran out. Ere the half-hour was done, he was back again, bawling cheerfully for another bottle. The business of salvation, it seemed, could be accomplished briskly when dinner was waiting.

When they rose from table, they returned to the ladies, and the card-tables were set out as they were for many hours each day. The whole party engaged. Madame de Bernstein could beat any of them at piquet; there was only the chaplain in the circle who proved at all her match. In this easy fashion the Sabbath slipped away, not in silence but in the steady click of pasteboard, the soft scold and laughter of players, the occasional call for wine, and—always—beneath it, the great house’s own music: distant servants’ feet, a door drawn to, the muted creak of beams, the rooks outside keeping their rough chorale over the trees.

The evening was beautiful; someone proposed a cool tankard and a game of whist in a summer-house. But the company voted to sit indoors. The ladies declared the aspect of three honours in the hand, and a few good court-cards, more beautiful than the loveliest scene of nature; and so the sun went down behind the elms while they still bent over their hands. The rooks came home cawing their evensong, and no one stirred save to change partners. The chapel clock tolled hour after hour unheeded. The moon and stars came out, pale and patient at the windows, and at nine the groom of the chambers announced supper.

They sat again to food and drink—lighter fare now, but still abundant—and as they ate, the postboy’s horn was heard twanging as he trotted into the village with his letter-bag: a thin, bright sound that cut through the comfortable room like a reed-pipe across a dance. My lord’s bag was brought in; he set the letters aside and opened his newspaper.

He smiled at a paragraph, looked at Harry, and handed the sheet to William, who by this time was very comfortable from good luck at the tables and a great deal of liquor.

“Read that, Will,” said my lord.

William read the line pointed out, and burst into an exclamation that made the ladies cry out at once.

“Gracious heavens, William! What has happened?”

“Mercy, child, why do you swear so dreadfully?” his fond mamma asked.

“What’s the matter?” inquired Madame de Bernstein, dozing after her usual punch and beer.

“Read it, Parson!” William cried, thrusting the paper at the chaplain, his face fierce as a Turk’s.

“Bit—by the Lord!” roared Mr. Sampson, dashing the paper down.

“Cousin Harry, you are in luck,” my lord said, taking up the sheet and reading aloud. “The Six Year Old Plate at Huntingdon was won by Jason, beating Brilliant, Pytho, and Ginger. The odds were five to four on Brilliant against the field, three to one against Jason, seven to two against Pytho, and twenty to one against Ginger.”

“I owe you a half-year’s income of my poor living, Mr. Warrington,” groaned the chaplain. “I will pay when my noble patron settles with me.”

“A curse upon the luck!” William growled. “That comes of betting on a Sunday”—and he took consolation in another great bumper.

“Nay, cousin Will—it was but in jest,” Harry cried, startled by how sharp pleasure and displeasure could taste in the same mouthful. “I can’t think of taking my cousin’s money.”

“Curse me, sir, do you suppose, if I lose, I can’t pay?” William cried. “That I want to be beholden to any man alive? That is a good joke. Isn’t it, Parson?”

“I think I have heard better,” Mr. Sampson replied; and William, with an oath, called for another bowl.

Let us hope the ladies did not remain for that last replenishment; for it was plain enough that in Castlewood, even on Sunday, the day’s holy sounds—the organ’s breath, the chapel bell, the posthorn’s twang—must compete with the hard bright music of cards, and with wine poured again and again until speech grew louder and meaning, like a language unspoken for too long, began to fray at the edges.

Harry Warrington, having won money from his cousin Will and from Mr. Sampson the chaplain, held himself—by a queer gentleman’s logic—obliged to offer them the means of winning it back. If Madam Esmond could have heard how that duty was discharged, she would have called it anything but duty. Cards, in that house, were as regular as the bell.

After the early dinner—served at three, with the lids lifted from dishes as solemnly as if they were opening a ceremony—there would be whist or quadrille with the ladies. The table smelled of beeswax and warmed baize; the candles sweated; the air carried the mingled savour of roast, extinguished by tea, and then revived by wine. The women’s laughter and the dry click of counters went on till supper. And then, when the family withdrew, and the long passages settled into their night-sounds—the last footfall of a maid, a door softly complaining on its hinge, a far-off clink from the pantry—Mr. Will would come stealing across to Harry’s quarters with a dice-box and a bottle of rum, as if he were bringing contraband spices.

There, with Hal and the chaplain, he would sit till dawn, the dice rattling like hail on a shutter, the glasses set down with little thuds upon the wood, and the talk rising and falling with that nocturnal boldness which men mistake for wit. The ladies had extracted from Cousin Will a thousand promises—he would not lead the Virginian into mischief, he would keep out of it himself. Will gave his word with the same ease that he shuffled a pack: light, quick, and meant to be handled again.

Harry had not meant to mislead Lord Castlewood when he spoke of his mother’s estate in America. He was honest by nature; but honesty, in a young man, does not always include a clear measure of what others will hear. At home, he had grown up among a rough plenty—horse-jockeys, tavern loungers, sporting men, card-players—such company as a tobacco colony breeds when its gentlemen have land, slaves to work it, and long evenings to fill. Their amusements were the hunt, the punch-bowl, the table where money slid from one hand to another like a dish passed at supper. Hospitality was without fence or lock: a neighbour’s house might as well have been your own, and the same venison, corn, and drink stood ready behind cracked windows and tumble-down rails. Harry had slept on straw mattresses that smelled of summer hay and old sweat; he had watched the sunrise come in through broken shutters while the last bowl of claret-punch sat emptied and sticky, the nutmeg grating still perfuming the air, and outside the hounds already giving tongue, impatient for daylight.

His brother George, he owned with a kind of shame, had been made of soberer stuff—books and tea rather than a gallop and Burgundy. Nature mixes her families so. Harry’s tastes showed themselves quickly in Hampshire. His English cousins did not love Puritan discipline; and if Harry was no milksop, they liked him the better. Manners were looser then; tongues freer; things were named and done that later generations would not bear to hear. The house, in its own way, was as indulgent as any Virginian hall, only the indulgence wore cleaner linen.

And yet Harry, keen-eyed under his good humour, suspected that his cousins meant to draw him out—pump him, as he phrased it—about his affairs. So he kept his counsel. In sport and chance he was no novice. At cards he met them with an easy hand; at backgammon and piquet he learned their English turns without losing his Virginian quickness. Even at billiards—“the noble game,” my lord called it—he held his own after a few days. His grandfather in Virginia had owned one of the few tables in the province; the green cloth, the balls, the chalk, were not foreign mysteries to Harry. Mr. Will, who beat him at first, found he could not keep him under long; and Will confessed, with a grudging respect, that the American was his match in most things and his better in many.

There was one contest, however, in which Harry often came off second—especially with one of the ladies. He was profoundly courteous to any creature in petticoats; that tradition has not yet left his country. Every woman in the Castlewood establishment softened towards him. The grim housekeeper unbent; the fat cook beamed, her hands always smelling of onion and thyme; the waiting-maids, French and English, smirked and giggled when he passed; even the porter’s pretty daughter at the lodge had always a shy, kind word ready. Madame de Bernstein said little, but watched much, and in her silence there was the sharpness of a knife laid aside, ready to be taken up again.

As for Lady Maria Esmond—who could say her age? In those days, peerage-books were fewer, and truth about women’s years was a thing handled like hot sugar. Will said she was five-and-thirty; he was abusive, and liked exaggeration. Maria was Will’s half-sister; she and my lord were children of the late Earl’s first wife, a German lady married in Queen Anne’s wars. Baron Bernstein—who married Maria’s Aunt Beatrix, Bishop Tusher’s widow—was German too, a Hanoverian nobleman and kin to the first Lady Castlewood. If Lady Maria had been born under George the First, and if George the Second had sat thirty years upon the throne, how could she be seven-and-twenty, as she told Harry? Yet she would say to him, when they were alone, in that voice that made every commonplace sound like confidence:

“I am old, child. I am a hundred years old. I am seven-and-twenty. I might be your mother almost.”

And Harry, with a boy’s heat and a man’s awkward daring, would answer, “Your ladyship might be the mother of all the Cupids, I am sure. You don’t look twenty, upon my word you do not!”

Lady Maria looked any age one wished—an easy, dazzling beauty with white-and-red complexion, fair hair in abundance, and round white arms shown to uncommon advantage when she played at billiards with Cousin Harry. When she leaned across the table for a stroke, the green cloth rising like a little field under her, Harry would catch sight of an ankle, a clocked stocking, a black satin slipper with a red heel—details small as spices, yet burning on the tongue of his mind. It filled him with a rapture he could not name without making himself ridiculous. And yet—foolish Harry—his own mother’s foot was slighter, shorter, finer. But boys do not look at their mothers’ slippers with rapture; they look where their blood tells them to look.

Lady Maria could be very kind when they were alone; and before her sister, aunt, stepmother, she made light of him—called him a chit, a simpleton, mimicked his Virginian accent with cruel exactness. Harry would blush and try to mend his intonation, coached by his English monitresses. “We shall make a pretty fellow of you,” his aunt said, as if she were seasoning a dish and knew the proper pinch.

Lord Castlewood, since that Sunday talk between them, became more familiar with Harry. Until the crops were off, there was little sport—an occasional cock-match at Winchester, a bull-baiting at Hexton Fair. Harry and Will rode out to fairs and races; Harry was shown, like a new coin passed from hand to hand, among county families—the Henleys of the Grange, the Crawleys of Queen’s Crawley, the Redmaynes of Lionsden. The neighbours came in their heavy coaches and stayed two or three days, eating, drinking, playing cards, and filling the house with the sound of wheels in the court, servants running, doors opening and shutting, and the constant clatter of plates. More would have come, but for the family’s fear of Madame de Bernstein. She disliked country company; their talk annoyed her; their laughter seemed to her too loud, their compliments too slow.

“We shall be merrier when my aunt leaves us,” the young folks whispered. “We have cause to be civil. You know what a favourite she was with our papa. She got him his earldom—she was very well at Court then, with the King and Queen. She commands here naturally—perhaps too much. We are all afraid of her. Even my elder brother stands in awe of her; and my stepmother is far more obedient to her than ever she was to my papa, whom she ruled with a rod of iron. But Castlewood is merrier when our aunt is not here. At least we have more company. You will come in our gay days, Harry—won’t you? Of course you will. This is your home, sir. I was so pleased—oh, so pleased—when my brother said he considered it your home!”

A soft hand accompanied the speech; blue eyes, well preserved, looked extremely friendly. Harry grasped her hand with ardour. He did not know what privilege cousinship might claim, only he was timid, and timidity made him honest in a way boldness never is. He had thought the English cold and selfish. How mistaken! How kind they were—especially the Earl, and dear, dear Maria. He longed to recall the first letter he had sent to his mother and Mrs. Mountain, in which he had hinted that his welcome was cool. My lord promised to introduce him in London, present him at Court, take him to White’s. Castlewood was to be his English home. Harry wrote all this with contrition in a second despatch to Virginia, adding—since his spelling was not yet the most exact of accomplishments—that “My cousin, the Lady Maria, is a perfect Angle.”

“Ille praeter omnes angulus ridet,” muttered little Mr. Dempster, at home in Virginia, wincing at the word as if it were a bone in the throat.

“The child can’t be falling in love with his angle!” cried Mrs. Mountain.

“Pooh, pooh! my niece Maria is forty!” said Madam Esmond. “I perfectly well recollect her—a great, gawky, carroty creature, with a foot like a pair of bellows.”

Where truth lies in such matters, who knows? Beauty is half the eye that beholds it, and half the tale that the heart repeats until it believes. The same face can be a paragon or a caricature depending on who tastes it—like wine that is nectar to one and vinegar to another.

Not only was Harry a favourite in the drawing-room and among the ladies of the servants’ hall; like master, like man, his valet Gumbo found himself admired in every corner. Gumbo had a hundred accomplishments. He could fish, hunt, shoe a horse, handle iron like a blacksmith. He dressed hair beautifully and improved himself under my lord’s Swiss gentleman, learning the little refinements of powder and ribbon as if they were sauces and garnishes. He was a cook of note in his own fashion—famous for Virginian dishes, and eager to steal new secrets from my lord’s French man. One day he would be roasting and basting with a patience that would shame a priest, the fat hissing and sending up its rich animal scent; another he would be stirring a pot with herbs bruised between his fingers, lifting the lid and sniffing as if the steam were a message. He sang exquisitely at church, and sang secular songs too—often inventing airs and rude words in the manner of his people. He played the fiddle so charmingly that he set the girls dancing in Castlewood Hall, and at the Three Castles in the village he was always welcome to a mug of ale—gratis—if he would but bring the fiddle. He loved to play for the village children, and the sound of his bow in the twilight—bright as a bird-call—made even the yard-dogs cease their barking. In a countryside where most music was measured by church bells and the groan of cartwheels, Gumbo’s fiddle seemed a new weather. It softened the house’s usual noises: the clank of kitchen-pots, the slap of wet linen, the scold of a cook; it made the place, for an hour, feel less like a machine of rank and more like a hearth.

The servants, who were no fools, soon perceived that Gumbo was a liar. The day at church when he pretended to read from Molly’s psalm-book, he sang quite other words than those printed there—he could not decipher a syllable. When he pretended to understand written music, the Swiss valet brought him some; Gumbo turned the page upside down. Such long-bow practice occurred daily and was patent to all; they did not think much the worse of him, because they liked him. But they did not know how great a liar he was—how vast a map of invention he carried in his head—and because they liked to believe, they believed.

Whatever wonder and envy he may have felt at first beholding Castlewood’s English comforts, Gumbo kept his sentiments to himself and examined park, stables, appointments coolly, as if he were judging a market. The horses were very well, he said—what there were of them—but at Castlewood in Virginia they had six times as many, and fourteen—eighteen—grooms to tend them. Madam Esmond’s carriages were much finer than my lord’s; a great deal more gold on the panels. Her gardens covered acres; they grew every kind of flower and fruit under the sun. Pineapples and peaches? So common they were given to pigs. They had twenty—forty—gardeners, not white gardeners, all black gentlemen like himself. In the house were twenty—forty—gentlemen in livery, besides women-servants; fifty women-servants, he thought, all Madam Esmond’s property, worth ever so many hundred pieces of eight apiece. A piece of eight was bigger than a guinea. Madam Esmond had twenty—thirty—thousand guineas a year, rooms full of gold and plate. She came to England in one of her ships; she had ever so many ships, Gumbo could not count them. Estates reached a week’s journey, all tobacco and negroes. Was Master Harry heir to all this? Of course—now Master George was killed and scalped by the Indians. Gumbo had killed ever so many Indians, tried to save Master George, but he was Master Harry’s boy—and Master Harry was as rich as ever he liked. He wore black because Master George was dead; but in Bristol were chests full of gold clothes and lace and jewels. Master Harry was the richest man in all Virginia and might have twenty—sixty—servants; only he liked traveling with one best, and that one was Gumbo.

This tale was not invented at once. It was coaxed out in draughts, like a stew that thickens the longer it simmers. Gumbo contradicted himself a little at first, but after he had told it twice or thrice in the servants’ hall or in the butler’s private room, he knew his story as a cook knows the order of courses. He could name precisely the number of Madam Esmond’s slaves and the amount of her income. There was, after all, a seed of truth: American establishments did swarm with servants, and a Virginian house could hold more negroes than an English one held men and maids.

Gumbo’s account travelled upward, borne like kitchen-smell up a staircase: from servants to valets, from waiting-women to their ladies. It reached my lord and Madame de Bernstein, and, in the retelling, lost nothing—except perhaps modesty. A young gentleman in England is not less liked for being thought heir to vast wealth. When Lady Castlewood heard of Harry’s prodigious expectations, she repented of her first coolness—repented too of having pinched her daughter’s arm black-and-blue for stretching it out too kindly towards the Virginian. Was it too late to coax him back into those fair arms? Lady Fanny was welcome to try; she resumed her dancing lessons, and the Countess would play the music with all her heart. But—how provoking—Lady Maria would always insist on being in the room; and as sure as Fanny walked in the garden or park, so sure would Maria come trailing after her, as if the elder sister’s shadow had learned to move of its own will.

Madame de Bernstein laughed at the rumours of the prodigious fortune. She knew her half-sister’s man of business in London and likely the real state of Madam Esmond’s money; but she did not contradict Gumbo’s splendid inventions. She was diverted by the way they altered the Castlewood family’s behaviour, as if a new dialect had been introduced into the house: the language of deference, sweetened and enlarged when money was supposed to be in the room.

“Hang him! Is he so rich, Molly?” said my lord to his elder sister. “Then good-bye to our chances with your aunt. The Baroness will be sure to leave him all her money to spite us—and because he doesn’t want it. Nevertheless, the lad is a good lad enough; and it’s not his fault being rich.”

“He is very simple and modest in his habits for one so wealthy,” Maria remarked.
