“Rich people often are,” my lord said. “If I were rich I often think I should be the greatest miser, live in rags and on a crust. There is no pleasure so enduring as money-getting. It grows on you, and increases with old age. But because I am as poor as Lazarus, I dress in purple and fine linen, and fare sumptuously every day.”

Maria went to the book-room and fetched the History of Virginia, by R. B. Gent, and read of its admirable climate; how fruit and corn grew there; how noble rivers—the Potomac, the Rappahannoc—abounded in fish. She wondered whether the climate would agree with her; whether Harry’s mother would like her. Harry declared his mother would adore her—so would Mountain. When asked of the number of servants at home, he said they certainly had more than in England—he did not know how many; the negroes did not do near as much work as English servants, hence the need of keeping so many. When some of Gumbo’s details were brought to him, he laughed and said the boy was wonderful as a romancer and, in telling such stories, was only trying to speak out for the honour of the family.

His denials, being modest, only served to confirm the others in their belief. More and more Lady Castlewood and the ladies grew affectionate. More and more Mr. Will betted with him and offered him bargains. Harry’s simple dress and equipage—one servant, no horses or carriage of his own—seemed to them not poverty but an almost heroic restraint. When he went to London, of course he would cut a better figure; Castlewood would introduce him at St. James’s; he would appear as he ought. Mr. Sampson, the chaplain, became more lively, wicked, obsequious than ever—so eager to show Harry “a little of London life,” to warn rogues off him and keep him out of harm. Everyone was kind. Harry liked the respect paid to him; as Madam Esmond’s son, he thought it perhaps his due, and, never having seen any place but his own province, took for granted he was the personage his family imagined. So from Castlewood House to Castlewood village, and thence through the county, it became a settled fancy that Mr. Harry Esmond Warrington was heir to immense wealth and a gentleman of great importance—because his negro valet told lies about him in the servants’ hall.

After a week or two, Harry’s aunt, Madame de Bernstein, began to tire of Castlewood, its inhabitants, and the neighbours who visited. She tired of most things sooner or later. She nodded and slept over the chaplain’s stories; dozed at her whist and over her dinner. She grew snappish, sarcastic, hitting out at my lord, at Will the jockey, at the ladies widowed and unmarried, who winced and bore it. The cook, once praised, now gave no satisfaction; the wine was corked; the house damp and draughty; doors would not shut; chimneys smoked. She declared the Tunbridge waters necessary, and ordered the doctor from Hexton to order them for her benefit.

“I wish to heaven she would go!” growled my lord, the most independent of the family. “She may go to Tunbridge, or Bath, or Jericho for me.”

“Shall Fanny and I come with you to Tunbridge, dear Baroness?” asked Lady Castlewood.

“Not for worlds, my dear! The doctor orders me absolute quiet; if you came I should have the knocker going all day, and Fanny’s lovers would never be out of the house,” replied the Baroness, weary of her sister-in-law’s company.

“I wish I could be of any service to my aunt,” said sentimental Lady Maria, demurely.

“My good child, what can you do? You cannot play piquet so well as my maid; and I have heard all your songs till I am perfectly tired of them! One of the gentlemen might go with me—at least make the journey, and see me safe from highwaymen.”

“I’m sure, ma’am, I shall be glad to ride with you,” said Mr. Will quickly.

“Oh, not you! I don’t want you, William,” cried his aunt. “Why do you not offer? Where are your American manners, you ungracious Harry Warrington? Don’t swear, Will. Harry is much better company than you are, and much better ton too, sir.”

“Ton, indeed! Confound his ton,” Will muttered to himself, sour as stale beer.

“I dare say I shall be tired of him, as I am of other folks,” Madame de Bernstein went on. “I have scarcely seen Harry at all these last days. You shall ride with me to Tunbridge, Harry!”

At the direct appeal—more to no one’s wonder than to the Baroness’s—Harry blushed, hemmed, hawed, and at last said, “I have promised my cousin Castlewood to go over to Hexton Petty Sessions with him to-morrow. He thinks I should see how the courts here are conducted—and—and—the partridge-shooting will soon begin, and I have promised to be here for that, ma’am.”

As he spoke, he grew red as a poppy. Lady Maria kept her meek face down and plied her needle with nimble diligence, the small sound of the thread drawn through cloth oddly loud in the sudden hush.

“You actually refuse to go with me to Tunbridge Wells?” cried Madame de Bernstein, her eyes flashing and her face flushing with anger.

“Not to ride with you, ma’am; that I will do with all my heart,” Harry said, striving to be respectful and firm. “But to stay there—I have promised—”

Harry Warrington’s refusal—sharp as a knife turned in a hand that had grown used to wielding it—fell upon Madame de Bernstein so suddenly that rage was her only seasoning for the moment. She flashed two eyes like struck flint at Lady Fanny and Lady Castlewood as she swept out. Lady Maria, behind her tambour-frame, scarcely lifted her sandy lashes; her needle went on pricking silk with the calm persistence of a kitchen clock that keeps time whether there’s a storm outside or none.

Between mother and daughter there passed those looks that speak louder than a viol in a drawing-room when the house has gone quiet. Fanny tried on puzzlement as if it were a borrowed lace cap; it sat ill. Had she been guilty, she would have made innocence as neat and finished as a trussed bird. Lady Castlewood’s glare promised a private reckoning later—smiles first, claws afterwards, as in households where public breeding is kept like silver: polished for company, locked away for use.

“So you don’t fancy going with the old lady to Tunbridge Wells?” Lady Castlewood said at last to Harry, her mouth simpering as if it had been taught good manners by a dancing-master, though the eyes behind it were all accounts and reckonings.

“And small blame to our cousin!” my lord broke in, and for one instant Maria’s head rose from the tambour, as if a familiar sound—some phrase, some cadence of power—had crossed her ear like the distant cry of hounds. “A young fellow must not have it all idling and holiday. Let him mix up something useful with his pleasures. Mr. Warrington has to conduct a great estate in America: let him see how ours in England are carried on. Will hath shown him the kennel and the stables; and the games in vogue, which, I think, cousin, you seem to play as well as your teachers. After harvest we will show him a little English fowling and shooting; in winter we will take him out a-hunting. Though there has been a coolness between us and our aunt-kinswoman in Virginia, we are of the same blood. Ere we send our cousin back to his mother, let us show him what an English gentleman’s life at home is. I should like to read with him as well as sport with him; and that is why I have been pressing him of late to stay and bear me company.”

He spoke with a frankness so well-cooked—clear, unclouded, carrying no visible spice of guile—that his mother-in-law and his half-brother and sister could not tell what dish lay hidden beneath. In that house they were used to little cabals, like servants whispering over the range when the master had stepped out; but when Castlewood chose this open tone, his meaning might not be tasted until months had passed. He did not say, This is true. He said, This shall be believed in my family. So it became, at once, a thing convenu: my Lord Castlewood had a laudable desire to cultivate domestic affections, to educate and amuse and improve his young relative; he had taken a great fancy to the lad; he wished Harry to stay.

Down a corridor hung with tapestries that muffled footfalls and swallowed laughter as bread swallows gravy, William drew his mother and sister aside.

“What is Castlewood’s game now?” he asked; and then, with a click as of a latch lifted, “Stop! By George, I have it!”

“What, William?”

“He intends to get him to play, and to win the Virginia estate back from him. That’s what it is!”

“But the lad has not got the Virginia estate to pay, if he loses,” Lady Castlewood said, her voice thin with calculation.

“If my brother has not some scheme in view, may I be—”

“Hush! Of course he has a scheme in view. But what is it?”

“He can’t mean Maria—Maria is as old as Harry’s mother,” Will mused; then, with the cruelty of a man who knows where to tap the bruise, “Pooh! with her old face and sandy hair and freckled skin! Impossible!” Lady Fanny sighed, though she tried to make it sound like scorn.

“Of course, your ladyship had a fancy for the Iroquois, too!” mamma snapped, in that tone which could sour milk at ten paces.

“I trust I know my station and duty better, madam! If I had liked him, that is no reason why I should marry him. Your ladyship hath taught me as much as that.”

“My Lady Fanny!”

“I am sure you married our papa without liking him. You have told me so a thousand times!”

“And if you did not love our father before marriage, you certainly did not fall in love with him afterwards,” Will broke in, laughing with the easy brutality of a man who never has to pay the reckoning for the household’s peace. “Fan and I remember how our honoured parents used to fight. Don’t us, Fan? And our brother Esmond kept the peace.”

“Don’t recall those dreadful low scenes, William!” cried Lady Castlewood. “When your father took too much drink, he was like a madman; and his conduct should be a warning to you, sir, who are fond of the same horrid practice.”

“I am sure, madam, you were not much the happier for marrying the man you did not like, and your ladyship’s title hath brought very little along with it,” Lady Fanny whimpered, stung into boldness. “What is the use of a coronet with the jointure of a tradesman’s wife?—how many of them are richer than we are? There is come lately to live in our Square, at Kensington, a grocer’s widow from London Bridge, whose daughters have three gowns where I have one; and who, though they are waited on but by a man and a couple of maids, I know eat and drink a thousand times better than we do with our scraps of cold meat on our plate, and our great flaunting, trapesing, impudent, lazy lacqueys!”

The complaint—so oddly domestic, so sharply gustatory—made the gallery itself seem to smell of yesterday’s beef, of congealed fat and vinegar too thin to wake it. One could almost hear the scrape of dull knives on pewter, the sigh of the household when a joint is carried out more bone than blessing. The acoustics of poverty were there: not silence, but the wrong kinds of sounds—lacqueys’ insolent heels, empty plates set down too hard to seem full, the rustle of gowns that could not afford to be careless.

“He! he! glad I dine at the palace, and not at home!” said Mr. Will. Through his aunt’s interest with Count Puffendorff, Groom of the Royal (and Serene Electoral) Powder-Closet, he had one of the many small court-crumbs—Deputy Powder—so that even his vanity smelled faintly of starch, pomatum, and the powdered air of a prince’s antechamber.

“Why should I not be happy without any title except my own?” Lady Frances persisted. “Many people are. I dare say they are even happy in America.”

“Yes!—with a mother-in-law who is a perfect Turk and Tartar, for all I hear—with Indian war-whoops howling all around you, and with a danger of losing your scalp, or of being eat up by a wild beast every time you went to church.”

“I wouldn’t go to church,” said Lady Fanny, pettishly.

“You’d go with anybody who asked you, Fan!” roared Will. “And so would old Maria, and so would any woman, that’s the fact.” He laughed at his own wit, loud enough to be heard through the hangings.

It was then that Madame de Bernstein’s head and shoulders appeared at the tapestried door, as if she had been listening all along and now chose to step into the very steam of their quarrel. The door fell back behind her with a soft hush, as cloth shuts on secrets.

“Pray, good folks, what is all your merriment about?” she asked.

Will told her, grinning, that his mother and sister had been having a fight—no novelty—because Fanny wanted to marry their cousin, the wild Indian, and Lady Castlewood would not let her. Fanny protested, coloring, that since the very first day her mother had warned her not to speak to the young gentleman, she had scarcely exchanged two words with him. She knew her station better. She did not want to be scalped by wild Indians, or eaten by bears.

Madame de Bernstein looked from one to the other, and the look was that of a woman tasting a sauce and finding in it a spice she had not put there herself.

“If he is not staying for you, for whom is he staying?” she asked. “At the houses to which he has been carried, you have taken care not to show him a woman that is not a fright or in the nursery; and I think the boy is too proud to fall in love with a dairymaid, Will.”

“Humph! That is a matter of taste, ma’am,” Mr. William said, with a shrug.

“Of Mr. William Esmond’s taste, as you say; but not of yonder boy’s. The Esmonds of his grandfather’s nurture, sir, would not go a-courting in the kitchen.”

“Well, ma’am, every man to his taste. A fellow might go farther and fare worse than my brother’s servants’ hall; and besides Fan, there’s only the maids or old Maria to choose from.”

“Maria! Impossible!”

Yet as she said it, the very word seemed to open a drawer in Madame de Bernstein’s mind where old recollections lay folded, scented, and dangerous. She had seen boys made fools by women old enough to be their aunts; she had heard the town’s whispered talk in doorways where the sound carries, in salons where laughter is arranged like a dessert course and the truth served under sugar. She remembered how often Harry had been absent of late—absences she had lazily salted down as field-sports. She remembered how often, when he was away, Lady Maria too had vanished from her tambour and her quiet corner. Walks under clipped hedges; pauses in cool avenues where leaves make a small sea-sound; garden temples where whispers gather and do not fly; hands that meet in twilight corridors, as accidentally as spoons touch in a crowded dish; glances exchanged on stairs like stolen sweetmeats. Madame’s fancy—trained by experience, sharpened by a lifetime of being spoken of—served all these images at once.

“Impossible, ma’am! I don’t know,” Will went on. “My mother warned Fan off him.”

“Oh, your mother did warn Fanny off?” Madame asked, as if she were innocently stirring a pot.

“Certainly, my dear Baroness!”

“Didn’t she? Didn’t she pinch Fanny’s arm black-and-blue? Didn’t they fight about it?”

“Nonsense, William! For shame, William!” cried both ladies together, as if the same whip had cracked over them.

“And now, since we have heard how rich he is, perhaps it is sour grapes, that is all. And now, since he is warned off the young bird, perhaps he is hunting the old one, that’s all. Impossible—why impossible? You know old Lady Suffolk, ma’am?”

“William, how can you speak about Lady Suffolk to your aunt?” Lady Castlewood cried.

A grin—half impudence, half a boy’s delight in naming forbidden things—passed over Will’s face. “Because Lady Suffolk was a special favourite at Court? Well, other folks have succeeded her.”

“Sir!” Madame de Bernstein cried. She may have had reasons, private and exquisitely sharp, to dislike such a hint.

“So they have, I say; or who, pray, is my Lady Yarmouth now? And didn’t old Lady Suffolk go and fall in love with George Berkeley, and marry him when she was ever so old? Nay, ma’am—if I remember right, and we hear a deal of town-talk at our table—Harry Estridge went mad about your ladyship when you were somewhat rising twenty; and would have changed your name a third time if you would but have let him.”

That last allusion—so notorious that it had long since passed from scandal into common vocabulary—did not anger Madame as the former had done. On the contrary, it warmed her, as a remembered cordial warms the chest on a cold day. She played her pretty little hand upon the table, and her mind, no doubt, went visiting mad young Harry Estridge.

“Au fait,” she said, musing, “’tis not impossible, William, that old folks, and young folks too, should play the fool.”

“But I can’t understand a young fellow being in love with Maria,” Will persisted, “however he might be with you, ma’am. That’s oter shose, as our French tutor used to say. You remember the Count, ma’am; he! he!—and so does Maria!”

“William!”

“And I dare say the Count remembers the bastinado Castlewood had given him. A confounded French dancing-master calling himself a count, and daring to fall in love in our family! Whenever I want to make myself uncommonly agreeable to old Maria, I just say a few words of parly voo to her. She knows what I mean.”

The words—parly voo—were like a counterfeit coin, passed with a wink. In a house where English titles sat on debts and foreign phrases served as both ornament and weapon, language itself became a kind of power: who may speak, who may mock, who may name. Maria’s French was a private country she had once lived in; Will used it as a stick to beat her with, as if stealing a woman’s dialect were the same as stealing her keys.

“Have you abused her to your cousin, Harry Warrington?” Madame asked quickly.

“Well—I know she is always abusing me—and I have said my mind about her,” Will replied.

“Oh, you idiot!” Madame cried, with sudden sincerity. “Who but a gaby ever spoke ill of a woman to her sweetheart? He will tell her everything, and they both will hate you.”

“The very thing, ma’am!” Will burst out laughing. “I had a sort of suspicion, you see, and two days ago, as we were riding together, I told Harry Warrington a bit of my mind about Maria—why shouldn’t I? She is always abusing me, ain’t she, Fan? And your favourite turned as red as my plush waistcoat—wondered how a gentleman could malign his own flesh and blood, and, trembling all over with rage, said I was no true Esmond.”

“Why didn’t you chastise him, sir, as my lord did the dancing-master?” Lady Castlewood demanded, the memory of old blows rising in her like smoke.

“Well, mother—you see that at quarter-staff there’s two sticks used,” Will answered. “And my opinion is, Harry Warrington can guard his own head uncommonly well. Perhaps that is one of the reasons why I did not offer to treat my cousin to a caning. And now you say so, ma’am, I know he has told Maria. She has been looking battle, murder, and sudden death at me ever since. All which shows—” He turned towards his aunt, triumphant, like a huntsman hearing the first cry in cover. “All which shows that I think we are on the right scent; and that we’ve found Maria—the old fox!” And he clapped his hand to his mouth and hallooed, loud and foolish, as if the hangings were hedgerows and the gallery a field.

How far had this pretty intrigue gone? That was the question now, and it lay in the house like a smell you cannot place at first—smoke, or singed sugar, or the faint sourness that warns you a cask has turned. Will said that at Maria’s age she would conduct matters as rapidly as possible, not having much time to lose. There was not a great deal of love lost between Will and his half-sister; their quarrels were old bones, gnawed down and still offered up at every meal.

Who was to sift the matter to the bottom? Scolding only hardens a will. Threats, in such cases, are like banging a pot-lid: they make more noise than change. Madame de Bernstein, who had lived long enough to know how easily a family mistakes clatter for control, spoke more quietly.

“I never was in danger but once, young people,” she said; “and I think that was because my poor mother contradicted me. If this boy is like others of his family, the more we oppose him, the more entêté he will be; and we shall never get him out of his scrape.”

“Faith, ma’am, suppose we leave him in it?” Will grumbled. “Old Maria and I don’t love each other too much, I grant you; but an English earl’s daughter is good enough for an American tobacco-planter, when all is said and done.”

His mother and sister broke out as if he had flung a coal among dry herbs. They would not hear of such a union.

“You are like the dog in the manger,” Will retorted. “You don’t want the man yourself, Fanny.”

“I want him, indeed!” Lady Fanny cried, tossing her head, and the denial sounded too quick—like a cook protesting she never tasted the sauce she made.

“Then why grudge him to Maria? I think Castlewood wants her to have him.”

“Why grudge him to Maria, sir?” Madame de Bernstein cried, with sudden fire that made them all look at her. “Do you remember who the poor boy is, and what your house owes to his family? His grandfather was the best friend your father ever had, and gave up this estate, this title, this very castle in which you are conspiring against the friendless Virginian lad, that you and yours might profit by it. And the reward for all this kindness is, that you all but shut the door on the child when he knocks at it, and talk of marrying him to a silly elderly creature who might be his mother! He shan’t marry her.”

“The very thing we were saying and thinking, my dear Baroness!” Lady Castlewood interposed at once, swift to wrap herself in the moral cloak when it suited. “Our part of the family is not eager about the match, though my lord and Maria may be.”

“You would like him for yourself, now that you hear he is rich—and may be richer, young people, mind you that,” Madame de Bernstein said, turning on the other women with the clean, cutting accuracy of a knife that knows the grain.

“Mr. Warrington may be ever so rich, madam, but there is no need why your ladyship should perpetually remind us that we are poor,” Lady Castlewood answered with more spirit than tenderness. “At least there is very little disparity in Fanny’s age and Mr. Harry’s; and you surely will be the last to say that a lady of our name and family is not good enough for any gentleman born in Virginia or elsewhere.”

“Let Fanny take an English gentleman, Countess, not an American,” Madame replied. “With such a name and such a mother to help her, and with all her good looks and accomplishments, sure she can’t fail of finding a man worthy of her. But from what I know about the daughters of this house, and what I imagine about our young cousin, I am certain that no happy match could be made between them.”

“What does my aunt know about me?” Lady Fanny asked, turning very red, as if the blood itself protested to be so read aloud.

“Only your temper, my dear,” Madame said. “You don’t suppose I believe all the tittle-tattle and scandal which one cannot help hearing in town. But the temper and early education are sufficient. Only fancy one of you condemned to leave St. James’s and the Mall, and live in a plantation surrounded by savages! You would die of ennui, or worry your husband’s life out with your ill-humour. You are born, ladies, to ornament courts—not wigwams. Let this lad go back to his wilderness with a wife who is suited to him.”

The other two declared at once—too quickly, too neatly—that for their parts they desired no better; and after a few more words, they went away down the corridor, their silks making that dry, expensive whisper which, in that house, so often took the place of kindness. Madame de Bernstein lifted the tapestried door and retired to her own chamber, where the air smelled faintly of past perfumes and closed drawers, and the only sound was the gentler, truer kind: the hush of cloth, the far-off tick of a clock, the faint murmur of a household living around her like a sea she had learned to navigate.

Now she saw the whole scheme; and she admired, with something like bitter amusement, the ways of women, calling back a score of little circumstances—glances on staircases, absences that had been explained by sport, Maria’s quiet vanishings, Harry’s sudden heat when her name was touched. She wondered at her own blindness. How far had it gone? Was Harry’s passion serious and tragical, or a mere fire of straw that burns bright and dies by morning? How deeply was he committed?

She dreaded the strength of Harry’s feeling and the weakness of Maria’s. A woman of Maria’s age may be desperate, she thought—desperate enough to make any efforts to secure a lover. Scandal? Bah. Maria would retire and be a princess in Virginia, and leave England to talk itself hoarse. There is always, is there not, some one thing women do not tell one another—some secret kept not in ink but in blood and breath—and about which they agree, without speaking, to deceive? Is it deceit, or modesty, or that deeper untranslatability of experience which makes even sisters speak different dialects when the heart is concerned? Men, as soon as inclination stirs, go seeking a friend to whom they can pour the delicious news. Women, with more or less art, bury it from their kind; and for days and weeks past had not this old Maria—Maria, the butt of the family—made fools of the whole house?

Madame de Bernstein did not care to examine Lady Maria’s antecedents too curiously; she had her own opinions about her own. A hundred years ago, people of the great world were not so straitlaced as they now pretend to be, when everybody is good, pure, moral, modest—when there is no skeleton in any closet; no scheming; no slurring over old stories; when no girl tries to sell herself for wealth, and no mother abets her. Suppose Lady Maria tries to play her little game: wherein is her great eccentricity? Thus the Baroness de Bernstein thought, alone with the muffled sounds of Castlewood, and the knowledge that in every great house there are languages spoken plainly at table, and others—older, darker, more intimate—whispered behind hangings where even truth must learn to lower its voice.

When my Lady Castlewood rose at last, gathering up her silks with that quick, practised hand which never seemed to fumble, and passed out of the saloon with her son and daughter, my Lord went his own way by another door, as if the house itself had been built to spare him the trouble of explanations. The room, left behind, held its great hearth like a patient mouth—blackened within, gilt without—with the portraits above it staring down as gravely as judges who never once have to dine on what they decree.

Lady Maria had sat all this while at her tambour-frame, the little ring of wood and tight-stretched linen on her lap, her needle dipping and drawing with a steady, pious industry. The flowers under her hand—violets and jonquils—were so innocent, so fragrantly pastoral in their very name, that they might have been plucked from the hedge-row by a child and pinned to a dairy-maid’s bodice. Yet the eyes that had pretended to live only among stitched petals lifted now, slowly, from their small garden to the living figure by the chimney.

Harry Warrington stood under an ancestral portrait, as if he had sought protection from a dead gentleman in full-bottomed wig and cuirass. The fire had warmed him; something else had set him alight. The heat climbed even to his ears. If blushes were herbs to be gathered, he had harvested them by the handful and worn them unashamed.

“Why did you refuse to go with our aunt, cousin?” Lady Maria asked, her tone demure as her needlework.

“Because your ladyship bade me stay,” Harry answered, and if his voice shook, it was not from fear.

“I bid you stay! La, child! What one says in fun, you take in earnest!” She bent again to her work, the needle pricking through the linen with small, decisive bites. “Are all you Virginian gentlemen so obsequious as to fancy every idle word a lady says is a command? Virginia must be a pleasant country for our sex if it be so!”

“You said—when—when we walked on the terrace two nights since—O heaven!” Harry broke out, the words tumbling as if his heart had tripped him. He stepped nearer, dragging the air with him, as if he could pull courage up by the roots.

“Ah, that sweet night, cousin!” said the tambour-frame, and the thread slipped through her fingers with the ease of long practice.

“When you gave me this rose—from your own neck,” Harry roared with the dreadful sincerity of the young; and he plunged his hand into his waistcoat and drew out, like a relic from a shrine, a crumpled thing—once a rose, now a brown and flattened vegetable, still faintly perfumed when it was warmed between his fingers. “Which I will never part with—no, by heavens, whilst this heart continues to beat! You said, ‘Harry, if your aunt asks you to go away, you will go; and if you go, you will forget me.’ Didn’t you say so?”

“All men forget,” Lady Maria replied, and sighed as prettily as her needle might have done. “In this cold selfish country they may, cousin.”

“Not in ours,” cried Harry, as though the very climate of Virginia would defend his constancy. “It went to my heart to say no to her, and she so kind to me, and the means of introducing me to—to—O heaven!” He advanced with a sudden fervour; a spaniel, asleep by the fender, ventured into his path. Harry’s boot struck it aside impatiently. The poor creature yelped and fled, its little protest swallowed by the thick carpet and the draught up the chimney.

“Look here, cousin! If you were to bid me jump out of yonder window, I should do it; or murder, I should do it.”

“La! but you need not squeeze one’s hand so, you silly child!” Maria said, and yet did not draw her hand away until she had been sure of its effect.

“I can’t help it—we are so in the south.” His fingers held hers with the pressure of a man who has never yet learned the politeness of restraint. “Where my heart is, I can’t help speaking my mind out, cousin—and you know where that heart is. Ever since that evening—that—O heaven! I tell you I have hardly slept since. I want to do something—to distinguish myself—to be ever so great. I wish there was giants, Maria, as I have read of in—in books, that I could go and fight ’em. I wish you was in distress, that I might help you somehow. I wish you wanted my blood, that I might spend every drop of it for you. And when you told me not to go with Madame Bernstein—”

“I tell thee, child? never.”

“I thought you told me.” He was not to be turned aside by a denial; he had already built the whole house of his devotion upon that one remembered sentence, and would not now pull it down because she declared the foundation imaginary. “You said you knew I preferred my aunt to my cousin; and I said then what I say now: ‘Incomparable Maria! I prefer thee to all the women in the world and all the angels in Paradise—and I would go anywhere, were it to dungeons, if you ordered me!’ And do you think I would not stay anywhere, when you only desired that I should be near you?”

“Men always talk in that way—that is—that is, I have heard so,” she answered, recovering herself with a little flurried dignity. “For what should a country-bred woman know about you creatures? When you are near us, they say you are all raptures and flames and promises and I don’t know what; when you are away, you forget all about us.”

“But I think I never want to go away as long as I live,” he groaned, as if the very notion bruised him. “I have tired of many things. Not books and that—I never cared for study much—but games and sports I used to be fond of when I was a boy. Before I saw you, it was to be a soldier I most desired. I tore my hair with rage when my poor dear brother went away instead of me on that expedition in which we lost him. But now I only care for one thing in the world, and you know what that is.”

“You silly child! Don’t you know I am almost old enough to be—”

“I know—I know! but what is that to me?” His honesty, like new wine, ran foaming over every sensible boundary. “Hasn’t your br—well, never mind who—some of ’em told me stories against you, and didn’t they show me the Family Bible where all your names are down, and the dates of your birth?”

“The cowards! Who did that?” cried Lady Maria, and in an instant the gentlewoman at her embroidery was gone, and something sharp and quick as vinegar flashed through her. “Dear Harry, tell me who did that? Was it my mother-in-law, the grasping, odious, abandoned, brazen harpy? Do you know all about her? How she married my father in his cups—the horrid hussey!—and—”

“Indeed it wasn’t Lady Castlewood,” Harry interposed, stunned to find what temper could live under such blue eyes.

“Then it was my aunt,” Maria continued, anger running on like a pot left unwatched. “A pretty moralist indeed! A bishop’s widow forsooth—and I should like to know whose widow before and afterwards. Why, Harry, she intrigues with the Pretender, and with the Court of Hanover, and I dare say would with the Court of Rome and the Sultan of Turkey if she had had the means. Do you know who her second husband was? A creature who—”

“But our aunt never spoke a word against you,” Harry broke in again, more and more amazed; for in Virginia he had seen anger, but not this sudden, polished fury that seemed to strike and glitter at once.

She stopped. In his open, enquiring face she fancied she read alarm—alarm not at what was said, but at the woman who could say it.

“Well, well! I am a fool,” she murmured, letting the heat sink and the smile return like icing laid back over a cake. “I want thee to think well of me, Harry.”

Somehow her hand went out again—how it escaped the tambour-frame, how it found his, who can tell?—and it was seized, and kissed, and pressed with the devout eagerness of youth.

“Angel!” he cried, staring into her face with those candid eyes that had never yet learned to read a mask as a mask.

Her eyes—those older orbs that could be cold as water when she chose and warm as wine when she wished—took fire under his gaze. They shone, and he plunged into them as if he were diving into a clear pool in summer, not seeing what lies under some calm surfaces: the sunk wreckage, the dropped treasures, the bones and broken promises that make a bed in such depths. A dog, Aesop tells us, once saw a meat-bone in the water and snapped at its reflection, losing what he held. So it is with more than dogs. There are quiet waters that smile and swallow. Have a care, you eager lads, how you lap.

Yet to Harry, the song was not stale; the voice did not crack; the witch did not seem old. He did not see the paint that could be laid on and washed off; he did not imagine the ringlets might be put away in a box; he heard only the lilting call that makes the heart step forward of its own accord.

And indeed, if any person who has ever read a tale, or lived one, had seen him draw out that faded rose just now—once red as a cook’s fresh pimento, now browned like an herb dried too long by the kitchen rafters—he might have drifted into his own reverie, as the writer himself does when lovers whisper in an alley or shoot glances across a room. These things follow each other by a law as old as people: a meeting in the garden, a hand taken by the old curtain where everyone may peep through the rent, an early walk in delicious weather, a charitable errand to some cottage, a basket carried by the one who longs to be useful. Whole chapters might be brewed out of such small domestic ingredients: a half-crown, a jar of calves’-foot jelly, a book of prayers read aloud into a deaf ear. The dish is ever the same, only served on a different plate.

Maria liked power over the young Virginian; but she did not want Harry to quarrel with his aunt for her sake, nor Madame de Bernstein to grow angry with her. He was not Lord of Virginia yet—only the Prince, and a Queen may marry again and bear other Princes; and who could tell what laws governed inheritance in that far country? My lord her brother and she spoke no words together on this delicate matter. They did not need to. The Earl had a way of understanding without speaking; Maria, in her brother’s house and under his eye for so much of her life, had had her little ways, tricks, faults, and schemes read as plainly as the household accounts. He would check or aid her as seemed good to him, and never with a scene.

Thus, three days before, when Maria had been tripping toward the gate-house on her errand to poor old Goody Jenkins—ill with a sore knee in the village—and when Harry had happened, quite by chance, to be walking behind the elms on the green, my lord crossed the court with his dogs about him and his gardener in attendance. He called to his sister.

“Molly, you are going to see Goody Jenkins. You are a charitable soul, my dear. Give Gammer Jenkins this half-crown for me—unless our cousin Warrington has already given her money. A pleasant walk to you. Let her want for nothing.”

At supper that night, my lord questioned Mr. Warrington about the poor in Virginia, and by what means they were maintained, and what the labourers ate and how they lived; questions that sounded, in the mouth of so great a man, like benevolence, and also like instruction. Harry answered as well as he could, thinking of corn-meal and bacon, of fish from the river and game from the woods, and of how different were the sounds of want in a country where land lay open like a table spread too wide for all the guests to reach. The Earl wished that in the old country there were no more poor people than in the new; and he recommended Harry to visit people of every degree—high and low—in the country to look at agriculture, in the city at manufactures and municipal institutions. Harry listened modestly, with few words; Madame Bernstein, at her piquet with the chaplain, nodded approval, her cards clicking softly like little bones.

The next day Harry was in my lord’s justice-room; the next he was out for hours with him on the farm, where the earth smelled of turnings and dung and damp straw, and the rooks complained overhead with that hoarse, rural parliament which has out-talked many human ones. Coming home, my lord looked in upon a sick tenant; and on that day too, Lady Maria was out, reading good books, no doubt, to Goody Jenkins, though it is not likely Madame Bernstein ever once asked after her niece’s charity.

In due course Harry wrote home, as sons will, trying to turn his heart into respectable sentences and his emotion into dutiful ink.

“CASTLEWOOD, HAMPSHIRE, ENGLAND,
August 5, 1757.

“MY DEAR MOUNTAIN,—At first, as I wrote, I did not like Castlewood, nor my cousins there, very much. Now, I am used to their ways, and we begin to understand each other much better. With my duty to my mother, tell her, I hope, that considering her ladyship’s great kindness to me, Madam Esmond will be reconciled to her half-sister, the Baroness de Bernstein. The Baroness, you know, was my Grandmamma’s daughter by her first husband, Lord Castlewood (only Grandpapa really was the real lord); however, that was not his, that is, the other Lord Castlewood’s fault, you know, and he was very kind to Grandpapa, who always spoke most kindly of him to us as you know.

“Madame the Baroness Bernstein first married a clergyman, Reverend Mr. Tusher, who was so learned and good, and such a favourite of his Majesty, as was my aunt too, that he was made a Bishop. When he died, Our gracious King continued his friendship to my aunt; who married a Hanoverian nobleman, who occupied a post at the Court—and, I believe, left the Baroness very rich. My cousin, my Lord Castlewood, told me so much about her, and I am sure I have found from her the greatest kindness and affection.

“The (Dowiger) Countess Castlewood and my cousins Will and Lady Fanny have been described per last, that went by the Falmouth packet on the 20th ult. The ladies are not changed since then. Me and Cousin Will are very good friends. We have rode out a good deal. We have had some famous cocking matches at Hampton and Winton. My cousin is a sharp blade, but I think I have shown him that we in Virginia know a thing or two. Reverend Mr. Sampson, chaplain of the famaly, most excellent preacher, without any biggatry.

“The kindness of my cousin the Earl improves every day, and by next year’s ship I hope my mother will send his lordship some of our best roll tobacco (for tennants) and hamms. He is most charatable to the poor. His sister, Lady Maria, equally so. She sits for hours reading good books to the sick: she is most beloved in the village.”

“Nonsense!” said the lady to whom Harry submitted this precious manuscript, as if he were offering her a dish he had laboured over and feared to season too boldly. She had taken it from him with an air of indulgence, and as she read, the room seemed to fill not with the crackle of the hearth but with the imagined hush of a cottage where a deaf old woman sat by a scant fire, hearing nothing of the fine phrases pronounced over her.

“Why do you flatter me, cousin?” Maria asked, though her eye brightened as if she had tasted the praise.

“You are beloved in the village and out of it,” said Harry, with a knowing emphasis, “and I have flattered you, as you call it, a little more still, farther on.”

He read, or pointed, and she continued, smiling at each line that served her.

“There is a sick old woman there, whom Madam Esmond would like, a most raligious, good, old lady.

“Lady Maria goes very often to read to her; which, she says, gives her comfort. But though her Ladyship hath the sweetest voice, both in speaking and singeing (she plays the church organ, and singes there most beautifully), I cannot think Gammer Jenkins can have any comfort from it, being very deaf, by reason of her great age. She has her memory perfectly, however, and remembers when my honoured Grandmother Rachel Lady Castlewood lived here. She says, my Grandmother was the best woman in the whole world, gave her a cow when she was married, and cured her husband, Gaffer Jenkins, of the collects, which he used to have very bad. I suppose it was with the Pills and Drops which my honoured Mother put up in my boxes, when I left dear Virginia. Having never been ill since, have had no use for the pills. Gumbo hath, eating and drinking a great deal too much in the Servants’ Hall.

“The next angel to my Grandmother (N.B. I think I spelt angel wrong per last), Gammer Jenkins says, is Lady Maria, who sends her duty to her Aunt in Virginia, and remembers her, and my Grandpapa and Grandmamma when they were in Europe, and she was a little girl. You know they have Grandpapa’s picture here, and I live in the very rooms which he had, and which are to be called mine, my Lord Castlewood says.

“Having no more to say, at present, I close with best love and duty to my honoured Mother, and with respects to Mr. Dempster, and a kiss for Fanny, and kind remembrances to Old Gumbo, Nathan, Old and Young Dinah, and the pointer dog and Slut, and all friends, from their well-wisher

“HENRY ESMOND WARRINGTON.”

At the bottom he had added, with the careful afterthought of a dutiful nephew:

“Have wrote and sent my duty to my Uncle Warrington in Norfolk. No anser as yet.”

He looked up from the page, anxious as a boy who has carried a dish into the parlour and waits to see if the company will praise it or push it away.

“I hope the spelling is right, cousin?” he asked.

“’Tis quite well enough spelt for any person of fashion,” Lady Maria answered, who did not choose to have her own orthography weighed too nicely, and who had no mind that any dominion of hers should be disputed, even by letters.

“One word, ‘Angel,’ I know I spelt wrong in writing to my mamma,” Harry said, his blushes coming again like heat from an opened oven, “but I have learned a way of spelling it right, now.”

“And how is that, sir?”

“I think ’tis by looking at you, cousin;” and with the words he made her a low bow—one of his best—offering it with such honest ceremony, and with such a red, fresh bouquet of colour rising over his cheeks, that it was as if he laid both bow and nosegay at her feet.

At the next meal the long table was set as if for a little festival, though the day had been as common as any: the cloth newly whitened, the napkins folded to stiff little peaks, the silver giving back the candlelight in soft, steady glints. The house itself seemed to hold its breath; even the familiar sounds—the low clink of spoons, the subdued scrape of chairs upon the boards—came gentled, as though Castlewood knew it must listen.

Madame de Bernstein entered with a face from which the morning’s storm had vanished as wholly as smoke from a quenched pan. She was all graciousness. She praised the cook—praised him with that exactitude which is half compliment, half command—declaring the fricassee to be excellent, and insisting that there were no eels anywhere like those drawn from the Castlewood moats: sweet as milk, she said, and clean as if they had been rinsed in spring-water and not in old, green-sleeping ditches.

The dish itself was a kind of homely glory: eels laid in their collars, the flesh pearled and firm, the gelée trembling clear about bay-leaf and peppercorn; beside it the fricassee—white with cream and yolk, thickened to a satin that clung to the spoon, smelling of lemon-peel, mace, and a handful of parsley chopped so fine it might have been green dust. When somebody hinted the wine was corked, the Baroness would not hear of such extravagance as opening a fresh bottle “for a useless old woman like me.” She lifted her glass when the new wine came, and gave, with a bright, steady voice, “Madam Esmond Warrington, of Virginia,” as her toast; and then, with a look that held Harry as a hook holds a fish, expressed a hope that he had brought away his mamma’s permission to take an English wife back with him.

He could not have told afterward whether the wine was rough or smooth upon his tongue; the room was full of scent—hot gravy, wax candles, damp stone beyond the windows where the moat lay—and yet his senses, which ought to have been masters at table, ran all one way: to Maria’s presence, to the turn of her head, to the soft rustle when she moved her sleeve. Madame de Bernstein, with an easy current of talk, began to amuse them with stories of her dear mother—Colonel Esmond’s widow—of her beauty and goodness, of her happiness with her second husband though she was so much older than Colonel Esmond. To see them together, she said, had been delightful; their attachment had been talked of through the country. After such a marriage, what was the use, she asked, of prating about disparity?

My Lady Castlewood and her two children held their peace while the Baroness prattled on. Harry was enraptured, and Maria—who had expected thunder—sat surprised, schooling her face into politeness as a scholar copies a harsh hand into fair. Lord Castlewood watched his aunt with the puzzled composure of a man who hears an unfamiliar bird-call in his own orchard. He showed no doubt; his countenance wore the stamp of perfect satisfaction; but his mind, no doubt, was busy with the question: what scheme had put this honey upon her tongue?

Her good-humour flowed down the table as gravy runs to the lowest trench. Not one person escaped a gracious word. When Mr. Will, with the blunt wonder of youth, let fall an expression of satisfaction at her behaviour, she answered him frankly.

“Complimentary, my dear! Of course I am. I want to make up with you for having been exceedingly rude to everybody this morning. When I was a child, and my father and mother were alive, and lived here, I remember I used to adopt exactly the same behaviour. If I had been naughty in the morning, I used to try and coax my parents at night. I remember in this very room, at this very table—oh, ever so many hundred years ago!—so coaxing my father, and mother, and your grandfather, Harry Warrington; and there were eels for supper, as we have had them to-night, and it was that dish of collared eels which brought the circumstance back to my mind. I had been just as wayward that day, when I was seven years old, as I am to-day, when I am seventy, and so I confess my sins, and ask to be forgiven, like a good girl.”

“I absolve your ladyship!” cried the chaplain, who made one of the party.

“But your reverence does not know how cross and ill-tempered I was. I scolded my sister, Castlewood: I scolded her children, I boxed Harry Warrington’s ears: and all because he would not go with me to Tunbridge Wells.”

“But I will go, madam; I will ride with you with all the pleasure in life,” said Mr. Warrington, and though his voice kept itself steady, the blood rushed to his face hot as if he had bent too near the fire.

“You see, Mr. Chaplain, what good, dutiful children they all are. ’Twas I alone who was cross and peevish. Oh, it was cruel of me to treat them so! Maria, I ask your pardon, my dear.”

“Sure, madam, you have done me no wrong,” Maria answered; and her accent, soft and slightly old-fashioned, had in it that unstudied music which made Harry think, absurdly, of a country air remembered from childhood. Even in that one phrase—so plain, so dutiful—there lay a whole inheritance of speech, the little turns and cadences that belonged to her blood and place, and which no London assembly could teach or buy.

“Indeed, I have, a very great wrong, child! Because I was weary of myself, I told you that your company would be wearisome to me. You offered to come with me to Tunbridge, and I rudely refused you.”

“Nay, ma’am, if you were sick, and my presence annoyed you—”

“But it will not annoy me! You were most kind to say that you would come. I do, of all things, beg, pray, entreat, implore, command that you will come.”

My lord filled himself a glass and sipped it, looking as unconcerned as if the whole matter were nothing but talk about sauces. Yet the meaning was plain enough. This, then, had been the object of the morning’s violence: not sickness, not whim, but a separation.

“Anything which can give my aunt pleasure, I am sure, will delight me,” Maria said, trying to wear happiness as one wears an uncomfortable ribbon—neatly, and without showing the pin.

“You must come and stay with me, my dear, and I promise to be good and good-humoured. My dear lord, you will spare your sister to me?”

“Lady Maria Esmond is quite of age to judge for herself about such a matter,” Lord Castlewood replied, bowing; and then, with the politeness of a man who offers a dish he does not mean to taste, added, “If any of us can be of use to you, madam, you sure ought to command us.”

“Oh, Tunbridge will be delightful!” sighed Lady Maria.

“Mr. Sampson will go and see Goody Jones for you,” my lord continued.

Harry drew idle figures with his finger upon the table as if tracing patterns in flour. A moment before, his mind had been laying out future hours with the particularity of a cook planning a feast: walks that would end in sheltered arbours; rides through lanes where leaves would make a whispering roof; long talks that would go on as slowly and richly as a well-stirred custard; afternoons at the harpsichord with music-books open, the paper smelling faintly of dust and ink; moonlight on the shrubbery; that soft, dangerous ease with which two young persons, left alone, begin to believe the world exists only to serve their hearts.

Now, with a single sentence, it all fell, like a soufflé struck by a door flung wide.

“I knew it couldn’t be,” he thought. “I knew something would happen to take her from me.”

“But you will ride with us to Tunbridge, nephew Warrington, and keep us from the highwaymen?” said Madame de Bernstein.

He hoped none observed how red he grew. “Yes,” he managed, and tried to sound calm, “I will ride with your ladyships; and I am sure you need fear no danger.”

Danger!—he felt, in his folly, that he would welcome it as a man welcomes a hard crust when he is starving, because it is something that proves life. Ten thousand highwaymen might come; he would cut them down, or at least ride so close to Maria’s coach that he might catch her eyes when the curtains stirred. Perhaps at an inn he might have the blessed chance to offer his hand, to feel hers rest for an instant upon it—light as a moth, warm as bread newly lifted from the oven.

They would be two whole days going to Tunbridge. One day or two he might stay there. Is not a poor wretch with the halter already measured thankful even for a short reprieve? If ever love made a man ridiculous, it had made Harry Warrington so; and if a man, in that fever, speaks like an idiot, it is a cheap bravery to write down his folly and laugh. Some are gently sick with it, and recover. Others take the malady so deep that the scar shows through the skin to old age. If you have never brayed, then jeer; but if you have ever been long-eared in the same pasture, recognise a brother.

“You will stay with us for a day or two at the Wells,” Madame Bernstein continued. “You will see us put into our lodgings. Then you can return to Castlewood and the partridge-shooting, and all the fine things which you and my lord are to study together.”

Harry bowed assent. A whole week, then—some remnant of heaven.

“And as there is sure to be plenty of company at the Wells, I shall be able to present you,” the lady added with an air of benevolence.

“Company! ah! I shan’t need company,” sighed Harry; and then, recollecting himself, he hastened to say, “I mean—I shall be quite contented in the company of you two ladies.”

No doubt Mr. Will wondered at his cousin’s taste.

As this was to be the last night of Harry’s present visit to Castlewood, cousin Will proposed that he, and his reverence, and Warrington should meet in the latter’s quarters and make up their accounts: a practice which, as Harry had been a considerable winner, he did not refuse. When the ladies withdrew and my lord retired—as was his custom—to his own apartments, the three gentlemen assembled in Mr. Harry’s little room before the punch-bowl, which was Will’s usual midnight companion.

The bowl steamed with its sugared breath, sharp with citrus and spirit; the grated nutmeg upon the surface sent up a fragrant dust whenever the ladle moved. It was comfort of a coarse sort, such as men take when they will not confess to loneliness. Outside, the court lay quiet; the house’s great body settled into night-sounds: a distant door-latch, a footfall fading, somewhere a clock that ticked as evenly as a cook’s knife upon a board.

But Will’s method of settling accounts was by producing fresh packs of cards, and offering to submit Harry’s debt to the process of being doubled or acquitted. The chaplain had no more ready cash than Lord Castlewood’s younger brother; and Harry, for his part, wanted to win the money of neither. Why should he pain Maria’s brother, or leave room for any of her kin to say the Virginian was grasping? Yet if they insisted upon play, he would not be made a gull, either. He had learned—at home, in those games young men call harmless—that there is a kind of honour even in vice: to play fairly, and to pay.

“Up to midnight,” he said, “I will play for what stakes you name.” And so they fell to it: the cards shuffled and dealt, the dice-box rattled, the little room filling with that thin, nervous music of chance.

Very likely he did not think of the cards at all. His mind, in spite of the noise, ran on another rhythm, another soundscape altogether: not the harsh snap of pasteboard, not Will’s oaths, not the chaplain’s muttered imprecations, but the imagined hush of Maria’s chamber; the soft combing of hair, the whisper of linen, a prayer spoken low in a voice whose particular turns of speech—its little archaic courtesies, its “sure” and “nay”—held for him a meaning no dictionary could ever render. How much of a person lives in such small words, and how easily the world, with its fashionable phrases and its loud, market-ready talk, rubs them away.

“You double us all round?” cried Will. “I will take a card upon each of my two. Thank you, that will do—a ten—now, upon the other, a queen—two natural vingt-et-uns, and as you doubled us you owe me so-and-so,” said Harry, not even lifting his eyes as if the winnings were no more than crumbs.

Will swore. The chaplain’s pious tongue grew very nimble with profanities. Harry kept calm. He won because he did not care to win. Fortune—that coquettish jade—came to him because he was thinking of another nymph, perhaps as fickle.

Will and the chaplain played against him, forever increasing their stakes, imagining the rich Virginian meant to let them recover their losses. But Harry’s notion was not so. Presently, as their growls thickened, he spoke with a quiet firmness.

“The luck does seem to be with me, cousin; and I am sure I do not want to press it; but you don’t suppose I’m going to be such a fool as to fling it away altogether? I have quite a heap of your promises on paper by this time. If we are to go on playing, let us have the dollars on the table, if you please; or, if not the money, the worth of it.”

“Always the way with you rich men,” grumbled Will. “Never lend except on security—always win because you are rich.”

“Faith, cousin, you have been of late for ever flinging my riches into my face. I have enough for my wants and for my creditors.”

“Oh, that we could all say as much!” groaned the chaplain. “How happy we, and how happy the duns would be! What have we got to play against our conqueror? There is my new gown, Mr. Warrington. Will you set me five pieces against it? I have but to preach in stuff if I lose. Stop! I have a Chrysostom, a Foxe’s Martyrs, a Baker’s Chronicle, and a cow and her calf. What shall we set against these?”

“I will bet one of cousin Will’s notes for twenty pounds,” cried Harry, producing one of those documents as coolly as if it were a recipe card. “Or I have my brown mare, and will back her—red against your honour’s notes of hand, but against ready money.”

“I have my horse,” bawled Will. “I will back my horse against you for fifty.”

Harry took the offers of both gentlemen. In the course of ten minutes the horse and the bay mare had changed owners, as simply as plates are changed between courses. Will swore more fiercely than ever. The parson dashed his wig to the ground and outdid his pupil in loudness. Harry was neither elated nor angry. They had asked him to play; he had played. He knew he should win.

And through it all his eyes strayed again and again to the window. Across the court, beneath a brilliant, flickering star, was the casement he knew to be hers. A lamp burned faintly behind it, making a pale square of light that looked, to his bewitched fancy, like a little hearth-fire set up for him alone. He forgot his victims, their groans, their ill-luck, even as they crossed the court at last and the night swallowed their voices. Behind yonder pane—behind that thin glass and curtain—lay his joy, his heart, his treasure; and the house’s quiet, after the clatter of cards, sounded like a great breath drawn in and held, as if Castlewood itself kept watch over what could not be spoken aloud.

If the old Archbishop of Cambray, in that courtly romance everyone quotes when they would make sorrow seem well-bred, took such pains to paint Calypso’s despair at Ulysses’ sailing, he might—had he been more curious about the world below the saloon—have spared a line for the grief in the kitchen. For every hero who leans, white-faced, into a last embrace in a great drawing-room, there is a waiting-woman with her apron to her eyes; and every queen who waves from a marble terrace has behind her some poor girl in a back passage, waving too, with a kerchief of coarser linen, yet wetted with tears of the same salt.

So it was at Castlewood. Harry Warrington rode away a captive to love; and Gumbo, his man, followed as surely taken, though his bonds were of another fashion and his sighs must be swallowed more carefully. The fellow had made himself beloved in those lower regions where the true life of a house goes on—among the copper pans and the smoky rafters, the scullery stones always damp, the bread rising by the hearth, the bustle of trenchers and ladles, and the perpetual talk of what must be served and how. Gumbo had a hand for a minuet and a hand for a sauce; he could bring a joint to table without drying it, and could set a pot to sing without letting it boil sullenly over. He played a tune too; and good humour, like good broth, went further then than many a fine speech. The women, who are charitable where men are censorious, were all for him. If the men in the servants’ hall muttered that the Virginian’s black man strutted too much, the maids thought his strut handsome, and the kitchen-maid forgave even the boldness of his Ashantee kingship. In those days they did not look upon a negro in England with the same sour, frightened hostility that later times have taught the white to practise—there was condescension enough, God knows, and a crude, half-laughing pity; but there was also an indulgence, and from women especially a kindness that could be as quick and warm as a fire suddenly fed with dry sticks.

One could have fancied the leave-takings in the grey of that morning: Molly the housemaid stealing out to the terrace-garden while the dew still held to the box-edges, choosing a sprig of something hardy and sweet—rosemary, perhaps, because it keeps its scent even after it is crushed. Betty from the kitchen, with hands that smelt of onions and flour in spite of all the rinsing, cutting off a thick lock of chestnut ringlets to barter for a woolly token, as she called it, from Gumbo’s crown. Such commerce of relics goes on always when youth is stung with parting. And Gumbo, with a face fit to break into laughter at any moment, would still look beyond them all towards one small window by the porter’s lodge, where a certain girl had been seen of late, and where, when she came, even the sparrows seemed to hush their quarrel.

On the morning fixed for Madame de Bernstein’s departure, Castlewood was not so much a great house as a fair. The doors and passages swarmed. They pressed in with the old human mixture—some for one last stare at my lady’s men and the fascinating black fellow; some to squeeze the hand of her ladyship’s maid; but most, in honest expectation, to waylay baroness and nephew for those parting gratuities which custom then demanded and which were accepted with as much gravity as if they were tithes.

Madame de Bernstein paid handsomely; Harry, who had been living at free charges and feeling himself a prosperous young conqueror, paid more handsomely still. He had gold in his pocket and love in his heart—two things that make a man liberal, at least for an hour. “My mother,” he told himself, “would have me remember every servant of the Esmonds.” So he scattered his guineas as if they were crumbs to pigeons: to the major-domo with his chain of office; to the butler in black and ruffles; to the housekeeper in her still-room among jars and cordials where dried lavender gave out a faint ghost of summer whenever the door opened; to the feeble old porter in his lodge, who smelled of dust and pipe-tobacco and old oak. From the shoeblack upward, none came near without a share.

There is a strange enchantment in a family when one loves a woman in it. A man finds every face connected with hers worth smiling on. He grows civil to the surly butler, patient with an old aunt, merry with the children, tender even to the lapdogs he would otherwise kick from his path. He drinks the sweet, warm port that would nauseate him at his club, because it is poured in that house. He applauds the little miss at the spinet and calls the boy a wag when the coffee is upset over his shirt. Harry, for a brief time—for love had but lately declared itself and been accepted—had been in this state of universal amiability.

He was shrewd enough too, with that shrewdness a sportsman learns early. In the midst of sighs and moon-gazing, he could still judge a horse and relish a fair win. Having played, and won, all the ready money Will had, and besides a bundle of Mr. Esmond’s autographs, Harry was particularly well pleased with one prize: Will’s brown horse, Prince William out of Constitution—the very beast that had almost shouldered him into the water on the first evening. Harry had watched the animal since; he knew the sound legs, the good wind, the breeding in the head and shoulder. When he had lingered long enough under the stars, staring up at the window where Maria’s candle had gone out, he went to his own room and fell asleep thinking of Maria and Prince William together—how easy it would be to have her hands (those two white arms of which he dreamed as other men dream of banners) about his waist as they made the tour of the island.

In the early morning the poor chaplain Sampson sent over his little black mare by the hands of a trembling trio—groom, footman, and gardener—who behaved as though the creature were a christened child. They kissed her white nose with loud sobs, and gave her a last pat as Gumbo took the rein. Gumbo wept too, moved by their sensibility; Harry, touched and amused in the same instant, quieted the storm with two guineas, which astonished and instantly comforted the chaplain’s boy. Then Gumbo and the late groom led the mare away to the stables with orders to bring her round after breakfast, along with Mr. William’s horse, when Madam Bernstein’s carriages should be ready.

So cordial was Lord Castlewood—whether out of politeness to his aunt, or gratitude for her departure—that he even came down to breakfast to take leave. The ladies and the chaplain were there. Will alone was absent; but he left a note for his cousin, scrawled in spelling that would have shamed a village school. He was obliged, he said, to go to Salisbury Races that morning; but he had left the horse Harry had won, and Tom, his groom, would deliver it to Mr. Warrington’s servant.

Tea was drunk in a kind of peace. Then wheels sounded on the gravel; the courtyard filled with movement. Servants packed the multiplied luggage—trunks and bandboxes and baskets enough to make a small caravan, though still modest beside the monstrous baggage of ladies in these latter days. A large open landau held the stout Baroness and her niece, with two armed men on the box—pistols and blunderbuss ready, in case the road should offer highwaymen. In another carriage rode the maids, and a servant kept guard over the trunks. Harry’s own modest valises were laid there too, under the maids’ eye. Gumbo proposed to ride by the window as much as he might.

Lord Castlewood, with his stepmother and Lady Fanny, went out to the steps and exchanged dutiful embraces with their kinswoman. Then Maria came last, in a riding-dress which, to Harry’s eyes, outshone all court finery. The colour of it, the neat fall of skirt and sleeve, the little points of leather and buckles, the clean scent of the cloth warmed on her by the house air—it made him think of movement, of roads, of liberty, of her beside him for miles. The servants stood about and called blessings after her. Beyond the gates, under the trees, the village had gathered—scores of faces, hats waving, cheers bursting like birds out of hedges when one shakes the branch. As the heavy vehicles rolled away, their iron-rimmed wheels spoke over the gravel in a slow, steady grind, and the cries rose and fell like surf.

Gumbo had gone for the horses. Lord Castlewood walked up and down the court with Harry, his arm thrust under the younger man’s with a familiarity that was half kindness and half command.

“I hear you carry away some of our horses out of Castlewood?” my lord said.

Harry coloured. “A gentleman cannot refuse fair play at cards,” he answered. “I never wanted to play, nor would have played for money, had not cousin William forced me. As for the chaplain, it went against me to win from him; but he was as eager as Will.”

“I know it. There’s no blame to you. At Rome—” and my lord shrugged—“you can’t help doing as Rome does. And I am glad you have been able to give Will a lesson. He is mad for play—would gamble his coat off his back. We have paid his debts ever so many times. How much have you won of him?”

“Eighteen pieces at first, and his note for a hundred and twenty besides; and the brown horse, sixty—near two hundred in all. But it was fair, my lord, though I played against my will. Will ain’t a match for me. That’s the truth.”

“He is a match for most,” my lord said dryly. “His brown horse, you say?”

“Yes. Prince William out of Constitution. You don’t suppose I’d set him sixty against his bay, my lord?”

“Oh. I didn’t know. I saw Will ride out this morning; I did not remark what horse he was on. And you won the black mare from the parson?”

“For fourteen. She’ll mount Gumbo well. Why does not the rascal come round?” Harry’s eyes kept darting to the lane where the dust cloud had gone; his mind was already trotting beside Maria’s carriage.

“When you come to Tunbridge, cousin Harry,” Lord Castlewood continued, “look out for sharper players than Will and the parson. There’s queer company at the Wells.”

“A Virginian learns to take care of himself,” Harry said, with a knowing nod.

“So it seems. I recommend my sister to you. Though she is no baby in years, she is as innocent as one. See she comes to no mischief.”

“I will guard her with my life,” Harry cried.

“And unless you are very fond of this tumble-down old place,” my lord went on, “I would not be in a hurry to return. I mean to go to another house, and scarce be back till partridge-shooting. You go, and take charge of the women—my sister and the Baroness.”

“Indeed I will,” said Harry; and his heart thumped as if it would break his ribs with gladness.

“I will send word when you shall bring my sister back. Ha! here come the horses. Have you bid adieu to the Countess and Lady Fanny? They are kissing their hands to you from the music-room balcony.”

Harry ran up, performed the farewells in haste—for what were those ladies to him now, beside the one who waited in the rolling dust?—and came down again to mount.

There was Gumbo, astride the chaplain’s black mare, holding another horse by the rein. But it was not the brown hunter Harry had imagined beneath him. It was a bay: old, with broken knees; a tired, sorry brute, whose coat had the dullness of a saucepan too long scoured with sand.

“What is this?” Harry cried.

“Your honour’s new horse,” said the groom, touching his cap.

“This brute? Go and bring me Prince William—Mr. William’s horse—the brown horse.”

“Mr. William have rode Prince William this morning to Salisbury Races. His last words was, ‘Sam, saddle my bay horse, Cato, for Mr. Warrington. He is Mr. Warrington’s horse now. I sold him to him last night.’ And I know your honour is bountiful: you will consider the groom.”

Lord Castlewood broke into a laugh that he did not try to hide. Harry, for his part, let fly a volley of expressions then common in England and Virginia, which the polite page does not repeat.

“Mr. William said he never could think of parting with the Prince under a hundred and twenty,” the groom added, peeping at Harry as if to measure how much anger was worth.

Lord Castlewood laughed the more. “Will has been too much for thee, Harry Warrington.”

“Too much for me? So may a fellow with loaded dice throw sixes and be too much for me. I do not call this betting; I call it—” And there Harry’s tongue went where it should not.

“Mr. Warrington!” Lady Maria’s voice rang from near the steps—clear, offended, and trembling with command. “Spare me bad words about my brother, if you please. Depend upon it, I will take care you are righted. Farewell. Ride quickly, or our coaches will be at Farnham before you.”

She had spoken like a princess of a house, using the lexicon of authority that women learn early when they must defend what men disgrace. The words were English enough, yet carried that untranslatable weight of blood and birth which no stranger, however beloved, can ever quite master. Harry swallowed the rest of his fury. Lord Castlewood, with a careless wave, turned back into the house; and Harry mounted the bay, feeling the animal’s old bones under him as plainly as if he sat on a bundle of sticks, and rode out of the courtyard with Gumbo at his heel.

In his impatience to overtake the carriages, Harry barely lifted his hat to the village cheers outside the gates. The people liked him; his open face and frank ways had won them. Old tales still went about of his grandparents—of Colonel Esmond in Queen Anne’s wars, and how he might have been Lord Castlewood and would not. Old Lockwood at the gate told those stories with relish, the words rolling in a rustic dialect that kept older turns of phrase alive like seeds in a dry pod. Such local speech holds memory the way a salt-cured ham holds the summer it was slaughtered in: cut it, and the smell rises again. But the present lord was a hard landlord, the village said; and poverty made him hated as much as harshness did. As for Mr. Will, no one loved him—brawls, broken heads, unpaid bills, dark doings with village girls, cudgellings in lanes by injured men. The village had heard too—because everything is known—how the young Virginian had beaten Will at riding, at jumping, at shooting, and then at cards. They respected Harry for it; and, more than all, they admired him because Gumbo’s busy tongue had made a prince of him in the county. Gold mines, diamond mines, tobaccos, furs—anything and everything, so long as it sounded rich. Prosperity has always had a loud music in English ears, and the crowd cheered it as naturally as it cheers a drum.

So Harry, leaving the hats tossing behind him, spurred his sorry bay. The horse’s hooves struck the road with a deadened, complaining sound, as if the animal itself protested the cheat; and the lane’s hedgerows answered with their proper summer noises—finches, a distant cart, the hushy rasp of wheels on dust. Harry heard none of it. His mind was already inside the moving cloud ahead.

He came up with the carriages at last, where the dust hung thick, smelling of hot leather, churned earth, and horses’ sweat. Pushing through, he found himself at the landau window. Maria had the back seat to herself; by keeping a little behind the wheels he could see her face framed between the bouncing curtains. She smiled; her eyes met his; she lifted a finger to her lip. Madame de Bernstein was dozing on her cushions, her capuchin bobbing softly with the carriage’s sway. Harry did not care to wake the old lady. To look at Maria’s eyes was enough; and if the hedgerow birds sang, they sang no music so sweet as her small, low monosyllables.

The Baroness’s horses were fat, accustomed to short stages and easy paces, and to feed at every stop. Thus, ill as Harry was mounted, he could keep alongside without much labour. At two o’clock they baited for dinner, and the inn received them with all the noise of a country halt: the sudden clatter of plates, the scrape of benches, the cry to the hostler, the stamping and snorting from the yard where oats rattled into troughs. The kitchen breathed out its own theology—roasting meat, ale, vinegar, herbs bruised in the mortar, and the comforting steam of bread broken open. Harry paid the landlord generously. What price could be too high, when it purchased an hour near Maria, and the chance of speech that seemed forbidden and therefore the sweeter?

Madame de Bernstein, after eating comfortably, sank into a half-hour’s slumber in her chair. In voices kept low, as if the very air might betray them, Maria and Harry repeated those delicious follies which lovers never exhaust. They were going to Tunbridge Wells, where beauty and fashion would crowd; timid Maria trembled lest, among younger faces, Harry should discover charms more worthy than hers. Harry swore by all the gods that Venus herself could not tempt him away. It was he, he said, who had cause to fear: for when the men of fashion saw his peerless Maria, they would gather round her carriage and make her forget the rough American who knew no wit and no fine ways, but only how to love faithfully.

Maria smiled, lifted her eyes as if to heaven, and vowed he knew nothing of women’s truth; it was men, she said, whose sex was proverbially faithless, whose sport was to play with hearts. He protested; she persisted. Their quarrel was all sugar and sparks, until, in the heat of defending the honour of his sex, Harry flung out his arm across the table to seize her hand. His broad cuff caught a glass; there was a clatter among knives and forks; the wine toppled and broke. An “Oh!” escaped from Maria’s lips—soft, startled, and instantly ashamed.

She glanced round, frightened the crash had wakened Madame de Bernstein. But the old lady slept on, breathing evenly, as if nothing in this world could disturb her after a good meal. And so Maria, seeing no witness but the harmless steam of dinner and the inn’s low murmur beyond the door, let her fingers yield under Harry’s gentle pressure.

How much those hands mean in love-making, and how foolishly lovers make them speak! What vows are kneaded into a thumb and four fingers, as if the flesh could hold promises the tongue scarcely dares. Yet there is a kind of language there that cannot be translated into any other—no dictionary catches it, no sermon can render it. It is all pressure and warmth, all pulse answering pulse; and each believes the other understands.

Then the horses were put to; the brief paradise ended until the next halt. When the landlord came with the bill, Harry was at a respectful distance, staring out of the window at the gathering cavalcade below, as if he had been discussing nothing but the state of the roads. Madame de Bernstein woke smiling, unconscious. With profound care Harry handed his aunt to her carriage; how demure and simple Maria looked as she followed, as if her hand had never been taken at all. Away they rolled, under the bows of landlord and waiters; past country-folk clustered under the blazing inn-sign; past shopmen in their low doors; past boys and market people under the old town-hall colonnade; past loungers along the gabled street.

“It is the famous Baroness Bernstein,” they said. “That is she, the old lady in the capuchin. And that is the rich young American from Virginia—worth millions and millions. Well—sure—he might have a better horse.”

The cavalcade disappeared in dust and summer sound, and the little town sank back into its ordinary quiet, while the landlord went to his friends to boast how great folks would sleep at The Bush at Farnham that night.

No tender-hearted soul need start at the thought that Henry Esmond Warrington—young, straight-limbed, scarcely out of boyhood—was flung by a broken-kneed brute into the grave. A man is not so easily discharged from his story as from his saddle; and if every gentleman were to perish at the first stumble of a horse, the roads about London would be paved with heirs and the churchyards would want for room. Harry was not dead. He lay, rather, in a good bed under a good roof, with clean linen to his skin, lavender in the air, and the quietest country sounds—wind through hedgerows, a distant cart creaking like a slow fiddle-string, the soft chime of a bell seldom used—washing over his half-waking fever.
