And to prove it, here is the very voice of the house that took him in: not the doctor’s report, nor a constable’s affidavit, but a letter—warm as bread, and as full of remembered flavours as it is of news—written by the lady who became, for a day, his Good Samaritan.

“TO MRS. ESMOND WARRINGTON, OF CASTLEWOOD  
At her House at Richmond, in Virginia

“If Mrs. Esmond Warrington of Virginia can call to mind twenty-three years ago, when Miss Rachel Esmond was at Kensington Boarding School, she may perhaps remember Miss Molly Benson—her class-mate—who has forgotten all the little quarrels which they used to have together (in which Miss Molly was very often in the wrong), and only remembers the generous, high-spirited, sprightly Miss Esmond, the Princess Pocahontas, to whom so many of our school-fellows paid court.

“Dear madam! I cannot forget that you were dear Rachel once upon a time, as I was your dearest Molly. Though we parted not very good friends when you went home to Virginia, yet you know how fond we once were. I still, Rachel, have the gold etui your papa gave me when he came to our speech-day at Kensington, and we two performed the quarrel of Brutus and Cassius out of Shakspeare; and ’twas only yesterday morning I was dreaming that we were both called up to say our lesson before the awful Miss Hardwood, and that I did not know it, and that as usual Miss Rachel Esmond went above me.

“How well remembered those old days are! How young we grow as we think of them! I remember our walks and our exercises, our good King and Queen as they walked in Kensington Gardens, and their court following them, whilst we of Miss Hardwood’s school curtseyed in a row. I can tell still what we had for dinner on each day of the week—what days the broth was thin as if it had heard of beef but never met it; what days the boiled mutton came grey and resigned; what mornings the porridge smelt of the copper pan, and what evenings the bread was newly cut and the butter set too hard to spread without tearing the crumb. I remember, too, how your little garden-plot was always better kept than mine, the earth neat as if you had combed it, whilst mine looked as if a hen had danced a jig upon it. So was Miss Esmond’s chest of drawers a model of order, whilst mine were in a sad condition.

“Do you remember how we used to tell stories in the dormitory, and Madame Hibou, the French governess, would come out of bed and interrupt us with her hooting?—a sound I can hear now, as plainly as I hear the sparrows in my eaves. Have you forgot the poor dancing-master, who told us he had been waylaid by assassins, but who was beaten, it appears, by my lord your brother’s footmen? My dear, your cousin, the Lady Maria Esmond (her papa was, I think, but Viscount Castlewood in those times), has just been on a visit to this house, where you may be sure I did not recall those sad times to her remembrance, about which I am now chattering to Mrs. Esmond.

“Her ladyship has been staying here, and another relative of yours, the Baroness of Bernstein; and the two ladies are both gone on to Tunbridge Wells. But another and dearer relative still remains in my house, and is sound asleep, I trust, in the very next room; and the name of this gentleman is Mr. Henry Esmond Warrington.

“Now, do you understand how you come to hear from an old friend? Do not be alarmed, dear madam! I know you are thinking at this moment, ‘My boy is ill. That is why Miss Molly Benson writes to me.’ No, my dear; Mr. Warrington was ill yesterday, but to-day he is very comfortable; and our doctor, who is no less a person than my dear husband, Colonel Lambert, has blooded him, has set his shoulder which was dislocated, and pronounces that in two days more Mr. Warrington will be quite ready to take the road.

“I fear I and my girls are sorry that he is so soon to be well. Yesterday evening, as we were at tea, there came a great ringing at our gate which disturbed us all, as the bell very seldom sounds in this quiet place unless a passing beggar pulls it for charity. You know that kind of ring, dear Rachel: not the civil little summons of a neighbour, but the harsh peal that sets the very spoons a-tremble in their saucers. The servants, running out, returned with the news that a young gentleman, who had a fall from his horse, was lying lifeless on the road, surrounded by the friends in whose company he was travelling.

“At this, my Colonel (who is sure the most Samaritan of men!) hastens away to see how he can serve the fallen traveller; and presently, with the aid of the servants and followed by two ladies, brings into the house such a pale, lifeless, beautiful young man! Ah, my dear, how I rejoice to think that your child has found shelter and succour under my roof! that my husband has saved him from pain and fever, and has been the means of restoring him to you and health! We shall be friends again now, shall we not?

“I was very ill last year, and ’twas even thought I should die. Do you know, that I often thought of you then, and how you had parted from me in anger so many years ago? I began then a foolish note to you, which I was too sick to finish, to tell you that if I went the way appointed for us all, I should wish to leave the world in charity with every single being I had known in it.

“Your cousin, the Right Honourable Lady Maria Esmond, showed a great deal of maternal tenderness and concern for her young kinsman after his accident. I am sure she hath a kind heart. The Baroness de Bernstein, who is of an advanced age, could not be expected to feel so keenly as we young people; but was, nevertheless, very much moved and interested until Mr. Warrington was restored to consciousness, when she said she was anxious to get on towards Tunbridge, whither she was bound, and was afraid of all things to lie in a place where there was no doctor at hand.

“My Aesculapius laughingly said he would not offer to attend upon a lady of quality, though he would answer for his young patient. Indeed, the Colonel, during his campaigns, has had plenty of practice in accidents of this nature, and I am certain, were we to call in all the faculty for twenty miles round, Mr. Warrington could get no better treatment.

“So, leaving the young gentleman to the care of me and my daughters, the Baroness and her ladyship took their leave of us, the latter very loth to go. When he is well enough, my Colonel will ride with him as far as Westerham, but on his own horses, where an old army-comrade of Mr. Lambert’s resides.

“And, as this letter will not take the post for Falmouth until, by God’s blessing, your son is well and perfectly restored, you need be under no sort of alarm for him whilst under the roof of, madam, your affectionate, humble servant,  
MARY LAMBERT.

“P.S. Thursday.

“I am glad to hear (Mr. Warrington’s coloured gentleman hath informed our people of the gratifying circumstance) that Providence hath blessed Mrs. Esmond with such vast wealth, and with an heir so likely to do credit to it. Our present means are amply sufficient, but will be small when divided amongst our survivors.

“Ah, dear madam! I have heard of your calamity of last year. Though the Colonel and I have reared many children (five), we have lost two, and a mother’s heart can feel for yours! I own to you, mine yearned to your boy to-day, when (in a manner inexpressibly affecting to me and Mr. Lambert) he mentioned his dear brother. ’Tis impossible to see your son, and not to love and regard him. I am thankful that it has been our lot to succour him in his trouble, and that in receiving the stranger within our gates we should be giving hospitality to the son of an old friend.”

So much for Harry’s death, and so much for the sort of face that buys credit without coin. Nature stamps some men early, as surely as a vintner brands his cask: frank brow, open eye, the very colour of health in the cheek, a look that seems to say, I have nothing hidden, ask me what you please. With such a countenance, Harry could hardly have begged a crust without being offered a chair. Even rogues trusted him while they robbed him.

Yet the boy—rosy as he looked—was not the simpleton that rosy cheeks sometimes advertise. He had his wits about him; and if age, with all its wrinkles, likes to pretend that cunning belongs chiefly to the grown, let any man recall the sly little commerce of schoolrooms: the practiced fibs, the obedient face masking rebellion, the delicate art of flattering Dr. Birch for five years, and calling it duty. The tongue learns early what the heart cannot translate; a child can speak humility in the master’s language while thinking mutiny in his own. There are dialects of the spirit that never pass into honest English, and perhaps never should.

Mrs. Lambert, at all events, had no mind for that sort of philosophy. Like most good women—and indeed like most bad—she was rich in sentiment, and her sentiment had a homely scent to it: tea-steam and clean sheets, beeswax, lavender, and the faint medicinal tang of whatever draught her husband had put between the patient and pain.

When Colonel Lambert had bled the young man, and with the steady hand of a soldier set the dislocated shoulder, he and his wife stood a moment at the bedside, fingers linked as if the touch itself were a prayer. Harry lay sunk in the best bed, the curtains drawn so the light fell mild upon his face. The laudanum—or whatever merciful mixture the Colonel favoured—kept him in a slumber that was not quite silence: now and then a small murmur, a word without shape, like a spoon tapping once against a cup in a dream.

“He is a pretty lad indeed,” Mrs. Lambert whispered; and in the same breath, because mothers compare as naturally as they breathe, she confessed with a pang that neither of her boys—Jack at Oxford nor Charles newly sent back to school after Bartlemytide—was half so handsome as the Virginian. The fallen stranger’s arm, where the bandage had been, was white as a lady’s; and the clean smell of soap on him made him seem not merely young but newly made.

“Yes, as you say, Jack might have been as handsome but for the small-pox,” she added; “and as for Charley—”

“Always took after his papa, my dear Molly,” said the Colonel, catching sight of his own honest face in a little looking-glass—cut border, japanned frame—that had served his guests for patches and powder, and himself for shaving.

“Did I say so, my love?” Mrs. Lambert asked, startled, as though her thought had spoken aloud.

“No; but you thought so, Mrs. Lambert.”

“How can you tell one’s thoughts so, Martin?”

“Because I am a conjurer, and because you tell them yourself, my dear,” he answered, with the quiet merriment of a man who has outlived cannon and can therefore afford to laugh at domestic alarms. “Don’t be frightened: he won’t wake after that draught I gave him. Because you never see a young fellow but you are comparing him with your own. Because you never hear of one but you are thinking which of our girls he shall fall in love with and marry.”

“Don’t be foolish, sir,” she said, and put her hand up to his lips to hush him, as if words themselves might be overheard through the wainscot. They had stepped softly into the dressing-closet adjoining the chamber: a snug little room with India curtains, Japan cabinets, and drawers that smelled of folded linen and dried lavender—an odour that seemed to sweeten the very breath. From the window one could see the garden-beds laid out as carefully as a cook’s mise en place: each herb in its place, each path swept clean, the green world trimmed to civility.

“You can’t deny it, Mrs. Lambert,” he resumed in a lower tone. “As you were looking at the young gentleman just now, you were thinking to yourself which of my girls will he marry? Shall it be Theo, or shall it be Hester? And then you thought of Lucy who was at boarding-school.”

“There is no keeping anything from you, Martin Lambert,” she sighed.

“There is no keeping it out of your eyes, my dear. What is this burning desire all you women have for selling and marrying your daughters? We men don’t wish to part with ’em. I am sure, for my part, I should not like yonder young fellow half as well if I thought he intended to carry one of my darlings away with him.”

“Sure, Martin, I have been so happy myself,” she answered, looking up at him with those best eyes which have coaxed and governed more surely than any rod, “that I must wish my girls to do as I have done, and be happy, too!”

“Then you think good husbands are common, Mrs. Lambert, and that you may walk any day into the road before the house and find one shot out at the gate like a sack of coals?”

“Wasn’t it providential, sir, that this young gentleman should be thrown over his horse’s head at our very gate, and that he should turn out to be the son of my old schoolfellow and friend?” she persisted. “There is something more than accident in such cases, depend upon that, Mr. Lambert!”

“And this was the stranger you saw in the candle three nights running, I suppose?”

“And in the fire, too, sir; twice a coal jumped out close by Theo. You may sneer, sir, but these things are not to be despised. Did I not see you distinctly coming back from Minorca, and dream of you at the very day and hour when you were wounded in Scotland?”

“How many times have you seen me wounded, when I had not a scratch, my dear? How many times have you seen me ill when I had no sort of hurt? You are always prophesying, and ’twere very hard on you if you were not sometimes right. Come! Let us leave our guest asleep comfortably, and go down and give the girls their French lesson.”

So the Colonel offered his arm, and she took it, and together they descended the broad oak staircase of the comfortable old hall. Along the walls hung the faces of foregone Lamberts—magistrates, soldiers, country gentlemen—each painted into a kind of stillness; and yet the house itself was never still. Its silence was alive: the faint clink of china in a cupboard, a servant’s step muffled by rush-matting, the distant lowing of cattle, and, now and then, that gate-bell—rare as thunder in a clear season.

Colonel Lambert was a gentleman with a pleasant, waggish humour, the sort that seasons authority without spoiling it. The French lesson he and his daughters conned together was not a dry list of verbs, but a scene from Monsieur Molière’s Tartuffe; and papa, amused at his own part, would call Miss Theo “Madam,” and bow with mock ceremony, as if they were at court and not in a country parlour.

They read a scene or two; the girls’ voices—fresh, careful, obedient—moving in and out like birds among branches, while the Colonel, arch and merry, took up Orgon’s lines with relish, tasting the French as if it were a sauce he knew well:

“ORGON. Or sus, nous voila bien. J’ai, Mariane, en vous  
Reconnu de tout temps un esprit assez doux,  
Et de tout temps aussi vous m’avez ete chere.  
MARIANE. Je suis fort redevable a cet amour de pere.  
ORGON. Fort bien. Que dites-vous de Tartuffe notre hote?  
MARIANE. Qui? Moi?  
ORGON. Vous. Voyez bien comme vous repondrez.  
MARIANE. Helas! J’en dirai, moi, tout ce que vous voudrez!  
ORGON. C’est parler sagement. Dites-moi donc, ma fille,  
Qu’en toute sa personne un haut merite brille,  
Qu’il touche votre coeur, et qu’il vous seroit doux  
De le voir par mon choix devenir votre epoux!”

Miss Theo, reading Mariane, could not keep from laughing and blushing on the right line, as if the very rhythm compelled her. The Colonel chuckled, pleased with his own art, and turned to his wife.

“Have we not read the scene prettily, Elmire?” he cried; and Elmira—Molly Lambert in her own name, but “Elmire” for the joke—admired him prodigiously, as did the daughters, and indeed almost everything their father said or did.

It is a sweet thing—more nourishing than many a fine dish—to see an honest man in his own house, with a loving wife by his side and loving, obedient children about him; to hear the unforced harmony of their daily talk, and the house’s natural music—voices not strained, doors not slammed, servants not bullied, silence not broken by needless racket. There are homes where every sound is a bruise; and there are homes where even the quiet has a flavour of peace, like warm milk with nutmeg at bedtime.

That first night at Oakhurst, Harry Warrington, sleeping under a potion and waking now and then with a feverish flutter, thought he heard an Evening Hymn. The sound came to him as if across an ocean and across years, threaded through the soft country hush—voices below, gathered together in a certain Name. In his half-delirium, the hymn was not Lambert voices at all, but his dearest brother George singing at home; and with that mistaken comfort, the boy’s breath eased, his fingers unclenched, and he went down again into sleep, as if the song itself had carried him there.

The lad sank into a sweetness of sleep, as though the very house had put a hand upon his forehead and hushed him. All night the air had been full of kindly household sounds—soft footfalls on boards rubbed smooth by generations, the faint clink of a spoon set down, a shutter eased to against the moths, and, floating through it all like a thread of balm, the last hymn of evening sung in a clear young voice. He woke with the sun strong at the casement, a warm square of light lying across the counterpane; and there, smiling at his bed-curtains as if they had watched beside him, stood his host and hostess.

Hunger came on him like a fever of its own—ravenous, shameless, hearty. His doctor, who had bled him soundly and left him with that light swimming weakness which follows, examined the bandage and declared that appetite was the surest sign of mending.

“You shall eat, then,” said he; “and you shall eat what will knit you. No beef for you yet. A mess of chicken, with rice, and a little of the broth it was dressed in. My wife will see to it.”

Mrs. Lambert, pleased with her patient’s eagerness as if it were a compliment to her care, told him, as she drew the curtain a little more to give him the full cheer of the morning, that the dish had been prepared by one of her daughters’ own hands.

“One of her daughters?” The words, simple as they were, struck a spark upon the half-burnt tinder of his memory. A faint picture rose—two young faces with red cheeks and black waving locks bending over him, smiles that had looked like sunshine through leaves, and then the quick withdrawing of them when he came a little to himself. And on the heel of that came another remembrance—of a female indeed lovely, but older; certainly much older; and with f—.

Oh, horror and remorse! He turned upon the pillow with a groan as though his wounded shoulder had been stabbed anew. An immense gulf of time seemed to yawn between him and what had been last night and what had been long ago: pearls he had once been told were false, locks that were pinchbeck gold—boyhood warnings returned now like a bell heard in a fog. He had slept from a draught, had been empty of food, had bled, had fever in him; and the mind, loosened by such physic, will make phantoms and call them realities.

“What is it, my dear child?” cried kind Mrs. Lambert, frightened by his start.

“Nothing, madam,” said he, mastering himself. “A twinge in my shoulder. I— I speak to my host and hostess? Sure you have been very kind to me.”

“We are old friends, Mr. Warrington,” she answered with a look which made her kindness feel like a right. “My husband, Colonel Lambert, knew your father; and your mamma and I were girls together at Kensington. You were no stranger to us when your aunt and cousin told us who you were.”

“Are they here?” Harry asked; and for the first time the simple question had a blankness in it, as if he feared what the answer must bring.

“They must have lain at Tunbridge Wells last night,” said Mrs. Lambert. “They sent a horseman from Reigate yesterday for news of you.”

“Ah! I remember,” said Harry, and his eyes went to his bandaged arm as if it were a seal to the whole strange passage.

“I have made a good cure of you, Mr. Warrington,” the Colonel said, coming up with that blunt cheer which belongs to men who have seen wounds in earnest. “And now Mrs. Lambert and the cook must take charge of you.”

“Nay; Theo prepared the chicken and rice, Mr. Lambert,” said the lady, with a sort of pride that would not be hidden. “Will Mr. Warrington get up after he has had his breakfast? We will send your valet to you.”

“If howling proves fidelity,” said Mr. Lambert, “your man must be a most fond, attached creature.”

“He let your baggage travel off after all in your aunt’s carriage,” Mrs. Lambert continued. “You must wear my husband’s linen, which, I dare say, is not so fine as yours.”

“Pish, my dear! my shirts are good shirts enough for any Christian,” cried the Colonel.

“They are Theo’s and Hester’s work,” said mamma; and the Colonel’s eyebrows rose as if that fact were both pride and reproof. “And Theo hath ripped and sewed your sleeve to make it quite comfortable for your shoulder,” she added, as though the stitch itself were a virtue.

Harry, whose senses had returned with hunger, took note of everything about him with a new, bodily gratitude: the clean scent of linen warmed by sun, the faint sharpness of vinegar from the sick-room washing, and—on the toilet-table, beneath a japan-framed glass—a great China vase of roses, their perfume spilling into the air like a draught.

“What beautiful roses!” he cried, for the sight almost hurt him with its living colour.

“My daughter Theo cut them this morning,” said Mrs. Lambert quickly. “Well, Mr. Lambert? She did cut them!”

The Colonel, I suppose, thought his wife named Theo too often, for he trod on her slipper or gave some little nudge toward discretion; but Mrs. Lambert’s pleasure in her child’s services was not to be stifled.

“And I fancied I heard some one singing the Evening Hymn very sweetly last night—or was it only a dream?” Harry asked.

“Theo again, Mr. Warrington!” said the Colonel, laughing. “My servants said your negro man began it in the kitchen as if he was a church organ.”

“Our people sing it at home, sir,” Harry said; and the sound of his own voice saying it seemed to carry him far across the sea. “My grandpapa used to love it very much. His wife’s father was a great friend of good Bishop Ken, who wrote it; and—and my dear brother used to love it too.” His words fell away, and there was an instant in which the room’s cheerful noises—the clock’s tick, a distant creak of a pump-handle in the yard, the muted coo of pigeons—seemed to grow tender with his grief.

Mrs. Lambert looked as if she could have kissed him then, not from any forwardness, but because maternal pity will put its mouth upon sorrow as if to soothe it by touch. His mishap, his weakness, the simple pieties of the house, the readiness of their care, had softened him. For some weeks past he had breathed an air tainted with worldliness and corruption, where even kindness carried a price, and the talk of men had the ring of coin in it; here was a different climate, where attention was given as bread is broken—because it is right that one should not be hungry.

They left him to his breakfast, and the Colonel sat by the bed while the dish was brought. It was no grand entertainment; it was only a plain country mess, but prepared with that patient accuracy which makes homely food memorable. The chicken had been simmered, not fiercely boiled, so the flesh held its sweetness and did not shred into dryness. The broth had been skimmed till it shone, with a mild savour of parsley and onion that had yielded without asserting themselves. The rice lay in it plump and separate, not clotted, each grain softened through but still keeping its own shape—such a thing is not done without a cook’s attention and a young housekeeper’s pride. A little salt, and a squeeze—no more—of lemon, made the whole taste clean and restorative, as if it were meant to put the blood back in a man.

Gratitude and that comfortable repletion which comes of wholesome food set Mr. Warrington in a genial mood. He was more ready to speak than was his habit; for, unless some strong feeling stirred him, he was commonly cautious and taciturn, and no great maker of fancies. Books had been neglected with him, and of such as he had seen he spoke without cleverness; but of horses and dogs and the plain business of living he could talk freely, because those things came to him by eye, ear, and hand.

Colonel Lambert—who had shrewdness enough for men, and experience enough for both cattle and books—took his measure quickly. In their talk Harry learned, for the first time, that Mrs. Lambert had been early friend to his mother, and that Lambert’s father had served with Harry’s grandfather, Colonel Esmond, in Queen Anne’s wars. The sense of being among his own sort—of finding old ties in a strange land—eased him more than any medicine.

“My boys are both away,” said the Colonel, “or they would have shown you the country when you got up, Mr. Warrington. Now you can only have the company of my wife and her daughters. Mrs. Lambert hath told you already about one of them—Theo, our eldest—who made your broth, cut your roses, and mended your coat. She is not such a wonder as her mother imagines her: but little Theo is a smart housekeeper, and a very good and cheerful lass—though her father says it.”

“It is very kind of Miss Lambert to take so much care for me,” Harry said, and meant it, thinking of the steady hand that had sewn his sleeve and the careful skimming of that broth.

“She is no kinder to you than to any other mortal, and doth but her duty.” The Colonel smiled as he said it. “I laugh at their mother for praising our children, and I am as foolish about them myself. The truth is, God hath given us very good and dutiful children, and I see no reason why I should disguise my thankfulness. You have never a sister, I think?”

“No, sir. I am alone now,” Harry answered; and the words were heavier than he intended.

“Ay, truly, I ask your pardon for my thoughtlessness. Your man hath told our people what befell last year. I served with Braddock in Scotland, and hope he mended before he died. A wild fellow, sir, but there was a fund of truth about him, and no little kindness under his rough swagger. Your black fellow talks very freely about his master and his affairs. I suppose you permit him these freedoms as he rescued you—”

“Rescued me?” cried Harry, lifting himself with sudden heat.

“From ever so many Indians on that very expedition. My Molly and I did not know we were going to entertain so prodigiously wealthy a gentleman. He saith that half Virginia belongs to you; but if the whole of North America were yours, we could but give you our best.”

Harry coloured. “Those negro boys, sir, lie like the father of all lies. They think it is for our honour to represent us as ten times as rich as we are. My mother has what would be a vast estate in England, and is a very good one at home. We are as well off as most of our neighbours, sir, but no better; and all our splendour is in Mr. Gumbo’s foolish imagination. He never rescued me from an Indian in his life, and would run away at the sight of one, as my poor brother’s boy did on that fatal day when he fell.”

“The bravest man will do so at unlucky times,” said Lambert quietly. “I myself saw the best troops in the world run at Preston, before a ragged mob of Highland savages.”

“That was because the Highlanders fought for a good cause, sir.”

“Do you think,” asked Harry’s host, “that the French Indians had the good cause in the fight of last year?”

“The scoundrels!” Harry cried, clenching his fist. “I would have the scalp of every murderous redskin among ’em! They were robbing and invading the British territories, too. But the Highlanders were fighting for their king.”

“We, on our side, were fighting for our king; and we ended by winning the battle,” said the Colonel, with a laugh that took the edge off contention.

“Ah!” cried Harry; “if his Royal Highness the Prince had not turned back at Derby, your king and mine now would be his Majesty King James the Third!”

“Who made such a Tory of you, Mr. Warrington?” asked Lambert.

“Nay, sir, the Esmonds were always loyal!” Harry answered hotly. “Had we lived at home, and twenty years sooner, brother and I often and often agreed our heads would have been in danger. We certainly would have staked them for the king’s cause.”

“Yours is better on your shoulders than on a pole at Temple Bar. I have seen them there, and they don’t look very pleasant.”

“I shall take off my hat, and salute them, whenever I pass the gate,” cried Harry, carried away, “if the king and the whole court are standing by!”

“I doubt whether your relative, my Lord Castlewood, is as staunch a supporter of the king over the water,” said Colonel Lambert, smiling: “or your aunt, the Baroness of Bernstein, who left you in our charge. Whatever her old partialities may have been, she has repented of them; she has rallied to our side, landed her nephews in the Household, and looks to find a suitable match for her nieces. If you have Tory opinions, Mr. Warrington, take an old soldier’s advice, and keep them to yourself.”

“Why, sir, I do not think you will betray me!” said Harry.

“Not I; but others might. You did not talk in this way at Castlewood? I mean the old Castlewood you have just come from.”

“I might be safe amongst my own kinsmen, surely, sir!” Harry cried, stung.

“Doubtless. I would not say no. But a man’s own kin can play him slippery tricks at times, and he finds himself none the better for trusting them. I mean no offence to you or any of your family; but lacqueys have ears as well as their masters, and they carry about all sorts of stories. For instance, your black fellow is ready to tell all he knows about you, and a great deal more besides, as it would appear.”

Harry’s face flamed. “Hath he told about the broken-kneed horse?”

“To say truth, my groom seemed to know something of the story, and said it was a shame a gentleman should sell another such a brute—let alone a cousin. I am not here to play the Mentor to you, or to carry about servants’ tittle-tattle. When you have seen more of your cousins, you will form your own opinion of them; meanwhile, take an old soldier’s advice again, and be cautious with whom you deal, and what you say.”

Soon after, with Gumbo’s help, Harry rose. He promised his valet for the hundredth time a sound caning if ever he heard that Gumbo had ventured to talk of his affairs again in servants’ hall. Gumbo swore with solemn eyes that he would obey for ever; and, I dare say, had his mouth running even then, for news travels in kitchens as briskly as fire along dry straw, and servants will feed one another on secrets as eagerly as on ale and dripping. Mrs. Lambert, at any rate, came by a number of stories concerning her guest which she could not prevent her housekeeper from repeating; though of course one would not accuse any worthy lady—man or woman—of undue curiosity. Yet how is one to forbid listening, when talk comes unasked, like a cart rumbling past your gate?

Mr. Lambert’s house stood on the outskirts of the little town of Oakhurst, upon the road between Farnham and Reigate. Madame Bernstein’s people, in their confusion, naturally pulled at the first bell at hand when the accident befell; and so, instead of carrying the wounded gentleman a few hundred yards farther to the long street where a tavern’s swinging tuns promised hospitality and a surgeon’s blazing gilt pestle and mortar promised physic, they brought him into the hands of one who could have tended him no more cleverly had he taken a fee, and could have made him no more welcome if he had been kin.

Two tall gates, each topped by heraldic monsters, led from the highroad to a neat broad stone terrace on which stood Oakhurst House—a square brick building with stone-faced windows, high chimneys, and a tall roof with a fair balustrade. Behind it stretched a garden roomy enough for cabbages as well as roses; and before, separated by the highroad, lay a field where cows and horses grazed with that steady tearing sound of contented beasts, which, when the wind is right, is as soothing as the sea. Over the centre window was a carved shield supported by the same monsters and crowned with a coronet; for the house had once been the jointure-house of Oakhurst Castle, whose turrets and chimneys showed over the surrounding woods now dark with full summer leaf. Oakhurst House was the greatest in the town; but the Castle was of more importance than the town put together. The Castle and jointure-house had been friends for years: their fathers had fought side by side in Queen Anne’s wars. Two small pieces of ordnance stood on Lambert’s terrace, and six before the Castle; all had been taken from the same privateer which Lambert and his kinsman and commander, Lord Wrotham, had brought into Harwich from Flanders with despatches from the great Duke.

When Gumbo had dressed his master’s fair hair and set him neat, and when the wounded shoulder was supported by a handkerchief hung from his neck, Harry made his way out, preceded by his host. They went down a broad oak stair round which hung pikes and muskets of ancient shape, and so into a square marble-paved hall from which the rooms branched. Arms were everywhere—pikes and halberts, pistols and jack-boots more than a century old, that had served in Cromwell’s wars; a tattered French guidon borne by a gendarme at Malplaquet; and a pair of cumbrous Highland broadswords which, having been carried as far as Derby, had been flung away on the fatal field of Culloden. Breastplates and black morions of Oliver’s troopers gleamed dully, and portraits of stern men in buff jerkins and plain bands looked down with cropped hair and uncompromising mouths.

“They fought against your grandfathers and King Charles, Mr. Warrington,” said Lambert, noticing the boy’s troubled gaze. “I don’t hide that. They rode to join the Prince of Orange at Exeter. We were Whigs, young gentleman—and something more. John Lambert, the Major-General, was a kinsman of our house, and we were all more or less partial to short hair and long sermons. You do not seem to like either?”

Harry’s face indeed showed no pleasure at the company of Parliamentary heroes. The house itself, with its relics and its words, spoke a dialect of loyalty different from his own; and in that difference there was a quiet power. A man might swear one thing in a drawing-room, and find it translated another way in a kitchen. Even names—Whig, Tory—were like spices: in one mouth they warmed, in another they bit.

“Be not alarmed,” Lambert continued, good-humoured. “We are very good Churchmen now. My eldest son will be in orders ere long. He is now travelling as governor to my Lord Wrotham’s son in Italy. And as for our women, they are all for the Church, and carry me with ’em. Every woman is a Tory at heart. Mr. Pope says a rake, but I think t’other is the more charitable word. Come, let us go see them.”

He flung open the dark oak door, and led Harry into the parlour where the ladies were gathered.

“Here is Miss Hester,” said the Colonel, “and this is Miss Theo—the soup-maker, the tailoress, the harpsichord-player, and the songstress who set you to sleep last night. Make a curtsey to the gentleman, young ladies! Oh, I forgot—Theo is mistress of the roses you admired awhile since in your bedchamber. I think she has kept some of them in her cheeks.”

Miss Theo, making a curtsey as deep and ceremonious as the times required, blushed in good earnest. She was not a particular beauty, nor did Harry fall headlong at first sight, faithless to that other person who had lately bewitched him. But she had kind eyes and a sweet voice; a ruddy freckled cheek; a round white neck from which, beneath a little cap such as misses wore, fell rich curling clusters of dark brown hair. She was no delicate, sentimental creature: her bare arms from the elbow were jolly and red with work and health; her feet were not so miraculously small but that one might see them without a telescope; her waist had nothing waspish about it. She was sixteen and looked older, as girls who manage household things often do. Yet she blushed as if she had done something bold in bringing a bowl of broth to a stranger, and rose from her curtsey with the innocence of one who has been praised too openly.

As she came up, her father tapped her under the chin—there was a hint of a double chin there, honest and wholesome—and hummed, laughing, a French line he had read that day. “Eh bien! que dites-vous, ma fille, de notre hôte?”

“Nonsense, Mr. Lambert!” cried mamma, shocked at his freedom.

“Nonsense is sometimes the best kind of sense in the world,” said Colonel Lambert. Harry looked puzzled, as if the language itself had slipped past him.

“Are you fond of nonsense?” the Colonel asked him, watching his face with a kindly mischief. “We consume a vast deal of it in this house. Rabelais is my favourite reading. My wife is all for Mr. Fielding and Theophrastus. I think Theo prefers Tom Brown, and Mrs. Hetty here loves Dean Swift.”

“Our papa is talking what he loves,” said Miss Hetty.

“And what is that, miss?” asked the father of his second daughter.

“Sure, sir, you said yourself it was nonsense,” she answered, with a saucy toss.

“Which of them do you like best, Mr. Warrington?” asked the Colonel.

“Which of whom, sir?”

“The Curate of Meudon, or the Dean of St. Patrick’s, or honest Tom, or Mr. Fielding?”

“And what were they, sir?”

“They! Why, they wrote books.”

“Indeed, sir. I never heard of either one of ’em,” said Harry, hanging down his head. “I fear my book-learning was neglected at home. My brother had read every book that ever was wrote, I think. He could have talked to you about ’em for hours together.”

At this, Mrs. Lambert’s eyes went to her daughter, and Miss Theo cast hers down and blushed anew—so quickly do households keep their own private histories, and so silently do certain names and losses pass between women like a thing understood. The room, full of sunlight and polished wood and the faint smell of yesterday’s beeswax, seemed to hold also a shadow of that absent brother—present by the very mention of him, and absent by the untranslatable gap between what one man can feel and another can say.

“Never mind; honesty is better than books any day, Mr. Warrington!” cried the jolly Colonel. “You may go through the world very honourably without reading any of the books I have been talking of; and some of them might give you more pleasure than profit.”

“I know more about horses and dogs than Greek and Latin, sir. We most of us do in Virginia,” Harry said.

“You are like the Persians; you can ride and speak the truth.”

“Are the Prussians very good on horseback, sir? I hope I shall see their king and a campaign or two, either with ’em or against ’em,” Harry remarked.

Why did Miss Theo glance at her mother, and why did that good woman’s face take on a sadness that was like a cloud crossing the sun? Because young lasses in humdrum country towns are not born without dreams. Because they wear caps and curtsey deep and have never quitted mother’s apron, do you suppose they have no inward story, no private language of the heart? The world’s great trumpet calls—war, travel, glory—sound to them even through garden walls and dairy doors. They hear it in the crack of a distant whip on the road, in the post-horn’s faint note, in the roll of a cart over stones, and they translate it into their own dialect of longing.

In fairy tales, you understand, the blessed hour always comes: the ivory horn is blown at the castle gate; and far off in her bower the princess starts up and knows it is the right champion. He is always ready; giants’ heads tumble as he gallops on his white charger, falchion flashing. How should a maiden locked in an inaccessible fortress, who has never seen any man not eighty, or humpbacked, or her father, know such beings as young men existed? Yet she does. There is an instinct; there is a season; there is that watchful expectancy which sits like a bird at the window of the breast.

Sister Ann, Sister Ann, do you see him? Surely it is a knight with curling mustachios and silver armour. Oh no—it is only a costermonger with his donkey and pannier of cabbages. Sister Ann, Sister Ann, what is that cloud of dust? Only a farmer’s man driving pigs from market. Sister Ann, Sister Ann, who is that splendid warrior in scarlet and gold? He nears the gate; he lifts the hammer; he knocks twice—ah me, it is only the postman with a double letter from Northamptonshire.

So we make false starts in life. I do not believe there is any such thing remembered as first love—no more than one remembers one’s christening. You fancy your spotless maiden never cared for any but you, and she tells you so? Oh, you innocent! When she was four years old she had a tenderness for the Buttons who carried coals up to the nursery, or the little sweep at the crossing, or the music-master, or never mind whom. She had a secret longing toward her brother’s schoolfellow, or the third charity boy at church; and had occasion served, the comedy enacted with you might have been performed with another. Not that she confessed it; only that she had it. Lay down this page and think how many times you were in love before you chose the present Mrs. Jones as partner of your name and affections.

Mrs. Lambert’s little holiday of fancy ended as such holidays commonly do: not with a thunderclap, but with the quiet click of a latch, and the sense of a room returning to its usual proportions. In the space of three days, Miss Theo and her mother had been obliged—tenderly, almost reluctantly—to confess to themselves that the pale young gentleman who had arrived at their gate with blood on his sleeve was not, after all, a creature minted out of romance, but an ordinary mortal with an ordinary appetite, an ordinary awkwardness, and a very real need of clean linen.

They spoke little of it. Love in a household has its own shorthand: a glance over the rim of a teacup, a pause while a ribbon is tied, a finger smoothing a crease in a sleeve that does not need smoothing. Mrs. Lambert, who could weep conscientiously over a printed sorrow, tried to console her daughter without naming the thing that hurt.

“Never mind, my dear,” she whispered in the way a kiss whispers, warm on Theo’s cheek. “Our hero proves human; and none such is good enough for my Theo. Thou shalt have a real husband ere long, if there be one in England. Why, I was scarce fifteen when your father first saw me at Bury Assembly; and while I was yet at school I vowed I’d never have any other man. If Heaven gave me such a husband—the best man in the whole kingdom—sure it will bless my child equally, who deserves a king if she fancies him!”

And indeed, with the same earnestness with which she ordered her still-room to be aired in damp weather, Mrs. Lambert seemed to order Providence to send greatness down her drive. No coach rattled past the gate but, in her mind, it might as well have been rolling straight from a fairy-tale: some young gentleman was sure to alight, ring the bell, and, between the tea-tray and the parlour fire, be gently apprenticed to love. It was even possible—she knew the Prince of Wales’s age, and had heard how handsome and good a young prince was—that she expected royalty itself to come cantering by, tumble obligingly from its horse, be carried in, cured, and afterwards reward Colonel Lambert with a regiment, and fall in love with Theo in the most proper and affecting manner.

Colonel Lambert, for his part, and his second daughter, Miss Hetty, took their stand on the laughing side, the side that pricks sentiment with a pin and then begs pardon for the prick by kissing hard. Mrs. Lambert had her novels; Hetty had her tongue. It ran as briskly as a spit before a clear fire, turning every subject and basting it with mischief.

She made a hundred sly allusions to their guest—so sly that they were not sly at all to the two listeners at whom they were aimed. She brought Prussia and Persia tumbling into talk with abominable pertness and frequency. She asked, with her head on one side, whether the present King of Prussia was called the Shaw or the Sophy; how far it might be from Ispahan to Saxony, which his Majesty was at present invading, as papa might see upon his maps and newspapers; and whether a person could travel thither with no more baggage than a gentleman’s valise and a set shoulder.

She fetched down the Persian Tales from her mamma’s closet and laid them, as if by accident, on the parlour table where the family sat. She declared she would not marry a Persian prince, not for her part: she preferred a gentleman who did not keep more than one wife at a time. She called Mr. Warrington Theo’s prince, and asked her mother, with a saucy bob, whether she wished Hetty to take the other visitor—the black prince—for herself. Then, after she had teased until Theo’s colour rose and Mrs. Lambert’s eyes filled, she would begin to cry too, as if she had been the injured party, and would rush in, kissing them violently one after the other, coaxing them back into good humour with the same hands that had pinched them.

All the while, Harry Warrington—simple Harry—knew nothing. He was the innocent occasion of this domestic play, and as ignorant of its plot as a fish is of the ripple made by a thrown stone. The arrows of “Prussia” and “Persia” whistled by him, and he did not so much as turn his head. A Shaw? A Sophy? He likely imagined a Sophy to be a lady, and would have laughed outright at the notion that a man with a great black beard should be called so. He was not stupid, though Miss Hetty in her impatience thought him so: he was merely full of his own honest affairs, and shy of women in that very common way of young men who have lived hitherto with horses and guns and plain household decencies, and have not yet learned that a look across a room can be a sentence in a language they do not know they are speaking.

So it happened that, three days after his arrival, the hospitable family walked with him in my Lord Wrotham’s park, where Colonel Lambert had leave to wander as a neighbour and friend. The day had the polished clearness that belongs to the end of autumn holidays: a thin sun, a faint bite in the air, and the steady, comforting hush of old trees holding back the wind. On a piece of water, the swans came sailing towards them with that calm authority which makes even a pond seem like court. The young ladies were accustomed to feed the birds with bread, and their fingers broke the crust into small white pieces as if they were preparing a dish rather than bribing a creature.

Hetty, with a queer look at her mother and sister and then a glance at her father—honest and content in a red waistcoat—said suddenly, “Mamma’s swans are something like these, papa.”

“What swans, my dear?” says mamma, puzzled.

“Something like, but not quite. They have shorter necks than these, and are, scores of them, on our common,” continues Miss Hetty with a gravity meant to be outrageous. “I saw Betty plucking one in the kitchen this morning. We shall have it for dinner, with apple-sauce and—”

“Don’t be a little goose!” cried Theo, with a quick, embarrassed laugh.

“—and sage and onions,” Hetty finished, as if she were dictating the very receipt. “Do you love swan, Mr. Warrington?”

“I shot three last winter on our river,” said the Virginian, as simply as if she had asked him whether he liked beef. “Ours are not such white birds as these—they eat very well, though.”

Mrs. Lambert gave a little sound between a protest and a sigh; Theo flushed; Colonel Lambert stared out over the water as if examining the birds’ wings. And Harry, who had answered honestly about the table-worth of a swan, had not the least notion that he himself had been served up in allegory and seasoned with Hetty’s impudence.

Theo’s first tender flutter—her soft shock of admiration when she had seen him at their gate, pale and bleeding—proved, in its own gentle way, like a lark’s note sounded before daybreak. It was not the great passion she had believed her heart capable of feeling. It had wakened too early, sung at a false dawn, and then, sensing the cold in the air, drawn back under the wing. A truer morning might come; but this was not it.

If the young gentleman could walk—and it appeared he could walk perfectly well—what business had he to be walking here at all? His shoulder was set; his health restored; he had not even a change of coats and was obliged to Colonel Lambert for raiment. He ought, by every tie of duty and convenience—by love, by relationship, by a gentle heart waiting for him, by the washerwoman, finally—to be at Tunbridge Wells with Lady Maria Esmond on the Pantiles. Why did he linger at Oakhurst unless he was in love with one of the young ladies (and he was not), or unless some invisible weight, some clinging fate, held him down?

Perhaps his fell aunt’s purpose was answered; perhaps Lady Maria’s late hope had been killed as neatly by poisonous communications as a garden plant is killed by a spoonful of brine. One may imagine the soundscape of Tunbridge without needing to be there: the bright, ceaseless chatter under the colonnade; the scrape of chairs; the fiddles that try too hard; the rattling of wheels on gravel; and, through it all, the harsher note of one dominating voice that makes every other voice smaller. Between her old aunt and her unhappy delusion, Lady Maria could be having no pleasant time. She was poor and hoped for money; she had secrets her aunt knew and brandished; and she stood alone in the crowd, where loneliness is loudest. One might fancy her, for all her faults and false adornments, as an antique Andromeda chained up for the dragon—her rich hair, true or not, falling over her shoulders—while the monster waited and waited, and Perseus loitered elsewhere, warm and comfortable, not in the least hurry.

Harry Warrington, who would not have allowed a mended shoulder to keep him from hunting, remained day after day at Oakhurst, and each day the kindly people who welcomed him grew more to his liking. Perhaps, since his grandfather’s death, he had not been in such good company. He had lived contentedly enough among fox-hunting Virginian squires, riding their horses, drinking their punch, and taking their talk as the measure of the world. The women of his home acquaintance were decorous and pious and well-bred, but narrow in their ways; the place itself had pompous little etiquettes and punctilios, small flatteries, small conversations, small scandals. He had not known, until he left it some time later, how confined his life had been, though he could ride and shoot for miles. The air at home was his mother’s air, and he breathed it whether it suited him or no.

Here, by contrast, was a circle incomparably gayer, brighter, freer; a house where the very sounds were different. The morning began not with a clatter of commands, but with the soft industry of a well-ordered kitchen—the crack of firewood, the steady chop of a knife, the low scold of a kettle coming to boil—sounds that promise sustenance rather than submission. Even the laughter in the parlour had a kind of clean echo, as if the walls had never learned to hoard malice.

Colonel Lambert had seen the world and come unwounded out of it, as he had out of dangers and battles. He had read more books than Harry could pretend to judge of, and had that unmistakable goodness and honesty written on his face and breathed from his lips which brave men instinctively recognise as their own coin. In such company Harry began, to his benefit, to learn that he was profoundly ignorant, and that there were many people far better than he had known how to imagine. He could be arrogant enough with those he thought his equals; in the presence of superiors he became docile with a magnanimity that did him more honour than any loud assurance could have done.

As for the women, they were the kindest, merriest, most agreeable he had yet known. They were pleasanter than Parson Broadbent’s black-eyed daughter at home, whose laugh could carry as far as a gun. They were as well-bred as the Castlewood ladies, save Madam Beatrix, who could be as grand as an empress on occasion. Yet after a talk with Madam Beatrix, for all the amusement and interest of her stories, Harry would come away with a bitter taste in his mouth, as though some bright dish had been flavoured with an herb too sharp, and he would fancy the world wicked round about him. Here there was no such aftertaste. Mrs. Lambert and her girls were not squeamish; they could laugh over pages of Mr. Fielding and cry over volumes of Mr. Richardson, though those books held jokes and incidents that would make Mrs. Grundy’s hair stand on end; yet their merry prattle left no bitterness behind. Their tales of neighbours were droll rather than cruel; their curtseys and salutations in the little town were kindly given and kindly received; their bounties were cordial, like well-made broth carried to a sick-bed without fuss.

Not much happened in those happy hours. It was sweet sleep, pleasant waking, friendly welcome, serene pastime: the kind of peace that later storms make memorable. The gates of the old house seemed to shut the wicked world outside, and the people within to be better and kinder than most. He was not in love—no, not in the least with saucy Hetty nor with generous Theodosia—but when the time came for him to go, he took both their hands and held them fast for a moment, and felt an immense regard for them. He thought he should like to know their brothers, and that they must be fine fellows. And as for Mrs. Lambert, she was as sentimental at his departure as if he had been the last volume of Clarissa Harlowe shut with a sigh.

From the terrace they saw him ride away on the road to Westerham, with Colonel Lambert beside him and servants following.

“He is very kind and honest,” said Theo gravely, watching the small figures diminish, the horses’ hoofbeats softening as the park swallowed sound.

“I don’t think him stupid at all now,” said little Hetty. “And, mamma, I think he is very like a swan indeed.”

“It felt just like one of the boys going to school,” said mamma, pressing her handkerchief to her mouth as if to hold the feeling in.

“Just like it,” Theo answered, and there was a sadness in her tone that was not only about Harry.

“I am glad he has got papa to ride with him to Westerham,” Hetty went on; “and that he bought Farmer Briggs’s horse. I don’t like his going to those Castlewood people. I am sure that Madame Bernstein is a wicked old woman. I expected to see her ride away on her crooked stick.”

“Hush, Hetty!”

“Do you think she would float if they tried her in the pond, as poor old Mother Hely did at Elmhurst? The other old woman seemed fond of him—I mean the one with the fair toupee. She looked very melancholy when she went away; but Madame Bernstein whisked her off with her crutch, and she was obliged to go. I don’t care, Theo. I know she is wicked. You think everybody good, you do, because you never do anything wrong yourself.”

“My Theo is a good girl,” Mrs. Lambert said, looking fondly at both daughters, as if the sight of their faces were a nourishment.

“Then why do we call her a miserable sinner?” Hetty demanded, quick as a sparrow.

“We are all so, my love,” said mamma, with a sigh that had been borrowed from sermons and sweetened by domestic habit.

“What, papa too? You know you don’t think so,” cried Miss Hester; and to allow that even Colonel Lambert might be a “miserable sinner” was almost more than Mrs. Lambert’s heart could afford.

Hetty’s eyes darted with sudden triumph. “What was that you told John to give to Mr. Warrington’s black man?”

Mamma coloured a little, shamefaced, and owned it was a bottle of her cordial water and a cake she had bid Betty make. It was the sort of cake her sons carried to school or college: rich with butter, close with eggs, studded perhaps with currants that had been soaked and dried, flavoured with a rasp of nutmeg from the still-room’s precious store; the kind that, when cut, gives off a warm, honest scent as of wheat and hearth and the hands that laboured for it.

“I feel quite like a mother to him, my dears,” she confessed softly. “I can’t help owning it—and you know both our boys still like one of our cakes to take with them.”

Mrs. Lambert had taken her stand with the girls at the window, a white handkerchief lifted like a small flag of surrender to the road. They watched the two horsemen go at a pace that was neither hurried nor ceremonious—just the easy, well-bred trot of men who had learned to make leave-taking look like an ordinary part of the day, as if departures were no more than stepping out to see to the orchard or the malt-kiln.

But at Oakhurst, even the road had its ritual.

They followed the riders with their eyes until the limes took them—those old trees whose leaves made a thin, constant whispering, like silk brushed the wrong way. The trunks were grey, as if rubbed with ash; the boughs clumped together into a green screen that hid the bend of the lane. Behind that screen Mrs. Lambert had watched, through the years, the shapes of her life go and vanish: a husband riding to danger, sons packed off to school, one after another swallowed by that same corner, and then, when Heaven pleased, returned again—bringing noise back into the house, boots on the flags, laughter in the passage, the sound of a whip unhooked from its peg.

The women’s hours made room for remembrance. When men were gone, the house itself became an archive. There was the vacant chamber where a boy had slept the night before, the bed still faintly pressed where his carpet-bag had lain. There was his rod and wicker creel set in the hall, smelling of river-water and damp rush. At dinner there would be a dish made because it had been his favourite—cherry-tart, perhaps, the crust browned to that point where butter turns nutty and the fruit keeps its sharpness; and a mother would notice, as if the noticing were a kind of prayer, that half of it had been eaten at two o’clock in spite of tears, with a choking little sister on either side trying to smile.

Even the day’s sound changed. At evening prayers a voice would be missing from the responses; at midnight the house’s silence would feel too deliberate, as though the very timbers had been trained to listen for absent footsteps. Mrs. Lambert, whose life had been stitched together by such comings and goings, grew quiet whenever she and the girls walked beneath those limes without the men. Once she had said she would like to carve their names upon the trunks—true-lovers’ knots and initials, as people did then—so that the trees would hold, in their living grain, what memory could not always keep. Miss Theo, who had a pretty talent for turning feeling into verse, had even written lines upon the trees which her delighted mother sent off to a magazine; and no doubt the limes, indifferent, went on whispering as before, taking poems and partings as they took weather.

The riders passed the screen of leaves.

“Now we are out of sight of the ladies,” Colonel Lambert said, lifting his hat in a last salute even though the window could no longer command the road. “My wife will be watching still. She always watches until we are round that corner. I hope we shall have you at Oakhurst again, Mr. Warrington. When the boys are home there may be better sport for you.”

“I never want to be happier, sir, than I have been,” Harry Warrington answered; and the words came out with a sincerity that surprised even himself. “It feels like leaving old friends.”

“The friend with whom we shall sup to-night has a son who is an old friend of our family too,” Lambert said. “My wife—she is an inveterate marriage-monger—would have made a match between him and one of my girls, but that the Colonel hath chosen to fall in love with somebody else.”

“Ah,” Harry sighed, with that sudden inwardness which came upon him whenever any man spoke lightly of love. “Other folks have done the same thing. There were brave fellows before Agamemnon.”

“I beg your pardon—Aga—?” the Virginian began, honestly puzzled.

“No, no—James Wolfe,” Lambert cried, laughing. “A young fellow still, or what we call so—scarce thirty. The youngest lieutenant-colonel in the army, unless you count the few scores of our nobility who take rank before us common folk.”

“Of course—of course,” Harry said, with the colonial reverence for precedence which could sit quite comfortably beside republican pride in other hours.

“I have seen him command captains thirty years his senior,” Lambert continued, “brave men too, who had neither his merit nor his fortune. Yet no one envies him. We acknowledge he is our superior. He is beloved by every man of our old regiment, knows each face, each voice. A scholar as well as a soldier, and master of many languages.”

At that, Harry’s mind—so often quickened by the jingle of bridles and the easy music of hoofbeats on hard road—fell into another kind of listening: a listening inward, towards what he lacked.

“Ah, sir,” he said, and the humility sounded raw in him, like a confession spoken too loudly. “I feel I have neglected my youth. I have come to England an ignoramus. Had my dear brother lived, he would have borne our name—and our colony—better than I can. George was a scholar; George was a musician; George could speak with learned men. I am glad to have come home, and to you especially, if only to learn how ignorant I am.”

“If you know that, ’tis a gain already,” Lambert said gently. “At home, and especially of late, I daresay you were flattered.”

Harry’s face, warmed by the morning’s ride and by a kind of shame, coloured. “Since we lost my brother, I used to think myself a mighty fine fellow. Folks about us—our gentry—know a deal about dogs and horses and betting and games. I wish I knew more about books, and less about them.”

“Nay,” Lambert replied. “Dogs and horses are books too, in their way. You may read truth out of ’em. Not all men are made to be scholars. If each does his best in his station, what matter high or low? His Royal Highness commands; Martin Lambert is colonel; Jack Hunt rides behind us now and was once a private and is a worthy groom. Who knows whether Jack’s currycomb, my epaulets, or a prince’s baton may not prove equal at the last? When I began, I dreamed of honour. Now I think of duty—and yonder folks from whom we parted. Let us trot on, else we shall not reach Westerham before nightfall.”

So they rode, the road’s own music changing as it passed from open country to village verge: the softer thud where earth lay over stone, the sharper ring when the shoe struck flint. There were hedges with late scents trapped in them—hawthorn lingering, bruised nettle, the green bitterness of leaves warming under sun. At one point they passed a farm where bread was being drawn; the air carried that plain miracle—yeast and heat and browned crust—and Harry, who could not help responding to such things, found his heart tugged a moment towards Oakhurst’s kitchen, towards the steady domestic comfort of meals that were not merely fuel but ceremony, memory, and love set on a plate.

At Westerham they were received with the solid hospitality of an old soldier’s house: the smell of beeswax on dark furniture; a hearth that had known generations of boots drying; and, in the parlour, a stately matron whose manner could be warm and severe in the same breath, as if she ruled affection by discipline.

The elder Colonel Wolfe was there too—grey now, with the posture of a man who had been trained to stand through discomfort. His recollections were of five-and-forty years back; he spoke of campaigns as if they were weather. And with them was their son—Lieutenant-Colonel Wolfe, come over from Maidstone where Kingsley’s regiment lay.

Harry looked at him with curiosity, for this was the man whose name had been tossed about like a talisman. The face did not answer to easy admiration: lean, pale, with red hair, high cheek-bones, a nose that seemed sharpened by thought and hardship. Yet when he spoke, an animation lit him; and when he listened, his attention was so exact and courteous that one forgot to measure his looks. His voice carried clearly through the room, not loud, but with a soldier’s habit of being understood; and it had the peculiar power of making others’ voices seem more honest, as if he drew truth out by the mere act of hearing.

At supper, when it was known that Mr. Warrington intended for Tunbridge Wells, the lady of the house declared that James should bear him company. She leaned to Lambert and whispered something that made the older officer smile and give a knowing wink. Wine was called for, and Lambert toasted “Miss Lowther.”

“With all my heart,” cried Wolfe, eager as a boy, and drained his glass.

His mother, enjoying her own little stage, whispered how James and the young lady were to make a match, and how she came of the famous Lowthers of the North.

“If she were the daughter of King Charlemagne,” Lambert said, “she is not too good for James Wolfe, or for his mother’s son.”

“Mr. Lambert would not say so if he knew her,” Wolfe declared, and his homely face took on that sudden tenderness which makes even plainness beautiful.

“Oh! of course she is the priceless pearl and you are nothing,” his mother retorted, half-scolding, half-proud. “No. I am of Colonel Lambert’s opinion,” she went on briskly, as if she would not allow humility to settle in her son too long. “If she brought Cumberland for a jointure, I should say it was my James’s due. That is the way with them, Mr. Warrington. We tend our children through fevers and measles and whooping-cough and small-pox; we send them to the army and cannot sleep for thinking; we break our hearts at parting, and have them at home a week or two in the year, or maybe not for ten years—then comes a lass with bright eyes, and away goes our boy, and never cares a fig for us afterwards.”

“And pray, my dear, how did you come to marry James’s papa?” the elder Colonel Wolfe asked dryly. “Why didn’t you stay with your parents?”

“Because James’s papa was gouty and wanted somebody to take care of him, I suppose,” she answered. “Not because I liked him a bit.”

So the evening went—easy talk, kindness, laughter that did not bite too hard.

In the morning Lambert, with many expressions of friendship, gave the young Virginian over to Wolfe’s care and turned his horse homeward. Harry watched him ride away with a longing that surprised him. Oakhurst, with its clean quiet and the limes’ whispering, had entered him like a scent that clings to clothes. He could almost hear again the domestic acoustics of that house: the clink of china, the soft tread of women on boards, the calmer air unshaken by the continual shouting of London or the brassy racket of fashionable places. It made him think—though he could not have said it aloud—how much of a man’s soul is ruled by what he hears all day, and how peace is not only a moral but a sound.

Wolfe, for his part, agreed readily with Harry’s praises of Lambert and his family.

“To have such a good name, and to live such a life as Colonel Lambert’s,” Wolfe said, “seems to me now the height of human ambition.”

“And glory and honour?” Harry asked. “Are those nothing? Would you give up the winning of them?”

“They were my dreams once,” Wolfe answered; and as he spoke, his voice took on a different cadence—less martial, more human. “I have followed arms since I was fourteen. I have seen almost every duty in my calling. I know the garrison towns in this country; I have served wherever there was work these ten years. I have done near the whole of a soldier’s duty—except the command of an army, which can hardly be hoped for at my years. And now, methinks, I would like quiet. Books. A wife to love me. Children to dandle on my knee. I have imagined such an Elysium. True love is better than glory; and a tranquil fireside, with the woman of your heart beside it, the greatest good the gods can send us.”

Harry pictured it—firelight, a woman’s face, the small warm weight of a child—and said “Yes.” But the assent was not cheerful; it had too much shadow in it, and Wolfe, quick to observe, glanced at him.

“You say ‘Yes’ as if a fireside and a sweetheart were not to your taste.”

“Why, look you, Colonel,” Harry replied, forcing a lighter tone, “there are other things a young fellow might like. You have had sixteen years of the world. I have been but a few months from my mother’s apron-strings. When I have seen a campaign or two—or six—as you have; when I have distinguished myself and made the world talk of me, then I may think of retiring.”

Wolfe’s heart, full of his own hope, answered by returning to it. He poured out praises of marriage, and then—warming, as men do when they speak of a single beloved name—fell into rhapsody about Miss Lowther: her virtues, her beauty, her manner, the very sound of her voice, as if each syllable were a promise. It was intensely interesting to him; to Harry, whose own thoughts of love were knotted with melancholy, it was a kind of distant music—sweet, but not meant for his ear.

They rode on. The afternoon was mild, the sky pale and wide. A mistake occurred a few miles from Tunbridge, when two horsemen stopped them; Harry, with the Virginian’s quick suspicion and a hand that had learned the habit of readiness, had pistol out, thinking them highwaymen.

Wolfe laughed. “Hold your fire, man. They are innkeepers’ agents.”

“Robbers, then,” Harry muttered, lowering the weapon.

“Only in their calling.”

At that instant Gumbo’s horse, catching some fright or fancy, bolted; and there was bawling enough from Harry to break the quiet of the hedgerows, sending birds out of cover and making the whole lane ring with it. The runaway was brought back after a clatter of hooves and a scramble; and then they rode on, the road narrowing as it drew into the little town where society gathered to drink waters, trade glances, and spend money as if it were part of the cure.

They alighted at their inn and parted—Wolfe in eager pursuit of the lady of his heart, Harry to seek his aunt.

He found Madame de Bernstein installed in handsome lodgings, with London lacqueys like tall furniture in her anteroom and behind her chair when she went abroad. The very air of her rooms seemed different—perfume laid upon perfume, powdery, sweet, and faintly stifling; the sounds were sharper too: the clack of heels, the rustle of stiff silk, the crisp little coughs and laughs of visitors who made noise because they could not bear silence.

She received him with the utmost kindness. His cousin, Lady Maria, was absent at his arrival; whether that absence made him unhappy, or whether he hid the fact, or whether the Baroness noticed anything at all, remained—like so many things between the sexes—unspoken.

A beau in a rich figured suit sat with her, the first of that brilliant species Harry had seen up close; and two dowagers were there too, monstrous with hoops and plentiful rouge, their faces like painted fans. Madame de Bernstein presented her nephew as the young Croesus out of Virginia. The phrase went off like a rocket.

They had heard of him.

His estate, she declared, was as large as Kent—and, as she had read, infinitely more fruitful. She spoke of Virginia’s marvels with the free invention of a woman determined to dazzle: spices, gold mines, strange beasts; perhaps, in the heat of display, she did not stop short of diamonds. As for his mother, she described Madam Esmond as “Princess Pocahontas” in her own country and did not tire of praising mother and son, their riches and their good qualities, as if she were seasoning a dish to please a fashionable palate—more and more sweetness, more and more spice, until the truth itself was drowned in flavour.

The beau shook Harry by the hand with delight and vowed himself honoured. The dowagers praised the young man’s good looks so loudly that he blushed, and blushed again at the absurdity of being admired for virtues he had not yet had time to prove.

They departed with curtseys and congees to carry the news through Tunbridge: that a rich young Virginian had arrived, handsome and well-bred, a prize to be viewed.

“You could not have come at a better moment, my dear,” Madame de Bernstein said the instant the door closed. Her voice changed—less honeyed, more briskly amused. “Those three have the most active tongues in the Wells. They will trumpet your good qualities everywhere. I have introduced you to a hundred people already and—Heaven help me!—told all sorts of fibs about Virginia to describe your estate. It is prodigious large, but I fear I magnified it. I filled it with wonderful animals, gold mines, spices—I am not sure I did not say diamonds. As for your negroes, I gave your mother armies of them and represented her as a sovereign princess reigning over a magnificent dominion. So she has a magnificent dominion. I cannot tell within a few hundred thousand pounds what her yearly income is, but it must be great. And you, sir, must prepare to be treated as heir-apparent to this royal lady. Do not let your head be turned. From this day forth you will be flattered as you have never been flattered in your life.”

“And to what end, ma’am?” Harry asked, bewildered and a little nettled. “Why should I be reputed so rich? Why all this flattery?”

“In the first place, sir, you must not contradict your old aunt,” she said sharply. “I have no desire to be made a fool of before company. As for your reputation—why, we found it almost ready-made. A London newspaper has somehow heard of you and printed a story of the immense wealth of a young gentleman from Virginia, lately landed, nephew of my Lord Castlewood. Immensely wealthy you are and can’t help yourself. All the world is eager to see you. You shall go to church to-morrow and witness the whole congregation turn from books and prayers to worship the golden calf in your person. You would not have had me undeceive them, and speak ill of my own flesh and blood?”

“But how am I bettered by being thought rich?”

“You are making your entry into the world, and the gold key opens most doors. To be thought rich is as good as to be rich. You need not spend; they will say you hoard, and your reputation for avarice will do you good. You shall see how the mothers smile and the daughters curtsey! Don’t look so surprised. When I was young, I did as the rest did and tried more than once—desperately—to better myself by a good marriage. Your poor grandmother, who was a saint—bating a little jealousy—scolded me and called me worldly. Worldly! So is the world worldly. We must serve it as it serves us and give it nothing for nothing.”

Then, leaning back, tapping her fingers as if counting coins or sins, she went on in a lower, more candid tone.

“Mr. Henry Esmond Warrington—I can’t help loving the first two names, old woman as I am—would have been nobody on coming here or to London. Our protection would help little. Our family has little credit and, entre nous, not much reputation. Castlewood was more than suspected in ’45, and hath since ruined himself by play.”

Harry had never heard this. The words struck him as a new sound in an old house—a crack where he had expected polish.

“He never had much to lose,” she continued, “but he has lost that and more. The estate is eaten with mortgages. He has been at all sorts of schemes to raise money. He has been so desperate, my dear, that I did not think my diamonds safe with him; and I have travelled to and from Castlewood without them. Terrible, is it not, to speak so of one’s own nephew? But you are my nephew too—and not spoiled by the world yet—and I wish to warn you of its wickedness. I heard of your play-doings with Will and the chaplain. They could do you no harm—nay, I am told you had the better of them. Had you played with Castlewood, you would have had no such luck. You would have played, had not an old aunt warned my Lord Castlewood to keep his hands off you.”

“What—did you interfere to preserve me?”

“I kept his clutches off,” she said coolly. “Be thankful you came out of that ogre’s den with any flesh on your bones. It has been the rage and passion of all our family. My poor silly brother played; both his wives played—especially the last, who has little else to live upon now but her nightly assemblies and the money for the cards. I would not trust her at Castlewood alone with you. The passion is too strong. They would fall upon you and fleece you; then fall upon each other and fight for the plunder. But for his place at Court my poor nephew hath nothing—and that is Will’s fortune too, sir, and Maria’s and her sister’s.”

“And are they too fond of the cards?”

“No. To do poor Molly justice, gaming is not her passion. But in London little Fanny will bet her eyes out of her head. I know what the passion is, sir. Do not look so astonished. I have had it—as I had the measles when I was a child. I am not cured quite. For a poor old woman there is nothing left but that. You will see some high play at my tables to-night. Hush. It was that I wanted, and without which I moped so at Castlewood! I could not win of my nieces or their mother; they would not pay if they lost. ’Tis best to warn you in time, lest you be shocked by the discovery. I cannot live without the cards, there’s the truth!”

A few days earlier, among the Castlewood people, Harry—who loved cards and cock-fighting and betting and every sport that made the blood move—might have laughed at such a confession. But since Oakhurst, since quiet meals and gentler company, laughter came harder. He had begun to hear, as if the ear of his mind had been newly tuned, the harshness in certain voices: how easily faith and honour were made a jest; how pure lives were treated as fables; how selfishness was spoken of as common practice and sacred duties shrugged away with a story.

These people were not hypocrites; they did not pretend to virtue. They flung no stones. They smiled, shrugged, and passed on, telling wicked funny tales about acquaintances whose tables they visited and whose hands they shook. Their speech itself—dominant, fashionable, careless—seemed to flatten every finer meaning into something marketable, like a song scraped of its native dialect to make it sell in town. Harry felt, without having words for it, that there were experiences that would not translate into their lexicon—not Oakhurst’s household hush, not the honest music of rural life, not the way a mother could taste a child’s absence in a dish set down for too many.

“How dreadfully dull you must have found those humdrum people at that village where we left you—but the savages were very kind to you, child!” Madame de Bernstein said, and patted his cheek with her pretty old hand.

“They were very kind,” Harry answered quickly; and his face flushed up, not with shame now but with anger. “And it was not at all dull, ma’am. I think they are some of the best people in the world.”

Her tone had jarred on him like a false note. He could not bear that she should speak lightly of the new friends who had fed him, tended him, and taken him in—friends whose very domestic routines had felt like a kind of history kept alive.

The Baroness, imperious and swift to resent, began to draw herself up; then checked. A second thought—mischievous, sharp as a pin—pricked her.
