“Those two girls,” she thought. “A sick-bed. An interesting stranger. Of course he has been falling in love with one of them.”

And as if the thought had summoned its object, she lifted her eyes with a quick, playful glance—just as Lady Maria entered the room.

Cousin Maria arrived as if she had been gathered out of a conservatory at dawn—herself the freshest blossom—and behind her came two gardener’s lads, their arms full of baskets whose damp wicker breathed the whole garden into the passage: bruised rose-leaves, crushed box, sweet-william, and the sharp green snap of cut stems. Madame de Bernstein’s great room was to be dressed for company, and the house began to hum with that peculiar music of preparation: footmen’s shoes whispering and scuffing, card-tables unfolded with a dry wooden sigh, the clink of brass against silver as sconces were set, the soft thud of wax candles laid down like little pale loaves waiting to be lit.

A major-domo in black, with a bag-wig and ruffles of fine lace, moved among them with the air of a man who ought to carry a sword, pointing with grave precision as pairs of candles were placed on each table and in the wall-sconces. The late sun slanted in and gilded the wainscot, gilded the green common beyond the windows—rocks, clumps of trees, and houses blinking in the light. Outside, hoops and brocades and powdered heads drifted over the grass like a bright flock; their shadows dappled the ground. From the Pantiles—on the far side—came a perpetual fair’s clatter: voices layered upon voices, heels on boards, vendors calling, and, threaded through all, the band’s tune, which rose and fell like a breeze. It was impossible to live here without taking in that soundscape as one takes in weather; it pressed into the rooms, it governed the pulse, it made solitude a kind of effort.

Madame de Bernstein’s chief sitting-room would have tortured a hermit. It was all cross-light, bustle, and view, with the world displayed like a moving picture. When evening came and the windows shone, the passers-by below knew her ladyship held her card-assembly, and that, for those with the smallest claim to be somebody, an introduction might be had as easily as a dish of tea.

Yet there was nothing, Harry Warrington thought, like the clean steadiness of daylight for judging things. Even as servants brought in the candles, he could not help remembering how much of the night in former days was swallowed by smoky darkness. There had been feasts and music and fine talk, but lit by mean stinking tallow that guttered, smeared ceilings, and made faces look as if they had been rubbed with soot. It was curious to think that the grandest courts had sat in that dimness, as if splendour itself were obliged to live by half-light and stink. Here, at least, wax would burn clear, and the room would be less like a cavern.

Maria moved from table to table setting her flowers. She chose her vases with a sort of domestic reverence—this bowl, that dragon jar—turning stems, stripping away bruised leaves, pinching them clean with her small fingers. The scent deepened where she worked: rose sweetened by the faint clove of pinks, a breath of earth still clinging to the roots. She lingered longer than mere duty required, and while she arranged a spray of sweet-william she stole shy glances toward Harry, as though the blossoms were an excuse for being in his sight. Harry, who could face a musket but not a young lady’s eyes, coloured until his very ears betrayed him.

If Maria hoped for a little unguarded moment, she was checked as promptly as a servant caught dawdling. The Baroness sat planted in her arm-chair like a garrison commander, her crooked tortoiseshell stick across her lap. Her gaze snapped from man to man; her voice cut as sharp as shears. Tom was rated for a darn in his stocking—how dared he show such beggary under her roof? John was attacked for greasing his hair too liberally from the candle-box, as if he thought to shine by oil. They scurried under her domination, and the whole room seemed to obey not the band outside but her imperious tapping stick.

“Where are you going to dine, Harry?” Madame de Bernstein asked, when the bustle of placing flowers and tables was done.

“My niece Maria and I shall have a chicken in the little parlour. You should go to the best ordinary. There is one at the White Horse at three—we shall hear his bell in a minute or two. And you will understand, sir, you ought not to spare expense, but behave like Princess Pocahontas’s son. Your trunks have been taken over to the lodging I have engaged for you. It is not good for a lad to be always hanging about the aprons of two old women. Is it, Maria?”

“No,” Maria said, dropping her eyes with obedient meekness, while her aunt’s eyes flared in triumph at having her agree.

Harry stood as if he were being marched from one post to another. The last five or six days had shown him that Madame de Bernstein could be, at pleasure, a dragon. If some Perseus had offered to relieve the neighbourhood by chopping off her head, Harry might have been tempted to think it not wholly unjust. But he had no sword for that; he only stared at the tawny-and-blue lacqueys creaking about their tasks, and listened to the ceaseless bustle from the Pantiles beyond, that lively human roar which made even insult feel public.

“And there are good mercers and tailors from London always here to wait on the company at the Wells,” Madame de Bernstein continued briskly. “You had better see them, my dear, for your suit is not of the very last fashion—a little lace—”

“I can’t go out of mourning, ma’am,” Harry said, looking down at his black clothes as if the very cloth were a promise.

“Ho, sir!” She rustled up from her chair, rising on her cane. “Wear black for your brother till you are as old as Methuselah, if you like. I am sure I don’t want to prevent you. I only want you to dress, and to do like other people, and make a figure worthy of your name.”

“Madam,” Harry said, drawing himself up with the stiff state of youth that feels its honour pressed on, “I have not done anything to disgrace it that I know.”

She gave a little start, so sudden it was almost as if the words had struck her physically. Then her mouth tightened and she moved on, as people do when they will not look at what has risen before them.

They had had many passages of this sort already—thrust and parry, quick heat, quick pride. She did not dislike him for meeting her. Indeed, something in her seemed to relish the resistance, as if a creature long used to obedience must poke for life wherever it can find it.

“Sure a little finer linen than that shirt you wear will not be a disgrace to you, sir,” she said, forcing a laugh which did not warm her eyes.

Harry bowed, and blushed again—this time with a different tenderness. That homely shirt had been a gift of his friends at Oakhurst. He could almost smell, in its clean folded linen, the quiet house that had given it: winter air outside, crackling logs within, hands of good women sewing by firelight, the faint scent of soap and sun-dried cloth. Wearing it, he had felt protected—as if the plainness itself were a charm and evil could not cling to it.

“I will go to my lodging,” he said, “and return as I should.”

“Come back here, sir,” Madame de Bernstein said. “And if our company has not arrived, Maria and I will find some ruffles for you!”

Under a footman’s guidance he was led away.

His new apartments were handsome and spacious, as if Madame de Bernstein meant to announce him to the world by the size of his rooms. A groom waited below to be engaged by his honour; there was even talk of a second valet, should he desire one to attend upon Gumbo. Before Harry had been many minutes within, emissaries arrived from a London tailor and a bootmaker—cards presented with bows and compliments from Messrs. Regnier and Tull, who knew, it seemed, the moment a new purse entered Tunbridge.

Gumbo laid out the best of Harry’s modest wardrobe, and, with a care that was almost priestly, placed the finest linen that Madam Esmond’s thrift had provided. The cloth was clean and stout and white, but as Harry looked at it amid these English refinements, a thought—a mean, new thought—crossed his mind: was it fine enough? were the clothes smart enough? It startled him as if he had heard himself speak in another man’s voice. At Castlewood, nobody would have questioned; the simple folk there were content with what their hands made and their land gave, and his mother had believed no young nobleman need be better furnished.

And yet, when his toilet was done, he cut a comely enough figure. Gumbo called a chair, and marched beside it with the grave air of one who had carried his master through worse press than a noisy spa-town, until they reached the ordinary where Mr. Warrington was to dine.

He expected to find the beau he had met earlier—who had named the White Horse the most modish place for dining at the Wells—and Harry mentioned the gentleman’s name to the host. But Monsieur Barbeau, the landlord, with a smile that showed practiced teeth, assured his honour that his honour needed no introduction but his own. He helped Harry hang coat and sword upon a peg, and, as though wine were a choice of sauces, asked whether his honour would drink Burgundy, Pontac, or champagne with his dinner.

Though the White Horse was called the most fashionable, it was not crowded that day. Monsieur Barbeau explained that a great entertainment at Summer Hill had drawn away most of the company. There were but four other gentlemen in the room. Two had finished their dinner and sat drinking wine; two young men were still at their meal. As Barbeau passed them, he must have whispered Harry’s name, for they looked up with interest, bowed slightly, and wished him welcome to Tunbridge, saying they hoped he would like the place better upon further acquaintance.

Then they smiled and exchanged waggish looks, and Harry—unpractised in the little codes of such places—could not tell why they cast knowing glances toward the pair of older diners over their wine.

One of those older men wore a somewhat tarnished velvet coat, with huge queue and bag, and ruffles and embroidery that had been splendid once and were now merely loud. The other was a little beetle-browed, hook-nosed, high-shouldered gentleman whom his opposite called milor—my lord—in a very high voice. My lord sipped his wine, glanced at Harry as one glances at a new chair brought into a room, and continued speaking to his companion.

A steaming soup was brought to Harry—so hot that its breath rose like a small fog and carried a rich scent of stock and herbs, the kind of careful simmering that tells of bones browned and vegetables sweated before the water ever touched them. Monsieur Barbeau laid it down with pride.

“Behold, sir! Behold a potage of my fashion!” he whispered, and, leaning closer, murmured the celebrated name of the nobleman opposite, as if offering a spice.

Harry thanked him in French. At that, the foreign gentleman turned and grinned at Harry with vast graciousness.

“Fous bossedez notre langue barfaidement, monsieur,” he said.

Harry had heard French spoken in Canada with a different music—clearer, sharper, less like a mouthful of wine. This was a French chewed and softened, as if it had travelled through many countries and picked up other tongues’ habits on the way. He bowed nevertheless.

Meanwhile the two elders, now speaking French themselves, were deep in a conversation whose subject Harry could not at first grasp.

“And so you know the nephew of the old woman—the Croesus who comes to arrive?” my lord was saying.

“You’re thrown out there, Jack!” one of the young men murmured to his companion, amused. “Never could manage the lingo.”

The elder with the great queue replied with energetic assurance.

“But assuredly, my dear lord! You have shown energy, my dear Baron! He has been here but two hours. My people told me of him only as I came to dinner.”

“I knew him before—I have met him often in London with the Baroness and my lord, his cousin,” the Baron answered.

Harry took a spoonful of soup. It was excellent—properly salted, the fat skimmed, the flavour deep and round. He felt the warmth travel down him, steadying him, as if food could set right what voices had begun to unsettle.

“Tell me more about the Croesus, my good Baron,” my lord continued, with a supercilious drawl. He did not look at Harry, which nettled the young man, though he would not yet admit how.

“What will you, that I tell you, my dear lord?” said the Baron. “Croesus is a youth like other youths; he is tall, like other youths; he is awkward, like other youths; he has black hair, as they all have who come from the Indies. Lodgings have been taken for him at Mrs. Rose’s toy-shop.”

Harry’s spoon paused. He had lodgings there too.

“He travels with a large retinue,” the Baron went on, “four servants, two postchaises, and a pair of outriders. His chief attendant is a black man who saved his life from the savages in America, and who will not hear, on any account, of being made free. He persists in wearing mourning for his elder brother from whom he inherits his principality.”

Harry felt a coldness spread under the warmth of the soup, like a shadow over a hearth. They were describing him. The French—crooked as it sounded—was plain enough to understand. It was strange how a man’s life, with its grief and its bonds of affection and its vows, could be reduced to the amusement of strangers at a public table.

“Could anything console you for the death of yours, Chevalier?” my lord cried.

“Milor! his property might,” said the Chevalier with the queue, and laughed thinly. “Which you know is not small.”

“Your brother lives on his patrimony—which you have told me is immense—you by your industry, my dear Chevalier.”

“Milor!” the Chevalier cried, with offended dignity.

“By your industry or your esprit—how much more noble! Shall you be at the Baroness’s to-night? She ought to be a little of your parents, Chevalier?”

The Chevalier looked sulkily blank, as if my lord’s English idioms had run away from him and left him behind.

“Again I fail to comprehend your lordship,” he said.

“Why, she is a woman of great wit—she is of noble birth—she has undergone strange adventures—she has but little principle (there you happily have the advantage of her). But what care we men of the world? You intend to go and play with the young Creole, no doubt, and get as much money from him as you can. By the way, Baron, suppose he should be a guet-apens, that young Creole? Suppose our excellent friend has invented him up in London, and brings him down with his character for wealth to prey upon the innocent folks here?”

The Baron put a finger to his nose with a knowing air.

“I have often thought it, milor. That Baroness is capable of anything.”

“A Baron—a Baroness, que voulez-vous? I mean the late lamented husband. Do you know who he was?”

“Intimately. A more notorious villain never dealt a card. At Venice, at Brussels, at Spa, at Vienna—the gaols of every one of which places he knew. I knew the man, my lord.”

“I thought you would. I saw him at the Hague, where I first had the honour of meeting you, and a more disreputable rogue never entered my doors. A minister must open them to all sorts of people, Baron—spies, sharpers, ruffians of every sort.”

“Parbleu, milor, how you treat them!” the Baron’s companion said, with a little snarl of laughter.

“A man of my rank, my friend—of the rank I held then—of course must see all sorts of people—entre autres your acquaintance. What his wife could want with such a name as his I can’t conceive.”

“Apparently, it was better than the lady’s own.”

“Effectively! So I have heard of my friend Paddy changing clothes with the scarecrow. I don’t know which name is the most distinguished, that of the English bishop or the German baron.”

“My lord,” cried the Chevalier, rising and laying his hand on a large star upon his coat, “you forget that I, too, am a Baron and a Chevalier of the Holy Roman—”

“Order of the Spur—not in the least, my dear knight and baron! You will have no more wine? We shall meet at Madame de Bernstein’s to-night.”

The knight-bar-on—his ruffles fluttering like noisy birds—felt in his embroidered pockets as if for money, then waved the waiter off with a hand blazing with rings, and stalked away.

It was only as the two men had spoken of the bishop’s widow and of the German baron’s wife that the full meaning struck Harry: his aunt had been the subject of their talk, and he himself the “Creole” to be fleeced. The room’s cheerful noise seemed to sharpen; the clink of glasses, the scrape of plates, even the band’s faint tune from outside, all pressed upon him as if the very air had turned into listeners.

Before the anger had settled into anything he could shape, my lord turned toward the two young diners and spoke in English.

“What a little sharper it is! Everything I said about Bernstein relates mutato nomine to him. I knew the fellow to be a spy and a rogue. He has changed his religion I don’t know how many times. I had him turned out of the Hague myself when I was ambassador, and I know he was caned in Vienna.”

“I wonder my Lord Chesterfield associates with such a villain!” Harry called out from his table, his voice leaping louder than he intended.

The two younger men stared at him. My lord—Lord Chesterfield—did not so much as flicker in response. He went on, still talking, still perfectly at ease.

“There cannot be a more fieffe coquin than this Poellnitz. Why, Heaven be thanked, he has actually left me my snuff-box! You laugh?—the fellow is capable of taking it.”

“You are quite right, sir,” said one of the younger diners, turning to Harry with a half-serious, half-amused face, “though, saving your presence, I don’t know what business it is of yours. My lord will play with anybody who will set him. Don’t be alarmed, he is as deaf as a post, and did not hear a word that you said; and that’s why my lord will play with anybody who will put a pack of cards before him, and that is the reason why he consorts with this rogue.”

“Faith, I know other noblemen who are not particular as to their company,” said the other young man—Jack—dryly.

“Do you mean because I associate with you?” his companion shot back. “I know my company, my good friend, and I defy most men to have the better of me.”

Lord Chesterfield, entirely unconscious of Harry’s indignation, now addressed Monsieur Barbeau in French, and complimented him on the dinner with an air of condescension that seemed as habitual as breathing. The landlord bowed again and again, delighted to be praised by such a customer.

His Excellency was satisfied? He had not forgotten the art he learned when he was a young man in his Excellency’s kingdom of Ireland. The salmi was to my lord’s liking? He had just served a dish to the young American seigneur opposite—the gentleman from Virginia.

“To whom?” Chesterfield asked. His pale face flushed suddenly, as if a hot coal had touched it, and he looked towards Harry across the room.

“To the young gentleman from Virginia who has just arrived, and who perfectly possesses our beautiful language!” Monsieur Barbeau said, pleased with his own diplomacy, thinking to flatter both at once.

“And to whom your lordship will be answerable for language reflecting upon my family, and uttered in the presence of these gentlemen,” Harry cried, standing and speaking with all the force he could summon, determined to drive his words through deafness itself.

“You must go and call into his ear, and then he may perchance hear you,” said one of the young men.

“I will take care that his lordship shall understand my meaning, one way or other,” Harry said, with a stiff dignity that scarcely covered the tremor in him. “And will not suffer calumnies regarding my relatives to be uttered by him or any other man!”

While Harry spoke, Chesterfield did not hear, but he had time enough to compose a reply as if he had. He rose, drew his handkerchief once or twice across his mouth, and laid his slim fingers upon the table with a measured grace.

“Sir,” he said, “you will believe, on the word of a gentleman, that I had no idea before whom I was speaking, and it seems that my acquaintance, Monsieur de Poellnitz, knew you no better than myself. Had I known you, believe me that I should have been the last man in the world to utter a syllable that should give you annoyance; and I tender you my regrets and apologies, before my Lord March and Mr. Morris here present.”

To this, Harry could only bow and mumble a few words—his heat checked by the sudden, formal civility, and by the oddity of being apologized to by a man who, in truth, had not heard the insult he was atoning for. Chesterfield, having made believe to hear Harry’s answer, returned a very profound bow.

He added, as if concluding a ceremony, that he should have the honour of waiting upon Mr. Warrington at his lodgings; then saluted the company and went away, leaving behind him the faint scent of snuff and wine, and the lingering vibration of voices that, once spoken, could not be taken back—words that clung to names like smoke clings to curtains.

The White Horse Tavern had set its pleasures in an English way: not merely within doors where plates were cleared and glasses replenished, but out upon the bowling-green itself, which came up close under the eating-room windows as if the lawn were another chamber of the house. A table or two stood there for those who liked their tea cooled by open air, or their punch sweetened with sunlight. The dinner of the three gentlemen ended much about the same time; and Mr. Morris, who found conclusions intolerable unless they led to fresh beginnings, proposed that they should adjourn to the Green and drink a cool bottle.

“Jack Morris would adjourn to the Dust Hole, if it served as pretext for a fresh drink,” said my lord, laughing.

To which Jack, with the candour of a man who could make a jest of his own vice while keeping the vice safe, replied that each gentleman had his own favourite road to the deuce; his weakness, he owned, was a bottle.

“My Lord Chesterfield’s deuce is deuce-ace,” says my Lord March. “His lordship can’t keep away from the cards or dice.”

“My Lord March has not one devil, but several devils,” said Morris. “He loves gambling, he loves horse-racing, he loves betting, he loves drinking, he loves eating, he loves money, he loves women; and you have fallen into bad company, Mr. Warrington, when you lighted upon his lordship. He will play you for every acre you have in Virginia.”

“With the greatest pleasure in life, Mr. Warrington!” my lord broke in, as quick as a knife finding the seam of a roast.

“And for all your tobacco, and for all your spices, and for all your slaves, and for all your oxen and asses, and for everything that is yours.”

“Shall we begin now? Jack, you are never without a dice-box or a bottle-screw. I will set Mr. Warrington for what he likes.”

“Unfortunately, my lord,” said Harry, whose plain honesty always sounded a little like stubbornness in such company, “the tobacco, and the slaves, and the asses, and the oxen, are not mine, as yet. I am just of age, and my mother, scarce twenty years older, has quite as good chance of long life as I have.”

The air on the Green carried the crisp clack of bowls from another party; from within the tavern came the muffled scrape of chair-legs on boards, and the thin treble of a spoon against porcelain. Those small sounds—the ecology of idleness—seemed to quicken the appetite of the two men of fashion for wagers, as the smell of cork and wine does.

“I will bet you that you survive her,” said my lord with the cool ease of one who could name death as if it were a point in a game. “I will pay you a sum now against four times the sum to be paid at her death. I will set you a fair sum over this table against the reversion of your estate in Virginia at the old lady’s departure. What do you call your place?”

“Castlewood.”

“A principality, I hear it is. I will bet that its value has been exaggerated ten times at least amongst the quidnuncs here. How came you by the name of Castlewood?—you are related to my lord? Oh, stay: I know,—my lady, your mother, descends from the real head of the house. He took the losing side in ’15. I have had the story a dozen times from my old Duchess. She knew your grandfather. He was friend of Addison and Steele, and Pope and Milton, I dare say, and the bigwigs. It is a pity he did not stay at home, and transport the other branch of the family to the plantations.”

“I have just been staying at Castlewood with my cousin there,” said Harry.

“Hm! Did you play with him? He’s fond of pasteboard and bones.”

“Never, but for sixpences and a pool of commerce with the ladies.”

“So much the better for both of you. But you played with Will Esmond if he was at home? I will lay ten to one you played with Will Esmond.”

Harry’s face answered before his tongue: the flush of a truth he had no mind to dress up in language.

He owned that, of an evening, his cousin and he had had a few games at cards.

“And Tom Sampson, the chaplain,” cried Jack Morris—who had that way of shouting a name as if it were a toast—“was he of the party? I wager Tom made a third, and the Lord deliver you from Tom and Will Esmond together!”

“Nay; the truth is, I won of both of them,” said Harry, smiling over his wine.

“And they paid you? Well, miracles will never cease!”

“I did not say anything about miracles,” said Harry, who liked credit but disliked cant.

“And you don’t tell tales out of school—the volto sciolto—hey, Mr. Warrington?” my lord said, tossing in foreign words as a cook tosses salt—carelessly, to show there is plenty.

“I beg your pardon,” said Harry, downright as ever; “French is the only language besides my own of which I know a little.”

“My Lord March has learned Italian at the Opera,” Morris remarked, “and a pretty penny his lessons have cost him. We must show him the Opera—mustn’t we, March?”

“Must we, Morris?” my lord answered, and there was a shade in his voice as if he half resented the familiarity that had been purchased with too many shared bottles.

Both of those gentlemen were dressed alike in small scratch-wigs without powder, in blue frocks with plate buttons, in buckskins and riding-boots, in little hats with narrow lace, and no outward mark of fashion; yet the very plainness had a studied air, like a dish served in earthenware to prove that silver is unnecessary.

“I don’t care about the Opera much, my lord,” said Harry, warming with his Burgundy; the wine had come to him with a full, ripe smell—berries crushed, a faint tang as of wet wood, and that velvet heat that rises into the cheeks and loosens the tongue. “But I should like to go to Newmarket, and long to see a good English hunting-field.”

“We will show you Newmarket and the hunting-field, sir. Can you ride pretty well?”

“I think I can,” Harry said; “and I can shoot pretty well, and jump some.”

“What’s your weight? I bet you we weigh even, or I weigh most. I bet you Jack Morris beats you at birds or a mark, at five-and-twenty paces. I bet you I jump farther than you on flat ground, here on this green.”

“I don’t know Mr. Morris’s shooting—I never saw either gentleman before—but I take your bets, my lord, at what you please,” cried Harry, who by this time was more than warm; the world had grown loud and bright, and the tavern’s laughter seemed a kind of music after all.

“Ponies on each!” cried my lord.

“Done and done!” cried my lord and Harry together. The young man thought it for the honour of his country not to be ashamed of any wager made to him.

“We can try the last bet now, if your feet are pretty steady,” said my lord, springing up and stretching, looking at the crisp dry grass as a man looks at a clean table he means to make a mess upon. He drew his boots off, then his coat and waistcoat, buckling his belt round his waist, and flinging his clothes down upon the ground.

Harry had more respect for his garments; it was his best suit, and he folded the velvet coat and waistcoat with a kind of carefulness that belonged to home habits—like wrapping yesterday’s bread to keep it from drying. Seeing the tables outside slopped with drink, he stepped to the eating-room window and laid his clothes within, where the air smelled of roasted fowl and peppered gravy gone cold, and of lemon peel from emptied punch-bowls.

A new guest sat there: Mr. Wolfe, soberly eating a chicken and salad, with a modest pint of wine. The chicken had been cut with soldierly exactness; the salad—sharp with vinegar, green with fresh herbs—stood as if it had not been allowed to wilt beneath the tavern’s noise.

Harry, in high spirits, told the Colonel he had a bet with my Lord March—would Colonel Wolfe stand him halves? Wolfe said he was too poor to bet. Would he come out and see fair play? That he would with all his heart. He set down his glass and stalked through the open window after his young friend.

“Who is that tallow-faced Put with the carroty hair?” said Morris, whose Burgundy made him bold and stupid.

Harry explained it was Lieutenant-Colonel Wolfe, of the 20th Regiment.

“Your humble servant, gentlemen!” said the Colonel, making the company a rigid military bow.

“Never saw such a figure in my life!” cried Morris. “Did you—March?”

“I beg your pardon, I think you said March?” the Colonel asked, eyes widening with a look half surprise, half scrutiny.

“I am the Earl of March, sir, at Colonel Wolfe’s service,” said the nobleman, bowing. “My friend, Mr. Morris, is so intimate with me, that, after dinner, we are quite like brothers.”

Why is not all Tunbridge Wells by to hear this? thought Morris, and in his delight shouted, “Two to one on my lord!”

“Done!” called out Harry; and the enthusiastic Jack, having trapped himself, was obliged to cry “Done!” too.

“Take him, Colonel,” Harry whispered.

But Wolfe said he could not afford to lose, and therefore could not hope to win.

“I see you have won one of our bets already, Mr. Warrington,” my Lord March remarked. “I am taller than you by an inch or two, but you are broader round the shoulders.”

“Pooh, my dear Will! I bet you you weigh twice as much as he does!” cried Morris.

“Done, Jack!” said my lord, laughing. “The bets are all ponies. Will you take him, Mr. Warrington?”

“No, my dear fellow—one’s enough,” said Jack, suddenly prudent when his purse was threatened.

“Very good, my dear fellow,” said my lord. “And now we will settle the other wager.”

Harry had already put himself into his best silk stockings, black satin-net breeches, and neatest pumps; he would not take off his shoes as his antagonist had done. My lord’s heavy riding-boots and spurs were little calculated for leaping, and he had shed them with a frankness that made the wager seem more sport than pride; but Harry’s pumps were as much a part of his dignity as the ribbon on a dish at table makes it fit for company.

They had before them thirty yards of even turf—enough for a run, enough for a jump. A gravel walk ran round the green; beyond it stood the wall and gate-sign with the Hanoverian White Horse rampant between two skittles, and for motto the landlord’s name and the animal’s—both equally advertised. The sign creaked a little in the afternoon air, and that small complaint of wood and iron seemed a thin prophecy of harsher noises that England would one day learn to call improvement.

Morris laid a handkerchief on the ground for the mark. Mr. Wolfe stood at the other end to note where each came down, as gravely as if he were marking ground for artillery.

“My lord went first,” Mr. Warrington later wrote to Mrs. Mountain at Castlewood, in a letter still extant, “He was for having me take the lead; but, remembering the story about the Battel of Fontanoy which my dearest George used to tell, I says, ‘Monseigneur le Comte, tirez le premier, s’il vous play.’ So he took his run in his stocken feet, and for the honour of Old Virginia, I had the gratafacation of beating his lordship by more than two feet—viz., two feet nine inches—me jumping twenty-one feet three inches, by the drawer’s measured tape, and his lordship only eighteen six. I had won from him about my weight before (which I knew the moment I set my eye upon him). So he and Mr. Jack paid me these two betts.”

The tape, produced with tavern importance, was stretched and called over; boots thudded back on, coats were resumed, and bank-notes—dry, crackling, smelling faintly of leather and pocket—passed hands. Harry’s purse, lately thinned by fees to Castlewood servants and by the purchase of a horse at Oakhurst, felt suddenly fat again, as if restored to its proper diet.

In the same letter Harry added, with dutiful anxiety, that his mother would not be displeased with him, for he had bet for the honour of the Old Dominion, and his opponent was a nobleman of the first quality, holding two earldoms and heir to a duke. “Betting is all the rage here,” he wrote, “and the bloods and young fellows of fashion are betting away from morning till night.”

And then—here the domestic, the remembered, slipped into the very centre of this public frolic—he told how he had spoken of a gentleman at home who could beat him by a good foot; and when asked who, he said Colonel G. Washington, of Mount Vernon. At that name Wolfe had pricked up as if at a trumpet, and questioned him closely; spoke of last year’s unhappy campaign as if he knew every inch of ground, naming rivers and roads with an exactness that made Harry laugh when Wolfe called the Potowmac the Pottamac. In that mispronunciation lay the whole tragedy of empire: the land known in a stranger’s mouth, the sound altered, the very syllables conquered before the soil.

These feats being over, the four gentlemen strolled from the tavern garden into the public walk, where a great deal of company was assembled. Here Mr. Morris, loud and free by nature and now made louder by drink, chose to scatter remarks as a cook scatters pepper—without much care whom it might make sneeze. If my Lord March made a joke, of which he was not sparing, Morris roared, “Oh, ho, ho! Oh, good Gad! Oh, my dear earl! Oh, my dear lord, you’ll be the death of me!” It seemed, as Harry sagaciously wrote, as if he wished everybody to know his companion was an earl.

A variety of characters passed, and the Walk had its own orchestra: the rustle of gowns, the click of buckles on gravel, the call of chairmen, the distant tap of bowls, and, over all, the soft busy murmur of polite society—less honest than the wind in trees, yet soothing in its way. M. Poellnitz, no finer dressed than at dinner, grinned and saluted with his great laced hat and tarnished feathers. Then came my Lord Chesterfield, in a pearl-coloured suit with blue ribbon and star, and saluted the young men in his turn.

“I will back the old boy for taking his hat off against the whole kingdom, and France either,” said my Lord March. “He has never changed the shape of that hat of his for twenty years. Look at it. There it goes again! Do you see that great, big, awkward, pock-marked, snuff-coloured man, who hardly touches his clumsy beaver in reply. D— his confounded impudence—do you know who that is?”

“No, curse him! Who is it, March?” asked Morris, with an oath.

“It’s one Johnson, a Dictionary-maker, about whom my Lord Chesterfield wrote some most capital papers, when his dixonary was coming out, to patronise the fellow. I know they were capital. I’ve heard Horry Walpole say so, and he knows all about that kind of thing. Confound the impudent schoolmaster!”

“Hang him, he ought to stand in the pillory!” roared Morris.

“That fat man he’s walking with is another of your writing fellows,—a printer,—his name is Richardson; he wrote Clarissa, you know.”

At that name, Colonel Wolfe and Mr. Warrington spoke together, their voices breaking through the general hum as if two birds had startled at once.

“Great heavens! my lord, is that the great Richardson? Is that the man who wrote Clarissa?”

Harry ran forward to look. The old gentleman toddled along with a train of admiring ladies about him, as if he were some kindly household saint come out into the sunshine to be worshipped. One lady—Miss Mulso—was saying, “Indeed, my very dear sir, you are too great and good to live in such a world; but sure you were sent to teach it virtue!”

“Ah, my Miss Mulso! Who shall teach the teacher?” said the good fat old man, raising a kind round face skywards. “Even he has his faults and errors! Even his age and experience does not prevent him from stumbl—. Heaven bless my soul, Mr. Johnson! I ask your pardon if I have trodden on your corn.”

“You have done both, sir. You have trodden on the corn, and received the pardon,” said Mr. Johnson; and he went on, swaying to and fro, mumbling verses to himself, eyes turned towards the ground, hands behind him, now and then endangering with his great stick the meek honest eyes of his companion-author.

“They do not see very well, my dear Mulso,” Richardson said to the young lady, with gentle alarm, “but such as they are, I would keep my lash from Mr. Johnson’s cudgel. Your servant, sir.” Here he made a low bow and took off his hat to Mr. Warrington, who shrank back with many blushes after saluting the great author.

Richardson was accustomed to be adored. A gentler wind never puffed mortal vanity. Enraptured spinsters flung tea-leaves round him and incensed him with the coffee-pot. Matrons kissed the slippers they had worked for him. There was a halo of virtue round his nightcap. All Europe had thrilled, panted, admired, trembled, wept over the pages of the immortal little kind honest man with the round paunch.

Harry came back glowing and proud at having received a bow. “Ah!” he said. “My lord, I am glad to have seen him!”

“Seen him! why, dammy, you may see him any day in his shop, I suppose?” said Morris, with a laugh that had more beer than brains in it.

“My brother declared that he, and Mr. Fielding, I think, was the name, were the greatest geniuses in England; and often used to say, that when we came to Europe, his first pilgrimage would be to Mr. Richardson,” cried Harry, impetuous and tender whenever he spoke of the dearest friend.

“Your brother spoke like a man,” cried Mr. Wolfe too, his pale face flushing up. “I would rather be a man of genius, than a peer of the realm.”

“Every man to his taste, Colonel,” said my lord, amused. “Your enthusiasm—I don’t mean anything personal—refreshes me, on my honour it does.”

“So it does me—by gad—perfectly refreshes me,” cried Morris.

“So it does Jack—you see—it actually refreshes Jack! I say, Jack, which would you rather be?—a fat old printer, who has written a story about a confounded girl and a fellow that ruins her,—or a peer of Parliament with ten thousand a year?”

“March—my Lord March, do you take me for a fool?” said Jack, and his voice, for all its bluster, turned suddenly tearful with wounded worship. “Have I done anything to deserve this language from you?”

“I would rather win honour than honours: I would rather have genius than wealth. I would rather make my name than inherit it, though my father’s, thank God, is an honest one,” said the young Colonel. And then, as if ashamed of having shown his heart among gamblers, he made them a hasty salutation and ran across the parade toward a young and elderly lady and a gentleman advancing.

“It is the beautiful Miss Lowther. I remember now,” said my lord. “See! he takes her arm! The report is, he is engaged to her.”

“You don’t mean to say such a fellow is engaged to any of the Lowthers of the North?” cried Morris. “Curse me, what is the world come to, with your printers, and your half-pay ensigns, and your schoolmasters, and your infernal nonsense?”

As if to answer that question with another kind of nonsense—solemn, ceremonious, and richly rewarded—Mr. Johnson, who had shown so little desire to bow to my Lord Chesterfield, was seen now to take off his beaver and bow almost to the ground before a florid personage in a large round hat with bands and a gown: my Lord Bishop of Salisbury, wearing complacently the blue riband and badge of the Garter, of which noble order his lordship was prelate.

Mr. Johnson stood hat in hand during the whole of his conversation with Dr. Gilbert, who made many flattering and benedictory remarks to Mr. Richardson, declaring that he was the supporter of virtue, the preacher of sound morals, the mainstay of religion—of all which points the honest printer himself was perfectly convinced.

And indeed, hearing these praises, one might fancy a book could be made a sort of sacrament; yet tastes alter, and with them the very permission of language. The old tears shed over Clarissa seemed to belong to a dialect of feeling now half lost; the words that once were household bread grew strange on the tongue, as if the nation’s palate had changed. A century may make a masterpiece into contraband, and the same shelves that once displayed it proudly may hide it away behind other titles, as families hide an old recipe no longer fashionable, though it once saved them from hunger.

“Who is yonder queer person in the high headdress of my grandmother’s time, who stops and speaks to Mr. Richardson?” asked Harry, as a fantastically dressed lady came up and performed a curtsey and compliment to the bowing printer.

Morris nervously struck Harry a blow in the side with the butt end of his whip. Lord March laughed.

“Yonder queer person is my gracious kinswoman, Katharine, Duchess of Dover and Queensberry, at your service, Mr. Warrington. She was a beauty once! She is changed now, isn’t she? What an old Gorgon it is! She is a great patroness of your book-men; and when that old frump was young, they actually made verses about her.”

The Earl quitted his friends for a moment to make his bow to the old Duchess, Morris explaining, with relish, how at the Duke’s death my Lord of March and Ruglen would succeed to his cousin’s dukedoms.

“I suppose,” said Harry simply, “his lordship is here in attendance upon the old lady?”

Morris burst into a loud laugh.

“Oh yes! very much! exactly!” he cried. “Why, my dear fellow, you don’t mean to say you haven’t heard about the little Opera-dancer?”

“I am but lately arrived in England, Mr. Morris,” Harry answered, smiling; “and in Virginia, I own, we have not heard much about the little Opera-dancer.”

Luckily for us, the secret about the little Opera-dancer never was revealed; for their talk was interrupted by a lady in a cardinal cape, with a hat not unlike those headpieces fashion loves to forget and then, generations later, to proclaim new. She made a profound curtsey to the two gentlemen and received their salutation. Then she stopped opposite Harry and held out her hand rather to his wonderment.

“Have you so soon forgotten me, Mr. Warrington?” she said.

Off went Harry’s hat in an instant. He started, blushed, stammered, and cried out Good Heavens! as though any celestial wonder lay in meeting a lady on a public walk. It was Lady Maria come out for air. The truth—cruel to his vanity and crueler still to hers—was that he had not been thinking of her at all. She had been, for a moment, so utterly out of his mind that her re-entry there, and her appearance in the body, startled his faculties and brought those guilty blushes crowding to his cheeks.

A week ago—a year, a hundred years ago it seemed—he would not have been surprised to meet her anywhere: gliding from dark shrubbery, loitering on stairs, hovering even in dreams, she had been his constant apparition. A week ago his heart used to beat at her very name. And it was only last Tuesday that his love had been stabbed and slain; now he had not only left off mourning but had forgotten.

“You will come and walk with me a little?” she said. “Or would you like the music best? I dare say you will like the music best.”

“You know,” Harry said, “I don’t care about any music much, except—” He was thinking of the evening hymn—“except of your playing.” He turned very red again; he felt he was perjuring himself horribly.

The poor lady was agitated too by the flutter she saw in him. Could that tremor mean she had been mistaken, and that the lad was still faithful? “Give me your arm, and let us take a little walk,” she said, waving a curtsey toward the other two gentlemen. “My aunt is asleep after her dinner.”

Harry could not but offer his arm, and press the hand that lay against his heart. Lady Maria made another fine curtsey to Harry’s bowing companions and walked off with her prize.

Meanwhile Morris, leaning on his noble friend’s arm, went away perfectly happy; he had dropped a light airy remark about a particular run of cards at Lady Flushington’s the night before; Lady Maria had replied graciously; and in his ears the Walk’s polite murmur had turned into applause. The tragedy passed beside him unheard—swallowed by the agreeable noise of the world.

“Tell me of those children, child,” Lady Maria said, as they paced the common where the turf lay close-cropped and resilient underfoot. The evening air held that mingled country-sweetness Tunbridge keeps—damp earth, trodden grass, a far hint of horse, and somewhere a kitchen-chimney sending up woodsmoke like a remembered comfort. “Those little ones I saw running about the house where they took you in—poor dear boy—after your dreadful fall. Oh, that fall, Harry! I thought I should have died when I saw it!”

“You needn’t squeeze one’s arm so,” she added, with a faint catch in her voice that tried to pass for playfulness. “You know you don’t care for me.”

“The people are the very best, kindest, dearest people I have ever met in the world!” Harry Warrington cried, turning his whole face toward praise as a hungry man turns toward supper. “Mrs. Lambert was a friend of my mother when she was in Europe for her education. Colonel Lambert is a most accomplished gentleman—has seen service everywhere: Scotland with his Royal Highness, Flanders, Minorca. No natural parents could be kinder than they were to me. How can I show my gratitude? I want to make them a present—I must make them a present!” And with that he clapped his hand into his pocket, as if the crisp bank-notes he had won were warm rolls that might be shared.

“We can go to the toy-shop, my dear, and buy a couple of dolls for the children,” Maria said quickly, seizing on the safest sort of generosity. “You would offend the parents by offering anything like payment for their kindness.”

“Dolls for Hester and Theo!” Harry broke out, laughing. “Why, do you think a woman is not woman till she is forty, Maria?”

The arm under his gave a small, involuntary wince—so slight it might have been from the evening chill; yet it had the same sharpness as when a too-bright knife hits bone.

“I can tell you Miss Hester by no means considers herself a child,” he went on, cheerfully blind, “and Miss Theo is older than her sister. They know ever so many languages. They have read books—oh! piles and piles of books! They play on the harpsichord and sing together admirable; and Theo composes, and sings songs of her own.”

“Indeed? I scarcely saw them,” Maria said, with care. “I thought they were children. They looked quite childish. I had no idea they had all these perfections, and were such wonders of the world.”

“That’s just the way with you women!” Harry cried, all young triumph and teasing, as if the world were a table set for him and he must taste everything. “At home, if me or George praised a woman, Mrs. Esmond—and Mountain too—would be sure to find fault with her!”

“I am sure I would find fault with no one who is kind to you, Mr. Warrington,” Maria sighed; and the sigh, though soft, seemed to drop into the grass between them like a spoon into an empty basin. “Though you are not angry with me for envying them because they had to take care of you when you were wounded and ill—whilst I—I had to leave you?”

“You dear good Maria!”

“No, Harry! I am not dear and good.” She withdrew her arm a hair’s breadth, then yielded it again—habit stronger than pride. “There, sir, you needn’t be so pressing in your attentions. Look! There is your black man walking with a score of other wretches in livery. The horrid creatures are going to fuddle at the tea-garden, and get tipsy like their masters. That dreadful Mr. Morris was perfectly tipsy when I came to you, and frightened you so.”

“I had just won great bets from both of them,” Harry said, pleased as a boy who has taken a hedge clean and lands with both feet. “What shall I buy for you, my dear cousin?”

And he told her, with the buoyancy that comes from sudden money and sudden applause, of his leap and his wagers—how, for the honour of Virginia, he would show them what jumping was; how, with a little practice, he could leap two foot farther. Maria listened and let herself be pleased; she had been trained to make others’ cheer her own, as a housekeeper sets out a dish she will not eat.

“But you must beware about play, child,” she said at last. “You know it hath been the ruin of our family. My brother Castlewood, Will, our poor father, our aunt—Lady Castlewood herself—they have all been victims to it: as for my Lord March, he is the most dreadful gambler and the most successful of all the nobility.”

“I don’t intend to be afraid of him, nor of his friend Mr. Jack Morris neither,” Harry answered, fingering the notes again, loving their dry crackle as if it were the crust of something baked to perfection. “What do you play at Aunt Bernstein’s? Cribbage, all-fours, brag, whist, commerce, piquet, quadrille? I’m ready at any of ’em. What o’clock is that striking—sure ’tis seven!”

“And you want to begin now,” Maria said, plaintive.

“Hey! Youth is youth, cousin!” Harry tossed his head. “And a young fellow must have his fling!”

So they turned toward the lodgings where pleasure waited, and already the Parade’s open orchestra was waking—fiddles scraping, testing, squeaking, that thin, nervous tuning like insects in a hedge. The sound lifted and worried the air; the very birds seemed to hold off until the humans had done with their noise. Maria heard it as one hears a door bolted on a room one longs for: her aunt was awake again, and she must go back to her slavery.

Harry never asked after that slavery. He must have known it, had he taken the trouble to think. He did not think. His mind was on cards and company, on the glittering cup held out to his age—he seized it as other lads do, not calculating the morning’s bitterness.

At Madame de Bernstein’s, they had, like worldly parents anxious to rid themselves of a troublesome child and go to their party, put the sun to bed while it was yet light. Curtains were drawn over day; candles flowered in sconces; and the rooms took on that warmed, crowded smell of wax and powder and hot spirits, of tea steeping too long, of lemon peel and grated nutmeg bruised into negus. There were little side-tables where plates appeared and vanished—biscuits, sugared comfits, slices of bread-and-butter curling at their edges—food not to nourish but to keep the hands busy while the eyes hunted.

One chair after another landed ladies at the Baroness’s door, more or less painted, patched, brocaded. Gentlemen arrived in gala raiment. Mr. Poellnitz’s star was the largest; his coat, the most embroidered. My Lord of March and Ruglen, when he came, was quite changed from the figure Harry had met at the White Horse: the tight brown scratch was exchanged for a neatly curled feather-top, with bag and grey powder; the jockey dress and leather breeches replaced by a rich French suit that gleamed like a well-glazed pastry. Mr. Jack Morris had just such another wig and suit of stuff, as close a copy as a kitchen-boy makes of his master’s dish.

Mr. Wolfe attended his beautiful mistress, Miss Lowther, and her aunt, who loved cards as the world loved them. And when Lady Maria appeared, it was plain her looks belied her aunt’s talk of her: her shape was very fine; her dress showed it; her complexion was exceeding fair by nature, and a dark frilled ribbon clasped by a jewel round her neck made her whiteness seem whiter. Her cheeks were no redder than other ladies’—and the roses, like the oranges in winter, were openly bought. An artful patch or two was supposed to add to her lustre. If the hoops were absurd, they were absurd in a way fashion forgives: the whole costume pleased, as sweetmeats please even when one knows they are more sugar than fruit.

As for the Baroness de Bernstein, when she took pains with her toilette she was magnificent still—handsome even—yet melancholy, and in a manner terrifying. Some faces show only the present; hers spoke in old accents of past power and passion. The rooms might glitter, the cards might slap and slide, yet there was something in that old lady’s eye like a winter pond—dark, still, reflecting flame without being warmed by it.

“My hostess,” said my Lord Chesterfield to his friend in a confidential whisper that he did not know was loud, “puts me in mind of Covent Garden in my youth. Then it was the court end of the town and inhabited by the highest fashion. Now, a nobleman’s house is a gaming-house, or you may go in with a friend and call for a bottle.”

“Hey! a bottle and a tavern are good things in their way,” my Lord March said, shrugging. “I was not born before the Georges came in, though I intend to live to a hundred. I never knew the Bernstein but as an old woman; and if she ever had beauty, hang me if I know how she spent it.”

“No, hang me—how did she spend it?” Jack Morris laughed out. “Here’s a table! Shall we sit down and have a game? Don’t let the Frenchman come in. He won’t pay. Mr. Warrington, will you take a card?”

So Harry found himself partnered with my Lord Chesterfield against Mr. Morris and the Earl of March.

“You have come too late, Baron,” Chesterfield said to the other nobleman advancing. “We have made our game. What, have you forgotten Mr. Warrington of Virginia—the young gentleman whom you met in London?”

“The young gentleman whom I met at Arthur’s Chocolate House had black hair, a little cocked nose, and was by no means so fortunate in his personal appearance as Mr. Warrington,” the Baron replied with easy presence, and with a smile that allowed truth to slip away without offence. “Warrington, Dorrington, Harrington—we of the continent cannot retain your insular names. I certify that this gentleman is not the individual of whom I spoke at dinner.”

He glanced kindly on Harry and sidled off to the embrasure where Mr. Wolfe and Miss Lowther talked in low tones. There the Baron chose to discourse on the Prussian manual exercise lately introduced into King George the Second’s army—matters Mr. Wolfe knew well, and which might have pleased him on any other night, but now fell like stale crumbs where a richer dish was desired. Still the Baron spoke, and believed himself charming.

At the start of the evening the Baroness received her guests personally, making her little speeches, laying out her courtesies as a cook lays out knives in order. But as rooms filled and tables were made up, Madame de Bernstein grew restless, then retreated at last with three friends to her own corner, where a table reserved for her was attended by her major-domo. There she sat down resolutely and never changed her place nor quit her game till cock-crow—fixed as a great landowner in her chair, drawing in and sending out coin and fate.

The charge of receiving the company devolved upon Lady Maria. She did not care for cards, but dutifully did the honours of the house, moving through the rooms with her silk rustling like dry leaves. Often she passed by Harry’s table and lingered—as if warmth might be had by standing near another’s fire.

“Come and cut the cards for us,” said Lord March as she paused on one of those wistful visits. “Cut the cards and bring us luck, Lady Maria! We have had none to-night, and Mr. Warrington is winning everything.”

“I hope you are not playing high, Harry?” Maria asked, timidly.

“Oh no, only sixpences,” my lord cried, dealing.

“Only sixpences,” echoed Mr. Morris, his round face fallen into such dismal lines that one might think each “sixpence” a slice cut from him. He must have been keenly alive to their value if the loss of a few could sour him so.

Lord Chesterfield sat opposite Harry, sorting his cards, calm as if he handled papers of state. No one could tell by that composed physiognomy whether fortune smiled or frowned on him. But a word—not altogether delicate—slipped from Mr. Morris, upon which his partner cried out with sudden heat, “Hang it, Morris, play your cards, and hold your tongue!”

Considering they were only playing for sixpences, his lordship too seemed strangely affected. Maria, still fondly behind Harry’s chair with her hand on its back, could see his cards, and saw a whole covey of trumps ranged in one corner. She had not taken away his luck. She was pleased, absurdly, to think she had cut the pack that dealt him those pretty trumps—pleased as a housewife is pleased when her yeast rises true, though another will eat the loaf.

As Lord March dealt, he said in a low voice to Harry, “The bet as before, Mr. Warrington, or shall we double it?”

“Anything you like, my lord,” Harry answered, very quietly, as if he were agreeing to a change of sauce.

“We will say, then—shillings.”

“Yes, shillings,” said Harry; and the game went on, the cards whispering and snapping like small wings, the counters clicking, the room’s talk and laughter swaying like a sea around that little island of play.

What came of that night—and of the succeeding nights—may be gathered from a letter written later, which was never delivered to the person addressed, but was found among Mr. Henry Warrington’s papers and made its way across the ocean like a bottle cast upon a tide:

“TUNBRIDGE WELLS, August 10, 1756.

“DEAR GEORGE—As White’s two bottles of Burgundy and a pack of cards constitute all the joys of your life, I take for granted that you are in London at this moment, preferring smoke and faro to fresh air and fresh haystacks. This will be delivered to you by a young gentleman with whom I have lately made acquaintance, and whom you will be charmed to know. He will play with you at any game for any stake, up to any hour of the night, and drink any reasonable number of bottles during the play.

“Mr. Warrington is no other than the Fortunate Youth about whom so many stories have been told in the Public Advertiser and other prints. He has an estate in Virginia as big as Yorkshire, with the incumbrance of a mother, the reigning Sovereign; but, as the country is unwholesome, and fevers plentiful, let us hope that Mrs. Esmond will die soon, and leave this virtuous lad in undisturbed possession. She is aunt of that polisson of a Castlewood, who never pays his play-debts, unless he is more honourable in his dealings with you than he has been with me. Mr. W. is de bonne race. We must have him of our society, if it be only that I may win my money back from him.

“He has had the devil’s luck here, and has been winning everything, whilst his old card-playing beldam of an aunt has been losing. A few nights ago, when I first had the ill-luck to make his acquaintance, he beat me in jumping (having practised the art amongst the savages, and running away from bears in his native woods); he won bets off me and Jack Morris about my weight; and at night, when we sat down to play, at old Bernstein’s, he won from us all round. If you can settle our last Epsom account please hand over to Mr. Warrington 350 pounds, which I still owe him, after pretty well emptying my pocket-book. Chesterfield has dropped six hundred to him, too; but his lordship does not wish to have it known, having sworn to give up play and live cleanly. Jack Morris, who has not been hit as hard as either of us, and can afford it quite as well, for the fat chuff has no houses nor train to keep up, and all his misbegotten father’s money in hand, roars like a bull of Bashan about his losses.

“We had a second night’s play, en petit comité, and Barbeau served us a fair dinner in a private room. Mr. Warrington holds his tongue like a gentleman, and none of us have talked about our losses; but the whole place does, for us. Yesterday the Cattarina looked as sulky as thunder, because I would not give her a diamond necklace, and says I refuse her because I have lost five thousand to the Virginian. My old Duchess of Q. has the very same story, besides knowing to a fraction what Chesterfield and Jack have lost.

“Warrington treated the company to breakfast and music at the rooms; and you should have seen how the women tore him to pieces. That fiend of a Cattarina ogled him out of my vis-à-vis, and under my very nose, yesterday, as we were driving to Penshurst, and I have no doubt has sent him a billet-doux ere this. He shot Jack Morris all to pieces at a mark: we shall try him with partridges when the season comes.

“He is a fortunate fellow, certainly. He has youth (which is not deboshed by evil courses in Virginia, as ours is in England); he has good health, good looks, and good luck.

“In a word, Mr. Warrington has won our money in a very gentlemanlike manner; and, as I like him, and wish to win some of it back again, I put him under your worship’s saintly guardianship. Adieu! I am going to the North, and shall be back for Doncaster.—Yours ever, dear George, M. et R.”

“To George Augustus Selwyn, Esq., at White’s Chocolate House, St. James’s Street.”

After two or three days at Tunbridge Wells, the young Virginian found himself, to his own wonder, promoted from stranger to spectacle, as though he were a rare dish newly set upon the board and every eye must taste him first. No coroneted lord drew half so much staring. Even the Bishop of Salisbury, grave as a winter pew, scarce commanded such bows. Folks wheeled about to look after Harry as he went by; farmers in from the lanes paused in market with their baskets and their brown eggs, gaping as if he were an Indian prince. At the Rooms, stout matrons beckoned him close with hands that smelt of lavender-water and orange-peel, contrived a vacancy upon the bench, and left him, by accident of motherly providence, alone with daughters who smiled like china shepherdesses.

The Wells had measured him to the acre and the shilling. At every tea-table where the spoons clinked against saucers and the kettle sang, his Virginian lands were cast up like sums, his income weighed as carefully as sugar. His winnings at play were bandied about with as much relish as a new receipt for syllabub; wonderful, the quickness with which neighbours season our names with their own conjectures. The interest ran so high that even his servant profited by it. People smiled upon Gumbo, drew him aside to the alehouse door, and treated him to cold meat and a foaming mug, as though truth might be coaxed out of him with beef and beer. Gumbo, who had always possessed a genius for enlargement, grew visibly rounder under this diet, became a principal person among the valets’ fraternity, and lied more enormously than ever—fed, as it were, upon other men’s curiosity.

No party, it seemed, was complete unless Mr. Warrington made one of it. Harry was amused, a little astonished, and carried his new consequence with tolerable ease. He had been bred in his own country to think well of himself; the sudden English homage did not lessen that natural opinion, though it did not wholly intoxicate him. He did not swagger about his victories, nor crow like a cock upon a dung-hill; yet he had a queer colonial notion of honour which bound him to meet any summons as if Old Virginia herself had been challenged. If a gentleman called him to a horse-match, or a drinking-bout, or a game at cards, Harry felt he must not draw back. And indeed they were ready enough to try him at all these trials. He had a strong head for wine, a steady hand for play, a firm seat, and nerves that did not flutter; and the representative of his province came off very handsomely in his friendly rivalry with the mother-country.

Madame de Bernstein—who had her fill of cards nightly, and no doubt repaired those losses of which we heard before—was delighted with her nephew’s credit. He shot with Jack Morris and beat him; rode a match with Mr. Scamper and won; took up tennis against Captain Batts, and though he had never tried the game, learned its springing, stinging strokes in a few days, as a good cook learns a new sauce by tasting it once. He played with the famous gamesters, my Lords Chesterfield and March, and both bore witness to his coolness, gallantry, and breeding.

At books Harry was no prodigy; but he wrote as well as many men of fashion, and the naïveté of his ignorance diverted the old lady. She had read in her time, and could talk learnedly with learned folk; she relished humour, had a taste for Molière and Mr. Fielding; yet she loved the world far better than the library, and would leave the best chapter for a rubber with the same promptness with which she would quit a dish of stewed prunes for a plate of hot fritters. She took a fond, tyrannical pleasure in Harry’s toilette—rummaged old laces for his ruffles, found him a pretty diamond brooch for his frill—dressing him as one garnishes a handsome capon with lemon and parsley, not for nourishment but for admiration. He became the prime favourite among her nephews and kin. Lady Maria, I fear, was only too well pleased at his successes, and did not grudge him his superiority over her brothers; but those gentlemen must have quaked when they heard of Harry’s astonishing luck and the advance he had made in their rich aunt’s affections.

After a fortnight at Tunbridge, he was a personage. He knew the best company in the place. Was it his fault if he grew acquainted with the bad likewise? Was he very wrong in taking the world as he found it, and drinking from that bright cup of pleasure which was held brimming to his lips? The old aunt enjoyed his triumphs, and bade him pursue his enjoyments. She was no rigorous moralist, nor perhaps a wholesome instructress for youth. Had the saucy Cattarina written him billets-doux, Aunt Bernstein would likely have told him to go; but Harry had brought from his thinly-peopled colonial home a stock of modesty that still sat upon him like honest homespun linen. Libertinism was not the fashion of those rough towns and wide plantations. The vices of great cities were scarcely known there, much less practised. Harry blushed at the daring talk of his new associates. Even Aunt Bernstein’s jests and freedom astonished him, so that the worldly old woman would call him Joseph, or simpleton.

Yet, innocent as he was, the world gave him credit for being as bad as the rest. How was he to guess there was harm in keeping company with Cattarina, when he had seen my Lord March driving her in his phaeton? Harry thought no sin lay in giving her his arm and walking openly with her in the public walks, where the gravel crunched beneath their feet and the band, in the distance, scraped out its fashionable airs. She took a fancy to a trinket in a toy-shop; and his pockets being full of money, he was pleased to buy her the locket she coveted. Next day it was lace; again he gratified her. Next day something else; Madame Cattarina’s desires were like a table that is never cleared. At last she asked for diamond drops for her pretty ears, and here Harry stopped—turned her off with a laugh and a jest. He was shrewd enough, not reckless nor prodigal, though generous. But who was to give him credit for his modesty? Old Bernstein would insist that her nephew played Don Juan and supplanted my Lord March; and she insisted the more when poor Maria was by, loving to stab that tender heart and enjoy her niece’s piteous silence.

“Boys will be boys, my dear,” the Baroness would say, “and I don’t want Harry to be the first milksop in his family!”

The bread Maria ate at her aunt’s expense choked her sometimes. O me! how hard and indigestible some women can make the very loaf.

Mr. Wolfe was forever coming from Westerham to pay court to the lady of his love; and as Harry knew the Colonel’s mind was wholly in that pursuit, he did not look to see much of him, though he liked the officer’s conversation. It was different from the ribald talk around Harry. Mr. Wolfe never spoke of cards, or horse pedigrees, nor bragged of his prowess in the hunting-field, nor boasted of women’s favours, nor retailed the innumerable scandals of the time. And it was not a good time. That old world was more dissolute than ours. There was an old King with mistresses openly in his train, whom great people honoured. There was a nobility mad for pleasure; there was a looseness in words and acts which we, as faithful historians, must note without particulars that would needlessly offend honest readers. Harry had fallen among some of the wildest of these wild people, and had found an old relative who lived in the thick of the rout.

So, at first, Harry did not remark how Colonel Wolfe avoided him, nor, when they met by chance, notice the coldness in the other’s manner. He did not know what stories were told of him. Who ever does know the stories that are told of him? Who makes them? Who fathers those wondrous lies? Poor Harry did not know the reputation he was acquiring; that whilst he rode and played and took his frolic, he passed among respectable folk for the most abandoned and profligate of young men. Alas, alas, to think that the lad we liked—gentle, quiet, easily pleased—should be, in report, a hardened spendthrift, a confirmed gamester, a frequenter of abandoned women! Such tales reached honest Colonel Lambert at Oakhurst: first one, then another, then a crowd of them, until his kind heart was full of care. His family saw plainly that something gnawed him.

At first Lambert would not speak. He put aside his wife’s fond questioning. Mrs. Lambert’s imagination ran to misfortune: ruin, dangerous orders, one of the boys ill or dead—an anxious woman can invent tragedies faster than a kitchen can boil water. Who can resist the cross-examination of the conjugal pillow? Lambert was forced at last to tell part of what he knew. His wife was as grieved and amazed as he had been. From their chamber the grief, stifled awhile under bed-pillows, came downstairs. Theo and Hester caught it from their parents, and had it very bad. Kind little wounded hearts! Hester at first flew into a passion, clenched her small fists, grew red, and vowed she would not believe a word of the wicked tales; but she ended by believing them. Scandal almost always masters people—especially the good and innocent. Oh, the serpent they had warmed at their fire! Oh, the wretched, wretched boy! To think of his walking about with that horrible painted Frenchwoman, giving her diamond necklaces, parading his shame before all society at the Wells!

The three ladies, after crying over it, and Lambert too deeply moved to bear it alone, took the parson into their confidence. In vain he preached next Sunday his favourite sermon against scandal and our propensity to think evil. We repent, we promise to do so no more; and when the next ill story comes we swallow it, as if it were physic and must be taken. So did those kindly Oakhurst people believe what they heard of poor Harry Warrington.

Meanwhile Harry was far too pleased with himself to guess how ill his friends were thinking of him. He pursued an idle, pleasant, unprofitable life, with no notion of the hubbub he made, nor of the dreadful repute in which many good men held him.

One day, coming out from a match at tennis with Mr. Batts—his limbs warmed, his spirits high, the very air at the Wells sounding, in his ears, like applause—Harry overtook Colonel Wolfe, returning from one of his visits to the lady of his heart. Harry held out his hand. Wolfe took it; but his salutation was so cold that Harry could not but observe it. And when Mr. Batts made a fine bow, the Colonel scarcely touched his hat with his forefinger. The tennis captain walked away, looking disconcerted, leaving Harry behind with his friend.

Mr. Wolfe strode on, very erect, silent, and chill as a north wall.

“I have not seen you these many days,” said Harry.

“You have had other companions,” Wolfe returned curtly.

“But I had rather be with you than any of them,” cried the young man.

“Indeed I might be better company for you than some,” said the other.

“Is it Captain Batts you mean?” asked Harry. “He is no favourite of mine, I own; he had a rascally reputation in the army, and I doubt he has not mended it since he was turned out. You certainly might find a better friend than Captain Batts. Pardon the freedom.”

“Friend? He is no friend: he only teaches me tennis. He is hand-in-glove with my lord and the people of fashion who play.”

“I am not a man of fashion,” said Mr. Wolfe.

“My dear Colonel, what is the matter? Have I angered you? You speak as if I had, and I am not conscious of having done aught to forfeit your regard.”

“I will be free with you, Mr. Warrington,” said Wolfe gravely. “I don’t like some of your friends.”

“Why, they are men of the first rank and fashion in England,” Harry answered, not choosing to take offence at bluntness.

“Exactly—too high for a hard-working poor soldier like me. If you continue to live with such, you will find numbers of us humdrum people can’t afford to keep such company. I am here paying my addresses to an honourable lady. I met you yesterday openly walking with a French ballet-dancer, and you took off your hat. I must tell you plainly, I had rather you would not take off your hat when you go out in such company.”

“Sir!” Harry cried, the blood rushing up under his skin till his face burned. “Do you mean that I am to forgo the honour of Colonel Wolfe’s acquaintance altogether?”

“I shall request you to do so when you are in company with that person,” said Wolfe angrily; and he used a word not fit to be written here, though Shakespeare puts it into Othello’s mouth.

“Great heavens! what a shame to speak so of any woman!” Harry burst out. “How dare any man say that poor creature is not honest?”

“You ought to know best, sir,” Wolfe said, looking at him with surprise, “or the world belies you very much.”

“What ought I to know best? I see a poor little French dancer come hither with her mother and ordered by the doctors to drink the waters. I know people of my rank don’t keep company with hers; but are you so squeamish? Have I not heard you say you did not value birth, and that all honest people ought to be equal? Why should I not give this little unprotected woman my arm? There are scarce half a dozen people here who can speak a word of her language. I can speak a little French, and she is welcome to it; and if Colonel Wolfe does not choose to touch his hat to me when I walk with her—by George he may leave it alone!”

“You don’t mean to say,” Wolfe answered, studying him, “that you do not know the woman’s character?”

“Of course she is a dancer, and I suppose no better or worse than her neighbours. But I mean to say, had she been a duchess—or your grandmother—I could not have respected her more.”

“You don’t mean to say you did not win her at dice from Lord March?”

“At what?”

“At dice. Everybody knows the story. Not a soul at the Wells is ignorant of it. I heard it but now in the company of that good old Mr. Richardson, and the ladies were saying you would be a character for a colonial Lovelace.”

“What on earth else have they said about me?” Harry asked; and then Wolfe, who was fair enough to speak out, told him. One charge after another—alarming accounts of his wickedness and profligacy—were laid before him. He was said to corrupt virtue, to drink habitually, to game like a professional, to blaspheme, to sneer at religion; to be a fitting companion for my Lord March and that society into which he had fallen.

“I tell you these things,” Wolfe said, “because it is fair you should know what is said of you; and because, from the way you met the last charge, I do heartily believe you are innocent of most of the rest. I feel I, for one, have been doing you wrong; and I ask your pardon sincerely.”

Harry, eager and honest, took his hand at once; and this time their grasp had warmth in it. As for most accusations, Harry rebutted them easily. Play he owned to; and he defended it with the same plain logic with which a hungry man defends a good supper. A gentleman, he thought, should not refuse a fair challenge from other gentlemen if his means allowed; he never would play beyond those means. After winning considerably at first, he could afford large stakes, since he was playing with other men’s money. Play was fair—certainly pleasant. Did not all England, except the Methodists, play? Had he not seen the best company at the Wells over the cards—his aunt among them?

Mr. Wolfe did not at once comment upon Harry’s notion of “best company,” but spoke frankly, because Harry’s own frankness had won him, and warned him that the life he led might be the pleasantest, but was not the most profitable.

“It can’t be, sir,” Wolfe said, “that a man is to pass his days at horse-racing and tennis, and his nights carousing or at cards. Every man was made to do some work; and a gentleman, if he has none, must make some. Do you know the laws of your country, Mr. Warrington? Being a great proprietor, you will doubtless one day be a magistrate at home. Have you travelled your own land, made yourself acquainted with its trades and manufactures? These are fit things for a gentleman to study, and may occupy him as well as a cock-fight or a cricket-match. Do you know anything of our profession? That, at least, you will allow is noble; and there is plenty in it to learn, and suited, I should think, to you. I speak of it rather than of books and learned professions, because, as far as I can judge, your genius does not lie that way. But honour is the aim of life; and every man can serve his country one way or another. Be sure, sir, idle bread is the most dangerous bread that is eaten. Cards and pleasure may be taken after work, but not instead of work, and all day. And do you know—though the world calls you the Fortunate Youth—I think you are rather Warrington the Unlucky; for you are followed by daily idleness, daily flattery, daily temptation; and the Lord send you deliverance out of your good fortune.”

Harry did not like to tell his aunt that afternoon why he looked grave. He meant not to drink; but at the ordinary there were jolly fellows and the bottle went round, the glass clinked, the room grew loud with laughter that did not so much answer the musicians outside as drown them. He meant not to play; but a fourth was wanted at his aunt’s table—how resist? The cards made their little dry music as they were dealt; gold slid and rang; phrases of fashionable wit fell like crumbs. He was the old lady’s partner again and again; he had Somebody’s own luck, to be sure; and once more he watched the dawn creep in, pale as watered milk, and feasted at sunrise on chickens and champagne—rich flesh torn hot from the bone, the wine sharp and yeasty on his tongue—while outside, the waking world began its daily murmur, and the Wells, already busy with talk, began to cook his name anew.

So long as there were cards to be cut at her lodging and a chair ready at the assembly-rooms, Madame de Bernstein remained tolerably content at Tunbridge Wells.
