She scolded her niece with the same steady relish with which she played her rubber; and, if the talk ran high or low, it ran always, like a brook, around her—never through her.

At Harry Warrington’s age, nearly every place is pleasant, provided there is brisk air to fill the lungs, company to quicken the blood, and some honest sport to set the limbs going. Youth has a cookery of its own: it can take a plain joint and swear it is a feast; it can drink thin port and call it nectar—because appetite, that best of sauces, seasons it. A man older will remember his first ball as he remembers the first loaf he ever helped to knead: not for the flour, but for the warmth of hands and the smell of it rising. When we are young, we go to pleasure like a hungry boy to table, counting the days until the dish comes on; later, we look at the same board with a cooler eye, and sometimes sit—as mothers do—while the daughters dance and the music carries them where we can no longer go.

Harry, being of that age when idleness itself tastes sweet, had little mind to be as severe upon his own otium as Colonel Lambert of the Twentieth was apt to be. There is a kind of leisure that is not noble, but is delicious all the same: the slatternly enchantress who lets a man lie late in his dressing-gown, draw a book to him as one draws a coverlet, and call for a glass mixed cold and sharp—sherry beaten with sugar and bruised mint, the ice clinking like small bells—while a cigar sends its blue ribbon into the afternoon. People may cry shame on her, and name her the mother of mischief; yet she is excellent company, and her voice is soft.

At the Wells the fashionable great came and went. My Lord of March rode northward; my Lord Chesterfield, finding that the water did not mend his deafness, returned to his lonely quiet at Blackheath—seeking a kinder soundscape than these public rooms afford, where every foot and fan makes its own small storm. Yet plenty of gentlemen remained, and Mr. Warrington lacked no companions at his ordinary at the White Horse.

He learned quickly to command a French dinner as neatly as any man who had been bred within sight of St. James’s. He could give his orders to Monsieur Barbeau in Barbeau’s own tongue with a fluency uncommon among those who borrowed foreign words as they would borrow a lace ruffle—only to show it. Harry liked the speech as he liked the food: for the taste of it in the mouth, and the world it carried with it. He had a decided palate for wines too, and could tell, with a certainty that made older topers stare, the deep, furred richness of Clos Vougeot from the more delicate, scented grace of a Romande. The bottles came up from the cellar sweating as if they, too, had traveled; the cork drew with a sigh; and the first pour sent its fragrance rising—berries and earth and old wood—as if some buried season were being uncapped.

Thus the young Virginian, in that little kingdom of pump-room and bowling-green, grew into what people called the young King of the Wells. The common frequenters were easy men of the world, not much shocked by the rumor of gallantry and extravagance which had begun to buzz about him, and which had frightened Mr. Wolfe. Yet, though Harry swam among loose fish, he had a natural shrewdness and honesty that kept him clear of many hooks. He made few foolish bets, and those jolly idlers who lived by taking in the unwary found him hard to handle. He played games indoors and out because he had a quick eye and a straight hand; but he was scrupulous about his company—playing only with gentlemen he knew—and he would settle his own debts on the spot, as a man pays for bread before he leaves the baker, unwilling to owe even the smallest crumb.

He would have cut a sorry figure at a college examination, perhaps; but there are other examinations in the world—tests of temper, of courage, of that fidelity which keeps a man whole. Harry had to sit for some of those.

For instance, when that unhappy little Cattarina—she who had already brought him into enough trouble—carried her importunities beyond the mark at which he thought generosity should stop, he drew away from the Opera-house siren with a coolness and skill that left her no hold upon him. The mermaid’s mother then appeared, a woman who could weep as quickly as she could grin. She came with a tale ready salted: a cruel bailiff, she vowed, had seized all her daughter’s goods for debt; the venerable father was languishing in a London gaol; nothing would serve but that Mr. Warrington should pay past accounts at Tunbridge and stand bail in town.

Harry answered that, between himself and a bailiff, there could be no dealings; and that because he had had the misfortune—or good fortune, as she chose to call it—to be known to Mademoiselle Cattarina, and had gratified her caprices with trinkets and knick-knacks, he was not thereby bound to discharge the old debts of her family. He would not be surety for her papa; he would not pay her outstanding bills.

The mother’s face shifted like a bad cook’s fire—now flaring, now sinking. She called him monster and ingrate; and then, with a veteran smirk, asked why he did not take pay for the services he had rendered to the young person. At first Harry did not understand what payment she meant. When the meaning was made plain, the honest lad rose as if he had been struck by a foul smell.

He told her he came from a country where even the savages would recoil from such trafficking; and that a woman who bartered a child’s dishonour was beyond his comprehension—beyond his language, too, for there are infamies which no clean word will carry. He bowed her out with ceremony, as if the formality of good breeding might keep the stain from his threshold, and ordered Gumbo to mark her well and never admit her again.

No doubt she went away breathing vengeance against the “Iroquois,” as she chose to call him; declaring that no Turk or Persian would treat a lady so. She and her daughter, in fact, retreated to London as soon as their anxious landlord would let them.

If Harry had escaped the perils of gallantry, there remained those of gaming. A man who plays at bowls—so the phrase ran—must expect rubbers. One evening after dinner at the ordinary, he declined to play piquet any further with Captain Batts. The Captain roughly demanded his reason. Harry told him fairly that he played only with gentlemen who paid, like himself; and he spoke with such readiness to satisfy Mr. Batts, as soon as the outstanding little account was settled, that the Captain declared himself satisfied in advance—satisfied d’avance—and straightway left the Wells without paying Harry or any other creditor.

There were other occasions when Harry’s spirit showed itself without calculation. One evening, as old Miss Whiffler was going to the assembly, a chairman was rude to her. Harry, who could not abide insolence laid upon age—any more than he could endure a harsh, needless noise in a quiet place—fell upon the fellow and beat him soundly; and the thump of it, though ungentle, seemed to many bystanders a wholesome correction in the day’s clatter.

Then, too, the calumny about himself and that unlucky opera-dancer was repeated aloud by Mr. Hector Buckler, one of the fiercest frequenters of the Wells. Buckler, in the pump-room, was regaling a circle of water-drinkers with the story, and the room was full of its particular din: the splashing of the fountain, the scraping of chairs, the thin laughter, the coughs and whispers, and that perpetual hum which public places breed—an acoustic fog that sets nerves jangling and makes scandal travel faster, because it has so many mouths to lodge in.

Harry stepped up to Buckler before them all and publicly informed him that the story was a falsehood; and that henceforth he would hold any man accountable who uttered it. He did not declaim: he spoke plainly, like one stating a fact, and the sudden stillness that followed—broken only by the water’s trickle—showed that plain words, when they are true, can master a crowd’s noise better than any flourish.

So, though our friend, being at Rome, did as Rome did in matters of diversion, he proved himself a valorous and worthy Roman; and, howling with the wolves, was acknowledged by Mr. Wolfe himself to be as brave as the best of the pack. If that officer had carried to Colonel Lambert the tales which had caused the latter so much pain, we may be sure that, when Wolfe found the young man innocent of the worse charges, he took the first opportunity to withdraw them.

At Lambert’s house, the retraction fell like rain upon a thirsty field. There was joy among them at Harry’s acquittal—something of that pure pleasure which better souls than ours may feel at the recovery of a sinner, though here it was rather the recovery of an unjustly suspected man.

Never had the little family been so happy—no, not even when they had news of Brother Tom winning his scholarship—as when Colonel Wolfe rode over with the account of his conversation with Harry Warrington.

“Hadst thou brought me a regiment, James, I think I should not have been better pleased,” said Mr. Lambert.

Mrs. Lambert called to her daughters, who were in the garden, and kissed them both when they came in, and cried out the good news. Hetty jumped for joy; Theo sat to the harpsichord and, in the evening, performed such uncommonly brilliant operations upon it that the very house seemed to ring more kindly than usual, as if the notes had brushed the corners clean of the old suspicion.

When Dr. Boyle came in for his backgammon, he could not at first account for the illumination in all their faces, until the three ladies, in a happy chorus, told him how right he had been in his sermon and how dreadfully they had wronged that poor dear, good young Mr. Warrington.

“What shall we do, my dear?” says the Colonel to his wife. “The hay is in, the corn won’t be cut for a fortnight,—the horses have nothing to do. Suppose we—” And here he leaned over the table and whispered in her ear.

“My dearest Martin! The very thing!” cries Mrs. Lambert, taking her husband’s hand and pressing it.

“What’s the very thing, mother?” cries young Charley, home for his Bartlemytide holidays.

“The very thing is to go to supper. Come, Doctor! We will have a bottle of wine to-night, and drink repentance to all who think evil.”

“Amen,” says the Doctor, “with all my heart!”

And with this the worthy family went to their supper; and if the fare was simple, it was made splendid by their spirits. The clink of plates, the soft bustle from the kitchen, the cork drawn clean, the first warm scent of bread and meat upon the table—these were honest domestic sounds, not the jangling of the pump-room; and in them, for that night at least, the Lamberts found their peace.

Harry Warrington went, as he had lately made a habit of doing, to dine at the White Horse ordinary; and the room met him with that agreeable tumult which belongs to a country table when it is pretending, for an hour, to be the town. Plates clattered; knives struck; the great joint at the board’s head sent up a warm steam of pepper and beef-fat; and under it all lay the steady music of a public room—boots creaking on sanded boards, pewter set down, corks eased from bottles with a soft pop, and then the long, contented draughting sound that follows.

Among the faces, red with good cheer and honest heat, was one that made Harry’s own spirits spring at once. Parson Sampson—round as a harvest moon, rosy as claret in a glass, and as ready with a story as a cook with salt—was in full command of the company. His voice rang above the rest, a bell in a flock, now dropping to a confidential relish, now flung wide with a laugh that set other men laughing before they had even caught the point. He had not been in London for months; but he possessed that talent, common enough in those days, of making yesterday’s invention sound like this morning’s post.

He dispensed news as the carver dispensed slices: a little of the King’s doings at Kensington; a little of the Duke’s in Pall Mall; how Mr. Byng bore himself in prison, who visited, who stayed away; what odds were given at Newmarket; which face in Covent Garden presently ruled the toasts. Names wandered and changed in his telling as herbs do when a country hand substitutes what grows nearest—Mrs. Polly became Mrs. Lucy; Lady Jane and Lady Mary traded passions; a quarrel in Marybone Gardens shifted from Horse Grenadiers to Foot Guards without injuring the flavor of the tale. The auditors—Hampshire gentlemen with their coats brushed for the Wells—asked only that the dish be lively and wicked, and were not inclined to quarrel with the cook about the exact receipt.

Harry had barely taken his place when Sampson’s eye caught him. Whether from modesty or claret, the parson’s already crimson cheeks deepened. He leaned to the squire beside him—a stout man in a drab coat and gold-laced red waistcoat—and whispered, with a solemn wag of his head, “Maxima debetur,” as though the Latin itself were part of the joke. Then he rose too quickly, stumbled, and made for Harry with arms half-open, like a man welcoming a long-lost son.

“My dear sir! my very dear sir! my conqueror of spades—and clubs—and hearts too!” cried the chaplain, taking Harry’s hand in both his own. “Delighted to see your honour looking so fresh and well!”

Harry returned the greeting warmly; he liked Sampson, for all his looseness, and the parson’s geniality had a warmth in it like a kitchen fire. “And I am glad to see your reverence so hearty,” Harry said, eyeing the clerical rosy gills with a grin. “You look as if English ale agreed with you.”

The drab-coated squire knew Harry, too, and slapped the bench to make room. “Here, Mr. Warrington! Here! Sit by me. Parson, come back and finish about Lord Ogle and the grocer’s wife in—” He never reached the place-name; Sampson, in his flurry, trod upon a gouty toe, and the sentence broke into a shout and an oath that made the table roar.

The chaplain begged pardon, turning from the offended foot to Harry and, by a kind of cheerful necessity, to all the room. In a few rolling breaths he delivered, as if they were tidings for the nation, all the private intelligence of Castlewood: my lord’s affectionate remembrances to his cousin; special orders that Sampson should come to Tunbridge Wells and look after the young gentleman’s morals; my Lady Viscountess and Lady Fanny gone to Harrogate for the waters; Mr. Will winning his money at Newmarket and bound to visit a duke; Molly the housemaid crying her eyes out about Gumbo, Harry’s servant. The names of high persons—introduced with that practised flourish which made small men feel themselves neighbour to greatness—fell into the parson’s talk like currants into a pudding.

“All Hampshire has heard of your successes at Tunbridge—successes of every kind,” Sampson said at last, with an arch look that set the squire chuckling. “My lord hopes—her ladyship hopes—you won’t be spoilt for quiet home.”

One by one the country gentlemen dropped away, called to their horses, or went to their lodgings to digest and doze. The room grew emptier, the noise thinned to a comfortable murmur, and at length there remained chiefly Harry and the chaplain, the bottle between them, and a pair of glasses that were never long dry.

“Though I have had plenty,” Sampson declared, filling again with that pious firmness with which some men refill, “that is no reason why I should not have plenty more.”

Toast followed toast. The claret had a smell like crushed berries and old wood; it warmed the throat, loosened the tongue, brightened the eye. Harry, who had been generous by nature, grew extravagant in kindness as the bottle sank. Why should Mr. Sampson pay for an inn when there was a room at Harry’s lodging? The invitation was pressed, insisted on, made a point of honour. The parson’s trunk was ordered over at once. Gumbo received commands—solemn, affectionate commands—to make Mr. Sampson comfortable, most comfortable; and Gumbo, who had grown sleek upon English beef and ale and the easy abundance of a rich young gentleman’s household, bowed and grinned, as though comfort were his own invention.

Harry would not stop at that. He must show Sampson his horses. He had several now—fine creatures, with groomed coats and patient eyes, steaming a little in their stalls. The stable air met them full in the face: sweet hay, dung, leather, warm animal breath, and the sharp iron scent of shoes against stone. The soundscape changed too—the soft stamp and shift of hooves, the jingle of bit and chain, the low, conversational nickering that seems always to be going on between beasts and men.

And there, turning its head at the parson’s voice, was the very horse Harry had won from him. The animal whinnied with such unmistakable pleasure, thrusting its nose into Sampson’s coat as if searching for old treats, that the chaplain stood arrested, ridiculous and touched at once.

“Why, you affectionate rogue,” Sampson murmured, rubbing the warm velvet of the muzzle, his laughter thickening oddly.

Harry, in a gust of feeling—claret feeding generosity as fat feeds flame—swore briskly by Jupiter and rapped out an oath or two in sheer good humour. “He’s yours again, Sampson! I’ll not keep him. Take your old horse back.”

The parson seized Harry’s hand, blessed him, and then, to complete the comedy, flung his arms round the horse’s neck and wept. Tears of Bordeaux and gratitude ran together. The groom stared; Gumbo showed his white teeth in a grin that might have been pity or amusement; and the horse endured the embrace with the grave patience of a creature accustomed to human folly.

Arm in arm, their clothes carrying the stable’s honest odors with them—leather, hay, and the faint animal musk—Harry and Sampson walked up to Madame Bernstein’s lodgings. Their cheeks were flushed; their eyes had that bright, friendly shine which in that age was as common as buckles on shoes.

Madame Bernstein received the chaplain kindly enough. She liked, now and then, a coarse jest as she liked a highly-spiced dish or a new entrée contrived by her cook: it delighted her for two or three appearances, and then she tired of it. The only entertainment she professed never to weary of was cards.

“The cards don’t cheat,” she used to say. “A bad hand tells you the truth to your face: and there is nothing so flattering in the world as a good suite of trumps.” When she was in a good humour, settling herself to her favorite pastime, she would bid her nephew’s chaplain, laughing, say grace—as if the parson were a sauce to the meal, to be sprinkled on before the carving began.

Honest Sampson at first hung back from the card-table at Tunbridge. Her ladyship played too high for him. He slapped his pocket with a comical, piteous look; its contents, he said, had already been transferred to that fortunate youth at Castlewood. Madame Bernstein, like most of her age and sex, was not lavish with money; yet, by some contrivance—most likely Harry’s overflowing purse and mood—Mr. Sampson presently found himself supplied with a little ready coin. Our young gentleman welcomed him to it as readily as he welcomed him to a chair, a bed, and a place at his bottle.

It was surprising how quickly Harry adapted himself to the life around him. His suits were still black, but of the finest cut and cloth; his linen and lace were as delicate as his aunt could wish. He purchased a fine shaving-plate from the toy-shop women, and two magnificent brocade bedgowns in which he lolled at ease, sipping his morning chocolate—a thick, fragrant draught, frothed and sweetened, that left a bitter cocoa perfume on the breath. He acquired swords and walking-canes; French watches with painted backs and diamond settings; snuff-boxes enamelled with a cunning that made the little pictures look moist and alive. Tradesmen learned his hours. Grooms and jockeys waited daily. There was now an anteroom full of men with petitions, parcels, and accounts; and Gumbo—grown important in his place—admitted them one by one over Harry’s chocolate, as though he were steward to a small court.

No single negro could have kept order among all the fine things Mr. Warrington had gathered—let alone the horses and the post-chaise he had bought. How many men Gumbo had under him no one exactly counted; but there were hands enough to polish, brush, fold, rub down, and carry, and the house smelled perpetually of fresh soap, beeswax, leather, and heated milk.

Harry instructed himself too in the accomplishments required of a gentleman. A French fencing-master and a dancing-master of the same nation resided at Tunbridge that season, and Harry frequented them with the steady appetite of youth that wishes to be complete. Within weeks he could handle the foils against his master and any frequenter of the school; and Lady Maria—who danced elegantly herself—owned with a sigh that there was no gentleman at court who could walk a minuet more gracefully than Mr. Warrington.

As for riding, he took a few lessons on the great horse from a master who came to the Wells; yet he declared their Virginian seat and manner good enough, and maintained he saw no one among the fine folks or jockeys who rode better than his friend Colonel George Washington of Mount Vernon. The boast was spoken not as vanity, but as loyalty to a remembered world—the red earth, the long fences, the quiet, wide sound of wind in trees and the honest creak of saddle-leather untroubled by the shrill racket of a fashionable course.

Sampson, meanwhile, found himself lodged better than he had been for a long while. He knew a great deal of the world and told a great deal more; and Harry—being twenty—looked up with delighted credulity to the man of thirty, whose old jokes and tarnished anecdotes had been washed anew in wine at a hundred tables. Sampson’s town pleasantries and college stories were all fresh to Harry, and his companionship came with the insinuating ease of a guide who takes a young man through bright rooms and never lets him see the kitchen where the reckoning is prepared.

There were, a hundred years ago, men in London who made a trade of attaching themselves to fashionable youth; of tickling their fancies with merry stories; of playing Mentors in playhouses and taverns; of attending them to gaming tables with an understanding perhaps with the punters; of drinking lemonade while Master Hopeful drank Burgundy, and then walking into the street with a cool head when the young lord reeled. Mr. Sampson was of that comfortable species; and if the diet was parasitical, it did not disagree with him. No man could look more healthy, or flourish more cheerfully, than the chaplain on such sustenance.

He became Harry’s confidential leader; and from the following letter—kept among the Warrington papers—it may be seen that Mr. Harry not only had fencing and dancing masters, but a tutor, chaplain, and secretary too; for the young gentleman’s pen, when it addressed his mother, carried an air of care and supervision, as if the very words had been dressed and powdered for her presence.

TO MRS. ESMOND WARRINGTON, OF CASTLEWOOD, AT HER HOUSE AT RICHMOND, VIRGINIA.

Mrs. Bligh’s Lodgings, Pantiles, Tunbridge Wells.
August 25th, 1756.

HONOURED MADAM,—Your honoured letter of 20 June, per Mr. Trail of Bristol, has been forwarded to me duly; and I have to thank your goodness and kindness for the good advice which you are pleased to give me, as also for the remembrances of dear home, which I shall love never the worse for having been to the home of our ancestors in England.

I writ you a letter by the last monthly packet, informing my honoured mother of the little accident I had on the road hither, and of the kind friends who I found and whom took me in. Since then I have been profiting of the fine weather and the good company here, and have made many friends among our nobility, whose acquaintance I am sure you will not be sorry that I should make. Among their lordships I may mention the famous Earl of Chesterfield, late Ambassador to Holland, and Viceroy of the Kingdom of Ireland; the Earl of March and Ruglen, who will be Duke of Queensberry at the death of his Grace; and her Grace the Duchess, a celebrated beauty of the Queen’s time, when she remembers my grandpapa at Court. These and many more persons of the first fashion attend my aunt’s assemblies, which are the most crowded at this crowded place.

Also on my way hither I stayed at Westerham, at the house of an officer, Lieut.-Gen. Wolfe, who served with my grandfather and General Webb in the famous wars of the Duke of Marlborough. Mr. Wolfe has a son, Lieut.-Col. James Wolfe, engaged to be married to a beautiful lady now in this place, Miss Lowther of the North—and though but 30 years old he is looked up to as much as any officer in the whole army, and has served with honour under his Royal Highness the Duke wherever our arms have been employed.

I thank my honoured mother for announcing to me that a quarter’s allowance of 52l. 10s. will be paid me by Mr. Trail. I am in no present want of cash, and by practising a rigid economy, which will be necessary (as I do not disguise) for the maintenance of horses, Gumbo, and the equipage and apparel requisite for a young gentleman of good family, hope to be able to maintain my credit without unduly trespassing upon yours. The linnen and clothes which I brought with me will with due care last for some years—as you say. ’Tis not quite so fine as worn here by persons of fashion, and I may have to purchase a few very fine shirts for great days: but those I have are excellent for daily wear.

I am thankful that I have been quite without occasion to use your excellent family pills. Gumbo hath taken them with great benefit, who grows fat and saucy upon English beef, ale, and air. He sends his humble duty to his mistress, and prays Mrs. Mountain to remember him to all his fellow-servants, especially Dinah and Lily, for whom he has bought posey-rings at Tunbridge Fair.

Besides partaking of all the pleasures of the place, I hope my honoured mother will believe that I have not been unmindful of my education. I have had masters in fencing and dancing, and my Lord Castlewood’s chaplain, the Reverend Mr. Sampson, having come hither to drink the waters, has been so good as to take a vacant room at my lodging. Mr. S. breakfasts with me, and we read together of a morning—he saying that I am not quite such a dunce as I used to appear at home. We have read in Mr. Rapin’s History, Dr. Barrow’s Sermons, and, for amusement, Shakspeare, Mr. Pope’s Homer, and (in French) the translation of an Arabian Work of Tales, very diverting.

Several men of learning have been staying here besides the persons of fashion; and amongst the former was Mr. Richardson, the author of the famous books which you and Mountain and my dearest brother used to love so. He was pleased when I told him that his works were in your closet in Virginia, and begged me to convey his respectful compliments to my lady-mother. Mr. R. is a short fat man, with little of the fire of genius visible in his eye or person.

My aunt and my cousin, the Lady Maria, desire their affectionate compliments to you, and with best regards for Mountain, to whom I enclose a note, I am,—Honoured madam, your dutiful son,
H. ESMOND WARRINGTON.

In the same packet, preserved by the careful hand at Richmond, Madam Esmond set down, as if she were entering stores in a great house-book, what she sent in answer—a domestic cargo crossing an ocean like a memory made edible:

From my son. Received October 15 at Richmond. Sent 16 jars preserved peaches, 224 lbs. best tobacco, 24 finest hams, per Royal William of Liverpool, 8 jars peaches, 12 hams for my nephew, the Rt. Honourable the Earl of Castlewood. 4 jars, 6 hams for the Baroness Bernstein, ditto ditto for Mrs. Lambert of Oakhurst, Surrey, and 1/2 cwt. tobacco. Packet of Infallible Family Pills for Gumbo. My Papa’s large silver-gilt shoe-buckles for H., and red silver-laced saddle-cloth.

One can almost hear, in that list, the old Virginian household again: the soft slap of peach flesh in the preserving-pan, the hiss when syrup meets heat, the steady stir with a wooden spoon; the smokehouse with its sweet, resinous perfume, hams darkening in slow time; the rustle of tobacco leaves like dry rain; the quiet authority of a mistress who knows that food, sent far, is not merely sustenance but command, comfort, and proof that the sender’s language still rules the receiver’s mouth.

Enclosed too was a second note, not dressed for a mother’s eye but dashed off as the heart ran, to Mrs. Mountain:

For Mrs. Mountain.

What do you mien, you silly old Mountain, by sending an order for your poor old divadends dew at Xmas? I’d have you to know I don’t want your 7l. 10, and have toar your order up into 1000 bitts. I’ve plenty of money. But I’m obleaged to you all same. A kiss to Fanny from—Your loving
HARRY.

Madam Esmond wrote beneath, in her own hand, with that mingling of shrewdness and tenderness that belongs to a woman who has ruled servants and children alike:

This note, which I desired M. to show to me, proves that she hath a good heart, and that she wished to show her gratitude to the family, by giving up her half-yearly divd. (on L500 3 per ct.) to my boy. Hence I reprimanded her very slightly for daring to send money to Mr. E. Warrington, unknown to his mother. Note to Mountain not so well spelt as letter to me.

Mem. to write to Revd. Mr. Sampson desire to know what theolog. books he reads with H. Recommend Law, Baxter, Drelincourt.—Request H. to say his catechism to Mr. S., which he has never quite been able to master. By next ship peaches (3), tobacco 1/2 cwt. Hams for Mr. S.

The mother of the Virginians and her sons have long since passed away; yet those two little pieces of writing remain like two voices caught in a shell—one formal, one natural; one speaking the careful English of duty, the other the affectionate dialect of home where spelling is less important than warmth. How is it that, under one enclosure and by one packet, one should march so correctly and the other stumble? The likeliest answer is the simplest: the long letter, with its proper names and respectful turns, was rewritten from a rough draft and had passed beneath a correcting eye—perhaps the chaplain’s, perhaps some other friendly hand in Tunbridge. The small note, flung to Mrs. Mountain, went straight from impulse to paper; it was not submitted to the same dominion of “who” and “whom.”

And indeed, who knows what noise may have broken in upon the young man’s pen? A fiddler in the Pantiles scraping a tune that wormed into the blood; a bear led past with pipe and tabor; a jockey under the windows showing off a horse; a pretty milliner turning her head at the very moment a difficult word came. There are days when any of us, however instructed, will spell ill and speak worse, because the world’s sounds and scents—music, hoofbeats, laughter, meat roasting somewhere, chocolate steaming—will not let us be orderly.

If Harry did not care to spell for Mrs. Mountain as for his mother, what is that to any later reader? And if, in the letter to Richmond, he showed a little reticence—set the best face on his doings, softened the pranks and sharpened the studies—he did what young men have always done when writing to those who love them and watch them from afar. There is, where there is not equality, always a certain decorous hypocrisy. A father (or mother) is king in the castle; the household steps backward before the chair; the children laugh at the old jokes; they are hushed as mice when authority nods after dinner. Away from the throne they may jump, skip, dance, tumble, and kick their heels as youth will; in presence, they compose their faces and their grammar.

So let the grandmammas and aunts cry out, if they please, “Oh, it was highly immoral and improper of Mr. Warrington to be writing home demure letters when he was playing merry pranks!” The young will curtsey and answer, “Yes, dear madam, it was very wrong of him,” and will add in their hearts, as the fiddles sing and the cakes and ale come round, that the sun did shine in other spring-times too, and blossoms did bud, and blood did dance—though the elders, with their gruel and slippers, protest that it never did.

Tunbridge had a way of turning lives into a dish served cold and then reheated with relish. What had been, in truth, a confused little sorrow between Harry Warrington and the luckless Cattarina became, in the mouths of watering-place matrons, a grand ragout of vice—richly seasoned, over-stirred, and passed from cup to cup as easily as the medicinal draughts at the Well. The old ladies, who took their sips of iron water with pinched faces and then loosed their tongues with astonishing vigour, could no more resist a scandal than they could resist a sweetmeat. They supposed the Virginian to be as dissipated as any young English lordling in lace ruffles and debt; and of all of them Madame de Bernstein was the most determined to believe it.

Her ladyship’s mind, like a pot kept too long at the fire, liked to bubble. She had known enough of wickedness in her day to be quick at recognising its smell—even when she mistook honest broth for something corrupt. Harry’s innocence displeased her almost as much as it would have surprised her; she preferred, from old habit and old Roman temper, that her nephew should do as Rome did. Let him be no better than his neighbours, since neighbours made the rule. So she accepted every story of his “Lovelace adventures” with a complacency that was almost maternal. The very idea of him being tempted, pursued, or fallen upon was comfortable to her. It made him common enough to manage.

He had, it is true, given tea and music at the Wells; and in those little assemblies, where china clinked and harpsichords tinkled and fiddles scraped in rooms heavy with perfume and damp woollen cloaks, he had been gallant and gentle to many ladies—ladies of far better figure and repute than the unfortunate dancer. By degrees Madame de Bernstein’s sharp watch over Lady Maria slackened. Old vigilance dozes, like an old cook who has stood too long by the hearth: the hand that once snatched away a child from the kettle grows slow; the eye that once saw everything through steam and smoke begins to ask for sleep.

The Baroness had her own concerns—her cards, her dinners, her rheumatic twinges that came like a knife between the bones. She could not for ever keep another’s heart under lock. Perhaps she thought the danger past; perhaps she grew indifferent to whether it existed or not; perhaps Maria, with that quiet craft young women learn as early as they learn to braid a ribbon, had soothed and cajoled her guardian until even the old Dragon’s scales felt soft. Dragons age. Teeth drop out. The claws, once fit to rake a reputation to ribbons, fall at last with a feeble pat. Their venom is no longer fatal; it is merely disagreeable, like wine turned sharp. And at roosting-time they trail their languid tails homeward, as helpless as any old creature that has spent its fire.

If good folks at Oakhurst had been ready enough to credit what was said against Harry, why should Madame Bernstein—who had seen more of the world’s evil than all Oakhurst put together—be less credulous? In such a place as Tunbridge, where women of fashion, women of reputation and demi-reputation, virtue and no virtue, all mixed as promiscuously as spices in a market-stall, no tale was too coarse to be whispered, no slander too bold to be believed. A century earlier, our ancestors met at Epsom, Bath, Tunbridge, Harrogate, as freely as modern folk go to foreign watering-places; they danced to the same fiddles, drank from the same glasses, and took health and pleasure in the same rooms until the air grew close with candle-smoke and wet silk.

So when the little dancer went back to London—as she did—why, it must be because heartless Harry had deserted her. Deserted her for somebody else, of course; and the company at the Wells could provide not only one name, but half-a-dozen, and would choose whichever best suited the whisperer’s spite. Each name was passed like a morsel from mouth to mouth; each came out altered—salted, peppered, overdone.

Harry’s bad reputation, thus manufactured, comforted his old aunt exceedingly. It eased her mind about his passion for Lady Maria. If he were wicked in the common way, he might be diverted in the common way; and the thought that he was like other young men was, to her, a pillow. She grew so easy that when the chaplain announced he had come to escort her home, she did not even care to separate Maria from her side. She preferred to keep her under her own eye, to gossip at her about her “wicked young cousin,” to speak with that indulgent cynicism old people call wisdom—boys would be boys—and to confide, with a smile that had more steel than mirth, her intention of finding Harry a proper wife: suitable age, suitable fortune, suitable everything that could be measured like flour.

Maria endured these pleasantries as best she might, as a hungry person endures talk of food that is not for them.

There lived in the last century a certain French duke and marquis, a man who made a profession of conquest and did posterity the unkindness of writing down, in sprightly memoirs, the names of many court-beauties he had ruined. Those pages, no doubt, are delightful reading for grandsons who discover their ancestresses there, like preserved fruit labelled and shelved for public tasting. In the course of his travels that nobleman visited North America, and, as in Europe, set himself promptly to fall in love and to win. Yet it is curious that, among the plain colonial people, he seems not to have made a single conquest—else he would certainly have recorded it. Travellers have complained loudly of transatlantic roughness; but one may say, from what one has seen, that American gentlemen are commonly modest in speech, and American women—at least to the best of belief—pure in life.

Harry Warrington had brought that colonial modesty with him. He lived among men of pleasure; he heard talk as free as wine; yet he sat silent through much of it, uneasy when double meanings were flung like bones under the table. He had no victories to boast. If others narrated their own exploits with laughter and coarse triumph, he blushed as if some hot stew had been suddenly splashed upon him. Mr. Sampson had observed this at Castlewood, when cousin Will, with his choice stories, had made Harry shift and redden; and my lord had even rebuked his brother, bidding him keep such jokes for the usher’s table at Kensington and not offend their kinsman. Hence the chaplain’s “Reverentia pueris” at the ordinary on Harry’s first appearance: Sampson, if he had not strength enough to do right, had at least enough grace not to revel in indecency before an innocent youth.

He was touched, too, by Harry’s gift of the horse; and gratitude, that honest appetite, warmed him. “You see, sir,” he said, “I am of the world, and must do as the rest of the world does. I have led a rough life, Mr. Warrington, and can’t afford to be more particular than my neighbours. Video meliora, deteriora sequor, as we said at college. I have a little sister at boarding-school not far from here; and as I keep a decent tongue in my head with my little Patty, and expect others to do the same, sure I may try to do as much by you.”

To Madame de Bernstein the chaplain was loud in praise of Harry. She liked praise of him as she liked good seasoning—liberal, unmistakable. She was as fond of him as she could be of anything; he pleased her eye and amused her temper. His good looks, his manly bearing, his bright eyes, his deep young voice, and—most of all—his blushes, which rose so readily, delighted her. Had he been clever, learned, witty, she would have tired of him. His shrewd simplicity entertained her like a plain dish well made. “We must find a good wife for him, Chaplain,” she said. “I have one or two in my eye who will suit. We must set him up here. He never will bear going back to his savages again, or to live with his little Methodist of a mother.”

On that point Sampson had his own private eagerness. He too had a wife in his eye for Harry. One may suppose he had had conversations at Castlewood with the Earl, who had hinted at rewarding his chaplain with a living or some provision, if only Sampson’s good offices could help my Lady Maria to a husband. Therefore he watched now, waiting to see how best to bring influence to bear.

And indeed Sampson could be agreeable. Within a few hours he and Harry were intimate. The parson rejoiced in high spirits, good appetite, and good humour; he had no sanctified drawl and no hypocritical squeamishness. Yet he took care not to shock Harry with needless grossness; whether from policy or compunction he initiated his pupil only into minor mysteries, keeping back the darker secrets of his own unlucky knowledge. With Harry he was brisk and jolly—ready for bottle, cards, cock-fight, shooting-match, a gallop across the common—yet his talk remained decent. He aimed rather to amuse than to corrupt. His success was easy: he had animal spirits, natural wit, and long apprenticeship in the business of toad-eating, which had been his livelihood since he first entered college as a servitor and began to seek whose favour might feed him.

Toad-eaters were by no means extinct; they only changed their manner. In those days a gentleman’s dependent made no pretence of equality. He openly paid court; called his patron “sir;” stood until bid to sit; ran errands, any errands; flattered ex officio. Mr. Sampson felt no shame in speaking of Harry as his young patron, recommended to him by his noble patron, the Earl of Castlewood. He was proud to appear at Harry’s side; he talked him up to company; he gave orders to Harry’s tradesmen—taking, no doubt, his perquisites as naturally as cooks take tastes from the pot—and played aide-de-camp with cheerful obedience. Since coming to Europe, poor Harry had not been uniformly lucky in his friendships.

“What a reputation, sir, they have made for you in this place!” cried Sampson, bursting in from the coffee-house. “Monsieur de Richelieu was nothing to you!”

“How do you mean, Monsieur de Richelieu? Never was at Minorca in my life,” said downright Harry, who knew nothing of the Frenchman’s famous home victories.

Sampson explained, laughing. The pretty widow Patcham, newly arrived, was certainly desperate about Mr. Warrington; her behaviour at the rooms last night proved it. As for Mrs. Hooper—there was no doubt. The Alderman had dragged his wife back to London for no other reason. It was the talk of the whole Wells.

“Who says so?” Harry broke out, colour rising in his face as quickly as heat under a lid. “I should like to meet the man who dares say so, and confound the villain!”

“I should not like to show him to you,” said Sampson, amused. “It might be the worse for him.”

“It’s a shame to speak with such levity about the character of ladies or of gentlemen either,” Harry continued, pacing the room, anger ringing in his voice like a struck pan. “It’s a shame, I say, to talk away the reputation of any man or woman as people do here. In our country a fellow’s ears would not be safe; and a little before I left home three brothers shot down a man for speaking ill of their sister.”

“Serve the villain right!” cried Sampson.

“Already they have had that calumny about me set a-going here, Sampson—about me and the poor little French dancing-girl.”

“I have heard,” said Sampson, shaking powder out of his wig with a care as delicate as a pastry-cook dusting sugar.

“Wicked; wasn’t it?”

“Abominable.”

“They said the very same thing about my Lord March. Isn’t it shameful?”

“Indeed it is,” Sampson answered, with an expression of astonishing gravity—though the truth was that indignation on such grounds had not visited him.

“I don’t know what I should do if these stories were to come to my mother’s ears. It would break her heart. Only a few days before you came, a military friend of mine, Mr. Wolfe, told me how the most horrible lies were circulated about me. Good heavens! What do they think a gentleman of my name and country can be capable of—I a seducer of women? They might as well say I was a horse-stealer or a housebreaker. I vow if I hear any man say so, I’ll have his ears!”

“I have read, sir, that the Grand Seignior of Turkey has bushels of ears sometimes sent in to him,” said Sampson, laughing. “If you took all those who had heard scandal against you or others, what basketsful you would fill!”

“And so I would, Sampson, as soon as look at ’em—any fellow’s who said a word against a lady or a gentleman of honour!” Harry cried, his voice thick with outraged pride.

“If you’ll go down to the Well you’ll find a harvest of ’em. I just came from there. It was high tide of Scandal. Detraction at its height. You may see the nymphas discentes and the aures satyrorum acutas,” the chaplain said, shrugging.

“That may be as you say,” Harry answered, “but if ever I hear any man speak against my character I’ll punish him. Mark that.”

“I shall be very sorry for his sake,” Sampson returned; “for you’ll mark him in a way he won’t like, and I know you are a man of your word.”

“And now shall we go to dinner, and afterwards to my Lady Trumpington’s tea?” Harry said, forcing himself down from anger as one forces a boil to subside.

“You know, sir, I can’t resist a card or a bottle,” said Sampson. “Let us have the last first, and then the first shall come last.”

So they went off to their accustomed place of refection.

It was an age when men drank as steadily as they breathed; and since General Braddock’s army had come through Harry’s native country, the young Virginian had learned to relish the filling of bumpers and the calling of toasts, having been taught it was a point of honour among officers never to decline a challenge. Thus he and his chaplain drank their claret in peace and plenty, naming with each glass some favourite lady, as easily as one names herbs while chopping them for a sauce.

Sampson had reasons of his own for wishing to know how far the affair between Harry and Lady Maria had gone—whether it advanced, whether it had been checked, whether it had ended. The claret warmed them to that dangerous friendliness which makes a man open his heart as if it were a larder door in a hungry house. The room had the thick, agreeable smell of wine and warm wood; outside, through the window, Tunbridge made its own music—wheels on gravel, distant laughter, the faint calling of sellers—sounds that rose and fell like a tide, and then were smothered again by the closeness indoors.

When the other diners had gone, and Monsieur Barbeau brought a bottle at dessert, Sampson found himself in an eloquent temper, with an urge to preach moralities; while Harry felt an almost physical need to pour out his private history as if it were wine that must be decanted before it soured.

“I am glad to hear what your conduct has really been with regard to the Cattarina, Mr. Warrington,” cried the chaplain, leaning forward with shining eyes. “I am glad from my soul. The wine is with you. You have shown you can bear down calumny and resist temptation. Ah, my dear sir, men are not all so fortunate. What famous good wine this is!” He drained a glass, then held it up. “A toast from you, dear sir, if you please?”

“I give you Miss Fanny Mountain, of Virginia,” said Harry, filling a bumper; and at the name his thoughts flew home, over sea and years, to a child in his mother’s household.

“One of your American conquests, I suppose?” Sampson asked.

“Nay, she is but ten years old, and I have never made any conquests at all in Virginia,” Harry said, almost sternly.

“You are like a true gentleman, and don’t kiss and tell, sir.”

“I neither kiss nor tell. It isn’t the custom of our country, Sampson, to ruin girls, or frequent the society of low women. We Virginian gentlemen honour women: we don’t wish to bring them to shame.” The words came out proud and simple, as if he were stating how bread should be baked or meat salted. “The young lady whose name I mentioned hath lived in our family since her infancy, and I would shoot the man who did her a wrong—by Heaven, I would!”

“Your sentiments do you honour!” Sampson cried, carried away either by the wine or by the usefulness of such sentiments in a patron. “Let me shake hands with you! I will shake hands with you, Mr. Warrington. And let me tell you ’tis the grasp of honest friendship offered, and not merely the poor retainer paying court to the wealthy patron. No! with such liquor as this, all men are equal—faith, all men are rich whilst it lasts! Tom Sampson is as wealthy with his bottle as your honour with all the acres of your principality!”

“Let us have another bottle of riches,” Harry laughed. “Encore du cachet jaune, mon bon Monsieur Barbeau!” And away went Barbeau to the caves below, where the bottles lay in their dusky coolness like stored summers.

“Another bottle of riches! Capital! How beautifully you speak French, Mr. Harry!”

“I do speak it well,” Harry said. “At least, when I speak, Monsieur Barbeau understands me well enough.”

“You do everything well, I think. You succeed in whatever you try. That is why they have fancied here you have won the hearts of so many women, sir.”

“There you go again about the women!” Harry snapped, though the flush rose in him more from unease than anger. “I tell you I don’t like these stories. Confound me, Sampson, why is a gentleman’s character to be blackened so?”

“Well—at any rate—there is one, unless my eyes deceive me very much indeed,” Sampson said, lowering his voice with an air of discretion.

“Whom do you mean?” Harry asked, colouring to the temples.

“Nay, I name no names,” the chaplain replied. “It isn’t for a poor chaplain to meddle with his betters’ doings, or to know their thoughts.”

“Thoughts! What thoughts, Sampson?”

“I fancied I saw, on the part of a certain lovely and respected lady at Castlewood, a preference exhibited. I fancied, on the side of a certain distinguished young gentleman, a strong liking manifested itself: but I may have been wrong, and ask pardon.”

“Oh, Sampson, Sampson!” Harry burst out, as if something tight had been cut. “I tell you I am miserable. I tell you I have been longing for some one to confide in, or ask advice of. You do know, then, that there has been something going on—something between me and—help Mr. Sampson, Monsieur Barbeau—and—and some one else?”

“I have watched it this month past,” said the chaplain.

“Confound me, sir, do you mean you have been a spy on me?” Harry flared, wounded pride flinging up again like a flame.

“A spy! You made little disguise of the matter, Mr. Warrington, and her ladyship wasn’t a much better hand at deceiving. You were always together—in the shrubberies, in the walks, in the village, in the galleries of the house—you always found a pretext for being together, and plenty of eyes besides mine watched you.”

“Gracious powers! What did you see, Sampson?” Harry cried, half terrified now at what the world might have harvested from their moments.

“Nay, sir—’tis forbidden to kiss and tell,” the chaplain said again, with a knowing smile.

Harry turned yet redder, the wine and shame mixing in him like heat and spice. “Oh, Sampson,” he said, voice dropping low, “can I—can I confide in you?”

“Dearest sir—dear generous youth—you know I would shed my heart’s blood for you!” exclaimed Mr. Sampson, squeezing his patron’s hand, and rolling his bright eyes upward as if appealing to Heaven for witness.

The secret which Colonel Lambert had whispered—half in mirth, half in that hopeful domestic daring which passes for romance in a country-house—could not be held long within Mrs. Lambert’s ear. It flew from her like the scent from a torn bunch of lavender; and in a moment the whole of Oakhurst seemed to inhale it and grow brisk.

The hay was stacked, the corn still stood green and unready, and the farm horses, for once, were not dragged and lathered by the day’s labour. “Why,” asked the Colonel, with a simplicity that made a holiday sound like a duty, “should we not put them into the coach, and carry all of you to Tunbridge Wells? We will take friend Wolfe at Westerham on the way.”

It was proposed as one proposes a feast when the pantry is not bare—an act of management as much as indulgence. Mrs. Lambert embraced the plan with a tenderness that very likely included the planner. The children, who could never keep still when joy came in, clapped and leapt as if the very flags of the hall had turned to a dancing-floor.

Instantly the girls were in a rustle and flutter of gear: calamancoes and paduasoys, falbalas and furbelows, capes, cardinals, sacks, caps, ribbons, mantuas, clocked stockings, and those high-heeled shoes which make a country step seem more courtly than it is. Mrs. Lambert’s best gowns were brought out from their lavender darkness—those grave, sweet-smelling robes that came forth only on solemn days, as if cloth could keep a Sabbath. The Colonel fetched his laced hat and waistcoat and his silver-hilted hanger; Charley, radiant, got into a holiday suit that had once been his father’s wedding bravery, and which Mrs. Lambert cut and altered with a little sigh, as though a garment could feel time passing through it.

Even the horses were dressed for the occasion. Ball and Dumpling had their tails and manes tied with ribbon, as if they too must be made conscious of company. Old Chump, the white cart-horse, was pressed into service as unicorn-leader, to give a steady pull up the first five hilly miles from Oakhurst towards Westerham, where a coach’s pride is apt to become a coach’s complaint.

The coach itself was ancient—one of those heavy, high-swung family chariots which seem built not to go but to be seen going. It was believed at Oakhurst, with a faith as firm as any creed, that this very vehicle had once been in the procession which brought King George the First from Greenwich to London. It had belonged to Mr. Lambert’s father; and the household, from the oldest down to the newest-born, had always spoken of it as one of the finest coaches in the three kingdoms. A family may be poor in ready money and yet rich in remembered splendours; and this coach was a kind of moving monument to what the Lamberts had been.

Brian—coachman, and, truth to tell, ploughman too—mounted the box; and Charley, by a right which only the young can claim without paying for it, sat by his side. The precious clothes were packed in imperials on the roof. The Colonel’s pistols were stowed into the pockets of the carriage, and the blunderbuss hung behind the box within Brian’s reach; for he was an old soldier, and liked the feel of defence as much as another man likes the feel of a warm loaf.

No highwayman, however, took the trouble of trying them. Not even an innkeeper made war upon Colonel Lambert’s slender purse; for there is a kind of poverty so plainly honest, and so plainly burdened with children, that even knavery passes it by. Young Colonel Wolfe, who had engaged for them a modest lodging at Tunbridge in the house where he himself commonly stayed, rode with them on horseback, and saw them safely to their quarters.

It happened that these lodgings stood opposite Madame Bernstein’s; and the family had scarcely set down their bags on a Saturday evening when the windows of the great world opened itself before them as if it were a show. Chair after chair came shouldering through the Pantiles, discharging powdered beaux and patched and brocaded beauties at the Baroness’s door; for she was holding one of those card-parties that were her trade as much as her pleasure.

The sun was not yet down. Our ancestors began their dissipations early, and were at meat, drink, or cards any time after three o’clock until any time in the night or morning. From their window, Mrs. Lambert and the girls could see the arrivals as distinctly as if they themselves had been invited. Colonel Wolfe, attentive, named the characters as they passed; it was almost as delicious, Hetty and Theo thought, as being in the room—perhaps more delicious, because one could watch without being watched.

When the Duchess of Queensberry went by, Mr. Wolfe told them who she was, and Martin Lambert, never at a loss for the garnish to any dish of life, was ready with lines out of his beloved Prior about “Kitty, beautiful and young.” The Colonel, pleased with his own recollection and with the girls’ bright listening faces, cried, “Think that that old lady was once like you, girls!”

“Like us, papa?” said Hetty, tossing up her little head. “Well, certainly we never set up for being beauties!”

“Yes, like you, you little baggage,” he answered, laughing; “like you at this moment, who want to go to that drum yonder:—‘Inflamed with rage at sad restraint / Which wise mamma ordained, / And sorely vexed to play the saint / Whilst wit and beauty reigned.’”

“We were never invited, papa,” Hetty returned. “And I am sure if there’s no beauty more worth seeing than that, the wit can’t be much worth the hearing.”

“Oh, but he’s a rare poet, Mat Prior!” the Colonel persisted, pleased to teach and tease at once. “Though, mind you, girls, you’ll skip over all the poems I have marked with a cross. A rare poet! and to think you should see one of his heroines! ‘Fondness prevailed, mamma gave way’—she always will, Mrs. Lambert!—‘Fondness prevailed, mamma gave way, / Kitty at heart’s desire / Obtained the chariot for a day, / And set the world on fire!’”

“I am sure it must have been very inflammable,” said Mrs. Lambert, smiling.

“So it was, my dear, twenty years ago—much more inflammable than it is now,” the Colonel remarked, with the air of a philosopher who measures time by the burn of youth.

“Nonsense, Mr. Lambert.”

“Look, look!” cried Hetty, darting forward, and pointing to the little square and the covered gallery where the door to Madame Bernstein’s apartments stood, ringed by street-urchins, idlers, and country yokels craning to see.

“It’s Harry Warrington!” Theo exclaimed; and she waved her handkerchief with that frank, impulsive joy which cannot help proclaiming itself. But Warrington did not see her. He walked arm-in-arm with a portly clergyman in a crisp, rustling silk gown, and the two passed in beneath Madame Bernstein’s door.

“I heard him preach a most admirable sermon here last Sunday,” said Mr. Wolfe. “A little theatrical, but striking and eloquent.”

“You seem to be here most Sundays, James,” Mrs. Lambert observed gently.

“And Monday, and soon till Saturday,” added the Colonel.

“See, Harry has beautified himself already,” said the Colonel, peering, “hath his hair in buckle, and I have no doubt is going to the drum too.”

“I had rather sit quiet generally of a Saturday evening,” said sober Mr. Wolfe, “at any rate, away from card-playing and scandal; but I own, dear Mrs. Lambert, I am under orders. Shall I go across and send Mr. Warrington to you?”

“No,” said meek Mrs. Lambert. “Let him have his sport. We shall see him to-morrow. He won’t care to be disturbed amidst his fine folks by us country-people.”

“I am glad he is with a clergyman who preaches so well,” Theo said softly; and her eyes pleaded on Harry’s behalf, as if virtue were something one might gather for another, like herbs for a broth.

“The clergyman has a very kind, handsome face.”

“Here comes a greater clergyman,” cried Mr. Wolfe. “My Lord of Salisbury, with his blue ribbon, and a chaplain behind him.”

“And whom a mercy’s name have we here?” Mrs. Lambert broke in, as a sedan-chair came up all gilding and insolence, topped with five earl’s coronets, carried by bearers in richly laced clothes, and preceded by three footmen in the same splendour.

The Bishop, who had been about to enter, stopped, turned, and ran back with bows and curtseys so low that respect seemed like servility. He gave his hand to the lady who stepped from the chair.

“Who on earth is this?” asked Mrs. Lambert, amazed.

“Sprechen sie Deutsch? Ja, meinherr. Nichts verstand,” said the Colonel, wagging his head with mocking gravity.

“Pooh, Martin.”

“Well, if you can’t understand High Dutch, my love, how can I help it? Your education was neglected at school. Can you understand heraldry?—I know you can.”

“I make,” cried Charley, eager as if reciting a recipe learnt by heart, “three merions on a field or, with an earl’s coronet.”

“A countess’s coronet, my son. The Countess of Yarmouth, my son.”

“And pray who is she?” asked Mrs. Lambert.

“It hath ever been the custom of our sovereigns,” the Colonel began solemnly, “to advance persons of distinction to honour; and this eminent lady hath been so promoted by our gracious monarch, to the rank of Countess of this kingdom.”

“But why, papa?” the daughters asked together.

“Never mind, girls,” said mamma quickly, with that instinct which tries to keep the young from learning too early the vocabulary by which power disguises itself.

But the Colonel was incorrigible. “Y, my children, is one of the last and the most awkward letters of the whole alphabet. When I tell you stories, you are always saying Why. Why should my Lord Bishop be cringing to that lady? Look at him rubbing his fat hands and smiling into her face! It’s not a handsome face any longer. It is all painted red and white like Scaramouch’s in the pantomime. See, there comes another blue-riband, as I live. My Lord Bamborough. The descendant of the Hotspurs. The proudest man in England. He stops, he bows, he smiles; he is hat in hand, too. See, she taps him with her fan. Get away, you crowd of little blackguard boys, and don’t tread on the robe of the lady whom the King delights to honour.”

“But why does the King honour her?” the girls insisted.

“There goes that odious last letter but one!” cried the Colonel. “Did you ever hear of her Grace the Duchess of Kendal? No. Of the Duchess of Portsmouth? Non plus. Of the Duchess of La Vallière? Of Fair Rosamond, then?”

“Hush, papa!” Mrs. Lambert pleaded, putting a finger to his lips. “There is no need to bring blushes on the cheeks of my dear ones, Martin Lambert!”

“’Tis not I; it is their sacred Majesties who are the cause of the shame,” the Colonel cried, his old republican blood rising. “Think of the bishops of the Church and the proudest nobility of the world cringing and bowing before that painted High Dutch Jezebel. Oh, it’s a shame! a shame!”

“Confusion!” broke out Colonel Wolfe; and snatching at his hat, he hurried from the room. He had seen the young lady he admired and her guardian walking across the Pantiles on foot toward the Baroness’s party; they came up while the Countess was still in talk with the two blue-ribboned lords, spiritual and temporal, who made the lowest reverences and waited to escort her in upon the Bishop’s arm.

Theo turned away from the window, her face suddenly grave, as if a cold draft had gone through her. Hetty stayed, rigid with indignation, a little red spot flaming on each cheek.

“A penny for little Hetty’s thoughts,” said mamma, coming to draw her from the casement.

“I am thinking what I should do if I saw papa bowing to that woman,” said Hetty, between anger and fear, as if she tasted something bitter and could not spit it out.

Tea was brought in; the kettle hissed like a small domestic serpent, and the family gathered to their evening meal. The table—plain enough, but honest—was set with that careful housewifery which makes even a lodging look for an hour like home. If across the way there were champagne and chickens, here there was the clean scent of brewed leaves, warm bread, and the mild comfort of being together. Yet Hetty, from her chair, begged that the window should not be closed, so she might keep her command of the show.

Charley had been down amongst the crowd, no doubt to read armorial bearings on sedans with as much relish as if they were chapters in a chronicle; and by his mother’s order and his own appetite, he invested sixpence in a cheese-cake. He came back with it wrapped in paper, the sweet warm smell rising as the crust broke under his fingers.

“Look, mother,” he said, mouth already hopeful, “do you see that big man in brown beating all the pillars with a stick? That is the learned Mr. Johnson. He comes to the Friars sometimes to see our master. He was sitting with some friends just now at the tea-table before Mrs. Brown’s tart-shop. They have tea there, twopence a cup; I heard Mr. Johnson say he had had seventeen cups—that makes two-and-tenpence—what a sight of money for tea!”

“What would you have, Charley?” asked Theo.

“I think I would have cheese-cakes,” said Charley with a sigh of devotion, as his teeth closed on a large slice; and, speaking as if the cake did not fill all his world, he went on: “and the gentleman whom Mr. Johnson was with was Mr. Richardson who wrote—”

“Clarissa!” cried all the women together, and ran to the window as if called by a bell.

By now the sun was down, and the stars pricked through; opposite, the footman began lighting candles in the Baroness’s rooms, so that the great chamber became a bright aquarium, with figures moving and glittering behind glass. Down by Mrs. Brown’s tart- and tea-shop there was a small illumination too, and by it the Lamberts could see one lady fetching Mr. Richardson’s hat and stick, and another tying a shawl about his neck before he walked away.

“Oh dear me! he does not look like Grandison!” cried Theo, dismayed, as if the author’s body had betrayed his book.

“I rather think I wish we had not seen him, my dear,” said mamma, who loved novels with a tender, hungry faith, as if printed words could keep one warm.

“Never mind that little fat man,” Hetty cried sharply, “but look yonder, mamma.”

And they looked, and saw Mr. Warrington receiving the honour of a presentation to the Countess of Yarmouth, who was still followed by her obsequious peer and prelate. The Countess sat down to a card-table; the Bishop, the Earl, and a fourth person took places as her partners. Presently Mr. Warrington stepped into the embrasure of a window with a lady whom they recognised—Lady Maria Esmond, whom they had seen for a few minutes at Oakhurst.

“How much finer he is!” remarked mamma. “How he is improved in his looks! What has he done to himself?”

“Look at his grand lace frills and ruffles!” cried the matron, half amused, half a little wounded. “My dear, he has not got on our shirts any more.”

“What are you talking about, girls?” asked papa from his sofa, where a doze had perhaps stolen upon him in the honest way of household fathers.

They told him Harry Warrington was visible, talking with his cousin Lady Maria.

“Come away!” cried the Colonel, rousing. “You have no right to be spying the young fellow. Down with the curtains, I say!”

And down the curtains went, shutting out that brilliant, noisy world as if one had closed a lid upon a glittering box.

If you will allow a remark, only by way of contrast between the two opposite houses: while Madame Bernstein and her guests—bishop, dignitaries, noblemen and such—were gambling or talking scandal, or devouring champagne and chickens (which I hold to be a venial sin), and doing honour to the King’s favourite, our country friends knelt around their own table. Even Brian the coachman came in as silently as his creaking shoes could manage; and Mr. Lambert, standing, read in a low voice the prayer that Heaven would lighten their darkness and defend them from the perils of the night, and grant the request of those few gathered together. The words had an old cadence, like a remembered dialect—something that does not glitter, but sustains. Outside, the Pantiles murmured with chairs, laughter, and the continual metallic clip of a town that sells amusement; within, the small, human hush of a family made its own music.

On Sunday morning the young folks were up betimes, in their smart dresses meant to fascinate Tunbridge. With brother Charley as escort, they paced the little town and the quaint Pantiles and the pretty common long before the company was at breakfast or the bells had rung to church. The morning had that clean sweetness which seems to taste of milk before it is even poured, and of grass before it is cut—a countryside flavour that Tunbridge could not quite buy away.

It was Hester who discovered where Harry Warrington lodged, by spying Mr. Gumbo at a window, in undress, with his lovely hair set in curl-papers. He drew aside a pair of red curtains and opened the sash, thrusting out his head to inhale the breeze as if it were a delicacy. He did not see the Oakhurst party, though they saw him well enough. He leaned gracefully; he waved a great feather-brush, and condescended to dust the furniture within; he chatted with a cherry-cheeked milkmaid lingering under the casement, and kissed his lily hand to her. That hand glittered with rings; his person blazed with jewellery—gifts, no doubt, from those who found novelty more moving than virtue.

Once or twice before breakfast the girls passed that window again. It stood open, but the room behind it was blank. No Harry appeared. Neither sister spoke of what both were thinking. Hetty, already in a mood, grew provoked with Charley, who clamoured for breakfast and seemed to her to care for nothing but eating.

“You are always thinking of it!” she cried.

He, artless as a child with a full mouth, owned he should like another cheese-cake.

Good-natured Theo laughed. “I have a sixpence,” she said. “If the cake-shop is open on a Sunday morning, Charley shall have one.”

The cake-shop was open. Theo drew out her little purse—netted by her dearest friend at school—and there lay her pocket-piece, her grandmother’s guinea, a scant store of shillings, and some copper at one end. She treated Charley to the thing he loved; and the tart, warm smell of it, the slight crack of the crust, the soft sweet within—these small, edible certainties made the morning feel safe, even when hearts were not.

A great deal of fine company was at church. There was the funny old Duchess; old Madame Bernstein with Lady Maria beside her; Mr. Wolfe, of course, close by Miss Lowther, singing with her out of the same psalm-book; and Mr. Richardson with a bevy of ladies. One of them, papa told them afterwards, was Miss Fielding, Harry Fielding’s sister.

“Oh, girls, what good company he was!” the Colonel cried after church, his spirits rising as if the sermon had been a glass of wine. “And his books are worth a dozen of your milksop Pamelas and Clarissas, Mrs. Lambert; but what woman ever loved true humour? And there was Mr. Johnson sitting amongst the charity children. Did you see how he turned round to the altar at the Belief, and upset two or three of the scared little urchins in leather breeches? And what a famous sermon Harry’s parson gave, didn’t he? A sermon about scandal. How he touched up some of the old harridans seated round! Why wasn’t Mr. Warrington at church? It was a shame he wasn’t at church.”

“I really did not remark whether he was there or not,” said Miss Hetty, tossing her head.

But Theo, who could not help being true even when truth pricked, said quietly, “Yes, I thought of him, and was sorry he was not there; and so did you think of him, Hetty.”

“I did no such thing, miss,” Hetty persisted.

“Then why did you whisper to me it was Harry’s clergyman who preached?”

“To think of Mr. Warrington’s clergyman is not to think of Mr. Warrington,” Hetty declared, fencing with words as if they were weapons. “It was a most excellent sermon, certainly, and the children sang most dreadfully out of tune.”

And indeed the little choir’s piping and the charity children’s dragged notes made a kind of rough music—honest, but painful—like a countryside dialect mangled by those who only half know it. Theo winced at it, not from pride, but from pity; for there is something in wrong sound that makes the heart uneasy, as if peace itself depends upon harmony.

“There is Lady Maria at the window opposite, smelling at the roses,” Hetty went on, eager to change the subject. “And that is Mr. Wolfe’s step—I know his great military tramp. Right left—right left! How do you do, Colonel Wolfe?”

Mr. Wolfe entered with a face overcast.

“Why do you look so glum, James?” asked Colonel Lambert. “Has the charmer been scolding thee, or is thy conscience pricked by the sermon. Mr. Sampson, isn’t the parson’s name? A famous preacher, on my word!”

“A pretty preacher, and a pretty practitioner!” said Mr. Wolfe with a shrug.

“Why, I thought the discourse did not last ten minutes,” said the Colonel, “and madam did not sleep one single wink during the sermon, didst thou, Molly?”

“Did you see when the fellow came into church?” Mr. Wolfe demanded, his indignation gathering voice. “He came in at the open door of the common, just in time, and as the psalm was over.”

“Well, he had been reading the service probably to some sick person,” Mrs. Lambert said, always charitable first, as if charity were her native tongue. “There are many here.”

“Reading the service! Oh, my good Mrs. Lambert!” Mr. Wolfe cried. “Do you know where I found him? I went to look for your young scapegrace of a Virginian.”

“His own name is a very pretty name, I’m sure,” burst out Hetty, hotly. “It isn’t Scapegrace! It is Henry Esmond Warrington, Esquire.”

“Miss Hester,” said Mr. Wolfe, stung into plainness, “I found the parson in his cassock, and Henry Esmond Warrington, Esquire, in his bedgown, at a quarter before eleven o’clock in the morning, when all the Sunday bells were ringing, and they were playing over a game of piquet they had had the night before!”

“Well, numbers of good people play at cards of a Sunday. The King plays at cards of a Sunday,” cried Hetty, reckless with her own anger.

“Hush, my dear!”

“I know he does,” Hetty insisted, “with that painted person we saw yesterday—that Countess what-d’you-call-her?”

“I think, my dear Miss Hester,” said Mr. Wolfe, “a clergyman had best take to God’s books instead of the Devil’s books on that day—and so I took the liberty of telling your parson.”

Hetty looked as if she thought it a liberty indeed.

“And I told our young friend,” Mr. Wolfe went on, “that I thought he had better have been on his way to church than there in his bedgown.”

“You wouldn’t have Harry go to church in a dressing-gown and nightcap, Colonel Wolfe?” Hetty cried, fiercely. “That would be a pretty sight, indeed!”

“I would have my little girl’s tongue not wag quite so fast,” remarked papa, laying a hand on her flushed cheek.

“Not speak when a friend is attacked, and nobody says a word in his favour? No; nobody!” Hetty cried.

Her lips clamped shut; her whole small frame shook. She flung a last look of defiance at Mr. Wolfe and hurried out, just in time to reach the stair before her self-command broke into sobbing.

Mr. Wolfe stood discomfited. “I am sure, Aunt Lambert, I did not intend to hurt Hester’s feelings.”

“No, James,” she said kindly—he had called her Aunt Lambert since early days—and she gave him her hand.

Mr. Lambert, to cover what could not be mended, began whistling “Over the hills and far away,” tapping a little drum accompaniment on the window with his fingers.

“I say, you mustn’t whistle on Sunday, papa!” cried Charley, literal as a rubric; and then, with a logic as steady as hunger, suggested it was three hours from breakfast and he should like to finish Theo’s cheese-cake.

“Oh, you greedy child!” cried Theo; yet even her scold had laughter in it.

But at a small sound outside—half sob, half strangled breath—Theo slipped away, closing the door behind her. We will not pursue her. That noise was the overflow of Hetty’s heart; and though we cannot see it, one may be sure the child flung herself on her sister’s neck and wept into Theo’s kind bosom, as into the only safe place in Tunbridge.

Hetty did not walk out in the afternoon when the family took the air upon the common. She pleaded a headache and lay upon her bed, while her mother watched her with that soft patience which is a sort of silent nursing. Charley found a comrade from Grey Friars; Mr. Wolfe, of course, paired off with Miss Lowther; and Theo, taking her sober walk with her father in the Sabbath sunshine, met Madame Bernstein herself basking on a bench under a tree, with her niece and nephew in attendance.

Harry ran up to greet his dear friends. He was radiant at seeing them—his pleasure so honest that for a moment all the talk of cards and bedgowns fell away like a bad dream. Madame Bernstein and Lady Maria were most gracious to the Colonel and his wife, thanking them by looks and words for their kindness to Harry. In that clear light, among the faint rustle of leaves and the distant murmur of Tunbridge voices—wheels far off, a hawker calling, the small, natural sound of a place breathing—Theo thought how noble and handsome he looked. She called him by his Christian name as if he were truly her brother.

“Why did we not see you sooner to-day, Harry?” she asked.

“I never thought you were here, Theo,” he said.

“But you might have seen us if you wished.”

“Where?” asked Harry.

“There, sir,” she said, pointing to the church.

She lifted her hand as if in reproof; yet a sweet kindness shone in her face, as though she scolded only because she cared. And if a young man is to be saved from the louder world—its glittering rooms, its false languages of honour and advancement—perhaps it is not by sermons only, but by the remembered look of a pure heart that calls him by his true name.

Colonel Lambert’s first heat, when his younger daughter’s sudden outbreak betrayed the little secret she had been keeping even from herself, was not tenderness, but a father’s sharp, possessive anger—anger that always masks fright.

“A plague upon all scapegraces, English or Indian!” he cried to his wife, as they sat in their lodgings with the windows shut against the thin Bath air and the distant clatter of wheels on the stones. “I would he had broken his nose on any doorpost but ours.”

Mrs. Lambert, who had been folding a little parcel of fine linen as neatly as if it were a ritual, laid it down with the softest patience. “Perhaps we are to cure him of being a scapegrace, my dear. Perhaps the fall at our door has something providential in it. You laughed at me when I said so before; but if Heaven did not send the young gentleman to us—who did? And it may be for the blessing and happiness of us all that he came, too.”

“It’s hard, Molly!” the Colonel groaned. “We cherish ’em and fondle and rear ’em; we tend ’em through sickness and health; we toil and scheme; we hoard money away in the stocking and patch our own old coats. If they’ve a headache we can’t sleep for thinking of it. If they have a wish or fancy we work day and night to compass it—and ’tis darling daddy and dearest pappy, and whose father is like ours? And so forth. On Tuesday morning I am king of my house and family. On Tuesday evening Prince Whippersnapper makes his appearance, and my reign is over. A whole life forgotten and forsworn for a pair of blue eyes, a pair of lean shanks, and a head of yellow hair.”

“’Tis written we women should leave all to follow our husband,” Mrs. Lambert said, and her voice had that quiet firmness which can hush even a soldier’s bluster. She put her hand on his sleeve as if smoothing a crease. “I think our courtship was not very long, dear Martin.”
