“’Tis human nature, and what can you expect of the jade?” he sighed, though the word “jade” came out as a caress in his mouth. “And I think I did my duty to my husband, though I own I left my papa for him,” she added, softly, with a smile that carried the scent of old lavender and the memory of white ribbons on a postillion’s hat.

“Excellent wench! Perdition catch my soul! but I do love thee, Molly!” he cried; and then, with the same breath, relapsed into the father again. “But mind you—your father never did me; and if ever I am to have sons-in-law—”

“Ever, indeed! Of course my girls are to have husbands, Mr. Lambert!” Mamma’s eyes flashed, not with anger, but with that pleased alarm women have when they foresee both sorrow and ceremony, separation and satin.

“Well—when they come, I’ll hate them, madam, as your father did me; and quite right too, for taking his treasure away from him.”

“Don’t be irreligious and unnatural, Martin Lambert! I say you are unnatural, sir!”

“Nay, my dear,” he answered, with a grimace as if biting a hard crust, “I have an old tooth in my left jaw here; and ’tis natural the tooth should come out. But when the tooth-drawer pulls it, ’tis natural I should feel pain. Do you suppose, madam, that I don’t love Hetty better than any tooth in my head?”

No woman, however, ever truly feared the notion of her daughter being married—fear belonged to fathers; mothers and grandmothers were married over again in their children’s marriages. The old bridal favours, stowed away like spices in the heart’s dark cupboard, were taken out and smelt again; the ribbons bloomed; the muslins rustled; and, in imagination, they fluttered into the post-chaise and drove away.

“It will be a sad thing, parting with her,” Mrs. Lambert said at last, with a sigh that was half pleasure and half pain.

“You have settled that point already, Molly,” the Colonel laughed sourly. “Had I not best go out and order raisins and corinths for the wedding-cake?”

“And then I shall have to leave the house in their charge when I go to her, you know, in Virginia. How many miles is it to Virginia, Martin? I should think it must be thousands of miles.”

“A hundred and seventy-three thousand three hundred and ninety-one and three-quarters, my dear, by the near way,” he answered gravely, as if reading out a provision list. “That through Prester John’s country. By the other route, through Persia—”

“Oh, give me the one where there is the least of the sea, and your horrid ships, which I can’t bear!” she cried.

“I hope Rachel Esmond and I shall be better friends,” she went on, already setting her mind to the domestic politics of a distant household. “She had a very high spirit when we were girls at school.”

“Had we not best go about the baby-linen, Mrs. Martin Lambert?” her husband put in, with a stare of wonder—as though he had been told to salt a ham for a child not yet born.

Mrs. Lambert, no doubt, saw nothing astonishing in it. She had likely been in Mrs. Bobbinit’s toy-shop already and noted some pretty lace caps and bibs; and that same Sunday afternoon, while Hetty lay upon her pillow—cheeks fever-hot, eyelids shut hard as if to keep the world out, her little mouth set in a piteous line—her mother looked at her with the most perfect ease of mind, almost with secret content, as if the girl’s woe were merely a first rising of bread that would, in time, make a good loaf.

But to Hetty herself it was no gentle fermentation: it was scorch and sting. She had not meant to publish her secret; perhaps she had not even known it until the sudden rush of feeling told her what lay in her. Now, having been surprised into confession, she chose to be ashamed as if she had been caught in a theft. Indignant at her own weakness, she turned her rage inward till it spilled out on everyone near her.

“What business has any young woman,” she cried, “to indulge in any such nonsense? Mamma, I ought to be whipped and sent to bed. I know perfectly well Mr. Warrington does not care a fig about me. I dare say he likes French actresses and the commonest little milliner-girl in the toy-shop better than me. And so he ought—and so they are better than me. Why, what a fool I am to burst out crying like a ninny about nothing, and because Mr. Wolfe said Harry played cards of a Sunday! I know he is not clever, like papa. I believe he is stupid—I am certain he is stupid: but he is not so stupid as I am. Why, of course I can’t marry him. How am I to go to America, and leave you and Theo? Of course he likes somebody else—at America, or at Tunbridge, or at Jericho, or somewhere. He is a prince in his own country and can’t think of marrying a poor half-pay officer’s daughter, with twopence to her fortune. Used not you to tell me how, when I was a baby, I cried and wanted the moon? I am a baby now, a most absurd, silly, little baby—don’t talk to me, Mrs. Lambert, I am. Only there is this to be said: he don’t know anything about it, and I would rather cut my tongue out than tell him.”

Dire were the threats she made against Theo, should her sister betray her. As for Charley—his whole soul, being set upon cheesecakes and the exact moment they might be procured, was unshaken by love’s earthquake; and the parents and kind sister, of course, promised to keep silence.

“I begin to think it had been best for us to stay at home,” Mrs. Lambert sighed to her husband later, when Hetty had worn herself into a sullen stillness and the household sounds—the shifting of a chair, the crackle of a coal, the thin music from some distant room in the lodging-house—came distinct in the hush.

“Nay, my dear,” Lambert replied. “Human nature will be human nature; surely Hetty’s mother told me herself she had the beginning of a liking for a certain young curate before she fell over head and ears in love with a certain young officer of Kingsley’s. And as for me, my heart was wounded in a dozen places ere Miss Molly Benson took entire possession of it. Our sons and daughters must follow in the way of their parents before them, I suppose. Why, but yesterday, you were scolding me for grumbling at Miss Het’s precocious fancies. To do the child justice, she disguises her feelings entirely, and I defy Mr. Warrington to know from her behaviour how she is disposed towards him.”

“A daughter of mine and yours, Martin,” the mother cried, drawing herself up with matronly dignity, “is not going to fling herself at a gentleman’s head!”

“Neither herself nor the teacup, my dear,” he answered.

In truth, little Miss Hetty treated Mr. Warrington like a vixen. He never came but she boxed his ears in one fashion or another—not with her hand, perhaps, but with her tongue, which could strike as quick as a spoon against a pan. Knowing what went on in the young hypocrite’s mind, her father was not angry at her rudeness: he watched it as one watches a saucepan threaten to boil over, half amused and half apprehensive.

“She hath no need to be rude at all, Martin; and our girl is good enough for any gentleman in England or America. Why, if their ages suit, shouldn’t they marry after all, sir?”

“Why, if he wants her, shouldn’t he ask her, my dear? I am sorry we came. I am for putting the horses into the carriage, and turning their heads towards home again.”

But mamma, with that tender obstinacy which is the match-making instinct in its purest form, said, “Depend upon it, my dear, these matters are wisely ordained for us. It was not for nothing Harry Warrington was brought to our gate in that way; and that he and our children are thus brought together again. If that marriage has been decreed in Heaven, a marriage it will be.”

“At what age, Molly, I wonder, do women begin and leave off match-making? If our little chit falls in love and falls out again, she will not be the first of her sex, Mrs. Lambert. I wish we were on our way home again, and, if I had my will, would trot off this very night.”

“He has promised to drink his tea here to-night. You would not take away our child’s pleasure, Martin?” she asked, softly—softly as warm milk poured into a cup.

In his fashion the father was not less good-natured. “You know, my dear,” he said, “that if either of ’em had a fancy to our ears, we would cut them off and serve them in a fricassee.”

Mrs. Lambert laughed—she, whose own ears were small and delicate, half hidden by hair combed smooth and drawn back, where a thread or two of silver glinted in the candlelight like fine sugar on a tart. When Lambert was most tender-hearted, his humour grew most grotesque. He took her ear between finger and thumb with a mock severity that could not hurt; and she, no doubt, was remembering her own first timid days—how courtship, like good preserving, sweetens what time would otherwise spoil.

Hallowed remembrances: if youthful love is pleasant, how much more moving is affection that has lasted through years—through illness, losses, faded beauty perhaps, and the small daily vexations that wear on a household like grit in flour.

In regard to her promise of disguise, Miss Hester was better—or worse—than her word. When Harry came that evening, it was not only to take tea with his friends, but to invite them, for the next day, to an entertainment at the Rooms—to be given in their special honour.

“A dance, and given for us!” cried Theo, clapping her hands. “Oh, Harry, how delightful! I wish we could begin this very minute!”

“Why, for a savage Virginian, I declare, Harry Warrington, thou art the most civilised young man possible!” said the Colonel. “My dear, shall we dance a minuet together?”

“We have done such a thing before, Martin Lambert!” Mrs. Lambert answered, and the words were a smile.

The Colonel hummed a minuet air; snatched a plate from the tea-table and, holding it like a hat, made a bow and flourish, whilst madam performed her best curtsey. The tea had that Bath smell—hot water, bruised leaves, milk warming, a faint sweetness from the sugar, and, under all, the coal’s dry breath; the spoons rang in their cups with bright domestic music that seemed, for a moment, to promise that nothing cruel could happen in such a room.

Only Hetty persisted in looking glum and displeased, as if she had been made to swallow something bitter.

“Why, child, have you not a word of thanks to throw to Mr. Warrington?” Theo asked, her eyes dancing.

“I never did care for dancing much,” said Hetty.

“What is the use of standing up opposite a stupid man, and dancing down a room with him?”

“Merci du compliment!” said Mr. Warrington; and there was a change on his face, as quick as a shadow passing over sunlit bread.

“I don’t say that you are stupid—that is—that is, I—I only meant country dances,” Hetty stammered, biting her lip as she caught Theo’s eye. She remembered her own cruel sentence—Harry is stupid—and Theo’s droll glance reminded her without saying a word.

But instead of softening, Hetty chose to be angry as if she had been wounded by an insult. “I hate dancing—there—I own it,” she said, tossing her head.

“Nay, you used to like it well enough, child!” her mother interposed.

“That was when she was a child: don’t you see she is grown up to be an old woman?” her father said.

“Or perhaps Miss Hester has got the gout?”

“Fiddle!” snapped Hetty, drubbing with her little foot.

“What’s a dance without a fiddle?” returned imperturbable papa.

Darkness had come over Harry Warrington’s face. He sat stiffly, hearing not only her words, but the way they struck the room—as if she had clapped a lid down on all the small cheerful sounds. In his mind there rose the manners of his own country, where a guest’s kindness is answered with kindness, and where, whatever a young person thinks, she does not so toss it at her elders.

“I come to try my best,” he thought, “and give them pleasure and a dance, and the little thing tells me she hates dancing. We don’t practise kindness, or acknowledge hospitality so in our country. No—nor speak to our parents so, neither.”

Nor did Miss Hester stop there. She must needs make sport of the company at the Wells—of their fineries and follies—and especially of Harry’s own pursuits and companions, till the honest lad felt the sting as plainly as if she had sprinkled pepper into his tea.

Later, when he found Mrs. Lambert alone, he asked her, with a grave simplicity that went straight to her heart, how or in what he had again offended, that Hester was so angry with him.

The kind matron, after her daughter’s behaviour, felt more than ever well disposed towards the boy. The secret burned at her tongue; she would have liked to tell it and so set all right. But she could not betray her child. Theo, too, remonstrated with her sister in private; but Hester would not listen. She carried her anger with her like a hot coal wrapped in paper: it did not cool; it only threatened to burn through.

In their bedroom, when they were alone and the house had quieted—when the murmur of other lodgers sank into a few coughs and footsteps, when even the street’s sound thinned and only the far-off Bath noises remained, like water in pipes—Hetty broke out again.

“Suppose he hates me?” she said. “I expect he will. I hate myself, I do, and scorn myself for being such an idiot. How ought he to do otherwise than hate me? Didn’t I abuse him, call him goose, all sorts of names? And know he is not clever all the time. I know I have better wits than he has. It is only because he is tall, and has blue eyes, and a pretty nose that I like him. What an absurd fool a girl must be to like a man merely because he has a blue nose and hooked eyes! So I am a fool, and I won’t have you say a word to the contrary, Theo!”

Theo thought her little sister, far from being a fool, a wonder; and if any girl were worthy of any prince in Christendom, Hetty was. Yet Theo spoke gently, as one takes a sharp knife from a child and replaces it with a spoon.

“You are silly sometimes, Hetty—that is when you speak unkindly to people who mean you well, as you did to Mr. Warrington at tea to-night. When he proposed to us his party at the Assembly Rooms, and nothing could be more gallant of him, why did you say you didn’t care for music, or dancing, or tea? You know you love them all!”

“I said it merely to vex myself, Theo, and annoy myself, and whip myself, as I deserve, child,” Hetty cried. “And besides, how can you expect such an idiot as I am to say anything but idiotic things? Do you know, it quite pleased me to see him angry. I thought, ah! now I have hurt his feelings! Now he will say, Hetty Lambert is an odious little set-up, sour-tempered vixen. And that will teach him, and you, and mamma, and papa, at any rate, that I am not going to set my cap at Mr. Harry. No; our papa is ten times as good as he is. I will stay by our papa, and if he asked me to go to Virginia with him to-morrow, I wouldn’t, Theo. My sister is worth all the Virginians that ever were made since the world began.”

Here, no doubt, the sisters kissed and clung together—Theo soothing, Hetty fierce in her affection as in her despair—until their mother’s knock came to the door. Mrs. Lambert, who had overheard more through the wainscot than daughters ever suspect, called, “Children, ’tis time to go to sleep.”

Theo’s eyes closed quickly; she had that gift of slipping into rest as a bird tucks its head under its wing. But poor little Hetty—her mind could not be lulled. She lay with her eyes wide in the dark, hearing the hours toll one after another, each sound falling into her like a weight. In the pauses between the strokes she heard everything: a late coach rumbling far off; the shifting of some neighbour; the faint creak of boards; the very small living noises of the house, as if the building itself breathed.

“It is a judgment upon me,” she whispered to herself. “For having thought and spoke scornfully of him.”

Then, as if love must always braid itself with sacrifice, she argued against her own heart.

“Only—why should there be a judgment upon me? I was only in fun. I knew I liked him very much all the time: but I thought Theo liked him too, and I would give up anything for my darling Theo. If she had—no tortures should ever have drawn a word from me. I would have got a rope-ladder to help her to run away with Harry, that I would, or fetched the clergyman to marry them. And then I would have retired alone, and alone, and alone, and taken care of papa and mamma, and of the poor in the village, and have read sermons, though I hate ’em, and would have died without telling a word—not a word—and I shall die soon, I know I shall.”

When dawn rose at last, thin and colourless at the window, Hetty had fallen asleep—nestling close to her sister, the stain of a tear or two dried upon her flushed, downy cheek, like salt left after boiling.

Most of us, at some time, play with edged tools and cut ourselves accordingly. The first cut stings: we drop the knife and cry out like wounded little babies, as we are. A very few, unlucky at the game, strike too deep and perish outright. But—heaven help us—many are pricked and scarred and tattooed all over with wounds, and yet recover, and live on lively enough.

Let us trust there is no present need of sexton for Miss Hetty. But the moment she wakes, there—tearing at her little heart again—will be that Care which had granted her a few hours’ reprieve, melted, no doubt, by youth and tears, but not dismissed.

Mr. Warrington, being young, flush of pocket, and resolved to play the man of the world because the town expected it, could not do less than set open his hand to his country neighbours, and give them an entertainment at the Assembly Rooms. It was the custom; and custom, like a well-seasoned dish, has a flavour that even those who pretend to scorn it cannot but taste. So he bade almost all the company remaining at the Wells; and the Rooms that night were portioned, as a housewife portions her work, into their several uses.

In one chamber the card-tables were spread—green cloths smoothed, corners weighted, counters laid ready, and candles trimmed so that the wax might not gutter upon the stakes. In another, the supper was ordered, with champagne in such profusion as a gentleman newly enriched believes to be the very proof of liberality; with bowls of negus, too—hot wine sweetened and spiced, sending up a steam of citrus and nutmeg that mingled with the warmed scent of beeswax and the faint, damp odour the company carried in from the walks. In the great room the dance was set; and at the farther end, in a little balcony, the music perched—harp, fiddle, flageolet—like three small birds compelled to sing all night whether they would or no.

There is a particular sound in such a place, and it governs the spirits as surely as weather governs rheumatism: the scrape of shoes on boards, the click of fans, the small coughs checked behind lace, the low, continuous rustle of silk that seems almost like wind passing through dry corn. Over all comes the thin, persevering thread of the instruments—tuneful, yet oddly plaintive; and one may marvel how men and women could ever have called such airs merry. The flageolet, especially, had a note like a child whistling in a cold passage. Yet they courted to it; they laughed under it; they made whole futures out of those melancholy measures, as farmers sow in a grey spring and trust the sun will come.

The beginning was as homely and ceremonious as our forefathers’ pleasure always was. First minuets were called, and two or three couple performed them with the gravity of people who believe a step to be a moral act. The spinsters of the highest rank went out for this dignified exercise; and as Lady Maria Esmond, being an earl’s daughter, was the highest in place of all present (saving only Lady Augusta Crutchley, who by reason of lameness could not stand up), Mr. Warrington led her forth first. He acquitted himself very prettily, and with more ease than Mr. Wolfe, who had Miss Lowther; and this was remarked with approval by the whole room, which loves to judge such matters, as it judges custards and sauces, with a keen palate and very little charity.

When Lady Maria’s minuet was done, Mr. Warrington begged Miss Theo Lambert to do him the honour of the next. The girl blushed—one could see the colour spread as if a warm hand had passed beneath her skin—and she went through her steps with a shy exactness that delighted her parents. It delighted them the more because it enraged Miss Humpleby of Liphook, who had expected, at least, to stand up after my Lady Maria, and now sat biting her lip with that peculiar sourness which is envy’s own taste.

After the minuets came the country dances; and the melancholy little band fell to thrumming through tune after tune. Between the sets, the room filled with the noises of breath and talk and laughter; then, at the first scraping summons of the fiddle, the boards again took the cadence of feet. There was even something like a domestic comfort in it, as if, for all the grandeur of titles and the sharpness of tongues, the company were no more than a great household keeping holiday.

Mr. Warrington had, among his guests, the honour of a duchess: the Duchess of Queensberry, heroine of those who write and whisper about great ladies as eagerly as cooks discuss great kitchens. Her Grace came with her usual insolence of manner—turning her back, laughing loudly, glancing over her shoulder, and pointing her fan as if it were a skewer—because a countess was present whom she chose to hate. Yet, for all the duchess’s fireworks, almost all the company pushed and bowed and cringed and smiled and backed, not before the duchess, but before that other lady; as if a whole room could be drawn by one magnet, and the rest of the iron left cold.

For this was the Countess of Yarmouth—Walmoden—the favourite whom his Majesty George the Second delighted to honour. In the morning, upon the walks, she had been mighty gracious to young Harry; had promised him a game at cards that night; and purblind old Colonel Blinkinsop, believing the invitation meant for him, had bowed till he was like to fall over. “Pooh! pooh!” the countess had cried, “I don’t mean you. I mean the young Firshinian!” and the whole place had congratulated Mr. Warrington upon his fortune, as if it were a dish newly set before him, hot and savoury, which others must smell but not taste.

So at night, out of loyalty doubtless—and out of that baser appetite which always sniffs round power as readily as round supper—everybody swarmed to my Lady Yarmouth. My Lord Bamborough was eager to make her party at quadrille. My Lady Blanche Pendragon, model of virtue; Sir Lancelot Quintain, pattern of knighthood; Mr. Dean of Ealing, exemplary divine; and a crowd besides—nobles, officers, matrons, and prim spinsters—waited for her smile, watched for a beck, sprang up at the least sign to join her table.

Lady Maria attended the countess with meek respect. Madame de Bernstein treated the Hanoverian lady with a gravity as deep as her curtsey. Harry’s bow had been no lower than hospitality required; but it was bow enough to kindle Miss Hester Lambert’s indignation. She scarce spoke a word to her partner while they danced; and when he led her towards the supper-room, she was no more communicative than a girl who has set herself to punish.

To reach the refreshments they must pass close by Madame Walmoden’s table. The countess, in good humour, called out to her host as he went by, and asked if his “breddy liddle bardner liked tanzing?”

“I thank your ladyship, I don’t like tanzing, and I don’t like cards,” says Miss Hester, tossing her head; and, dropping a curtsey as stiff and tasteless as a lump of cheese, she strutted away.

Mr. Warrington felt as if a hot spoon had been thrust into him. Sarcasm from young to old pained him; flippancy towards himself hurt him. He was simple in his courtesy, and because it was simple he believed it should be returned. Hetty knew perfectly well what offence she gave; she could see displeasure redden on his honest face with a sidelong glance; and yet she kept on, wearing the most ingenuous smile, as some children keep on nibbling at forbidden sweets while watching the rod.

When they reached the sideboard—the table crowded with cut-glass, silver, little piles of ratafias, and dishes from which rose the warm, eggy sweetness of custards—she said, as artlessly as if she had been praising the music, “What a horrid, vulgar old woman that is; don’t you think so?”

“What woman?” asked Harry.

“That German woman—my Lady Yarmouth—to whom all the men are bowing and cringing.”

“Her ladyship has been very kind to me,” says Harry, grimly. “Won’t you have some of this custard?”

“And you have been bowing to her, too! You look as if your negus was not nice,” continues Miss Hetty, with that cruel innocence.

“It is not very good negus,” says Harry, swallowing more than the bad liquor.

“And the custard is bad too! I declare ’tis made with bad eggs!” cries Miss Lambert, tasting, and flinging her displeasure as lightly as she flung her words.

“I wish, Hester, that the entertainment and the company had been better to your liking,” says poor Harry.

“’Tis very unfortunate; but I dare say you could not help it,” she answers, tossing her little curly head.

Something in him clenched—fists, teeth, pride, and patience all together. She went on, still in that tone that pretended kindness. “You seem disturbed: shall we go to my mamma?”

“Yes—let us go to your mamma,” cries Mr. Warrington, with eyes that had fire in them; and to an unlucky waiter who got between him and his path he broke out with a “Curse you, why are you always standing in the way?”

“La! Is that the way you speak in Virginia?” asks Miss Pertness.

“We are rough there sometimes, madam, and can’t help being disturbed,” he answers slowly, with a quiver through his whole frame, looking down upon her as if she were some bright, stinging insect.

Hetty, for her part, saw nothing distinctly afterwards until she came to her mother. Never had she seen Harry look so handsome, so noble. Mrs. Lambert, with the quick anxiety of all frightened mothers, cried, “You look pale, child!”

“’Tis the cold—no, I mean the heat. Thank you, Mr. Warrington,” and the girl made him a faint curtsey, while Harry bowed a tremendous bow and went away amongst his guests, scarcely knowing what he did, so hot was his blood.

He was roused from his own anger by another—an altercation between his aunt, Madame de Bernstein, and the Duchess of Queensberry. As the royal favourite passed, the duchess gave her an awful stare with eyes no longer so bright as in the old days when they “set the world on fire;” turned to her neighbour with an affected laugh; and, with fan and giggle, poured a ceaseless rain of sneers upon the jolly Hanoverian. The countess pursued her cards, not knowing—or not choosing to know—how she was being gibed at. There had been feud of many years between the duchess and the family on the throne; and the duchess’s malice, like strong spice, kept its savour long.

“How you all bow down to the idol! Don’t tell me! You are as bad as the rest, my good Madame Bernstein!” cries her Grace. “Ah, what a true Christian country this is! and how your dear first husband, the Bishop, would have liked to see such a sight!”

“Forgive me, if I fail quite to understand your Grace,” Madame de Bernstein answered, very grave.

“We are both growing old, my good Bernstein—or perhaps we won’t understand when we don’t choose to understand. That is the way with us women, my good young Iroquois.”

“Your Grace remarked that it was a Christian country,” said Madame de Bernstein, “and I failed to perceive the point of the remark.”

“Point?—Indeed, my good creature, there is very little point in it! I meant we were such good Christians because we were so forgiving. Don’t you remember reading, when you were young—or your husband the Bishop reading, when he was in the pulpit—how, when a woman amongst the Jews was caught doing wrong, the Pharisees were for stoning her out of hand? Far from stoning such a woman now, look how fond we are of her! Any man in this room would go round it on his knees if yonder woman bade him. Yes, Madame Walmoden—you may look up from your cards with your great painted face and frown with your great painted eyebrows at me. You know I am talking about you; and I intend to go on talking about you too. I say any man here would go round the room on his knees if you bade him!”

“I think, madam, I know two or three who wouldn’t!” says Mr. Warrington, with spirit.

“Quick, let me hug them to my heart of hearts!” cries the duchess. “Which are they? Bring ’em to me, my dear Iroquois! Let us have a game of four—of honest men and women; that is to say, if we can find a couple more partners, Mr. Warrington!”

“Here are we three,” says the Baroness de Bernstein, with a forced laugh; “let us play a dummy.”

“Pray, madam, where is the third?” asks the old duchess, looking round.

“Madam!” cries Madame Walmoden at last, the colour rising under her paint, “I leave your Grace to boast of your honesty, which I have no doubt is spotless: but I will thank you not to doubt mine before my own relatives and children!”

“See how she fires up at a word! I am sure, my dear creature, you are quite as honest as most of the company,” returns the duchess. “Which may not be good enough for her Grace the Duchess of Queensberry and Dover, who, to be sure, might have stayed away in such a case; but it is the best my nephew could get, madam, and his best he has given you. You look astonished, Harry, my dear—and well you may. He is not used to our ways, madam.”

“Madam, he has found an aunt who can teach him our ways, and a great deal more!” cries the duchess, rapping her fan. “She will teach him to try and make all his guests welcome, old or young, rich or poor. That is the Virginian way, isn’t it, Harry? She will tell him, when Catherine Hyde is angry with his old aunt, that they were friends as girls, and ought not to quarrel now they are old women. And she will not be wrong, will she, Duchess?”

Whereupon Madame de Bernstein made the other dowager a superb curtsey, as if she had laid a cloth smooth over a stain; and the battle that seemed ready to blaze passed away into smoke.

Next morning, when Harry talked over the night’s work with his tutor, the chaplain cried, “Egad, it was like Byng and Galissonière!”

“Seventy-fours at least—both of ’em!” laughs Harry. “But the Baroness declined the battle, and sailed out of fire with inimitable skill.”

“Why should she be afraid? I have heard you say my aunt is as witty as any woman alive, and need fear the tongue of no dowager in England.”

“Hem! Perhaps she had good reasons for being peaceable!” Sampson answered; and his handsome eyes had a look which said he knew more than he would tell. Poor Bernstein’s reputation, cracked long ago, was such that any jests thrown at Madame Walmoden might splash her too; and in such a world the innocent are often punished by the very words meant for others.

“Sir,” cried Harry, in amazement, “you don’t mean to say there is anything against the character of my aunt, the Baroness de Bernstein!”

The chaplain stared at him with such wonder that Harry saw there must be old stories, and charges not to be spoken. “Good heavens!” he groaned, “are there two then in the family, who are—?”

“Which two?” asked the chaplain; and Harry stopped short, blushing to the temples, bit his lip, and was silent, remembering too well whence he had learned of another family offender.

“Bygones are always unpleasant things, Mr. Warrington,” said Sampson at last. “We had best hold our peace regarding them. No man or woman can live long in this wicked world without some scandal attaching. We cannot escape calumny, my dear young friend—you have had proof enough of that in your brief stay amongst us. But we can have clear consciences, and that is the main point!” And he lifted his eyes upward, as if his conscience were as white as the ceiling.

“Has there been anything very wrong, then, about my Aunt Bernstein?” Harry persisted, remembering how his mother at home had never spoken of the Baroness.

“O sancta simplicitas!” the chaplain muttered. “Stories, my dear sir, much older than your time or mine. Stories such as are told about everybody—de me, de te; and you know with what degree of truth in your own case.”

“Confound the villain! I should like to hear any scoundrel say a word against the dear old lady,” cried Harry. “Why, this world, parson, is full of lies and scandal!”

“And you are just beginning to find it out,” said the clergyman, with that beatified air which sat on him as naturally as a napkin on a well-trained servant.

At this moment Colonel Lambert came in to pay a morning visit; and behind him loitered Mr. Gumbo, who moved through life as if he were carrying a brimming bowl. Harry—suiting action to speech—had just been tweaking the nose of Calumny with his fist on the table.

“The ladies are purely. Whose nose were you pulling when I came in, Mr. Warrington?” says the Colonel, laughing.

“Isn’t it a shame, sir? The parson here was telling me there are villains who attack the character of my aunt, the Baroness of Bernstein!”

“You don’t mean to say so!” cries Mr. Lambert.

“I tell Mr. Harry that everybody is calumniated!” says the chaplain with clerical intonation; and at the same time he looks at Lambert and winks, as much as to say, He knows nothing—keep him so.

“Yes,” says Lambert, taking the hint, “the jaws of slander are for ever wagging. Witness that story about the dancing-girl that we all believed against you, Harry Warrington.”

“What, all, sir?”

“No, not all. One didn’t—Hetty didn’t. You should have heard her standing up for you, Harry, t’other day, when somebody—a little bird—brought us another story about you; about a game at cards on Sunday morning, when you and a friend of yours might have been better employed.” And here the Colonel cast a look of humour and reproof at the chaplain.

“Faith, I own it, sir!” says Sampson. “It was mea culpa, mea maxima—no, mea minima culpa—only the rehearsal of an old game at piquet which we had been talking over.”

“And did Miss Hester stand up for me?” asks Harry.

“Miss Hester did. But why that wondering look?” says Lambert.

“She scolded me last night like—like anything,” Harry answers, with the blunt honesty that makes its own trouble. “I never heard a young girl go on so. She made fun of everybody—hit about at young and old—so that I couldn’t help telling her that in our country, leastways in Virginia (they say the Yankees are very pert), young people don’t speak of their elders so. And, do you know, sir, we had a sort of quarrel; and I’m very glad you’ve told me she spoke kindly of me.” And he shook Lambert’s hand, cheeks glowing, eyes moist with boyish readiness.

“You won’t come to much hurt if you find no worse enemy than Hester, Mr. Warrington,” said the Colonel gravely, and looked at the young man with a deep interest. Is he fond of her? he thought. And how fond? Miss Het has been playing her tricks. He is a fine honest lad; God bless him.

“And the young lady of the minuet?” asked the chaplain smoothly. “She distinguished herself to perfection: the whole room admired. I trust Miss—Miss—”

“Miss Theodosia is perfectly well, and ready to dance at this minute with your reverence,” says Lambert. “Or stay, Chaplain, perhaps you only dance on Sunday?”

Then the Colonel turned again to Harry. “You paid your court very neatly to the great lady, Mr. Flatterer. My Lady Yarmouth has been trumpeting your praises at the Pump Room. She says she has got a leedel boy in Hannover dat is wery like you, and you are a sharming young mans.”

“If her ladyship were a queen, people could scarcely be more respectful to her,” says the chaplain.

“Let us call her a vice-queen, parson,” says Lambert, with a twinkle.

“Her Majesty pocketed forty of my guineas at quadrille,” cries Harry, laughing.

“She will play you on the same terms another day. The Countess is fond of play, and she wins from most people,” Lambert answered drily.

“Why don’t you bet her ladyship five thousand on a bishopric, parson? I have heard of a clergyman who made such a bet—and lost it—and paid it—and got the bishopric.”

“Ah! who will lend me the five thousand? Will you, sir?” asks the chaplain.

“No, sir! I won’t give her five thousand to be made Commander-in-Chief or Pope of Rome,” says Lambert stoutly. “I fling no stones at the woman; but I bow no knee to her, as I see a pack of rascals do. No offence—I don’t mean you. And I don’t mean Harry Warrington, who was quite right to be civil to her and to lose his money with good-humour.”

Then the Colonel’s face changed to that look men have when they are about to take a leave that matters. “Harry, I am come to bid thee farewell, my boy. We have had our pleasuring—my money is run out, and we must jog back to Oakhurst. Will you ever come and see the old place again?”

“Now, sir, now! I’ll ride back with you!” cries Harry eagerly.

“Why—no—not now,” Lambert answered, hurried. “We haven’t got room—that is, we’re—we’re expecting some friends.” (And under his breath: The Lord forgive me for the lie.) “But you’ll come to us when—when Tom’s at home. Yes, when Tom’s at home. That will be famous fun. And I’d have you know my wife and I love you sincerely, sir—and so do the girls, however much they scold you. And if ever you are in a scrape—and such things have happened, Mr. Chaplain—you will please to count upon me. Mind that, sir!”

He would have taken his leave then and there; but Harry followed him down the stairs, and would not be denied saying good-bye to the ladies. Yet instead of going straight to Lambert’s lodging, the two gentlemen turned towards the common; and from Harry’s windows Mr. Sampson saw them walking there, deep in earnest talk. Lambert smiled first, and looked roguish; then, as the talk went on, he flung up both hands and made gestures of surprise and agitation.

“The boy is telling him,” thought the chaplain.

When Mr. Warrington returned an hour later, he found his reverence sunk in the composition of a sermon, as if ink could wash away knowledge. Harry’s face was grave and melancholy. He flung down his hat, dropped into a chair, and something like an execration broke from him.

“The young ladies are going, and our heart is affected?” says the chaplain, looking up.

“Heart!” sneers Harry. “Which of the young ladies is the conqueror, sir? I thought the youngest’s eyes followed you about at your ball.”

“Confound the little termagant!” Harry broke out. “What does she mean by being so pert to me? She treats me as if I was a fool!”

“And no man is, sir, with a woman!” says Sampson, dipping his pen.

“Ain’t they, Chaplain?” growls Harry, and then adds more words of inward disquiet which were not fit for a pulpit, nor for any well-ordered table.

“By the way, have you heard anything of your lost property?” the chaplain asked presently.

“No!” says Harry, with another oath that would not bear repeating.

“I begin to suspect there was more money than you like to own in that book. I wish I could find some.”

“There were notes in it,” Harry said gloomily, “and—and papers that I am very sorry to lose. What the deuce has come of it? I had it when we dined together.”

“I saw you put it in your pocket,” cried the chaplain. “I saw you take it out and pay at the toy-shop a bill for a gold thimble and workbox for one of your young ladies. Of course you have asked there, sir?”

“Of course I have,” says Harry, sunk in his ill-humour as in a bog.

“Gumbo put you to bed—at least, if I remember right. I was so cut myself that I scarce remember anything. Can you trust those black fellows, sir?”

“I can trust him with my head,” says Harry; and then, as if the words had bitten him, he groaned, “With my head? I can’t trust myself with it.”

“‘Oh, that a man should put an enemy into his mouth to steal away his brains!’” quotes the chaplain.

“You may well call it an enemy,” says Harry. “Hang it, I have a great mind to make a vow never to drink another drop! A fellow says anything when he is in drink.”

The chaplain laughed. “You, sir, are close enough!” he said; and indeed, for the last few days, no amount of wine would unseal Mr. Warrington’s lips when Sampson, by chance or art, touched upon the subject of his patron’s loss.

“And so the little country nymphs are gone, or going?” the chaplain resumed. “They were nice, fresh little things; but I think the mother was the finest woman of the three. I declare, a woman at five-and-thirty or so is at her prime. What do you say, sir?”

Mr. Warrington looked askance at him for a moment, as if he tasted something sour in the air.

“Confound all women, I say!” muttered the young misogynist; for which sentiment every well-conditioned person will surely rebuke him.

Colonel Lambert, who had seen men bleed from the mouth and yet swear they were sound, took counsel with his lady upon a sickness far less easy to physic. They agreed—quietly, as householders agree upon the ordering of a kitchen for winter—that their little Hetty should be carried away from Tunbridge Wells, and from the reach of that young gentleman whose very laugh seemed to set her heart in motion.

Absence, which is a fair purge for many a man, is no such simple draught for a girl. A man will be marched from a temptation as from a tavern door; he will busy himself with cards, horses, commissions, and forget. A young woman, once her mind has tasted a sweetness, may travel a hundred miles, and yet the flavour goes with her like spice in a closed box: you open it, and there is the scent still, in the linen and the wood. The mother, who knew the way of hens and children and hearts, looked to distance as to a cool pantry; the father, who knew the way of camps, trusted in removal as in a change of air. They forgot that love is not cured by climate, and that memory, once seasoned, keeps.

So why not, one might say, let the child take leave? Why not permit her to stand in the doorway, while the harness jingles and the post-boy clucks to the horses, and say, with a steady little voice, “Good-bye, Mr. Warrington. I was wilful last night, and you were kind. Good-bye”? She would show no special emotion. Shame sits in the throat like a dry crust; it will not let the words come as tears. She would smile her innocent smile, which is often but an artifice to hide pain, and he—preoccupied, full of his own concerns, and of the bustle of men—would not read what lay behind her eyes.

And indeed he did not. When the time came, Harry Warrington did not even ride beside the Lambert carriage a part of the homeward way. He had made some other party for that afternoon—an engagement of pleasure, as men call it, that takes the place of duty—and when he returned, the good people were gone from Tunbridge Wells. Their windows stood open to the air, and a card in one pane announced, with that cold civility of lodging-houses, that the apartments were once more to let.

A little sorrow, passing as swiftly as the shadow of a cloud over a table-cloth, may have touched him at the blankness of the rooms which had lately held such frank faces, such friendly voices. But four o’clock brings dinner. He dined at the White Horse, and the hot savour of roasted meat and gravy, the clatter of plates, the scrape of chairs, the cork drawn with that small sigh of glass and air—these common sounds and smells of the world took him up as they always do. He ate his meal, and called fiercely for his bottle, as though a man could drown a thought as he drowns a biscuit in wine.

At that same hour, poor little Hester, jolting away toward Westerham, would choke over her tea when it was offered—tea that tasted of tin and sorrow. When at last the Lambert cavalcade reached the house of their friends, she went to bed with the sound of wheels still in her head, and in the morning the young roses in her cheeks were wan, and there were dark circles about her eyes. It was the thunder, she said; the night was hot; she could not sleep. She would be better when she got home next day. She spoke as children speak, naming weather and not naming the secret storm.

Home they came, and every familiar thing stood waiting, as if it had not stirred while she had lived whole years in two nights. There was the gate where he fell. There was the bed he lay in. There was the chair in which he used to sit. The very boards seemed to remember the tread of those days, and the yard had its own music—the steady pecking of hens, the small cries of chickens, the soft drip from a watering-pot into thirsty earth. Who was that child yonder calling her chickens, or bending to the rose-bushes with a little jug? Was she the same Hester Lambert who, a week ago, had thought only of music and poultry and her flower-garden? She looked older than Theo now—Theo, always composed, clever, and old for her age. But Hester had crossed a gulf in the night, and though she still moved among kettles and coops and beds as before, she moved like one who has learned a new tongue of pain which she cannot translate to anyone.

In Tunbridge Wells, Maria Esmond watched the Lamberts drive away and felt a grim relief, as if a door had closed between her and a draught of cold air. She had that relief which comes when a rival is removed—not by one’s own hand, but by Providence or prudence—and yet relief is seldom clean; it leaves a taste.

When Harry came into his aunt’s card-room that evening, he was flushed with Barbeau’s good wine; his laughter ran too loud against the hush of upholstery and candlelight. Madame Bernstein’s tables were set as carefully as any supper-board: green cloth smoothed, counters ranged, the cards in their neat tyranny. But there is a kind of hunger in play too, and a thirst.

His aunt asked, with her mocking ease, which of the girls was his sweetheart. He rattled an answer as he might toss a dice-box: he loved them both like sisters. He had never seen better people than the Lamberts; Lambert should be a general; the Duke was fond of him. And Madame Bernstein, who seasoned every sentence with malice as a cook seasons with salt, bade him make interest with Lady Yarmouth for his protégé.

“Elle raffole de fous, cher petit!” she said, mimicking the Countess’s German accent until it turned coarse in her mouth. The Baroness was delighted with her boy’s success, and turned a sneer upon her niece.

“You carry off the hearts of all the old women, doesn’t he, Maria?” she said; and Maria, who had been braced like a string, quivered at the touch.

“You were quite right, my dear,” Madame Bernstein went on, “not to perceive that she cheated at cards, and you play like a grand seigneur.”

“Did she cheat?” Harry cried, honestly amazed. “I am sure, ma’am, I saw no unfair play.”

“No more did I, my dear,” said the old woman lazily, “but I am sure she cheated. Bah! every woman cheats, I and Maria included, when we can get a chance. But when you play with the Walmoden, you don’t do wrong to lose in moderation; and many men cheat in that way. Cultivate her. She has taken a fancy to your beaux yeux. Why should your Excellency not be Governor of Virginia, sir? You must go and pay your respects to the Duke and his Majesty at Kensington. The Countess of Yarmouth will be your best friend at court.”

“Why should you not introduce me, aunt?” Harry asked.

The old lady’s rouged cheek took on a deeper colour, as if the paint itself were ashamed.

“I am not in favour at Kensington,” she said. “I may have been once; and there are no faces so unwelcome to kings as those they wish to forget. All of us want to forget something or somebody. I dare say our ingénu here would like to wipe a sum or two off the slate. Wouldst thou not, Harry?”

At that, Harry reddened; and Maria reddened too. Madame Bernstein laughed one of those wicked laughs that have no merriment in them, only the crackle of spite. What guilt had signalled itself in those two blushes? What account lay scored upon either memory which each would be glad to rub out? Most of us—be we ever so powdered and perfumed—carry some ugly reckonings, and dread an audit.

Had Maria known one cause of Harry’s disquiet, her own anxiety would have risen like dough in heat. For days past, he had missed a pocket-book. He remembered it in his possession on the day he drank so much claret at the White Horse—claret whose warm fumes mingle with the smell of roast and tobacco until a man’s head becomes a noisy market—and Gumbo had carried him to bed. He searched for it in the morning; none of his servants had seen it. He made inquiry at the White Horse, but the house yielded nothing—no trace in the bedding, no forgotten bundle in a drawer, no tell-tale scuff under a settle. He could not cry the book openly; he could only ask with cautious words, as though he were feeling for a bruise.

He must not have it known the book was lost.

For in it were letters—Lady Maria’s letters—those long outpourings of the heart, which, like over-rich sauces, are delightful to those at the table and nauseous when found cold by strangers. They contained disclosures of family matters, little histories, confidences, and that rash satire which lovers write because they believe the ink will be buried with the secret. There were jokes, scorn, scandal; appeals and protests of eternal fidelity; reproaches about his attentions to other women. There was the whole foolish farrago that people will pour out when they love and fear and have nothing but paper to receive it. Foolishness is not a crime; but it is a peril, especially when a private tongue is committed to a public alphabet.

While Madame Bernstein dozed after dinner—for eating and drinking too much were among her ladyship’s indulgences—Harry went to play billiards with Count Caramboli. The click of the balls, sharp and exact, is a sort of music too, but a hard one; it does not soothe the mind, it drives it. In the neighbouring room, Mr. Chaplain Sampson sat with Lady Maria and spoke low, that he might not disturb the Baroness’s sleep. Sampson had the air of a man who has walked long in other men’s houses and learned to tread softly; his voice was full of unction, as if every word had been dipped in oil.

“A gentleman of Mr. Warrington’s means can afford to be idle,” Maria said, trying for ease.

“I don’t say, madam, my practice is good, only my doctrine is sound,” Sampson replied with a sigh that seemed meant to be heard. “This young gentleman should have some employment. He should appear at court, and enter the service of his country, as befits a man of his station. He should settle down, and choose a woman of a suitable rank as his wife.”

As he said it, he looked straight into her face. Maria’s cheeks warmed, as if he had held them briefly over a fire.

“Indeed, my cousin is wasting his time,” she answered, and tried to keep her voice even.

“Mr. Warrington might see his relatives of his father’s family,” Sampson suggested.

“Suffolk country boobies drinking beer and hallooing after foxes!” Maria cried, too quickly. “I don’t see anything to be gained by his frequenting them, Mr. Sampson!”

“They are of an ancient family,” said the chaplain calmly, “of which the chief has been knight of the shire these hundred years. I have heard Sir Miles hath a daughter of Mr. Harry’s age—and beauty, too.”

“I know nothing, sir, about Sir Miles Warrington, and his daughters, and his beauties!” Maria exclaimed, flustered, and then, as if to cover the sound, glanced toward the room where her aunt lay.

Sampson listened, and smiled a faint smile. “The Baroness stirred—no—her ladyship is in a sweet sleep,” he murmured. Then, leaning in a little as a man leans to smell whether a pot is boiling over, he went on: “I fear, madam, for your ladyship’s cousin, Mr. Warrington. I fear for his youth; for designing persons who may get about him; for extravagances, follies, intrigues even into which he will be led, and into which everybody will try to tempt him. His lordship, my kind patron, bade me come and watch over him, and I am here accordingly, as your ladyship knoweth. I know the follies of young men. Perhaps I have practised them myself. I own it with a blush”—and he spoke of blushes with great sincerity, though his face did not much alter—“Between ourselves, I fear Mr. Warrington is in some trouble now, madam.”

“What, again?” Maria cried, too sharply.

“Hush! Your ladyship’s dear invalid!” whispered Sampson, and pointed with his eyes toward Madame Bernstein.

Maria lowered her voice. “What trouble?”

“Do you think your cousin has any partiality for any—any member of Mr. Lambert’s family? for example, Miss Lambert?”

“There is nothing between him and Miss Lambert,” said Maria at once, with the eagerness of one who puts a lid on a pot.

“Your ladyship is certain?”

“Women are said to have good eyes in such matters, my good Sampson,” Maria answered, forcing an easy air. “I thought the little girl seemed to be following him.”

“Then I am at fault once more,” the chaplain said, with a frankness that looked like honesty. “Mr. Warrington said of the young lady, that she ought to go back to her doll, and called her a pert, stuck-up little hussy.”

Maria let out a breath that was half a sigh. “Ah!”

“Then, madam, there must be somebody else,” Sampson continued, watching her steadily. “Has he confided nothing to your ladyship?”

“To me, Mr. Sampson? What? Where? How?” Maria stammered; and the room, though close, seemed suddenly airless.

“Some six days ago,” said Sampson, “after we had been dining at the White Horse, and drinking too freely, Mr. Warrington lost a pocket-book containing letters.”

“Letters?” Maria gasped, and the word struck her like a blow to the breast.

“And probably more money than he likes to own,” Sampson added gravely. “He is very much disturbed about the book. We have both made cautious inquiries about it. We have—Gracious powers, is your ladyship ill?”

For Lady Maria gave three shrill screams—so piercing that they seemed to cut clean through the soft hangings and sleeping-room silence—and fell from her chair in a heap, as if her bones had been drawn out of her. The house itself seemed to start at the noise; in such a quiet place, sound is a tyrant.

“I will see the Prince. I have a right to see him. What’s this?—Where am I?—What’s the matter?” cried Madame Bernstein, waking as if out of some feverish dream. She shook in her limbs; her face was flushed under the rouge; her eyes stared wildly before she gathered herself. Then she tottered forward on her tortoiseshell cane, the tapping of it sharp on the boards.

“What—what’s the matter?” she demanded again. “Have you killed her, sir?”

“Some sudden qualm must have come over her ladyship,” Sampson cried, all innocence and alarm. “Shall I cut her laces, madam? or send for a doctor?”

“What has passed between you, sir?” the old Baroness asked fiercely, her voice hard as a knife on a plate.

“I give you my honour, madam,” he said, “I have done I don’t know what. I but mentioned that Mr. Warrington had lost a pocket-book containing letters, and my lady swooned, as you see.”

Madame Bernstein snatched a glass of water and dashed it on Maria’s face. Presently a feeble moan came; the younger woman’s eyelids fluttered as if weighed with lead. Madame Bernstein sent Sampson away for the doctor, but her eyes followed him with a suspicion that was almost a glare.

When Maria opened her eyes, the first thing she saw was her aunt’s grim countenance bent over her—no comfort there, only judgment.

“What has happened?” Maria asked, bewildered and gasping.

“H’m! You know best what has happened, madam, I suppose,” the Baroness replied, her mouth twisting bitterly. “What hath happened before in our family?”

“Ah, yes! the letters have been lost—ach lieber Himmel!” Maria cried, and in her agitation slipped into her mother’s tongue, as she did when much moved.

“Yes! the seal has been broken, and the letters have been lost—’tis the old story of the Esmonds,” cried the elder woman. “Seal broken, letters lost? What do you mean—aunt?” Maria asked, faintly.

“I mean that my mother was the only honest woman that ever entered the family!” Madame Bernstein cried, stamping her foot so that the cane jarred. “And she was a parson’s daughter of no family in particular, or she would have gone wrong, too. Good heavens! is it decreed that we are all to be—”

“To be what, madam?” Maria whispered.

“To be what my Lady Queensberry said we were last night. To be what we are! You know the word for it!” the Baroness cried, her anger rising like a boil. “I say, what has come to the whole race? Your father’s mother was an honest woman, Maria. Why did I leave her? Why couldn’t you remain so?”

“Madam!” Maria exclaimed, struggling to sit upright, “I declare, before Heaven, I am as—”

“Bah! Don’t madam me! Don’t call heaven to witness—there’s nobody by! And if you swore to your innocence till the rest of your teeth dropped out of your mouth, my Lady Maria Esmond, I would not believe you!”

Maria’s eyes widened. “Ah! it was you told him!” she gasped. She knew that thrust; she had felt it before, like a pin set in a sleeve.

“I saw some folly going on between you and the boy,” Madame Bernstein replied without shame, “and I told him that you were as old as his mother. Yes, I did! Do you suppose I am going to let Henry Esmond’s boy fling himself and his wealth away upon such a battered old rock as you? The boy shan’t be robbed and cheated in our family. Not a shilling of mine shall any of you have if he comes to any harm amongst you.”

That last threat snapped something in Maria that had been habit and fear. She rose, trembling but upright.

“Ah! you told him!” she cried, and her voice, for once, had steel in it. “Well, then! I’d have you to know that I don’t care a penny, madam, for your paltry money! I have Mr. Harry Warrington’s word—yes, and his letters—and I know he will die rather than break it.”

“He will die if he keeps it!” the old lady screamed.

Maria shrugged, as if to fling off the weight of that prophecy. “But you don’t care for that—you’ve no more heart—”

“Than my father’s sister, madam!” Maria shot back. The meekness that had been her daily bread was gone; she spoke now as if she had swallowed fire.

Madame Bernstein’s fury faltered into something like despair, and she shook her head, suddenly old.

“Ah! Why did not I marry an honest man?” she said. “Henry Esmond was noble and good, and perhaps might have made me so. But no, no—we have all got the taint in us—all! You don’t mean to sacrifice this boy, Maria?”

“Madame ma tante, do you take me for a fool at my age?” Maria asked, and her laugh was bitter.

“Set him free! I’ll give you five thousand pounds—in my—in my will, Maria. I will, on my honour!”

“When you were young,” Maria answered, “and you liked Colonel Esmond, you threw him aside for an earl, and the earl for a duke?”

“Yes,” said Madame Bernstein, and her mouth tightened.

“Eh! Bon sang ne peut mentir! I have no money, I have no friends. My father was a spendthrift, my brother is a beggar. I have Mr. Warrington’s word, and I know, madam, he will keep it. And that’s what I tell your ladyship!” Maria cried, sweeping her hand as if she were clearing a table.

“Suppose my letters are published to all the world to-morrow? Après? I know they contain things I would as lieve not tell. Things not about me alone. Comment! Do you suppose there are no stories but mine in the family? It is not my letters that I am afraid of, so long as I have his, madam. Yes, his and his word, and I trust them both.”

“I will send to my merchant, and give you the money now, Maria,” the old lady pleaded, changing tack as quickly as a cook who sees a sauce about to split.

“No, I shall have my pretty Harry, and ten times five thousand pounds!” Maria cried, reckless now with desperation and pride.

“Not till his mother’s death, madam, who is just your age!” Madame Bernstein retorted.

“We can afford to wait, aunt,” Maria answered. “At my age, as you say, I am not so eager as young chits for a husband.”

“But to wait my sister’s death, at least, is a drawback?”

“Offer me ten thousand pounds, Madam Tusher, and then we will see!” Maria flung out.

“I have not so much money in the world, Maria,” the Baroness said, and for an instant her voice was small.

“Then, madam, let me make what I can for myself!” Maria replied.

“Ah, if he heard you—”

“Après? I have his word. I know he will keep it. I can afford to wait, madam,” Maria said; and with that she swept out of the room, her skirts whispering like a departing tide, at the very moment Mr. Sampson returned with news of the doctor.

It was Madame Bernstein who wanted cordials now. The old lady, shaken by the suddenness of the discovery and the violence of her niece’s rebellion, sank back as if the strength had run out of her. The house, which a moment ago had been full of shrieks and stamping and accusations, fell again into its domestic hush—the muffled creak of a chair, the far-off rattle of carriage-wheels in the street, the soft crackle of a coal settling—sounds that should have soothed, but which, after such a storm, seemed only to mark how thin the walls were between a family’s secrets and the listening world.

Though she had plainly been worsted in the skirmish of the previous day, the Baroness Bernstein met her niece as if no wound had been given and none received. Her voice came smooth as warmed wine, and her smile lay upon her face like a well-placed mask.

“Of course, my Lady Maria,” she said, “you can’t suppose that I, as Harry Warrington’s near relative, can be pleased at the thought of his marrying a woman as old as his mother, and with not a penny to her fortune. But if he chooses to do so silly a thing, the affair is none of mine; and I doubt whether I should have been much inclined to be taken au sérieux touching that offer of five thousand pounds which I made in the heat of our talk. So it was at Castlewood that this pretty affair was arranged? Had I known how far it had gone, my dear, I should have spared some needless opposition. When a pitcher is broken, what railing can mend it?”

“Madam!” Maria cut in, her colour rising.

“Pardon me—I mean nothing against your ladyship’s honour or character, which, no doubt, are quite safe. Harry says so, and you say so—what more can one ask?”

“You have talked to Mr. Warrington, madam?”

“And he has owned he made you a promise at Castlewood: that you have it in his writing.”

“Certainly I have, madam!” said Lady Maria, drawing herself up as if the paper were stitched into her very stays.

“Ah!” The elder lady did not wince. “And I own, too, that at first I put a wrong construction upon the tenor of your letters to him. They implicate other members of the family—”

“Who have spoken most wickedly of me, and endeavoured to prejudice me in every way in my dear Mr. Warrington’s eyes. Yes, madam, I own I have written against them, to justify myself.”

“But, of course, are pained to think that any wretch should get possession of stories to the disadvantage of our family, and make them public scandal. Hence your disquiet just now.”

“Exactly so,” Lady Maria said quickly. “From Mr. Warrington I could have nothing concealed henceforth, and spoke freely to him. But that is a very different thing from wishing all the world to know the disputes of a noble family.”

“Upon my word, Maria, I admire you, and have done you injustice. These—these twenty years, let us say.”

“I am very glad, madam, that you end by doing me justice at all,” said the niece, and her curtsey was the smallest a woman ever gave.

“When I saw you last night, opening the ball with my nephew, can you guess what I thought of, my dear?”

“I really have no idea what the Baroness de Bernstein thought of,” said Lady Maria, icily.

“I remembered that you performed to that very tune with the dancing-master at Kensington, my dear!”

“Madam, it was an infamous calumny.”

“By which the poor dancing-master got a cudgelling for nothing!”

“It is cruel and unkind, madam, to recall that calumny—and I shall beg to decline living any longer with any one who utters it,” Maria returned, with a spirit that made the words ring like a snapped fan.

“You wish to go home? I can fancy you won’t like Tunbridge. It will be very hot for you if those letters are found.”

“There was not a word against you in them, madam: about that I can make your mind easy.”

“So Harry said, and did your ladyship justice. Well, my dear, we are tired of one another, and shall be better apart for a while.”

“That is precisely my own opinion,” said Lady Maria again, dropping a deeper curtsey, as if she sealed the bargain with it.

“Mr. Sampson can escort you to Castlewood. You and your maid can take a postchaise.”

“We can take a postchaise, and Mr. Sampson can escort me,” echoed the younger lady. “You see, madam, I act like a dutiful niece.”

“Do you know, my dear, I have a notion that Sampson has got the letters?” said the Baroness, with a frankness that was its own sort of cruelty.

“I confess that such a notion has passed through my own mind,” Lady Maria answered; and her gaze did not flicker, only tightened, like thread drawn through cloth.

“And you want to go home in the chaise, and coax the letters from him! Delilah! Well, they can be no good to me, and I trust you may get them. When will you go? The sooner the better, you say? We are women of the world, Maria. We only call names when we are in a passion. We don’t want each other’s company; and we part on good terms. Shall we go to my Lady Yarmouth’s? ’Tis her night. There is nothing like a change of scene after one of those little nervous attacks you have had, and cards drive away unpleasant thoughts better than any doctor.”

Lady Maria, who could accept an insult as she accepted a compliment—without yielding an inch—agreed to go.

She was dressed and ready first, waiting in the drawing-room. When Madame Bernstein came down, she remarked, as if by accident, that Maria’s door was left open.

“She has the letters upon her,” thought the old lady; and the thought sat in her mind as steadily as a stone in a pocket.

They went off to their entertainment in their respective chairs, and the two of them, who had wounded each other so neatly, displayed that charming cordiality and respect which women can produce after, and even during, the bitterest quarrels. The city’s night-noise took them up—the hollow drum of sedan-poles, the clop and scrape of horses, the far-off bawl of a watchman, the near chatter at every lit doorway. Even the air seemed to have a sound, being thick with the rustle of silk and the click of fans, as if the town itself played at cards with them, shuffling and dealing.

Upon their return from the Countess’s drum, Mrs. Brett, Madame Bernstein’s maid, presented herself at Lady Maria’s call, when that lady rang her hand-bell on retiring. Betty, Mrs. Brett confessed with shame, was not in a condition to come before my lady. Betty had been a-junketing and merry-making with Mr. Warrington’s black gentleman, with my Lord Bamborough’s valet, and several more ladies and gentlemen of that station; and the liquor—Mrs. Brett was shocked to own it—had proved too much for Mrs. Betty.

Should Mrs. Brett undress my lady?

My lady said she would undress without a maid, and gave Mrs. Brett leave to withdraw.

“She has the letters in her stays,” thought Madame Bernstein.

They had bid each other an amicable good-night on the stairs.

Mrs. Betty had her scolding the next morning, when she came to wait on her mistress from the closet adjoining Lady Maria’s apartment in which Betty lay. She owned, with contrition, her partiality for rum-punch, which Mr. Gumbo had the knack of brewing most delicate. It was not mere spirit flung together with coarse haste, but a draught contrived with a cook’s patient cunning: the clean bite of lime, the burnt-sugar sweetness melted down to a dark edge, spice that rose after the first swallow and warmed the throat like a well-laid coal. Even now, speaking penitently, the girl’s mouth betrayed the memory of it, as if she still tasted the citrus on her tongue.

She took her scolding with meekness; and, having performed her usual duties about her lady’s person, retired.

Now Betty was one of the Castlewood girls who had been so fascinated by Gumbo, and was a very good-looking, blue-eyed lass, upon whom Mr. Case, Madame Bernstein’s confidential man, had also cast the eyes of affection. Hence, between Messrs. Gumbo and Case, there had been jealousies and even quarrels; which had caused Gumbo, who was of a peaceful disposition, to be rather shy of the Baroness’s gentlemen, the chief of whom vowed he would break the bones, or have the life of Gumbo, if he persisted in his attentions to Mrs. Betty.

But on the night of the rum-punch, though Mr. Case found Gumbo and Mrs. Betty whispering in the doorway in the cool breeze, and Gumbo would have turned pale with fear had he been able so to do, no one could be more gracious than Mr. Case. It was he who proposed the bowl, which was brewed and drunk in Mrs. Betty’s room, and which Gumbo concocted with exquisite skill. He complimented Gumbo on his music. Though a sober man ordinarily, he insisted upon more and more drinking, until poor Mrs. Betty was reduced to the state which occasioned her ladyship’s just censure.

As for Mr. Case himself—who lay out of the house—he was so ill with the punch that he kept his bed the whole of the next day, and did not get strength to make his appearance and wait on his ladies until supper-time; when his mistress good-naturedly rebuked him, saying it was not often he sinned in that way.

“Why, Case, I could have made oath it was you I saw on horseback this morning galloping on the London road,” said Mr. Warrington, who was supping with his relatives.

“Me! law bless you, sir! I was a-bed, and I thought my head would come off with the aching. I ate a bit at six o’clock, and drunk a deal of small beer, and I am almost my own man again now. But that Gumbo, saving your honour’s presence, I won’t taste none of his punch again.”

And the honest major-domo went on among the bottles and glasses, drawing corks with the neat snap of long practice, rinsing a glass to silence the last ghost of claret, setting decanters in their places as a gardener sets pots: domestic order against the day’s confusions.

As they sat after their meal, Madame Bernstein was friendly enough. She prescribed strong fortifying drinks for Maria against the recurrence of her fainting fits. The lady had such attacks not unfrequently; and the Baroness spoke of them with that worldly tenderness which is half care and half command.

She urged Maria to consult her London physician, and to send up an account of her case by Harry.

“By Harry?” asked the lady, and the question sounded too sharp for so smooth a room.

“Yes. Harry is going for two days on an errand for his aunt to London. I do not care to tell you, my dear, that it is on business which will do him good. I wish Mr. Draper to put him into my will, and as I am going travelling upon a round of visits when you and I part, I think, for security, I shall ask Mr. Warrington to take my trinket-box in his postchaise to London with him, for there have been robberies of late, and I have no fancy for being stopped by highwaymen.”

Maria looked blank at the notion of the young gentleman’s departure, but hoped she might have his escort back to Castlewood, whither her elder brother had now returned.

“Nay,” said his aunt, “the lad hath been tied to our apron-strings long enough. A day in London will do him no harm. He can perform my errand for me, and be back with you by Saturday.”

“I would offer to accompany Mr. Warrington, but I preach on Friday before her ladyship,” said Mr. Sampson; for he was anxious that my Lady Yarmouth should judge of his powers, and Madame Bernstein had exerted her influence with the king’s favourite to induce her to hear the chaplain.

Harry relished the notion of a rattling journey to London and a day or two of sport there. He promised his pistols were good, and that he would hand the diamonds over in safety to the banker’s strong-room. Would he occupy his aunt’s London house? No; that would be a dreary lodging with only a housemaid and groom in charge. He would go to the Star and Garter in Pall Mall, or to an inn in Covent Garden.

“Ah! I have often talked over that journey,” said Harry, and his face, which could brighten so boyishly, now clouded in a moment.

“And with whom, sir?” asked Lady Maria, who had an ear for every name that might be spoken.

“With one who promised to make it with me,” said the young man, thinking—as he always did—with extreme tenderness of the lost brother.

“He has more heart, my good Maria, than some of us!” said Harry’s aunt, witnessing his emotion.

Uncontrollable gusts of grief would still, not unfrequently, pass over the young man: the parting from his brother; the scene and circumstances of George’s fall last year; a remembered word, or some excursion at home which they had planned together—these would return with a force that made the present fall away like a loosened ribbon.

“I doubt, madam,” whispered the chaplain demurely to Madame Bernstein after one of these bursts, “whether some folks in England would suffer quite so much at the death of their elder brother.”

But sorrow is not a climate in which youth can breathe for ever; and we can fancy Mr. Warrington setting out eagerly enough, and very gay and happy, if it must be owned, to be rid—though he could scarce confess it even to himself—of his elderly attachment.

Yes. There was no help for it. At Castlewood, on one unlucky evening, he had made an offer of his heart and himself to his mature cousin, and she had accepted the foolish lad’s offer. But the marriage now was out of the question. He must consult his mother. She was mistress for life of the Virginian property. Of course she would refuse her consent to such a union. The thought of it was deferred to a late day. Meanwhile it hung like a weight about his neck, and caused him remorse and disquiet; no wonder that his spirits lifted as he came near London, and that he looked with a kind of delighted hunger from his postchaise windows upon the city as he advanced.

No highwayman stopped him on Blackheath. The road’s sounds—wheel-rim on flint, the leather creak of harness, the steady breath of the horses—seemed to thicken as the world grew fuller. Yonder were the gleaming domes of Greenwich, canopied with woods. There was the famous Thames, with its countless shipping; a forest of masts that chimed faintly in the wind like rigging-strung harps. There—there actually was the Tower of London.

“Look, Gumbo! There is the Tower!”

“Yes, master,” said Gumbo, who had never heard of the Tower; but Harry had, and remembered how he had read of it in Howell’s Medulla, and how he and his brother used to play at the Tower; and he thought with delight now of seeing the armour, the jewels, the lions—those old marvels which, told in a boy’s dialect and then heard again in a man’s, are never the same marvel, nor ever quite translatable from one age of the blood into another.

They passed through Southwark and over that famous London Bridge, which had been covered with houses like a street two years ago; now there was only a single gate left, and that too was coming down. Then the chaise rolled through the City; and—

“Look, Gumbo, that is Saint Paul’s!”

“Yes, master; Saint Paul’s,” said Gumbo, obediently, little struck by architecture, more struck by the smell of the town—the coal-smoke, hot tallow, river-mud, roasting meat, brewer’s yeast, and the sharp stink of narrow lanes that seemed never to air.

And so by the well-known course they reached the Temple, and Gumbo and his master looked up with awe at the rebel heads on Temple Bar. The crows made their own commentary on politics; the wind gave the poles a creaking note; and the city’s roar carried on as if it had forgotten, long ago, the individual voices it had swallowed.

The chaise drove to Mr. Draper’s chambers in Middle Temple Lane. Harry handed the precious box over to Mr. Draper, together with a letter from his aunt. The gentleman read it with some interest, carefully put it away, then consigned the trinket-box to his strong closet. He went into the adjoining room, taking his clerk with him, and then returned, at Mr. Warrington’s service to conduct him to an hotel.

An hotel in Covent Garden was fixed upon as best for his residence.

“I shall have to keep you for two or three days, Mr. Warrington,” the lawyer said. “I don’t think the papers which the Baroness wants can be ready until then. Meanwhile I am at your service to see the town. I live out of it myself, and have a little box at Camberwell, where I shall be proud to have the honour of entertaining Mr. Warrington; but a young man, I suppose, will like his inn and his liberty best, sir?”

Harry said yes: the inn would be best. So the postchaise, with a clerk of Mr. Draper’s inside, was despatched to the Bedford, whither the two gentlemen agreed to walk.

They sat and talked for a while first. The Drapers, father and son, had been lawyers time out of mind to the Esmond family; and the attorney told Mr. Warrington stories of the Castlewood ancestors, as if rummaging an old pantry for jars with labels half-faded—this one full of a quarrel preserved in vinegar; that one a feud sweetened with sugar and yet sharp on the tongue. Of the present Earl Mr. Draper was no longer agent: his father and his lordship had had differences, and his lordship’s business had been taken elsewhere; but the Baroness was still their honoured client, and very happy indeed was Mr. Draper to think her ladyship so well disposed towards her nephew.

As they were taking their hats to go, a young clerk of the house stopped his principal in the passage.

“If you please, sir, them papers of the Baroness was given to her ladyship’s man, Mr. Case, two days ago.”

“Just please to mind your own business, Mr. Brown,” said the lawyer sharply. “This way, Mr. Warrington. Our Temple stairs are rather dark. Allow me.”

Harry saw Mr. Draper throw a Parthian look of anger at Mr. Brown.

“So it was Case I saw on the London road two days ago,” Harry thought. “What business brought the old fox to London?”

But he was not curious to pry into other folk’s affairs, and dismissed it from his mind.

Whither first? Harry was for seeing the place where his grandfather and Lord Castlewood had fought their duel fifty-six years ago in Leicester Field. Mr. Draper knew the spot and the story; they might take Covent Garden on their way and see that Mr. Warrington was comfortably lodged.

“And order dinner,” said Harry; for even in pleasure he had a soldier’s method, and liked to have his provisions made sure.

No; Mr. Draper could not consent. Mr. Warrington must do him the honour to dine with him. In fact he had made so bold as to order a collation from the Cock: fowls trussed and roasted till the skin took a proper colour; cold ham shaved thin and glossy; a raised pie with its crust firm as a box; pickles and anchovies; bread crisp at the edge; and wine that set a warm note in the body as music sets a key. Mr. Warrington could not decline so pressing an invitation.

So they walked away gaily together, passing under that arch where the heads were. Harry took off his hat to them, much to the lawyer’s astonishment.

“They were gentlemen who died for their king, sir. My dear brother George and I always said we would salute ’em when we saw ’em,” Mr. Warrington said.

“You’ll have a mob at your heels if you do, sir,” said the alarmed lawyer.
