“Confound the mob, sir,” said Mr. Harry loftily; but the passers-by, intent on their own errands, did not heed him, and he walked up the thronging Strand gazing with delight on all he saw, storing it away—sounds as much as sights: the rattle of carts, the hawkers’ cries, a distant hammering like a great heart beating in timber, the thin violin of a street-fiddler losing his tune beneath the heavier roar. Mr. Draper chattered ceaselessly; Harry heard little of it, not caring to let the lawyer know how much he was moved, nor the public perceive he was a stranger.

Nor was Mr. Draper displeased by the young Virginian’s silent and haughty reserve. A hundred years ago a gentleman was a gentleman, and his attorney his very humble servant.

At the Bedford the chamberlain showed Mr. Warrington his rooms, bowing with delightful obsequiousness; for Gumbo had already trumpeted his master’s greatness, and Mr. Draper’s clerk announced the new-comer as a “high fellar.” Then the rooms surveyed, the two gentlemen went to Leicester Field—Mr. Gumbo strutting behind—looked upon the scene of his grandsire’s wound and poor Lord Castlewood’s tragedy, and returned to the Temple to Mr. Draper’s chambers.

Who was that shabby-looking big man Mr. Warrington bowed to as they went out after dinner for a walk in the gardens? That was Mr. Johnson, an author he had met at Tunbridge Wells.

“Take the advice of a man of the world, sir,” said Mr. Draper, eyeing the shabby man of letters superciliously; “the less you have to do with that kind of person, the better. The business we have into our office about them literary men is not very pleasant, I can tell you.”

“Indeed!” said Mr. Warrington; and he liked his new friend the less as the latter grew more familiar and more ready with contempt, as if contempt were a sauce fit for all dishes.

The theatres were shut. Should they go to Sadler’s Wells? or Marybone Gardens? or Ranelagh? or how?

“Not Ranelagh,” said Mr. Draper, “because there’s none of the nobility in town.”

But seeing in the paper that at Sadler’s Wells, Islington, there would be a most singular diversion on eight hand-bells by Mr. Franklyn, as well as the surprising performances of Signora Catherina, Harry—who had already had his fill of city-bellow and wanted something not made of iron and wheels—wisely determined on Marybone Gardens; where there was a concert of music, a choice of tea, coffee, and all sorts of wines, and the benefit (or burden) of Mr. Draper’s ceaseless conversation. The clarinets and fiddles there seemed, for an hour, to cleanse the ear: a pocket of ordered sound against the grinding din beyond the gates.

Mr. Draper’s obsequiousness only ended at Harry’s bedroom door, where, with haughty grandeur, the young gentleman bade his talkative host good-night.

Next morning Mr. Warrington, in his brocade bedgown, took his breakfast, read the newspaper, and enjoyed his ease in his inn—hot rolls whose crusts broke with a small crackle, butter softening into their steaming crumb, and coffee strong enough to lay a steady hand upon the nerves. He read news from his own country; and when he saw the words, Williamsburg, Virginia, June 7th, his eyes grew dim somehow.

He had just had letters by that packet of June 7th, but his mother did not tell how—

“A great number of the principal gentry of the colony have associated themselves under the command of the Honourable Peyton Randolph, Esquire, to march to the relief of their distressed fellow-subjects, and revenge the cruelties of the French and their barbarous allies. They are in a uniform: viz., a plain blue frock, nanquin or brown waistcoats and breeches, and plain hats. They are armed each with a light firelock, a brace of pistols, and a cutting sword.”

“Ah, why ain’t we there, Gumbo?” cried Harry, and the words tasted bitter in his mouth, as if London’s richness had turned suddenly to ashes.

“Why ain’t we dar?” shouted Gumbo.

“Why am I here, dangling at women’s trains?” continued the Virginian; and the phrase itself—women’s trains—seemed to catch him like a hook, for it was the language of the town, neat and contemptuous, and it did not fit what he felt. What he felt had no clean English for it; it was a home-sound in him, a cadence of field and river, too thick with memory to be spoken in drawing-rooms.

“Think dangling at women’s trains very pleasant, Master Harry!” said the materialistic Gumbo, who was little affected by further home news which his master read—viz., that The Lovely Sally, Virginia ship, had been taken in sight of port by a French privateer.

And now, reading that the finest mare in England, and a pair of very genteel bay geldings, were to be sold at the Bull Inn, the lower end of Hatton Garden, Harry determined to go look at the animals, and asked his way.

He then and there bought the genteel bay geldings, and paid for them with easy generosity; for horseflesh spoke a universal tongue to him—muscle and wind, bright eye, sound leg—more honest than the smoothest phrases of law or love.

He never said what else he did that day, being shy of appearing a stranger; but it is believed he took a coach and went to Westminster Abbey, then to the Tower, then to Mrs. Salmon’s Waxwork, then to Hyde Park and Kensington Palace; and then, having given orders to go to the Royal Exchange, catching a glimpse of Covent Garden on his way, he bade Jehu take him back to his inn, and cut short the coachman’s enumeration of places by flinging the fellow a guinea.

Mr. Draper had called in his absence and said he would come again; but Mr. Warrington, having dined sumptuously by himself, went off nimbly to Marybone Gardens again, in the same noble company.

As he issued forth next day, the bells of St. Paul’s, Covent Garden, were ringing for morning prayers; and their measured peal—so different from the ragged racket of carts and cries—reminded him that friend Sampson was going to preach his sermon.

Harry smiled. He had begun to have a shrewd and just opinion of the value of Mr. Sampson’s sermons.

The London Advertiser lay beside Mr. Warrington’s breakfast like a second plate set for temptation. The coffee—dark as walnut shell and sharp with a faint tang of burnt sugar—sent up its steam in little banners; the rolls were hot enough to tear with the fingers; a dish of kidneys swam in gravy peppered to a Londoner’s liking. Gumbo had contrived, out of the inn’s indifferent butter and some shred of herb begged from the cook, to make the bread taste less like yesterday’s loaf and more like morning. The room, for all its snugness, could not keep out the city’s ceaseless undertone—wheels worrying the stones, hawkers calling as if their throats were brass instruments, and the thin quarrel of a distant fiddle sawing at nothing in particular.

Between mouthfuls, Harry read an invitation to all lovers of manly British sport to witness the trial of Sutton and Figg. It was printed boldly, with that London assurance which makes even bloodshed sound like a public benefit. By the time his cup was drained and the last salt of the kidneys lingered on his tongue, the decision was made; the page had done its work as thoroughly as any sermon.

He drove himself to Marybone Fields with the pair of horses he had bought only yesterday—spirited brutes, quick to take the bit, and needing a hand steadier than his impatience. He did not know the road. London was not like Virginia, where a lane kept its name by being the only lane for miles and where one might follow a creek’s voice or the smell of turned earth and come right at last. Here the streets tacked and veered as though the town had been built by men in a hurry, and then mended by other men who hated the first. He found himself behind Mr. Whitfield’s round Tabernacle on the Tottenham Road, where the preaching-house sat in its green as solemnly as a fat goose in a yard; he passed fields with a few cows cropping, and the Middlesex Hospital standing in the midst like a white warning, and more than once he had to pull up to ask a ragged boy, who answered as if language were a thing to be sold by the syllable.

At length the Wooden House showed its flag and its crowd. The place was a kind of shrine to an English appetite that asked for blows as other men asked for pudding. Around the doors surged London blackguards, their voices rising and falling like a kennel of hounds; with them were a few carriages of fashion, lacquer and crest glinting among the mud-splashed hacks. Beggars and cripples worked the edges of the press; shoeblack-boys flung themselves upon one another for the honour of his boots; nosegay-women offered damp bunches whose crushed leaves gave out a green, bruised scent; flying fruiterers darted through with apples and oranges, their baskets brushing coats and dripping juice. Piemen cried their wares, the pastry smelling of suet and pepper; ale steamed from open mugs; and every sound—horn, drum, shout, oath—seemed to argue with every other, as if the city could not bear silence for fear it might remember something.

A manager, accompanied by a drummer and a horn-blower, repeatedly issued upon the little stage out front to proclaim that the noble English sports were just about to begin. The horn’s brazen note made the ears ache; Harry, who had grown with the rustle of tobacco leaves and the low talk of slaves in the quarters, felt how a man’s spirit is pressed and shaped by the noises that surround him. Here the very air seemed battered.

He paid his money and was placed in a gallery where he could command the platform. Gumbo sat below in the amphitheatre until the crush and the heat offended him; then he would go out into the outer world, drink a pot of beer, and fall in with his brother-lacqueys and the coachmen perched on boxes outside. London, Harry observed, had a prodigious quantity of those liveried creatures. They were everywhere—at chapel-doors, in theatre galleries, on landings, swarming in anterooms—powdered, buckled, nosegayed, melancholy in their finery as if they were the last of a tribe. Their talk was of vails and cards and small tyrannies; their laughter was loud and empty. One could not help thinking of other peoples being pushed aside—how a tongue and a way of living can be made to look quaint, then useless, then vanish, leaving only a few specimens for the curious to stare at. In Virginia, Gumbo’s speech carried the cadence of home and captivity together—no Londoner could hear in it what Harry heard, and what could not be translated: the salt of tidewater, the lash remembered, the kitchen-fire at night. Here, voices were made to conform; the city’s lexicon ruled like a magistrate.

Before the principal combatants appeared, minor warriors exhibited themselves. A boxing-match came off; the men feinted and hugged and panted, but neither had much stomach for punishment. The crowd grumbled as if served stale bread. Then came cudgel-playing; a few heads were tapped, a few trickles of blood shown, but the wounds were so trifling that even the women selling fruit looked disappointed. Hisses rose. “The masters! the masters!” the people bawled, demanding the true dish.

At last Sutton strode up the steps, sword in hand, in his shirt with his head shaven clean. The scars on his scalp looked like old seams in leather. He saluted the company with his weapon, and made an especial bow to a private box where sat a stout gentleman, hands folded, expression as calm as if he were at table. Presently Figg followed—also bare to the waist, his head clean-shorn and marked by former fights. Each wore on his burly sword-arm an armiger of his colour, ribbons like cockades, the way soldiers wear signs to be known even when their faces are blown to pieces.

They shook hands. The crowd’s roar rolled up to the roof. Then the word was given, and the air on the platform seemed to harden.

Figg opened with a blow so tremendous that, had it met Sutton’s honest head, it would have lopped it off as neatly as the cook’s carving-knife takes the top from a carrot—Harry had just watched such a knife at breakfast, and the comparison came to him with a sick exactness. Sutton caught the blade on his own sword; Figg’s stroke was delivered so mightily that his weapon broke in his hands. There was a shout as when a dish is dropped in a kitchen and everyone turns at once.

Other swords were brought. The first blood drawn spouted from Figg’s side; Sutton’s supporters yelled as if they had won a campaign. But Figg turned, panting, and appealed to his audience—especially to the stout personage in the private gallery—showing that the broken sword in the previous encounter had caused the wound. There was parley, cries, gestures; and while the dispute buzzed, Harry saw a gentleman in a riding-frock and plain scratch-wig enter the stout man’s box. It was his acquaintance from Tunbridge Wells, my Lord March and Ruglen.

Lord March was no great dealer in politeness; yet here he showed singular deference. Harry watched him bend profoundly as the stout gentleman produced bank-bills from a pocket-book and handed them over. The exchange was as neat as a serving of coin with dessert—no talk, no flourish, only the quiet transfer of power. Then March’s eye caught Harry; his business finished, he crossed over and greeted the young Virginian with warmth that seemed almost good-humoured.

They sat together while the combat renewed, the swords clashing with a sound like cleavers on bone. Skill and valour were on both sides, and the crowd drank it in, shouting and stamping so that the whole building rang. When the swords had done their work, the gladiators took up the quarter-staff. The long staves whistled through the air; the blows landed with a dull, meal-sack thud that made Harry’s stomach turn, though his eyes would not look away. It ended, after a long and satisfying battle to the audience, with victory to Figg, ancient champion.

All the while a thunderstorm had gathered and broken over the Wooden House. Rain drummed on the roof, and the thunder rolled like cannon over the fields. For a moment, beneath that natural tumult, the human clamour seemed thin—mere shouting against the sky’s deeper voice. Harry breathed more freely, as if the storm’s great sound cleared the air of some of its foulness.

When the fight was done, Lord March offered him a seat in his chariot. Harry gladly accepted, leaving his own phaeton to be driven home by his groom. The rain made the streets smell of wet earth and horse, of chimney soot washed down, of raw wood and damp leather. Harry, warmed with wine-less excitement, declared the sight he had witnessed to be sport indeed—better than any he had seen since coming to England. As always, any pleasure brought with it the impulse to share it with the dear companion of his boyhood. He drew breath and began, “I wish—” and then stopped as though the words had bitten him.

“No, I don’t,” he said, and stared out at the streaming windows.

“What do you wish, and what don’t you wish?” asked March, lolling among his cushions, watching him with that lazy curiosity which can be sharper than attention.

“I was thinking of my elder brother,” Harry answered, the taste of iron and rain in his mouth. “I wished he had been with me. We promised to have our sport together at home. We talked of it many’s the time. But he wouldn’t have liked this rough sort. He didn’t care for fighting—though he was the bravest lad alive.”

“Oh, he was the bravest lad alive, was he?” March drawled, eyes narrowing with amusement.

Harry, carried on by feeling, spoke of a quarrel George had had with a very gallant officer—an absurd affair, but hard to keep George off him. “I never saw a fellow so cool,” Harry said, “nor more savage and determined, God help me. For the honour of the country, I wish he could have come here instead of me, and shown you a real Virginian gentleman.”

“Nay, sir, you’ll do very well,” said March. “What is this I hear of Lady Yarmouth taking you into favour?”

“I will do as well as another,” Harry replied, stubbornly, then softened. “I can ride, and I think I can shoot better than George. But my brother had the head, sir—the head!” He tapped his own skull with a rueful candour. “Why, upon my word, he had read almost every book that was ever written; could play both on the fiddle and harpsichord; could compose poetry and sermons most elegant. What can I do? I’m only good to ride and play at cards, and drink Burgundy.”

He hung his head, as if shamed by the smallness of his own list. Yet even that list was full of sensations—horseflesh under him, the click of cards, the dark velvet warmth of wine—and he could not help adding, with a sudden rally, “But them I can do as well as most fellows. In fact, my lord, I’ll back myself.”

March laughed, relishing the naivete as a jaded voluptuary still relishes a wholesome mutton-chop. “By Gad, Mr. Warrington, you ought to be taken to Exeter ’Change and put in a show.”

“And for why?”

“A gentleman from Virginia who has lost his elder brother and absolutely regrets him. The breed ain’t known in this country. Upon my honour and conscience, I believe you would like to have him back again.”

“Believe!” Harry cried, flushing, his throat tightening. The word felt like an insult because it questioned what, to him, had no need of proof.

“That is, you believe you believe you would like him back again,” March continued, untroubled, turning his gaze out to the new houses they passed. “But depend on it you wouldn’t. ’Tis not in human nature, sir; not as I read it, at least.” He pointed as they rolled by: Sir Richard Littleton’s at the corner, my Lord Bingley’s great house beyond; Cavendish Square fenced with unsightly boards, a waste of space; Montagu House turned into a confounded museum with books and stuffed birds and rhinoceroses; the cursed New Road cut behind Bedford House Gardens. His complaints about the town’s growth came like the rattle of a cook who hates new fashions in the kitchen—too much slicing and rearranging, not enough respect for the old stock that once made everything taste right.

“Shall we go down Tyburn Road and the Park,” he asked, “or through Swallow Street and into the habitable quarter? We can dine at Pall Mall, or, if you like, with you; and we can spend the evening as you like—with the Queen of Spades, or—”

“With the Queen of Spades, if your lordship pleases,” Harry said, blushing at the name that was half woman and half card-table.

So the chariot drew up at his hotel in Covent Garden. The landlord came forward with his usual obsequiousness; recognising my Lord March and Ruglen, he bowed his wig almost to my lord’s shoes, as though humility were an art he practised for tips. In the dining-room a dinner was ordered that London called the best: soups rich with long-simmered bones; fish with a sharp sauce; roast meat with its fat crisped; vegetables boiled into submission; and a pudding heavy enough to silence talk for a minute. Yet it was the wine that truly made March attentive—Burgundy of a quality to satisfy even an epicurean earl, its scent rising when poured like warmed cherries and old oak.

Over wine there was talk of fireworks at Vauxhall or else of cards. Harry, who had never seen a firework beyond a dozen squibs let off at Williamsburg on the fifth of November—an exhibition he had thought sublime—would have liked Vauxhall for the novelty: lights over water, the crackle and bloom of fire against the night. But he yielded to March’s preference for piquet. The cards were brought; the table cleared; the world narrowed to pasteboard, fingers, and calculation.

Harry began by winning, as usual, his luck coming briskly like a good wind. Then, within half an hour, it turned and favoured March, whose skill belonged to the clubs and whose face hardly altered whether he gained or lost. Mr. Draper, Harry’s man of business, came bowing into the room. Harry, in his way, always asked everybody to sit and drink and partake of his best. He would share a crust, a haunch, a jug of water, a bottle of Burgundy, with the same open-handedness; and there was in it a country welcome that had not yet withered in him under London’s smoke.

Draper did not care much for wine, but he delighted in great company. He protested he liked nothing better than to see piquet played by two consummate players and men of fashion. He sat down, undismayed by March’s sidelong scowls, and watched. The gentlemen said they played for shillings; yet they counted gains and losses in a manner too quiet for shillings to be the whole matter. Their voices dropped; their faces stayed grave; courtesy sat between them like a third player.

Then came the first sign of trouble: a scuffling without, a whispering, an outcry like a woman in tears. The door flew open and a female burst in, producing from March an explosion of language fit to sour a cask of wine.

“I wish your women would take some other time for coming, confound ’em,” he said, flinging his cards down.

“What—Mrs. Betty!” Harry started up. It was indeed Lady Maria’s maid; and behind her stood Gumbo, his fine countenance wet and shining with tears, his chest heaving as if he had run miles.

“What has happened?” Harry asked, the room suddenly tasting of cold ashes. “The Baroness is well?”

“Help! help, sir—your honour!” Betty cried, and dropped to her knees as though the floor were a church. “Help whom?”

A howl came from Gumbo—one long sound dragged out of him, half grief and half outrage, and in it Harry heard the helplessness that no gentleman’s English can properly name.

“Gumbo! you scoundrel!” Harry demanded, startled into anger by that sound. “Has anything happened between Mrs. Betty and you?”

Gumbo stepped back with a wounded dignity, laying his hand on his heart. “No, sir; nothing hab happened ’twix’ this lady and me.”

“It’s my mistress, sir,” Betty sobbed. “Help! help! here’s the letter she have wrote, sir! They have gone and took her, sir!”

“Is it only that old Molly Esmond?” March said, taking up his cards again as if misfortunes were flies to be brushed away. “She’s known to be over head and heels in debt. Dry your eyes in the next room, Mrs. Betty, and let me and Mr. Warrington go on with our game.”

“Help! help her!” Betty cried again, and the old name, Molly, sounded in her mouth not like a jest but like a prayer. “Oh, Mr. Harry! you won’t be a-going on with your cards, when my lady calls out to you to come and help her! Your honour used to come quick enough when my lady used to send me to fetch you at Castlewood!”

March swore at her to hold her tongue, but she would not cease weeping; and the noise of her grief, in that close room, drove the game from the table as surely as a gust snuffs a candle. Harry rose, went to the bell, and said, with a steadiness that surprised even himself, “My dear lord, the game must be over for to-night. My relative writes to me in great distress, and I am bound to go to her.”

“Curse her! Why couldn’t she wait till to-morrow?” March cried, testily, as if a woman in trouble were no more than a creditor tapping at the door of his amusement.

Harry ordered a postchaise instantly. His own horses, he said, would take him to Bromley. March, who could turn any circumstance into a wager as some men turn any scraps into broth, began instantly: “Bet you you don’t do it within the hour! Bet you you don’t do it within five quarters of an hour! Bet you four to one—or I’ll take your bet, which you please—that you’re not robbed on Blackheath! Bet you you are not at Tunbridge Wells before midnight!”

“Done,” Harry said, his face hot, his mind already on the road and Lady Maria’s peril. March, with careful relish, noted down the terms of the four wagers in his pocket-book, as though writing a recipe he meant to use again.

Lady Maria’s letter was thrust into Harry’s hand. The paper was crumpled, the ink uneven, the spelling that of a woman whose tongue and schooling were at war. He read:

“MY DEAR COUSIN—  
I am fell into a trapp, which I perceive the machinations of villians. I am a prisner. Betty will tell you all. Ah, my Henrico! come to the resque of your  
MOLLY.”

The words, with their misshapen certainty, struck him harder than any cudgel blow he had seen that day. “Trapp.” “Machinations.” “Prisner.” The very letters seemed caught and cramped, as if her language itself had been seized along with her person—an old woman’s voice forced to plead in the dominant tongue of lawyers and bailiffs, where every term carries a hook.

Within half an hour of receiving the missive, Mr. Warrington was in his postchaise, cloaked against the rain, galloping over Westminster Bridge to the road that would lead him to Bromley and beyond, to succour his kinswoman. Behind him London roared on—cards shuffled, ale poured, drums beat—heedless as ever; but ahead, through the wet dark, the wheels hummed their urgent song on the road, and the horses’ breathing made the only music he could bear.

In my youth I fell, by a piece of luck that now seems less luck than providence, into the intimacy of a man of decent exterior and scandalous memory, born—so he swore, and so the world of sailors swore with him—in an island praised, by impartial dealers in maritime jewellery, as the first gem of the ocean. He never let that gem shine for long. He preferred to show it by candle-end, in a back kitchen, with the light full upon its cracks.

He would sit where the peat-smoke and the kitchen-steam made one soft haze, and from under that haze draw, as from an old pot set to simmer, story after story of his nearest blood: every commandment broken as if they had taken the holy table and dashed it upon a stone; murders that would have made Turpin blink; robberies as bare-faced as a butcher’s cleaver. Yet he remembered each wickedness with an exactness a food historian might envy in the cataloguing of sauces—who added what, who stole what, whose hand slipped into which drawer, at what hour, and in what weather. It was a wonder, he said, that any of them lived out of the hulks.

“My brother Tim,” he would begin, and then go on until Tim was dragging a father’s grey hairs down to the grave; “me brother Mick,” until Mick had stripped a parish church as regularly as a cook strips thyme; “me sister Annamaroia,” until she had jilted the Captain for the Ensign, forged a grandmother’s will, and made off with the spoons that poor Larry the knife-boy swung for. The house of Atreus, he maintained, was a small household compared to his own roaring clan—though no power on earth, of course, would induce me to name the country whence he came.

And then—this was what made my young blood curdle more than the crimes themselves—he would tell how these very same hands, still reeking in his telling, would pour each other drink; how these lips, black with perjury, would kiss a sister’s cheek; how they would weep over “the dear old Castle What-d’ye-call-’em,” and the regiment once quartered there, and the tomb of their sainted mother (who had cheated them out of the property), and cry “Heaven bless her soul!” with such tender violence that a stranger might have believed them a family of lambs.

What can there be finer than forgiveness? It is a noble art, particularly among those accustomed to bad language as they are to strong waters. They fling the decanter at a man’s head in the morning; in the evening they retrieve the same decanter, wipe the dust from it, and drink together as if the glass had never flown. Habit blunts the sting of words. Where oaths are daily bread, a curse is chewed and swallowed without choking.

So it was at Tunbridge Wells: our two ladies, aunt and niece, had, the day before, snapped and scratched with admirable spirit; and now, having kissed and made truce with the ease of veterans who know when the bugle calls halt, they played at cards in perfect amity. They drank to each other’s health. They divided the chicken between them—each took a wing with a neat, practised pinch, and they drew the merry-thought with smiling hands. In talk, they scratched their neighbours’ eyes out, not each other’s. They were like Peninsular warriors who, during truce, exchange tobacco and wine with the enemy—firelock always near, flint cocked, the powder dry.

Aunt Bernstein’s threatened gout? The twinges had obligingly vanished. Maria was all solicitude. Maria’s fainting fits? None to speak of—only a slight recurrence the night before. The Baroness was all compassion. Her niece must have the best doctor; she must continue the steel; she must be fortified; she must even, if need were, have bottled waters sent after her when she left Tunbridge. How kind the aunt was. How grateful the niece.

What passed in whispers behind curtains we need not swear to. Suppose the old lady said to her own woman, with a sniff as sharp as gin, “Fainting fits—pooh! Epilepsy, inherited from that scrofulous German mother!” Suppose Lady Maria, with her soft voice and hardened heart, bade her maid taste every medicinal glass first, declaring her aunt capable of poison. Such private talk is the concealed pistol beneath the embroidered cloak. It does not disturb the smile in the public room.

Lady Maria, with Harry Warrington’s bond safe in her pocket like a spice wrapped and hidden from thieves, did not choose to press for payment. She knew the world: you do not force a young man’s hand when you mean to keep him under your thumb. Better to give him day-rule, let him frisk, let him fancy himself free, while the chain lies quiet round the ankle. “Take your ease and amusement, cousin,” she said aloud. Grey Grimalkin purred in the corner: frisk, little mousekin; I watch.

And amusements came readily. Mr. Jack Morris, who delighted to lose money in the company of titled persons, became one of Lady Maria’s diversions. To him it was almost pleasure to have an earl’s daughter take his guineas; to her it was a pleasant, steady income. Madame Bernstein procured him entrance to the Countess of Yarmouth’s assembly; they played; and so, in the first eight-and-forty hours after Mr. Warrington’s departure, Tunbridge rolled on very cheerily—cards, gossip, and those small domestic economies of genteel life: the ordering of a breakfast, the pinning of a lace ruffle, the cutting of a wing, the pouring of tea, the little click of porcelain, and beneath it all the steady undertone of calculation.

Friday arrived: the day for the sermon which Mr. Sampson had been preparing.

The Wells folk, if no conjurer, breakfast, dancing bears, or concert offered itself as rival entertainment, would put up with a discourse; and Sampson had a name for being amusing and eloquent. Moreover, Lady Yarmouth was coming; and Lady Yarmouth, with her vermilion cheeks and flaming taffeta, had a great voice in the giving of livings and the dispensing of bishoprics, the Defender of the Faith of that day having an admirable confidence in her ladyship’s judgement. So Sampson polished his best phrases as carefully as a cook polishes copper, laid out his points like dishes in order, and hoped to serve them hot.

He was the domestic chaplain of Madame Bernstein’s nephew; and both ladies patronised him. On the morning, the Baroness gave a little breakfast in his honour. Sampson appeared rosy and handsome, his wig fresh-flowered, his new cassock rustling—credit, no doubt, from some church-admiring mercer at the Wells. There was a pleasant smell about him of lavender and warmed cloth, that clean, shopman’s scent of novelty which makes even sanctity seem purchasable.

Then, with their ladyships, their lacqueys behind with great gilt prayer-books, Mr. Sampson marched from breakfast to church. The gravel underfoot gave its crisp music; the morning air carried the faint chirp of sparrows and the distant clatter of chairs and hoofs; and over all floated that peculiar Tunbridge hum—polite voices, rustling silk, the town’s shallow merriment.

At the door was a dazzling conflux of fashion. Lady Yarmouth shone among them, a blaze of colour and rouge. Yet there were shabby people too—always a few shadows at the edge of a candlelit room. As the organ stopped, in slipped an odd pair in ragged coats; one had carroty hair peeping from under a scratch-wig. He could not be Protestant, for he crossed himself by instinct and muttered to his comrade, “Bedad, Tim, I forgawt!”—which, if one had ears trained, as I had, by my earlier island acquaintance, betrayed a birthplace without naming it. Wherever they went, a rich fragrance of whisky went too, like a bold seasoning that overpowers every dish.

And not only Catholics appeared. Two men with hooked noses and sallow faces—disciples of a creed older still—worked their way in despite the beadle’s opposition. The beadle, seeing their greasy coats and counting their worth with his eyes, barred the door with his mace. One whispered, “We wants to be conwerted, gov’nor!” and the other slid coin into the beadle’s palm. The mace lifted. In they went.

The organ began again. The doors closed. Mr. Sampson, preceded by the gold-laced beadle, walked up to the pulpit as jolly a figure as you could wish to see, his face full, his cheek bright, his manner prosperous.

Presently he rose from his plump cushion—and turned as pale as death.

He looked to the western door. There, on either side, lingered the two Hebrew caryatides. He glanced then towards the vestry door hard by the rector’s pew, where he had been sitting during the service alongside his patronesses. And suddenly—like cats taking their places before a mouse-hole—two perfumed Hibernian gentlemen slipped out of an adjacent seat and seated themselves close by that vestry door and pew. They sat meekly, eyes cast down, hands still. Only the faintest ghost of whisky and hair-powder marked them, and the soft creak of their boots when they shifted weight.

How can one describe that sermon, if the preacher himself never knew how it came to an end? He spoke; the words came out in their proper order; the cadence rose and fell; the congregation listened and approved; and all the while his mind was like a kitchen where a roast is set too close to the fire—one watches the browning and cannot look away. The sound of his own voice seemed distant to him, muffled by the rushing in his ears. Yet the company pronounced it excellent.

When it was over, the fine ladies buzzed their praise across pews. Madame Walmoden declared it bewdiful and said it made her dremble all over. Madame Bernstein said it was excellent. Lady Maria, pleased that the family chaplain should distinguish himself, looked up and tried to catch his eye. She gave him a little wave of her hand and fluttered her handkerchief. He scarcely noted it; his eyes kept straying towards the font, where the Hebrew strangers still remained.

The people streamed out—first a rush, then a throng, then twos and threes, then a slow dribble of laggards. The organ ceased. The air changed: incense of hair-powder and perfume thinned, replaced by the damp scent of stone and the sharper odour of the crowd’s wool. The church grew emptier, the acoustics barer; each footstep and cough became distinct, as in a house after the feast when only the servants remain.

Everybody was gone. The two Hebrews still waited by the door. Madame Bernstein and her niece still lingered in the rector’s pew, the old lady deep in conversation with a gentleman—some compliment, some sly enquiry, some spoonful of honey with a pin concealed within it.

“Who are those horrible men at the door? And what a smell of spirits there is!” Lady Maria whispered to Mrs. Brett, her aunt’s woman, who waited behind.

“Farewell, doctor,” Madame Bernstein was saying; “you have a darling little boy—will he be a clergyman too?”

“Are you ready, my dear?” she added, and the pew was thrown open.

Because Madame Bernstein’s father was only a viscount, she insisted—out of punctilio or mock humility—that her niece, an earl’s daughter, should precede her out of the pew. Lady Maria stepped forward; and at that moment the two whiskified gentlemen advanced.

One drew a long strip of paper from his pocket.

Lady Maria started, turned pale, and made for the vestry as if she could slip through and bolt the door behind her. But the gentlemen were up with her. One actually laid his hand upon her shoulder—lightly, almost respectfully, yet with the firmness of a hand that knows its right.

“At the shuit of Misthress Pincott, of Kinsington, mercer,” he said, “I have the honour of arresting your leedyship. Me neem is Costigan, madam—a poor gentleman of Oireland, binding to circumstances and forced to follow a disagrayable profession. Will your leedyship walk, or shall me man go fetch a cheer?”

Lady Maria answered with three shrieks and fell swooning to the ground, her fine cloak spreading like a spilled sauce across the flags.

“Keep the door, Mick!” shouted Mr. Costigan.

“Best let in no one else, madam,” he added, very politely to Madame Bernstein. “Her leedyship has fallen in a feenting fit, and will recover here, at her aise.”

“Unlace her, Brett!” cried the old lady; and there was an odd twinkle in her eyes, as if she watched not a niece in distress but a dish at last turning as she wished. As soon as the stays were loosened, Madame Bernstein seized the little bag that Lady Maria wore about her neck on a hair chain, and with a small, sharp snip cut the necklace in twain and had the bag for her own.

“Dash some cold water over her face,” the Baroness said. “It always recovers her. You stay with her, Brett. How much is your suit, gentlemen?”

Mr. Costigan, with the air of a man reciting a bill of fare, answered, “The deem we have against her leedyship for one hundred and thirty-two pounds, in which she is indebted to Misthress Eliza Pincott—”

Meanwhile, where was the Reverend Mr. Sampson?

Like the fabled opossum that, spying the unerring gunner from its gum-tree, says, “It’s no use, Major; I will come down,” Sampson gave himself up. He knew this business; he knew the faces; he had met them before, as a man meets the same creditors again and again, until their footsteps become as familiar as the rattling of a saucepan lid.

“At whose suit, Simons?” he asked sadly.

Sampson knew Simons. “Buckleby Cordwainer,” said Mr. Simons.

“Forty-eight pound and charges, I know,” said Sampson with a sigh. “I haven’t got the money. What officer is there here?”

Mr. Simons’s companion, Mr. Lyons, stepped forward and said, with the smoothness of a host offering a guest a chair, that his house was most convenient, often used by gentlemen, and he should be proud to accommodate his reverence.

Two chairs happened to be waiting outside the chapel. Into those two chairs were placed Lady Maria Esmond and Mr. Sampson, and so they were carried to Mr. Lyons’s residence, escorted by the gentlemen newly introduced to them. The chairmen’s poles creaked; the leather straps groaned; the rhythm of footsteps made a dull drum upon the road. Tunbridge heard it all and understood: the acoustic of disgrace is always louder than the acoustic of prayer.

Not long after the capture, the Baroness Bernstein sent Mr. Case, her confidential servant, with a note to her niece full of the most ardent expressions of affection—regretting only that heavy losses at cards rendered the payment of such a sum quite impossible. She had written to Mrs. Pincott by that very post to entreat time; as soon as she had an answer she would not fail to acquaint her dear unhappy niece.

Mrs. Betty, Lady Maria’s maid, came to console her mistress. The two women, poor in cash and rich in rage, cast about for money enough to send Betty to London. Both mistress and maid had been unlucky at cards; between them they could muster no more than eighteen shillings. It was agreed Betty should sell a gold chain belonging to her lady and, with the money, travel to London.

Now Betty took the chain to the very toy-shop man who had sold it to Mr. Warrington—who had given it to his cousin. The shopman, seeing the bauble in a servant’s hand, supposed she had stolen it and was for bringing in a constable. So Betty had to make explanations; and once she confessed her mistress was in durance, the tale ran through Tunbridge as quickly as the smell of hot punch runs along a gaming-table. Before night closed, everybody knew Lady Maria Esmond was in the hands of bailiffs—knew the house where she lay, the amount (and ten times the amount) for which she was taken, and that she had pawned her trinkets for a little money to keep her in jail. And everybody said, of course, that old fiend of a Bernstein was at the bottom of it.

But money was found at last; and Mrs. Betty whisked up to London in search of the champion in whom the poor prisoner confided.

“Don’t say anything about that paper being gone!” Lady Maria cried. “Oh, the wretch, the wretch! She shall pay it me!”—meaning, no doubt, her aunt. Mr. Sampson read her a sermon; and they passed the evening over revenge and backgammon, consoling themselves with the well-grounded hope that Harry Warrington would rush to their rescue the moment he heard.

The Wells did not cease its music for them.

Though, before the evening was out, every soul knew what had happened, society remained civil and bland. At my Lady Trumpington’s cards that night, where Madame Bernstein appeared, and as long as she was within hearing, not a word was said of the morning’s transactions. Lady Yarmouth asked after the Baroness’s breddy nephew and heard Mr. Warrington was in London. My Lady Maria was not coming? She was indisposed—had fainted at church—must keep her room.

The cards were dealt; the fiddles sang; the wine went round. The gentlefolks talked, laughed, yawned, chattered. The footmen waylaid the supper—the clink of plates and the breathy hiss of lifted covers in the pantry; the chairmen drank and swore in the yard; the stars climbed the sky; and the world, as worlds do, went on as though no lady were imprisoned and no parson arrested.

It is a mortifying truth, and a consoling one: the little stings that pierce us do not keep our neighbours from sleeping. Were we forced to feel every other person’s tight boot upon our own corn, every slander upon our own cheek, every death upon our own heart, the burden would be intolerable. Better, perhaps, that the fiddles play on while somebody rages in a room with a locked door.

Madame Bernstein, for her part, stayed at the assembly until the very last—perhaps to deny the company a chance to speak of her the moment her back turned. It is a comfort we have backs, and that our ears do not grow upon them.

“Don’t tell me!” said Lady Yarmouth. “The Bernstein would play at cards over her niece’s coffin. Talk about her heart! Who ever said she had one? That old spy lost it to the Chevalier a thousand years ago, and has lived ever since perfectly well without one. For how much is the Maria put in prison? If it were only a small sum we would pay it—it would vex her aunt so. Find out, Fuchs, in the morning.”

Faithful Fuchs bowed and promised.

About midnight, Madame de Bernstein went home and presently fell into a sound sleep. She woke late, summoned her attendant, and received her morning dish of tea. If I told you she took a dram with it, you would be shocked; yet many of our great-grandmothers kept cordials in their closets, and a morning mouthful of strong water was counted almost medicinal—an old custom with old scents, like rosemary pressed in a Bible.

Having tipped off the cordial, the Baroness settled among her pillows and asked Mrs. Brett for news.

“He can give it you,” said Brett sulkily.

“He? Who?”

Mrs. Brett named Harry, and said Mr. Warrington had arrived about midnight—and Betty, Lady Maria’s maid, was with him.

“And my Lady Maria sends your ladyship her love and duty, and hopes you slept well,” Brett added, as if repeating a phrase from a lesson-book.

“Excellently, poor thing!” said the Baroness, with sweet calm. “Is Betty gone to her?”

“No; she is here,” said Mrs. Brett.

“Let me see her directly,” cried the old lady.

“I’ll tell her,” replied the obsequious Brett, and went away, leaving her mistress placidly reposing, her tea-cup’s faint perfume mingling with the sharper ghost of spirits.

Presently two pairs of high-heeled shoes were heard pattering over the bare deal floor—carpets being luxuries scarce known in bedrooms of those days. The sound came nearer, brisk and certain, like a knife’s tap on a board.

“So, Mrs. Betty, you were in London yesterday?” called Bernstein from within her curtains.

“It is not Betty—it is I! Good morning, dear aunt! I hope you slept well?” cried a voice that made old Bernstein start upon her pillow.

It was Lady Maria.

She drew the curtains aside and dropped her aunt a low curtsey. Lady Maria looked very pretty—rosy and happy, as if the air outside Mr. Lyons’s house had been a restorative cordial, and the night’s adventure a mere sauce piquante to sharpen appetite. And with that little surprise—her appearance there, in her aunt’s very bedchamber—we may bring this passage to a close.

On Saturday morning, the five-and-twentieth of August, 1756, Mr. Harry Esmond Warrington, with the clean, eager hand of youth and the confident flourish of a gentleman who had tasted both hazard and speed, set down his news to Lord March from Tunbridge Wells.

He wrote of wagers won, and of new horses that had “kep a-going at a capital rate,” as if the very muscle of the beasts and the clink of harness were part of his triumph. He had driven them himself—postilion beside to point the way—while his black servant sat within the carriage with Mrs. Betty, steadying her against the jolts. He described Blackheath and the two horsemen who rode up to peer at them, then wheeled off again as though discouraged by the set of their faces. The wheels had never slackened; the air had cut; the road had hummed under the spokes; he was at Bromley within two minutes of his hour, and into Tunbridge by forty-five minutes after eleven, where he “transacted” what must be transacted. The whole note had the briskness of a man who thinks the world a course and himself the whip.

It was by that same hurry of wheels—by that same hard-ridden haste—that Lady Maria Esmond was able, before the day was well in, to pass from a house of restraint into liberty.

For she had sent Mrs. Betty away to London as an emissary, and did not look to see her again so quickly; and she and the chaplain, Mr. Sampson, had sat up late, playing their little game of cards to hold their spirits together. The bailiff’s wife—who knew what it is to put comfort into a poor room—had provided them a small refection: cold meat laid out with careful parsimony, a heel of bread, a bit of cheese that smelt of the dairy and the cellar, and a mug of ale whose yeasty sweetness made a kind of courage. The house was quiet in the way country houses are at midnight, when even the boards seem to listen. Outside, the night had its own music: a distant dog that barked once and was ashamed; the long hush between gusts; the soft brush of leaves. It was a world made of breathing.

Then came a sound that did not belong to that order: the rapid whirling of wheels, a hard, eager thunder on the road, drawing nearer as if the night itself were being driven back. The lady laid her trumps down. Her heart beat with a strange violence, as though it recognized, before her mind dared, what the ears had already translated.

Whirr came the wheels; the carriage stopped at the very door. A parley at the gate—voices low, metal clinking, a latch complaining—then steps. Mrs. Betty appeared, her face radiant with joy though her eyes were full of tears, the way a saucepan will shine even while the contents boil over. And behind her—tall, young, flushed with the ride, smelling of road-dust and horse-sweat and the sharp clean leather of reins—entered Harry.

The chaplain, forgetting his clerical gravity, slapped his cards down with a huzzay. Lady Maria turned as white as linen, rose, tottered a pace, and with a shriek that was half laughter and half a sob, flung herself into her cousin’s arms.

If he kissed her a hundred times, or a thousand, or ran through all Catullus’s reckoning and still found himself in debt, no honest person need cry out. She clung to him as though the world had tried to unhand her and he alone was firm. Her tears came hot and plentiful upon his shoulder. In that homely room, with its poor supper and its stale candle-smell, she looked handsomer than she had looked in any fine drawing-room; for there is a beauty that is not bought with powder and silk, but with relief.

“You are both free to go home,” were Harry’s first words, brisk as a key turning.

“Get my lady’s hat and cardinal, Betty. And, Chaplain, we’ll smoke a pipe together at our lodgings. It will refresh me after my ride.”

The chaplain, whose feelings were a tinder always ready, burst into tears as he seized Harry’s hand and kissed it, praying God to bless his generous young patron. Harry felt, with a pleasant glow, the sweetness of being the cause of joy. It is a good thing, indeed, to turn sorrow into comfort; to see faces brighten as a hearth brightens when the fire has been fed. He walked beside his rescued princess with his hat cocked and his young vanity not a little pleased. In his mind, trumpets and shawms played; the very air seemed to applaud him; and if it was only that he had paid money and driven hard, he felt as though he had slain a dragon.

Yet the night did not end at the gate.

Back at their lodgings, Monsieur Barbeau—ever obsequious—had sent over a cold supper as if to crown the adventure: partridges with their skin browned and aromatic even when cold, the bird’s faint wild sweetness lingering under the salt; and ancient Burgundy, deep and perfumed, that rose from the glass with a rich, cellar-breathed warmth. The crackle of the pipe—tobacco’s dark, earthy smell—filled the room. Their talk ran on; the wine ran on; the hours, like a good sauce, reduced themselves to a potent thickness.

Mr. Sampson continued prodigiously affected. He was one of those men whose whole nature is an instrument—quick to take any tune, grief or gratitude, laughter or hate. His profession had trained him to summon tears as readily as he might summon a text, and, for the moment, he was exactly what he acted: a grateful dependant, melted by kindness. He would weep with the widow and the orphan, and, as soon as the door closed, roar with Jack over a bottle in the tavern opposite. He gave money readily and forgot repayment as easily as he forgot last week’s resolution. This night, his heart—if heart it was—overflowed in adoration of Harry Warrington; and in all London, perhaps, the unlucky Fortunate Youth could not have found a more dangerous companion than a man so fluent in feeling.

With each bumper, the chaplain’s admiration swelled; with each bumper, Harry’s notion of the splendour of his house swelled too, for Burgundy had always made him eloquent on that point.

“The younger branch of our family,” said Harry, with a superb air, “have treated you scurvily; but, by Jove, Sampson my boy, I’ll stand by you!”

Sampson’s eyes shone wet. Harry, warmed by wine and the delight of playing Providence, went further still.

“You said you had a sister at boarding-school. You will want money for her, sir. Here is a little bill which may help to pay her schooling.”

And he pushed a bank-note across the table, as lightly as a man might push across the salt.

Again Sampson was affected almost beyond bearing. He set the note a little away from him, like something too hot to touch.

“Mr. Warrington,” he cried, “I—I don’t deserve your kindness—by George, I don’t!” and he swore it as if an oath could make it true.

“Psha!” said Harry. “I have plenty more of ’em. There was no money in that confounded pocket-book which I lost last week.”

“No, sir. There was no money,” said Sampson, dropping his head.

“Hallo!” Harry’s colour rose. “How do you know, Mr. Chaplain?”

“I know because I am a villain, sir,” Sampson said. “I am not worthy of your kindness. I told you so. I found the book, sir, that night, when you had too much wine at Barbeau’s.”

“And read the letters?” Harry started up, crimson with shame and anger.

“They told me nothing I did not know, sir,” said the chaplain, with that odd mixture of boldness and abasement some men can contrive. “You have had spies about you whom you little suspect—from whom you are much too young and simple to be able to keep your secret.”

Harry’s voice sharpened. “Are those stories about Lady Fanny, and my cousin Will and his doings, true then?”

“Yes, they are true,” sighed Sampson. “The house of Castlewood has not been fortunate, sir, since your honour’s branch—the elder branch—left it.”

“Sir, you don’t dare for to breathe a word against my Lady Maria!” Harry cried.

“Oh, not for worlds!” Sampson answered quickly, with a queer look—half fear, half calculation. “I may think she is too old for your honour, and that ’tis a pity you should not have a wife better suited to your age, though I admit she looks very young for hers, and hath every virtue and accomplishment.”

“She is too old, Sampson, I know she is,” Harry said, with a dignity that tried to master the hurt. “But she has my word, and you see, sir, how fond she is of me. Go bring me the letters, sir, which you found, and let me try and forgive you for having seized upon them.”

“My benefactor, let me try and forgive myself!” cried Sampson; and he went to his chamber, leaving Harry alone with the remnants of supper—the partridge bones, the wine-stains, the tobacco-smoke that hung in the curtains like a confession.

Sampson returned presently, looking very pale.

“What has happened, sir?” Harry asked imperiously.

The chaplain held out the pocket-book.

“With your name in it, sir.”

“My brother’s name in it,” said Harry; “it was George who gave it to me.”

“I kept it in a locked chest, sir, in which I left it this morning before I was taken by those people. Here is the book, sir, but the letters are gone. My trunk and valise have also been tampered with. And I am a miserable, guilty man, unable to make you the restitution which I owe you.”

He clasped his hands, and his whole body took the attitude of tragedy—as if grief were a garment he could put on.

Who had been in the rooms during their absence? The landlady, white with alarm at being suspected, was ready to drop to her knees and swear nobody had entered. Indeed, Harry’s room showed no disorder; and from Sampson’s scanty wardrobe and possessions, nothing seemed missing save those papers—those letters—that the chaplain lamented.

Whose interest was it to seize them?

Not Lady Maria’s. She had been a prisoner all day when the seizure was made. If there was guilt here, it was elsewhere. The sudden taking of the two; Case, the house-steward’s secret journey to London; Case, who knew the shoemaker at whose house Sampson lodged in town, and who knew the hidden arrangements and old sores of the Esmond family—these things might have pointed, in Sampson’s mind, to the Baroness Bernstein. Yet why arrest Lady Maria? Sampson knew nothing of the particular letter Maria had lost; the poor lady had not thought to confide that secret to him.

But Harry—swollen with self-satisfaction, warmed by wagers won, by the feeling of rescue, by the savour of partridge and the velvet punch of ancient Burgundy—was in no humour to sift the matter. He accepted Sampson’s vows of contrition, his promises of future fidelity. He reached out his hand with a grand forgiveness.

When the chaplain swore that henceforth he would be Harry’s truest, humblest friend and follower, ready to die for him at any moment, Harry answered, majestically, “I think, Sampson, you would; I hope you would. My family—the Esmond family—has always been accustomed to have faithful friends round about ’em—and to reward ’em too. The wine’s with you, Chaplain. What toast do you call, sir?”

“I call a blessing on the house of Esmond-Warrington!” cried the chaplain, with real tears.

“We are the elder branch, sir. My grandfather was the Marquis of Esmond,” Harry declared, his noble voice growing slightly thick. “Here’s to you, Chaplain—and I forgive you, sir—and God bless you, sir—and if you had been took for three times as much, I’d have paid it. Why, what’s that I see through the shutters? I am blest if the sun hasn’t risen again! We have no need of candles to go to bed, ha, ha!”

And with that, extending his blessing once more, he went off to sleep.

About noon, Madame de Bernstein sent a servant to say she would be glad if her nephew would come over and drink a dish of chocolate with her. Harry rose, dressed, and walked to his aunt’s lodgings.

She remarked at once, not without pleasure, a change in his toilette: the cut of his coat, the air of his linen, the small new elegancies that London tailors and my Lord March’s purveyors could bestow. She called him “my dearest child,” thanked him for his noble, generous behaviour to dear Maria, and spoke with dramatic emphasis of the shock of that seizure in church—how it had struck her as if a pistol had gone off at the altar.

Then, as if the world always must come back to accounts, she sighed over Wednesday night: she had lost three hundred to Lady Yarmouth, and was quite a sec.

“Why,” said the Baroness, “I had to send Case to London to my agent to get me money to pay—I could not leave Tunbridge in her debt.”

“So Case did go to London?” Harry asked, the words coming out with more meaning than he meant them to carry.

“Of course he did: the Baroness de Bernstein can’t afford to say she is court d’argent. Canst thou lend me some, child?”

“I can give your ladyship twenty-two pounds,” Harry said, blushing. “I have but forty-four left till I get my Virginian remittances. I have bought horses and clothes, and been very extravagant, aunt.”

“And rescued your poor relations in distress, you prodigal good boy. No, child, I do not want thy money. I can give thee some. Here is a note upon my agent for fifty pounds, vaurien! Go and spend it, and be merry! I dare say thy mother will repay me, though she does not love me.”

She looked quite affectionate as she held out her hand; Harry kissed it. Her fingers were neat still, though age lived in the joints.

“Your mother did not love me,” she went on, “but your mother’s father did once. Mind, sir, you always come to me when you have need of me.”

When Beatrix chose to be gracious, no one could exceed her. Yet her grace had a blade in it.

“I can’t help loving you, child,” she continued, “and yet I am so angry with you that I have scarce the patience to speak to you. So you have actually engaged yourself to poor Maria, who is as old as your mother? What will Madam Esmond say? She may live three hundred years, and you will not have wherewithal to support yourselves.”

“I have ten thousand pounds from my father, of my own, now my poor brother is gone,” Harry answered. “That will go some way.”

“Why, the interest will not keep you in card-money.”

“We must give up cards,” said Harry, with the brave simplicity of a man who has never yet been truly hungry.

“It is more than Maria is capable of. She will pawn the coat off your back to play. The rage for it runs in all my brother’s family—in me too, I own it. I warned you. I prayed you not to play with them, and now a lad of twenty to engage himself to a woman of forty-two!—to write letters on his knees and signed with his heart’s blood (which he spells like hartshorn), and say that he will marry no other woman than his adorable cousin, Lady Maria Esmond. Oh! it’s cruel—cruel!”

“Great heavens! madam, who showed you my letter?” Harry cried, the blood mounting again.

“An accident. She fainted when she was taken by those bailiffs. Brett cut her laces for her; and when she was carried off, poor thing, we found a little sachet on the floor, which I opened, not knowing in the least what it contained. And in it was Mr. Harry Warrington’s precious letter. And here, sir, is the case.”

She held out the little locket. Harry’s heart gave a sick pang—less at her having read, than at what might be made of it.

“Great heavens! why didn’t she destroy it?” he thought; and aloud, “I—I will give it back to Maria,” he said, reaching for it.

“My dear, I have burned the foolish letter,” the old lady said quietly.

It was as if a hot cinder had been dropped into the conversation: a sharp shock, then a spreading heat. Harry drew back, struck through with relief and shame in the same instant.

“If you choose to betray me I must take the consequence,” Madame Bernstein went on. “If you choose to write another, I cannot help thee. But, in that case, Harry Esmond, I had rather never see thee again. Will you keep my secret? Will you believe an old woman who loves you and knows the world better than you do? I tell you, if you keep that foolish promise, misery and ruin are surely in store for you. What is a lad like you in the hands of a wily woman of the world, who makes a toy of you? She has entrapped you into a promise, and your old aunt has cut the strings and set you free. Go back again! Betray me if you will, Harry.”

“I am not angry with you, aunt—I wish I were,” Harry said, his voice thick with conflicting feeling. “I—I shall not repeat what you told me.”

“Maria never will, child—mark my words!” the Baroness cried eagerly. “She will never own that she has lost that paper. She will tell you that she has it.”

“But I am sure she—she is very fond of me; you should have seen her last night,” Harry faltered.

“Must I tell more stories against my own flesh and blood?” the Baroness sobbed out. “Child, you do not know her past life!”

“And I must not, and I will not!” Harry cried, starting up. “Written or said—it does not matter which! But my word is given; they may play with such things in England, but we gentlemen of Virginia don’t break ’em. If she holds me to my word, she shall have me. If we are miserable, as I dare say we shall be, I’ll take a firelock, and go join the King of Prussia, or let a ball put an end to me.”

“I—I have no more to say.” The Baroness’s voice grew stiff again, as if she were drawing on armour. “Will you be pleased to ring that bell? I—I wish you a good morning, Mr. Warrington.”

She dropped a stately curtsey, rose with the help of her tortoiseshell stick, and turned toward the door. But at the first step she put her hand to her heart, sank back upon the sofa, and shed—strange sight—the first tears that had fallen for long years from Beatrix Esmond’s eyes.

Harry was moved beyond any courtly speech. He knelt by her, seized her cold hand, and kissed it.

He told her, in his artless way, how keenly he had felt her love, and how with all his heart he returned it.

“Ah, aunt!” he said, bowing his comely head over her hand, “you don’t know what a villain I feel myself. When you told me, just now, how that paper was burned—oh! I was ashamed to think how glad I was.”

Hot drops fell from his eyes onto her hand. She had loved this boy; and in half a century of wit and world, never perhaps had she felt anything so tender and so pure as the pain of seeing him honest.

Her hard heart, long practised in mastery, was wounded into softness. She put both her hands on his shoulders and lightly kissed his forehead.

“You will not tell her what I have done, child?” she whispered.

He declared never—never.

And at her summons, demure Mrs. Brett entered, and found aunt and nephew in that sentimental attitude: the old woman’s tears drying like salt on fine china, the young man’s loyalty set like bread in the oven—warm, swelling, and not yet aware what it would cost to eat.

Tunbridge had begun to taste of itself—warm mineral water and colder talk, the same hands forever shuffling the same greasy cards, the same compliments turned and returned until their edges wore thin. Madame de Bernstein, whose appetite for company was as exacting as her palate, declared Bath would restore her: more tables, more lights, more bustle; and, before that, a round of country visits to remind old acquaintances that she had not forgotten them, only outgrown them.

Harry promised—without the softness that makes a promise a gift—to ride with Lady Maria and the chaplain as far as Castlewood. The road took them again by Oakhurst, by that trim village where hedges clipped the wind into a mild whisper, and where the kitchen-smoke hung low and honest over the chimneys as if the very air were being fed. Lady Maria, perched in her carriage like a judge in ribbons, made keen, pecking remarks about the Oakhurst young ladies—the way they had looked, the way they had lingered, the way their mother had measured him as though he were a side of beef to be bargained for.

Her words pricked him. He said, sharply, that since her ladyship hated and abused those kind folk, he would not inflict them upon her again; and he would not so much as turn his head toward their gate. At the inn a few miles on, he carried his sulk like a cloak. Supper was set—roast fowl gone dry at the joints, a dish of eggs over-browned, bread that smelled faintly of the last loaf’s sourness, and wine warmed by the room rather than the hand. Lady Maria tried smiles, those little sugared pellets of the face meant to sweeten bitterness; Harry’s mouth stayed flat. She tried tears—she could summon them as easily as a cook can summon steam by lifting a lid; he watched them as one watches rain on a window, without reaching to wipe.

Her querulous remarks fetched only a growl. The chaplain sat on, pipe and patience, as if by instruction, and Lady Maria—thwarted of the private moment she wanted—was forced at last to rise, to be bowed out with stubborn politeness, and handed to landlady and maid like a parcel he was glad to see sealed away.

What horse was it, then, that galloped out of the inn-yard ten minutes after she had gone? An hour later, when Mrs. Betty came bustling for the smelling-salts, she found Parson Sampson alone, the room hazed with tobacco, the pipe’s faint crackle the loudest sound. Mr. Warrington? Gone to bed, perhaps; gone to take a walk in the moonlight, perhaps—how was a chaplain to know? Sampson answered with a dull calm that made the maid sniff, as if truth itself had an odour she distrusted.

In the morning, Harry was ready as if he had slept like a stone—only his brow looked like a storm. He took his place beside Lady Maria’s carriage, and rode black-faced, hardly speaking. Lady Maria, in her own mind, turned a fear over and over like a bead between finger and thumb: Great heavens! she must have told him that she stole it.

It had begun, indeed, on that steep hill three miles from Oakhurst on the Westerham road. They had walked to ease the horses, Lady Maria leaning on Harry’s arm as though she had a right to his strength. She was in love with him—warmly, shamelessly, with the zeal of one who has endured long hunger and thinks herself at last seated before a feast. She warbled into his ear vows and protests, lines remembered from the few plays she knew, the scraps stuck in her mind like herbs in a mortar, pounded out for use when she thought them needed. As she grew fonder, he grew colder. Her face, fresh enough, well preserved by prudence and powders, still showed the fine webbing of forty years; and the weight of her arm upon his seemed suddenly intolerable. To think—so his mind ran—that all his life that weight was to be there, that clinging fondness, that claim. He cursed the hot evening, the hot wine, the moonlight walk that had ended in a pledge; he felt fatally bound by his own foolish mouth.

And she, delighted by her own tenderness, praised him until praise became an instrument of torture. “My champion—my Henrico—my preserver!” she sighed, clinging closer. “Thy Molinda faithful ever, ever!” And then, with that eager menace lovers use when they fear losing what they have not earned, she murmured, “Ah, child! have I not thy precious image, thy precious hair, thy precious writing here? Shall it not go with me to the grave? It would, sir—were I to meet with unkindness from my Henrico!”

Harry started—felt his arm jerk as if it would drop hers. That little silken case: Madame Bernstein had given it him; she had sworn she burned what it held—hair and note. And yet Lady Maria had it still, pressed to her heart, warm as bread kept under a cloth. Lady Maria felt, at his start, her first pang of remorse—not at lying, but at being found out in a lie; for discovery is the whip many consciences require. Heaven help us: if some people were put to sackcloth and ashes for fibbing, they would never be out of them.

Castlewood received them with its old dignity: damp stone, tall trees that turned the wind into a low organ-note, and a stable-yard alive with the clop and snort of horses, the familiar music of a great house that feeds and is fed by beasts. My lord was away; the ladies too. The only Esmond at home was Mr. Will, who came back from partridge-shooting as the chaise rolled in. The smell of gunpowder still hung about him, and feathers were caught in the seams of his coat like evidence. He turned very pale when he saw Harry; Harry gave him a scowl that was a recognition and a sentence at once.

At supper they sat with Lady Maria and spoke civilly, because her presence was a napkin laid over the mess of their feelings. The talk was flat: races, bets, the common fodder of such men. Will had been to some? To several. He had done well? Pretty well. Harry’s voice stayed too calm.

“And you have brought back my horse sound?” Harry asked.

“My horse! what horse?” Will said.

“What horse? My horse,” Harry returned, curt as a butcher’s cleaver.

“Protest I don’t understand you,” Will said, and tried to laugh.

“The brown horse for which I played you, and which I won of you the night before you rode away upon it,” Harry said, with a sternness that made the very knives seem sharper. “You remember the horse, Mr. Esmond.”

“Mr. Warrington, I perfectly well remember playing you for a horse, which my servant handed over to you on the day of your departure.”

“The chaplain was present at our play,” Harry said, still mild. “Mr. Sampson, will you be umpire between us?”

“I am bound to decide that Mr. Warrington played for the brown horse,” Sampson answered, with a glance that begged Will to be wise.

“Well, he got the other one,” Will muttered, and showed his teeth in a grin.

“And sold it for thirty shillings,” Harry said—always that careful calm, like a cook’s hand steady over a dangerous flame.

“Thirty shillings? and a devilish good price, too, for the broken-kneed old rip! Ha, ha!”

“Not a word more. ’Tis only a question about a bet, my dear Lady Maria. Shall I serve you some more chicken?” Harry’s courtesy, while she remained, was studied and bright as a polished dish. When she rose, he followed, bowed, and shut the door on her with the most courtly farewell—as if closing a pantry against vermin.

He stood a moment listening to her retreating rustle. Then he bade the servants leave. When they were out, he locked the heavy door and put the key in his pocket.

The click sounded like the snap of a trap.

Will, pale now not from surprise but from fear forced into anger, stared over his punch and swore, asking what the devil Harry meant by that.

“I guess there’s going to be a quarrel,” Harry said, almost gently, “and there is no use in having these fellows look on at rows between their betters.”

“Who is going to quarrel here, I should like to know?” Will said, and his hand went to a knife as if it knew its own business better than he did.

“Mr. Sampson,” Harry said, “you were present when I played Mr. Will fifty guineas against his brown horse?”

“Against his horse!” Will bawled.

“I am not such a fool as you take me for,” Harry answered, and his Virginian blood, long held in, spoke through his civility. “Although I do come from Virginia!” He repeated, steadily, “Mr. Sampson, you were here when I played the Honourable William Esmond, Esquire, fifty guineas against his brown horse?”

“I must own it, sir,” Sampson said, deprecatingly.

“I don’t own no such a thing,” Will said, forcing a laugh that sounded like a cracked bell.

“No, sir: because it costs you no more pains to lie than to cheat,” Harry said, and walked up to him. “Hands off, Mr. Chaplain, and see fair play! Because you are no better than a—ha—”

What he called him was swallowed by action. Will, with the swiftness of one who prefers violence to being named, snatched a wine bottle and flung it full at Harry’s head. Harry bobbed aside; the bottle flew across the room and smashed against the opposite wainscot, cracking the painted face of an Esmond ancestor—port spilling in a dark gush that splattered the chaplain’s white wig and cheeks so that he looked, for a moment, baptized in blood.

“Great heavens, gentlemen, I pray you to be quiet!” cried Sampson, dripping with wine and indignation.

But men in that heat do not remember the Church’s commands. Will seized the large silver-handled knife and lunged. Harry caught his right wrist in his left, just as he had seen the boxers do at Marybone, and drove a quick, hard blow into Will’s nose. The crack of it seemed to change the room’s acoustics: the oak panels threw back the sound, sharp and mean. Will reeled against the wall; the knife fell; Harry kicked it under the table with the neatness of one clearing a kitchen floor of broken crockery.

Will had been to Marybone too—to Hockley-in-the-Hole; he knew the language of fists. Blood ran; his breath rasped; then he dashed forward, head down, as if his skull were a ram and Harry’s belly a door.

Harry had seen that blunt savage charge among the negroes on his mother’s estate—two bodies meeting like cannon-balls. But he had also marked the white man’s trick. He skipped aside, and, as Will rushed past, Harry swung a tremendous blow on the right ear. Will went down, striking his head on the heavy oak table with a thud that made the glasses tremble, and lay senseless on the floor.

“Chaplain, you will bear witness that it has been a fair fight!” Harry said, still quivering but forcing his face into coolness. He drew the key, opened the door. Behind it, in the lobby, three or four servants were gathered, their ears and fear pressed close. The crash and shout and oath had carried through the house like a harsh drumbeat.

They entered and saw two victims bedabbled with red: the chaplain painted in port, and Mr. Will stretched out in his own gore.

“Mr. Sampson will bear witness that I struck fair, and that Mr. Esmond hit the first blow,” Harry said. “Undo his neckcloth, somebody—he may be dead; and get a fleam, Gumbo, and bleed him. Stop! He is coming to himself! Lift him up, you, and tell a maid to wash the floor.”

In a minute Will did begin to return. First his eyes rolled—rather, his eye, one swollen shut by Harry’s earlier blow. Then came a gasp and a moan, then a flood of swearing, fluent as ale from a tapped cask.

“He is getting well,” Harry said, dryly.

“Oh, praise be Mussy!” sighed sentimental Betty, whose heart was soft even when her tongue was sharp.

“Ask him, Gumbo, whether he would like any more?” Harry said, with a stern humour.

“Massa Harry say, wool you like any maw?” Gumbo asked obediently, bending over the prostrate gentleman with that grave politeness that can sting worse than insult.

“No, curse you, you black devil!” Will cried, striking up at Gumbo. Gumbo explained afterward to pitying Betty, “So he nearly cut my tongue in two in my mouf!” “No—that is, yes! You infernal Mohock! Why does not somebody kick him out of the place?”

“Because nobody dares, Mr. Esmond,” Harry answered, arranging his ruffles—his ruffled ruffles—with the air of a man setting his table after a disturbance.

“And nobody won’t neither,” growled the men. They had come to love Harry, who spoke to them like men when he remembered to, whereas Will had no one’s good word.

“We know all’s fair, sir. It ain’t the first time Master William have been served so.”

“And I hope it won’t be the last,” shrilled Betty. “To go for to strike a poor black gentleman so!”

Will, wiping his bleeding face with a napkin, gathered himself and slunk toward the door like a whipped cur. His curses left him in a thick trail, as if his mouth were a chimney belching soot.

“Surely it’s manners to say good night to the company. Good night, Mr. Esmond,” Harry called after him; the joke was not brilliant, but it warmed Harry inwardly like a dram.

“He’s ad his zopper, and he goes to baid!” Betty said in her native dialect, and everyone laughed outright except Will, who disappeared.

Harry’s wit continued next morning. He sent Will a note to ask if he fancied a ride to town or anywheres else; if for London, Harry would frighten the highwaymen on Hounslow Heath and look a very genteel figure at the Chocolate House. Will’s reply, if he sent one, suggested a destination not on Hounslow.

And there came, too, the inevitable domestic intrusion of romance: a simpering maiden at Harry’s door, and Gumbo entering with something white and triangular pinched between his dark fingers. A letter, of course. Harry groaned before he opened it, as one groans when a dish arrives too sweet, too rich, too much of itself.

Molinda greeting her Enrico, and so forth—no sleep, no peace, vows, fears, jealousy dressed as devotion; he must never, never quarrel and be so cruel again. The words ran on, a syrup with no sharpness to cut it, and for Harry, already sickened by his own pledge, the sweetness cloyed.

After the scandal with cousin Will, Harry’s dignity would not permit him to stay longer at Castlewood. He wrote a majestic letter to my lord of the house explaining what had passed; and as he called in Parson Sampson to supervise the document, it no doubt contained none of the odd spellings that straggled through his common correspondence. He told poor Maria that, having blackened the eye and damaged the nose of a son of the family, he could hardly remain under that roof with grace; she was forced to agree that his absence would best become him.

Of course she wept at parting. He would go to London and see younger beauties; he would find none who would love him like his fond Maria. Harry, if he felt anything, did not show it. The moment he crossed Castlewood Bridge his spirits rose as if the air itself had changed flavour. He made his horses whisk at ten miles an hour; he sang to them to go along; he nodded to pretty girls by the roadside; he chucked the landlady under the chin. He was not inconsolable.

Truth was, London called him like music heard far off: the thrum of wheels on stones, the shouting of link-boys, the fiddles and laughter from pleasure gardens, the rattle of dice on baize at clubs—an acoustic feast after Tunbridge’s tame murmur. The petty society of women and cards had become child’s-play now that he had tasted the city.

By the time he reached London again, almost all the four-and-forty pounds he had at Tunbridge had slipped away—like flour through careless fingers. Further supplies were necessary. Regarding these he made himself easy. There were two sums of five thousand pounds, in his own and his brother’s name, of which he was master. He would take up a little money; a run or two of good luck at play could replace it. Meanwhile he must live as became his station, and Madam Esmond must understand that a gentleman of his rank cannot keep fitting company, nor appear as he ought, upon a miserable pittance of two hundred a year.

He lodged at the Bedford Coffee-House as before, but only briefly; he wanted a more fashionable kitchen, as it were, for his life—nearer the Court-end, where reputations were baked and served hot.
