He fixed on rooms in Bond Street and installed himself and Gumbo; his horses stood at a neighbouring livery-stable, where the constant stamping and whinnying, the ring of iron shoes, made a rough counterpoint to the street’s finer noises.

Tailors, mercers, shoemakers were summoned. Not without a pang—like setting aside a mourning cloth too soon—he laid aside black and appeared in lace, hat and waistcoat. Gumbo, deft at hair as any French valet, dressed Harry’s locks, flung powder into them until they smelled of starch and faint perfume; and soon Harry’s head was as modish as any gentleman’s in the Mall. He drove his phaeton in the Ring, where eyes appraised him as they appraise a new dish—curiosity first, then judgement. Reports of his great wealth had long preceded him; London, which loves nothing so much as an exotic fortune, was eager to taste this fortunate Virginian.

Until he could be balloted for in season, Lord March had written down his name at White’s Chocolate-House as a distinguished gentleman from America. There were as yet but few people of fashion in town; but with a pocket full of money at one-and-twenty, a young man can make himself happy even out of season. Harry was determined to enjoy.

He ordered Mr. Draper to sell five hundred pounds of his stock. What would his poor mother have said, could she have heard the scratch of that pen as the first slice was cut from his patrimony? He dined at taverns where the air was thick with roasted meat and old smoke, where gravy clung to plates and laughter rose in waves; he supped at the club, introduced by Jack Morris with loud eulogies to such gentlemen as were in town. Life and youth and pleasure were before him; the wine was set a-running, and he was greedy to drink. Far away in the west, a pious widow might be at her prayers, shaping his name in a tongue that held the old country’s cadences; behind the trees at Oakhurst, perhaps, a tender little heart beat for him, keeping time with the farm’s honest sounds—milk pails, swishing brooms, the lowing of cows. When the Prodigal Son was away carousing, were not love and forgiveness still watching for him?

Among the unprinted letters of the late Lord Orford there is one the learned editor Mr. Peter Cunningham has omitted, perhaps doubting its truth. I have seen only a copy among the Warrington papers in Madam Esmond’s prim handwriting, noted, “Mr. H. Walpole’s account of my son Henry at London, and of Baroness Tusher,—wrote to General Conway.”

“ARLINGTON STREET, Friday Night.

“I have come away, child, for a day or two from my devotions to our Lady of Strawberry. Have I not been on my knees to her these three weeks, and aren’t the poor old joints full of rheumatism? A fit took me that I would pay London a visit, that I would go to Vauxhall and Ranelagh. Quoi! May I not have my rattle as well as other elderly babies? Suppose, after being so long virtuous, I take a fancy to cakes and ale, shall your reverence say nay to me? George Selwyn and Tony Storer and your humble servant took boat at Westminster t’other night. Was it Tuesday?—no, Tuesday I was with their Graces of Norfolk, who are just from Tunbridge—it was Wednesday. How should I know? Wasn’t I dead drunk with a whole pint of lemonade I took at White’s?

“The Norfolk folk had been entertaining me on Tuesday with the account of a young savage Iroquois, Choctaw, or Virginian, who has lately been making a little noise in our quarter of the globe. He is an offshoot of that disreputable family of Esmond, Castlewood, of whom all the men are gamblers and spendthrifts, and all the women—well, I shan’t say the word, lest Lady Ailesbury should be looking over your shoulder. Both the late lords, my father told me, were in his pay, and the last one, a beau of Queen Anne’s reign, from a viscount advanced to be an earl through the merits and intercession of his notorious old sister Bernstein, late Tusher, née Esmond—a great beauty, too, of her day, a favourite of the old Pretender. She sold his secrets to my papa, who paid her for them; and being nowise particular in her love for the Stuarts, came over to the august Hanoverian house at present reigning over us. ‘Will Horace Walpole’s tongue never stop scandal?’ says your wife over your shoulder. I kiss your ladyship’s hand. I am dumb. The Bernstein is a model of virtue. She had no good reasons for marrying her father’s chaplain. Many of the nobility omit the marriage altogether. She wasn’t ashamed of being Mrs. Tusher, and didn’t take a German Baroncino for a second husband, whom nobody out of Hanover ever saw. The Yarmouth bears no malice. Esther and Vashti are very good friends, and have been cheating each other at Tunbridge at cards all the summer.

“‘And what has all this to do with the Iroquois?’ says your ladyship. The Iroquois has been at Tunbridge, too—not cheating, perhaps, but winning vastly. They say he has bled Lord March of thousands—Lord March, by whom so much blood hath been shed, that he has quarrelled with everybody, fought with everybody, rode over everybody, been fallen in love with by everybody’s wife except Mr. Conway’s, and not excepting her present Majesty, the Countess of England, Scotland, France and Ireland, Queen of Walmoden and Yarmouth, whom Heaven preserve to us.

“You know an offensive little creature, de par le monde, one Jack Morris, who skips in and out of all the houses of London. When we were at Vauxhall, Mr. Jack gave us a nod under the shoulder of a pretty young fellow enough, on whose arm he was leaning, and who appeared hugely delighted with the enchantments of the garden. Lord, how he stared at the fireworks! Gods, how he huzzayed at the singing of a horrible painted wench who shrieked the ears off my head! A twopenny string of glass beads and a strip of tawdry cloth are treasures in Iroquois-land, and our savage valued them accordingly.

“A buzz went about the place that this was the fortunate youth. He won three hundred at White’s last night very genteelly from Rockingham and my precious nephew, and here he was bellowing and huzzaying over the music so as to do you good to hear. I do not love a puppet-show, but I love to treat children to one, Miss Conway! I present your ladyship my compliments, and hope we shall go and see the dolls together.

“When the singing woman came down from her throne, Jack Morris must introduce my Virginian to her. I saw him blush up to the eyes, and make her, upon my word, a very fine bow, such as I had no idea was practised in wigwams. ‘There is a certain jenny squaw about her, and that’s why the savage likes her,’ George said—a joke certainly not as brilliant as a firework. After which it seemed to me that the savage and the savages retired together.

“Having had a great deal too much to eat and drink three hours before, my partners must have chicken and rack-punch at Vauxhall, where George fell asleep straightway, and for my sins I must tell Tony Storer what I knew about this Virginian’s amiable family, especially some of the Bernstein’s antecedents, and the history of another elderly beauty of the family, a certain Lady Maria, who was au mieux with the late Prince of Wales. What did I say? I protest not half of what I knew, and of course not a tenth part of what I was going to tell, for who should start out upon us but my savage, this time quite red in the face; and in his war paint. The wretch had been drinking fire-water in the next box!

“He cocked his hat, clapped his hand to his sword, asked which of the gentleman was it that was maligning his family? so that I was obliged to entreat him not to make such a noise, lest he should wake my friend, Mr. George Selwyn. And I added, ‘I assure you, sir, I had no idea that you were near me, and most sincerely apologise for giving you pain.’”

In the London of Harry Warrington’s first season, men still quarrelled in coffee-houses over the ancients and the moderns—over whether Homer or Pope held the richer marrow, whether the old tongues were a better storehouse than the new. It was a dispute conducted with as much heat as a stew set too suddenly upon the fire, and with about as much regard for the tenderness of the meat. Meanwhile the city itself went on, chopping and boiling and broiling its daily life with a hard, metallic perseverance: wheels on stones; hammers in alleys; the thin cry of hawkers threading the thicker roar of coaches; the forever-clap of doors; the drone of the great town like a kettledrum under every conversation.

Harry, for his part, had no more mind for those learned skirmishes than a hungry young gentleman has for a sermon when the cover is just lifting from the dish. He was newly made of age, newly made of fashion, newly made (so he fancied) of consequence; and he took London as he took his suppers—rapidly, with appetite, and with a youth’s confidence that the bill will somehow be paid.

If one were to set down in plain ink the entertainments of that world—its late tables, its bold wagers, its painted faces, its careless oaths and careless quarrels—there are daughters of our present decorum who would clap a hand to the page as a cook claps a lid upon a pot beginning to boil over. There are guardians who would cry out, “Away with it!” as though a frank description were a contagion. And yet a century makes saints and sinners of the same people by a mere change of vocabulary, by the slow drift of what words may be spoken aloud. The thing is, society—like a master in a kitchen—sets rules not because the ingredients alter, but because the diners’ palates grow delicate. You may cover the legs of a table with muslin and call it modesty; you also muffle the sound of the room and pretend the silence is virtue.

So, when Harry Warrington is found in lodgings in Bond Street; when he rides down to Newmarket for October; when he dines at White’s ordinary and stays over cards; when he is seen in company at the Shakspeare’s Head or the Bedford; when he keeps late hours and bright company, and is no enemy to a bowl of punch—who shall affect astonishment? Youth has its own seasoning, sharp and heady, and too often it is shaken in by other hands.

The town’s pleasures had their music, and their ugliness too. In the daytime, St. James’s Park could sound almost pastoral for an instant—wind in a row of trees, the splash of waterfowl—until the next carriage crushed that fragile hush under iron-bound wheels. At night, taverns and gaming-rooms made their own ecology of noise: dice clicking like teeth; cards slapped down; laughter, which was sometimes only cruelty with a ribbon on it; quarrels that rose in pitch until steel sang out of scabbards. The very language of the place encouraged excess—each oath a kind of percussion, each boast a brass note—so that a man could be driven to folly as much by the room’s din as by the wine in his blood.

Mr. Sampson—who in a pulpit could lash Vice as though he had it tied to a post—was not above stepping from chapel into supper with the very lads he had just anathematised. He would trample Drunkenness in rhetoric, and then, after service, accept a chair at the Star and Garter; mix a bowl at the Bedford Head; take a hand at whist in Mr. Warrington’s lodgings or in my Lord March’s rooms, wherever there was good company and something savoury on the table. He was, in this, as London is: condemning with one voice, indulging with another; and the two voices seldom heard each other clearly for the general uproar.

I am told I judge Harry too harshly. Perhaps I do. Perhaps I have imagined him a rake because I know the town is a rake, and because I know human nature will lean toward the warm hearth and the rich sauce when it is offered. But if you would have proof of his propriety, there lies a letter from him to his mother in Virginia; and in it you will find no confession, no midnight riot, no scent of spilled wine or singed wig, no admission of the watch-box or the roundhouse—only dutiful phrases, careful news, and the sort of domestic detail that can make a distant plantation kitchen seem nearer than Bond Street.

“BOND STREET, LONDON, October 25, 1756.

“HONORD MADAM— I take up my pen to acknowledge your honored favor of 10 July per Lively Virginia packet, which has duly come to hand, forwarded by our Bristol agent, and rejoice to hear that the prospect of the crops is so good. ’Tis Tully who says that agriculture is the noblest pursuit; how delightful when that pursuit is also prophetable!

“Since my last, dated from Tunbridge Wells, one or two insadence have occurred of which it is nessasery [the word is cut upon with a penknife, yet left, as if the writer thought the scar itself a sort of improvement] I should advise my honored Mother. Our party there broke up end of August: the partridge-shooting commencing. Baroness Bernstein, whose kindness to me has been most invariable, has been to Bath, her usual winter resort, and has made me a welcome present of a fifty-pound bill. I rode back with Rev. Mr. Sampson, whose instruction I find most valluble, and my cousin, Lady Maria, to Castlewood.

“I paid a flying visit on the way to my dear kind friends Col. and Mrs. Lambert, Oakhurst House, who send my honored mother their most affectionate remembrances. The youngest Miss Lambert, I grieve to say, was dellicate; and her parents in some anxiety.

“At Castlewood I lament to state my stay was short, owing to a quarrel with my cousin William. He is a young man of violent passions, and alas! addicted to liquor, when he has no controul over them. In a triffling dispute about a horse, high words arose between us, and he aymed a blow at me or its equivulent—which my Grandfathers my honored mothers child could not brook. I rejoyned, and feld him to the ground, whents he was carried almost sencelis to bed. I sent to enquire after his health in the morning: but having no further news of him, came away to London where I have been ever since with brief intavles of absence.

“Knowing you would wish me to see my dear Grandfathers University of Cambridge, I rode thither lately in company with some friends, passing through part of Harts, and lying at the famous bed of Ware. The October meeting was just begun at Cambridge when I went. I saw the students in their gownds and capps, and rode over to the famous Newmarket Heath, where there happened to be some races—my friend Lord Marchs horse Marrowbones by Cleaver coming off winner of a large steak. It was an amusing day—the jockeys, horses, etc., very different to our poor races at home—the betting awful—the richest noblemen here mix with the jox, and bett all round. Cambridge pleased me: especially King’s College Chapel, of a rich but elegant Gothick.

“I have been out into the world, and am made member of the Club at White’s, where I meet gentlemen of the first fashion. My Lords Rockingham, Carlisle, Orford, Bolingbroke, Coventry are of my friends, introduced to me by my Lord March, of whom I have often wrote before. Lady Coventry is a fine woman, but thinn. Every lady paints here, old and young; so, if you and Mountain and Fanny wish to be in fashion, I must send you out some roogepots: everybody plays—eight, ten, card-tables at every house on every receiving-night. I am sorry to say all do not play fair, and some do not pay fair. I have been obliged to sit down, and do as Rome does, and have actually seen ladies whom I could name take my counters from before my face!

“One day, his regiment the 20th being paraded in St. James’s Park, a friend of mine, Mr. Wolfe, did me the honour to present me to his Royal Highness the Captain-General, who was most gracious; a fat, jolly Prince, if I may speak so without disrespect, reminding me in his manner of that unhappy General Braddock; whom we knew to our sorrow last year. When he heard my name, and how dearest George had served and fallen in Braddock’s unfortunate campaign, he talked a great deal with me; asked why a young fellow like me did not serve too; why I did not go to the King of Prussia, who was a great General, and see a campaign or two; and whether that would not be better than dawdling about at routs and card-parties in London? I said, I would like to go with all my heart, but was an only son now, on leave from my mother, and belonged to our estate in Virginia. His Royal Highness said, Mr. Braddock had wrote home accounts of Mrs. Esmond’s loyalty, and that he would gladly serve me. Mr. Wolfe and I have waited on him since, at his Royal Highness’s house in Pall Mall. The latter, who is still quite a young man, made the Scots campaign with his Highness, whom Mr. Dempster loves so much at home. To be sure, he was too severe: if anything can be top severe against rebels in arms.

“Mr. Draper has had half the Stock, my late Papa’s property, transferred to my name. Until there can be no doubt of that painful loss in our family which I would give my right hand to replace, the remaining stock must remain in the trustees’ name in behalf of him who inherited it. Ah, dear mother! There is no day, scarce any hour, when I don’t think of him. I wish he were by me often. I feel like as if I was better when I am thinking of him, and would like, for the honour of my family, that he was representing of it here instead of— Honored madam, your dutiful and affectionate son,

“HENRY ESMOND WARRINGTON.”

And then, as if even duty must have its aftertaste, he adds in the postscript—where so many hearts, like careful housekeepers, hide their richest morsel—

“P.S.—I am like your sex, who always, they say, put their chief news in a poscrip. I had something to tell you about a person to whom my heart is engaged. I shall write more about it, which there is no hurry. Safice she is a nobleman’s daughter, and her family as good as our own.”

Thus does a young man write home: of crops, of chapels, of princes; of a quarrel made to sound like honour; of card-tables described with a decent frown; and of an engagement touched as lightly as a finger testing whether a loaf is done. Not a syllable of the kitchen heat of his life—no mention of the way town suppers smell after midnight, when candles have been burning too long and the air has taken in spilled claret, snuffed tallow, powder, pomatum, and the sweet-sour breath of fatigue. He gives his mother Cambridge stone and Newmarket turf; he does not give her the rasp of London’s nightly din, which gets into a man as smoke gets into cloth.

But there is another voice in the chapter of his life, and it comes from one who knows how the world seasons its traps.

“CLARGIS STREET, LONDON, October 23, 1756.

“I think, my good sister, we have been all our lives a little more than kin and less than kind, to use the words of a poet whom your dear father loved dearly. When you were born in our Western Principallitie, my mother was not as old as Isaac’s; but even then I was much more than old enough to be yours. And though she gave you all she could leave or give, including the little portion of love that ought to have been my share, yet, if we can have good will for one another, we may learn to do without affection: and some little kindness you owe me, for your son’s sake; as well as your father’s, whom I loved and admired more than any man I think ever I knew in this world: he was greater than almost all, though he made no noyse in it. I have seen very many who have, and, believe me, have found but few with such good heads and good harts as Mr. Esmond.

“Had we been better acquainted, I might have given you some advice regarding your young gentleman’s introduction to Europe, which you would have taken or not, as people do in this world. At least you would have sed afterwards, ‘What she counselled me was right, and had Harry done as Madam Beatrix wisht, it had been better for him.’ My good sister, it was not for you to know, or for me to whom you never wrote to tell you, but your boy in coming to England and Castlewood found but ill friends there; except one, an old aunt, of whom all kind of evil hath been spoken and sed these fifty years past—and not without cawse too, perhaps.

“Now, I must tell Harry’s mother what will doubtless scarce astonish her, that almost everybody who knows him loves him. He is prudent of his tongue, generous of his money, as bold as a lyon, with an imperious domineering way that sets well upon him; you know whether he is handsome or not: my dear, I like him none the less for not being over witty or wise, and never cared for your sett-the-Thames afire gentlemen, who are so much more clever than their neighbours. Your father’s great friend, Mr. Addison, seemed to me but a supercillious prig, and his follower, Sir Dick Steele, was not pleasant in his cupps, nor out of ’em. And (revenons a luy) your Master Harry will certainly, pot burn the river up with his wits. Of book-learning he is as ignorant as any lord in England, and for this I hold him none the worse. If Heaven have not given him a turn that way, ’tis of no use trying to bend him.

“Considering the place he is to hold in his own colony when he returns, and the stock he comes from, let me tell you, that he hath not means enough allowed him to support his station, and is likely to make the more depence from the narrowness of his income—from sheer despair breaking out of all bounds, and becoming extravagant, which is not his turn. But he likes to live as well as the rest of his company, and, between ourselves, has fell into some of the finist and most rakish in England. He thinks ’tis for the honour of the family not to go back, and many a time calls for ortolans and champaign when he would as leaf dine with a stake and a mugg of beer. And in this kind of spirit I have no doubt from what he hath told me in his talk (which is very naif, as the French say), that his mamma hath encouraged him in his high opinion of himself. We women like our belongings to have it, however little we love to pay the cost. Will you have your ladd make a figar in London? Trebble his allowance at the very least, and his Aunt Bernstein (with his honored mamma’s permission) will add a little more on to whatever summ you give him. Otherwise he will be spending the little capital I learn he has in this country, which, when a ladd once begins to manger, there is very soon an end to the loaf. Please God, I shall be able to leave Henry Esmond’s grandson something at my death; but my savings are small, and the pension with which my gracious Sovereign hath endowed me dies with me. As for feu M. de Bernstein, he left only debt at his decease: the officers of his Majesty’s Electoral Court of Hannover are but scantily paid.

“A lady who is at present very high in his Majesty’s confidence hath taken a great phancy to your ladd, and will take an early occasion to bring him to the Sovereign’s favorable notice. His Royal Highness the Duke he hath seen. If live in America he must, why should not Mr. Esmond Warrington return as Governor of Virginia, and with a title to his name? That is what I hope for him.

“Meanwhile, I must be candid with you, and tell you I fear he hath entangled himself here in a very silly engagement. Even to marry an old woman for money is scarce pardonable—the game ne valant gueres la chandelle—Mr. Bernstein, when alive, more than once assured me of this fact, and I believe him, poor gentleman! to engage yourself to an old woman without money, and to marry her merely because you have promised her, this seems to me a follie which only very young lads fall into, and I fear Mr. Warrington is one. How, or for what consideration, I know not, but my niece Maria Esmond hath escamote a promise from Harry. He knows nothing of her antecedens, which I do. She hath laid herself out for twenty husbands these twenty years past. I care not how she hath got the promise from him. ’Tis a sin and a shame that a woman more than forty years old should surprize the honour of a child like that, and hold him to his word. She is not the woman she pretends to be. A horse jockey (he saith) cannot take him in—but a woman!

“I write this news to you advisedly, displeasant as it must be. Perhaps ’twill bring you to England: but I would be very cautious, above all, very gentle, for the bitt will instantly make his high spirit restive. I fear the property is entailed, so that threats of cutting him off from it will not move Maria. Otherwise I know her to be so mercenary that (though she really hath a great phancy for this handsome ladd) without money she would not hear of him. All I could, and more than I ought, I have done to prevent the match. What and more I will not say in writing; but that I am, for Henry Esmond’s sake, his grandson’s sincerest friend, and madam,—Your faithful sister and servant,

“BEATRIX BARONESS DE BERNSTEIN.

“To Mrs. Esmond Warrington of Castlewood, in Virginia.”

Read that, and you will see how differently the same life is salted, according to the hand that sprinkles. Harry’s letter is all clean linen and proper phrases, the speech of a son who knows which words his mother can bear; Beatrix’s is sharp with experience, flavoured by old grudges, and by a knowledge of what promises cost when spoken in the wrong dialect to the wrong listener. In her French turns of phrase—naïf, escamote, ne valant guères la chandelle—there is a little of the old world still living and still asserting itself: a private language used like a knife, a way of naming folly so it cannot hide behind English politeness. And beneath her counsel about ortolans and champagne—those tiny, ruinous dainties of fashion—runs the practical wisdom of a household economist: the loaf is not infinite; once you begin to cut it too thin, you find your fingers.

On the back of this letter, in Madam Esmond’s hand—plain, decisive, as a good housekeeper’s marking of jars in a storeroom—was written: “My sister Bernstein’s letter, received with Henry’s December 24 on receipt of which it was determined my son should instantly go home.”

Harry Warrington held, with that stubborn Virginian conscience of his, to the melancholy promise his cousin had wrung from him; yet no charitable soul could fancy the engagement was sweet to his palate. It sat on him like meat swallowed too hastily—honour, yes, but dry as yesterday’s bread. If ever a man wished to be quit of a bond without seeming to cut it, it was Harry.

And so—whether by design, by hot blood, or by that quick temper which is the same in the field and at the card-table—there came the bout with Will Esmond. A private payment of a private score: fists in a room, no witnesses to go gossiping through drawing-rooms as through poultry-yards. Harry’s thought (if he owned it even to himself) ran in this fashion: a boxing-match must breed a family quarrel; a family quarrel might set Maria against him; he would not retract; Will, stung, might call him out; and in that smoke and confusion the hateful compact might burn away, leaving him free. He laid his little train and touched it off.

The powder flashed—then settled to a mere bruise and a swollen nose. Will’s eye went black for a week; his pride, one suspects, for longer; but he sent no challenge. He was knocked down and got up again—an act of sense many men might practise, could they only settle their accounts in a back room and keep the reckoning off the public ledger. Presently the cousins met in other people’s houses and did not maul each other.

Nor did Maria, as Harry had perhaps hoped, run to her family’s colours. She declared for her cousin. So did my lord Castlewood when the disturbance reached him. By the chaplain’s showing, Will had struck first; and it was neither the first nor the tenth time he had been found quarrelsome in his cups. Mr. Warrington, said my lord, had shown proper spirit in resenting an injury; it was for Will to ask pardon, not Harry. Harry answered he would accept no apology while his horse was not returned and his wager not paid. How the matter of the bet was cooked and served at last, this chronicler cannot discover; only that it ended, like many a disputed dish, in being eaten without further clatter.

My lord had at first been willing enough that his sister—unmarried so long, her life trailing behind her like a gown that has brushed too many thresholds and gathered too many burrs—should accept any bridegroom who offered, and, if a gentleman from Virginia, so much the better: let her be carried off to his wigwam in the forest and done with. In the natural course, Harry would outlive so elderly a bride, and console himself afterward or not, as suited him.

But after my lord’s talk with Aunt Bernstein upon coming to London, his mind altered; he even tried to dissuade Maria, and spoke—miracle of tenderness!—of pity for the young fellow forced into misery by a foolish promise given at one-and-twenty. Misery! Maria could not taste the word. What misery? Pity indeed! She knew what pity meant, and it was not my lord’s flavour of it. Her brother had been with Aunt Bernstein; Aunt Bernstein had offered money to break the match. Maria understood very well what his lordship’s compassion signified; but Mr. Warrington was a man of honour, and she could trust him.

My lord, balked and irritated, went off to White’s, or to whatever kennel of fashionable noise then yelped him welcome. And there, in the roaring tide of London—dice rattling like hail on shutters, voices cracking, chairs scraping, snuff-boxes snapping, the very air thick with oaths and laughter—he brooded with a bitterness that made the room’s din seem almost medicinal. Had his sister guessed too neatly the drift of his conversation with Madame Bernstein? If so, the guess galled him.

“And so,” he thought, “the end of my virtue will be that the Mohock falls into other hands; and there is no use in sparing him. If I don’t have him, somebody else will—that is plain. My brother has had a slice; my dear sister would swallow him whole. And here have I been playing guardian, refusing to play beyond a sixpence, fattening a goose for other people to carve! Remorse? By all the furies, my remorse is for what I have not done and might have done. Why did I spare Lucretia? She hated me ever after, and her husband went where he was destined. Why let this lad off—only that March and the rest, who do not want him, may pluck him? And I have the bad name; I am the wicked lord pointed at; women warn their sons against me. Pardi, I am not a penny worse—only more unlucky than my neighbours; my cursed weakness is my worst enemy!”

Perhaps no man ever spoke such a speech aloud; but historians have long put words into dead mouths, and if Livy may do it for heroes, why may not we, who know Lord Castlewood’s temper, set down the shape of his thoughts? One pack of wolves on the hunt for the lamb, and one hungry old hunter to stand aside without so much as a cutlet? The world is amazed when men, on counting their opportunities, find they took so little.

Madame Bernstein, however, was loth to lay before her Virginian nephew all the sour knowledge she kept of his family. She had even been touched by my lord’s forbearance when Harry first came to Europe, and pleased to have her wishes obeyed. Yet in that later talk—when Castlewood spoke of Maria’s designs—he had thrown off restraint with his customary cynicism, called himself a fool for sparing a lad whom sparing would not save from ruin, and pointed to Harry’s undeniable extravagances: nights at faro and hazard, rides to Newmarket, a troop of spendthrift companions always hungry for another course. Why should he alone keep his hands off?

Madame Bernstein pleaded that Harry was poor. Bah! said my lord; he was heir to a principality that ought to have been Castlewood’s and might have set their ruined house on its legs. Were there not money-lenders enough in town who would advance on post-obits? Castlewood knew those gentry to his cost: he had tasted their usury in his father’s lifetime, and they had gnawed away two-thirds of his wretched income, as rats work through a sack of grain.

He spoke with such desperate candour and ill-humour that Madame Bernstein, alarmed for her favourite, resolved to warn him at the first chance.

That evening she began a billet to Mr. Warrington; but all her life she had been slow with her pen and mistrustful of ink. “I never knew any good come of writing more than bon jour or business,” she would say. “Why write ill, when there are so many who can do it well? and even then it were best left alone.” So she sent one of her men to Harry’s lodgings, bidding him come next day for a dish of tea, when she meant to caution him.

But the next morning she was indisposed and could not receive him when he came; then she kept her chamber a couple of days; then there was some great engagement; then Harry was off on an expedition of his own. In the whirl of London, who sees his neighbour? What brother meets his sister? What schoolfellow finds his old friend? Days slipped by before aunt and nephew had their confidential talk.

When at last they sat together, she began by scolding him mildly on his extravagance and madcap frolics—though in truth she was charmed with him for both, as some people are charmed by a young cook’s bold hand even while pretending to fear the spice. Harry replied that young men would be young men; and that, in dutifully attending on his aunt, he had made the acquaintances with whom he chiefly lived now. Then, after some prelude, she began to warn him of Lord Castlewood.

At this Harry broke into a bitter laugh. The good-natured world, he said, had told him plenty already about his cousin.

“To say of a man of his lordship’s rank—of any gentleman—‘Don’t play with him,’ is more than I like to do,” Madame Bernstein continued; “but—”

“Oh, you may say on, aunt,” Harry said, with something like an oath biting the back of his teeth.

“And have you played with your cousin already?” asked the old monitress, who had lived long enough to know how quickly warning turns into prophecy.

“And lost and won, madam!” Harry answered, with a gallantry that tried to make light of the thing. “It don’t become me to say which. If we have a bout with a neighbour in Virginia—a bottle, a pack of cards, a quarrel—we don’t go home and tell our mothers. I mean no offence, aunt!”

And, blushing, he rose and kissed her. He looked brave and brilliant—rich lace at his wrists, fair face and hair, velvet and gold new on his back. He took leave with that easy kindness which made his generosity seem as natural as breathing. The servants gathered round him, and he gave them his usual sumptuous benefaction, so that even gratitude had a sound in that house: curtseys, murmured blessings, the soft clink of coin—a kinder music than the harsh chorus of the gaming rooms.

Outside, the day was rainy and winter-grey; to save his fine silk stockings from the street’s wet filth, he must needs come in a chair. He called through the curtains, “To White’s!” and away the chairmen carried him—feet splashing, poles creaking, voices calling in the watery air—to the place where he spent far too much of his time.

If his friends could have wished him less constant there, so much may yet be said for him: once engaged in play, he fought his battle like a hero. Good luck did not make him noisy; ill luck did not make him mean. Fortune is proverbially fickle to gamblers; but how many gamblers are fickle to Fortune—run frightened from her advances, desert her, and then swear she was faithless first?

“By George, Mr. Warrington,” cried Mr. Selwyn, waking up into one of his rare fits of enthusiasm, “you deserve to win! You treat your luck as a gentleman should. So long as she stays with you, you behave to her with perfect politeness. Si celeres quatit pennas—you know the rest—no? Well, you are none the worse off. You will call her ladyship’s coach, and make her a bow at the step. Look at Lord Castlewood yonder, passing the box. Did you ever hear a fellow curse and swear so at losing five or six pieces? She must be a jade indeed, if she long gives her favours to such a niggardly canaille as that!”

“We don’t consider our family canaille, sir,” Harry said, stiffening, “and my Lord Castlewood is one of them.”

“I forgot—forgot, and ask your pardon! And I make you my compliment upon my lord, and Mr. Will Esmond, his brother,” Selwyn said, with his dry grin. “The box is with me. Five’s the main! Deuce Ace!—my usual luck. Virtute mea me involvo!” and he sank back as if virtue were a cloak he drew over his face to sleep.

Whether this was the very occasion when Harry threw those fifteen mains spoken of in one of Mr. Walpole’s letters I cannot tell; but certain it is that, upon his first appearance at White’s, Harry had five or six evenings of prodigious good fortune. The five hundred pounds taken from his inheritance multiplied into thousands; the purse seemed bewitched, as if Fortunatus had slipped it into his pocket with a wink.

And Harry—who was not one of those Fortunati that tie up the endless purse, drink small beer, and go to bed with a tallow candle—spent as freely as he breathed. Fine clothes came as regularly as bread from an oven; fine horses, too, sleek as if groomed by gold; grand entertainments where the rooms steamed with candle-wax, roast meats, wine, perfume, and wet wool from cloaks hung to dry. The five thousand pounds never seemed to diminish. Giving was easy when the hand felt always full; and yet it must be said, it was his nature to give, not merely his luck.

In the very height of this vein, what must Mr. Harry do but find out from Lady Maria what her debts were—and pay them off to the last shilling. Her stepmother and half-sister, who did not love her, he loaded with magnificent presents.

“Had you not better get yourself arrested, Will?” my lord said sardonically to his brother. “Although you bit him in that affair of the horse, the Mohock will certainly take you out of pawn.”

Then Mr. William felt a true remorse—though not of the humble kind that sends prodigals to their knees. “Confound it,” he groaned, “to think I have let this fellow slip for such a little matter as forty pound! Why, he was good for a thousand at least.”

As for Maria, that generous creature accepted the good fortune sent her with a grateful heart—and was ready to accept as much more as one pleased. Having paid off her debts to milliners, tradesmen, purveyors, she forthwith proceeded to contract new ones. Mrs. Betty, her maid, went round with news on her tongue like a bellman’s cry: her mistress was about to form a matrimonial alliance with a young gentleman of immense fortune; therefore they might give my lady credit to any amount. The tradesfolk, having heard that tune twice or thrice before, might not believe every note; but their bills were paid, and payment is a persuasive language in any dialect. Even to Mrs. Pincott of Kensington Maria showed no rancour; she ordered fresh supplies with a smile, as if former humiliations were only yesterday’s dish set aside for today’s sweeter course.

So she drove about from mercer to toy-shop, from toy-shop to jeweller, in a coach with her maid and Mr. Warrington inside; and the shopkeepers, hearing the wheels, the horses’ snort and jingle, the coachman’s call, thought her a fortunate woman indeed to have secured the Fortunate Youth—though they might wonder at the young man’s taste in choosing so elderly a beauty.

Mr. Sparks, of Tavistock Street, Covent Garden, took the liberty of waiting upon Mr. Warrington at his lodgings in Bond Street with the pearl necklace and the gold étui bought in Lady Maria’s company the day before, and asked whether he should leave them at his honour’s lodgings or send them to her ladyship with his honour’s compliments. Harry, in that mood when money seems to have the lightness of feathers, added a ring from the jeweller’s stock to the necklace and the étui, bade Sparks send in the bill, and dismissed him with a grandeur that made even Gumbo receive a bow as the tradesman withdrew.

Nor did his bounties end there. Within days the pleased young fellow drove up in his phaeton to Sparks’s shop and chose a couple of trinkets for two young ladies whose parents had been kind to him and for whom he felt a sincere regard.

“Ah,” thought he, as the jewels winked in their trays like bright eyes in candlelight, “how I wish I had my poor George’s wit and genius for poetry! I would send these presents with pretty verses to Hetty and Theo. If goodwill and real regard could make a poet of me, I should have no difficulty finding rhymes.”

And so he called in Parson Sampson, and together they fell to concocting a billet. Outside, London went on clattering—coaches, cries, bells, the ceaseless hard-edged music of the town—while inside the young man’s fortune, like a sauce left too long on the fire, thickened fast and sweet, and threatened, even as it pleased, to change its flavour.

So Harry Warrington of Virginia took rooms in Bond Street, and for a while it seemed London had been laid out like a table expressly for his appetite. He lived where coaches rolled day and night like a ceaseless surf; where the street-cries stitched the hours together—oysters! hot pies! broom!—and where, beneath the winter soot, kitchens sent up their honest signals: beef fat browning, coffee scorching, wet wool steaming in passages. In such a town a young man might fancy fortune itself had a smell—made of warm wine, truffles, wax candles, and new-guinea gold.

The world called him Fortunate Youth, and—being young, comely, well-born, and, above all, visibly provided—society found him eminently tolerable. He was liked because he could like in return: because he could sing when the bottle made men tender; because he could ride when the morning made men rash; because he had that modest blush with ladies which is often taken for virtue, and is at least a kind of courtesy; because with tradesmen, chairmen, and serving folk he had a way of paying largely and speaking as if their annoyance were an affront to him. He carried his rank like a sword worn easy in its belt: not always drawn, but always there.

The winter of ’56-’57 offered him its round of pleasures: Italian operas, which he praised with the politeness of a man who would rather hear a hunting-horn; the theatres where Garrick and Pritchard made whole houses breathe together; masquerades with their rustle of silk and their false laughter; and private assemblies that began and ended in cards, where the air grew stale with melted tallow and hot hands, and where Harry, who preferred higher and fairer play, found himself missing the downright, roaring honesty of White’s.

One day his kinsman, Lord Castlewood, carried him to Court and presented him at St. James’s. The King had come in from Kensington, and looked as if he had brought the damp with him. His Majesty received the young Virginian with a glance as short as a snapped thread.

“Oh—heard of you from Lady Yarmouth,” he said; then, turning to Castlewood and speaking in German, added a sentence which ended like a slap. And with that the Defender of the Faith showed Harry the royal back.

Castlewood withdrew, yellow with dismay, as if a chill had struck him through his lace.

“What did he say?” Harry asked, not much troubled, only curious.

“His Majesty thinks they play too high at White’s, and is displeased,” Castlewood whispered.

“If he does not want us, we had better not come again,” Harry said, simply. “I never somehow considered that German fellow a real King of England.”

“Hush! for Heaven’s sake, hold your confounded colonial tongue!” Castlewood hissed. “Don’t you see the walls have ears?”

“And what then?” Harry said, looking about him. “Why, hang me, it is a curiosity. They were shaking hands with me and bowing and sweetening their voices a moment ago—and now they step away as if I carried the plague.”

A hand like a ham, brown and hard as a block on a butcher’s stall, came out of the crowd and closed on Harry’s.

“Shake hands, nephew,” said a broad-faced gentleman in a great old-fashioned wig and scarlet-laced waistcoat. “I heard what you said. I have ears like the wall, look you. If other folk show you the cold shoulder, I’ll give you my hand. There’s something of my brother about your eyes. Though in your island you grow more wiry and thin, I reckon. I am thine uncle, child. Sir Miles Warrington. My lord knows me well enough.”

Castlewood, made suddenly smaller by fear, bowed as if a pistol were at his head. “Yes—my dear Harry—this is your paternal uncle, Sir Miles.”

“Might as well have come to see us in Norfolk as dangle about playing the fool at Tunbridge, Mr. Warrington—or Mr. Esmond—which do you call yourself?” the Baronet went on, in that downright, farm-yard voice that seemed to bring the smell of stable and roast meat into the gilded room. “The old lady calls herself Madam Esmond, don’t she?”

“My mother is not ashamed of her father’s name, nor am I,” Harry answered, the pride rising in him like heat.

“Well said, lad!” Sir Miles cried, clapping him with approval. “Come home and eat a bit of mutton with Lady Warrington at three, in Hill Street—if you can do without your White’s kickshaws. You needn’t look frightened, my Lord Castlewood! I shall tell no tales out of school.”

“I—I am sure Sir Miles Warrington will act as a gentleman!” Castlewood stammered.

“Belike he will,” growled the Baronet, wheeling on his heel. “And thou wilt come, young man, at three. Mind, good roast mutton waits for nobody. Thou hast a great look of thy father. Lord bless us, how we used to beat each other! He was smaller and younger, but often had the best of it. Take it he was henpecked when he married, and Madam Esmond took the spirit out of him when she got him in her island. Virginia’s an island. Ain’t it an island?”

Harry laughed. “No.”

“Well, island or not, thou must come and tell all about it to my lady. She’ll know whether ’tis an island or not.”

When Sir Miles had tramped away, Castlewood drew nearer with an anxious, confidential air, as if the very draughts in the corridor might carry tales.

“My dear Mr. Warrington,” he said, “in this great city every man has enemies; there is detraction and scandal beyond belief. I never spoke to you about Sir Miles precisely because I did know him, and because we have had differences. Should he permit himself remarks to my disparagement, you will receive them cum grano, and remember it is from an enemy they come.”

They went out into St. James’s Street, where the coach-wheels made their perpetual thunder, and the cries and hoofbeats rose and fell like a living thing. By the time Harry reached White’s, the sound of his cold reception had flown ahead of him as swiftly as a rumour always does when it can feed on envy. The King had turned his back upon him. The King was jealous of his favour with the favourite. Harry was au mieux with Lady Yarmouth. Men who would have crossed the room to avoid him yesterday now pressed near to congratulate him, as if royal sulkiness were a badge.

And when Harry, obedient to roast mutton and blood, appeared at three in Hill Street, Sir Miles rallied him at table in his plain, hearty fashion, as though a King’s back were no more than a weathercock.

Lady Warrington at first received him with a majesty so stiff it seemed starched; she had the air of a woman who had taken up salvation as one takes up housekeeping—resolutely, with rules and a cupboard of admonitions. Later, when the first scrutiny had passed, she confessed (with a chill candour) that the town’s account of him had been so bad she had scarcely known how to greet him.

The Misses Warrington—prim young women with clean collars and careful voices—curtsied and said, “How d’ye do, cousin?” and “No, thank you, cousin,” as if even gratitude must be rationed. The little boy, the heir, dined too, guarded by his governor. After dinner Sir Miles gave the child a small glass of port, and the warm wine loosened the innocent tongue as surely as any sermon.

Master Miles stared long at Harry, as if he sought wickedness the way a child seeks a bruise beneath a stocking.

“Are you wicked, cousin Harry?” he asked at last. “You don’t look very wicked!”

“My dear Master Miles!” the tutor, Mr. Walker, protested, reddening to the ears.

“But you said he was wicked!” the boy cried. “You did. And mamma said so too—that Lady Yarmouth was a wicked woman.”

“We are all miserable sinners, Miley,” Sir Miles said, half laughing. “Haven’t you heard the clergyman say so every Sunday?”

“Yes,” the child insisted, “but not so very wicked as cousin Harry. Is it true you gamble, cousin, and drink all night with wicked men, and go with wicked women? You know you said so, Mr. Walker—and mamma said so.”

“And you are a little pitcher,” Sir Miles roared, pleased and vexed at once. “Take him to his sisters, Mr. Walker, and Topsham shall give thee a ride in the park on thy little horse.”

The promise of the pony dried the tears that had been swelling; for Master Miles began to bawl that he would rather stay with his wicked cousin than go to his sisters.

“They’ve made you a sad reputation among ’em, nephew,” Sir Miles said when the child was gone. “My wife, since my poor eldest died, has took to—hum!—Tottenham Court Road and Mr. Whitfield’s preaching; and we’ve had one Ward about the house, a friend of Mr. Walker’s, who has told bad stories about you and your brother at home.”

“As for me, sir, let him say what he pleases,” Harry cried, warmed with port and quick blood; “but I’ll break any man’s bones who dares say a word against my brother! That fellow wasn’t fit to buckle my dear George’s shoe; and if I find him repeating in England what he dared to say in our house in Virginia, I promise him a second caning.”

“You stand up for your friends, nephew Harry,” Sir Miles said, looking at him with a rough liking. “Fill thy glass. Thou art not as bad as thou hast been painted. I always told my lady so. I drink Madam Esmond Warrington’s health—of Virginia—and will have a full bumper for that toast.”

Harry emptied his glass, filled again, and drank Lady Warrington and Master Miles.

“Thou wouldst be heir to four thousand acres in Norfolk, did he die, though,” Sir Miles added, with the bluntness of a man who counts fields as other men count cards.

“God forbid,” Harry said quickly, “and be praised that I have acres enough in Virginia of my own.”

After dinner he drank coffee with Lady Warrington—the bitter fragrance rising from the cup like an old friend calling him back to mornings at home—and talked easily with the young ladies. One of them had a look that made him think of Fanny Mountain, and his manner softened toward her, as if memory were a seasoning that changed the whole dish. When he took his leave, they agreed their wicked cousin was not nearly so wicked as rumour had made him; Lady Warrington, indeed, conceived strong hopes of plucking him from the pit by a steady diet of improving pages.

That evening she sent him a good book—Law’s Call—with a pretty note praying it might profit him. And then, having discharged conscience, she and her daughters went to a rout at the house of a minister’s lady, where piety and vanity took hands and danced without blushing.

Harry, before going to White’s, had driven to Mr. Sparks in Tavistock Street and purchased more trinkets for his cousins—“from their aunt in Virginia,” he said. He was full of kindness in those days; prosperity made him blaze like a well-fed fire. The girls in Hill Street were delighted and wrote a collective note to Madam Esmond Warrington across the seas—a letter that would astonish her when it reached Virginia in spring, when she and Mountain and Fanny were visiting the grim, deserted Castlewood again, and the snows were gone and a thousand peach-trees stood flushed with bloom like a young bride’s cheek.

“Poor boy,” the mother would think then. “This is some present he gave his cousins in my name, in the time of his prosperity—nay, of his extravagance and folly. How quickly his wealth has passed away! But he ever had a kind heart for the poor Mountain; and we must not forget him in his need. It behoves us to be more than ever careful of our own expenses, my good people!”

And so, one may fancy, they warmed themselves by one log, and ate from one dish, and worked by one candle, while the house’s sounds—scrape of ladle in pot, creak of spinning-wheel, the quiet crackle of stingy fire—made their own small music against the wind. Yet pinching a household does not always save it: the servants, pressed more and more, lied and stole more and more; what was hoarded in one corner went missing in another, as if thrift and loss were sisters who could not be separated.

Meanwhile, in Bond Street, one afternoon, Harry sat in his dressing-gown—satin against his wrists, fine linen at his throat—sipping chocolate that had been whipped to a froth and scented faintly of vanilla. The cup was warm in his hand, the room handsome, the fire bright; but care lay on him like a heavy cloak. Outside, the city’s roar kept its endless sermon: wheels, cries, iron-shod hoofs, the occasional hammering that made a man’s teeth clench without knowing why. London’s noise could turn rich rooms into cages.

A few weeks before, when luck had sat by him at the table like a flattering companion, he had royally bidden Parson Sampson draw up a list of his debts which he, Harry Warrington, would pay. Sampson had gone to work, and brought him—not all (no man ever sets down all), but enough to make a decent show of conscience.

The chaplain waited humbly at breakfast until Harry chose to appear. At last the young man came in pale and languid, curl-papers still in his hair, his appetite gone. Sampson, fingering his schedule in his pocket, ventured to ask whether his patron had had a bad night. Indeed he had: Harry had been brought home from White’s by two chairmen at five in the morning; one of the chair windows would not shut, and rain and snow had blown in, and he had caught a confounded cold and an even worse humour. Sampson tried his small jests, talked of muffins and eggs, tea and news, plays and players; but the smiles he sought were as hard to raise as a soufflé in a draught.

At last, however, Harry broke into a laugh—sudden, loud, and anything but merry—when Sampson drew out his paper and said in a piteous tone, “Here is that schedule of debts which your honour asked for—two hundred and forty-three pounds—every shilling I owe in the world, thank Heaven!—that is—ahem!—every shilling of which the payment will in the least inconvenience me—and I need not tell my dearest patron I shall consider him my saviour and benefactor!”

Harry took the paper, eyed Sampson with a look that made the poor divine’s stomach sink, and laughed again with a bitter edge. An oath or two followed—hot, disconnected words, like sparks that fly from a pokered coal.

“Confound it,” Harry said, “why didn’t you bring it on Monday?”

“Confound me, why did I not bring it on Monday?” Sampson echoed, timidly, as if agreeing might mend it. “It is my luck—my usual luck. Have the cards been against you, Mr. Warrington?”

“Yes,” Harry said, with a scowl. “A plague on them. Monday night and last night both went against me. Don’t be frightened, chaplain; there’s money enough in the locker yet. But I must go into the City and get some.”

“What—sell out, sir?” Sampson asked, his voice pretending alarm and betraying relief.

“Sell out, sir? Yes. I borrowed a hundred off Mackreth in counters last night, and must pay him at dinner-time. I will do your business nevertheless, and never fear, my good Mr. Sampson. Come to breakfast to-morrow, and we will see and deliver your reverence from the Philistines.”

When the chaplain had gone, Harry’s shoulders dropped, and his head sank toward his chest. He sat over the fire, beating the coals about with the poker as if he could stir luck into them, muttering disjointed wicked words that showed his agitation without easing it. The chocolate on the table cooled and thickened, its sweetness turning cloying; the room smelled of scorched sugar and damp wool from his cloak, and he felt as if all London’s noise were inside his skull.

In this mood he was interrupted by a visitor who, on any other day—even on this day with conscience gnawing—would have been welcome: Colonel Lambert. The Colonel came in his military dress, a cloak over it, smelling of cold air and the road, as if he had brought the country’s silence (and the memory of it) into Bond Street’s din. He had been to the Captain-General’s levee and came thence to see his young friend.

Harry fancied Lambert’s greeting colder than usual, but his own affairs were too loud within him for him to attend closely. How were the ladies of Oakhurst? and Miss Hetty, who had been ailing when he passed in autumn? Better? He was glad. They were in London now, staying with their friend Lord Wrotham? Harry said he was delighted—though his face, truthfully, did not brighten as the words required.

“And so you live at White’s and with the great folks,” Lambert said, watching him, “and you fare sumptuously every day, and you pay your court at St. James’s, and make one at my Lady Yarmouth’s routs, and at all the card-parties in the Court end of the town?”

“My dear Colonel,” Harry answered, a little stiffly, “I do what other folks do.”

“Other folks are richer folks than some folks, my dear lad.”

“Sir!” Harry cried, rising on pride as on sudden wind. “I would thank you to believe I owe nothing for which I cannot pay!”

“I should never have spoken of your affairs,” Lambert said, not taking up the heat, “but that you yourself confided them to me. I hear all sorts of stories about the Fortunate Youth. Only at his Royal Highness’s even to-day they were saying how rich you were already, and I did not undeceive them—”

“Colonel Lambert, I cannot help the world gossiping about me!” Harry broke in, impatience sharpening.

“—And what prodigious sums you had won,” Lambert continued steadily. “Eighteen hundred one night—two thousand another—six or eight thousand in all. Oh, there were gentlemen from White’s at the levee too, I can assure you, and the army can fling a main as well as you civilians.”

“I wish they would meddle with their own affairs,” Harry said, scowling.

“And I, too, you look as if you were going to say,” Lambert replied. “Well, my boy, it is my affair, and you must let Theo’s father and Hetty’s father—and Harry Warrington’s father’s old friend—say how it is my affair.”

He drew from his pocket a packet, the generous skirts and lappets of his coat accommodating it with ease, and laid it down as if laying down a charge.

“Look you, Harry. These trinkets you sent with the kindest heart in the world to people who love you, and would cut off their little hands to spare you needless pain—could never be bought by a young fellow with two or three hundred a year. Why, a nobleman might buy these things, or a rich City banker, and send them to his—to his daughters, let us say.”

“Sir,” Harry said, burning red, “as you say, I meant only kindness.”

“But you must not give them to my girls,” Lambert said. “Hester and Theodosia Lambert must not be dressed up with the winnings off the gaming-table, saving your presence. It goes to my heart to bring them back. Mrs. Lambert will keep her present, which is of small value, and sends you her love and a God bless you—and so say I, Harry Warrington, with all my heart.”

His voice thickened; his face grew very red; he passed a hand across his eyes, and then held that same hand out to Harry—an honest hand, offered as it had been offered in old days, without bargain.

But rebellion was strong in Harry; shame and pride, like two cooks quarrelling over the same pot, spoiled what might have been wholesome. He rose and did not take the hand.

“Give me leave to tell Colonel Lambert,” he said, each word rustling like stiff silk, “that I have had somewhat too much advice from him. You are forever volunteering it, sir, and when I don’t ask it. You make it your business to inquire about my gains at play and the company I keep. What right have you to control my amusements or my companions? I strive to show my sense of your former kindness by little presents to your family, and you fling—you bring them back.”

“I can’t do otherwise, Mr. Warrington,” Lambert said, looking very sad.

“Such a slight may mean nothing here, sir,” Harry cried, the Virginian in him leaping up, “but in our country it means war, sir! God forbid I should talk of drawing a sword against the father of ladies who have been as mother and sister to me; but you have wounded my heart, Colonel Lambert—you have, I won’t say insulted, but humiliated me—and this is a treatment I will bear from no man alive. My servants will attend you to the door, sir!”

And with that, in his brocade dressing-gown and all the state a young man can borrow from cloth, Harry Warrington turned away and walked into his bedroom, shutting out with the door not only an old friend, but for a moment the very possibility that any language—English or Virginian, courtly or homely—could translate what he felt without wounding him anew.

Harry Warrington’s peace-offerings lay where he had flung them down—two morocco cases, their lids gaping like mouths that had been made to praise and were now forced to gape in stupid silence. Within, on white satin, the gold toys shone the more impudently because nobody would accept them: a repeater with its little pearl circlet and diamond knob; a necklace and rings that had cost him not merely coin but heat and haste in foreign shops; trifles that had been chosen with the bright, foolish notion that gratitude might be weighed and paid for like sugar or spice.

Colonel Lambert had rejected all.

And so Harry, who had come in with offerings like a penitent at a communion rail, went out with the wrath of a young conqueror balked, and with shame in the same breath. They had humbled him—before the girls. That was the sting. Not the money. Not even the slight. It was the sense of being exhibited once more as a prodigal, a scapegrace, a lesson for the family to point at while they polished their own virtue.

“They are so fine they won’t touch my hand,” he told himself, pacing his rooms. “And when I try to show common gratitude, they fling it back in my face.”

Parson Sampson, who had no notion of dignity that was not borrowed, had been staring at the open cases with a look that was almost hunger.

“Why, sir,” he said, his eyes lingering as a hungry man’s will linger on a roast fowl trussed and ready for the spit, “the things must be worth a fortune.”

“They cost money,” Harry answered shortly. “Not that I’d grudge ten times as much to people who have been kind.”

“No, faith, sir, not if I know your honour!” Sampson cried, quick to season his flattery as a cook seasons broth—too much salt, and always at hand.

Harry touched the repeater’s case, and his anger sharpened at the thought of Hetty’s eager face when she had once sighed for such a watch, as if wishing for it were only another kind of prayer. “They told me at Paris it was a bargain. Miss Hetty said she longed for a repeating watch.”

“Oh, what a love!” Sampson gushed. “The pearls—look, sir, the pearls! And the diamond knob—why, ’twould win any woman’s heart.”

“There’s an apple-woman passing with a basket,” Harry broke out. “I’ve half a mind to fling the thing to her.”

Sampson made a little cry as if the notion were a dagger aimed at his own ribs. Harry laughed once, harshly, and went out.

He had business in the City; business that now, each time he crossed those streets, seemed to him like a man walking through a market where his own flesh was for sale. Sampson, for all his devotion, peeled away early in the Strand with a confession of terror for Chancery Lane and its grim precincts. Harry went on alone.

At his broker’s he did what he had come to do. There were papers, signatures—light scratches of pen on parchment that felt, absurdly, like knives on bone—and presently he walked out with crisp bank-notes folded in his pocket. The broker, as if to sweeten the transaction with a supper-sauce, took him to one of the great City dining-houses. The rooms were warm with the thick smell of meats and beer, the clatter of plates, the comfortable roar of men who believed the world was stable because dinner came at the hour. Beef cut in shining slices, greens steamed to a dull surrender, bread that had the faint sour of yesterday’s leaven—Harry ate without tasting, or tasted only bitterness. Under the talk and knives and tankards, the City’s own sound rose like surf: wheels grinding, hawkers calling, bells, and that perpetual human hum which, if a man listened too closely, seemed less like life than like the turning of a millstone.

Afterwards the broker showed him the Virginian walk upon ’Change, where the tobacco-men loitered with their grave faces and their provincial air. Harry passed through it shamefacedly, as if each step sounded his disgrace.

What would his mother say—Madam Esmond far away, with the river wind in her windows and the quiet of the plantations about her—if she knew her son was carrying off, in a gambler’s bottomless pocket, so much of his father’s patrimony? He imagined those Virginia merchants looking at him and hearing their own voices name him: Young Esmond of Castlewood on the Potomac; losing at play; selling out again and again. The thought made his ears burn. Even the street-noise seemed to mock him. In Virginia, the loudest thing at daybreak might be a cock and the rattle of a pail; here the city never ceased clanging and scolding, as if it could drown thought by sheer racket.

Not until he passed under the traitors’ heads at Temple Bar and felt the City behind him did his spirits rise a little, like a man who has escaped a close room into air. He walked home by the Strand, glanced in at St. James’s Street—too early yet for the chocolate-house crowd—and reached his lodgings.

There he drew out his bank-notes. He took three—three small squares of rescue—and slipped them into a sheet of paper. On the inside he wrote, “Much good may they do you. H. E. W.” He sealed it carefully and directed it to the Reverend Mr. Sampson. He left the packet on the chimney-glass and told the servants to hand it to the parson when he came.

His phaeton was brought round. He meant to drive in the Park; but the east wind had teeth, and rain began to sift down, cold and straight as needles. Some irritation—weather, mood, fate—made him snap the reins instead toward St. James’s Street. By three he was at White’s again.

The club was still drowsy at that hour, men at dinner elsewhere; only a few loungers and the servants moving with trained silence. Lord Castlewood sat yawning over the Public Advertiser, newly come from Court.

“What shall we do?” my lord drawled. “A little piquet? Just an hour. I dine in Arlington Street at four.”

Harry, with that fatal readiness which in him passed for good nature, had no objection. “Just for an hour,” he said; and cards were called for.

“Upstairs?” Castlewood suggested. “Out of the noise?”

“Certainly,” Harry answered. “Out of the noise.”

It was a curious phrase for him to cling to, as if sound itself could be a moral influence. Down below, the club murmured, chairs scraped, glasses clinked; above, in the little tea-room, the world narrowed to green baize, the soft shuffle of cards, the click of counters, and two men’s breath. It was quieter—and therefore, perhaps, more dangerous. In the hush, each loss had a weight, each gain a pulse. There are silences that heal, like a field at dusk; and there are silences that sharpen appetite, like a kitchen before service when knives are being honed.

At five the club filled. Gentlemen came in after dinner; the play-room began to wake. Some put on gaming-jackets kept there for long sittings. In the coffee-room two toothpick-bearing wits leaned out through the blinds into the wet street.

“Whose phaeton?” asked one.

“The Fortunate Youth’s,” said the other.

“Not so fortunate the last three nights. Thirteen hundred lost last night to the table. Is Warrington here?”

“In the little tea-room with Lord Castlewood since three,” the waiter said. “Piquet.”

“What fun for Castlewood,” one of the men sneered, showing all his polished teeth.

The other growled. “Curse him. No right to be here. He doesn’t pay when he loses. Sir Miles Warrington told me Castlewood has owed him money on a bet these three years.”

“Castlewood doesn’t lose if he plays alone,” the first replied, shrugging. “A company flurries him. That’s why he doesn’t sit at the table.”

“Let’s go up and stop ’em,” the second muttered.

“Why? Better sport here. Look—the lamplighter’s up his ladder. And that old putt in the chair—did you ever see such a quiz?”

Just then Harry came out of the house. In the wet afternoon he seemed to have forgotten his phaeton had been waiting. The two men watched him spring in and lash the horses as if whipcord could beat back misfortune. Coachmen and chairmen scattered; he drove with a reckless speed that was like an insult to the rain. Presently Lord Castlewood was seen to enter a chair and be carried away.

Harry rattled up to his own door. The horses had stood all that time on the pavement, steaming under the drizzle; now their flanks quivered as if a cook had set a spit too close to the fire. At the door Gumbo, his servant, was talking with a country-looking girl who curtsied and tripped off. Gumbo, wherever he went, contrived to season the servants’ hall with pretty friendships.

“Has Mr. Sampson been here?” Harry asked from the seat.

“No, sar. Mr. Sampson have not been here,” Gumbo answered.

Harry told him to fetch the letter addressed to Sampson—the sealed one on the mantel in the glass. Gumbo, who could not read, took his time; Harry’s fingers drummed impatiently. When the packet was brought, Harry snatched it, turned his horses’ heads at once, and in the same instant the idlers at White’s saw him galloping back again through the wet street.

He entered the club with his jaw set. In the little tea-room he had noticed the bank already set, gentlemen bending over it with that absorbed look which is neither pleasure nor pain but a kind of fever. He went to the clerk’s desk, paid his account of the previous night, and sat down calling for fresh counters.

The week had been unlucky; to-night was worse. He could not win. The counters slid away from him as if the green cloth were a slope. He called for more. He was pale and very quiet; when spoken to, he answered with ease and politeness, like a man entertaining guests while his house burns behind him.

Lord March, with a heap of green and white counters in front of him, laughed as Harry rose at last.

“Hang it! Stay and mend your luck,” March said. “Take a hundred of mine and go on.”

“I have had enough for to-night, my lord,” Harry answered; and he went away.

He ate a broiled bone in the coffee-room—hot fat hissing under the fork, salt and smoke, the simple honest smell of meat scorched at the edge. It was the sort of food a man eats standing, without ceremony, when he can’t bear the softness of a chair. Then, about midnight, he walked back to his lodgings.

After a catastrophe, men often sleep. It is the waking that punishes. The night comes like a cook laying a heavy lid on a pot; all boils and passions are muffled. But at dawn the lid is lifted, and the stench of what has been left to scorch rises sharply.

Harry woke before the light. The room was a grey cave. He tried to pull his nightcap down and the blankets up, as if cloth could smother Yesterday. The watchman bawled some hour in the street, his voice part of London’s perpetual din—a city that never quite hushes, even in the darkest watch of the night. Harry remembered the repeater under his pillow, the pretty toy he had meant for Hetty. He pressed the knob.

Ting, ting, ting—six times, and then the half-hour in its little added flourish, like a bird foolishly singing in a storm.

Poor bright Hetty. And Maria—good Heaven, Maria, who was beginning to feel, in his irritated mind, like a refrain repeated too often. And his mother at home, who had built her life on old names and old duties and the sound of her own people’s speech, the Potomac words that Londoners laughed at when they heard them. What would she say when she learned that he had lost every shilling of his ready money—his winnings, and five thousand pounds besides—in three nights?

Castlewood could not have played him false. No. His lordship knew piquet better, but he was his kinsman. Harry forced himself to believe it, because there are lies a man must tell himself to keep from going mad. And yet the arithmetic was plain: when Harry counted his losses at the gaming-table and saw that they would swallow the remainder of his patrimony, he had passed the box and left the table. He had meant, at least, to stop before the last plank broke. But he had gone back. He had always gone back. That was the shame that tasted like bile.

Dawn seeped in at last, a miserable London light, thin as watered milk. The housemaid came to light the fire and admit the dun morning. Gumbo followed with the warmed dressing-gown, shaving-plate, and linen. The hairdresser arrived to curl and powder him; the soft swish of brush and puff made a ridiculous domestic music against his despair, as if a man could be made respectable by starch and scent.

At breakfast Parson Sampson came, eager and smiling, smelling faintly of last night’s wine and tavern cheer. He had been meant to return yesterday afternoon, but companions had held him to dinner at the St. Alban’s and made a night of it. He entered with the air of a man arriving at the second course, not knowing the first has been burnt.

“Oh, Parson,” Harry groaned, “’twas the worst night you ever made in your life! Look here, sir!”

He thrust the paper at him.

Sampson, with quick eyes, saw the broken seal. “Here is a broken envelope with the words ‘Much good may it do you,’ written within,” he said.

“Look on the outside!” Harry cried. “It was directed to you.”

Sampson’s face changed at once. Alarm—then calculation—then dread. “Has some one broke it open, sir?”

“Some one, yes. I did. Had you come as you said, you’d have found it full of bank-notes. As it is, they were all dropped at the infernal macco-table last night.”

“What, all?” Sampson whispered.

“All. With what I brought from the City, and all the ready money I have left in the world. Yesterday afternoon I played piquet with my cous—with a gentleman at White’s—and he eased me of what I had about me. Remembering there was still some money here, unless you’d fetched it, I came home, carried it back, and left it at the macco-table—every shilling besides that belongs to me.” Harry’s breath came short. “And—great Heaven, Sampson—what’s the matter, man?”

Sampson’s mouth worked, and then he burst into tears—real tears, not the theatrical dew he could summon for a sermon.

“It’s my luck,” he cried. “It’s my usual luck!”

“What!” Harry flared, anger snapping as a pan flares when grease catches. “You’re whimpering like a baby at the loss of a loan of a couple hundred pounds? Leave the room, Gumbo! Confound you, why are you always poking your woolly head in at that door!”

Gumbo, offended and slow, explained somebody below wanted to see master with a little bill.

“Tell him to go to Jericho!” Harry roared. “Let me see nobody. I am not at home!”

There was a murmur and scuffle on the landing and then silence. The noise, slight as it was, rasped Harry’s nerves; he turned on Sampson with savage contempt.

“Hadn’t you better take a bumper of brandy to keep your spirits up, Mr. Sampson? Hang it, man! Don’t snivel like a woman!”

“Oh, it’s not me,” Sampson said, tossing his head, struggling for pride. “I am used to it, sir.”

“Not you! Who then? Are you crying because somebody else is hurt?”

“Yes, sir,” the chaplain said, with a sudden spark. “Because somebody else is hurt, and through my fault. I have lodged many years with a bootmaker—a very honest man. A few days since, relying upon—upon a friend who promised to accommodate me with a loan, I borrowed sixty pounds from my landlord, which he was about to pay to his own. I can’t get the money. My poor landlord’s goods will be seized for rent; his wife and dear young children turned into the street; and this honest family ruined through my fault. But as you say, Mr. Warrington, I ought not to snivel like a woman. I will remember you helped me once—and I will bid you farewell, sir.”

He took his broad-leafed hat and walked out.

Harry, in a fury with himself, with the whole world’s crookedness, let out an execration and then—shamefully—a savage laugh. It sounded to his own ears like something low and foreign in his throat. From the stairs he called after the chaplain, “Sampson! hang you! come back! It’s a mistake! I beg your pardon!”

But Sampson, cut to the soul, went on. Harry heard the street-door slam. The thump of it seemed to strike his breast.

He sank into his chair. In his mind the filthy herd came crowding—gambling, debauchery, extravagance, reckless companions, dangerous women—wallowing and trampling like swine over the prostrate prodigal. The city’s morning noise filtered in, carts and cries and the far-off beat of London’s unceasing labour: a harsh soundscape in which repentance itself seemed drowned, as if the very air were too loud for prayer.

Yet he was not utterly overcome. He sprang up as if shaking animals from his clothes. He seized a great glass of brandy—the same fire-water he had mocked Sampson with—and swallowed it. Then he flung off his damask robe, rang for Gumbo, and ordered his coat.

Gumbo brought a fine green coat with plated buttons and a gold cord.

“Not that!” Harry roared. “A plain suit—the plainer the better. The black clothes.”

So Gumbo fetched the mourning-coat Harry had discarded months before. In it, he looked more like his own conscience.

Then, as a man in a ruined pantry gathers what silver remains before the bailiff arrives, Harry took up his valuables: his fine new gold watch; the repeater meant for Hetty; the necklace meant for Theo; his rings—half a dozen, save his grandfather’s old seal-ring which he kissed and laid back as if it were a relic that must not be pawned; three gold snuff-boxes; and lastly his purse knitted by his mother, with three shillings and sixpence and a little pocket-piece from Virginia. That purse—coarse wool, honest work—smelled faintly of home in a way the gold never could. It was a scent memory, untranslatable into London’s jargon, and it stung him.

He put on his hat and went out.

On the landing Mr. Ruff, his landlord, met him with bowing and cringing and a strip of paper a yard long. Ruff was one of the chief waiters and aides-de-camp of Mr. Mackreth at White’s; Mrs. Ruff was a milliner and had “accounts to make up.”

“Much obliged if Mr. Warrington will settle,” Ruff whined, thrusting the bill forward.

The sight of him was like a fly on a dish. Harry looked down over Ruff’s head with glum disdain.

“Of course I will settle,” he said.

“Perhaps his honour will settle now?”

“No, sir, I will not settle now!” Harry snapped, pushing forward.

“I’m very—very much in want of money, sir,” Ruff pleaded. “Mrs. Ruff is—”

“Hang you, sir, get out of the way!” Harry cried, and drove him backward against the wall so that the man almost toppled down his own landing. Harry tramped past and out into Bond Street.

As he went, the Guards were at exercise at the King’s Mews near Charing Cross. Drums and fifes cut through the air—clean, martial sounds, ordered and measured. For a moment the rhythm steadied him, as if a better life could be marched into by keeping step. He looked in at the gate and watched the drill.
