“I can shoulder a musket at any rate,” he thought gloomily, and strode on.

He crossed St. Martin’s Lane for a little business, then made his way into Long Acre, to the bootmaker’s house where Sampson lodged. The air there was different: leather and wax and damp wool, the small domestic smell of honest poverty. A child cried somewhere; a kettle sang thinly in a back room. Compared with St. James’s, where money and noise and fashion made a glittering storm, this place had the worn quiet of a kitchen after supper, when the fire is low but human beings still breathe close together.

The woman of the house said Mr. Sampson was not at home but had promised to be in at one. Since she knew Mr. Warrington, she showed him up to the parson’s little room. Harry sat down by the window-seat and, having nothing to do with his hands but wring them, took up an unfinished sermon lying there.

The title—or rather, the subject—made him start: the Prodigal Son.

He tried to read, but the words slid like grease on a plate. The parson’s phrases about husks and swine and repentance seemed not doctrine but mockery.

Presently he heard the landlady’s shrill voice on the stairs, pursuing someone who climbed. Sampson burst into the room, breathless, followed by the sobbing woman.

“There’s only thirteen pound in the house, and he will be here at one, I tell you!” she was bawling, her apron half pulled off her shoulder as she clutched at Sampson like a creditor clutching a coat.

Sampson saw Harry and started; the landlady stopped short, then, in her agitation, seemed not to understand that a gentleman’s presence altered anything.

“Hush, hush! my good creature!” Sampson gasped, pointing. “Don’t you see Mr. Warrington? I’ve business with him—most important business. It will be all right, I tell you!”

He coaxed and ushered her out, the anxious children clinging to her skirts like burrs.

When the door shut, Harry rose.

“Sampson,” he said, “I have come to ask your pardon again. What I said this morning was cruel and unjust, and unlike a gentleman.”

“Not a word more, sir,” Sampson answered, cold and sad. He bowed and scarcely pressed the hand Harry offered.

“I see you are still angry.”

“An apology is an apology,” Sampson said, with bitterness that tried to pass for humility. “A man of my station can ask for no more from one of yours. No doubt you did not mean to give me pain. And what if you did?” His eyes moved round the poor little room as if counting its humiliations—the cracked mirror, the few books, the sermon sheets. “And you are not the only one of the family who has. I wish I had never known the name of Esmond or Castlewood—or that place yonder.”

He glanced at a picture above the fireplace—some view of the great house he had haunted so long in hope.

“My lord, your cousin, took a fancy to me,” Sampson went on. “Said he would make my fortune. Kept me as his dependant till fortune passed by me, and now refuses me my due.”

“How do you mean—your due?” Harry asked.

“Three years’ salary,” Sampson answered. “Owed me as chaplain of Castlewood. Seeing you could give me no money, I went to his lordship this morning and asked him. I fell on my knees, sir. But his lordship had none. Civil words, at least—saving your presence, Mr. Warrington—but no money. Five guineas, which he declared was all he had, and which I took. But what are five guineas among so many? Oh, those poor little children!”

“Lord Castlewood said he had no money?” Harry cried, the blood rushing to his face. “He won eleven hundred pounds yesterday of me at piquet—which I paid him out of this pocket-book.”

Sampson gave a short, ugly laugh. “I dare say, sir. One can’t believe a word his lordship says.”

“But there’s execution in this house, and ruin upon these poor folks to-morrow,” he added, and his voice broke on the last word as if it were bread too hard to swallow.

“That need not happen,” Harry said.

He drew out what he had—eighty guineas—and laid them down.

“Here are eighty, Sampson. As far as they go, God help you. ’Tis all I have to give. I wish to my heart I could give more as I promised; but you did not come at the right time, and I am a poor devil now until my remittances come from Virginia.”

Sampson stared as if the coins were a miracle and an accusation together. Then he went white. He dropped on his knees and seized Harry’s hand.

“Great powers, sir!” he cried. “Are you a guardian angel Heaven hath sent? You quarrelled with my tears this morning; I cannot help them now. They burst from a grateful heart. A rock would pour them forth before such goodness! May Heaven eternally bless you and give you prosperity! May my unworthy prayers—”

“Nay, nay! Get up, friend—get up,” Harry said, annoyed despite himself at the flood of words. He had come to give money, not to be drenched in worship. “There—there! Don’t be on your knees to me.”

“To Heaven who sent you!” Sampson cried, and flung open the door. “Mrs. Weston! Mrs. Weston!”

The landlady appeared instantly—she had been listening at the door all along, her domestic terror too sharp for manners.

“What is it, sir?”

“We are saved!” Sampson shouted. “We are saved! Kneel, kneel, woman, and thank our benefactor! Raise your innocent voices, children, and bless him!”

A universal whimpering rose. The children, tugged into the room, stared and began to cry by contagion; the mother fell to her knees. One child, bewildered, remained standing until the mother slapped her ear and hissed, “Drat it, Jane, kneel down and bless the gentleman!”

Harry stood among them, simpering in spite of himself, warmed by the consciousness of doing one good action in the midst of so much folly. Their gratitude had a sound—raw, high, broken, like a choir of kettles and crying infants—but it was human, and for a moment it quieted the harsher noises inside him.

He slipped away at last, leaving them in their benedictions, and walked out into Long Acre feeling lighter than he had in days, as if generosity were a kind of food that could nourish even the giver, and as if—by some old, half-forgotten Virginia measure of honour—a man might still redeem himself with bread and coin, even when he had wasted so much.

And all this while, in another thread of the day’s weaving, the girl Gumbo had been talking with at Harry’s door—countrified, curtseying—was Mrs. Molly from Oakhurst, attendant to the ladies there. Wherever that fascinating Gumbo went, he left admirers behind him in kitchens and servants’ halls, and the air of his partings was always full of soft laughter and whispering, like the last low talk over a banked hearth. It had been, I think, on a Wednesday evening that he and Mrs. Molly had taken a walk together; and they were lingering in the amiable courtesies of farewell when Gumbo’s master drove up from White’s and put an end to their twilight murmurs.

There is a kind of villain whom plays delight to powder with flour and display upon the boards—your professional saint, your pulpit-thumper whose lips are forever honeyed with salvation while his heart keeps no more faith than a dry husk keeps sap. Yet in the common run of men and women, in the slow honest press of a Sunday street, hypocrisy is rarer than the satirist would have it. The chapel bell’s thin chink comes through the evening air; pattens clap on the stones; hobnailed shoes beat their blunt rhythm; umbrellas knock and open with a little gust of canvas and whalebone. The very sound of a congregation has its own weather: a sough of woollen gowns, the swish of ribbons, the stiff creak of prayer-books, the small coughs that try to be discreet and only advertise themselves the more.

Look at them filing in, and do not be too eager to call them false because their minds wander. The maid-servant’s thoughts fly, as naturally as a sparrow, to the lad who waits for her beyond the railings; the tradesman measures sugar and credit in his head even while he measures grace with his lips; the schoolboy mouths the responses and hears, under them, the Latin he must construe on Monday. Another thinks, not of the sermon, but of the pie to come after it—spiced, steaming, a comfort promised at the end of restraint. The parish clerk drones the psalm, his voice a weary pump drawing water from a deep place, and all the while his heart is at home with a daughter’s trouble. The parson himself, when he hides his face in his cushion, may be tasting in his mind the sourness of a bill due on Monday. They are not saints; they are not airy angels with feet lifted off the earth. But they are not stage hypocrites either. For most folk keep religion as they keep a cordial or a purge: a bottle in the cupboard, to be taken in the hour of sickness, and pressed upon a neighbour with that eager charity which loves to prescribe.

Of such household physic—bodily and spiritual—women are the most ardent dispensers. A century ago every great house had its still-room, where rosemary and lavender hung drying, where lemon-peel and angelica lay in sweet heaps, where syrups thickened in glazed pans and cordials brightened in glass, and where remedies stood labelled in a hand that believed its own authority. My Lady Warrington, at Sir Miles’s, took charge of consciences and digestions with the same sure air. She kept the servants’ hall as another woman might keep a dairy: everything must be ordered, wholesome, obedient; the dose measured, the doctrine measured; the swallow expected and praised. Whether her pill or her text was well chosen, Heaven can tell; but she administered each as one who never doubted that she was born to prescribe.

Sir Miles’s dinner, to do him justice, made a handsome show. The sideboard shone with plate enough to dazzle a poor man into thinking he had eaten his fill merely by seeing it. Liveries moved solemnly about the room as if the household had been raised, by broadcloth and buttons, into a sort of ceremony. Yet it required a steady mind to notice that the beer, brought in a tankard fit for a lord’s October, was small and thin upon the tongue; and that the grand silver dish carried but a single joint of mutton, carved with as much importance as if it were venison for a hunting party. Sir Miles smacked his lips over his wine, and looked upon the ruby in his glass as though it were nectar poured from Olympus. He asked Harry Warrington—our young Virginian, so lately the darling of fortune and the favourite at every table—whether they had port like that in Virginia; and vowed it was nothing to what Harry should taste in Norfolk.

Harry, who had known better wine, nearly believed by force of his uncle’s praising that this, too, must be excellent; and he held the glass up, squinting into it as if merit might be spied by close looking, like a bubble in amber. It is one of the small enchantments of society that a man may drink sour liquor and, if all around him swear it is ambrosia, find his own tongue wavering between truth and politeness.

As in many well-ordered families then and now, the Warringtons had their two paragons. Lady Warrington told Harry, with a pious pride that rose like leaven in all her speech, that of her grown daughters one was the greatest Beauty and the other the greatest Genius and Angel of any young lady alive. The Beauty—Flora—was, in her mother’s confidence, already engaged to dear Tom Claypool. The Genius and Angel—Dora—set herself, with unwearied zeal, to improve Harry’s wits and morals. She sang to him at the harpsichord; an angel, Harry thought, might have kept better time, but he did not say so. She was ready with advice, instruction, earnest conversation; and she gave it with such a plentiful hand that, though Harry was a good-natured young fellow, he often would have preferred the simpler company of the little cousin who reminded him of Fanny Mountain at home—a child’s voice, a child’s laugh, a child’s appetite for simple pleasures, like new bread.

That youngest maiden, however, after dinner commonly retired to her nursery. Beauty went off upon her own avocations. Mamma had her poor to visit, her voluminous letters to write, her conscience to inspect. Papa dozed in his great chair with a contented grunt, like a man who had eaten enough to forget that the world required effort. And Dora remained, the Angel, to keep her cousin company and to rescue him—so she imagined—from the world.

Yet there was a calm in the house that pleased Harry. He, who lived so much in riot and late hours, liked at times to take shelter under this roof where the evening sounded differently: not the clatter of dice and the shrill laughter that follows them, but the quiet tick of a clock, the low stir of servants clearing away, the faint jangle of the harpsichord when Dora tried a passage again, dissatisfied. Such domestic noises are a kind of music too, and they steadied him. The welcome he received was unfailing. The doors were open at all hours. If Flora was not at home, Dora was ready to receive him; if Dora was busy in her angelic labours, mamma herself would be motherly. In a few days he and his little cousin Miles had had a galloping-match in the Park, hoof-beats drumming on the softer ground, the boy’s laughter carried away on the wind like a lark’s. Harry, generous to everybody who came near him, even began to think of buying the lad a better horse than the poor little beast he rode—when events, with the suddenness of a snapped trace, brought all Harry’s coaches and horses to an abrupt standstill.

Sir Miles, who had once imagined Virginia to be an island, was not the best instructed in geography; but the ladies were more curious, and more knowing, and eager to hear of Harry’s home. Harry was not loth to talk of it. To speak of the rivers and woods of his birth was to feel, for a moment, his feet planted on something real. He described the length and breadth of his estate; the rivers that coasted it; the produce it bore. He had, as a boy, taken some pleasure in surveying with a friend, and now, in Lady Warrington’s drawing-room, he set to work with paper and pencil, making a map of his county. He placed towns here and there—fine towns upon his draught which, in truth, were little more than log-huts; but for the honour of his country he would have them look handsomer than they were. Here ran Potomac; here James River; here the wharves from which his mother’s ships carried tobacco to the sea. The estate, in truth, was as large as an English county. Harry did not brag; he spoke as a young man might speak of his mother’s domain with a natural pride, and because the telling itself warmed him.

To see him, handsome in his velvet and silver lace, bending over his draught, pointing to a hill, a forest, a water-course, you might have imagined him a travelling prince describing a realm. He almost fancied himself so at times. In Virginia he had miles where English gentlemen had acres. Dora listened, intent, as if maps could be moral lessons. Flora, too, bowed her fair head and heard him with a new attention. And why should she not? What was young Tom Claypool—Sir Miles’s nephew in Norfolk, with his great boots and great voice and heirship to a poor five thousand acres—compared to this American cousin with his wide rivers and woods and the air of a charming stranger? Dora, angel as she was proclaimed, began to lose her angelic temper and to twit Flora with being a flirt. Claypool, when he came, would sit dumb in his red waistcoat before splendid Harry, who talked of March and Chesterfield, Selwyn and Bolingbroke, and the whole glittering company of macaronis, as if London were his pantry and he knew where every sweetmeat lay.

Lady Warrington’s affection for Harry grew in proportion as she discovered his importance. She became anxious about the spiritual welfare of the poor Indians and poor negroes in Virginia, and asked what she might do to help dear Madam Esmond in her good work—Madam Esmond being, as Lady Warrington was sure, a precious woman. She had a serious butler and a serious housekeeper; and they were delighted with the spiritual behaviour and sweet musical gifts of Gumbo, Harry’s black servant, who could sing as if he had swallowed a little bell. “Ah, Harry, Harry!” she would cry. “You have been a sad wild boy! Why did you not come sooner to us, sir, and not lose your time amongst the spendthrifts and the vain world? But ’tis not yet too late. We must reclaim thee, dear Harry! Mustn’t we, Sir Miles? Mustn’t we, Dora? Mustn’t we, Flora?”

At this appeal, the three would look up to the ceiling—as if heaven were painted there and could be consulted at leisure—and agree, each in her own way, that the prodigal must be reclaimed. It became a little contest of virtue, which should rescue him most. Dora watched Flora; Flora smiled with that softness which is not an argument but often wins them. When the girls were away, mamma talked to Harry more tenderly, more seriously. She would be a mother to him, she said, in the absence of his admirable parent. She gave him a hymn-book, pressed it upon him as she might press a vial of cordial into a trembling hand. She kissed his forehead. She was moved, she believed, by the purest love and religious regard toward her dear, wayward, amiable nephew.

While these domestic sanctities were being kneaded and shaped in the Warrington parlour, Harry kept his own counsel about his affairs out-of-doors. For fortune, which had smiled upon him with a broad easy grin for weeks, had suddenly turned her face away; and in a few days she had kicked down, with a careless foot, all his heap of winnings. If my Lord Castlewood—his own kinsman—had dealt unfairly with the young man at the table, who shall say? We insinuate nothing so disrespectful. But the fact remained: Castlewood had won from Harry every shilling that properly belonged to him; and would have played him for his reversions too, had not Harry, seeing himself beaten past remedy, flung up his hands and declared the battle must end. One spar remained from the wreck, as it were—that portion he had set aside for poor Sampson. In an hour of rash hope he ventured that too at the table; and it went down with the rest, and fortune fluttered off into the storm, leaving him almost naked on the shore.

When a man is young and hearty, the loss of money does not at first bite so deep as it will later. Harry told himself he would sell his horses, dismiss his coach, lessen his train. If he wanted immediate supplies, were there not friends? Would not his Aunt Bernstein be his banker? Might not his kinsman, who had won so much from him, be appealed to? Or his kind Uncle Warrington and Lady Warrington, always preaching benevolence and calling him a son—would they not help? He could call on any of these at leisure.

But Sampson’s story of his landlord’s distress touched him more sharply than his own. The young gentleman, who could feel another man’s hunger more readily than his own ruin, determined to raise a hasty supply for the poor clergyman. He gathered his trinkets—rings, a repeater, little ornaments bought in prosperous days—and carried them to a pawnbroker in St. Martin’s Lane. The shop had its own smell: old metal, stale cloth, oiled wood, and that sour breath of coins handled by many hands. Behind the counter, under dim light, the broker weighed gold with a grave face, as though virtue itself were being measured in drachms. Harry left his finery there as a man might leave pieces of himself.

Now this broker was a relative or partner of that very Mr. Sparks in Tavistock Street from whom Harry had once purchased—purchased, did we say? No: taken—the trinkets meant for his Oakhurst friends. And it happened that Mr. Sparks came to visit his brother-tradesman soon after Harry had pledged his goods. Recognising at once the little enamelled, diamond-handled repeater he had sold to the Fortunate Youth, the jeweller broke into such expressions regarding Harry as need not be repeated. A man acquainted with a pawnbroker is likely to have acquaintances among bailiffs; and bailiffs have followers who, at the bidding of the impartial Law, will lay a hand with equal readiness on a captain’s epaulet or a macaroni’s shoulder.

The very gentlemen who had seized upon Lady Maria at Tunbridge were now set upon her cousin in London. From Gumbo—garrulous, pleased with his own importance, and at that moment engaged in courting Mrs. Lambert’s maid in the adjoining mansion—they learned that his honour was at Sir Miles Warrington’s house in Hill Street. So while the black fellow dallied and whispered and listened for the maid’s laugh over the area railings, Mr. Costigan and his assistant waited, patient as cats, opposite the Warrington door.

Within, poor Harry was enjoying the delights of a virtuous family circle. Never had Uncle Miles been more cordial; never had Aunt Warrington been more gracious and affectionate. Flora looked unusually lovely; Dora more than ordinarily amiable. At parting, my lady gave Harry both her hands and called benedictions down from the ceiling upon him. Papa, in his most jovial manner, cried, “Hang it, nephew! when I was thy age I should have kissed two such fine girls as Do and Flo ere this—and my own flesh and blood too! Don’t tell me! I should, my Lady Warrington! Odds-fish! ’tis the boy blushes, and not the girls! I think—I suppose they are used to it. He, he!”

“Papa!” cried the virgins.
“Sir Miles!” said the august mother at the same instant.

“There, there!” quoth papa. “A kiss won’t do no harm, and won’t tell no tales: will it, nephew Harry?”

And so, during those brief phrases, the harmless little ceremony was performed: blushing cousin Harry touched the damask cheek of cousin Flora and cousin Dora—two soft, perfumed touches, like pressing one’s lips to rose-petals. Then he went downstairs with his uncle. Lady Warrington, when the door had closed behind him, addressed the girls with her usual upward gaze, as if virtue itself sat in the cornice. “What precious qualities your poor dear cousin has! What shrewdness mingled with his simplicity, and what a fine genteel manner—though upon mere worldly elegance I set little store. What a dreadful pity to think that such a vessel should ever be lost! We must rescue him, my loves. We must take him away from those wicked companions, and those horrible Castlewoods—not that I would speak ill of my neighbours. But I shall hope, I shall pray, that he may be rescued from his evil courses!”

And again she looked at the ceiling with a most determined piety, while the girls, less celestial, looked wistfully toward the door through which their interesting cousin had vanished.

Sir Miles went with Harry into the hall. “God bless you, my boy!” he cried, pressing Harry’s hand, repeating his benediction at the very threshold with a hearty shake, as if blessing were a thing that could be kneaded into the palm like dough.

As the door closed and the light from within fell full upon Harry’s face and figure, two men who had been standing on the opposite side of the way advanced quickly. One took a strip of paper from his pocket; the other laid a hand upon Harry’s shoulder. The touch was not paternal like Sir Miles’s; it was the dry grip of business. The man declared Harry his prisoner.

A hackney-coach waited, its wheels standing in the gutter, its horse shifting with a tired jingle of harness. And thus—so swiftly that the warmth of Hill Street’s parlour seemed a dream already—poor Harry Warrington, Madam Esmond’s son, was carried away to sleep in Chancery Lane.

To think of it: a Virginian prince’s back slapped by a ragged follower of the law; that young man, who had talked of broad rivers and forests under English candles, lying now in a spunging-house in Cursitor Street. The night there had its own cruel soundscape: not the pleasant clink of glasses at Sir Miles’s, but the oaths and jollifications of hardened inmates boozing in the next room, their laughter striking the walls like knuckles on a coffin-lid; the scrape of a bench; the groan of a bedstead; the murmur of the street outside, where wheels went on turning for those who were free.

Let us, if we please, imagine him wakeful on his dingy pillow, the stings of remorse as sharp as vinegar on a raw tongue; shame burning in him hotter than any punch-bowl; rage beating time with his heart to the coarse chorus next door. There is no need to pity him overmuch—so the world says—for surely none of us have ever been extravagant or foolish, nor ever paid the reckoning of regret.

Harry Warrington, caged in that sour little lock-up off Cursitor Street, had leisure enough for remorse and for rage; remorse—yes, for the follies that had led him here; rage—hotter still, at the indignity of a sheriff’s hand on a gentleman’s shoulder. Yet he would not grant the thing its full weight. It must be a passing inconvenience. He had twenty friends in London who would unlatch any door for him: Mr. Draper, all bows and deference; his kind baronet-uncle, who had offered him hearth and home; his cousin Castlewood, lately so lucky at cards; the great men at White’s and the Chocolate-House; good Aunt Bernstein herself. Only—let it be done quietly. Let no buzzing town-mouths make a dish of it, spicing his name for their amusement.

As if London were not a kitchen where every whisper is minced fine and tossed from table to table. As if the world cannot smell out a man’s mischance through closed shutters, the way hungry folk smell roast-meat down a passage. Still, Harry, with the vanity of youth, imagined all of St. James’s already chewing on his disgrace, Selwyn cracking bone-dry jests over it, March fretting about the bet, the whole club clattering their plates in cruel congratulation at the “Savage” being taken.

No—he would not begin with family, nor with lords. He would send for Sampson. Sampson had been in such scrapes before; Sampson knew the turns of such locks, the price of such keys. So at the first watery light of dawn—so late it seemed that morning, as though the sun had forgotten the alleyways of bondage—Harry got a message carried to Long Acre, begging the chaplain to come with counsel and comfort.

Having done that, his mind settled enough to condescend to breakfast. It came on a tray like a sentence: pale bread, a weak pot, and the smell of yesterday’s grease clinging to everything, as if the very boards had been basted with old misery. The attendant, with the practised civility of a tavern-waiter and the hard eye of a gaoler, asked whether his honour would order dinner, or take his meal at Mrs. Bailiff’s table with other gentlemen. No. Harry would be gone before dinner. The fellow’s mouth twitched as if he had heard that promise from a hundred young blades before.

“Well, if your honour does stay,” he said, shutting the door upon Harry and his pride, “there is good beef and carrot at two o’clock.”

So the morning dragged—hour after hour, each one a spoon scraping the bottom of a pot. A return message came from Sampson: he would attend as soon as might be. Ten o’clock came, eleven, noon; no parson. Instead, near midday, in burst Gumbo with a portmanteau, and with such howling grief as might have raised the dead. He flung himself at Harry’s feet, clasped at his knees, sobbed out oaths of fidelity; he would die, he would sell himself into slavery again, he would do anything to save Master Harry from this calamitous place.

Harry—touched in spite of himself—ordered him up sharply. “Give me my clothes. Dress me. And hold your tongue. Not a word of this business to anybody. Mind you—not a word.”

“Oh no, sir—nebber to nobody!” Gumbo swore, solemn as a judge; and set about his work with the devotion of a man who loved with his hands. He brushed and shook out linen, laid out stockings and waistcoat, and set his master’s coat as carefully as a cook trusses a bird for a great table. He flung a dash of powder through Harry’s hair—too much, perhaps, for a prison room, but Gumbo would have his gentleman look like a gentleman, even among walls that stank of fear. Buttons were fastened, cravat coaxed into place, cuffs set straight; and when the black had done, Harry might have been stepping from his lodgings into a chair for St. James’s, not waiting for a key in a shabby den.

Love and servility did all they could. But there are things no hands can mend once done; and there are truths that crouch away when a man has been trained to fear. Gumbo, for all his warmth, had been schooled in that old lesson of dependence: to slip, to excuse, to lie prettily where plain truth might bring a blow. Such training is a chain of the tongue, whether the neck beneath it be black or white; and the slave’s habit clings like smoke to cloth.

For indeed—his oath to keep silence was the very kind of promise his nature could not keep. Gumbo’s heart might ache honestly enough, but his tongue wagged with its own appetite: for story, for brag, for company. Long before he entered Harry’s room with that portmanteau, he had carried the news as fast as feet and vanity could take him—chiefly to gentlemen with shoulder-knots and worsted lace, who live by other people’s fortunes and misfortunes. He had told Colonel Lambert’s people; he had told Lord Wrotham’s; he had proclaimed it at his footmen’s club over ale, with every repetition adding a fresh garnish; he had repeated it in Sir Miles Warrington’s butler-room, where the tale was swallowed with relish; he had gone on to Madame Bernstein’s household, to those with whom he kept affectionate commerce; and, having nothing to do that evening now his master was “captured,” he had even climbed to Lord Castlewood’s and fed the news to that kitchen too. So when he looked holy-eyed and vowed, “nebber to nobody,” it was already all over town in the way kitchen-savour runs—under doors, up stairs, into drawing-rooms.

Harry sat dressed, breakfast finished, pride propped up as if clothes could armour him. Still no Sampson. At last, after noon, a billet arrived—not the man, but his writing, sealed with a wafer still damp, the ink hardly dry.

It ran—blotted with haste and misery—to this effect: that Sampson had done all that could be done; that Harry little knew what danger he had called his chaplain into; that Sampson, hastening to him with gratitude and zeal, had been seized by two villains with a writ, and was now lodged in Naboth’s, three doors off; so close, he wrote, that they might almost hear each other across the garden walls of their respective prisons. He had much of importance to say, but would not put it on paper. He ended with a prayer that both their cursed fortunes might mend, and signed himself, “Your honour’s afflicted Chaplain-in-Ordinary, J. S.”

So the friend Harry had summoned into the pit had tumbled in beside him.

And since Sampson would not speak plainly on paper, the rest must be told without his voice.

Gumbo’s babble had not reached as far as Long Acre. Sampson had known nothing of Harry’s arrest until Harry’s messenger found him. Still freshly grateful for the service Harry had lately done him, the chaplain’s first impulse was to run to Lord Castlewood—who had, after all, won so much from his cousin—and try to wring pity from that fine-bred hardness.

Sampson spoke with genuine feeling. He pleaded, he painted Harry’s distress, he reminded the nobleman of kinship and of winnings. But Lord Castlewood, whom life had made peevish and inwardly desperate, cut him short.

“Did I not tell you, two days since, when you came for money, that I was as poor as a beggar, Sampson?” he said. “Has any one left me a fortune since? The little sum I won from my cousin was swallowed up by others. I not only can’t help Mr. Warrington, but—upon my word, not knowing his calamity—I had written to him this morning to ask him to help me.”

And he had: a letter to that very effect was even then making its slow, cruel way by penny post to Harry’s lodgings.

“I must get him money, my lord,” Sampson cried. “He had scarcely anything left after relieving me. I’ll pawn my cassock and bands—he must have money!”

“Amen,” Castlewood said with an indifferent sneer. “Go and pawn your bands, your cassock—anything you please. Your enthusiasm does you credit.” And he went back to his paper as though he had dismissed a beggar from his door.

Sampson went out with despair in his throat—and was seized, just beyond that house, by Lady Maria.

She drew him into the dining-room, her face already worked into grief and anger. “Tell me,” she demanded, “what is this that has happened to Mr. Warrington?”

“Your ladyship knows, then?” Sampson asked.

“Have I not been in mortal anxiety since his servant brought the dreadful news last night?” she said. “We had it as we came from the opera—from my Lady Yarmouth’s box—my lord, my Lady Castlewood, and I.”

“His lordship, then, did know?” Sampson pressed.

“Benson told the news when we came from the playhouse to our tea,” she repeated.

The chaplain’s patience snapped. He swore, and told her—hotly—of Castlewood’s refusal; of his pretence of ignorance; of the sums he had taken from Harry; and of Harry’s generosity to himself. Sampson spoke as only a man can speak when gratitude and indignation boil together.

Then Lady Maria—who did not commonly love truth, yet could fling it like stones when rage armed her—burst into a torrent against her own blood. Tears, curses, and words worse than curses; she flung open family histories as if they were cupboards and dragged out the sour contents. Her voice rose so shrill, her gestures so wild, that Sampson, fearing the storm she meant to loose, edged away toward the street.

But Maria dashed to her brother’s library door and broke in upon him.

Castlewood looked up, surprised as a man is surprised when a quiet room is invaded by a sudden hawk-cry. He chose a strong oath, as one chooses a stick, and threw it at her to beat her back.

She did not flinch. Fear of him had been her habit; fury unmade it.

“So, my lord!” she cried. “You sit with him in private to cards and pigeon him! You get the poor boy’s last shilling, and you won’t give him a guinea out of his own winnings now he is penniless!”

“So that infernal chaplain has been telling tales!” Castlewood said.

“Dismiss him—do! Pay him his wages, and let him go. He’ll be glad enough!” she flung back.

“I keep him to marry one of my sisters, in case he is wanted,” he answered, glaring.

“What can the women be in a family where there are such men?” Maria cried.

“Effectivement!” said my lord, with a shrug.

“What can we be, when our fathers and brothers are what they are?” she went on. “We are bad enough—but what are you? You have neither courage—nor honour—nor common feeling. As your equals won’t play with you, you must take this poor lad out of Virginia—your own kinsman—and fleece him! Oh, it’s a shame—a shame!”

“We are all playing our own game,” Castlewood said coolly. “Haven’t you played and won one, Maria? Is it you that are squeamish of a sudden about the poor lad from Virginia? Has Mr. Harry cried off, or has your ladyship got a better offer? If you won’t have him, one of the Warrington girls will, I promise you; and the old Methodist woman in Hill Street will give him the choice of either. Are you a fool, Maria Esmond? A greater fool, I mean, than in common?”

“I should be a fool if I thought either of my brothers could act like an honest man, Eugene!” she cried. “I am a fool to expect you will help a relative in distress; that if you find a victim you won’t fleece him.”

“Fleece him? Psha! What folly! Have you not seen, from the course the lad has been running for months, how he would end? If I had not won his money, some other would. I never grudged you your little plans regarding him. Why fly into a passion because I put out my hand to take what he was offering to the world? I reason with you—I don’t know why. You think this money belonged by right to Lady Maria Warrington and her children? I tell you that in three months every shilling would have found its way to White’s macco-table, and it is much better spent paying my debts. So much for your anger, tears, menaces, and naughty language. See! I am a good brother, and repay you with reason and kind words.”

“My good brother might have given a little more than kind words,” Maria broke in, “to the lad from whom he has taken hundreds.”

“Great heavens, Maria!” Castlewood cried, suddenly changing his tone to one of sly instruction. “Don’t you see that even out of this affair—unpleasant as it seems—a clever woman may make her advantage?”

“I don’t understand you,” she said.

“C’est possible; but sit down, and I will explain in a manner suited to your capacity.” And Maria, who had entered like a raging creature, found herself—by habit, by family training, by the old authority of the elder male voice—sinking into a chair to listen.

Meanwhile, in Clarges Street, Madame de Bernstein had not slept. The news Gumbo brought her the night before—one more bitter draught for a weary spirit—had struck her with a real, unwilling tenderness. Arrests were common enough in her world; she knew the process as she knew the prices at market. But what scrape had her scapegrace nephew fallen into now? How much money would be demanded for his release? Had he spent all his own?

If he had not committed himself beyond remedy, she was disposed to help. She liked even his follies; they were at least alive. For long years he had been almost the only creature upon whom she could lay anything like natural affection; and so, while he lay wakeful behind his prison door and she lay wakeful behind her curtains, their thoughts, in different rooms, kept the same uneasy vigil.

Early in the morning she sent to her man of business, Mr. Draper, commanding him to learn at once for what sums Mr. Warrington had been arrested, and to report to her. Draper’s people were quick. They found Harry locked up close by, and they counted the detainers already laid against him. Others would follow, they warned, as soon as creditors scented the confinement—like flies that find a spilled pot of syrup.

So much to Mr. Sparks, the jeweller, for those unlucky presents; so much to the Bond Street landlord for board, fire, and lodging. These, for the present, were all. Draper stood ready to settle them the moment she gave word. Especially the jeweller’s bill must be paid; for Harry had acted with a rashness that could turn to scandal: taking goods on credit and pledging them with a pawnbroker. It spoke of sudden pressure, not of dishonour; perhaps he meant to redeem at once. Still, in London, appearances are currencies too; and this coin had an ugly stamp unless melted down quickly.

“There cannot be the least difficulty about a thousand pounds more or less,” Madame de Bernstein said, “for a gentleman of Mr. Warrington’s rank and expectations.” She knew very well where funds lay that could be touched at once with her guarantee.

Mr. Draper, ever eager to smooth a disturbance, proposed to go instantly to Messrs. Amos, settle the matter, and have Mr. Harry free in time to dine with her at two—and so confound the club gentlemen “who are no doubt rejoicing over his misfortunes.”

But the Baroness, with that hard practical mercy of hers, had other views.

“I think, my good Mr. Draper,” she said, “that my young gentleman has sown wild oats enough; and when he comes out of prison I should like him to come out clear—and without any liabilities at all. You are not aware of all his.”

“No gentleman ever does tell all his debts, madam,” Draper answered. “No one I ever had to deal with.”

Gumbo’s kind offices—his soft-footed comings and goings, his murmured assurances, his very way of setting a cracked jug of water and a coarse napkin as though they were silver and damask—had worked upon Harry Warrington’s anger like a slow simmer upon tough meat. The second night in that sour spunging-house was not so noisome as the first; for there was, at least, one faithful creature near him who could warm a corner of the cold place with human care.

Yet the warmth went no further than that corner. Toward the rest of the world Harry’s heart stayed hard, proud, and impatient. He lay listening to the house breathe—chains clinked below, a cough worried the next room, a key turned with that metallic scrape that seemed made to rasp a man’s spirit raw—and he told himself that England was a land where friendship had been turned to trade, and trade to cruelty. Aunt Warrington with her pieties; March with his great airs; Castlewood with his easy scorn: each had been tested, and each, in Harry’s mind, had failed. Not for twenty years of prison, not for famine, not for the shame of being pointed at in the street, would he stoop to ask their aid again.

He would leave. He would go anywhere that did not have this perpetual jangling of metal and coin in its very speech. Germany, perhaps—where a king made war openly and a man might be ruined by cannon instead of by creditors. Or Virginia—where the woods kept old sounds in their branches, where the whippoorwill and the creek’s talk were honest, and a man’s name meant what it meant in his mother’s mouth. He pictured, with a hunger that was almost bodily, the clean snap of tobacco leaves curing in barns, the sweet damp of earth at dawn, a kitchen where bacon hissed and corn-cakes browned, where the dialect of the quarter and the drawl of Tidewater—those languages that carried memory in their very vowels—had not been beaten thin by London’s sharp, fashionable tongue. He would be factor and steward; he would hunt all day; he would marry Polly Broadbent or Fanny Mountain; he would become anything—planter, farmer, even a plain tobacco-grower—rather than remain among these fine gentlemen whose politeness had the sound of knives.

So he rose with an outward face made cheerful by obstinacy, and an inward temper still burning. Early in the morning Gumbo appeared, punctual as any steward in a great house, having come from Bond Street with Mr. Harry’s letters.

“I wanted to bring some more clo’es, master,” honest Gumbo said, with that look of patient shame he wore whenever a white man’s pride had been brought to beggary; “but Mr. Ruff, de landlord, he wouldn’t let me bring no more.”

Harry scarcely cared to see the papers. He broke one seal, then another, then a third: all were bills, all with that same cold, printed certainty, as if money itself had learned to write in a harsher hand than men. A fourth was from the landlord: no more goods to go out; the debt must be paid; if not, the goods should be sold; and the black man must sleep elsewhere. Ruff had almost refused Gumbo his own clothes and portmanteau.

Gumbo, however, had refuge. He said it simply, but his eyes were busy on Harry’s face. “I been stayin’ wid friends at Lord Wrotham house. Wid Colonel Lambert people,” he added, as though dropping a stone into still water to see what circles would come.

“And Miss Hetty,” Gumbo continued, lowering his voice as if sorrow must be spoken softly, “she fall down in a faint when she hear you taken up; and Mr. Lambert, he very good man, and he say to me dis mornin’, he say, ‘Gumbo, you tell your master if he want me he send to me, and I come to him.’”

At the mention of Hetty, something in Harry’s breast gave way for a moment. Whatever else England had been to him—its gaming-tables, its drawing-rooms, its scornful laughter—Hetty Lambert’s gentleness had not been a lie. He did not altogether believe in Gumbo’s fainting tale; he knew how the man embroidered kindness into legend, as if affection must be made larger to cover misfortune. But that she had been distressed—yes, he believed that. It touched him, and the touch stung.

Then Colonel Lambert’s name came, and the softness curdled at once. The colonel—who had flung back his gifts, who had insulted him with that calm superiority which is a whip without a lash. Send to Lambert? Ask the man for help? Harry’s jaw set as though he were biting iron.

“I send to Lambert,” he said to himself, grinding his teeth. “If I were starving I would not ask him for a crust.”

He dressed with the same punctilious care he would have used in his best days, as though a clean neckcloth and ordered hair could silence the dirty clatter of bolts and bars. He called for breakfast. The bread was coarse, the tea thin, the room steeped in the smell of stale spirits and damp wool; still, he made himself eat, not from appetite but from that stubborn discipline that had been beaten into him by plantation and camp. The house was full of sound—men bickering in low voices, a distant shout, a laugh that ended in coughing—each noise an insult, each echo a reminder that he was penned.

He sent Gumbo away with a brief note to Mr. Draper, attorney in the Temple, requiring that gentleman’s attendance.

The note, indeed, had the air of a command flung to a slave. Draper, who had long endured Harry’s condescension with a sour patience, read it and coloured.

“It’s all very well for a fine gentleman to give hisself airs; but for a fellow in a spunging-house! Hang him!” Draper said to himself. “I’ve a great mind not to go!”

Nevertheless he went. He came in a mood bristling with small resentments, and found the young Virginian more lordly in adversity than he had ever been in prosperity.

Harry sat upon the bed as if it were a chair of state, wrapped in a splendid brocaded dressing-gown that made a kind of mockery of the dingy room. His hair was dressed; his hands were clean. He motioned to Gumbo as though Gumbo were a footman in Clarges Street.

“Gumbo, a chair to Mr. Draper.”

“Excuse me, madam, but such haughtiness and airs I ain’t accustomed to!” Draper had exclaimed, afterwards, when he went to report proceedings to Madame de Bernstein; and the old Baroness, far from being angered, had smiled. There was a relish in her for pride—especially pride that bit when it was wounded. It amused her that the boy could still carry himself like a gentleman while the law had him by the throat.

She and Draper had arranged beforehand what line he should take. Draper was capable, even shrewd; but like many men whose living depended upon phrases and forms, he could not understand the kind of pride that is not a bargaining chip. He went in thinking he should manage Harry as he managed common clients: a push here, a threat there, a promise dangled, a paper thrust under the nose. He did not see that Harry’s very sense of language—what was binding, what was base, what words could be endured—was of another country, another upbringing, another music.

“Sit down, if you please,” Harry said, with a cold civility that made the request sound like an order. “Let us talk my business over. Much obliged to you for coming so soon in reply to my message. Had you heard of this piece of ill-luck before?”

“Bad news travel quick, Mr. Warrington,” Draper replied. “And I was eager to offer my humble services as soon as ever you should require them. Your friends, your family, will be much pained that a gentleman of your rank should be in such a position.”

“I have been very imprudent, Mr. Draper. I have lived beyond my means.”

Draper bowed—one of those bows which seem to say, I expected no better.

“I played in company with gentlemen much richer than myself. A cursed run of ill-luck has carried away all my ready money, leaving me with liabilities to the amount of five hundred pounds, and more.”

“Five hundred now in the office,” Draper said promptly.

“Well,” Harry continued, staring straight at him, “it is such a trifle that I thought by sending to one or two friends yesterday I could have paid my debt and gone home without further to do. I have been mistaken. I thank you to put me in the way of raising the money as soon as may be.”

Draper pulled a long face, as though five hundred pounds were a mountain.

“Why, sir, it can be done!” Harry said sharply, provoked by the display.

“It can be done in time,” Draper answered, enjoying the chance to look grave, “but it will require a considerable time. To touch the property in England which is yours on Mr. George Warrington’s death, we must have the event proved, the trustees released—and who is to do either? Lady Esmond Warrington in Virginia, of course, will not allow her son to remain in prison, but we must wait six months before we hear from her. Has your Bristol agent any authority to honour your drafts?”

“He is only authorised to pay me two hundred pounds a year,” Harry said.

“I suppose I have no resource, then, but to apply to my aunt, Madame de Bernstein,” Harry went on, forcing the words through his pride. “She will be my security.”

“Her ladyship will do anything for you, sir; she has said so to me, often and often,” Draper replied. “And if she gives the word at this moment you can walk out of this place.”

“Go to her, then, from me,” Harry said. “I did not want to have troubled my relations; but rather than continue in this horrible needless imprisonment, I must speak to her. Say where I am, and what has befallen me. Disguise nothing. And tell her that I confide in her affection and kindness for me to release me from this—this disgrace.”

His voice shook on the last word. For an instant he heard, under the present sounds, other remembered sounds: his mother’s voice in Virginia, calling him by his name in that slow, native music; the kitchen’s steady labour; the crackle of a fire fed with pine; words that did not cut, because they belonged.

Draper watched him, then said, with a dry relish, “Sir, I was with her ladyship yesterday, when we talked over the whole of this here most unpleasant—I won’t say, as you do, disgraceful business.”

“What do you mean, sir? Does Madame de Bernstein know of my misfortune?” Harry demanded.

“Every circumstance, sir. The pawning the watches, and all.”

Harry flushed as though he had been struck.

“It is an unfortunate business,” Draper continued, “the pawning them watches and things which you had never paid for.”

Harry sprang up from the bed. There was something in his look that made Draper feel, for a moment, the difference between a man who has been taught to command bodies and a man who has only ever commanded papers.

“It may lead to litigation and unpleasant remarks being made, in court,” Draper went on, half frightened, half delighted to be giving pain. “Them barristers respect nothing; and when they get a feller in the box—”

“Great Heaven, sir!” Harry cried. “Do you suppose a gentleman of my rank can’t take a watch upon credit without intending to cheat the tradesman?”

“Of course you meant everything that’s honourable,” Draper said, winking, “only, you see, the law mayn’t happen to think so. Your aunt says it’s the most imprudent thing ever she heard of—to call it by no worse name.”

“You call it by no worse name yourself, Mr. Draper?” Harry said, speaking each word slowly, as if he were measuring them, trying to keep mastery over his own voice.

“Heaven forbid that I should say anything as between gentleman and gentleman,” Draper answered; “but between me and my client, it’s my duty to say, ‘Sir, you are in a very unpleasant scrape,’ just as a doctor would tell his patient, ‘Sir, you are very ill.’”

“And you can’t help me to pay this debt off,” Harry said, with a bitter astonishment, “and you have come only to tell me I may be accused of roguery?”

“Of obtaining goods under false pretences? Most undoubtedly, yes. I can’t help it, sir. Don’t look as if you would knock me down. A young gentleman who has only two hundred a year from his ma’, orders diamonds and watches, and takes ’em to a pawnbroker. You ask me what people will think of such behaviour, and I tell you honestly. Don’t be angry with me, Mr. Warrington.”

“Go on, sir,” Harry said, and the words came like a groan.

Draper now felt the moment was his. “But you ask if I can’t help to pay this debt off? And I say Yes—and that here is the money in my pocket to do it now, if you like—not mine, sir; my honoured client’s; your aunt, Lady Bernstein. But she has a right to impose her conditions, and I’ve brought ’em with me.”

“Tell them, sir,” Harry said, his pride bending because he saw the door open.

“They are not hard. They are only for your own good. If you say Yes, we can call a hackney-coach, and go to Clarges Street together, which I have promised to go there whether you will or no. Mr. Warrington, I name no names, but there was a question of marriage between you and a certain party.”

“Ah!” Harry breathed; and his face, for the first time that day, showed something like relief. The very thought of being unknotted from that foolish promise was like drawing a thorn from the flesh.

“To that marriage my noble client, the Baroness, is most averse,” Draper continued. “Having other views for you, and thinking it will be your ruin to marry a party—of noble birth and title it is true; but, excuse me, not of first-rate character, and so much older than yourself. You had given an imprudent promise to that party.”

“Yes,” Harry said, “and she has it still.”

“It has been recovered,” Draper replied. “She dropped it by an accident at Tunbridge, so my client informed me; indeed her ladyship showed it me, for the matter of that. It was wrote in bl—”

“Never mind, sir!” Harry cried, turning as red as the ink he imagined, and as ashamed as though his folly had been shouted down the whole passage.

“At the same time letters, wrote to you, and compromising a noble family, were recovered,” Draper went on. “You had lost ’em. It was no fault of yours. You were away when they were found again. You may say that that noble family, that you yourself, have a friend such as few young men have. Well, sir, there’s no earthly promise to bind you—only so many idle words said over a bottle, which very likely any gentleman may forget. Say you won’t go on with this marriage—give me and my noble friend your word of honour. Cry off, I say, Mr. W.! Don’t be such a d—-fool, saving your presence, as to marry an old woman who has jilted scores of men in her time. Say the word, and I step downstairs, pay every shilling against you in the office, and put you down in my coach—either at your aunt’s, or at White’s Club, if you like—with a couple of hundred in your pocket. Say yes; and give us your hand! There’s no use in sitting grinning behind these bars all day!”

All this, in substance, was what Harry desired. His flame for Maria Esmond had long since guttered out; it had been vanity and youth, and the intoxication of being pursued by a famous woman’s notice. If she would release him, he would bless the release. Yet Draper’s tone—his coarse jokes, his familiarity—fell on Harry’s ear like the clank of the keys below: the sound of a man trampling another man’s pride for sport.

“Come! Give us your hand, and say done!” Draper pressed, with a knowing wink. “Don’t stand shilly-shallying, sir. Law bless you, Mr. W., if I had married everybody I promised, I should be like the Grand Turk, or Captain Macheath in the play!”

The attorney’s easy profanity in the presence of an oath disgusted Harry. He drew back, scarcely aware that he did so, and gathered the brocaded gown about him as if to shut out not cold but familiarity.

“Give me a little time to think of the matter, if you please, Mr. Draper,” he said. “And have the goodness to come to me again in an hour.”

“Very good, sir—very good, sir!” Draper answered, biting his lip till it whitened. “Most parties would not want an hour to consider about such an offer as I make you; but I suppose my time must be yours. I’ll come again, and see whether you are to go or to stay. Good morning, sir—good morning.”

He went down the stairs muttering. “Won’t take my hand, won’t he? Will tell me in an hour’s time! Hang his impudence! I’ll show him what an hour is!”

In his chambers he vented himself on clerks and clients. He sent a messenger to the Baroness to say he had waited on the young gentleman, who had demanded time for consideration—mere form, no doubt. Then he went to dinner at his leisure and did business as though a man’s liberty were an item to be entered when convenient. It was late afternoon before he turned toward Cursitor Street.

“He’ll be at home when I call, the haughty beast,” Draper sneered.

At the spunging-house the double doors were opened by a sheriff’s follower with a face both flushed and solemn, and an air of importance so comic that it might have been harmless, had the smell not betrayed the truth. The little passage between the doors was rich with spirituous fumes; gin and sour breath lay there like a fog.

“The Fortunate Youth in his room?” Draper asked.

“Mr. Warrington is in his apartment,” the fellow said, “but—” and here he winked and laid a finger to his nose with drunken significance.

“But what, Mr. Paddy from Cork?” Draper snapped, pushing forward.

“My name is Costigan,” the man returned, swelling and scowling. “Me familee is noble, and me neetive place is the Irish methrawpolis, Mr. Six-and-eightpence!”

“Confound you, sir, let me pass!” Draper bawled.

“I can hear you perfectly well, Six-and-eightpence,” Costigan retorted, slurring and blustering, “except your h’s, which you dthrop out of your conversation. I’ll thank ye not to call neems, me good friend, or me fingers and your nose will have to make an intimate hic-quaintance. Walk in, sir! Be polite for the future to your shupariors in birth and manners, though they may be your infariors in temporary station. Confound the kay! Walk in, sir, I say—Madam, I have the honour of saluting ye most respectfully!”

A lady came down the stairs at that moment, her face covered with a capuchin, further hidden by a handkerchief. She gave a small cry, startled to find herself confronted by a man like Draper pressing forward with bold curiosity.

Draper would have peered at her—he had that vulgar gallantry which mistakes intrusion for compliment—but Costigan thrust his leg between them, barring the way like a gate.

“Keep your own distance, if you plaise! This way, madam! I at once recognised your ladysh—”

He stopped himself and, with a sudden drunken discretion, slammed the door on Draper’s nose, leaving the attorney to find his own way upstairs, fuming and bewildered amid the sour, echoing sounds of the place.

In Clarges Street, meanwhile, the old Baroness de Bernstein paced upon her drawing-room floor, leaning on her crutch, turning her head at every rumble of wheels. The street’s noises—coach-horses, calls, the far-off clatter of a city always buying and selling—came to her like a taunt. She, who on ordinary days would have scourged a cook for five minutes’ delay, had put off dinner from hour to hour. She had ordered two covers. She had commanded extra dishes, as though to tempt a boy’s appetite back into him with rich gravies and crisped pastry, as if liberty itself might be served hot and fragrant upon a plate.

Four o’clock passed. Five. At six she went again to the window, and at last a coach did stop at her door.

“Mr. Draper,” the servant announced.

He entered bowing profoundly. The Baroness trembled upon her stick, her old eyes bright and impatient.

“Where is the boy?” she demanded. “I told you to bring him, sir! How dare you come without him?”

“It is not my fault, madam,” Draper said, with a wounded dignity. “Mr. Warrington refuses to come.”

And then, in the same room where soups and roasts were cooling for want of the one guest they were meant to warm, Draper began to give his version of the interview—each word chosen to make his own affront sound like the young man’s insolence, and each syllable carrying, under its meaning, that harsh London note which had already begun to corrode Harry Warrington’s faith in kindness.

Mr. Draper went off in his heat with the echo of his own peroration snapping at his heels. In the close passage outside the room, he thought he heard the young prisoner call after him—indeed Harry had started up from the bed, half a word on his lips, his pride already bending as need would have it. But the attorney’s dignity was in arms, and Harry’s was wounded too; the one would not pause, the other would not beg. The door shut. A draught from the corridor chilled the sour air of the chamber; the bolts and bars seemed to answer it with a little iron music that set the teeth on edge.

“An hour hence will do as well,” Harry told himself, and dropped back upon the coverlet with that stubborn sullenness which is only despair wearing a soldier’s coat. He would not—he did not—care for Maria Esmond. No. The very thought of her was an insult to his own liberty. He had been trapped into the engagement; a woman older, wily, instructed in the tricks by which hearts are hooked and held, had taken advantage of a boy’s heat as her brother had taken advantage of a boy’s rashness at the cards. They were his own blood; they should have spared him. Instead they had made him their convenience, their instrument—hospitality turned to snare, a kinsman welcomed within their gates only to be used.

He lay and stared at the stained ceiling, yet saw, as if laid upon a trencher before him, the table at Castlewood—the soft nap of the cloth, the shining of glasses, the steam of a dish uncovered, the honest Virginia abundance he had fancied in his mind when he first came to England with his simple confidence and his hungry youth. Had they come to Virginia, he thought, they should have had a different welcome: smoke from hickory, a ham cured sweet and salt both, a great dish of hominy set to swell and soften till each grain gave up its heart, chicken browned in a Dutch oven and basted till the skin shone, apple-tarts with the edges crimped by a careful hand. A house where the voices were kind and the sounds at night were only frogs and wind in the trees—not this perpetual London grind of wheels, iron upon stone, men bawling beneath windows, and keys clanking like threats.

His throat thickened, his pride melted into bitterness, and bitter tears, hot as broth, ran down and wet the pillow. He turned his face into it, as if even his sobbing must be muffled, not to give the place the satisfaction of hearing him break.

A shuffle at the door, a familiar cough smothered in a grin, roused him. Gumbo’s black face, half lighted, peeped in like a friendly moon.

“A lady come see Master Harry,” the man said; and before Harry could do more than wipe his eyes with the back of his hand, the lady herself entered, wrapped in a capuchin.

He sat up, pale and hollow-cheeked, the loose dressing-gown slipping from his shoulder. The lady gave a sob that seemed to carry with it all the warmth of a hearth into that cold room. Almost before the servant had withdrawn, she ran to him and put her arms round his neck with a real emotion and a motherly tenderness. She kissed his cheek again and again, not caring that it was fevered, and her tears fell plentifully there.

“Oh, my Harry! Did I ever, ever think to see thee here?”

He started back as if the sight of her were too strange to be borne—an apparition indeed in that place; and yet she sank down at the bedside and caught his hand, pressing it against her lips, and then, as if she could not help herself, embraced his knees, clinging to him as one clings to a living thing in a flood.

“I—I thought none of you would come!” Harry groaned; for all his anger of the morning, that one sentence unlocked something in him that had been hard shut.

Her answer was kisses and more kisses, her fingers closing over his hand as if she would warm it by mere will. There was no coquetry now, no small tyrannies of a drawing-room; she wept outright, and the poor room was the witness of a tenderness that needed no audience.

“Oh, my dear! my dear! I cannot bear to think of thee in misery,” she sobbed.

Hardened though her heart might be by practice, it was not all marble; and that dreary life of hers, with its painted smiles and desperate shifts, was not all desert. Harry’s own mother could not have spoken more softly than this kinswoman kneeling at his feet.

“Some of the debts, I fear, were owing to my extravagance,” she said—speaking truth, for she knew how he had flung away prudence to buy her pleasures. “You bought trinkets and jewels in order to give me delight. Oh, how I hate them now! I little thought I ever could! I have brought them all with me, and more trinkets—here! and here! and all the money I have in the world!”

From a little bag and a pocket in her cloak she poured out upon his lap brooches, rings, a watch, and guineas—yellow, heavy, and bright as a hoard of sun. They made a sound upon the quilt—a small clink and tumble—that seemed in that silence loud as a tavern’s till. The very sight of them, the proof of her sacrifice, shook him. It was as though she had brought not metal but her own flesh to ransom him.

“Dearest—kindest cousin!” he sobbed, his voice breaking like a boy’s. His lips could find no more words, but they found her hand, and kissed it with a gratitude too deep for speech.

Presently, as her tears lessened, his spirits rose in that strange way they will when kindness comes after cruelty. He became almost gay; he smiled as he gathered some of the trinkets—those he had bought for her—back into her keeping, and told her with rueful candour into what danger he had fallen by selling other goods purchased on credit: how he had tried to patch one hole with another, as a cook spoils a dish by over-salting to cover a burnt. He told her too of the lawyer’s insolence that morning.

He would not—he could not—take her money. He had enough for the moment, he said. And yet he prized her twenty guineas as if they were twenty thousand; their weight was not in gold but in love. He swore he would never forget her goodness, not by any thing sacred. His mother should hear of it. It had cheered him when he was upon the point of breaking under disgrace.

So they talked on, cousins again and not adversaries, until the early darkness of the London season began to creep in, turning the small window to a dull mirror. Maria rose with a sigh, her eyes still red, and bade him farewell. The air where she had been seemed warmer a moment after she went, as if the very room remembered her perfume and the rustle of her cloak.

The door had scarcely closed upon her when it opened again and admitted Mr. Draper.

“Your humble servant, sir,” said the attorney.

His voice grated upon Harry’s ear like a knife on a plate. After Maria’s weeping tenderness it sounded the more hard, the more commercial.

“I had expected you some hours ago, sir,” Harry returned curtly.

“A lawyer’s time is not always his own, sir,” Draper answered, who had been consulting not parchments but a bottle of port at the Grecian. He wore that slightly flushed assurance which comes of wine and self-approval. “Never mind; I’m at your orders now. Presume it’s all right, Mr. Warrington. Packed your trunk? Why, now there you are in your bedgown still. Let me go down and settle whilst you call in your black man and titivate a bit. I’ve a coach at the door, and we’ll be off and dine with the old lady.”

“Are you going to dine with the Baroness de Bernstein, pray?” Harry asked, with a coldness that tried to be polite and could not.

“Not me—no such honour. Had my dinner already. It’s you are a-going to dine with your aunt, I suppose?”

“Mr. Draper,” said Harry, drawing his brocade dressing-gown close about him, standing up so tall that the lawyer instinctively looked upward, “you suppose a great deal more than you know.”

“Great goodness, sir, what do you mean?” Draper asked; and there was in his tone a touch of fear, as if he heard some note in the room besides the human voices—the faint ring of the bar, the dull thud of a boot, the prison’s patience wearing thin.

“I mean, sir, that I have considered; and that having given my word to a faithful and honourable lady, it does not become me to withdraw it.”

“Confound it, sir!” shrieked Draper. “I tell you she has lost the paper. There’s nothing to bind you—nothing. Why she’s old enough to be—”

“Enough, sir,” Harry said, stamping his foot so that the boards spoke. “You seem to think you are talking to some other pettifogger. I take it, Mr. Draper, you are not accustomed to have dealings with men of honour.”

“Pettifogger, indeed!” Draper cried, all his wine turning to vinegar. “Men of honour, indeed! I’d have you to know, Mr. Warrington, that I’m as good a man of honour as you. I don’t know so many gamblers and horse-jockeys, perhaps. I haven’t gambled away my patrimony, and lived as if I was a nobleman on two hundred a year. I haven’t bought watches on credit, and pawned—touch me if you dare, sir!” He sprang to the door.

“That is the way out, sir. You can’t go through the window, because it is barred,” Harry said, pointing with a contempt that cut more than a blow.

“And the answer I take to my client is No, then!” screamed Draper.

Harry stepped forward, both hands clenched, the blood pounding in his ears so loud he could scarcely hear his own voice—a harsh little private thunder that seemed to drown even the street-noise outside.

“If you utter another word,” he said, “I’ll—”

The door banged rapidly; the sentence was never finished. Draper went off in a fury to Madame de Bernstein. He told his tale in the best dress he could give it, but even so he got fiercer language than Harry had used.

“What? Shall she trust me, and I desert her?” Harry paced up and down his narrow room, his brocade gown rustling with every turn like angry leaves. “Dear, faithful, generous woman! If I lie in prison for years, I’ll be true to her.” And he repeated it, not to persuade himself, but as men repeat a vow to keep the world from shaking it.

Meanwhile, the desolate old Baroness, her lawyer dismissed after that storm, sat down at the meal she had hoped to share with her nephew. The chair was set before her which he was to have filled. The glasses shone beside the silver; the candles burned steady, though the noise of the great town beat round the house like an endless sea.

One dish after another was laid before her by the silent major-domo: a soup that should have been taken hot, and now cooled a little as she hesitated; a fowl trussed neatly, its skin browned, the savour rising in a delicate steam; a dish of fish, the lemon sliced thin as paper; sweets and fruits brought in season by money and care. She tasted and pushed away each plate, as if the very abundance mocked her loneliness. There are meals that nourish, and meals that turn to ashes in the mouth.

At last the man pressed his mistress, his voice low, as though he too feared the sound of his own words in that room.

“It is eight o’clock,” he said. “You have had nothing all day. It is good for you to eat.”

She could not. She would have her coffee. Let Case go get her coffee.

Coffee—something dark and bitter, with a perfume strong enough to cut through sorrow—was all she could imagine taking. The lacqueys bore the dishes away, leaving their mistress sitting at the table before the vacant chair. The silence had a sound of its own then: the faint ticking of a clock, the soft stir of a curtain, the distant rumble of a cart in the Strand—London’s coarse bass note under every private grief.

Presently old Case re-entered without the coffee. His face was strangely scared, as though he had seen a ghost in the corridor. His mouth opened once and closed; then he found breath enough to say, in a voice that shook:

“Mr. WARRINGTON!”

The old woman uttered an exclamation, rose from her arm-chair, and sank back in it trembling. Her rouge, laid on by habit as a mask against age and the world, made her face look the ghastlier now, as if colour itself were a lie told too boldly.

“So you are come, sir, are you?” she said, her voice fond and shaking. “Bring back the—Ah!”

She screamed, staring wildly, clutching the arms of her chair as the visitor approached her.

A gentleman whose face and figure exactly resembled Harry Warrington—so exactly that the household might have sworn to him by candlelight—came forward. When he spoke, the tones had the same family ring, as if one voice had been divided between two brothers.

“You expected my brother, madam?” he said. “I am but now arrived in London. I went to his house. I met his servant at your door, who was bearing this letter for you. I thought I would bring it to your ladyship before going to him.” And he laid down a letter before Madam Bernstein.

“Are you—” the Baroness gasped, as if language itself failed and she must drag each word from the depths—“are you my nephew, that we supposed was—”

“Was killed—and is alive!” he answered. “I am George Warrington, madam; and I ask his kinsfolk, what have you done with my brother?”

The old lady’s bewilderment, her joy, her fright, all fought together in her. She looked from the letter to his face, as if her eyes could not be taught this new truth at once.

“Look, George!” she cried at last, as one snatches at anything firm. “I expected him here to-night—that chair was set for him—I have been waiting for him, sir, till now—till I am quite faint—I don’t like—I don’t like being alone. Do stay and sup with me!”

“Pardon me, madam,” George said; and though his bow was stately, there was iron under his politeness. “Please God, my supper will be with Harry to-night.”

“Bring him back. Bring him back here on any conditions! It is but five hundred pounds! Here is the money, sir, if you need it!” She spoke as if ransom were a household purchase—like buying spices dearer than usual because the dish must be made.

“I have no want, madam. I have money with me that can’t be better employed than in my brother’s service.”

“And you will bring him to me, sir! Say you will bring him to me!”

George Warrington made her a grave bow for answer and quitted the room, passing the amazed domestics as if he were master there already. In the hall his voice rang with authority, and the sound of it steadied the servants as a bell steadies a church.

“Gumbo!” he called. “Follow me.”

Had Mr. Harry received no letters from home? Master Harry, Gumbo stammered as he hurried after, had not opened all his letters the last day or two. Had he received no letter announcing his brother’s escape from the French settlements and return to Virginia? No—no such letter had come, else Master Harry would certainly tell Gumbo.

Quick, then: horses. Quick by Strand to Temple Bar. The street roared and rattled; the wheels struck sparks; men cried and cursed; the city’s noise, that perpetual iron commerce of sound, seemed for once to be turned to purpose, driving the Deliverer through the din toward the house of Captivity, where his brother waited unwitting, and the door stood between them like a chapter not yet read.

Rattle and plunge, you poor hackney-coach, through the Strand and Fleet Street; stumble, weary wheels, over stones that never learnt kindness; and you, spent horses, drag George Warrington to his brother as if each jolt were a fresh insult added to the night.

London in winter had a sound of its own—iron-rimmed wheels grinding in ruts, hoofs sucking at black mud, an oath cracking like a whip in the dark, and then, just for a breath, the thin rush of wind between the houses, as though the city exhaled. There were few lamps: only the link-boys’ torches, flaring tallow and resin, spitting in the damp, casting greasy halos on puddles and on the faces of men who looked as if they had been carved out of soot. The coach-lamps shook; the springs groaned; the streets answered with their endless, unmusical clatter. To George, that short passage from Piccadilly to the Temple seemed as long as his morning journey from Marlborough—perhaps longer, because now his blood was hot with dread and haste.

He had written to Harry from Bristol, announcing his landing. He had written before that—written the great, incredible news of himself: the brother left for dead at Braddock’s defeat, the brother who had not stayed dead; who had crawled back into the world after eighteen months among the French. But there was war, and the sea was a net of privateers. Somewhere, between ship and shore, a letter had been swallowed. Harry never broke its seal. That other letter—the one from Bristol—came too late as well: it lay, unopened, at Harry’s lodgings, delivered on the third morning after the arrest, when Mr. Ruff, in his anger, refused to yield up one single item more of his lodger’s property, as though paper itself could be held to ransom.

George’s first step in London had been to those apartments, to the very door where his brother’s name still hung in the air like the ghost of tobacco-smoke. A maid opened; seeing the likeness, she screamed and ran, as if the dead had come to collect his due. The mistress, unwilling to confess that Captain Warrington was in a bailiff’s house at her husband’s suit, lied clumsily: Mr. Warrington had gone away; she did not know where.

George did know where to go next. Clarges Street lay close to Bond Street. He had studied London’s map again and again on the far side of the ocean, tracing lanes with a finger as other men trace rivers. Aunt Bernstein would tell him. Harry’s letters to Virginia had spoken of her kindness; even Madam Esmond had been softened by it—softened, too, by a letter from the Baroness, written in a hand which, for all its elegance, carried the weight of urgency that had sent George packing post-haste for Europe. Madam Esmond hoped—heartily hoped—that Madam Beatrix had at last found occasion to repent. At her age, indeed, it was time. Heaven knows there was much to repent of.

And yet in families, as in nations, forgiveness keeps a narrow pantry. Some faults are salted down and kept for ever; the tongue preserves them when it lets all else decay. Rachel Esmond never named her eldest daughter. Madam Esmond Warrington never named her sister. No handwriting on the Temple floor, no remission signed and sealed, can make certain people unhear the old word once spoken. Female virtue, especially, can be inexorable—its lexicon full of harsh finalities, and no translation possible from one heart to another. George, fresh from battlefields and captivity, did not yet understand the London dialect of kinship: the polite, decisive vocabulary by which those nearest in blood can turn away as if the stranger were you.

Still, he went to Aunt Bernstein’s. Gumbo met him at the door—Gumbo, who had mourned his young master as dead, and now stood blinking at him as though at a miracle that had walked in off the road. The lad’s terror passed into a trembling delight; and then, in hurried, broken phrases, he let slip enough about Harry—where he was, and in what pitiable condition—to make George’s face set hard when he was shown in to the old lady.

George had thought it simple: a brother in trouble would be rescued by his relations. Oh, George—how little you knew of London ways! In the streets, you could not walk a furlong without meeting hunger and misfortune, and if a man undertook to redeem them all, the riches of all America would not do it. Help in London was a commodity; sympathy often a performance sold by the hour. Yet the agitation and real feeling in Aunt Bernstein—her quick, frightened breath; her hands working together as if kneading some invisible dough of worry; the way her voice thickened when she spoke of Harry—touched George in spite of himself.

As the coach jolted on towards the Temple, George’s anger cooled into shame. She does feel it, he told himself. I was too hasty. Again and again in life, he would have to scold himself with that same fault. And the worst of it is: once a harsh word has been served, no repentance can take it back and make it fresh again.

“Quick, coachman!” he cried, as if speed could mend what time had already spoilt.

Gumbo knew the way to the bailiff’s house as well as he knew the way to market. The house received them like a trap.
