First a bell rung sharply; then a door opened; then it was locked behind them with caution, as though they carried plague. They stood in a narrow passage under the eye of a small Jewish janitor holding a flaring tallow-torch. Its smoke carried the rancid smell of cheap fat, and the flame made every shadow jump. A second door was unbolted; they were admitted deeper, as into the belly of a careful beast.

The janitor stared hard when the torchlight fell on George’s face—as if he had already seen that face in the house, and could not make his mind accept two of them.

“Come to see that gentleman?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“But wait.” The man’s eyes slid to Gumbo. “This Mr. Warrington’s brother from America?”

Gumbo nodded, swollen with importance, and was sent upstairs—“to prepare the gentleman,” as the porter put it, for the shock of it.

George was led into a little room called Mr. Amos’s office. A guttering candle stood on a table, and the air was stale with ink, damp wool, and the sour reek of smoke that had no proper chimney. There sat the bailiff, and beside him a stout gentleman in a cloak and laced hat, who, hearing the new arrival, rose with a frank cheerfulness.

“We are not angry any more, Harry!” the stout gentleman cried, thrusting out his hand. “Thank God, my boy! Mr. Amos says there will be no difficulty—James and I will be your bail, and we will do your business by breakfast in the morning. Why—”

He halted as though struck. His hand was taken—held firmly—and he peered into George’s face.

“Angels and ministers of grace! Who are you?”

The stranger’s grip tightened, not in threat but in gratitude that could not help being forceful.

“God bless you, sir,” George said, his voice unsteady. “I know who you are. You must be Colonel Lambert, whose kindness my poor Harry wrote of. And I am the brother you have heard of—the one left for dead at General Braddock’s action; who came to life again after eighteen months among the French; and who lives to thank God, and to thank you, for your goodness to my brother.”

“James! James! Here is news!” Colonel Lambert called, half-laughing, half-crying, to a gentleman in red who entered at that moment. “Here are the dead come alive! Here is Harry Scapegrace’s brother come back—with his scalp on his head too!”

George had removed his hat; the candle caught his hair and the hard travel-lines about his mouth.

“This is my brother-bail, Mr. Warrington,” Lambert continued, recovering his humour as a man does when emotion is too sharp and laughter must cover it. “This is Lieutenant-Colonel James Wolfe, at your service. You must know there has been a little difference between Harry and me, Mr. George. He is pacified, is he, James?”

“He is full of gratitude,” said Wolfe, bowing—plain-featured, brisk, with that air of exactness which makes one think a man even measures his words like rations.

“Harry wrote home about Colonel Wolfe too,” George said quickly. “And I hope my brother’s friends will be so kind as to be mine.”

“I wish he had no other than us,” Lambert returned, the cheer in him edged with something bitter. “His fine folks have been too fine for him, and have ended by landing him here.”

Mr. Amos, who knew a sound security when he saw it—rank, respectability, and ready money—shifted his manner as a cook shifts a sauce when a guest of consequence enters. His voice grew obsequious.

“Nay, your honours, I have done my best to make the young gentleman comfortable; and knowing your honour before, when you came to bail Captain Watkins, and that your security is perfectly good—if your honour wishes, the young gentleman can go out this very night, and I will make it all right with the lawyer in the morning.”

“The debt is five hundred and odd pounds, I think?” George asked.

“Ay, sir.”

“With a hundred thanks to these gentlemen, I can pay the amount at this moment into the officer’s hands, taking the usual acknowledgment,” George said. “But I can never forget, gentlemen, that you helped my brother at his need. For doing so, I say thank you—and God bless you—in my mother’s name and mine.”

While they spoke below, Gumbo had gone up to Harry’s room.

Harry sat there in his morning-gown, with a pipe of Virginia between his fingers. The tobacco’s scent—sweet, grassy, and homely as a summer field—seemed out of place in that hired prison, where the walls smelled of old breath and boiled cabbage from some lower kitchen, and the street outside kept up its hard, sleepless racket. Even Maria’s goodness, shown but now with a tenderness that ought to have been balm, had not wholly consoled him. Her fidelity bound him; and he had looked, with a kind of dismay, at the consequences of being loved so honestly when one is not honest enough to deserve it.

Then Wolfe came in with his homely face lit by good intention, and his hand thrust out as if the gesture could drag a man up from his own sulks.

He told Harry how Lambert was below, and for what errand the two officers had come.

In spite of himself, Lambert would be kind. In spite of Harry’s ill-temper, suspicion, and foolish anger, the good man was resolved to help him—help him even against Wolfe’s advice, as Wolfe now told the prisoner with soldierly frankness.

“For you were wrong, Mr. Warrington,” said Wolfe, “and you would not be set right; and you, a young man, used hard words and unkind behaviour to your senior—and what is more, to one of the best gentlemen who walks God’s earth. You will bear with a friend who speaks plainly? Martin Lambert hath acted in this as he always doth—as the best Christian, the best friend, the most kind and generous of men. If you want proof, here it is: he has converted me, who was angry with you for your treatment of him, and has brought me down to be your bail. Let us both cry Peccavimus, Harry, and shake our friend by the hand. He is sitting in the room below. He would not come here till he knew how you would receive him.”

“I think he is a good man,” Harry groaned, as if the admission cost him physically. “I was very angry and wild when we met last, Colonel Wolfe. Nay, perhaps he was right in sending back those trinkets, hurt as I was. Go down to him, will you be so kind, and tell him I am sorry, and ask his pardon—and—God bless him for his generous behaviour.”

He turned his face away and rubbed his hand across his eyes, ashamed of tears and ashamed of the pride that had earned them.

“Tell him thyself, Harry!” Wolfe cried, seizing his hand. “No deputy will ever say it half so well. Come now.”

“You go first,” Harry pleaded, clinging to the last rag of dignity as a man clings to a blanket in the cold. “I’ll—I'll follow. On my word I will. See—I am in my morning-gown. I will but put on a coat and come. Give him my message first—just—just prepare him for me.”

Wolfe smiled as he went out; he understood the taste of humble-pie, and that it is best swallowed quickly, but that some palates need a moment’s warning.

As Wolfe opened the door, Gumbo came tumbling in, almost forgetting his usual bows and flourishes. His eyes rolled; his mouth split in a vast grin; his hands shook as though he had been set to sift flour in a gale.

“What, Gum?” Harry asked, startled into irritation. “What has happened to thee? Hast thou got a new sweetheart?”

“No, mas’r. No new sweetheart,” Gumbo said, and could hardly get the words out for delight. “I see a ghost, mas’r!”

“A ghost? Whose, and where?”

“Whar? Saw him at Madame Bernstein’s house. Come with him here in de coach. He downstairs now with Colonel Lambert!”

While he spoke, he helped Harry into his coat, fingers clumsy with excitement.

“Ghost—what ghost?” Harry demanded, the pipe forgotten. A strange agitation seized him. “Is anybody—is—my mother come?”

“No, sir. No, Master Harry!” Gumbo’s head wagged so violently it seemed near to rolling off.

Harry stared at him one sharp second, then flung the door open and went rapidly down the stairs, the boards answering his steps with a hollow clack that sounded suddenly like a drum.

He reached the foot just as a voice in the little office—its door ajar—was saying, “…and for doing so, I say thank you, and God bless you, in my mother’s name and mine.”

“Whose voice is that?” Harry cried, and his own voice sounded to him oddly—too high, too bare, as if the air had been knocked out of him.

“It’s de ghost’s, mas’r!” Gumbo whispered behind.

Harry ran forward to the room—and there, before we follow him over the threshold, let the moment hold, like a breath held over a pot lest it boil over.

Inside, the two officers turned their heads away, giving privacy as men do when something sacred has entered the everyday. The lost was found. The dead stood living. The prodigal—if prodigal he had been—fell upon his brother’s heart; and George, whose sternness had been born of fear and love, felt that heart fill with gratitude, repentance, and a warmth so sudden it was almost pain.

“Come away, James,” Colonel Wolfe said softly to Lambert. “I think we are not wanted any more here. Good-night, boys. Some ladies in Hill Street won’t sleep for this strange news. Or will you go home and sup with them, and tell the story?”

No—with many thanks, the brothers would not go to sup that night. They had a tale of their own to eat and to digest, and no table in Hill Street could serve it.

“Quick, Gumbo, with the trunks!” Harry called at last, when speech returned to him in scraps. “Good-bye, Mr. Amos!”

And yet, when he went away from that place—free, with his brother beside him, with the night’s noise suddenly sounding less like a sentence and more like mere weather—Harry felt, oddly, almost unhappy, as though joy itself had its aftertaste, and the sweetest leaf could still carry a hint of smoke.

When first I had the honour to be presented to Sir Miles Warrington at the King’s drawing-room in St. James’s, I confess my senses—those foolish, hopeful sentinels—were taken in at once. His face was as round and coloured as an October pippin; his waistcoat broad as a harvest moon; his manner that of a man who has spent his life in fields and coverts and believes the world was created chiefly that a good horse might carry him over it. I thought I had at last stumbled upon that celebrated creature, trumpeted in ballad and sermon—the good old English country gentleman: the landlord who smiles upon his tenants as if they were sheep he has named, the squire whose very sneeze is supposed to be a blessing to the parish.

And indeed, if felicity had a savour, it would be tasted at such a man’s table: the roast sent up brown and crackling, the gravy clear, the beer of his own brewing with a head like whipped cream, and the air in his hall loud with the wholesome noises of domestic plenty—the click of knives, the clink of glass, the crackle of logs, and the deep, satisfied hum with which Englishmen praise their own cookery. To ride to church in health, to drop into the pew under the sound of a village chorus—coughs, shufflings, the clerk’s nasal leading—while the vicar looks down with dutiful reverence; to say, in a voice of proper gravity, “Have mercy upon us, miserable sinners,” as if misery were a customary condiment sprinkled over prosperity—why, it is a phrase served like grace before meat: uttered because printed, not because tasted.

Give any man five thousand a year, an appetite that never fails him, and a parish trained to touch forelocks at the mere creak of his saddle, and you will not make him feel “miserable” except when the claret is stopped and the doctor puts him upon arrowroot. Misery, in such weather, is a word for other people: for Colin Ploughman with his ague and his seven children and his eight shillings a week; for the widow whose broth is as thin as the parish’s pity. The rich man’s penitence is commonly as light as the foam on his ale.

Yet there is a flavour to hypocrisy too, and it is rancid. There are country houses in which charity is dealt out as one deals out small beer—sour, watered, and only to those who bow low enough; and where the broth for the poor has been skimmed until it will hardly grease a spoon. There are excellent Christians who cry “Amen!” loud as the clerk, who would as soon give their last guinea away as give up their opinion of themselves; who patronise the miserable without relieving them, and buy virtue as they cheapen a goose—proud of the bargain, and persuaded that the seller ought to be grateful.

Poor Harry Warrington, in his extremity, had appealed to his relations. His aunt answered with a tract and her blessing, as if paper could be stewed into nourishment; his uncle had business out of town and could not, of course, be troubled with a petition that smelt of debt. How often, in respectable life, does this same cold cookery go on—refusals dressed up as duties, stinginess spiced with Scripture? One can imagine a Macbeth with blood on his hands shrinking from his own wife’s look; but a Lord and Lady Skinflint can refuse a starving kinsman, go straight down to family prayers, discourse of Providence, and afterward sit nose to nose as serenely as if they had fed him rather than turned him away. They are indignant with the prodigal for being foolish; they are never ashamed of themselves for being hard.

It was in this spirit that Lady Warrington, in her drawing-room, was at that moment preparing one of her moral ragouts—an excellent dish in appearance, made up of much piety cut into neat slices, seasoned with indignation, and served cold.

“Very sad, very sad, my dear!” said Sir Miles, wagging his head with a genial gravity, as if sorrow were a thing to be performed like carving.

“To think of so much extravagance in one so young!” cried Lady Warrington. “Cards, bets, feasts at taverns of the most wicked profusion—carriages and riding-horses—the company of the wealthy and profligate of his own sex, and, I fear, of the most iniquitous persons of ours.”

“Hush, my Lady Warrington!” her husband interposed, with a glance towards Dora and Flora, whose downcast eyes and carefully arranged blushes seemed to say they knew perfectly well what their mamma meant, though they would faint sooner than name it.

“They can’t go to an opera or the Park without seeing ’em, to be sure,” Sir Miles remarked, with that easy tolerance men often keep for sins they do not pay for.

“To think we should have introduced such a young serpent into the bosom of our family,” pursued my lady, raising her voice as if she were in the pulpit, “and have left him in the company of that guileless darling!” She indicated Master Miles, the cherished Innocent, who sat stoutly planted, a small, rosy tyrant, with a top-string in his fingers.

“Who’s a serpent, mamma?” inquired that youth. “First you said cousin Harry was bad: then he was good: now he is bad again. Which is he, Sir Miles?”

“He has faults, like all of us, Miley, my dear,” said Sir Miles, who could season a sermon with humour. “Your cousin has been wild, and you must take warning by him.”

“Was not my elder brother—who died—my naughty brother—was not he wild too?” the child persisted, in that fearless way in which the young speak truth, having not yet learned the parish custom of silence. “He was not kind to me when I was quite a little boy. He never gave me money, nor toys, nor rode with me, nor—why do you cry, mamma? Sure I remember how Hugh and you were always fight—”

“Silence, sir!” cried papa and the girls together, as if the very name were a draught of poison.

“I know I love Harry, and I didn’t love Hugh,” said little Miles sturdily. “And if cousin Harry is in prison, I’ll give him my half-guinea that my godpapa gave me, and anything I have—yes, anything, except—except my little horse—and my silver waistcoat—and—and Snowball and Sweetlips at home—and—and, yes, my custard after dinner.”

This last exception was prompted by a sisterly whisper; yet even then the boy’s generosity fought with his appetite as if both were born warriors.

“But I’d give him some of it,” he added, after a pause—meaning, no doubt, the custard, for there are limits to saintship when it comes in a glass dish and smells of nutmeg.

“Shut thy mouth with it, child, and then go about thy business,” said Sir Miles, laughing. He had a considerable fund of easy humour, and liked the honest noise of a family squabble almost as much as the honest noise of knives on trenchers.

“Who would have thought he should ever be so wild?” Lady Warrington resumed, for she could not let her dish cool. “That we should have been so misled in him!”

“And that he should kiss us both!” cried Sir Miles, with a rogue’s twinkle.

“Sir Miles Warrington, I have no patience with that sort of vulgarity!” said the majestic matron, as if kissing were a crime and her own coldness a virtue.

“Which of you was the favourite yesterday, girls?” Sir Miles continued, delighted to prick their vanity.

“Favourite, indeed!” cried Flora, handsome and quick as a flame. “I told him over and over again of my engagement to dear Tom—I did, Dora—why do you sneer, if you please?”

“Nay, to do her justice, so did Dora too,” said papa.

“Because Flora seemed to wish to forget her engagement with dear Tom sometimes,” Dora remarked, with that precise malice which can be cut as thin as lemon-peel and yet flavour the whole room.

“I never, never, never wished to break with Tom!” Flora exclaimed, tossing her head and turning, by instinct, towards the glass, as if her own reflection were her truest confidante. “It is wicked of you to say so, Dora! It is you who are for ever sneering at him: it is you who are always envious because I happen—at least, because gentlemen imagine that I am not ill-looking, and prefer me to some folks, in spite of all their learning and wit!”

“Why are you always looking there, sister?” asked little Miles, with blunt innocence. “Sure, you must know your face well enough!”

“Some people look at it just as often, child, who haven’t near such good reason,” said Sir Miles gallantly, tossing his compliment as a cook tosses herbs—lightly, and to make the dish smell better.

“If you mean me, Sir Miles, I thank you,” cried Dora, accepting the seasoning gravely. “My face is as Heaven made it, and my father and mother gave it me. ’Tis not my fault if I resemble my papa’s family. If my head is homely, at least I have got some brains in it. I envious of Flora, indeed, because she has found favour in the sight of poor Tom Claypool! I should as soon be proud of captivating a ploughboy!”

“Pray, miss, was your Mr. Harry of Virginia much wiser than Tom Claypool? You would have had him for the asking!” Flora flung back.

“And so would you, miss, and have dropped Tom Claypool into the sea!” Dora returned.

“I wouldn’t.”

“You would.”

“I wouldn’t.”

And thus the shuttlecock of wrath went briskly from hand to hand—an old domestic sport, accompanied by the little sounds that make a house alive: a chair creaking, a silk sleeve whispering, Master Miles’s top-string rasping between his teeth. Lady Warrington laid down her embroidery with an air of martyrdom.

“Oh, my children! Is this the way you dwell together in unity?” she cried, as if unity were a pudding liable to be spoiled by over-stirring. “What an example you set to this Innocent!”

“Like to see ’em fight, my lady!” roared the Innocent, rubbing his hands with glee. “At her, Flora! Worry her, Dora! To it again, you little rogues!” Sir Miles encouraged, for he loved the honest sound of life when it did not threaten his dignity.

But Lady Warrington, who could never allow noise to be merely noise, must turn it into edification.

“These disputes are unseemly,” she said, pressing a hand to her bosom as if her heart were being carved. “They tear a fond mother’s heart. What cause for thankfulness ought we to have that watchful parents have prevented any idle engagements between you and your misguided cousin! If either of you had any preference for him, your excellent good sense will teach you to overcome—to eradicate—the vain feeling. That we cherished and were kind to him can never be a source of regret. ’Tis a proof of our good-nature. What we have to regret is, that your cousin should have proved unworthy of our kindness, and, coming away from the society of gamblers, play-actors, and the like, should have brought contamination—pollution, I had almost said—into this pure family!”

“Oh, bother mamma’s sermons!” Flora muttered, under her breath; and Sir Miles, whistling softly, edged away on tiptoe as if escaping a draught. Meanwhile the artless Miles junior wound up his top, pegged it under his sisters’ robes, and sent it humming across the carpet—its little wooden music—a brief, brave buzzing—staggering, falling, and dying in its usual tipsy manner long before Lady Warrington’s discourse had run itself out.

“Were you listening to me, my child?” she asked, laying a hand upon his head.

“Yes, mother,” he answered, with the whipcord in his mouth, already winding again.

“You was a-saying that Harry was very poor now, and that we oughtn’t to help him. That’s what you was saying; wasn’t it, madam?”

“My poor child,” she replied, turning her eyes upward to the ceiling—her usual refuge, as if Heaven were painted there—“thou wilt understand me better when thou art older!”

At that moment Dora, stung by the top at her toes, cried, “Get out, you little wretch!” and the boy laughed in pure delight at having made a noise and a commotion—those small domestic earthquakes by which children learn they have power.

But suddenly a different sound entered the room, and with it a change of air, as when a door opens upon a colder passage: brisk footsteps; the scrape of a boot; a voice too eager to be ceremonious.

Sir Miles returned, and after him came Tom Claypool, striding as if pursued, his face heated, his breath puffing, his waistcoat straining like a soldier’s. The very hush that followed them had its own note—an expectant silence, sharp as a knife poised over a joint.

“Here’s a pretty business, my Lady Warrington!” Sir Miles cried. “Here’s a wonderful wonder of wonders, girls!”

“For goodness’ sake, gentlemen, what is your intelligence?” asked the virtuous matron, lifting her hands as if for prayer and scandal together.

“The whole town’s talking about it, my lady!” Tom gasped. “I seen him.”

“Seen both of them,” Sir Miles continued. “At Ranelagh last night, with a regular mob after ’em. And so like, that but for their different ribbons you would hardly have told one from the other. One was in blue, the other in brown; but I’m certain he has worn both the suits here.”

“What suits?” cried the girls together.

“Why, your fortunate youth, to be sure,” said Sir Miles, swelling with the pleasure of a discovery. “Our precious Virginian, and heir to the principality!”

“Is my nephew, then, released from his incarceration?” Lady Warrington asked, already arranging the face with which she would receive a penitent.

“Confound him!” Sir Miles roared, with an oath too hearty for her taste. “What should you think, my Lady Warrington, if this precious nephew of mine should turn out to be an impostor—by George! no better than an adventurer?”

“An inward monitor whispered me as much!” cried the lady, instantly promoting her suspicion into prophecy. “But I dashed from me the unworthy thought. Speak, Sir Miles, we burn with impatience.”

“I’ll speak, my love, when you’ve done,” Sir Miles returned, his humour not quite vanquished. “Well, what do you think of my gentleman, who comes into my house, dines at my table, is treated as one of this family, kisses my—”

“What?” Tom Claypool barked, turning suddenly as red as his waistcoat.

“Hem! Kisses my wife’s hand,” Sir Miles amended, “and is treated in the fondest manner. What do you think of this fellow, who talks of his property and his principality—turning out to be a beggarly SECOND SON! A beggar, my Lady Warrington, by—”

“Sir Miles Warrington,” she cut in, “no violence of language before these dear ones! I sink to the earth, confounded by this unutterable hypocrisy. And did I entrust thee to a pretender, my blessed boy? Did I leave thee with an impostor, my innocent one?” She clutched at Master Miles as if the child were a silver spoon in danger of being stolen.

“Who’s an impostor, my lady?” the boy asked.

“That confounded young scamp of a Harry Warrington!” Sir Miles bawled; whereupon little Miles, after a puzzled pause, seemed struck by some hidden grief and burst out crying—great honest sobs that made more truth in the room than all Lady Warrington’s morals. She tried to gather him up, but he kicked and bawled and flung off the caress as if affection, when it is too late, hurts like rough wool.

And then the butler’s voice—steady as if announcing dinner—rang out: “Mr. George Warrington, Mr. Henry Warrington!”

Lady Warrington dropped Master Miles from her lap as if he had suddenly become inconvenient. Sir Miles’s face grew as hot as Claypool’s waistcoat. Dora and Flora rose with the chillest of curtseys; their mother with a third, majestic and frozen. The air itself seemed to tighten, the domestic sounds silenced, as when a kitchen stops clattering because the master has entered.

George Warrington and Harry came in.

Little Miles, wiping his face with the back of his hand, darted forward. “Oh, Harry! No! which is Harry? You’re my Harry!”—and he chose rightly, flinging his small arms about the younger brother with the fierce fidelity of childhood. “Oh, you dear Harry! I’m so glad you are come! and they’ve been abusing you so!”

“I am come to pay my duty to my uncle,” said George, the dark-haired gentleman, his voice measured and grave, “and to thank him for his hospitalities to my brother Henry.”

“What, nephew George? My brother’s face and eyes!” cried Sir Miles; and in an instant the honest delight broke through his anger as sun through cloud. He seized a hand of each young man and held them fast, as if touch itself could make amends. “Boys both, I am delighted to see you!”

“This indeed hath been a most mysterious and most providential resuscitation,” Lady Warrington said, as if she were reading the caption to a monument. “Only I wonder that my nephew Henry concealed the circumstance until now,” she added, letting suspicion peep sidelong from beneath her propriety.

“He knew it no more than your ladyship,” George answered quietly.

The young ladies looked down, and their silence had its own language, like a dish refused without a word.

“Indeed, sir! a most singular circumstance,” Lady Warrington continued. “We had heard of it, sir; and Mr. Claypool—our county neighbour—had just brought us the intelligence, and it even now formed the subject of my conversation with my daughters.”

“Yes,” cried a small voice—too truthful to be safe—“and do you know, Harry, father and mother said you was a—a imp—”

“Silence, my child! Screwby, convey Master Warrington to his own apartment!” Lady Warrington commanded, as if she could banish the sound itself. “These, Mr. Warrington—or I suppose I should say nephew George—are your cousins.”

Two frigid curtseys followed—two cheeses made of young faces; two hands held out as if charity were being given. George made a profound bow that included all three ladies, but embraced none. He laid his hat to his heart.

“It is my duty, madam, to pay my respects to my uncle and cousins,” he said, “and to thank your ladyship for such hospitality as you have been enabled to show to my brother.”

“It was not much, nephew, but it was our best. Ods bobs! it was our best!” Sir Miles cried, eager to pour warmth over the frost.

“And I appreciate it, sir,” George said, and looked gravely round the family as if taking inventory of what had been given and what withheld.

“Give us thy hand. Not a word more,” Sir Miles insisted, smacking George’s hand into his with a hearty sound, like a cook clapping dough. “Do you think I’m a cannibal and won’t extend the hand of hospitality to my dear brother’s son? What say you, lads? Will you eat our mutton at three? This is my neighbour, Tom Claypool—son to Sir Thomas Claypool, Baronet—and my very good friend. Hey, Tom! Thou’lt be of the party, Tom? Thou knowest our brew, hey, my boy?”

“Yes, I know it, Sir Miles,” Tom answered, without any rapture, his eyes still smouldering.

“And thou shalt taste it, my boy!” Sir Miles persisted. “What is there for dinner, my Lady Warrington? Our food is plain, but plenty, lads—plain, but plenty!”

“We cannot partake of it to-day, sir,” George replied. “We dine with a friend who occupies my Lord Wrotham’s house—your neighbour. Colonel Lambert—Major-General Lambert he has just been made.”

“With two daughters, I think—countrified-looking girls—are they not?” Flora asked, in that tone with which fine ladies speak of rustic poultry.

“I think I have remarked two little rather dowdy things,” Dora added, sharpening the point.

“They are as good girls as any in England!” Harry broke out suddenly—Harry, who had sat there burning, dismissed by everybody’s eyes as if his reign were over and he had become invisible. The words escaped him hot and unguarded, as a hungry man defends bread.

“Oh, indeed, cousin!” Dora said, turning at last to look at him, and letting the glance do what words might deny. “You are very charitable—or very lucky, I’m sure. You see angels where we only see ordinary little persons. I’m sure I could not imagine who were those odd-looking people in Lord Wrotham’s coach, with his handsome liveries. But if they were three angels, I have nothing to say.”

“My brother is an enthusiast,” George interposed smoothly. “He is often mistaken about women.”

“Oh, really!” Dora returned, and for an instant looked uneasy, as if she felt the ground shift under her well-planted superiority.

“I fear my nephew Henry has indeed met with some unfavourable specimens of our sex,” Lady Warrington remarked, with a sigh manufactured for the occasion. “We are so easily taken in.”

“We are both very young yet, madam,” George said. “We shall grow older and learn better.”

“Most sincerely, nephew George, I trust you may. You have my best wishes, my prayers, for your brother’s welfare and your own. No efforts of ours have been wanting. At a painful moment, to which I will not further allude—” She paused, enjoying the pause like a moralist who knows the power of silence.

“And when my uncle Sir Miles was out of town,” George added, looking towards Sir Miles, who smiled at him with affectionate approval.

“—I sent your brother a work which I thought might comfort him, and I know might improve him. Nay, do not thank me; I claim no credit; I did but my duty—a humble woman’s duty. For what are this world’s goods compared to the welfare of a soul? If I did good, I am thankful; if I was useful, I rejoice. If, through my means, you have been brought, Harry, to consider—”

“Oh! the sermon, is it?” Harry broke in, plain as a kitchen-boy and twice as sincere. “I hadn’t time to read a single syllable of it, aunt—thank you. You see I don’t care much about that kind of thing—but thank you all the same.”

“The intention is everything,” George said, with a quiet courtesy that did not concede a line. “And we are both grateful. Our dear friend General Lambert intended to give bail for Harry; but, happily, I had funds of Harry’s with me to meet any demands upon us. But the kindness is the same, and I am grateful to the friend who hastened to my brother’s rescue when he had most need of aid, and when his own relations happened—so unfortunately—to be out of town.”

Sir Miles’s face changed—shame and affection wrestling there like two dogs. “Anything I could do, my dear boy—my brother’s son—my own nephew—ods bobs! you know—that is, anything—anything, you know!” He struck George’s hand again with that generous smack.

“You can’t stay and dine with us? Put off the Colonel—the General—do, now! Or name a day. My Lady Warrington, make my nephew name a day when he will sit under his grandfather’s picture, and drink some of his wine!”

But the young men, having paid duty, must go. They took their leave; and with them went a certain honest warmth, leaving behind the faint chill of virtue congratulating itself.

“His intellectual faculties seem more developed than those of his unlucky younger brother,” Lady Warrington observed as soon as the door closed, as if a nephew were a text to be anatomised. “The younger must be reckless and extravagant about money indeed; for did you remark—the loss of his reversion in Virginia, the amount of which has no doubt been grossly exaggerated, but nevertheless must be something considerable—did you remark that the ruin of Harry’s prospects scarcely seemed to affect him?”

“I shouldn’t be at all surprised that the elder turns out to be as poor as the young one,” Dora tossed out, for she could not bear admiration to go unpunished.

“He! he!” Flora tittered. “Did you see that cousin George had one of cousin Harry’s suits of clothes on—the brown and gold—that one he wore when he went with you to the oratorio, Dora?”

“Did he take Flora to an oratorio?” Tom Claypool demanded, fiercer than a man whose roast has been stolen.

“I was ill and couldn’t go, and my cousin went with her,” Dora answered coolly, and the lie of emphasis was that she seemed to take pleasure in Tom’s smart.

“Far be it from me to object to any innocent amusement, much less to the music of Mr. Handel, dear Mr. Claypool,” Lady Warrington began, rallying her morality once more like a cook bringing out a second course. “Music refines the soul, elevates the understanding, is heard in our churches, and ’tis well known was practised by King David. Your operas I shun as deleterious; your ballets I would forbid to my children as most immoral; but music, my dears! May we enjoy it, like everything else in reason—may we—”

“There’s the music of the dinner-bell,” Sir Miles said, rubbing his hands; and indeed, from below came that metallic summons, a sound that ruled the house more surely than sermons. In that clang lay the promise of steam and savour: the hiss of gravy upon hot metal, the sweet animal smell of mutton, the yeasty breath of ale drawn fresh, and the blessed domestic chorus of plates and appetite.

“Come, girls. Screwby, go and fetch Master Miley. Tom, take down my lady.”

“Nay, dear Thomas, I walk but slowly,” Lady Warrington said, arranging herself as if moving were a virtue. “Go you with dearest Flora downstairs.”

And Dora—who had resolved, by some spiteful instinct, that if she could not choose the menu she would at least choose the noise—made the evening pleasant by talking of Handel and oratorios constantly during dinner, until even the clink of knives seemed to keep time to her discourse.

Across the street—if you will cross with me, and hush your step upon the flags—you may look in at Lord Wrotham’s town-house, lent with a noble carelessness to his friend the General. There, in a snug front parlour (not the state dining-room, where every chair seems to sit at attention), the little household from Oakhurst and Tunbridge has gathered again, drawn close as a family draws close about a hearth when the wind frets the shutters.

James Wolfe has promised to dine; but James is elsewhere, keeping watch and ward in a drawing-room for the least soft encouragement from Miss Lowther’s eyes, preferring that to all Lord Wrotham’s kitchen can contrive—be it ragout as delicate as a whisper, or a pyramid of sugared fruits that would make a bishop forget a sermon. He will not come. You may take his place. As for me, I will not intrude upon your chair, but stand where I can see and hear, near the sideboard, where the smells of the dinner still linger like the last notes of a tune after the fiddles have stopped.

The room has that comfortable after-feast warmth: wax and wood and woollen cloth, and, under it all, the kitchen’s ghost—roast meat drawn from the fire at the proper moment, onions melted down to sweetness, a faint sting of mustard from the cold meats, and the steady perfume of oranges bruised in the peeling. Even the sounds have changed now the servants are gone: no clink of plate, no hiss of a ladle in sauce, no brisk footfall; only the soft settling of chairs, the cough held back, the breath before speech. Silence here is not emptiness; it is a kind of ecology, a small domestic weather. One may live by it as surely as by bread.

Mark first how happy the women look; how the peace in their faces seems newly baked, still rising.

When Harry Warrington was carried off by those bailiffs, I had meant earlier to tell you how good Mrs. Lambert—who can never hear of a young creature in trouble without her heart flying before her—ran to her husband, and begged him with a thousand reasons, each reason kissed into an entreaty.

“Never mind his rebeldom the other day. Never mind his being angry that his presents were returned—why, who would not be angry, much more such a high-spirited lad as Harry? Never mind that we are poor, and every spare guinea is as carefully portioned as sugar in a hard winter for the boys at college. There must be some way of getting him out. Did you not get Charles Watkins out of his scrape two years ago, and did he not pay you every halfpenny? Yes; and you made a whole family happy, blessed be God! and Mrs. Watkins prays for you and blesses you to this very day. I think everything has prospered with us since. And I have no doubt it has made you a major-general—no earthly doubt,” cries the fond wife, who will always find a providence in her husband’s goodness.

Now Martin Lambert, who needs little coaxing to do a kind act (and is never so tall as when he stoops to help), lets himself be persuaded readily. Having made up his mind to seek friend James Wolfe and give bail for Harry, he takes his leave and his hat; squeezes Theo’s hand, who seems to divine his errand (or perhaps that foolish mamma has already spilled the whole story, as she spills rose-water into every dish); kisses little Hetty’s hot cheek; and goes out. Mrs. Lambert follows him to the door.

When she is alone with him in the passage, her feelings break through all the stays and seams of propriety. She flings her arms round his neck, kisses him—no, not once or twice, but with the prodigality of one who has long been hoarding tenderness like a housewife hoards spice—and calls Heaven to bless him, and cries on his shoulder in such a storm of gratitude that the very house seems softer for it.

In this posture the pair are discovered by old Mrs. Quiggett, the housekeeper—bustling keys and all, sharp as vinegar, and long-lived as a parrot; a white, hook-nosed, vigilant old creature who seems made of starch and curiosity.

“We have had a tiff, and we are making it up! Don’t tell tales out of school, Mrs. Quiggett!” says the General, marching off with as much dignity as a man may carry who has just been embraced like a schoolboy.

“Well, I never!” cries Mrs. Quiggett, with a shrill laugh that startles the air like a cracked trumpet; and she shakes till her keys jingle and clatter, as if the very metal upon her girdle were gossiping too.

“Oh, Quiggett!” sobs out Mrs. Lambert, “what a man that is!”

“You’ve been a-quarrelling, have you, mum, and making it up? That’s right.”

“Quarrel with him? He never told a greater story. My General is an angel, Quiggett. I should like to worship him. I should like to fall down at his boots and kiss ’em, I should! There never was a man so good as my General. What have I done to have such a man? How dare I have such a good husband?”

“My dear, I think there’s a pair of you,” says the old cockatoo. “And what would you like for your supper?”

When Lambert comes back very late to that meal and tells what has happened—how Harry is free, and how his brother has, as it were, risen out of the earth to rescue him—you may fancy what a commotion follows. If Mrs. Lambert’s General was an angel in the morning, what is he now by candlelight? If she longed to embrace his boots at breakfast, pray what further abasement of worship will satisfy her at night?

Little Hetty steals close to her father, silent as if words were too coarse for the moment, and sips a tiny drop from his glass, as children will, tasting not the wine so much as the triumph and safety in it. Theo and mamma beam like two moons set side by side. After supper, at a certain signal known to their small household, the four kneel down together—glad homage in a mirth that is almost solemn, the sort of joy we read angels have when a sinner repents.

Then, in the midst of their kneeling, comes a great knocking at the door. The sound seems enormous in so hushed a house; it shakes the quiet as a sudden drum shakes a pastoral tune. Past midnight—my lord in the country—who can it be?

Mrs. Lambert, I think, guesses before anyone speaks.

“This is George,” says a young gentleman, leading in another. “We have been to Aunt Bernstein. We couldn’t go to bed, Aunt Lambert, without coming to thank you too. You dear, dear, good—”

There is no more speech; it is swallowed in kisses and hands and sobs. Aunt Lambert clasps Harry as if she would keep him safe inside her very ribs. Theo snatches up Hetty—who has turned pale as if the knock had been a cannon-shot—and hugs her back into life. George Warrington stands hat in hand; when Harry’s first storm of gratitude has passed, he steps forward and kisses Mrs. Lambert’s hand. The General wipes his eyes with the back of his fingers and looks away, as men do who would rather face a battery than be seen in tears.

Generous hearts know that moment: when wrong is forgiven, when peace returns, when love—thought lost—comes back and sits down quietly again like a familiar cat by the fire.

“We came from Aunt Bernstein’s,” says Harry at last; “we saw lights here, you see; we couldn’t go to sleep without saying good-night to you all. Could we, George?”

“’Tis certainly a famous nightcap you have brought us, boys,” says the General. “When are you to come and dine with us? To-morrow?”

No: to-morrow they must go to Madame Bernstein’s.

The next day, then. Yes—the next day. And that is the very day we are now upon: this is the dinner. Lieutenant-Colonel Wolfe is absent on private affairs, and you sit in his stead.

And why, if you please, are we assembled? Not to a mere Barmecide meal; no, no—though the table still bears, like a memory upon the tongue, the savour of what has been eaten. The cloth is withdrawn; the General has given the King’s health; the servants have gone. A hush lies over the room, as if every ear were a doorway. Even the house seems to listen—those old timbers and plaster accustomed to holding voices the way casks hold wine.

It is Mr. George Esmond Warrington’s statement they wait for.

Here they sit, conticuere omnes—women with their hands folded, men with their mouths set as if bracing against bad news. After a little hemming and a blush that rises and falls like a sudden flame in an oven, Mr. George begins.

“I remember,” says he, “at our General’s table, how the little Philadelphia agent—whose wit and shrewdness we had remarked at home—made the very objections to the campaign which its disastrous issue proved just. ‘Of course,’ says he, ‘your Excellency’s troops once before Fort Duquesne, such a weak little place will never be able to resist such a general, such an army, such artillery as will be found attacking it. But do you calculate, sir, on the difficulty of reaching the place? Your Excellency’s march will be through woods almost untrodden, over roads you must make yourselves, and your line will be some four miles long. This slender line, threading the forest, will be subject to endless attacks in front, in rear, in flank, by enemies you will never see, and whose constant practice in war is the dexterous laying of ambuscades.’—‘Psha, sir!’ says the General; ‘the savages may frighten your raw American militia’ (thank your Excellency for the compliment, Mr. Washington seemed to say, who sat at the table), ‘but the Indians will never make any impression on his Majesty’s regular troops.’—‘I heartily hope not, sir,’ says Mr. Franklin, with a sigh; and of course the gentlemen of the General’s family sneered at the postmaster, as at a pert civilian meddling beyond his comprehension.

“We despised the Indians on our own side; our commander made light of them and their service. Our officers disgusted the chiefs with us by outrageous behaviour to their women. There were not above seven or eight who remained with our force. Had we had a couple of hundred in our front on that fatal ninth of July, the event must have been different. They would have flung off the attack of the French Indians; they would have prevented the surprise and panic. ’Tis known now the French had even made ready to give up their fort, never dreaming of the possibility of a defence; and that the French Indians themselves remonstrated against the audacity of attacking such an overwhelming force as ours.

“I was with our General in the main body when the firing began in front, and one aide-de-camp after another was sent forwards. At first the enemy’s attack was answered briskly by our advanced people, and our men huzzaed and cheered with good heart. But very soon our fire grew slacker, whilst from behind every tree and bush round about us came single shots that laid man after man low. We were marching in orderly line—skirmishers in front, colours and two small guns in the centre, baggage well guarded in the rear—moving over ground open and clear for a mile or two, and for some half mile in breadth, with thick tangled covert of brushwood and trees on either side. After the firing had continued a brief time in front, it opened from both sides of the wood upon our advancing column.

“The men dropped rapidly; the officers in greater number than the men. At first, as I said, our fellows cheered and answered; our guns even opened on the wood, and seemed to silence the French in ambuscade. But the hidden rifle-firing began again. Our men halted, huddled together, in spite of shouts and orders to advance, and fired wildly into brushwood—of course making no impression. Those in advance came running back frightened, many wounded. They reported five thousand Frenchmen and a legion of yelling Indian devils in front, scalping our people as they fell. We could hear cries from the wood around as our men dropped under their rifles.

“There was no inducing the people to go forward now. One aide-de-camp after another was sent, and never returned. At last it came to be my turn, and I was sent with a message to Captain Fraser of Halkett’s in front—a message he was never to receive nor I to deliver.

“I had not gone thirty yards when a rifle-ball struck my leg and I fell straightway. I recollect a rush forward of Indians and Frenchmen after that—the former crying their war-cries, the latter as fierce as their savage allies. I was amazed and mortified to see how few whitecoats there were. Not above a score passed me; indeed there were not fifty in the accursed action in which two of the bravest regiments of the British army were put to rout.

“One of them, half Indian half Frenchman, with mocassins and a white uniform coat and cockade, saw me prostrate and turned back, musket clubbed over his head to dash my brains out and plunder me. I had my little fusil which my Harry gave me when I went on the campaign; it had fallen by me and within reach. I seized it; down fell the Frenchman dead at six yards. I was saved for that time; but I bled and grew faint. I swooned almost in trying to load; the piece dropped from my hand; my hand itself sank lifeless to the ground.

“I was scarcely in my senses, yells and shots ringing dimly, when I saw an Indian before me, busy over the body of the Frenchman I had just shot, but glancing towards me as I lay bleeding. He rifled the Frenchman, tore open coat and pockets; then scalped him; and with his bleeding knife in his mouth advanced towards me. I saw him coming as through a film, as in a dream; I had no power to move or resist.

“He put his knee upon my chest; with one bloody hand he seized my long hair and lifted my head. And as he lifted it, I saw a French officer rapidly advancing behind him.

“Good God—it was young Florac, who was my second in the duel at Quebec. ‘A moi, Florac!’ I cried. ‘C’est Georges! aide moi!’

“He started, ran up at the cry, laid his hand on the Indian’s shoulder and called him to hold. But the savage did not understand French—or chose not to. He clutched my hair the tighter, and waved his dripping knife, motioning Florac away. I could only cry again, piteously, ‘A moi!’

“‘Ah, canaille, tu veux du sang? Prends!’ said Florac, with a curse; and the next moment, with an ugh, the Indian fell over my chest dead, Florac’s sword through him.

“My friend looked round. ‘Eh!’ says he, ‘la belle affaire! Where art thou wounded?—in the leg?’ He bound it tight with his sash. ‘The others will kill thee if they find thee here. Ah, tiens! Put on this coat, and this hat with the white cockade. Call out in French if any of our people pass. They will take thee for one of us. Thou art Brunet of the Quebec Volunteers. God guard thee, Brunet! I must go forward. ’Tis a general débâcle, and the whole of your redcoats are on the run, my poor boy.’ Ah, what a rout it was! What a day of disgrace for England.

“Florac’s rough binding stopped the bleeding. He helped me to rest against a tree, and to load my fusil, which he placed within reach to protect me if any other marauder should fancy my scalp. He gave me the gourd of that unlucky French soldier I had killed; the drink within refreshed and invigorated me. Taking a mark of the tree, noting bearings so as to find me again, he hastened on. ‘Thou seest how much I love thee, George,’ he said, ‘that I stay behind in a moment like this.’

“I forget whether I told thee, Harry, that Florac was under obligation to me. I had won money of him at cards at Quebec—only playing at his repeated entreaty—and there was difficulty about paying; I remitted his debt and lighted my pipe with his note-of-hand. You see, sir,” and here George glances with a half-smile at his younger brother, “that you are not the only gambler in the family.

“At evening, when the dismal pursuit was over, the faithful fellow came back with a couple of Indians—each with reeking scalps at his belt—whom he informed that I was a Frenchman, his brother, wounded early and to be carried back to the fort. They laid me in one of their blankets and carried me groaning, Florac by my side. Had he left me, they would assuredly have set me down, plundered me, and added my hair to those bleeding spoils at their girdles. He promised them brandy at the fort if they brought me safely there. I have but a dim recollection of the journey; the anguish of my wound was extreme; I fainted more than once. We came at last. I was taken into the fort, carried to the officers’ log-house, and laid upon Florac’s own bed.

“Happy for me was my insensibility. I had been brought in as a wounded French soldier. I heard afterwards that during my delirium the few prisoners made in our disaster were brought under the walls of Duquesne by their savage captors, and there horribly burned, tortured, and butchered by the Indians, under the eyes of the garrison.”

A shiver goes round the little room, as if a draught had found a crack in the window. Theo takes Hetty’s hand and looks at George with alarm. Harry’s fist comes down upon the table so that the glasses jump and ring—a sharp little music in the midst of horror.

“The bloody, murderous, red-skinned villains!” cries he. “There will never be peace for us until they are all hunted down!”

“They were offering a hundred and thirty dollars apiece for Indian scalps in Pennsylvania when I left home,” says George, very quietly, “and fifty for women.”

“Fifty for women, my love! Do you hear that, Mrs. Lambert?” cries the Colonel, lifting up his wife’s hair, as if even that domestic gesture must now be pressed into service of indignation.

“The murderous villains!” Harry breaks out again. “Hunt ’em down, sir! Hunt ’em down!”

“I know not how long I lay in my fever,” George resumes. “When I awoke to my senses, my dear Florac was gone. He and his company had been despatched on an enterprise against an English fort in Pennsylvanian territory, which the French claimed too. In Duquesne, when I came to be able to ask and understand, there were not above thirty Europeans left. The place might have been taken over and over again had any of our people had courage to return after the disaster.

“My old enemy the ague-fever set in again as I lay by the river-side. ’Tis a wonder I survived. But for the goodness of a half-breed woman in the fort, who took pity on me and tended me, I never should have recovered; and my poor Harry would be what he fancied himself yesterday—our grandfather’s heir, our mother’s only son.

“I remembered how, when Florac laid me in his bed, he put under my pillow my money, my watch, and a trinket or two. When I woke, these were gone; and a surly old sergeant—the only authority left in that quarter—told me with a curse I was lucky enough to be left with life at all; that only the white cockade and coat saved me from the fate the other canaille of Rosbifs had deservedly met.

“At the time of my recovery the fort was almost emptied. The Indians had retired enriched with British plunder; the chief part of the French regulars were gone upon expeditions northward. My good Florac had left me upon his service, consigning me to the care of an invalided sergeant. Monsieur de Contrecoeur had accompanied one of these expeditions, leaving an old lieutenant—Museau by name—in command at Duquesne.

“This man had long been out of France and serving in the colonies. His character, doubtless, had been indifferent at home; and he knew that, by the system pursued in France where almost all promotion is given to the noblesse, he never would advance. And he had made free with my guineas, I suppose, as with my watch; for I saw it one day on his chest when I was sitting with him in his quarter.

“Monsieur Museau and I managed to be pretty good friends. If I could be exchanged or sent home, I told him, my mother would pay liberally for my ransom. I suppose the idea excited his cupidity; for a trapper coming in winter, whilst I still lay very ill, Museau consented that I should write home—but the letter must be in French, he must see it, and I must say I was in the hands of the Indians and should not be ransomed under ten thousand livres.

“In vain I said I was prisoner to the troops of his Most Christian Majesty; that I expected the treatment of a gentleman and officer. Museau swore that letter should go and no other; that if I hesitated he would fling me out of the fort, or hand me to the tender mercies of his ruffian Indian allies. He would not let the trapper speak with me except in his presence. Life and liberty are sweet. I resisted awhile, but I was pulled down with weakness and shuddering fever; I wrote such a letter as the rascal would let pass, and the trapper went away with my missive, promising in three weeks to deliver it to my mother in Virginia.

“Three weeks, six, twelve, passed. The messenger never returned. Winter came and went; the little plantations round the fort—where French soldiers had cleared corn-ground, planted gardens, peach- and apple-trees down to the Monongahela—were in full blossom. Heaven knows how I crept through the weary time. When I was pretty well, I made drawings of the soldiers of the garrison, and of the half-breed and her child—Museau’s child—and of Museau himself, whom I am ashamed to say I flattered outrageously. There was an old guitar left in the fort; I sang to it and played French airs I knew; and I ingratiated myself as best I could with my gaolers. So the months passed—but the messenger never returned.

“At last news arrived he had been shot by some British Indians in Maryland: so there was an end of my hope for some months more. This made Museau savage and surly toward me; the more so as his sergeant inflamed him by telling him the Indian woman was partial to me—as I believe, poor thing, she was. I was always gentle with her and grateful. My small accomplishments seemed wonders in her eyes; I was ill and unhappy too, and these are always claims upon a woman’s affection.

“A captive pulled down by malady, a ferocious gaoler, and a young woman touched by the prisoner’s misfortunes—sure you expect, with these three prime characters, some pathetic tragedy is to be enacted? You, Miss Hetty, are about to guess the woman saved me?”

“Why, of course she did!” cries mamma.

“What else is she good for?” says Hetty, with that cruel sprightliness of youth which has never yet been made to swallow its own tears.

“You, Miss Theo, have painted her already as a dark beauty—is it not so? A swift huntress—”

“Diana with a baby,” says the Colonel.

“—who scours the plain with her nymphs, who brings down the game with her unerring bow, who is queen of the forest—and I see by your looks you think I am madly in love with her?”

“Well, I suppose she is an interesting creature, Mr. George?” says Theo, blushing; her voice low, as if she feared to disturb the story’s spell.

“What think you,” says George, “of a dark beauty the colour of new mahogany, with long straight black hair usually dressed with a hair-oil or pomade by no means pleasant to approach; with little eyes; with high cheek-bones; with a flat nose sometimes ornamented with a ring; with rows of glass beads round her tawny throat; her cheeks and forehead tattooed; a great love of finery; and an inordinate passion for—oh! must I own it?”

“For coquetry. I know you are going to say that!” cries Miss Hetty.

“For whisky, my dear Miss Hester—in which appetite my gaoler partook; so that I have often sat by on nights when I was in favour with Monsieur Museau, and seen him and his poor companion hob-and-nobbing until they could scarce hold the noggin out of which they drank. In these evening entertainments they would sing, they would dance, they would fondle, they would quarrel, and knock the cans and furniture about; and when I was in favour I was admitted to share their society—for Museau, jealous of his dignity, or not willing that his men should witness his behaviour, would allow none of them to be familiar with him.

“Whilst the result of the trapper’s mission to my home was yet uncertain—and Museau and I expected the payment of my ransom—I was treated kindly enough: allowed to crawl about the fort, even to go into adjoining fields and gardens, always keeping parole and returning before gun-fire. And I exercised a piece of hypocrisy, for which I hope you will hold me excused. When my leg was sound—the ball came out in winter after some pain and inflammation, and the wound healed presently—I yet chose to walk as if disabled; I hobbled on two sticks and cried Ah! and Oh! at every minute, hoping that a day might come when I might treat my limbs to a run.”

We dragged on through months of that weary fort-life: the commandant and I snarling and making it up again like ill-sorted spouses; greasy packs of cards slapping the table; his asthmatic flute wheezing alongside my cracked guitar; the drum at retreat cutting clean through any little comfort our noise contrived. Outside the palisade the woods kept their own music—wind in the high leaves, the low talk of water where the rivers met—yet within, the fort’s sounds were meaner: a cough, a curse, a bottle knocked against a cup, a sentry’s boots pacing the plank. It is a curious tyranny, that of a place: it teaches you how a man’s temper can be tuned by nothing more than the pitch of a whistle and the constant rasp of a file on iron.

La Biche—“the Fawn,” as they called her, with that brutal fondness by which conquerors make pets of what they have broken—took her beatings and her drams as Museau dispensed them. She was made to nurse everything that needed nursing: her own papoose, the commandant when the gout made him howl, and once, when fever shook me like a dog in winter, me too. She moved about the fort’s little domestic labours with a quiet exactness that only those learn who must keep order in a life where they are allowed none. She fetched in from the river and the fields the small necessities of our table—corn, onions, a handful of herbs bruised between her fingers to wake them; she made a thin soup out of what there was, and, when she could, she thickened it with a trick of patience, letting it simmer until even poor roots tasted of something like home. Her face rarely altered; but her ears—hers were always working. She listened as if the very air might betray a danger before eyes could.

At the beginning of the fall of last year a hunter came in with news, and the fort, which had been languid as a sickroom, stirred like a pot just set over a high fire. Montcalm, they said, had sent up a considerable detachment to garrison the posts already in French hands and to thrust further into the enemy’s—meaning our—possessions. The troops had left Quebec and Montreal and were coming up the St. Lawrence and the lakes in bateaux, bringing artillery and provisions and all the heavy furniture of war. Museau would be superseded by an officer of higher rank; and such a change, while it made the soldiers clap and sing and swear of victories to come—Albany, Philadelphia, the Rosbifs driven into the sea—put an altogether different taste in my mouth. A new commander might exchange me; or, with a shrug, might hand me to the Indians in reprisal for cruelties our own backwoodsmen had practised on captured Frenchmen. In these border wars, men paid for other men’s sins as if guilt were a coin passed from palm to palm.

The garrison swaggered about their conquest of all America from Mississippi to Newfoundland; yet, for all their boasting, I noticed that the prospect did not sweeten Museau’s humour.

“Eh, commandant,” said I, “’tis fort bien. But meanwhile—your farm in Normandy, your pot of cider, your trippes à la mode de Caen—where are they?”

“Ay,” says he, making a face as if he could already smell the apple-press and the stewing onions of his parish, “it is very well, my garcon. But where will you be when old Museau is turned out? Other officers are not companions like me. Very few men in the world have my humanity. When there is a great garrison here, will my successor give you indulgences as honest Museau has? You will be kept in a sty like a pig for killing. And as sure as one of our officers falls into your frontier brigands’ hands and harm comes to him, so surely will you pay with your skin. You will be given to our red allies—to La Biche’s brethren. Did you see last year what they did to your countrymen we took with Braddock? Roasting was the smallest punishment—was it not, La Biche?”

Then, with that ghastly cheerfulness some men assume when they talk of horrors as if they were recipes, he went on with a list of torments—eyes burned, teeth and nails wrenched, flesh gashed and hacked—until the very air of the room seemed thick with imagined smoke. La Biche did not flinch. She had seen such work. She came of the Senecas by the great cataract between Ontario and Erie; her people had fought now for the English, now against them; and in the wars among tribes and between tribes and whites, it is hard to say which skin has worn the more savage heart.

“They may chop me into cutlets and broil me, ’tis true, commandant,” said I, keeping my voice cool. “But again I say: you will never have the farm in Normandy.”

“Go get the whisky-bottle, La Biche,” said Museau.

“And it is not too late even now,” said I, leaning into the one appetite that ruled him best. “I will give the guide who takes me home a large reward. And I promise, as a man of honour, ten thousand livres—to whom shall I say? To one who brings me any token—my watch and seal, with my grandfather’s arms—which I have seen in a chest somewhere in this fort.”

“Ah, scelerat!” he roared with hoarse laughter. “You have eyes! All is good prize in war.”

“Think,” I whispered, as if to myself, though I meant every word for him, “of a house in your village; a fine field hard by; half a dozen cows; an orchard covered with fruit.”

“And Javotte at the door with her wheel,” he whimpered suddenly, “and a rascal child or two, cheeks as red as the apples! O my country! O my mother! Quick, La Biche—the whisky!”

All that night he sat deep in thought, and La Biche, too, silent and melancholy. She kept apart nursing her infant; and whenever my eyes drifted to her, I found hers fixed on me—not boldly, not beseeching, but with a steady attention, as if she were holding in her mind some path that must not be forgotten. The little one began to cry, and Museau—his tenderness always reserved for the idea of Normandy—ordered her away with foul language to the hut where she slept with her child. When she was gone, the commandant and I spoke freely, and I laid before him such reasons as his cupidity could not resist.

“How do you know,” he asked, “that this hunter will serve you?”

“That is my secret,” said I. And, since we were dealing in anything but honour, I may as well say how it came to pass.

When hunters came in for trade, they often stayed a day or two for rest and drink and company, and our new friend loved all three. He gambled with the men; he set his furs against their liquor; he sang and danced with them. There being little else to fill the hours, I was often made to sing and scrape my guitar, and there would be a kind of concert in the smoky room: men clapping time with their palms, boots stamping, voices joining in chorus until the drum called them back to discipline, that blunt instrument which flattens all human noise into obedience.

The hunter was present at one such evening, and I watched him as I sang our French catches. Then, as if on a whim, I said, “My lads, I will give you an English song.” To the tune of “Over the hills and far away”—an air my good old grandfather used to hum, loving it as a soldier loves what carries him out of mud and hunger—I made doggerel words of my plight:

“This long, long year, a prisoner drear;
Ah, me! I’m tired of lingering here:
I’ll give a hundred guineas gay,
To be over the hills and far away.”

“What is it?” says the hunter. “I don’t understand.”

“’Tis a girl to her lover,” I answered. But I saw by the twinkle in his eye that he understood well enough.

Next day, when no one stood within hearing, he passed me and hummed low, in perfectly good English, “Over the hills and far away”—the burden of my nonsense.

“If you are ready,” says he, “I am ready. I know who your people are, and the way to them. Talk to the Fawn; she will tell you what to do. What! you will not play with me?” Here he pulled out cards as two soldiers came up, and shifted into French with a grin. “Milor est trop grand seigneur? Bonjour, my lord!”

He mocked me with a bow and went off to drink elsewhere, shrugging as if my fate were merely another hand dealt and thrown away.

I knew now that La Biche was to be the agent, and that my offer had found its mark in Museau. The poor Fawn performed her part with a dexterity that would have been admired in any court where people call cunning “policy.” She had long been allowed free communication with me: she had tended me when I lay weak, helped with the work of my little chamber, my cooking, and so forth. (Prison fare is mostly noise and want; yet even there the body begs for some small mercy of the senses—warmth, salt, the remembered smell of bread. Many a day I watched her coax a better flavour out of mean stores: a sprig of potherb bruised and dropped at the right moment; corn boiled until it lost its rawness; a bone kept back to give tomorrow’s pot a ghost of richness. Such arts are a language too, and the conquerors did not even know they were hearing it.)

She was free to go out of the fort, to the river and the fields whence our scant corn and garden-stuff were brought. Meanwhile the trapper—Silverheels was the name he went by—having gambled away most of the money he got for his peltries, gathered his store of flints, powder, and blankets and took his leave. Three days after his departure, La Biche gave me the sign that the time was come.

When first wounded, kind Florac had placed me on his own bed in the officers’ room. Later, when the fort was emptied of all officers save the old lieutenant left in command, I had been allowed to remain in my quarters—sometimes pretty free, sometimes locked and fed on prisoners’ rations, sometimes invited to share Museau’s mess when my gaoler was in a good humour and a bad sobriety.

This officers’ house was of logs like the others, one of a half-dozen buildings within a fort that mounted only four small guns. One piece stood on the bastion behind my cabin. Looking westward over that gun you could see a small island at the meeting of the Ohio and Monongahela, where Duquesne sat; and on the opposite shore some trees stood in a clump.

“You see those trees?” La Biche said to me the day before, in her broken French. “He wait for you behind those trees.”

In daylight my door was open, and she came and went. That day she returned from the fields with a pick in her hand and a basketful of vegetables and potherbs for soup—the smell of damp earth clinging to the roots, the sharp green of bruised leaves rising when she shifted them. She sat on the bench at my door with the pick leaning against it and the basket at her side. I stood talking to her, stupid with anxiety; I believe I should never have thought to use that pick even if she had struck the wall with it before my eyes. At last, with a motion swift as a bird’s, she pushed it into my doorway so it fell into my room.

“Hide it,” she whispered. “Want it soon.”

And that afternoon she pointed again, silently, to the clump of trees.

Next day she came pretending to be very angry, calling out loud in her jargon, “My lord! my lord! why you not come to commandant’s dinner? He very bad! Entendez-vows?” As she peeped in, she flung a coil of rope at me.

“I am coming, La Biche,” said I, and hobbled after her on my crutch. As we went, she breathed, “Pour ce soir.” Then I knew.

Museau, for his part, knew nothing—nothing at all. He growled at me that the soup was cold. He looked steadily in my face and talked of this and that, not only while his servant was present but afterwards as we smoked and played piquet, while La Biche, in her wonted posture, sat cowering in a corner like a shadow. The soup—thin as it was—carried the faint taste of the garden she had brought in; it was a domestic thing in a place made for murder, and the contradiction sickened me.

Museau’s whisky-bottle was empty. With a knowing look he said he must have another glass—we must both have a glass that night. Rising, he stumped to the inner room where he kept his fire-water locked, away from La Biche, who could no more resist that temptation than a starving man can resist bread.

As he turned his back, La Biche raised herself. He was scarcely gone before she was at my feet, kissing my hand, pressing it to her heart, and bursting into tears over my knees—silent at first, then shaking as if some dam had broken in her. I had not understood—until that instant—the full measure of her attachment, nor how, in helping me, she was perhaps reaching for the one act in her life that belonged to her alone. When Museau returned I had not recovered my composure, though La Biche had slipped back to her corner and pulled her blanket up, face hidden.

He remarked nothing. We sat down again to cards, though my mind was so preoccupied the painted kings and knaves seemed like strangers.

“I gain everything from you to-night, milor,” says he grimly. “We play upon parole.”

“And you may count upon mine,” I answered.

“Eh! ’tis all that you have!” says he.

“Monsieur,” said I, “my word is good for ten thousand livres.” And the game went on, the cards whispering on the table like dry leaves.

At last he said he had a headache and would go to bed, and I understood the order that I was to retire too.

“I wish you a good night, mon petit milor,” says he. “Stay—you will fall without your crutch.” His eyes twinkled; his mouth wore a sarcastic grin. In the agitation of the moment I had forgotten my lameness and was walking away at almost a grenadier’s pace.

“What a vilain night!” says he, looking out; and indeed a tempest was abroad, roaring in the trees, rain driving in sheets. “Bring a lanthorn, La Tulipe, and lock my lord comfortably into his quarters!” He stood a moment in his doorway watching me, and I caught a glimpse of La Biche behind him, still as a carved figure.

The night was so wet that the sentries clung to their boxes and did not trouble me. The log-house was built with upright posts sunk deep, with horizontal logs laid on them. With the pick hidden in my room I began to dig under the lowest timber soon after tattoo. The earth was cold and heavy; each scrape sounded in my skull like a shout, though the storm kindly swallowed it. I worked in darkness until my hands were raw and my breath came short. It was some while after midnight when my fingers, feeling upward, found rain falling from without—the first cold touch of freedom. For two hours after that I worked more cautiously, widening the hole enough to admit my body.

Then I crept through to the parapet and flung my rope over the gun, not without a tremor lest the sentry should look down and send a charge of lead into me. The wall was but twelve feet; my drop into the ditch easy enough. I waited there a moment, letting my eyes accustom themselves, peering under the gun to find the river and the island. Above me the sentry paced and hummed—careless, domestic, as if the storm and the dark were his kitchen and he the master of it.

The darkness clarified; the moon rose, and I saw the river shining and the island’s rocks and trees crouched in the water. I made for the clump of trees as swiftly as my weakened leg allowed. Oh, the relief—sharp as the first mouthful of hot broth to a starving man—when I heard, low among the trunks, a voice humming, “Over the hills and far away.”

When I came to this part of my narrative, Miss Theo—seated by the harpsichord—turned round and dashed off the tune, and all the little company broke into the merry chorus; for people who sit warm by candlelight love to borrow the edge of danger and turn it into music.

“Our way,” I continued, “lay through a level tract of forest on the right bank of the Monongahela, which my guide knew as well as a cook knows the shelves of his pantry. He moved by sound as much as sight—the hush of a hollow, the different rustle of oak and maple, the far-off complaint of a night-bird—choosing the quieter paths, for even the wilderness has its alarms, and the loudest thing in it is often a man.”

By daylight we came to clearer ground, and Silverheels asked had I ever seen the spot before. It was the fatal field where Braddock fell, whence I had been wonderfully rescued the previous summer. Now the leaves were beginning to tint with our magnificent autumn—maples turning like embers, oaks bronze and wine-coloured, the whole forest as if some vast hearth had been stirred. Yet even that splendour had its own sorrow: it was a language the season spoke for a brief while, and then forgot, leaving bare branches that could not translate their own former glory.

“Ah, brother!” cries Harry, seizing my hand, when I told it. “I was gambling and making a fool of myself at the Wells and in London, when my George was flying for his life in the wilderness! Oh, what a miserable spendthrift I have been!”

“But I think thou art not unworthy to be called thy mother’s son,” said Mrs. Lambert very softly, with wet eyes. And indeed, if Harry had erred, the mark of his repentance—his love, his unselfish joy and generosity—made one feel there was hope even for the humbled young sinner.

“We presently crossed the river,” I resumed, “and took our course along the base of the western slopes of the Alleghanies, through grand forest of oaks and maples and enormous poplars rising a hundred feet without a branch. It was Indians we had chiefly to avoid, besides the outlying French. Always of doubtful loyalty, the savages have been specially against us since our ill-treatment of them and the French triumph two years ago.

“I was weak still, and our journey lasted a fortnight or more. As we advanced, the woods grew redder and redder; frost nipped sharply at night. We lighted fires at our feet and slept in blankets as best we might, listening always—listening for a twig snapped where it ought not, for a far cry, for that sudden hush in which even insects seem to hold their breath. At that time of year mountain hunters get their sugar from maples. We came on more than one such family camped by their trees near mountain streams; they welcomed us at their fires, and gave us venison—smoked, or roasted on spits, the fat hissing as it fell into the coals. The smell of it in the cold air was like a promise, and the taste brought back, for a moment, the idea of a table where people speak their own tongue without fear of who might overhear and punish the very words.

“So we crossed the two ranges of Laurel Hill and the Alleghanies. The last day’s march took us down that wild pass of Will’s Creek, a valley between cliffs near a thousand feet high—bald, white, broken into towers like fortifications—with eagles wheeling round the summits and watching their nests among the crags. Their cries rang thin and clean above us, and after the fort’s petty noises it seemed a kind of liberty merely to hear a sound that no man had trained or priced.

“And thence we descended to Cumberland, whence we had marched the year before, and where now there was a considerable garrison of our people. Oh, you may think it was a welcome day when I saw English colours again on the banks of our native Potomac.”

George Warrington had told the same history the night before to Madame de Bernstein—so much of it as could be kept above water whilst an old lady, like a ship in a calm, drifted perpetually into sleep and as perpetually woke with a start when the voice ceased. Each time George paused, she blinked, gathered the lace at her throat with three little mittened fingers, and said, with the air of granting him an audience out of pure beneficence, that it was “most interesting,” and that he was to proceed.

He did proceed, but ill at ease; hemming, stammering, reddening as though he were confessing theft, and not recounting marches, hunger, fort-prisons, and the dumb, stubborn endurance of men who have no choice but to go on. He spoke with half the spirit he had found in Hill Street, where the very room listened to him: Hetty’s eyes, wide as bowls; Theo’s quick sympathy, like a hand set on the shoulder; mamma’s ready tears; and the General’s comic gravity which, by mere good-nature, could make a timid young man eloquent. The General had said, laughing, that Mrs. Lambert was as serviceable as Mr. Addison’s trunk-maker; you had only to seat her in the front box, engaged to cry, and any tragedy might take its fortune. That was why they had chosen my Lord Wrotham’s drawing-room for George’s first performance: a theatre where a youth might be understood, not cross-examined by a shrewd, wakeful cynic who slept through the tender passages and opened her eyes at the hard ones.

“Very good and most interesting, I am sure, my dear sir,” Madame de Bernstein said now, and lifted her fingers to hide a twitch at the corner of her mouth, half laughter and half malice. “And your mother must have been delighted to see you.”
