George’s shoulders moved the merest fraction, like a man shrugging off a cloak; he bowed low, and met, for an instant, his aunt’s keen gaze.

“Have been delighted to see you,” she went on, dry as a chip in the grate, “and killed the fatted calf, and—and that kind of thing. Though why I say calf, I don’t know, nephew George, for you never were the prodigal. I may say calf to thee, my poor Harry! Thou hast been amongst the swine sure enough. And evil companions have robbed the money out of thy pocket and the coat off thy back.”

“He came to his family in England, madam,” George said, with heat rising into his throat, “and his friends were your ladyship’s.”

“He could not have come to worse advisers, nephew Warrington—and so I should have told my sister earlier, had she condescended to write to me by him, as she has done by you,” the old lady answered, tossing up her head as if to shake off both sister and reproach.

And later, when she had dismissed them to make her toilette for the night’s rout, she chuckled in her chair as her maid laced, pinned, and smoothed her into splendour.

“Hey! hey!” she said. “This young gentleman’s mother is half sorry that he has come to life again—I could see that in his face. She is half sorry, and I am perfectly furious. Why didn’t he lie still where he dropped there under the tree, and why did that young Florac carry him to the fort? I knew those Floracs when I was at Paris, in the time of Monsieur le Régent. Of Ivry. No great house before Henri Quatre. His ancestor was the King’s favourite—his ancestor—he! he!—his ancestress! Brett! entendez-vous? Give me my card-purse. I don’t like the grand airs of this Monsieur George; and yet he resembles, very much, his grandfather—the same look and sometimes the same tones. You have heard of Colonel Esmond when I was young? This boy has his eyes. I suppose I liked the Colonel’s because he loved me.”

Cards were her true sacrament; she never missed them—weekday or Sabbath—so long as she could sit upright and hold trumps. Therefore, soon after George ended his unwilling narration, she dismissed her nephews briskly. To the elder she gave two fingers and a curtsey stiff as a state paper; to Harry, she extended both hands and patted his cheek with an odd, almost maternal kindness.

“My poor child, now thou art disinherited, thou wilt see how differently the world will use thee!” she said. “There is only, in all London, a wicked, heartless old woman who will treat thee as before. Here is a pocket-book for you, child! Do not lose it at Ranelagh to-night. That suit of yours does not become your brother half so well as it sat upon you! You will present your brother to everybody, and walk up and down the room for two hours at least, child. Were I you, I would then go to the Chocolate-House, and play as if nothing had happened. Whilst you are there, your brother may come back to me and eat a bit of chicken with me. My Lady Flint gives wretched suppers, and I want to talk his mother’s letter over with him. Au revoir, gentlemen!”

Her chairmen, her flambeaux, the whole little machinery of rank and habit were already at the door; and in a moment she was borne away into the night, where coaches rolled like distant thunder and London’s evening began its usual racket—iron wheels, calling footmen, fiddles tuning, laughter spilling from open doors.

The gentlemen went to Ranelagh.

If you would know a place by its sound as much as by its sight, you must remember that famous rotunda not merely as a lantern of light, but as a shell filled with music. The crowd made a continuous surf: the rustle of stiff silks, the soft click of fans, the scrape of buckles on the boards, the murmuring exchange of gossip—names dropped like coins—and over all a full orchestra, not the thin piping of a tavern, but a body of instruments breathing together. George, who loved music far more than Harry ever did, stood as though he had been led into church. It was his first time hearing such a band, and a piece of Mr. Handel done with satisfaction: the violins bright as poured wine, the bass like a steady pulse underfoot, the hautboys carrying a keen scent through the air, as if sound itself had an aroma.

Harry, master of ceremonies, brought George round the circle, pointing out the curiosities with the practiced ease of a man who knew how to move, how long to pause, whom to greet, whom to avoid. They met Mr. Tom Claypool with some country friends; they listened; they took tea in a box where steam rose faintly from the cups and mingled with perfume and candle-smoke. There was lemon-peel in the air, and the sharp, comforting tannin of the leaves, and beneath it the hot, animal tang of crowded humanity. For all its gaiety, Ranelagh had its fatigue: noise that pressed upon the ear until the mind grew tired of itself. Yet for George, new-come from a prison-fort’s silence and the harsher music of wilderness—wind in pine, musket-crack, the wooden thump of a sentry’s step—this ordered harmony seemed almost miraculous; a civilised soundscape, made by men agreeing, for once, not to shout.

Harry’s humility showed itself in a small thing. In those days, fiddling was voted effeminate; the patriotic prints called daily upon Britons to sneer at the foreign accomplishments of Squallinis and Monsieurs. Yet Harry, who could laugh at much, did not laugh at George’s attention. He let his brother listen, and even looked pleased that George could take delight in what the town despised. It is a strange point in our national character, that we once prided ourselves upon ignorance as if it were courage. There is less of that conceit now; art has, in some fashion, taken out her letters of naturalisation among us, and lives here almost as an equal. If a great heiress chose to marry a music-master and kept a good cook, there are many who would go dine with her nevertheless, and treat the musician with civility—nay, perhaps forget to call his art frivolous if the capon were well roasted and the sauce properly reduced.

After Ranelagh, pursuant to Madame de Bernstein’s counsel, George returned to her ladyship’s house; whilst Harry showed himself at the club where gentlemen assembled nightly to sup and then to gamble away, with solemn faces, what their cooks and tailors had earned for them.

At the club no one alluded to Mr. Warrington’s little temporary absence. Mr. Ruff, his ex-landlord, waited on him with the utmost gravity, as though there had never been any scene between them; as though debt, like yesterday’s dish, might be scraped away and forgotten. Harry’s trunks and habiliments had been removed from Bond Street that morning; he and George were lodged elsewhere now, with the freedom of men who pay in ready money—or can borrow it.

Supper was served; and if London’s great world had any religion beyond cards, it was supper: the bright clink of glass, the low argument over wine, the knife’s short stroke through meat, the fat hissing as it met heat, the thick scent of pepper, vinegar, and smoke. There were bones cracked for marrow; there were sauces too rich to be honest; there was bread torn and buttered with the unconscious tenderness men reserve for what will not contradict them. The very room had its own acoustic: talk rising and falling like flame, laughter snapping, the scrape of chairs as men leaned in, the occasional thud of a bottle set down with decision. A man might almost persuade himself such noises were health, and not merely the din of appetite.

When the cloth was removed and, as usual, the gentlemen prepared to seek the macao-table upstairs, Harry said quietly that he was not going to play any more. He had burned his fingers already, and could afford no more extravagance.

“Why,” Mr. Morris said, rather flippantly, “you must have won more than you have lost, Mr. Warrington, after all is said and done.”

“And of course I don’t know my own business as well as you do, Mr. Morris,” Harry replied sternly—he had not forgotten the other’s manner when the arrest was spoken of; “but I have another reason. A few months or days ago, I was heir to a great estate, and could afford to lose a little money. Now, thank God, I am heir to nothing.”

He looked round, blushing not a little, to the knot of his gaming companions lounging by the tables and gathered round the fire.

“How do you mean, Mr. Warrington?” cried my Lord March. “Have you lost Virginia too? Who has won it? I always had a fancy to play you myself for that stake.”

“And grow an improved breed of slaves in the colony,” said another, with that light cruelty which passes, in such places, for wit.

“The right owner has won it,” Harry answered. “You have heard me tell of my twin elder brother.”

“Who was killed in that affair of Braddock’s two years ago! Yes. Gracious goodness, my dear sir—I hope in Heaven he has not come to life again?”

“He arrived in London two days since. He has been a prisoner in a French fort for eighteen months; he only escaped a few months ago, and left our house in Virginia very soon after his release.”

“You haven’t had time to order mourning, I suppose, Mr. Warrington?” Mr. Selwyn asked very good-naturedly; and simple Harry did not catch the joke until later, when his brother explained it to him.

Harry took his leave.

As the door closed, the room’s sound altered—the way a kitchen changes when the cook steps out and the scullions begin to whisper. My Lord March, who had a gift for making every sentiment look like a vice, broke out laughing.

“Hang me, if I don’t believe the fellow is absolutely glad of the reappearance of his confounded brother!”

“These savages practise the simple virtues of affection—they are barely civilised in America yet,” Selwyn yawned.

“They love their kindred, and they scalp their enemies,” simpered Mr. Walpole. “It’s not Christian, but natural. Shouldn’t you like to be present at a scalping-match, George, and see a fellow skinned alive?”

“A man’s elder brother is his natural enemy,” said Mr. Selwyn placidly, ranging his money and counters before him.

“Torture is like broiled bones and pepper. You wouldn’t relish simple hanging afterwards, George!” continued Horry.

“I’m hanged if there’s any man in England who would like to see his elder brother alive,” said my lord.

“No, nor his father either, my lord!” cried Jack Morris.

“First time I ever knew you had one, Jack. Give me counters for five hundred.”

Jack, once set going, loved the sound of his own suspicion.

“I say, ’tis all mighty fine about dead brothers coming to life again,” he continued. “Who is to know that it wasn’t a scheme arranged between these two fellows? Here comes a young fellow who calls himself the Fortunate Youth, who says he is a Virginian Prince and the deuce knows what, and who gets into our society—”

A great laugh went round at Jack’s “our society,” as though the phrase itself were a jest too plump to swallow.

“—Who is to know that it wasn’t a cross?” Jack persisted. “The young one is to come first. He is to marry an heiress, and, when he has got her, up is to rise the elder brother! When did this elder brother show? Why, when the younger’s scheme was blown, and all was up with him! Who shall tell me that the fellow hasn’t been living in Seven Dials, or in a cellar dining off tripe and cow-heel until my younger gentleman was disposed of? Dammy, as gentlemen, I think we ought to take notice of it: and that this Mr. Warrington has been taking a most outrageous liberty with the whole club.”

“Who put him up? It was March, I think, put him up?” asked a bystander.

“Yes. But my lord thought he was putting up a very different person. Didn’t you, March?”

“Hold your confounded tongue, and mind your game!” said the nobleman; but Jack’s opinion, like a bad smell, found its way into more than one corner. In the world outside that room, too, there were many willing to agree that it was indecorous of Mr. Harry Warrington ever to have believed his brother dead; that there was something suspicious in his first appearance and subsequent actions; and that, regarding foreigners, adventurers, and the like, one ought to be especially cautious—especially when such caution cost nothing but another man’s reputation.

Yet Harry, for his part, though he was out of prison and difficulty; though he had Madame Bernstein’s liberal donation of money in his pocket; though his dearest brother was restored to him—whose return to life Harry never once thought of deploring, as the gentlemen at White’s supposed he must—though Maria had shown herself in so favourable a light by her behaviour during his misfortune: yet, when he was alone, he was not cheerful.

He sat and smoked his pipe of Virginia, and the tobacco’s sweet, resinous heaviness filled his mouth and nose, and seemed to lay a warm hand on his thoughts without soothing them. The room about him was quiet—no dice rattling, no fiddles, no coach-wheels—only the faint tick of London life beyond the panes, and the occasional settling of the fire. After the club’s rattle, that quieter soundscape ought to have been peace; but it made space for anxiety to speak.

It was not that he was deposed from his principality: the loss of it never once vexed him. He knew George would share with him, as he would have done with George. But after all those struggles and doubts in his own mind, to find himself poor—and yet irrevocably bound to his elderly cousin!

Yes, she was elderly; there was no doubt. When she came to that horrible den in Cursitor Street and the tears washed her rouge away, she looked as old as his mother. Her face, without its paint, had seemed yellow and wrinkled; and thinking of it now gave him the same sick qualm he had felt when she was taken ill in the coach on the Tunbridge road. What would his mother say when he brought her home? What battles there would be between them! He would go and live on one of the plantations—the farther from home the better—and have a few negroes, and farm as best he might, and hunt a good deal. But at Castlewood, or in any home he could make for her, what a life for poor Maria, used to court, to cards, to balls and assemblies every night! The very silence of a country evening would ring in her ears like punishment.

If he could be but the overseer of the estates—oh, he would be an honest factor, and try to make up, by labour and care, for his useless life and extravagance in Europe. Five thousand pounds—his patrimony and the accumulations of his long minority—squandered in six months! He a beggar, except for dear George’s kindness, with nothing left him but an old wife: a pretty beggar, dressed out in velvet and silver lace forsooth. He had been in his best clothes; he had made, to the eye, so fine a figure; and here was the end of the show.

With all his fine friends at White’s and Newmarket, with all his extravagance, had he been happy a single day since he had been in Europe? Yes—three days, four days: yesterday evening, when he had been with dear, dear Mrs. Lambert, and those affectionate kind girls, and that brave good Colonel. The Colonel had been right to rebuke him; and he had been a brute to be angry. God bless them all for their generous exertions in his behalf.

Such were the thoughts Harry put into his pipe, and smoked there, in the hush between one London noise and the next, whilst he waited his brother’s return from Madame Bernstein.

Colonel Esmond—whose name, like a well-worn family seal, had been pressed into this tale so often already—had carried into his long American leisure a habit of setting things down. In Virginia, where the summers were loud with cicadas and the nights rang with frogs and distant drums from quarters, he had written his memoirs in a firm, old-fashioned hand, as if to keep the past from washing away like a footprint in tide-sand. In those pages Madame de Bernstein—then Beatrice Esmond—moved with a brightness that seemed, even on paper, to throw candle-glare on the surrounding sentences. George Warrington had read that manuscript many times, and so came to know his aunt twice over: first as the young, handsome, wilful woman of fifty years ago; then as the lady who now sat near him in rouge and jewels, with age at her temples and malice and wit still quick as a knife.

There is a particular cruelty in time: it does not merely dim a face; it changes the sound a room makes around that face. Where once there might have been music and the soft rush of admirers’ feet, now there were the tired creak of chair-legs, the click of a cane, the dry cough of servants keeping wakefulness by habit. George, watching his aunt come in late from her rout, thought—against his will—of fireworks he had seen as a boy at Williamsburg: the rockets’ brief splendor, and afterward the blackened frame, the empty sockets, the wheel that had been a sun and now was only a skeleton.

He had kept to himself how closely he knew her early history. It did not seem to him a kindness to tell an old woman—however formidable—that her youth had been long since rehearsed and bound between covers in his grandfather’s study.

When their supper was done, Madame Bernstein tapped her cane toward her escritoire, and ordered her attendant to bring the letter lying beneath the inkstand. George knew the superscription at once. It was the letter he had carried from Virginia.

“It would appear by this,” said the Baroness, fixing him with a stare that seemed to search for lies among his eyelashes, “that since your return you and my sister have had differences.”

“Indeed? I did not know Madam Esmond had chosen to name them,” George answered.

She set a great pair of glasses upon her nose—an absurd harness for eyes that, in their day, had made men reckless—and after a glance, passed the paper to him. He read.

“RICHMOND, VIRGINIA, December 26th, 1756.

“HONOURED MADAM! AND SISTER!—I have received, and thankfully acknowledge, your ladyship’s favour….”

It was his mother’s voice upon the page: pious, exact, tender where it chose, and firm as a locked pantry where it must. She spoke of the season of goodwill, and of sorrow still decreed. She told how her eldest son, returned “miraculously out of the Valley of the Shadow of Death,” would bring her answer. She mourned that Harry, in England, had been presented “under false colours,” as heir, while George yet lived, though “dead to us” in captivity. She praised Harry’s tenderness—his heart, she insisted, the softest alive—and assured her sister that in the joy of George’s return, Harry would accept his altered place without a pang, obedient, generous, giving up the inheritance that had seemed his “but for the accident of birth.”

Then came money—always money beneath the prayers, as sure as salt beneath sweetness in a sauce. She reminded her sister how an opportunity had once arisen to establish Harry in Virginia with “a noble estate and negroes,” had her wishes been complied with and his portion invested, but “the forms of the law” and “my elder son’s scruples” had prevailed. She sent a sum now—carefully entrusted—meant to cover Harry’s expenses in fine company, for surely a grandson of the Marquis of Esmond “may claim equality with any other nobleman in Great Britain.” And she prayed the Baroness to add what she would.

George, unable to help himself, broke in, his tone controlled but edged. “It took him out of prison yesterday, madam. I think that was the best use to which we could put it.”

Madame Bernstein lifted her brows as if he had spoken heresy over the pudding. “Nay, sir, I don’t know any such thing! Why not keep it to buy him a pair of colours—or to help toward another estate and some negroes, if he has a fancy for home? Besides, I had a fancy to pay that debt myself.”

“I hope you will let his brother do that. I ask leave to be my brother’s banker in this matter—and consider I have borrowed so much from my mother, to be paid back to my dear Harry.”

“Do you say so? Give me a glass of wine!” she cried. “You are an extravagant fellow. Read on, and you will see your mother thinks so. I drink your health, nephew George. ’Tis good Burgundy. Your grandfather never loved Burgundy. He loved claret—the little he drank.”

George read on. His mother’s letter, like one of her own Virginia broths, had been skimmed and strained until only her chosen flavors remained. She professed fear of George’s prudence. She spoke of humility, of fond blessings, of every act dictated by love for her “dearest boys’ welfare.” Yet between the lines, George saw the scratches and blots—literal upon the page and figurative in the heart that wrote it: the penknife mark, the heavy stain as of water fallen, as though the ink had been forced to run by a tear or an angry hand.

“There is a scratch with a penknife, and a great blot upon the letter there, as if water had fallen on it,” his aunt remarked, not unkindly. “Your mother writes well, George. I suppose you and she had a difference?”

“Yes, ma’am—many,” George said quietly.

“The last was about money,” he continued, because the truth had a pressure of its own and would not be kept down. “About the ransom I promised the old lieutenant at the fort—Museau—who aided my escape.”

He told her what had happened: how, six weeks after his return, the Indian woman—Museau’s poor mistress—had found her way through the woods to Richmond, guided by the same perilous track he had taken, bearing his grandfather’s watch and a line scrawled from a prison-bed. A new commandant had arrived at Duquesne; Museau had been accused—of what peculation the messenger could hardly make clear—put under arrest, attempted to flee, and been shot on the rampart. With his last breath he begged George to send “ce que je scavais” to a notary at Havre de Grace, to be transmitted to his kin at Caen.

Silverheels, the hunter, had helped the woman; without him, she might have been scalped and left to the crows. But in Richmond, she met not gratitude but suspicion—suspicion that had its own harsh music: whispers in doorways, laughter from servants, pulpit-thunder from a sanctimonious fellow who used a sermon like a cudgel. She drank when she could. George ordered her food and shelter, and she became a jest among their negroes and a subject for the old town’s sharp tongues. At last he obtained a pass from the Governor—“a man of sense,” he said—to send her back to her people. Her grief at parting from him only confirmed those who wished to be scandalised. He had to cane one man; he believed another preached against him. And at home, Madam Esmond and he had come to a violent quarrel because he insisted on paying Museau’s heirs the money he had promised.

“You see,” George concluded, “that scandal flourishes at the borders of the wilderness, and in the New World as well as the Old.”

“I have suffered from it myself, my dear,” Madame Bernstein said, demure as a saint in a comedy. “Fill thy glass, child! A little tass of cherry-brandy! ’Twill do thee all the good in the world.”

He tasted it—hot and perfumed, with that winter-stored sweetness of cherries steeped until they surrender their color—and the room seemed for a moment to change its sound: the crackle of the fire, the faint far-off rumble of carriages, the rustle of silk as the Baroness adjusted herself. London at night had its own ecology of noise—less honest than Virginia’s, more mechanical, more restless—wheel on cobble, chairmen calling, a drunken catch from a side-street, all of it like commerce turned into weather. In such a city, even art was hawked and shouted, and song itself could feel like a thing for sale.

His mother’s letter went on to speak of Harry’s marriage. Madam Esmond declared herself shocked at the match with Lady Maria Esmond, “out of the question” because of her age—almost the same as Rachel’s—and because Castlewood’s daughters had been left with the smallest portions. Harry, she said, was so obedient that a desire from her would suffice to end the engagement. She reminded her sister—unnecessarily—that she herself had never contemplated a second union, whatever foolish people had supposed; she knew what was due to her children. George, she wrote, was amply provided for as heir; her task now was to save for the younger brother, and to have him return without delay to his “fond and loving mother,” since she did not love to live alone.

She praised Harry’s refinement gained in Europe, spoke with gratitude of his time among his English cousins, and ended with gratitude to her sister for kindness, with a pious flourish over their father—“one of the best of men”—and a postscript: she had communicated with Lady Maria, and there was no need to tell her or Harry that his mother or his aunt hoped to increase his small fortune. “The match is altogether unsuitable.”

George laid the paper down. “As far as regards myself, madam, my mother’s letter conveys no news. I always knew Harry was the favourite son—he deserves it. He has a hundred good qualities I have not. He has better looks—”

“Nay, that is not your fault,” the Baroness said, looking him over with a sly approval. “And but that he is fair and you are brown, one might almost pass for the other.”

George bowed; a faint color came to his cheek. “His disposition is bright, and mine is dark. Harry is cheerful, and I am otherwise. He knows how to make himself beloved by every one, and it has been my lot to find but few friends.”

“My sister and you have pretty little quarrels. There were such in old days in our family,” Madame Bernstein said. “And if Madam Esmond takes after our mother—”

“My mother has always described hers as an angel upon earth,” George said quickly.

“Eh! That is a common character for people when they are dead!” cried the Baroness. “Rachel Castlewood was an angel, if you like—at least your grandfather thought so. But angels are sometimes not very commodes à vivre. They are too good to live with us sinners; the air down below doesn’t agree with them. My poor mother was so perfect she never could forgive me for being otherwise. Ah, mon Dieu, how she used to oppress me with those angelical airs!”

George’s eyes dropped. He thought of his own youth, of prayers measured out like rations, of moral precepts spoken in a tone that allowed no answering. It was not that he wished to blacken his mother; rather, he could not bear to have her anatomised by this glittering cynic, who seemed, for all her worldliness, to read him as easily as if he were print.

“I comprehend you, sir, though you hold your tongue,” the Baroness went on. “A sermon in the morning, a sermon at night, and two or three of a Sunday—that is what people call being good. Every pleasure cried fie upon; all us worldly people excommunicated; a ball an abomination of desolation; a play forbidden; a game of cards perdition. Mon Dieu, what a life!”

“We played at cards every night, if we were so inclined,” George said, allowing himself a small smile; “and my grandfather loved Shakespeare so much, my mother had not a word to say against her father’s favourite.”

“I remember. He could say whole pages by heart—though for my part I like Mr. Congreve better. And then there was that dreadful, dreary Milton, whom he and Mr. Addison pretended to admire!” Madame Bernstein tapped her fan as if beating time to an unwanted hymn. “If your ladyship does not like Shakespeare, you will not quarrel with my mother for being indifferent to him too.”

“And indeed,” George added, attempting a defence that sounded, even to himself, like dutiful recitation, “you don’t do her justice. Wherever there are poor she relieves them; wherever there are sick she—”

“She doses them with horrible purges and boluses!” the Baroness broke in. “Of course, just as my mother did!”

“She does her best,” George said, steadying his voice. “She acts for the best and performs her duty as far as she knows it.”

“I don’t blame you for doing yours and keeping your own counsel about Madam Esmond,” the old lady returned. “But at least there is one point upon which we all three agree—that this absurd marriage must be prevented. Do you know how old the woman is? I can tell you—though she has torn the first leaf out of the family Bible at Castlewood.”

George said his mother had not forgotten her cousin’s age and was shocked at the disparity. And beyond age there was the matter of place: a London-bred lady, used to luxury and routs, might find little comfort in the plain routine of a Virginian plantation, where the day began with horns and hammering, where even the air had a different weight and smell—woodsmoke, damp earth, boiled hominy, curing meat. Besides, the house was not Harry’s; he was welcome there—more welcome, perhaps, than George, though George was the natural heir. But, George admitted with a blush and a stumble of speech, he doubted how Harry’s wife would like their colony.

The Baroness laughed—shrill, pleased, a laugh that made the glasses on the sideboard tremble. “He, he! Nephew Warrington! Speak your mind out. I shall tell no tales to your mother—though it is no news to me she has a high temper and loves her own way. Harry held his tongue; but it needed no conjurer to see who was mistress at home and what sort of a life my sister led you. I love my niece, my Lady Molly, so well I could wish her two or three years of Virginia with your mother reigning over her. You may well look alarmed, sir! Harry has said quite enough to show me who governs the family.”

“I may say as much as this,” George replied, forcing a smile, “that I don’t envy any woman coming into our house against my mother’s will. And my poor brother knows it perfectly.”

“What? You two have talked it over? No doubt you have. And the foolish child considers himself bound in honour—of course he does, the gaby!”

George told her Harry said Lady Maria had behaved nobly: when he was sent to prison she brought him her trinkets and jewels and every guinea she had. It touched him; he felt bound more than ever. Yet George owned that his brother seemed bound by honour rather than by love—at least in his present feeling.

“My good creature,” cried Madame Bernstein, leaning forward as if to press the point physically into him, “don’t you see Maria brings a few twopenny trinkets and a half-dozen guineas to Mr. Esmond—the heir of the great estate in Virginia—not to the second son who is a beggar and has just squandered away every shilling? I swear to you, on my credit as a gentlewoman, knowing Harry’s obstinacy and the misery he had in store, I tried to bribe Maria to give up her engagement and only failed because I could not bribe high enough! When he was in prison I sent my lawyer with orders to pay his debts immediately if he would part from her—but Maria had been beforehand with us, and Mr. Harry chose not to go back from his stupid word. Let me tell you what has passed in the last month!”

And she told it—what the reader already knows, though spoken now in that bold, unblushing idiom of her world, where even delicate ladies named greed and lust as if they were dishes on a bill of fare. Her phrases came out sharp, seasoned with contempt; she served up motives as if carving a fowl, laying bare joints and sinews that polite speech pretends are not there. She talked long, and cleverly, and with the satisfaction of one who believes herself the only honest tongue in a room of liars.

At last she surrendered herself to Mrs. Brett to be undressed, and announced, with the briskness of one who changes her mind as she changes gloves, that she had altered her opinion of her eldest nephew. Mr. George, she said, was handsome; certainly wittier than poor Harry (whom Heaven, it must be confessed, had not furnished with a great supply of brains); and he had the bel air—a melancholy, noble, distinguished je ne sais quoi—which reminded her of the Colonel. Had she ever told Brett about the Colonel? Scores of times, no doubt—and now she told her again, as if repeating a recipe whose taste she could not forget though the ingredients had long since soured.

George, walking home late through the city, was less pleased with her than she with him. The night had thinned; fashion’s last guests issued from bright doorways into cold air; chairmen yawned over expiring torches; somewhere a watchman’s call threaded through the street’s rumble like a mournful refrain. He felt as if the Baroness had peeled back a painted panel and shown him not merely her own face but the structure beneath their entire notion of nobility: family after family scrambling for small advantages, trampling through stale dissipations and faded pleasures, turning “ancient names” into counters in a game.

Are these the inheritors of noble blood? he asked himself. In the old romances, when a knight found a friend in want, did he turn away? When a nobleman received a young kinsman, did he cheat him at dice, trick him in horseflesh, buy and sell him with smiles? Had his poor Harry been inveigled into this engagement by a worldly woman’s skill—and would she, finding him poor, desert him? Would it not be better to pack trunks at once and take a cabin in the next ship home, to the quieter soundscape of fields and rivers, where the loudest thing at dawn might be geese, not coaches?

His own door answered these thoughts with domestic plainness. Gumbo came up yawning with a candle, the small flame making the hallway smell of tallow and smoke. In the sitting-room Harry lay asleep before the extinguished fire, his pipe emptied, its grey ashes spilled on the table like sifted flour. The city’s roar was muffled here; only the faint crack of settling wood and the far-off wheels remained, like surf heard indoors.

Harry started up at the candle’s movement. For a moment his eyes were dulled by sleep; then they brightened with honest pleasure at sight of George. He laughed like a boy and put his arm round his brother.

“There he is in flesh and blood, thank God!” he cried. “I was dreaming of thee but now, George, and that Ward was hearing us our lesson! Dost thou remember the ruler, Georgy? Why, bless my soul, ’tis three o’clock! Where have you been a-gadding, Mr. George? Hast thou supped? I supped at White’s, but I’m hungry again.”

His words tumbled out with that cheerful appetite for life that belonged to him: the hunger that was not only for food, but for company, for warmth, for reassurance.

“I did not play, sir—no, no; no more of that for younger brothers!” he went on quickly, as if reporting a victory. “And my Lord March paid me fifty he lost to me. I bet against his horse and on the Duke of Hamilton’s! They both rode the match at Newmarket this morning, and he lost because he was under weight. And he paid me, and he was as sulky as a bear. Let us have one pipe, Georgy—just one.”

And so, in a room that smelled of cold hearth and stale tobacco, with London’s restless noises held at bay by a closed door, the brothers shared their smoke like a small rite—one more thread binding them back to childhood and to home. Afterward they went to bed; and it is a good and pleasant thing, indeed, to see brethren who love one another.

Naturally the brothers, once the first embrace was over and the astonishment of finding each other breathing and warm in the same room had settled into the ordinary miracle of companionship, fell to their reckoning of home—reckoning it as men do who have been long starved of familiar things: by naming them, tasting them again on the tongue.

“How are Harry’s dogs?” George asked first, because he knew his brother’s heart went in front of him, like a hound. “And little Dempster—does he still cry when the kitchen door shuts? And old Nathan—does he yet pretend he cannot hear unless you speak civil?”

Harry, who had been nibbling at a bit of bread as if it were a comfort rather than a food, brightened at once. He could tell you the condition of every creature at Castlewood as a cook can tell you, by scent and touch, whether a ham will keep. The dogs were sleek, Dempster had grown a finger taller and a pound thinner (for he would run after anything with a tail), Nathan’s rheumatism made his temper sharper than his carving-knife. Mountain—dear Mountain—was well and match-making as ever; and Fanny had shot up into that perilous prettiness which makes a household suddenly cautious of its own laughter.

“And Polly Broadbent?” George asked, with the half-smile of a man who has filed away his youth in books and yet remembers where it used to sting. “They say she is to marry Tom Barker of Savannah and go to Georgia.”

“Polly? Oh, Lord!” Harry broke into a laugh that was half shame and half relish. “I was mighty sweet upon her once. I lost a deal of pocket-money at cards, and drank more strong-waters with the Parson than was good for me, only to have a pretext to be near the girl. But Madam would never have consented to my throwing myself away upon Polly Broadbent, no more than she would let Nathan salt a joint twice.”

George’s mouth tightened at the name of their mother, though he spoke lightly. He told, for Harry’s entertainment, of Colonel Washington’s pretty young wife—good-natured, pleasant, and with a fortune—and of the visit of state she had paid to Madam Esmond at Richmond. George, who had an eye for ceremony as other men have for spices, described the whole as if he had been forced to sit at a table where every dish was cold from politeness: the bows, the pauses, the compliments laid on so thick you could have spread them with a knife.

“Never mind, George, my dear!” Mountain had said afterward, according to George, in her cheery way. “The Colonel has taken another wife, but I feel certain that at one time two young gentlemen I know of ran a very near chance of having a tall stepfather, six feet two in his boots.”

Harry roared at that; yet it was a laugh that stuck. Mountain, good soul, matched people as she matched cups and saucers, putting them together because they were near to hand. Two folk could scarce sit to a dish of tea without her fancying their conjunction was for life. It had been she—the foolish tattler—who set abroad the talk about the poor Indian woman, Biche.

When George came to that, his voice changed, and the room itself seemed to thin, as if the air had been drawn off by a bad story. Madam Esmond, when Parson Stack brought the insinuation, repelled it with scorn.

“I should as soon fancy Mr. Esmond stealing the spoons,” she had said, “or marrying a negro woman out of the kitchen.”

And she did not believe Biche guilty, not even when all Richmond took pleasure in believing; she even thanked the poor creature for nursing her son in his illness. Yet she froze her with such proud coldness—like laying one’s hand on a jug and willing the ale to sour—that the Indian slunk away into the servants’ quarters, and there, with the harsh clink of bottle against cup and the low mutter of the quarters at night, tried to drown her disappointments with drink. George, who heard everything when he could not bear to speak, remembered the sound of it: the stealthy step, the suppressed laughter, the sudden hush when Madam passed.

“It was not cheerful,” he told Harry. “Two months at home, and I felt as though the house itself had grown narrow. The birthright is mine, Harry—but thou art the favourite, and God help me, I think my mother almost grudges it to me.”

Harry began at once, hot as a hearth in winter, to deny and protest. George stopped him with a weary motion.

“Why should I have taken the pas, and preceded your worship into the world?” George went on, the bitterness breaking through his usual restraint. “Had you been the eider, you would have had the best cellar, ridden the best nag, and been the most popular man in the country; whereas I have not a word to say for myself and frighten people by my glum face. I should have been second son, set up as lawyer, or come to England, got my degrees, turned parson, and said grace at your honour’s table. The time is out of joint, sir. O cursed spite, that ever I was born to set it right!”

“Why, Georgy, you are talking verses,” Harry cried, delighted in spite of the gloom. “I protest you are!”

“I think some one else talked those verses before me,” George said, and allowed himself a small smile.

“It’s out of one of your books. You know every book that ever was wrote, that I do believe!” Harry exclaimed; and then, with that boyish impulse to offer his heart in anecdotes, told how he had seen two famous authors at Tunbridge and taken off his hat to them.

“Not that I cared much about their books, not being clever enough. But I remembered how my dear old George used to speak of ’em,” Harry said; and his voice caught, as if the words had scraped a tender place. “That’s why I liked to see them. I say, dear, it’s like a dream seeing you over again. Think of that bloody Indian with his knife at my George’s head! I should like to give that Monsieur de Florac something for saving you—but I haven’t got much now, only my little gold knee-buckles, and they ain’t worth two guineas.”

“You have got the half of what I have, child,” George answered. “We’ll divide as soon as I have paid the Frenchman.”

At this Harry broke out into blessings and then into oaths—those rough benedictions of a passionate fellow who cannot keep his love neat—and swore there never was such a brother in the world as his brother George. For some days after George’s arrival, Harry’s eyes followed him as if he feared he would vanish again. At table he would lay down knife and fork mid-cut and begin to laugh softly to himself, as though the very act of chewing in company with George was a marvel. When they walked on the Mall or in Hyde Park, the sounds of London—carriages on gravel, the distant cries of hawkers, the wind combing the trees—seemed to Harry only a frame for his triumph. He would gaze at the company with a look that said, Look here, gentlemen. This is he. This is my brother that was dead and is alive again. Can any man in Christendom produce such a brother as this?

Of course, in Harry’s judgment, George must pay to Museau’s heirs the money promised for his ransom. To Harry the matter was as plain as a debt for supper: a man had pledged his word, therefore he must discharge it, whether the creditor lived to count it or no. But at home the question had been the very millstone about George’s neck.

Museau dead, Madam Esmond had argued—eagerly, sharply—that the bargain fell to the ground and her son was free. The man was a rogue from the first. She would not pay the wages of iniquity. Mr. Esmond had some small independence from his father; he might squander his patrimony if he chose; he was of age and the money was in his power. But she would be no party to such extravagance as giving twelve thousand livres to a parcel of peasants in Normandy with whom they were at war, and who would very likely hand it all to priests and the Pope. She would not subscribe to such wickedness. If George wanted to throw away his father’s money—she could not but remark that formerly he had not been so eager, and when Harry’s benefit was in question had refused to touch a penny of it—then why not give it to his own flesh and blood, to poor Harry suddenly deprived of his inheritance, instead of to a priest-ridden set in France?

It had raged so between mother and son during George’s last days in Virginia that the house seemed to have taken sides: the very doors shut more loudly, the floorboards reported footsteps like accusations. It was never settled. On the morning of George’s departure, Madam Esmond came to his bedside after a sleepless night and asked him, with that pale steadiness which admits no appeal, whether he still persisted in his intention to fling away his father’s property.

He answered from a depth of grief and perplexity that his word was passed; he must do as his honour bade him.

She said she would continue to pray that Heaven might soften his proud heart and enable her to bear her heavy trials; and the last view he had of her face was as she stood a moment by the bed, pale and with tearless eyes, before turning away and leaving the chamber slowly, like a judge who will not look back lest she be moved.

“Where didst thou learn the art of winning over everybody to thy side, Harry?” George asked now, in their London lodging, where the city’s constant murmur pressed against the windows like the sea. “How is it you and all the world begin by being friends? Teach me a few lessons in popularity—nay, I don’t know that I will have them. When I find and hear certain people hate me, I think I am rather pleased than angry.”

He told how, at first in Richmond, Mr. Esmond Warrington—the only prisoner escaped from Braddock’s field, the victim of illness and hardship—had been a favourite with town-folks. The parson glorified his escape in a sermon; neighbours came to visit the fugitive; the family coach was ordered out; Madam Esmond and George paid visits in return. “I think some pretty little caps were set at me,” George said with a dry amusement, “but our mother routed them off and frightened them with the prodigious haughtiness of her demeanour.”

And then, because George would not drink like the officers nor dice and swagger and swear, they judged him dull. Because he could not endure the ladies’ tea-table tattle—how it buzzed like flies around a sugar bowl—they judged him cold and sarcastic, never knowing whether he was in earnest. Richmond’s soundscape, as he painted it, was not the honest music of a farm—wind in corn, an axe biting wood, a kettle beginning to sing—but a weary clatter of gossip, squabbles, and boasts; and it gnawed at him until he found himself more than once wishing for the silence of Duquesne, for the prison’s “freedom of thought,” as he called it, and its easier hush.

“I am very shy, I suppose,” he said. “I can speak unreservedly to very few people. Before most, I sit utterly silent. When we two were at home, it was thou who used to talk at table and get a smile now and then from our mother. When she and I were together we had no subject in common, and we scarce spoke at all until we began to dispute about law and divinity.”

So the gentlemen decided he was supercilious, and the ladies decided he was disagreeable—before his character was “gone quite away.” And that, he said, went with the appearance of poor Biche and Museau’s unlucky messenger.

“Oh, a nice character they made for me,” George cried then, anger flaring in him at last. “And a pretty life they led me after that messenger appeared! The boys hooted the poor woman if she showed in the street; the ladies dropped me half-curtseys and walked to the other side. That precious clergyman went from one tea-table to another preaching on the horrors of seduction and the lax principles young men learn in Popish countries and bring back. The poor Fawn’s appearance at home a few weeks after my return was declared to be a scheme between her and me; the best informed agreed she had waited on the other side of the river until I gave the signal to come join me in Richmond. The officers bantered me at the coffee-house and cracked their clumsy jokes about the woman I had selected.”

He paused, and in the pause Harry could hear the city again: wheels, distant shouts, a bell. Against that London din, George’s Virginia sounded—its gossip louder than its crickets, its sermons sharper than its scythes.

“I was so enraged,” George went on, “I thought of going to Castlewood and living alone there—for our mother finds the place dull and the greatest consolation in Mr. Stack’s ministry—when the news arrived of your female perplexity; and I think we were all glad I should have a pretext for coming to Europe.”

“I should like to see any infernal scoundrel that said a word against you and break his rascally bones,” Harry bellowed, striding up and down as if the room were too small for his indignation. “I had to do something like it for Bob Clubber.”

“What!” George cried, contempt and astonishment together. “That little sneaking, backbiting, toad-eating wretch who’s forever hanging about my lord at Greenway Court and spunging on every gentleman in the country? If you whipped him, I hope you whipped him well.”

“We were bound over to keep the peace,” Harry said, with a shrug that tried to make light of it. “And I offered to go into Maryland with him and settle our difference there. And of course the good folk said that having made free with the seventh commandment I was inclined to break the sixth.”

“So by this and by that,” George concluded, “and being as innocent of the crime imputed to me as you are, I left home, my dear Harry, with as awful a reputation as ever a young gentleman earned.”

Then, as if the narrative itself could not resist stepping aside to hear its own echo, George spoke—half mocking, half wounded—of how the world will always invent the rest of one’s story, and tell it with a confidence that drowns truth as a mill-wheel drowns a bird’s song. Names, he said, are altered; words are twisted; a man’s life is translated into another dialect and comes out as something else entirely, like a receipt repeated from mouth to mouth until the seasoning is wrong and yet everybody swears it is authentic. Harry, who cared less for the philosophy than for the bruise beneath it, only growled and poured his brother more wine.

And because George had offered up his martyrdom, Harry must unbosom himself in turn. He confessed he had given up all the family at Castlewood—my lord not for winning from him at play (for Harry was sporting and expected to pay when he lost and receive when he won), but for refusing to aid the chaplain in necessity and dismissing him with false, heartless pretexts. About Mr. Will he had made up his mind after the horse-dealing matter and had marked his sense of that gentleman’s conduct freely upon Mr. Will’s eyes and nose.

As for the Countess and Lady Fanny, Harry spoke more guardedly, yet not favourably. He had heard stories: the Countess a card-playing old cat, Lady Fanny a desperate flirt. Who told him? Well—he had heard them from a person who knew both ladies very well indeed. Maria, in those days of confidence of which he spoke with a kind of stubborn tenderness, had imparted to him a number of anecdotes of her stepmother and half-sister by no means to their advantage.

But when he came to speak of Maria herself, his whole nature warmed, as a kitchen warms when bread is in the oven: not merely heated, but filled with a living smell and promise.

“It may be imprudent,” he said. “I don’t say no, George. I may be a fool—I think I am. I know there will be a dreadful piece of work at home, and that Madam and she will fight. Well! We must live apart. Our estate is big enough to live on without quarrelling, and I can go elsewhere than Richmond or Castlewood. When you come to the property, you’ll give me a bit—at any rate Madam will let me off at an easy rent—or I’ll make a famous farmer or factor. I can’t and won’t part from Maria. She has acted so nobly by me, that I should be a rascal to turn my back on her. Think of her bringing me every jewel she had in the world, dear brave creature, and flinging them into my lap with her last guineas—and—and—God bless her!”

He dashed his sleeve across his eyes and stamped, ashamed of weeping and yet unable not to.

“No, brother, I won’t part with her—not to be made Governor of Virginia to-morrow; and my dearest old George would never advise me to do so, I know that.”

“I am sent here to advise you,” George said quietly; and there was something in his tone that reminded Harry of their mother, though without her hardness. “I am sent to break the marriage off, if I can; and a more unhappy one I can’t imagine. But I can’t counsel you to break your word, my boy.”

“I knew you couldn’t.” Harry’s jaw set, and the warmth in him turned to a gloomy steadiness, as when broth cools and begins to film. “What’s said is said, George. I have made my bed, and must lie on it.”

So it had stood between them when first they talked over Harry’s love affair: George fearing, Harry resolved; George honour-bound, Harry heart-bound. Yet after George’s conversation with his aunt—after that keen old woman of the world had poured her information with a steady hand, like vinegar into oil until the mixture would not reconcile—Mr. Warrington, naturally sceptical, began to doubt Lady Maria as well as her brothers and sister, and to look at Harry’s engagement with increased distrust and alarm.

Was it for his wealth that Maria wanted Harry? Was it his handsome young person she longed after? Were those stories true which Aunt Bernstein had told? George could not bid Harry break his word; but he began, in the secret pantry of his mind, to consider how one might put Maria’s affection to the trial. And his ensuing conduct—which did not appear very amiable—sprang, no doubt, from that deliberation.

Lord Castlewood kept a house in Kensington Square, broad-fronted and dignified, with a gravel sweep before the steps and a thin strip of garden that tried, bravely, to be green in a city whose soot fell like black flour. It was large enough for the whole noble brood when the Court lay near, and for those evenings when her ladyship held her assemblies—cards, compliments, and that measured laughter which is the first music of fashionable life. Kensington, a hundred years ago, was not the easy suburb it has since become: the road out of town had stretches where the wheels fell silent in ruts, and the hedges seemed to listen. A man could hear his own coach springs complain, and, beyond them, the far-off mutter of London like a sea behind walls. George Selwyn would say he feared to go so far lest he be robbed of a night—whether by highwaymen with crepe masks or by ladies in rouge at quadrille, it came to much the same loss.

About noon, the day after Harry Warrington showed his face again at White’s, chance—or that domestic Fate that times its entrances better than any prompter—brought all Lord Castlewood’s virtuous kinsfolk together at breakfast. There was chocolate, thick as varnish, sent up steaming in painted cups; there were rolls split and toasted, their faces browned, and butter softening into them; there were eggs brought to table in their shells and opened with the little silver taps that made a neat, polite sound. Even the room itself had its palate: beeswax on the wainscot, coal-dust in the grate, and the faint medicinal perfume of pomatum lingering where my lord’s wig would presently sit.

The ladies came first and took their chocolate with that air of piety which society assumes towards any morning indulgence. Then Mr. Will clattered in, already dressed for the afternoon’s waiting in his court suit, bright as a toy soldier and twice as restless. At last the master of the house appeared, languid and yawning, in bedgown and nightcap, his wig not yet donned; his Daily Advertiser opened with the indifference of a man who expects to find the world behaving itself.

Here was news, Will said—news he had brought from the Star and Garter, where he had supped last night with men who had heard it at White’s and swore they had seen proof of it at Ranelagh.

“Heard what? seen what?” my lord asked, lifting his paper as though it were a shield.

“Ask Maria,” Lady Fanny said, and turned her bright eyes, trained to mischief, upon her elder sister.

Lord Castlewood looked at Lady Maria. She sat pale as linen, her hands lying in her lap as if they had been placed there by someone else. The chocolate before her had a skin upon it; she had not touched it.

“’Tis one of Will’s usual elegant and polite inventions,” Maria said, and her voice, though steady, had the thinness of a string drawn too tight.

“No,” Will swore—he had oaths ready like small coins in a pocket, and threw them down liberally. “No invention of mine. Tom Claypool of Norfolk saw ’em both at Ranelagh; Jack Morris came out of White’s where he heard it from Harry Warrington’s own lips. Curse him, I’m glad of it!” And he slapped the table so that the spoons rang, that little bright chorus of metal which makes a breakfast sound like battle. “What do you think of your Fortunate Youth, your Virginian—whom your lordship made such a pet of—turning out to be only a second son?”

“The elder brother not dead?” my lord said.

“No more dead than you are. Never was. It’s my belief there was a cross between the two.” And Will leaned back, exulting as though he had tasted a sauce that pleased him: sharp, sour, and triumphantly salted.

“Mr. Warrington is incapable of such duplicity!” Maria cried—too swiftly, as if she feared her own words would be snatched away.

“I never encouraged the fellow,” my lady put in, smoothing her napkin with the exactness of a woman who believes in order as in virtue. “Nor did Fanny. Not we, indeed!”

“Not we, indeed!” echoed Lady Fanny, as obedient in phrase as she was inventive in smile.

“The fellow is only a beggar,” Will went on, “and, I dare say, hasn’t paid for the clothes on his back. I’m glad of it, for, hang him, I hate him!”

“You don’t regard him with favourable eyes—especially since he blacked yours, Will,” my lord said, grinning. “So the poor fellow has found his brother and lost his estate!” He turned to Maria, and though she sat the very picture of woe, something in her rigid propriety—or perhaps the way misery itself can seem absurd to the comfortable—tickled his humour. He gazed at her a moment, then burst into a shrill laugh. At that sound, her face flushed as if scalded; her eyes brimmed and ran. “It’s a shame! it’s a shame!” she sobbed, and hid her face in her handkerchief.

Maria’s stepmother and sister exchanged a glance over their cups. “We never quite understand your lordship’s humour,” her ladyship said gravely, as if humour were a foreign dish badly described.

“I don’t see there is the least reason why you should,” my lord answered coolly; and then, with an easy change to gentleness: “Maria, my dear, pray excuse me if I have said—that is, done—anything to hurt your feelings.”

“Done anything!” Maria rose, her chair scraping—a harsher note in the room’s morning music. “You pillaged the poor lad in his prosperity, and you laugh at him in his ruin!” She glared round at them all as if they were a jury she despised. “Oh, never mind at what or whom else, my lord. You have taken from him all he had to lose. All the world points at you as the man who feeds on his own flesh and blood. And now you have his all, you make merry over his misfortune!” With that she swept out, her silk rustling like dry leaves dragged by wind.

“Tell us what has happened,” Lord Castlewood said, settling his paper again as if it were only a slight inconvenience that tears had fallen on the carpet, “and my sister’s grief will not interrupt us.”

Will obliged, at great length, rolling out the story that now hummed through London like a fiddler’s tune everybody knows: George Warrington’s sudden apparition; the elder brother alive; the estate gone from Harry’s hands as quickly as a dish snatched away at table. Will told it with a relish that belonged less to speech than to eating—he chewed each detail. Lord Castlewood, for all his worldly appetite, felt a certain regret. Harry was brave, open-handed, and pleasant company; my lord liked him as much as certain men like one another when each is useful to the other and neither cares to think too closely of the bargain. To be sure he had played Harry at cards, and taken the advantage of the market upon him; but why not? If another man would pluck the peach, why should not he eat it? If that were all a conscience had to reproach him with, it need not keep him awake.

“Where does Mr. Warrington live?” he asked at last.

Will declared himself ready for reprobation if he knew or cared.

“He shall be invited here, and treated with every respect,” my lord said.

“Including piquet, I suppose!” Will growled.

“Or will you take him to the stables and sell him one of your bargains of horseflesh, Will?” Lord Castlewood asked. “You would have won of Harry Warrington fast enough if you could; but you cheat so clumsily at your game that you got paid with a cudgel. I desire, once more, that every attention be paid to our cousin Warrington.”

“And that you are not to be disturbed when you sit down to play, of course, my lord!” Lady Castlewood said, with that smooth malice which can be poured like cream.

“Madam, I desire fair play—for Mr. Warrington, and for myself, and for every member of this amiable family,” my lord retorted, flashing.

“Heaven help the poor gentleman if your lordship is going to be kind to him,” her ladyship said with a curtsey; and Heaven only knows how far their quarrel might have gone, had not wheels at that instant crunched the gravel without, and a phaeton drawn up.

In it sat the two young Virginians.

It was the carriage Harry had bought in his prosperity, and he still drove it, as if motion itself could argue against misfortune. George sat beside him; their negroes followed behind. Harry had been trying, with a meekness that was new upon him and sat oddly on his lively spirit, to give up whip, reins, and all, to his brother.

“What business has a poor devil like me with horses and carriages, Georgy?” he had said. “Beyond the coat on my back and the purse my aunt gave me, I’ve nothing in the world. You take the driving-seat, brother; it will ease my mind if you’ll take the driving-seat.”

George, laughing, said he did not know the way and Harry did; and as for the carriage, he would claim only half, as he had already done with Harry’s wardrobe. “A bargain’s a bargain; if I share thy coats, thou must divide my breeches’ pocket, Harry; that’s fair dealing!” Harry had sworn again and again there never was such a brother on earth. He rattled the horses over the road with a boy’s pride, delighted to be seen driving so noble a companion, even though that nobility had just stripped him.

Gumbo’s thunder on Lord Castlewood’s door might have belonged to the biggest footman in St. James’s. There is a particular sound to a great house’s knocker struck with conviction: it is not merely noise, but announcement; it enters the body and tells it to stand straighter.

Only Lady Castlewood and her daughter, Lady Fanny, were in the room where the gentlemen were shown. Will had no appetite to face Harry; my lord was not long dressed; Maria had her reasons for being away at least until her eyes were dry. And there is this curious mercy in good breeding—that it can arrange itself in an instant like a table set for guests, napkins folded, crumbs brushed away, as though the knives had not just been drawn.

Lady Castlewood advanced with perfect ease and good humour. “We have heard, Harry,” she said, and gave him a look of particular friendliness, “of this most extraordinary circumstance. My Lord Castlewood said at breakfast he should wait on you this very day, Mr. Warrington; and, cousin Harry, we intend not to love you any the less because you are poor.”

“We shall be able to show now that it is not for your acres that we like you, Harry!” Lady Fanny cried, following her mamma’s lead as neatly as a well-trained echo.

“And I to whom the acres have fallen?” George asked, smiling, and bowed.

“Oh, cousin, we shall like you for being like Harry!” Lady Fanny answered, arch as a pastrycook’s twist of sugar.

They were civil enough to George; but to Harry they were tender—softly familiar, gently kind, affectionately reproachful. Why had he stayed away days and days? Better, Lady Castlewood said, to have had a dish of tea and a game at piquet with them than to have haunted other tables. If they had won enough to buy a paper of pins from him they would have been content; young gentlemen, she sighed, did not know what was for their own good.

“Now you have no more money to play with, you can come and play with us, cousin!” cried fond Lady Fanny, lifting her finger. “So your misfortune will be good fortune to us.”

George watched, puzzled. He had expected London to be all claws and coldness; yet here were caresses offered to the brother who had not a guinea. Perhaps people were not so black as painted. Or perhaps they were—only in a subtler dye that does not run at first washing.

After near twenty minutes of this sweet seasoning, Lord Castlewood entered at last, wig on head and sword at side, composed and shining like a man who has been basted and served. He greeted both young men with equal politeness.

“If you were to come to us—and I, for one, cordially rejoice to see you—what a pity you did not come a few months earlier!” he said to George. “A certain evening at piquet would then most likely never have taken place. A younger son would have been more prudent.”

“Yes, indeed,” Harry said, obediently.

“Or a kinsman more compassionate,” my lord went on, with a fine air of candour. “But I fear the love of play runs in the blood of all of us. I have it from my father, and it has made me the poorest peer in England. Those fair ladies before you are not exempt. My poor brother Will is a martyr to it; and what I win one day, I lose the next. ’Tis shocking—the rage for play in England. All my poor cousin’s bank-notes parted company from me within twenty-four hours after I got them.”

“I have played, like other gentlemen,” George said, “but never to hurt myself, and never indeed caring much for the sport.”

“When we heard that my lord had played with Harry, we did so scold him,” cried the ladies, as if scolding were a ribbon tied over wrongdoing.

“But if it had not been I,” Lord Castlewood said, “some other person would have had your money. ’Tis a poor consolation; but Harry must take it and be glad that friends won his money who wish him well, not strangers who cared nothing for him and fleeced him.”

“Eh! a tooth out is a tooth out, though it be your brother who pulls it, my lord,” George said, laughing. “Harry must bear the penalty of his faults and pay his debts like other men.”

“I am sure I have never said or thought otherwise,” Harry declared. “’Tis not like an Englishman to be sulky because he is beaten.”

“Your hand, cousin! You speak like a man!” cried my lord, delighted; and the ladies smiled to each other, pleased to see virtue seasoned with masculine bravado.

“My sister in Virginia has known how to bring up her sons as gentlemen!” Lady Castlewood exclaimed.

“I protest you must not be growing so amiable now you are poor, cousin Harry!” Lady Fanny cried. “Why, mamma, we did not know half his good qualities when he was only Fortunate Youth and Prince of Virginia! You are exactly like him, cousin George, but I vow you can’t be as amiable as your brother!”

“I am the Prince of Virginia,” George said gravely, “but I fear I am not the Fortunate Youth.”

Harry was beginning, “By Jove, he is the best—” when a harpsichord sounded above: a few cautious notes, then a little run, as if fingers trembled and corrected themselves. The sound fell down the staircase like something private overheard. Harry blushed; the ladies smiled.

“’Tis Maria, above,” Lady Castlewood said. “Let some of us go up to her.”

They rose and moved to the door; and Harry, colouring deeply, followed them. George was about to go too, but Lord Castlewood checked him.

“Nay—if all the ladies follow your brother,” his lordship said, “let me at least have the benefit of your company and conversation. I long to hear the account of your captivity and rescue, cousin George!”

“Oh, we must hear that too!” cried one of the ladies, lingering.

“I am greedy, and should like it all by myself,” Lord Castlewood answered, and gave her such a stern look that she obeyed, smiling. He followed the women to the door, bowed low, and closed it upon them.

“Your brother has no doubt acquainted you with the history of what has happened to him in this house, cousin George?” Lord Castlewood asked, when they were alone.

“Yes, including the quarrel with Mr. Will and the engagement to my Lady Maria,” George replied, and bowed. “I may be pardoned for saying he hath met with ill fortune here, my lord.”

“Which no one can deplore more cordially than myself,” Lord Castlewood said readily. “My brother lives with horse-jockeys and trainers and the wildest bloods of the town; between us there is very little sympathy. We should not all live together were we not so poor. This is the house our grandmother occupied before she went to America and married Colonel Esmond. Much of the furniture belonged to her.”

George looked round with interest at the wainscoted parlour: the old chairs with their faded needlework, the table scarred by candle and spilled wine, the very air seeming to hold the ghost of other breakfasts, other quarrels. It is strange how a room can keep memory better than many a tongue; and yet a tongue can change its word and lose a world.

“Our house has not flourished in the last twenty years,” my lord continued. “We had a promotion of rank a score of years since, through court interest; but the malady of play has been our ruin. I am a miserable victim to it—only too proud to sell myself and title to a roturière, as many noblemen, less scrupulous, have done. Pride is my fault, my dear cousin. I remember how I was born!” And he laid his hand upon his shirt-frill, turned out his toe, and looked nobly into George’s face.

Young George’s disposition was to believe what people said, as a child believes a recipe written in a fair hand. But once undeceived, he could taste deceit in a sentence the way a careful palate detects rancid butter beneath fine spices. He kept his gravity; his scorn stayed inward, like a laugh swallowed.

“We have all our faults, my lord,” he said. “That of play hath been condoned over and over in gentlemen of our rank. Having heartily forgiven my brother, I cannot presume to be your judge; and instead of playing and losing, I wish sincerely you had both played and won!”

“So do I, with all my heart!” my lord sighed. “I augur well for your goodness when you can speak thus; and for your experience too—you seem to possess more of the world than most young men of your age. Your poor Harry hath the best heart in the world; but I doubt whether his head be very strong.”

“Not very strong, indeed,” George said. “But he hath the art to make friends wherever he goes; and in spite of all his imprudences most people love him.”

“I do—we all do, I’m sure! as if he were our brother!” my lord cried.

“He has often described in his letters his welcome at your lordship’s house,” George went on. “My mother keeps them all, you may be sure. Harry’s style is not learned; but his heart is so good that to read him is better than wit.”

“I may be mistaken,” Lord Castlewood said obstinately gracious, “but I fancy his brother possesses a good heart and good wit too!”

“I am as Heaven made me, cousin,” George said, “and perhaps some more experience and sorrow than has fallen to the lot of most young men.”

“This misfortune of your poor brother—I mean this piece of good fortune, your sudden reappearance—has not quite left Harry without resources?” Lord Castlewood asked, very gently, as if he were lifting a lid to see what remained in the pot.

“With nothing but what his mother can leave him, or I, at her death, can spare him. What is the usual portion here of a younger brother, my lord?”

“Eh! a younger brother here is—you know—in fine, everybody knows what a younger brother is,” my lord said, and shrugged.

George continued, with a frankness that cut. “We are the best of friends, but we are flesh and blood. I don’t pretend to do more for him than is usually done for younger brothers. Why give him money—that he should squander it at cards or horse-racing? My lord, we have cards and jockeys in Virginia too; and my poor Harry hath distinguished himself in dissipation at home before he came to yours. He inherits the family failing.”

“Poor fellow, poor fellow—I pity him!”

“Our estate is great, but our income is small,” George said. “We have little more money than what we get from England for our tobacco—and very little of that too—for our tobacco comes back to us in the shape of goods: clothes, leather, groceries, ironmongery—nay, wine and beer for our people and ourselves. Harry may come back and share all these: there is a nag in the stable for him, a piece of venison on the table, a little ready money to keep his pocket warm, and a coat or two every year. This will go on while my mother lives—unless, which is far from improbable, he gets into some quarrel with Madam Esmond. Then, while I live, he will have the run of the house and all it contains; then, if I die leaving children, he will be less and less welcome. His future is dismal unless some strange luck turn up on which we were fools to speculate. Henceforth he is doomed to dependence; and I know no worse lot than to be dependent on a self-willed woman like our mother. The means he had to make himself respected at home he hath squandered away here. He has flung his patrimony to the dogs; poverty and subserviency are now his only portion.”

He spoke with spirit and speed, as if he feared his own pity might rise and spoil the argument. Lord Castlewood listened respectfully, as men listen to a hard truth when it is not their hard truth.

“You speak well, Mr. Warrington. Have you ever thought of public life?” my lord asked.

“Of course,” George replied. “Like every man of my station—every man, that is, who cares for something beyond a dice-box or a stable. I hope to take my own place; my unlucky brother must content himself with his. I say this advisedly, having heard from him of certain engagements he has formed, and which it would be misery to all parties were he to attempt to execute now.”

“Your logic is very strong,” my lord said. “Shall we go up and see the ladies? There is a picture above-stairs which your grandfather is said to have executed. Before you go, my dear cousin, you will please to fix a day when our family may have the honour of receiving you. Castlewood is always your home when we are there. It is something like your Virginian Castlewood, from your account. We have beef and mutton and ale and wood in plenty; but money is woefully scarce amongst us.”

They went up. In the drawing-room they found only Lady Maria, who came out of the embrasure of a window where she and Harry had been talking. The light struck her face and showed plainly what powder and composure could not hide: swollen lids, a mouth held firm by sheer will, the look of a woman whose heart has been pulled at like thread from a seam.

George made his best bow; Maria curtseyed low. “You are indeed wonderfully like your brother,” she said, giving him her hand. “And from what he says, cousin George, I think you are as good as he is.”

At the sight of her tearful face George felt a pang of remorse. Poor thing, he thought: Harry has been vaunting my generosity and virtue to her, and I have been downstairs playing the selfish elder brother. How old she looks! How could he ever have a passion for such a woman as that? How? Because Harry did not see with George’s eyes. He saw with his own—and perhaps he was beginning now, painfully, to see differently.

After the introduction there was a little talk, which Maria managed at first with that trained ease society demands—words laid like a cloth over the bare board. But even ladies, consummate hypocrites of cheer, cannot keep up the mask for long when the face beneath is wet. After a sentence or two she broke into a sob; then, motioning Harry away with her hand—as though she would not even take comfort that might shame her—she fled from the room.

Harry sprang forward, then stopped, checked by that sign. Lord Castlewood said his poor sister was subject to fits of nerves and had already been ill that morning. After this, the young gentlemen judged it needless to prolong their visit. Lord Castlewood went down with them, admired the horses at the door, spoke of their points as if horseflesh were the one honest subject left in the world, waved them off with friendliness.

“And so we have been coaxing and cuddling in the window, and we part good friends, Harry—is it not so?” George said, as Harry gathered the reins.

“Oh, she is a good woman!” Harry cried, and flicked the whip; the harness chimed, that bright, domestic music of leather and brass. “I know you’ll think so when you come to know her.”

“When you take her home to Virginia? A pretty welcome our mother will give her. She will never forgive me for not breaking the match off—nor you for making it.”

“I can’t help it, George!” Harry said, and leaned forward, driving as if speed could carry him out of consequence. “Don’t you be popping your ugly head so close to my ears, Gumbo! After what has passed between us, I am bound in honour to stand by her. If she sees no objection, I must find none. I told her all. I told her Madam would be very rusty at first; but she is very fond of me, and must end by relenting. And when you come to the property, I told her I knew my dearest George so well that I might count upon sharing with him.”

“The deuce you did!” George said sharply. “Let me tell you, my dear, that I have been telling my Lord Castlewood quite a different story—that as an elder brother I intend to have all my rights—there, don’t flog that near horse so—and that you can but look forward to poverty and dependence.”

“What! You won’t help me?” Harry cried, turning quite pale.

Madame de Bernstein was scarcely less content than her two Virginian nephews when Harry came back from his last audience with Lady Maria, free—so the word went—from that engagement which had bound him and galled him by turns. George sent his news to the Baroness that very evening in a little note, crisp as a wafer and as carefully folded; and not long after, her nephew Lord Castlewood—who visited her as men visit dentists, seldom and with a face composed beforehand—came to her house and spoke of the matter without any of the silk-and-velvet disguises which polite people so love.

For now that the match was ended, what was the use of parrying? The cards had been played, the stakes lifted, the table cleared. Eugene Castlewood knew well enough how to be frank when frankness could no longer lose him anything.

“She is my own sister,” said he, with a kind of warmth that sounded the more credible because it came out of so practised a mouth. “She won’t have many more chances—many more such chances—of marrying and settling herself. I might not approve of the match in every respect; I might pity your ladyship’s young Virginian favourite; but such fortune was not to be thrown away. I was bound to stand by my own flesh and blood.”

“Your candour does your lordship honour,” Madame de Bernstein replied, as if tasting a sauce to see whether it needed salt. “And your love for your sister is quite edifying.”

“Nay, we have lost the game, and I am speaking sans rancune,” Castlewood said, bowing. “It is not for you, who have won, to bear malice.”

Malice? The Baroness declared she had never been in better humour in her life. There are moods in which an old woman’s good-nature has the crackle of dry kindling: it warms all the room, and can burn any one who comes too near.

“Confess now, Eugene,” she cried, leaning forward as if she scented a secret as plainly as hot bread, “that visit of Maria to Harry at the spunging-house—that touching giving up of all his presents to her—was a stroke of thy invention?”

“Pity for the young man,” said Castlewood, demure as a priest at a christening, “and a sense of what was due from Maria to her friend—her affianced lover—in misfortune. These motives might well suffice.”

“But ’twas you advised her, my good nephew?”

He shrugged, and owned he had advised his sister to see Mr. Henry Warrington.
