“And yet we should have won, in spite of your ladyship,” he continued, taking snuff with that air of a man sprinkling seasoning on a dish already his own, “had not the elder brother made his appearance. I have been trying to console my poor Maria by showing her what a piece of good fortune it is, after all, that we lost.”

“Suppose she had married Harry, and then cousin George had made his appearance?” the Baroness asked.

“Effectivement,” cried Eugene; and his little laugh was like the click of a lid on a box. “As the grave was to give up its dead, let us be thankful to the grave for disgorging in time! I am bound to say Mr. George Warrington seems a man of sense, and not more selfish than other elder sons and men of the world. My poor Molly fancied he might be—a greenhorn perhaps is the term—like his younger brother. She fondly hoped he might be inclined to go share and share alike with Twin junior; in which case, so infatuated was she about the young fellow, that I believe she would have taken him. ‘Harry Warrington, with half a loaf, might do very well,’ says I, ‘but Harry Warrington with no bread, my dear!’”

“How no bread?” Madame de Bernstein asked, bristling.

“Well, no bread except at his brother’s side-table. The elder said as much.”

“What a hard-hearted wretch!” she cried.

“Ah, bah! I play with you, aunt—cartes sur table!” Castlewood answered, with the easy cruelty of a man who thinks truth is always an excuse. “Mr. George only did what everybody else would do. We have no right to be angry with him; really we haven’t. Molly herself acknowledged as much after her first burst of grief was over, and I brought her to listen to reason. The silly old creature! to be so wild about a young lad at her time of life!”

“’Twas a real passion, I almost do believe,” said Madame de Bernstein, and her eyes—so quick to judge others—softened for once.

“You should have heard her take leave of him. C’était touchant, ma parole d’honneur! I cried. Before George, I could not help myself. The young fellow, with muddy stockings and his hair about his eyes, flings himself amongst us when we were at dinner; makes his offer to Molly in a very frank and noble manner, and in good language too; and she replies. Begad, it put me in mind of Mrs. Woffington in that new Scotch play Lord Bute’s man has wrote—Douglas—what d’ye call it? She clings round the lad; she bids him adieu in heartrending accents. She steps out of the room in a stately despair—no more chocolate, thank you. If she had made a mauvais pas no one could retire from it with more dignity. ’Twas a masterly retreat after a defeat. We were starved out of our position, but we retired with all the honours of war.”

“Molly won’t die of the disappointment,” Madame de Bernstein said, sipping her cup as calmly as if it were only thin chocolate and not another woman’s bruised heart that had been served with it.

My lord showed his yellow teeth in a grin that creaked. “He, he! She hath once or twice before had the malady very severely, and recovered perfectly. It don’t kill, as your ladyship knows, at Molly’s age.”

How should her ladyship know? She had not married Doctor Tusher until she was far advanced in life; and Madame de Bernstein came later still, as names and fortunes often do, trailing their histories behind them like the smell of smoke in an old gown. Yet even those who have been slow to happiness are not ignorant of misfortune; and misfortune, like a harsh seasoning, teaches the palate to recognize bitterness in another dish.

In the little world, people quarrel and scratch like cats in a back-yard, and keep their bristles up for months. In the great world, folks are wiser in their generation. They differ; they cease to meet; then, when the game is over and the stakes have changed hands, they make it up and come together again, no questions asked. A stray prodigal—or a stray puppy—will be brought in under the benefit of an amnesty though you know well enough what ugly company he has kept. So it happened now. For six months past, while the Castlewoods and Madame de Bernstein had been tugging at poor Harry as if he were a prize joint to be carved and divided, these two branches of the Esmond family had held apart. But the question being settled, they were free to meet again as though no difference had ever separated them. The Baroness drove in her great coach to Lady Castlewood’s rout; and the Esmond ladies appeared smiling at Madame de Bernstein’s drums; and they loved each other just as much as they previously had done—no more and no less, which is to say, as much as their interests could bear.

“So, sir, I hear you have acted like a hard-hearted monster about your poor brother Harry!” Madame de Bernstein cried when George came within reach; and she menaced him with her stick, delighted as a cook who has found a nephew stealing cream and can scold him for it.

“I acted but upon your ladyship’s hint,” George answered, colouring like a man caught with his hand in the spice-box, “and desired to see whether it was for himself or his reputed money that his kinsfolk wanted to have him.”

“Nay, Maria could not marry a poor fellow who was utterly penniless, and whose elder brother said he would give him nothing!”

“I did it for the best, madam,” George said, still blushing.

“And so thou didst, O thou hypocrite!” cried the old lady.

“Hypocrite, madam! and why?” George asked, drawing himself up with a dignity that sat oddly on a young man who had lately been a ghost to his own friends.

“I know all, my infant!” she said in French, her voice dropping into that intimate tone which makes a secret sound like a dish passed under the cloth. “Thou art very like thy grandfather. Come—that I embrace thee! Harry has told me all, and that thou hast divided thy little patrimony with him!”

“It was but natural, madam. We have had common hearts and purses since we were born. I but feigned hard-heartedness in order to try those people yonder,” George replied; and his eyes filled, honest with the simple habit of affection, as if he had been cutting onions for a stew and could not help the tears.

“And thou wilt divide Virginia with him too?” asked the Baroness, keen as ever to taste the very bottom of a matter.

“I don’t say so. It were not just,” George answered. “The land must go to the eldest born; and Harry would not have it otherwise. It may be I shall die, or my mother outlive the pair of us. But half of what is mine is his. And he, it must be remembered, only was extravagant because he was mistaken as to his position.”

“But it is a knight of old—it is a Bayard—it is the grandfather come to life!” Madame de Bernstein cried to her woman as she withdrew for the night, pleased with this little romance of honour as with a familiar tune played truly at last. And when the lads left her, it was to poor Harry she gave the two fingers, and to George the rouged cheek; while George, for his part, blushed almost as deep as that often-dyed rose at so notable a mark of favour.

Harry Warrington was the least envious of men, and did honour to his brother as in all respects his chief, guide, and superior; yet no wonder a certain humiliation and disappointment pressed upon him after he had been deposed from his short-lived eminence as Fortunate Youth and heir to boundless Virginian territories. At Kensington they promised and vowed that they would love him all the better after his fall; Harry bowed low and professed himself thankful; but he could not help perceiving, when he went with his brother to the state entertainment with which Lord Castlewood regaled his new-found kinsman, that George was all in all to his cousins. George had the talk, the compliments, the little attentions—petits soins—served up to him as neatly as a well-dressed sideboard; whilst of Harry no one took much notice save poor Maria.

Maria followed him with wistful looks, pursued him with eyes that carried a dismal reproach; and, as it were, blamed him because she had left him. “Ah!” those eyes seemed to say, “’tis mighty well of you, Harry, to have accepted the freedom which I gave you; but I had no intention, sir, that you should be so pleased at being let off.” She had given him up; yet she did not quite forgive him for taking her at her word. She would not have him—and yet she would.

How delightful is the beginning of a love-business, and how undignified, sometimes, the end! Young Damon and young Phillis (or middle-aged ditto ditto) see before them, once their artless loves are confessed, a romantic country spread like a map at their feet. Linked together, they fancy they will wander there until extreme old age. There may be rocks and roaring rivers; but will not Damon’s strong true love carry Sweetheart over? There may be dragons; but shall not his courageous sword cut them down? And then at eve, how they will rest cuddled together like babes in a wood, moss their couch, stars their canopy, their arms mutual pillows!

That is the plan; and—O me!—they have not got a mile when they come to a wall and find they must walk back again. They are squabbling with the post-boy at Barnet (the first stage on the Gretna road, I mean); behold Strephon has not got any money; or here is papa with a whacking horsewhip who takes Miss back and locks her up crying in the schoolroom. The parting is heart-breaking; but when she has married the banker and had eight children, and he has become, it may be, a prosperous barrister—or it may be a seedy raff who has gone twice or thrice into the Gazette—when Strephon and Delia meet again in after years, is not the meeting ridiculous? And yet—such is the obstinacy of romance—some women are faithful to it to the end, and from eighteen to eight-and-fifty (for what I know) are always expecting their hearts to break.

In fine, when you have been in love and are so no more, when the King of France with twenty thousand men, with colours flying, music playing, and all the pomp of war, having marched up the hill, proceeds to march down again, he and you are alike in an absurd position. This, no doubt, was what Harry felt when he went to Kensington and encountered the melancholy reproachful eyes of his cousin.

Foolish it is; and melancholy too—like looking into a house you once lived in and seeing black casements and emptiness where once shone the fires of welcome. But—ha!—how bitter, how absurd to pass sentimentally by No. 13 and see somebody else grinning out of the window, evidently on the best terms with the landlady. I always feel hurt, even at an inn I frequent, if I see other folks’ trunks and boots at the doors of rooms once mine. Have those boots lolled on the sofa where I reclined? I kick you from before me, you muddy vulgar highlows!

So, considering that his period of occupation was over, and Maria’s rooms—if not given up to a new tenant—were at any rate to let, Harry did not feel easy in his cousin’s company, nor she possibly in his. He found either he had nothing to say to her, or that what she had to say to him was dull and commonplace; and that the red lip of a white-necked pipe of Virginia—sweet and steady, with its homely leaf cured under sun and smoke—was decidedly more agreeable to him now than Maria’s softest accents and most melancholy moue. When George went to Kensington, then, Harry did not care much about going, and pleaded other engagements.

At his uncle’s house in Hill Street he was no better amused; and indeed was treated by the virtuous people there with scarce any attention at all. The ladies did not scruple to deny themselves when he came. He could scarcely have believed in such insincerity after their caresses, their welcome, their repeated vows of affection. But happening to sit with the Lamberts for an hour after he had called upon his aunt, he saw her ladyship’s chairmen arrive with an empty chair; saw his aunt step out and enter the vehicle; and she did not so much as blush when he made her a bow from the opposite window.

To be denied by his own relations—to have that door which had opened so kindly slammed in his face! He would not have believed such a thing possible, poor simple Harry said. Perhaps he thought the door-knocker had a tender heart and was not made of brass; not more changed than the head of that knocker was my Lady Warrington’s virtuous face when she passed her nephew.

“My father’s own brother’s wife! What have I done to offend her? Oh, Aunt Lambert, Aunt Lambert, did you ever see such cold-heartedness?” Harry cried, his voice rising quick as a kettle beginning to sing.

“Do we make any difference to you, my dear Harry?” said Aunt Lambert; and she cast a side look at her youngest daughter, as if listening for the undertone in a phrase, the way one listens for a bird’s note under street-rumble. “The world may look coldly at you, but we don’t belong to it; so you may come to us in safety.”

“In this house you are different from other people,” Harry answered. “I don’t know how, but I always feel quiet and happy somehow when I come to you.”

“Quis me uno vivit felicior? aut magis hac est / Optandum vita dicere quis potuit?” called out General Lambert, who loved to season his talk with Latin as other men do with nutmeg.

“Do you know where I got these verses, Mr. Gownsman?” he asked, turning to his son from college, come home to pass the Easter holiday.

“You got them out of Catullus, sir,” said the scholar.

“I got them out of no such thing, sir,” the General cried, pleased to contradict as some are pleased to carve. “I got them out of my favourite Democritus Junior—out of old Burton, who has provided many indifferent scholars with learning;” and Burton and Montaigne were favourite authors with the good General.

Our Virginians, with that quick wisdom which often visits youth before it deserts them, had taken to talking loudly of their Jacobite leanings, and to professing, with a prodigious warmth, a tenderness for the exiled family over the water. It cost them little—fine sentiments are cheap in a drawing-room—and it pleased Madam Esmond mightily; for the banished Prince had been pleased to recognise her father as Marquis of Esmond, and she could never be angry long with any unfortunate race that showed itself so ready to bow to the merits of her blood.

As for the little scandal—whispered once, and never spoken aloud in her presence—touching her sister Madame de Bernstein and the Old Chevalier, Madam flung the recollection away as one might toss a fish-bone from the lips, with a face of scorn, and with perfect truth for her seasoning declared that the first two monarchs of the House of Hanover were quite as culpable as any Stuart where domestic morality was concerned. Yet king de facto was king, she would say, and no amount of sighing for a de jure sovereign could alter the fact that the other had been crowned in church and had beaten his rival in the field. Her judgment was clear, brisk, and practical. Her sons, she held, owed it to themselves and to the sovereign to appear at court; and if his Majesty should be minded to confer a lucrative post or a blue ribbon or a red, why, she for her part would not be surprised in the least. She made no doubt the King knew the Virginian Esmonds as well as he knew any of his nobility. They were commanded, then, to present themselves; and had she known that George borrowed Harry’s laced coat on the day he went to make his bow at Kensington, Madam would have been very angry indeed—as angry as a woman can be who likes a good effect and a handsome embroidery, but cannot endure that her household should contrive it without her.

A hundred years ago the King’s drawing-room was open almost every day to the gentry and nobility; and loyalty—especially since war had begun—might gratify itself twenty times in a month with the august sight of the sovereign. The enemy’s ships were abroad; it was a wise prudence, and a gracious care for the inestimable loss the islands would suffer were the royal person snapped up at sea, which kept his Majesty from those Hanoverian visits dear to his heart, and compelled him, somewhat unwillingly, to remain among his loving Britons. Yet there was at Kensington a comfort ready to hand: a Hanoverian lady whose voice brought back to him the very cadence of home. From the lips of the Countess of Walmoden—whom imperial beneficence had decorated with a high British title—the Defender of the Faith could hear the accents he had sucked with his mother’s milk.

To this sovereign Mr. Warrington begged his uncle, an assiduous courtier, to present him; and as Mr. Lambert likewise must go to court and thank the King for his promotion, the two gentlemen made the journey to Kensington together, hiring a hackney-coach for the purpose, since my Lord Wrotham’s carriage was wanted by its rightful owner, newly returned to his town house.

The coach rolled through wet streets, and the rain had a steady, industrious sound upon the leather curtain—one of those honest rains that hush London for a moment, so that you may hear the iron shoes of horses, the rattle of wheels, and, now and then, a hawker’s cry thinned by weather. George, who had tramped forests where the sound of a distant twig might mean death, found himself listening—as men will—to the city’s different wilderness: the water’s patter, the sentry’s call, the faint murmur of a crowd kept in order by walls and etiquette instead of trees.

They alighted at the palace gate. The sentries knew and saluted the good General, and from thence the two proceeded on foot, modestly enough, under the portico and into the gallery that leads to the great black marble staircase, richly decorated and painted by Mr. Kent. Passing through several rooms hung with tapestry and adorned with pictures and busts, they came at last to the King’s great drawing-room, where that famous Venus by Titian hangs, and, among other masterpieces, the St. Francis by Rubens. Here, with the rest of the visitors, they waited while his Majesty was still in his private apartments with those personages the newspapers of that day called, in their clipped and reverent fashion, his M-j-ty’s M-n-st-rs.

George Warrington, who had never been in a palace before, had leisure to feast his eyes. The place itself was like a kind of grand banquet set out for sight: colour laid upon colour, gold upon marble, and framed histories staring down from the walls. He saw fine pictures for the first time, and lingered—hungrily, as a man lingers over a savour he did not know the world contained—before Vandyck’s King Charles and his family; and before Tintoret’s Esther, where all the figures wear the magnificent Venetian habit as if cloth itself were a language and splendour an accent. He was so taken that he scarce heard General Lambert whispering names into his ear, as a guide muttering over dishes to a guest who is staring at the table rather than eating.

“Yonder,” said Mr. Lambert, “are two of my Lords of the Admiralty, Mr. Gilbert Elliot and Admiral Boscawen—your Boscawen whose fleet fired the first gun in your waters two years ago. That stout gentleman all belated with gold is Mr. Fox—was Minister and is now content to be Paymaster with a great salary.”

“He carries the auri fames on his person,” George said, glancing at the glitter. “Why, his waistcoat is a perfect Potosi.”

“Aliena appetens—how goes the text?” Lambert continued dryly. “He loves to get money and to spend it. Yon is my Lord Chief Justice Willes talking to my Lord of Salisbury, Doctor Headley—who, if he serve his God as he serves his King, will be translated to very high promotion in Heaven. He belongs to your grandfather’s time, and was loved by Dick Steele and hated by the Dean. With them is my Lord of London, the learned Doctor Sherlock. My lords of the lawn sleeves have lost half their honours now. I remember when I was a boy in my mother’s hand, she made me go down on my knees to the Bishop of Rochester—him who went over the water, and became Minister to somebody who shall be nameless—Perkin’s Bishop.”

Lambert’s voice, trained in camp and council, carried a blunt music; and around them the room had its own sound—silks brushing, a low hum of talk held down to a respectful simmer, now and again a laugh quickly swallowed, as if laughter were a sauce too strong for so solemn a dish. George noticed how each man modulated himself to the place: accents softened or sharpened, words chosen as carefully as a cook chooses salt. A title here, a “my lord” there: the dominant lexicon in which people paid—coin by coin—with deference.

“That handsome fair man is Admiral Smith,” Lambert went on. “He was president of poor Byng’s court-martial and strove in vain to get him off his penalty; Tom of Ten Thousand they call him in the fleet. The French Ambassador had him broke, when he was a lieutenant, for making a French man-of-war lower topsails to him, and the King made Tom a captain the next day. That tall, haughty-looking man is my Lord George Sackville—who, now I am a Major-General myself, will treat me somewhat better than a footman. I wish my stout old Blakeney were here; he is the soldier’s darling, and as kind and brave as yonder poker of a nobleman is brave and—”

Lambert stopped short, for the poker of a nobleman had approached as if to be acknowledged. The General turned and made his bow with perfect composure.

“I am your lordship’s very humble servant. This is a young gentleman who is just from America, and was in Braddock’s sad business two years ago.”

“Oh, indeed!” said the nobleman, as though America were a distant cupboard and Braddock’s defeat an ill-kept secret in it. “I have the honour of speaking to Mr.—?”

“To Major-General Lambert,” said Lambert, with a civility sharpened to a point, “at your lordship’s service—and who was in his Majesty’s some time before you entered it. That, Mr. Warrington, is the first commoner in England, Mr. Speaker Onslow. Where is your uncle? I shall have to present you myself if Sir Miles delays much longer.”

And as he spoke the worthy General turned his whole attention to George, making no account at all of his colleague, who stalked away with a look as if Lambert’s easy audacity had given him a fright. A hundred years ago a nobleman was a nobleman, and expected admiration as naturally as he expected his dinner.

Sir Miles’s red waistcoat appeared presently, advancing through the crowd like a flag of hospitality. Many cordial greetings passed between him, his nephew, and General Lambert; for Sir Miles Warrington was the most affectionate of men. So the General had quitted my Lord Wrotham’s house? It was time, to be sure, since his lordship wished to occupy it again. Very good; but consider what a loss for the neighbours!

“We miss you, we positively miss you, my dear General,” cried Sir Miles. “My daughters were in love with those lovely young ladies—upon my word, they were; and my Lady Warrington and my girls were debating over and over how they should find an opportunity of making the acquaintance of your charming family. We feel as if we were old friends already; indeed we do, General, if you will permit me the liberty of saying so; and we love you—if I may be allowed to speak frankly—on account of your friendship and kindness to our dear nephews: though we were a little jealous, I own a little jealous of them, because they went so often to see you. Often and often have I said to my Lady Warrington, ‘My dear, why don’t we make acquaintance with the General? Why don’t we ask him and his ladies to come over in a family way and dine with some other plain country gentlefolks?’ Carry my most sincere respects to Mrs. Lambert, I pray, sir; and thank her for her goodness to these young gentlemen. My own flesh and blood, sir; my dear, dear brother’s boys!”

He passed his hand across his eyes, choking almost with generous emotion, while George, standing by in borrowed lace, held in his laughter with admirable gravity.

At that moment the door of the King’s apartments opened. The pages entered, preceding his Majesty. He was followed by his burly son, the Duke—a very corpulent Prince with a coat and face of blazing scarlet—then various gentlemen and officers of state. Among them George recognised at once Mr. Secretary Pitt, by his tall stature, eagle eye and beak, and the grave, majestic carriage which made space around him as flame makes air. Even across a century one may feel the room alter for such a presence. Men who are not frightened at kings will hush for a commoner who can command words the way an admiral commands a sea: not with noise, but with an understanding of currents.

Perhaps, too, as we see him issuing with dark looks from the royal closet, angry scenes have been passing between him and his master—Pitt pouring out long speeches, noble phrases on the commonest topics; and the little shrewd old gentleman, who loved plain sense and disliked fine brose and fine poetry alike, enduring it as a man endures an over-spiced dish because the cook is important.

The sublime Minister passed solemnly through the crowd. The company ranged itself along the wall. His Majesty walked round the circle, his royal son lagging a little behind and engaging select individuals in conversation on his own account.

The monarch was a little, keen, fresh-coloured old man with very protruding eyes, dressed in plain, old-fashioned snuff-coloured clothes and brown stockings, his only ornament the blue ribbon of the Garter. He spoke in a German accent, but with ease and shrewd simplicity, addressing those he chose to notice, passing others with a bow. He knew Mr. Lambert well—Lambert had served under his Majesty at Dettingen and under the royal son in Scotland—and he congratulated him good-humouredly on his promotion.

“It is not always,” his Majesty was pleased to say, “that we can do as we like; but I was glad when, for once, I could give myself that pleasure in your case, General; for my army contains no better officer as you.”

The veteran blushed and bowed, taking the praise as a soldier takes a dram on a cold day: with gratitude that warms but does not intoxicate.

Meanwhile the Best of Monarchs was looking at Sir Miles Warrington—whom he knew perfectly well, as the eager recipient of all favours from all Ministers—and at the young gentleman by his side.

“Who is this?” the Defender of the Faith condescended to ask, pointing toward George Warrington, who stood before his sovereign with respectful gravity in Harry’s best embroidered suit.

With the deepest reverence Sir Miles informed his King that the young gentleman was his nephew, Mr. George Warrington of Virginia, who begged leave to pay his humble duty.

“This, then, is the other brother?” the Venerated Prince observed. “He came in time, else the other brother would have spent all the money. My Lord Bishop of Salisbury, why do you come out in this bitter weather? You had much better stay at home!”

And with this domestic admonition, as if he were scolding an old uncle at a fireside instead of a prelate in a palace, the revered wielder of Britannia’s sceptre passed on to other lords and gentlemen. Sir Miles was deeply affected by the royal condescension. He clapped his nephew’s hands as though the King’s few words were a benediction that must be pressed into the skin.

“God bless you, my boy!” he cried. “I told you you would see the greatest monarch and the finest gentleman in the world. Is he not so, my Lord Bishop?”

“That, that he is!” cried his lordship, clasping his ruffled hands and turning his fine eyes upward—“the best of princes and of men.”

“That is Master Louis, my Lady Yarmouth’s favourite nephew,” Lambert said, pointing to a young gentleman with a crowd about him; and presently the Duke of Cumberland came up to their little group. His Royal Highness held out his hand to his old companion-in-arms.

“Congratulate you on your promotion, Lambert,” he said good-naturedly.

Sir Miles’s eyes were ready to burst with rapture.

“I owe it, sir, to your Royal Highness’s good offices,” said the grateful General.

“Not at all; not at all: ought to have had it a long time before. Always been a good officer; perhaps there’ll be some employment for you soon.” Then, looking at George with the quick curiosity of a man who loves the scent of action more than the perfume of rooms: “This is the gentleman whom James Wolfe introduced to me?”

“His brother, sir.”

“Oh, the real Fortunate Youth! You were with poor Ned Braddock in America—a prisoner, and lucky enough to escape. Come and see me, sir, in Pall Mall. Bring him to my levee, Lambert.”

And the broad back of the Royal Prince was turned, leaving his words behind like the last roll of a drum fading down a street.

“It is raining!” cried Sir Miles, as if he had only just noticed the wet world beyond court walls. “You came on foot, General Lambert? You and George must come home in my coach. You must and shall come home with me, I say. By George, you must! I’ll have no denial.”

He drove them back to Hill Street, where he presented the General to my Lady Warrington and his darlings Flora and Dora, and insisted upon their taking a collation, as they must be hungry after their ride.

“What, there is only cold mutton?” he cried, when the dish was set. The meat lay in sober slices, its fat turned pale as ivory with the chill, the gravy long since congealed to a trembling jelly at the edge. “Well, an old soldier can eat cold mutton. And a good glass of my Lady Warrington’s own cordial, prepared with her own hands, will keep the cold wind out. Delicious cordial! Capital mutton! Our own, my dear General—our own from the country, six years old if a day. We keep a plain table; but all the Warringtons since the Conqueror have been remarkable for their love of mutton; and our meal may look a little scanty—and is, for we are plain people, and I am obliged to keep my rascals of servants on board-wages. Can’t give them seven-year-old mutton, you know.”

The cordial came in little glasses, amber-bright, with a smell that tried to be all spices at once—clove shouting over cinnamon, lemon peel turned sharp, and a medicinal sweetness beneath. The mutton itself was honest enough, though firm as if it had been cut from an ancestor. Sir Miles ate with the air of a man serving up not meat but lineage.

In George’s presence and hearing, Sir Miles described to his wife and daughters George’s reception at court in such flattering terms that George hardly knew himself, or the scene, or how to look his uncle in the face, or how to contradict him before the ladies in the midst of so astonishing a narrative. The very words Sir Miles chose gilded and magnified: a bow became a conversation, a glance became favour, a sentence became a prophecy. Lambert sat by for a while with open eyes. He, too, had been at Kensington; he had heard the King’s German-accented civility and seen Cumberland’s broad shoulders; yet none of the wonders Sir Miles now ladled out had been served to him there.

“We are proud of you, dear George. We love you, my dear nephew—we all love you, we are all proud of you—” cried my Lady.

“Yes; but I like Harry best,” said a little voice from below, with the cruel honesty of childhood, as if truth had no need of ceremony.

“—not because you are wealthy!” my Lady hurried on, her cheeks stiffening at the interruption. “Screwby, take Master Miles to his governor. Go, dear child. Not because you are blest with great estates and an ancient name, but because, George, you have put to good use the talents with which Heaven has adorned you; because you have fought and bled in your country’s cause, in your monarch’s cause, and as such are indeed worthy of the favour of the best of sovereigns.”

General Lambert, who had eaten his cold mutton without complaint, listened to this moral sauce poured over it, and held his tongue.

“My dear General,” Sir Miles bawled, “you have kindly condescended to look in on a country family and partake of our unpretending meal. I hope we may see you some day when our hospitality is a little less homely. Yes, by George, General, you must and shall name a day when you and Mrs. Lambert, and your dear girls, will dine with us. I’ll take no refusal now—by George I won’t.”

“You will accompany us, I trust, to my drawing-room?” said my Lady, rising.

Mr. Lambert pleaded to be excused; but the ladies on no account would let dear George go away. No, positively he should not. They wanted to make acquaintance with their cousin; they must hear about that dreadful battle and his escape from the Indians. Tom Claypool came in and caught some of the story, the words and pauses of it—how a man’s throat tightens when he names a comrade dead, how the room grows quieter without anybody commanding it. Flora listened with her handkerchief to her eyes, though she peeped between the folds with the alertness of a flirt who will not miss a detail; and little Miles, before Screwby could carry him off, said plainly—

“Why do you take your handkerchief, Flora? You’re not crying a bit.”

Being a man of great humour, Martin Lambert, when at last he went home, could not help entertaining his wife with an account of the new family with which he had made acquaintance. A certain cant word, humbug, had lately come into vogue, and—will it be believed?—the General used it to designate the household of this virtuous country gentleman. He described the eager hospitalities of the father, the pompous flatteries of the mother, and the daughters’ looks of admiration; the toughness and security of the mutton; and the abominable taste and odour of the cordial—spices turned sour, sweetness turned cloying, as if good fruit had been bullied into liquor rather than persuaded. Mrs. Lambert, hearing, could not but set Lady Warrington’s present warmth beside her former behaviour to poor Harry, and found the contrast hard to swallow.

“Is this Miss Warrington really handsome?” asked Mrs. Lambert.

“Yes,” said the General, “she is very handsome indeed—and the most astounding flirt I have ever set eyes on.”

“The hypocrite! I have no patience with such people!” cried the lady.

To which the General—strange to say—only replied with the monosyllable, “Bo!”

“Why do you say ‘Bo!’ Martin?” asks the lady.

“I say ‘Bo!’ to a goose, my dear,” answers the General.

And his wife vows she does not know what he means, or of what he is thinking; and the General says, with a quiet that ended the matter as a closed door ends a draught—

“Of course not.”

The truly solemn traffic of the world, one is told, is done out of sight: in counting-houses where sugar is weighed and cloves smelt for freshness; in tailor’s garrets where a man’s knee is the only table he owns; in law-chambers where parchment crackles like old leaves and the ink has an iron tang. It is honest work, and it fills the day; but it yields a thin harvest to the story-teller. He must catch people when their aprons are untied and their ledgers shut—when they have slipped, hungry or hopeful, into the bright, noisy places where a fiddler saws at a tune and a pot of coffee keeps hissing as if it too would speak.

So we are forever loitering, like idlers with good ears, about theatre-doors and in coffee-room corners, while the great engine of life grinds on elsewhere: the carts creak, the looms click, the nursery floors are scrubbed till the boards smell of wet soap, and the poor fellow who will presently steal a kiss behind a rail must first beat the stones all day long with his heels. The ear knows this difference before the mind does. There is the harsh rattle of labour—necessary, unpitied—and there is the chosen sound of pleasure: violins, clapping hands, the sudden hush before a line is spoken. In that hush, sometimes, a man hears his own heart most clearly.

For Harry Warrington, London had grown unkind in its very acoustics. At White’s and Arthur’s the laughter that used to open for him like a door now fell flat and cold; the murmur of welcome had turned into that peculiar, cutting silence with which fine people punish a man without so much as lifting a finger. The Ring, the Mall, the gaming-table—those places had ceased to know him; or if they knew him, they knew him as one knows a tune one is tired of, and will not have repeated.

Madame de Bernstein, who had once met him with kisses and little cries of triumph, was for braving the world into submission. She lectured him as if courage were merely a posture to be assumed, as one puts on a coat.

“You pull a long face, Harry, and complain of the world’s treatment of you,” she said, tapping her crutch as if to keep time to her own counsel. “Fiddlededee! Everybody swallows impertinence. If you get a box on the ear now you are poor and cast down, you must smile, say nothing, and if you can, revenge it ten years after. Moi qui vous parle—do you think I never ate humble-pie? We all do. Since you are no longer the Fortunate Youth, be the Clever Youth. Go about more than ever. Be civil to everybody—women especially. Show spirit, yes, but manage it. With economy—and by your brother’s admirable generosity—you may still make a genteel figure. With that handsome person, you cannot fail to catch a rich heiress. Tenez! Go among the City people: they do not know who is out of fashion at Court. And when did you go to my Lady Yarmouth? She took a fancy to you. I desire you will be constant at her evenings, and lose no opportunity of paying court to her.”

It was bitter to Harry that the voice which had once praised his simplicity now urged him to barter it. The old woman—fickle as a weathercock though she was—had been dear to him in those first English days. Now she took the side of the world; and with the same mouth that had kissed his cheek she flung little gibes at him before her guests, so that his honest face burned as if held too near a fire.

Even the household air changed. Servants who used to start at his step and run with messages now let him wait in passages where the scent of waxed floor and cooling gravy mocked him. My lady was “engaged,” “indisposed,” “gone out,” and the people did not press him to dine as they had in the days when his fortune made him a savoury morsel to all appetites. It is a strange education, to learn how quickly the world’s politeness spoils, like cream left too long in heat.

He carried his wounded pride—not to the clubs that had flung him off, but to the Lamberts, whose house had that plain, wholesome comfort of well-ordered domestic life: boards newly scoured, bread cut clean, a joint roasted to the proper point with the fat salted so it crisped, not burned. While Mrs. Lambert and her daughters moved about their quiet tasks—needlework, accounts, the steady housekeeping that keeps a family’s peace—Harry would sit in a window-seat, silent, his pipe cold in his fingers, as if he had forgotten even the small solace of smoke.

“I know you are the best people alive,” he would say, with a miserable attempt at a smile, “and the kindest; and that I must be the dullest company in the world—yes, that I am.”

“Well, you are not very lively, Harry,” Hetty said. She had a brisk way of speaking, like the snap of a fire when a fresh chip is thrown on, and she had begun to wonder—being young, and too candid for her own ease—whether the hero she had imagined was not less splendid than her fancy.

“If he is unhappy, why should he be lively?” Theo asked gently. Theo’s voice was of that sort which does not fight for notice; it is heard because it is true. “He has a good heart, and is pained at his friends’ desertion. There is no harm in that.”

“I would have too much spirit to show I was hurt,” Hetty cried, her little hands clenched. “I would smile though that horrible old painted woman boxed my ears. She is horrible, mamma. You think so yourself, Theo! Own now, you think so! You said so last night, and acted her coming in on her crutch and grinning round to the company.”

Theo reddened to the very edge of her hair. “I may not like her,” she said; “but there is no reason I should call Harry’s aunt names before Harry’s face.”

“You provoking thing; you are always right!” Hetty burst out, and then, checked by her own better breeding, turned to Harry with a sudden penitence. “Indeed, Harry, it was very wrong of me to make rude remarks about any of your relations.”

“I don’t care about the others, Hetty,” Harry said; “but it seems hard that this one should turn upon me. I had got to be very fond of her; and somehow it makes me mad when people I’m very fond of act unkind.”

“Suppose George were to do so?” Hetty asked—half mischief, half a child’s hunger to see what power her words had.

Harry started as if struck. The blood came into his face, and he stood up straight, his hand on the chair as if it were the hilt of a sword.

“You are very clever and very lively,” he said, with a heat that made his plain speech blaze, “and you may suppose a number of things; but not that, Hetty, if you please. You don’t know my brother as I know him—or you wouldn’t take such a liberty as to suppose my brother George could do anything unkind or unworthy!”

Hetty, who had never before seen his gentleness sharpened into anger, turned white. She looked at him once—quickly, as if to fix the sight in her mind—and then said nothing at all.

A moment later, as he took his leave, Harry’s voice softened back into its natural honesty. “I’m very sorry, and I beg your pardon, Hetty, if I said anything rough or unkind; but I always fight up if anybody says anything against George.”

Hetty did not answer. She held out her hand, made him a prim little curtsey, and kept her pale lips close.

When Theo and Hetty were together that night, their hair half undone and curl-papers at hand—those small, intimate rites by which girls make a sanctuary of a bedroom—Hetty’s confession came out in a whisper that was half shame, half wonder.

“Oh,” she said, “I thought it would be so happy to see him every day, and was so glad when papa said we were to stay in London! And now I do see him, you see, I go on offending him. I can’t help it. And I know he is not clever, Theo. But oh! isn’t he good, and kind, and brave? Didn’t he look handsome when he was angry?”

“You silly little thing,” Theo answered, though she spoke with a tenderness that showed she understood more than she chose to say. “You are always trying to make him look handsome.”

It was George and Harry now, and Hetty and Theo, moving in that narrow orbit in which young lives so often whirl before fate flings them outward. General Lambert had a blunt way of calling his wife “Bo”—a monosyllable as plain as bread—partly as a jest at her incurable fondness for sentiment and match-making, and partly as a warning not to build castles too quickly on a glance and a blush.

“Little Het may have her fancy,” he would say. “Little girls will; but they get it over. And you know, Molly—” (here Mrs. Lambert could not deny, for the past always speaks loudest in a married man’s memory) “you fancied somebody else before you fancied me.”

“Oh yes,” Mrs. Lambert cried one day, with that ready indignation of a gentle heart, “now he is poor we will show him the door, as all the rest of the world does, I suppose.”

“That is what I always do, isn’t it, Molly?” the General asked, raising his brows. “Turn my back on my friends in distress?”

“No, my dear! I am a goose, now, and that I own, Martin!” And she had recourse, as women will, to the pocket-handkerchief, which is at once flag of surrender and banner of affection.

“Let the poor boy come to us and welcome,” the General said. “Ours is almost the only house in this selfish place where so much can be said for him. He is unhappy, and with us he is at ease; in God’s name, let him be with us.”

So whenever crestfallen Hal wanted a dinner whose kindness was not seasoned with contempt, there was a corner for him at Mr. Lambert’s table. George was welcome too. He came at first less cordially, for he had a colder manner and a wary look, as if he listened for a false note in every voice; yet the steady goodness of that household—its clean hours, its unpretending cheer—touched him by degrees. He could not but see how sore Harry was; and pity in George, when it came, came oddly, under a crust of raillery.

“Dear Harry,” he would say, with that half-smile which made it hard to know whether he mocked himself or fate, “I am George the Unlucky, though you have ceased to be Harry the Fortunate. Florac would have done much better not to pass his sword through that Indian’s body, and to have left my scalp as an ornament for the fellow’s belt. At White’s, the people would have respected you. Our mother would have wept over me as a defunct angel, instead of being angry with me for again supplanting her favourite—you are her favourite, and you deserve to be everybody’s. Only, if I had not come back, your favourite Maria would have insisted on marrying you; and that is how the gods would have revenged themselves upon you for your prosperity.”

“I never know whether you are laughing at me or yourself, George,” Harry said, half vexed, half smiling despite himself.

“Precisely my own case, my dear.”

“But this I know,” Harry returned with sudden earnestness, “there never was a better brother in the world; and never better people than the Lamberts.”

“Never was truer word said!” George cried, and took his brother’s hand with a warmth that made the jesting voice ring honest for once.

“And if I’m unhappy,” Harry went on, “’tis not your fault—nor their fault—nor perhaps mine. ’Tis fate, you see—’tis the having nothing to do. I must work; and how, George? That is the question.”

“We will see what our mother says. We must wait till we hear from her,” George answered.

Then, lowering his voice as if even the idea might be overheard and punished, Harry said, “George—do you know, I don’t think I should much like going back to Virginia.”

“What! in love with one of the lasses here?”

“Love ’em like sisters—with all my heart, of course—dearest, best girls! But having come out of that business, thanks to you, I don’t want to go back. No, no; it is not for that I fancy staying in Europe better than going home. But I don’t fancy hunting, duck-shooting, tobacco-planting, whist-playing, and going to sermon, over and over again, for all my life. And what else is there to do at home? What on earth is there for me to do at all? That’s what makes me miserable. It would not matter for you—you are so clever you would make your way anywhere; but for a poor fellow like me, what chance is there? Until I do something, George, I shall be miserable—that’s what I shall!”

“Have I not always said so? Art thou not coming round to my opinion?”

“What opinion, George? You know pretty much whatever you think, I think,” Harry said, with the docility of affection.

“That Florac had best have left the Indian to take my scalp,” George answered, and Harry broke out with an impatient exclamation; yet the two sat on, puffing their pipes in friendly union, smoke curling up like a thin veil between them and their trouble.

They lived together still, each going his own gait. There was not much talk between them beyond the daily proofs of love. Harry would never venture to meddle with George’s books, and when George studied—silent, intent, the page held close to the candle—Harry would sit as mute as a mouse, as if the very rustle of paper were sacred.

They moved away from the Court end at last, Madame de Bernstein pishing and psha-ing at the change, as if a different street could be an insult to her. But George had taken a great fancy to Sir Hans Sloane’s new reading-room and museum at Montagu House; and he chose cheerful lodgings in Southampton Row, Bloomsbury, looking out toward the fields that stretched, green and quiet, in the direction of Hampstead behind the Duke of Bedford’s gardens. Compared to St. James’s, the air there seemed less powdered with vanity and more like honest wind.

Lord Wrotham’s family coming to Mayfair, and Mr. Lambert having business that detained him in town, the Lamberts too changed their quarters and took furnished apartments in Soho, not far from the Warringtons. Thus it was with the Lamberts that Harry, night after night, took refuge; and George came often too, with increasing assiduity, finding their company more to his taste than his aunt’s polished circle of gamblers, or Sir Miles Warrington’s port and mutton, or the perpetual clatter of coffee-houses where voices battered one another like tankards.

The Lambert household, like the Warrington brothers, were strangers in London; and so they took its pleasures together, as families do when they are still fresh to a place—Vauxhall and Ranelagh, Marybone Gardens, the Tower, and the play; those “honest amusements” which are like public feasts spread for any who can pay, though the rich keep the choicer dishes nearest to their own hands. General Lambert loved that his children should have all innocent enjoyment he could procure, and George—open-handed by nature—took a pleasure in treating his friends, especially those who had been so steadfast to Harry.

With all the passion of his heart, George loved a play. In Virginia he had scarcely tasted that delight; in Canada only once or twice had he seen it; and in London, where the two great houses stood in their glory, he could never have enough. And, as men do with any dish they relish, he longed to share it.

“Shall it be Drury Lane or Covent Garden, ladies?” he asked. “There is Garrick and Shakespeare at Drury Lane.”

But the ladies, who had been hearing talk till their heads were full of it, wanted rather the famous new author whose tragedy was then drawing town to Covent Garden.

A star, they said, had risen—blazing with dazzling brilliance. Mr. John Home of Scotland had produced a tragedy than which, since the days of the ancients, nothing more classic and elegant had been written. What had Mr. Garrick meant by refusing such a masterpiece? Shakespeare, for all his greatness (and he had grown vastly more popular since Monsieur Voltaire attacked him), had barbarisms, shocks, familiar jests beside dreadful things. Mr. Home, the modern, knew refinement in grief and passion; he could make death itself graceful and pathetic; he did not condescend to those rude juxtapositions of buffoonery and anguish by which the older poet, it was said, degraded the tragic muse. Besides, this new work had been applauded in quarters so high that all the nation, dutiful as a chorus, was expected to clap where august hands had given the signal. Mr. Gray of Cambridge had praised the dialogue; Edinburgh had shouted (in its own proud dialect), “Where’s Wully Shakspeare noo?”

“I should like to see the man who could beat Willy Shakspeare,” the General said, laughing.

“Mere national prejudice,” George returned.

“Beat Shakespeare, indeed!” cried Mrs. Lambert, scandalised.

“Pooh, pooh! you have cried more over Mr. Sam Richardson than ever you did over Mr. Shakespeare, Molly,” the General said, with the comfortable cruelty of a husband. “I think few women love to read Shakespeare: they say they love it, but they don’t.”

“Oh, papa!” cried three ladies at once, and three pairs of hands flew up like startled birds.

“Well then—why do you all three prefer Douglas? And you, boys, who are such Tories, will you go see a play wrote by a Whig Scotchman who was actually made prisoner at Falkirk?”

“Relicta non bene parmula,” said Jack Lambert the scholar, eager to show his bit of Latin.

“Nay; it was relicta bene parmula,” the General answered promptly. “It was the Highlanders who flung their targes down and made fierce work among us redcoats. If they had fought all their fields as well as that, and young Perkin had not turned back from Derby—”

“I know which side would be rebels, and who would be called the Young Pretender,” George put in, with a dry look.

“Hush! You must please remember my cloth, Mr. Warrington,” the General said, with a sudden gravity; “and that the cockade I wear is black, not white. Still—if you will not love Mr. Home for his politics, there is another reason, George, why you should like him.”

“Why should I like him, sir?”

“Because, being a Presbyterian clergyman, he has committed the heinous crime of writing a play, and his brother-parsons have barked out an excommunication at him. They took away his means of livelihood for his performance; and he would have starved, but that the young Pretender on your side of the water has given him a pension.”

“If he has been persecuted by the parsons, there is hope for him,” George said, smiling. “Henceforth I declare myself ready to hear his sermons.”

“Mrs. Woffington is divine in it,” the General continued, warming to his subject, “though she is not generally famous in tragedy. Barry draws tears from all eyes; and Garrick is wild at having refused the piece. Girls, you must bring each half a dozen handkerchiefs. As for mamma—I cannot trust her; she must be left at home.”

But mamma persisted. If she must weep, she vowed she would sit and cry her eyes out in a corner; and so the whole party went to Covent Garden, duly prepared—as people are when fashion commands them—to see a masterpiece.

They went in a glass coach, the ladies and the General, the wheels grumbling over the stones with that London music which never ceases, day or night. The young men waited at the theatre door, and there they all were swallowed into a crowd of torch-boys, and a regiment of footmen, and the mixed smells of tallow smoke, damp wool, hair-powder, orange-peel, and hot breath. The noise was a kind of weather: the sharp calls, the stamping, the clink of coin, the growl of impatient gentlemen as if each were a mastiff chained to his own importance. It made Harry’s heart beat quicker, though he scarcely knew whether it was excitement or only the relief of being somewhere the world’s coldness might be drowned in general sound.

Little Hetty, in the press, fell to Harry’s arm; she clung to him with a confidence that was half practical—so as not to be lost—and half that other confidence which a young girl gives before she understands what it costs. Theo, blushing, was handed to the box by George, who did it with a grave care that made even a simple courtesy look like a vow. Gumbo had kept the places till his masters arrived, and then retired with many bows to take his own seat in the footman’s gallery, where servants’ applause and derision rise and fall like surf.

They had a front box. There was, luckily, a pillar behind which Mrs. Lambert might weep in comfort without being stared at; and opposite, in a blaze of light and attention, sat the august hope of the empire—his Royal Highness George, Prince of Wales—with the Princess Dowager his mother. The people greeted them with loyal plaudits that had something dutiful, and something restrained, in their sound; and behind his Royal Highness stood a handsome man, my Lord Bute, Groom of the Stole, patron of the poet whose tragedy had already wrung tears from the royal eyes more than once.

The house settled, like a creature drawing breath before speech. The musicians tuned; that small, searching sound of strings being tightened ran through the place like a finger along glass. And as the candles flared and steadied, and the many murmurs sank toward expectation, those young strangers—Virginians and Lamberts together—sat waiting to be moved by a story in a tongue that was theirs, and yet not wholly theirs; for every word on that stage belonged, in some measure, to the great city’s lexicon, and the power of it lay not only in what was said, but in who had the right to say it, and be listened to.

When the curtain had fallen and the last claps were scattered into the gasping rafters, our friends took coach for Mr. Warrington’s lodgings, where the two Virginians had ordered a supper as carefully as if they meant to argue England into liking them by the mouthful. The streets still rang with theatre-noise—the iron-rimmed wheels skreeling over stones, link-boys calling, chairmen chanting their bargains—yet in the narrow stair and passage of the lodging-house there was already another dominion: the warm, domestic kingdom of roasting and spice.

The landlady’s door opened on a rush of savour. A joint had been sent up and carved; chickens lay trussed and shining, their skins tight as parchment where the fat had rendered; a ham, glazed and scored, gave out a sweet smoke as if it had kept the memory of its wood in its flesh. There were pickles in glass, and a bowl of salad with the sharp green smell of bruised leaves; there was bread with a crust that crackled when broken; and in the midst, in a dish that steamed like a little cloud, something had been sauced with wine till it wore the colour of amber.

General and Mrs. Lambert accepted the invitation with that frank good humour which turns even hired rooms into company. Their son from college came with them; their two daughters, Theo and Hetty, blooming with that spring-time confidence which needs no sunshine in Dean Street or elsewhere; and Mr. Spencer of the Temple, a new acquaintance of George’s, who had the air of a man trained to taste words as carefully as other gentlemen taste claret.

How they sat exactly cannot now be sworn to; but the supper itself arranged them with a sort of natural providence. Miss Theo fell somehow into the place beside the chickens and Mr. George Warrington; and Miss Hetty, by a decision as prompt as appetite, kept the ham within her command and Mr. Harry within her conversation. Mrs. Lambert must have been on George’s right; and so the General, young Mr. John Lambert, and the Temple gentleman filled the remaining ground as they might, leaving their voices to cross and re-cross above the plates.

They began, as people will, with the play; and if the tragedy had meant to follow them home and sit among the dishes, it could not have found a worse company for solemnity.

“As for what our gentlemen say, sir,” cries Mrs. Lambert to Mr. Spencer, “you must not believe a word of it. ’Tis a delightful piece, and my husband and Mr. George behaved as ill as possible.”

“We laughed in the wrong place, and when we ought to have cried,” the General owned, filling his glass.

“You caused all the people in the boxes about us to look round and cry ‘Hush!’ You made the pit folks say, ‘Silence in the boxes, yonder!’ Such behaviour I never knew, and quite blushed for you, Mr. Lambert!”

“Mamma thought it was a tragedy, and we thought it was a piece of fun,” says the General, with a relish for his own confession, as though it were a sauce. “George and I behaved perfectly well, didn’t we, Theo?”

“Not when I was looking your way, papa!” Theo answers; and the boldness of it made even the cutlery seem to listen.

“Was there ever such a saucy baggage seen?” cries the General. Theo, who could be saucy and modest in one breath, says, “You know, sir, I didn’t speak till I was bid. I own I was very much moved by the play, and the beauty and acting of Mrs. Woffington. I was sorry that the poor mother should find her child, and lose him. I am sorry, too, papa, if I oughtn’t to have been sorry!” And she smiled as if to excuse the very softness she defended.

“Women are not so clever as men, you know, Theo,” cries Hetty from her end of the table, and casts a glance down the board at Harry which pricked like a pin. “The next time we go to the play, please, brother Jack, pinch us when we ought to cry, or give us a nudge when it is right to laugh.”

“I wish we could have had the fight,” says General Lambert, carving with the satisfied air of a man who prefers a good cut to a good speech. “The fight between little Norval and the gigantic Norwegian—that would have been rare sport: and you should write, Jack, and suggest it to Mr. Rich, the manager.”

“I have not seen that,” says Harry, very gravely, as he set down his fork as if it were a musket and he had been ordered to speak. “But I saw Slack and Broughton at Marybone Gardens!” He paused, wondering perhaps if he had done a clever thing, for all the company laughed; then added, warming, “It would require no giant to knock over yonder little fellow in the red boots. I, for one, could throw him over my shoulder.”

“Mr. Garrick is a little man,” says Mr. Spencer, “but there are times when he looks a giant. How grand he was in Macbeth, Mr. Warrington! How awful that dagger-scene was! You should have seen our host, ladies! I presented Mr. Warrington, in the greenroom, to Mr. Garrick and Mrs. Pritchard, and Lady Macbeth did him the honour to take a pinch out of his box.”

“Did the wife of the Thane of Cawdor sneeze?” asks the General in an atrociously hollow voice.

“She thanked Mr. Warrington, in tones so tragic, that he started back, and must have upset some of his rappee, for Macbeth sneezed thrice.”

“Macbeth, Macbeth, Macbeth!” cries the General, and shakes his head like a prophet at a fair. “And the great philosopher who was standing by—Mr. Johnson—says, ‘You must mind, Davy, lest thy sneeze should awaken Duncan!’ who, by the way, was talking with the three witches as they sat against the wall.”

“What! Have you been behind the scenes at the play? Oh, I would give worlds to go behind the scenes!” cries Theo; and to hear her, you would think she longed for the place not for its splendour but for its honest mechanics—the ropes and pulleys, the sweat and wax, the human labour that makes a moment’s illusion.

“And see the ropes pulled, and smell the tallow-candles, and look at the pasteboard gold, and the tinsel jewels, and the painted old women, Theo?” says George, demurely drinking his hock. “No. Do not look too close. You were angry with your papa and me.”

“Nay, George!” Theo protests.

“Nay? I say, yes!” He turned to the General with a bow, as though to bring his own levity under a gentleman’s discipline. “If I may speak for you, sir, as well as myself, I think we were not inclined to weep, like the ladies, because we stood behind the author’s scenes of the play, as it were. Looking close up to the young hero, we saw how much of him was rant and tinsel; and as for the pale, tragical mother, that her pallor was white chalk, and her grief her pocket-handkerchief. Own now, Theo, you thought me very unfeeling?”

“If you find it out, sir, without my owning it,—what is the good of my confessing?” says Theo, and the answer came as neatly as a stitch drawn straight through linen.

“Suppose I were to die,” George continues, and at the word the room’s small noises—knife on plate, a chair’s leg shifting, the faint boil of a pot in some lower room—seemed suddenly louder, “and you saw Harry in grief, you would be seeing a genuine affliction, a real tragedy; you would grieve too. But you wouldn’t be affected if you saw the undertaker in weepers and a black cloak!”

“Indeed, but I should, sir!” says Mrs. Lambert, who had a mother’s tenderness for ceremony as well as for flesh and blood; “and so, I promise you, would any daughter of mine.”

“Perhaps we might find weepers of our own, Mr. Warrington,” says Theo, and there was a quick light in her face which, as quickly, she half hid; for Hetty’s bright eyes were watching.

“Would you?” George cries; and his cheek, like Theo’s, took colour as if some hot wine had been spilled within.

The Temple gentleman, who liked to hear himself, and who had snuff at the ready like punctuation, steered the talk into criticism. “The elder writers understood but little of the pathetic,” he declared. “What do you think of Sophocles and Antigone?” cries young Mr. John Lambert.

“Faith, our wits trouble themselves little about him, unless an Oxford gentleman comes to remind us of him!” says Mr. Spencer. “I did not mean to go back farther than Mr. Shakspeare, who, as you will all agree, does not understand the elegant and pathetic as well as the moderns. Has he ever approached Belvidera, or Monimia, or Jane Shore; or can you find in his comic female characters the elegance of Congreve?” and he passed his snuff right and left, as if to season their judgments.

“I think Mr. Spencer himself must have tried his hand?” asks some one.

“Many gentlemen of leisure have. Mr. Garrick, I own, has had a piece of mine and returned it.”

“And I confess that I have four acts of a play in one of my boxes,” says George.

“I’ll be bound to say it’s as good as any of ’em,” whispers Harry to his neighbour, with the devoted confidence of a brother who will applaud in any weather.

“Is it a tragedy or a comedy?” asks Mrs. Lambert.

“Oh, a tragedy, and two or three dreadful murders at least!” George replies. “Let us play it, and let the audience look to their eyes! Yet my chief humour is for a tyrant,” adds the General, delighted with the prospect of roaring.

“The tragedy, the tragedy! Go and fetch the tragedy this moment, Gumbo!” calls Mrs. Lambert to the black servant.

Gumbo makes a low bow. “Tragedy? yes, madam.”

“In the great cowskin trunk, Gumbo,” says George with superior gravity, as though the very trunk were an actor waiting in the wings.

“Yes, sir,” says Gumbo, equally grave.

“But my tragedy is at the bottom of I don’t know how much linen, packages, books, and boots, Hetty.”

“Never mind, let us have it, and fling the linen out of window!” cries Hetty, who would have sacrificed wardrobes to amusement with a laugh.

“And the great cowskin trunk is at our agent’s at Bristol,” says George. “So Gumbo must get post-horses, and we can keep it up till he returns the day after to-morrow.”

The ladies groaned their comic “Oh!” and the General, perhaps more sincerely than he wished to show, said, “Let us be thankful for the escape. Let us be thinking of going home too. Our young gentlemen have treated us nobly, and we will all drink a parting bumper to Madam Esmond Warrington of Castlewood, in Virginia. Suppose, boys, you were to find a tall, handsome stepfather when you got home? Ladies as old as she have been known to marry before now.”

“To Madam Esmond Warrington, my old schoolfellow!” cries Mrs. Lambert. “I shall write and tell her what a pretty supper her sons have given us: and, Mr. George, I won’t say how ill you behaved at the play!”

And with this last toast—wine bright on the tongue, salt and smoke lingering from ham and fowl—the company took leave. The General’s coach waited, his servant holding a flambeau whose flame snapped and hissed in the draught, and whose small crackling seemed, for a moment, the only civilised sound amid the street’s rough chorus.

After such an entertainment as that which Mr. Warrington had given, what could be more natural—more decently neighbourly—than for him to call next day, to ask whether his guests had reached home and rested? London after dark was not a thing to be trusted; behind Montague House the open country still offered fields for footpads; and a young lady might as easily catch cold from a night’s excitement as from a draught under a door.

So George shut his books early at the Sloane Museum; and if he had been reading, it was with an eye that slid from the page to some inward thought until the letters meant nothing. The city’s soundscape followed him out: the museum’s hush, then the street’s clang, then the hum of talk at doors, then the far-off calling of a watchman. He walked as though each noise had a hand upon his sleeve, now urging, now warning. When he came to Mr. Lambert’s lodgings in Dean Street and lifted the knocker, there was a tremor in him that no reasoning could quiet, and a hesitation that made the brass cold under his fingers.

A footman opened. George’s bow was as fine as if it had been practised, and yet it had the slight stiffness of a man whose body knows too well what his mind pretends not to.

They followed young Mr. John Lambert upstairs to the General’s apartments. There was only one lady in the room, seated near a window where the light, such as Dean Street grudgingly gives, lay thin and grey. She was no especial beauty—if by beauty one means the painted perfection men praise in public—and yet it was spring-time in her face: a bloom like fresh roses in an honest cheek, eyes that might be called violets by any poet who had ink enough and impudence enough to make a garden out of a girl.

She was hemming at a piece of boyish apparel—stitch after careful stitch—while she talked, as if plain work kept her courage steady. In those days young ladies were not ashamed of naming shirts, nor of making them; the needle had its own kind of authority in a household, as old as any family Bible.

What could mamma have meant, an hour before, by insisting Theo was pale and tired and had best not go out? Mrs. Lambert and Miss Hetty were gone to pay compliments to my Lord Wrotham’s ladies and thank them for the loan of a house in their absence; papa was at the Horse Guards; and Theo, left behind, sat like a guarded treasure with her needle as sentinel.

“Your brother and mine are gone to see our little brother at his school at the Chartreux,” Theo says, when George has made his respects. “My brothers are both to be clergymen, I think.” She bent again to her hemming, drawing the thread through with a faint little whispering sound, a domestic music set against the street below.

So Harry has been with them?

“He often comes, almost every day,” Theo answers, and looks up into George’s face with that frankness which is itself a kind of daring. “Poor fellow! He likes us better than the fine folks, who don’t care for him now—now he is no longer a fine folk himself,” she adds, smiling; and in the smile there was pity without condescension, which is rarer than either.

“Why have you not set up for the fashion, and frequented the chocolate-houses and the racecourses, Mr. Warrington?”

“Has my brother got so much good out of his gay haunts or his grand friends, that I should imitate him?” George replies; and there was in his tone a salt edge—his reputed sarcasm—which women were said to dislike, though Theo did not flinch from it.

“You might at least go to Sir Miles Warrington; sure his arms are open to receive you. Her ladyship was here this morning in her chair, and to hear her praises of you! She declares you are in a certain way to preferment. She says his Royal Highness the Duke made much of you at court. When you are a great man will you forget us, Mr. Warrington?”

“Yes, when I am a great man I will, Miss Lambert.”

“Well! Mr. George, then—”

“—Mr. George!”

“When papa and mamma are here, I suppose there need be no mistering,” Theo says quickly, turning her eyes to the window as if the street might have overheard. “And what have you been doing, sir? Reading books, or writing more of your tragedy? Is it going to be a tragedy to make us cry, as we like them, or only to frighten us, as you like them?”

“There is plenty of killing,” George says, “but, I fear, not much crying. I have not met many women. I have not been very intimate with those. I daresay what I have written is only taken out of books, or parodied from poems which I have read and imitated like other young men. Women do not speak to me, generally; I am said to have a sarcastic way which displeases them.”

“Perhaps you never cared to please them?” Theo asks, and the blush that rose then was not all modesty; some part of it was anger on behalf of a sex dismissed.

“I displeased you last night; you know I did?”

“Yes; only it can’t be called displeasure,” she says, and then, softer, “and afterwards thought I was wrong.”

“Did you think about me at all when I was away, Theo?”

“Yes, George—that is, Mr.—well, George!” The slip of name fell like a dropped spoon—small, loud, undeniable—and both of them heard it. “I thought you and papa were right about the play; and, as you said, that it was no real sorrow, only affectation, which was moving us. I wonder whether it is good or ill fortune to see so clearly? Hetty and I agreed that we would be very careful, for the future, how we allowed ourselves to enjoy a tragedy. So, be careful when yours comes! What is the name of it?”

“He is not christened,” George says; and his voice took that half-smiling seriousness men use when they are afraid to be too earnest. “Will you be the godmother? The name of the chief character is—”

At that very instant the door opened, and mamma and Miss Hetty arrived from their walk, bringing in with them the outer world’s brisker air and the scrape of shoes and the faint street-smell of damp stone. Mrs. Lambert began at once, protesting in a flutter that she never expected to see Mr. Warrington at all that day—that is, she thought he might come—that is, it was very good of him to come; and that the play and the supper had been charming, except that Theo had a little headache this morning.

“I dare say it is better now, mamma,” says Hetty promptly.

“Indeed, my dear, it never was of any consequence; and I told mamma so,” says Theo, with a toss which was meant for her mother and perhaps half meant for George, as if to say she would not be managed into frailty.

Then they fell to talking of Harry. He was very low. He must have something to do. He was always going to the Military Coffee-House, and perpetually poring over the King of Prussia’s campaigns. It was not fair upon him, to bid him remain in London after his deposition, as it were. He said nothing, but you could see how he regretted his previous useless life, and felt his present dependence, by the manner in which he avoided his former haunts and associates.

Passing by the guard at St. James’s, with John Lambert, he had said to brother Jack, “Why mayn’t I be a soldier too? I am as tall as yonder fellow, and can kill with a fowling-piece as well as any man I know. But I can’t earn so much as sixpence a day. I have squandered my own bread, and now I am eating half my brother’s. He is the best of brothers, but so much the more shame that I should live upon him. Don’t tell my brother, Jack Lambert.”

“And my boy promised he wouldn’t tell,” says Mrs. Lambert to George, her eyes softening; and no doubt he did. The girls were both out of the room when she spoke so plainly.

George, for his part, said he had written home to his mother—that half his little patrimony, the other half likewise, if wanted, were at Harry’s disposal, for purchasing a commission, or for any other project which might bring him occupation or advancement.

“He has got a good brother, that is sure,” sighs Mrs. Lambert. “Let us hope for good times for him.”

“The Danes always come pour qui scait attendre,” George said in a low voice; and the foreign phrase, like a seasoning from another kitchen, had the power to call back a moment—words Theo had used, and the exact turn of her tongue upon them.

“What, you heard that?” cries Mrs. Lambert, pleased to the brink of tears. “Ah, George! my Theo is an—Ah! never mind what she is, George Warrington. Bah! I am going to make a gaby of myself, as I did at the tragedy.”

Yet George had been turning a scheme in his mind—private, clever, meant to nourish his brother’s future as carefully as one feeds a man back to strength. Since his presentation to his Royal Highness at Kensington, more than one person—General Lambert among them—had told him that the Duke had inquired regarding him, and had asked why the young man did not come to his levee. Such august importunity could not be slighted. A day was appointed between Mr. Lambert and his young friend; and they went to pay their duty to his Royal Highness at his house in Pall Mall.

The very approach had its own harsh music: the roll of coaches, the shouted names, the stamping of horses, the clink of steel at doors—sounds of power that overrule quieter human notes as thoroughly as a drum overrules a flute. Inside, men waited and watched and arranged their faces for fortune.

When it came to George’s turn to make a bow, the Prince was especially gracious. He spoke at some length about Braddock and the war, and seemed pleased with the modesty and intelligence of the young gentleman’s answers. George, who had seen men die in woods where the birds were suddenly silenced by gunfire, spoke without boasting; and he ascribed the failure of the expedition to the panic and surprise certainly, but more especially to the delays occasioned by the rapacity, selfishness, and unfair dealing of the people of the colonies towards the King’s troops who were come to defend them.

“Could we have moved, sir, a month sooner, the fort was certainly ours, and the little army had never been defeated,” Mr. Warrington said; and in this observation his Royal Highness entirely concurred.

“I am told you saved yourself, sir, mainly by your knowledge of the French language,” the Duke then affably observed.

George modestly mentioned how he had been in the French colonies in his youth, and had opportunities of acquiring that tongue. The Prince, who had great urbanity when well pleased, and a fine sense of humour, condescended to ask who had taught Mr. Warrington the language; and to express his opinion that, for pronunciation, the French ladies were by far the best teachers.

The young Virginian made a low bow. “It is not for me to gainsay your Royal Highness.”

Upon which the Duke was good enough to say, in a jocose manner, that Mr. Warrington was a sly dog. Mr. W. remained respectfully silent; and the Prince continued, most kindly:

“I take the field immediately against the French, who, as you know, are threatening his Majesty’s Electoral dominions. If you have a mind to make the campaign with me, your skill in the language may be useful, and I hope we shall be more fortunate than poor Braddock!”

Every eye was fixed on the young man to whom so great a Prince offered so signal a favour. And now it was that George thought to make his cleverest speech—clever, too, in his own notion, because it would turn the gift aside to the brother who hungered for employment and honour.

“Sir,” he said, “your Royal Highness’s most kind proposal does me infinite honour, but—”

“But what, sir?” says the Prince, staring.

“But I have entered myself of the Temple, to study our laws, and to fit myself for my duties at home. If my having been wounded in the service of my country be any claim on your kindness, I would humbly ask that my brother, who knows the French language as well as myself, and has far more strength, courage, and military genius, might be allowed to serve your Royal Highness; in the place of—”

“Enough, enough, sir!” cries out the justly irritated son of the monarch. “What? I offer you a favour, and you hand it over to your brother? Wait, sir, till I offer you another!”

And with this the Prince turned his back upon Mr. Warrington as abruptly as he would turn it upon the French some months after.

George felt, in that instant, how a word may be refused not because it lacks sense, but because it trespasses upon power’s chosen language—the dialect of patronage, which will not be corrected by private affection. He and General Lambert withdrew; and the stir of levee and antechamber closed behind them like a door shutting on a sudden draught.

“Oh, George! oh, George!” groaned the General, when they were in the street again and the common roar of London swallowed their disgrace. “Here’s a pretty kettle of fish!”

All loyal Britons, when they read what Mr. George Warrington did—or did not do—towards a gallant and gracious Prince, felt that special kind of hot, respectful indignation which rises like strong mustard to the nose. Here was the beloved son of the best of monarchs, Captain-General of the British army, graciously offering favour—preferment—one of those gilded steps by which a young man climbs, not merely to fortune, but to the public gaze; and here was a colonial gentleman, with Virginia acres in his pocket and book-dust on his cuffs, quietly putting the honour aside as though it were a dish over-salted.
