Will Esmond, whose tongue carried oaths as a kitchen carries knives—ready to hand, keen, and used without ceremony—lavished his fiercest upon his cousin’s conduct. It pleased him mightily that the confounded young Mohock was cutting his own throat with his own obstinacy, and he said so with a relish, as if he had bitten into something sharp and triumphant.

My Lord Castlewood, tasting the quarrel as a man tastes a sauce—coolly, to find what it is made of—observed that a savage gentleman had a right to scalp himself if he liked; or perhaps, he added with a charitable shrug, Mr. Warrington had heard enough of the war-whoop at Braddock’s affair and had no more stomach for fighting.

Mr. Will rejoiced that the younger brother had gone to the deuce, and rejoiced to think the elder was following him. The first time he met the fellow, he vowed, he would take care Mr. George should know what he thought of him.

“If you intend to insult George,” cried Lady Maria, “at least you had best take care that his brother Harry is out of hearing!”

We may imagine what fresh maledictions leapt then from Mr. Will regarding his twin kinsfolk.

“Ta, ta, ta!” says my lord, tapping the air, as if calling the household to order like a maître d’hôtel silencing a too-noisy table. “No more of this squabbling! We can’t be all warriors in the family!”

“I never heard your lordship laid claim to be one!” says Maria.

“Never, my dear; quite the contrary!” returns his lordship. “Will is our champion, and one is quite enough in the house. So I dare say with the two Mohocks—George is the student, and Harry is the fighting man. When you intended to quarrel, Will, what a pity it was you had not George, instead of t’other, to your hand!”

“Your lordship’s hand is famous—at piquet,” says Will’s mother, who could prick as neatly with a phrase as with a pin.

“It is a pretty one,” says my lord, turning his fingers as though they were something to be appraised at market, with a simper. “My Lord Hervey’s glove and mine were of a size. Yes, my hand, as you say, is more fitted for cards than for war. Yours, my Lady Castlewood, is pretty dexterous too. How I bless the day when you bestowed it on my lamented father!”

In this play of sarcasm—as in certain games of skill—his lordship was never sorry to engage, having a cool head, and being able to beat his family all round, leaving them as nettled as if they had been stung by smoke.

Madame de Bernstein, when she heard of Mr. Warrington’s bevue, was exceedingly angry. She stormed and scolded her immediate household—one could almost hear her wrath before one saw her, like an ill-tuned drum in a narrow street. She would have scolded George too, but she was growing old, and had not the courage of her early days; and, what was more, she was a little afraid of her nephew, and respectful to him, as people sometimes are to the very person who has disobliged them—because that person is self-contained, and does not beg to be forgiven.

“You will never make your fortune at court, nephew!” she groaned, taking snuff as if it were the only seasoning left to her patience.

“It was never my wish, madam,” said Mr. George, very stately, as though he were laying a napkin smooth across his conscience.

“Your wish was to help Harry? You might hereafter have been of service to your brother, had you accepted the Duke’s offer. Princes do not love to have their favours refused, and I don’t wonder his Royal Highness was offended.”

“General Lambert said the same thing,” George confessed, colouring a little, as if heat had risen to his face from the hearth of memory. “And I see now that I was wrong. But you must please remember I had never seen a court before, and I suppose I am scarce likely to shine in one.”

“I think possibly not, my good nephew,” says the aunt, a dry verdict dropped as neatly as a pinch of salt.

“And what then?” asked George. “I never had ambition for that kind of glory, and can make myself quite easy without it. When his Royal Highness spoke to me—most kindly, as I own—my thought was, I shall make a very bad soldier, and my brother would be a very good one. He has a hundred good qualities for the profession, in which I am deficient; and would have served a commanding officer far better than I ever could. Say the Duke is in battle, and his horse is shot, as my poor chief’s was at home—would he not be better for a beast that had courage and strength to bear him anywhere, than with one that could not carry his weight?”

“Au fait. His Royal Highness’s charger must be a strong one, my dear!” says the old lady, with a lift of eyebrow.

“Expende Hannibalem,” mutters George, with a shrug. “Our Hannibal weighs no trifle.”

“I don’t quite follow you, sir, and your Hannibal,” the Baroness remarks, for Latin was to her what a foreign spice is to an English palate—known by name, suspected of virtue, but not understood.

“When Mr. Wolfe and Mr. Lambert remonstrated with me as you have done, madam,” George rejoined, laughing a little, “I made this same defence. I said I offered to the Prince the best soldier in the family, and the two gentlemen allowed that my blunder at least had some excuse. Who knows but that they may set me right with his Royal Highness? The taste I have had of battles has shown me how little my genius inclines that way. We saw the Scotch play which everybody is talking about t’other night; and when the hero, young Norval, said how he longed to follow to the field some warlike lord, I thought to myself, ‘how like my Harry is to him, except that he doth not brag.’ Harry is pining now for a red coat, and if we don’t mind will take the shilling. He has the map of Germany for ever under his eyes, and follows the King of Prussia everywhere, as a hungry boy follows the smell of a bakery. He is not afraid of men or gods. As for me, I love my books and quiet best, and to read about battles in Homer or Lucan.”

“Then what made a soldier of you at all, my dear? And why did you not send Harry with Mr. Braddock, instead of going yourself?” asked Madame de Bernstein.

“My mother loved her younger son the best,” said George, darkly—an old bitterness, like old coffee left too long on the grounds. “Besides, with the enemy invading our country, it was my duty, as the head of our family, to go on the campaign. Had I been a Scotchman twelve years ago, I should have been a—”

“Hush, sir! or I shall be more angry than ever!” said the old lady, with a perfectly pleased face; for there are women who rebuke treason as a duty, and enjoy the flavour of it all the same.

George’s explanation might appease Madame de Bernstein, whose principles, we fear, were not so tight-laced as her cap; but to the loyal heart of Sir Miles Warrington and his lady, the young man’s conduct gave a severe blow indeed—like a dish sent back untouched, not because it is ill-cooked, but because it is offered by the wrong hand.

“I should have thought,” her ladyship said, “from my sister Esmond Warrington’s letter, that my brother’s widow was a woman of good sense and judgment, and that she had educated her sons in a becoming manner. But what, Sir Miles—what, my dear Thomas Claypool—can we think of an education which has resulted so lamentably for both these young men?”

“The elder seems to know a power of Latin, though, and speaks the French and the German too. I heard him with the Hanover Envoy at the Baroness’s rout,” says Mr. Claypool. “The French he jabbered quite easy; and when he was at a loss for the High Dutch, he and the Envoy began in Latin, and talked away till all the room stared.”

“It is not language, but principles, Thomas Claypool!” exclaims the virtuous matron. “What must Mr. Warrington’s principles be, when he could reject an offer made him by his Prince? Can he speak the High Dutch? So much the more ought he to have accepted his Royal Highness’s condescension, and made himself useful in the campaign! Look at our son—look at Miles!”

“Hold up thy head, Miley, my boy!” says papa, with that hearty household voice which, when it sounds, sets the servants moving and the very spoons seeming to listen. “I trust, Sir Miles, that, as a member of the House of Commons, as an English gentleman, you will attend his Royal Highness’s levee to-morrow, and say, if such an offer had been made to us for that child, we would have taken it, though our boy is but ten years of age.”

“Faith, Miley, thou wouldst make a good little drummer or fifer!” says papa. “Shouldst like to be a little soldier, Miley?”

“Anything, sir, anything! a Warrington ought to be ready at any moment to have himself cut in pieces for his sovereign!” cries the matron, pointing to the boy, as if he were a joint offered up upon the altar of duty.

But the child, as soon as he comprehended his mother’s proposal, protested against it by a loud roar—one of those honest domestic noises, more true than speeches at a levee—midway through which he was carried off by Screwby, the house absorbing him again like a pantry door shutting on a squall.

In obedience to conjugal orders, Sir Miles went to his Royal Highness’s levee the next day, and made a protest of love and duty which the Prince deigned to accept, saying, “Nobody ever supposed that Sir Miles Warrington would ever refuse any place offered to him.”

A compliment gracious indeed—and repeated everywhere by Lady Warrington, as showing how implicitly the august family on the throne could rely on the loyalty of the Warringtons; she served it up to every visitor, warm again and again, till it was known in all her circles, as certain family dishes are, by repetition rather than novelty.

Accordingly, when this worthy couple saw George, they received him with a ghastly commiseration—such as dear relatives will sometimes extend when we have done something fatal or clumsy; when we have come badly out of a lawsuit; when we enter just as the company has been abusing us; when our banker has broke; or we have had to figure in the commercial columns of the London Gazette. Who does not know that face of pity—pity doled out like thin broth, with a look that says you have brought hunger on yourself?

It was not, indeed, just on Sir Miles’s part to turn upon George and be angry with his nephew for refusing the offer of promotion; for Sir Miles himself had agreed in George’s view of pursuing quite other than a military career, and it was in respect to this plan that Madam Esmond had written from Virginia. George had announced his intention of entering at the Temple, and qualifying himself for those magisterial and civil duties which, in the course of nature, he would be called to fulfil; nor could any one applaud his resolution more cordially than his uncle, who introduced him to a lawyer of reputation, under whose guidance we may fancy the young gentleman reading leisurely, with that patient appetite which belongs to studious minds—taking in clause and precedent as others take in a well-stewed dish, slowly, tasting the structure, noting what gives strength and what gives savour.

Madam Esmond from home signified approval, fully agreeing with Sir Miles (to whom and his lady she sent grateful remembrances) that the British Constitution was the envy of the world and the proper object of every English gentleman’s admiring study. The chief point to which George’s mother objected was the notion that Mr. Warrington should have to sit down in the Temple dinner-hall and cut at a shoulder of mutton, and drink small-beer out of tin pannikins, by the side of rough students who wore gowns like the parish-clerk. It was not the mutton—Virginia had made her no stranger to plain meat—but the company and the vessels: pewter and tin, like coarse words, seemed to her to rub away gentility by contact.

George’s loyal younger brother shared the repugnance. Anything was good enough for him, Harry said; he was a younger son, prepared to rough it. But George, in a gown, dining in a mess with three nobody’s sons off dirty pewter platters! Harry never could relish this condescension on his brother’s part, nor fancy George in his proper place at any table except the high one; and he was sorry that a plan Madam Esmond hinted at in her letters was not feasible—namely, that an application should be made to the Master of the Temple, to be informed that Mr. George Warrington was a gentleman of most noble birth, and of great property in America, and ought only to sit with the very best company in the hall.

Rather to Harry’s discomfiture, when he communicated his own and his mother’s ideas to the gentlemen’s new coffee-house friend, Mr. Spencer, Mr. Spencer received the proposal with roars of laughter, loud as the rattle of cups and saucers in a crowded room; and I cannot learn, from the Warrington papers, that any application was made to the Master of the Temple upon this subject.

Besides his literary and historical pursuits—which he loved best, and followed as others follow hunting or gaming—Mr. Warrington studied the laws of his country, attended the courts at Westminster, where he heard a Henley, a Pratt, a Murray, and those other famous schools of eloquence and patriotism, the two houses of parliament: rooms in which voices—trained, various, and powerful—made their own weather, and where a word, like a note struck true, could set a whole bench murmuring.

Gradually Mr. Warrington made acquaintance with some of the members of the House and the Bar; who, when they came to know him, spoke of him as a young gentleman of good parts and good breeding in terms so generally complimentary, that his good uncle’s heart relented towards him, and Dora and Flora began once more to smile upon him.

This reconciliation dated from the time when his Royal Highness the Duke, after having been defeated by the French in the affair of Hastenbeck, concluded the famous capitulation with the French, which his Majesty George II refused to ratify. His Royal Highness, as ’tis well known, flung up his commissions after this disgrace, laid down his commander’s baton—which, it must be confessed, he had not wielded with much luck or dexterity—and never again appeared at the head of armies or in public life.

The stout warrior would not allow a word of complaint against his father and sovereign to escape his lips; but as he retired with wounded honour, and as he would have no interest or authority more, nor any places to give, it may be supposed that Sir Miles Warrington’s anger against his nephew diminished as his respect for his Royal Highness diminished—resentment cooling when there was no longer any heat of patronage to keep it simmering.

As our two gentlemen were walking in St. James’s Park one day, with their friend Mr. Lambert, they met his Royal Highness in plain clothes and without a star, and made profound bows to the Prince, who was pleased to stop and speak to them. He asked Mr. Lambert how he liked my Lord Ligonier, his new chief at the Horse Guards, and the new duties in which he was engaged; and recognising the young men with that fidelity of memory for which his Royal race hath ever been remarkable, he said to Mr. Warrington, “You did well, sir, not to come with me when I asked you in the spring.”

“I was sorry, then, sir,” Mr. Warrington said, making a very low reverence, “but I am more sorry now.”

Upon which the Prince said, “Thank you, sir,” touched his hat, and walked away—the sound of his steps falling back into the Park’s general hush, mingling with the far-off wheel-rumble and the bird-notes, as if even royal displeasure, once passed, became only another tone in London’s great sound.

The circumstances of this interview, and the discourse which passed at it, being related to Mrs. Esmond Warrington in a letter from her younger son, created so deep an impression in that lady’s mind, that she narrated the anecdote many hundreds of times, until all her friends and acquaintances knew it and, perhaps, were tired of it; for memory, like a household recipe, is repeated not only because it delights, but because it proves something about the teller’s house and name.

Our gentlemen went through the Park and so towards the Strand, where they had business. And Mr. Lambert, pointing to the lion on the top of the Earl of Northumberland’s house at Charing Cross, says, “Harry Warrington! your brother is like yonder lion.”

“Because he is as brave as one,” says Harry.

“Because I respect virgins!” says George, laughing.

“Because you are a stupid lion. Because you turn your back on the East, and absolutely salute the setting sun. Why, child, what earthly good can you get by being civil to a man in hopeless dudgeon and disgrace? Your uncle will be more angry with you than ever—and so am I, sir.”

But Mr. Lambert was always laughing in his waggish way, and indeed he did not look the least angry.

War lay thick over Europe that year, like woodsmoke that will not quit the curtains. In London, in the rooms where gentlemen warmed themselves by talk and coffee, the very air seemed pricked with names of battles and generals; and every street-crier’s paper, snapped open with impatient fingers, carried fresh tinder for a young man’s temper. The King of Prussia—spoken of as though he were a figure stamped on a medal before the metal had cooled—was winning victories which all the clubs rehearsed with ardour, as if the telling were a kind of marching. Harry Warrington heard these tales until they rang in his ears like drums heard from afar, and the sound made him restless rather than brave; for he was not where the drum was.

So he chafed. He did not go. He wanted to go, and could not. He drifted instead, useless and sore with idleness, through the military coffee-houses where the smell of damp greatcoats and ink and toasted crumbs rose together; where pipes were lit and knocked out; where the scrape of chairs and the clink of spoons against cups made a small, ceaseless clatter—an indoor sort of campaign. He read nothing but the newspaper, as if letters printed yesterday were ration enough for a life. Books sent him to sleep. Novels he declared absurd; and when women spoke with wet eyes of Mr. Richardson, he laughed, hearty, honest, and a little too late, as though the jest had had to travel some distance through him before it could find its way out.

With no work for his broad hands, no calling but to sit, and think, and be ashamed, he grew like a strong horse kept too long in stall—stamping, sulky, starting at every noise. And it was almost lucky that his great energies found no battle; for a man who has been denied the honest outlet of peril will sometimes seek worse sport in safer places.

The Lambert ladies—Mrs. Lambert and her elder daughter Theo—took pity on him with the quiet industry of women who cure by small daily ministrations. They had a way of making their drawing-room feel less like a tribunal and more like a hearth: the rustle of silk, the soft tap of a fan laid down, the faint scent of tea and preserved fruit from the sideboard, the low, considerate murmur with which they received him. There are few gentlenesses like that kind of constancy: the steady hand that lays a warm poultice over a man’s pride without saying it is a wound.

But Miss Hetty Lambert’s kindness, if it existed at all, came in the shape of a whip. Her heart, at least in Harry’s cause, was flinty. She was angry that he was idle. She was angrier still that he seemed to accept his idleness as fate. While all Europe clashed, must he sit? While harvest came and men went out with sickles that flashed like bright steel, must he—who had hands made to grasp—do nothing but drink, stroll, and be pitied?

“Why, how savage the little thing is with him!” Mr. Lambert said once, after Hetty had peppered Harry with her quick shots, each one light as a pinprick and twice as stinging because it was laughed off.

“Her conduct is perfectly abominable!” cried Mrs. Lambert, who, being the gentlest of women, could be the fiercest in defence of gentleness. “She deserves to be whipped and sent to bed.”

Theo, whose colour came and went quickly, said in a low voice, “Perhaps, mother, it is because she likes him better than any of us do; and it is for his sake that Hetty is angry. If I were fond of—of some one—I should like to admire him always—to think everything he did right—and my gentleman better than all the gentlemen in the world.”

“The truth is,” Mrs. Lambert answered, “your father is so much better than all the world, he has spoiled us. Did you ever see any one to compare with him?”

“Very few, indeed,” Theo admitted, blushing.

“Who is so good-tempered?”

“Nobody, mamma.”

“Or so brave?”

“I dare say Mr. Wolfe—or Harry—or Mr. George—are very brave.”

“Or so learned and witty?”

Theo, who could not keep a certain bright seriousness out of her face when George Warrington’s name was spoken, said, “Mr. George seems very learned, and witty too, in his way; and his manners are very fine—you own they are. Madame de Bernstein says they are, and she hath seen the world. Indeed, Mr. George has a lofty way with him, which I don't see in other people; and, in reading books, I find he chooses the fine noble things always, and loves them in spite of all his satire. He is bitter only against mean things. No gentleman hath a more tender heart, I am sure. Yesterday, after he had been speaking so sharply as you said, I looked from the window and saw him stop and treat a whole crowd of little children to apples at the stall at the corner. And the day before, when he brought me the Molière, he gave money to a beggar—and how charmingly, sure, he reads the French! I agree with him about Tartuffe, though ’tis so wonderfully clever, that a mere hypocrite is too mean to be the chief of a great piece. Iago, he said, is near as great a villain; but then he is not the first character—Othello is, with his noble weakness. But what fine ladies and gentlemen Molière represents—so Mr. George thinks—and—oh, I don’t dare to repeat the verses after him.”

“But you know them by heart, my dear?” asked Mrs. Lambert, watching her.

“Oh yes, mamma! I know them by—Nonsense!”

Theo fled, a rose that had suddenly remembered it was being looked at.

After that, any one might have observed a little domestic miracle of timing—so neatly managed that the girls would have died rather than confess it. When George came, Theo appeared as if summoned by the click of his step on the pavement; when Harry knocked, Theo kept to her work upstairs, and Hetty, who had been nowhere in particular, suddenly materialised in the drawing-room. Theo had excellent eyes, and watched the street from the window as though it were a pageant: she could distinguish, even at dusk, the difference between Harry’s fair head and George’s dark; and though strangers forever mistook the brothers for one another, Theo never did. Hetty, for her part, showed no flutter at all when it was the black-haired gentleman. Her pert speeches were saved for the other.

Thus it happened, on a morning when the house held its usual comfortable sounds—the faint grind of a carriage-wheel outside, the creak of a stair, the soft chink of china being set in order—that Harry sat on the couch in an attitude of more than common despondency. He had the look of a man who has eaten nothing but air and finds himself empty. He was listening, not to music, but to London: the distant calls, the rattle, the persistent hum that never quite becomes silence. It was not the clean, living noise of a farm—wind in trees, hens fussing, a pump-handle squeaking, men calling across a field—but the manufactured, unceasing grind of a city; and it fretted him as an ill-tuned instrument frets a musician, though he had not words for it.

Down came Miss Hetty Lambert, as if sent by fate to prod him.

“And pray, sir,” she began, standing before him with her small hands planted like an officer’s, “what makes your honour look so glum this morning?”

“Ah, Hetty,” he said, with a weary attempt at smile, “I have nothing else to do but to look glum. When we were boys I used always to be begging my tutor for a holiday. I would spend it swinging on a gate, or making ducks and drakes over the pond; and those do-nothing days were always the most melancholy. What have I got to do now from morning till night?”

“Breakfast, walk—dinner, walk—tea, supper, I suppose; and a pipe of your Virginia,” Hetty said, tossing her head, as if she could smell that sweet leaf already and despised it because it came too easily.

“I tell you what: when I went back with Charley to the Chartreux t’other night, I had a mind to say to the master, ‘Teach me, sir. Here’s a boy knows a deal more Latin and Greek at thirteen than I do, who am ten years older. I have nothing to do; I might as well go to my books again and see if I can repair my idleness as a boy.’ Why do you laugh, Hetty?”

“I laugh to fancy you at the head of a class, and called up by the master!”

“I shouldn’t be at the head,” Harry said, simply. “George might be, but I am not a bookman. When I was young I neglected myself, and was very idle. We would not let our tutors cane us much at home; but if we had, it might have done me good.”

Hetty drubbed the carpet with her foot and looked at him—at the strong shoulders doing nothing, at the honest face grown slack with regret.

“Upon my word, it might do you good now!” she was almost tempted to say; and instead she asked, with a hard brightness, “What does Tom say about the caning at school? Does his account set you longing for it, pray?”

“His account makes me see I’ve been idle when I ought to have worked,” Harry answered, in the same plain voice that made his self-condemnation sound like a verdict. “And I have no genius for books. And for what am I good? Only to spend my patrimony when I come abroad; to lounge at coffee-houses or race-courses; to gallop behind dogs at home. I am good for nothing, I am.”

“What, such a great, brave, strong fellow as you good for nothing?” Hetty cried. “I would not confess as much to any woman, if I were twice as good for nothing!”

“What am I to do? I ask leave to go into the army, and Madam Esmond does not answer me. ’Tis the only thing I am fit for. I have no money to buy. Having spent all my own, and so much of my brother’s, I cannot and won’t ask for more. If my mother would but send me to the army—if she would but say the word—you know I would jump to go.”

“Eh! A gentleman of spirit does not want a woman to buckle his sword on for him, or to clean his firelock!” Hetty returned, quick as flint. “What was that papa told us of the young gentleman at court yesterday? Sir John Armytage—”

“Sir John Armytage?” Harry said, rousing at the name. “I used to know him at White’s and the club-houses. A fine, noble young gentleman; a great estate in the North.”

“And engaged to be married to a famous beauty too—Miss Howe, my Lord Howe’s sister—but that, I suppose, is not an obstacle to gentlemen?”

“An obstacle to what?”

“An obstacle to glory!” Hetty cried. “I think no woman of spirit would say ‘Stay!’ though she adored her lover ever so much, when his country said ‘Go!’ Sir John has volunteered for the expedition preparing; and being at court yesterday, his Majesty asked him when he would be ready. ‘Tomorrow, please your Majesty,’ replies Sir John; and the King said that was a soldier’s answer. My father himself is longing to go, though he has mamma and all us brats at home. Oh dear, oh dear! Why wasn’t I a man? Both my brothers are for the Church; but as for me, I know I should have made a famous little soldier!”

And she strode about the room with a warrior’s air, her dress swishing like a banner behind her, her small chin lifted, as bold as if she wore a casque. Yet the boldness was all in the carriage and the voice; her slightness betrayed her at every turn, as a sparrow’s bravery does.

Harry watched her with a tenderness that was half amusement and half a pang.

“I think,” he said, “I would hardly like to see a musket on that little shoulder, nor a wound on that pretty face, Hetty.”

“Wounds! Who fears wounds?” she cried. “Muskets? If I could carry one, I would use it. You men fancy we women are good for nothing but to make puddings or stitch samplers.”

The word puddings, spoken with contempt in a house where Mrs. Lambert’s cook took pride in her suet and spice, brought with it, absurdly, the very smell of the kitchen—warm flour, a whiff of citrus peel laid out for candied slices, the rich, animal sweetness of butter melting. Such domestic scents, honest and sustaining, floated up even into the drawing-room and made Hetty’s scorn sound like a child striking at the very thing that feeds it.

“Why wasn’t I a man, I say? George was reading to us yesterday out of Tasso—look, here it is—and I thought the verses applied to me. See! Here’s the book, with the mark in it where we left off.”

“With the mark in it?” Harry repeated dutifully, as though the ribbon were a military order.

“Yes! It is about a woman who is disappointed because—because her brother does not go to war; and she says of herself—

‘Alas! why did not Heaven these members frail
With lively force and vigour strengthen, so
That I this silken gown—’”

“Silken gown?” Harry interrupted, with his plain puzzled face.

“Well, sir, I know ’tis but calimanco; but so it is in the book—

‘—this silken gown and slender veil
Might for a breastplate and a helm forgo;
Then should not heat, nor cold, nor rain, nor hail,
Nor storms that fall, nor blust’ring winds that blow,
Withhold me; but I would, both day and night,
In pitched field or private combat, fight—’

Fight? Yes, that I would! Why are both my brothers to be parsons, I say? One of papa’s children ought to be a soldier!”

Harry laughed softly, looking at her as if she were something fierce in miniature—like a kitten arching its back at a mastiff. He held up a finger.

“Why, I think here’s a finger nigh as big as your arm. How would you stand up before a great strong man? I should like to see a man try and injure you, though; I should just like to see him! You little, delicate, tender creature! Do you suppose any scoundrel would dare do anything unkind to you?”

And at the notion, he began pacing too, fired now not by glory but by protective wrath—his boots thudding on the carpet in a quick martial rhythm, as if his body could find relief in sound if his life could not find it in action. He imagined, with sudden heat, a Frenchman insolent to Hetty; and his hands, made for holding reins and sword-hilts, clenched as if they had found at last something honest to do.

This was what conquered Hetty when her speeches could not. She admired in him that dumb readiness to spring—an unadvertised courage that seemed to live in his blood and not in his boasting. In truth she was no virago at all; her bravery was a bright ribbon she liked to wear, not armour she could endure. She wanted, without knowing it, not to be a soldier, but to have one near her.

Still, her tongue went on. Her darts were her way of keeping power in a world where girls had little else.

“Pray, what is the use of having a strong hand if you only use it to hold a skein of silk for my mother?” she cried, watching him stride. “And what is the good of being ever so strong in a drawing-room? Nobody wants you to throw anybody out of window, Harry. A strong man indeed! I suppose there’s a stronger at Bartholomew Fair. James Wolfe is not a strong man. He seems quite weakly and ill. When he was here last he was coughing the whole time, and as pale as if he had seen a ghost.”

“I never could understand why a man should be frightened at a ghost,” Harry said.

“Pray, have you seen one, sir?” Hetty asked, her eyes bright with mischief.

“No. I thought I did once at home—when we were boys—but it was only Nathan in his night-shirt. I wasn’t frightened when I thought he was a ghost. I believe there’s no such things. Our nurses tell a pack of lies about ’em,” Harry said gravely. “George was a little frightened; but then he’s—” He stopped short.

“Then George is what?” Hetty pressed.

“Different from me, that’s all. Our mother’s a bold woman as ever you saw, but she screams at seeing a mouse—always does—can’t help it. It’s her nature. So perhaps my brother can’t bear ghosts. I don’t mind ’em.”

“George always says you would have made a better soldier than he.”

“So I think I should, if I had been allowed to try. But he can do a thousand things better than me, or anybody else in the world. Why didn’t he let me volunteer on Braddock’s expedition? I might have got knocked on the head; and then I should have been pretty much as useful as I am now; and then I shouldn’t have ruined myself, and brought people to point at me and say I had disgraced the name of Warrington. Why mayn’t I go on this expedition and volunteer like Sir John Armytage? Oh, Hetty! I’m a miserable fellow—that’s what I am.”

He paced faster, as if he could outrun his own words.

“I wish I had never come to Europe,” he groaned.

“What a compliment to us! Thank you, Harry!” Hetty flung back; and then, seeing his face—how his simplicity made his suffering almost childish—she softened in spite of herself. “Are you—are you thinking of going home?”

“And have all Virginia jeering at me! There’s not a gentleman there that wouldn’t—except one, and him my mother doesn’t like. I should be ashamed to go home now. You don’t know my mother, Hetty. I ain’t afraid of most things; but somehow I am of her. What shall I say when she says, ‘Harry, where’s your patrimony?’ ‘Spent, mother.’ ‘What have you done with it?’ ‘Wasted it, mother, and went to prison after.’ ‘Who took you out of prison?’ ‘Brother George, ma’am.’ And now I’m come back having done no good for myself—no profession, no prospects, no nothing—only to look after negroes, and be scolded at home; or to go to sleep at sermons; or to play at cards and drink and fight cocks at the taverns. How can I look the gentlemen of the country in the face? I’m ashamed to go home in this way. I must and will do something. What shall I do, Hetty? Ah! what shall I do?”

“Do?” Hetty repeated, seizing on the word as if it were a handle. “What did Mr. Wolfe do at Louisbourg? Ill as he was, and in love as we knew him to be, he didn’t stop to be nursed by his mother, Harry, or to dawdle with his sweetheart. He went on the King’s service, and hath come back covered with honour. If there is to be another great campaign in America, papa says he is sure of a great command.”

“I wish he would take me with him,” Harry burst out, “and that a ball would knock me on the head and finish me.”

“Life indeed!” Hetty said, with a shrug, as if he had offered her a penny.

“You don’t seem to think that of much value,” Harry said sadly. “No more it is—to anybody. I’m a poor useless fellow. I’m not even free to throw it away as I would like, being under orders here and at home.”

“Orders indeed! Why under orders?” Hetty cried, and now her voice had the sharp crack of a whip. “Aren’t you tall enough and old enough to act for yourself? Must you have George for a master here, and your mother for a schoolmistress at home? If I were a man, I would do something famous before I was two-and-twenty. I would have the world speak of me. I wouldn’t dawdle at apron-strings. I wouldn’t curse my fortune—I’d make it. I vow and declare I would!”

For the first time, her words struck deep enough to draw blood. Harry stopped short; the colour rose hot in his face, not with shame only but with a kind of anger at being handled so.

“No negro on our estate is more a slave than I am, Hetty,” he said, turning full upon her, his voice thickening. “But then, Miss Lambert, we don’t reproach the poor fellow for not being free. That isn’t generous. At least, that isn’t the way I understand honour. Perhaps with women it’s different—or I may be wrong, and have no right to be hurt at a young girl telling me what my faults are. Perhaps my faults are not my faults—only my cursed luck. You’ve been talking ever so long about this gentleman volunteering, and that man winning glory, and cracking up their courage as if I had none of my own. I don’t brag, but I’m not afraid of Mr. Wolfe, nor of Sir John Armytage, nor of anybody else that ever I saw. How can I buy a commission when I’ve spent my last shilling? Or ask my brother for more, who has already halved with me? A gentleman of my rank can’t go common soldier—else, by Jupiter, I would! And if a ball finished me, I suppose Miss Hetty Lambert wouldn’t be very sorry. It isn’t kind, Hetty—I didn’t think it of you.”

“What is it I have said?” Hetty asked quickly, as if her own pride had been struck now. “I have only said Sir John Armytage has volunteered, and Mr. Wolfe has covered himself with honour, and you begin to scold me! How can I help it if Mr. Wolfe is brave and famous? Is that any reason you should be angry, pray?”

“I didn’t say angry,” Harry answered, holding himself stiffly as if to keep from breaking. “I said I was hurt.”

“Oh, indeed! I thought such a little creature as I am couldn’t hurt anybody. I’m sure ’tis mighty complimentary to me to say that a young lady whose arm is no bigger than your little finger can hurt such a great strong man as you!”

“I scarce thought you would try,” Harry said, with a look that went to her more than any scolding. “You see, I’m not used to this kind of welcome in this house.”

At that moment, the door opened, and Mrs. Lambert appeared—soft-footed, as mothers are, with a face ready at once for inquiry and comfort. Behind her came the house’s familiar hush: the distant rattle of teaspoons, the low talk of servants, the steady, homely sounds that stitched a day together.

“What is it, my poor boy?” she asked, seeing Harry’s worn countenance.

“Oh, we have heard the story before, mamma,” Hetty said hastily, stepping between them with an air of careless impatience that was too quick to be quite natural. “Harry is making his old complaint of having nothing to do. And he is quite unhappy; and he is telling us so over and over again—that’s all.”

George Warrington did not suffer his law to starve his body, nor his body to dull his mind. The gown of a student sat upon his shoulders; but his mother’s letters sat nearer his conscience, and they were stitched with that old Esmond pride which holds a man upright as a stays-bone holds a coat.

“You have a name,” Madam Esmond wrote, “and a very ancient one. You are not bound to grind like a clerk with ink in his pores. Study as a gentleman.”

So he obeyed, and contrived to give Themis her due without giving her his marrow. He went to hall with the crowd of unknown young men and ate the same commons—mutton that had marched too long in the pot, bread whose crust remembered yesterday’s oven, ale that smelt of the cask’s damp staves—yet he took care, when he could, to refresh himself elsewhere, as a man will turn from thin broth to a stew that has been tended. The law even then was a jealous mistress; she liked her votaries pale and sleepless. But a century ago she had not yet learned the modern tyranny of denying a man his dinner. She allowed more coffee-house air, more bowls of punch, more nights wherein talk and tobacco could make their own kind of study.

George, who loved letters as other men love hunting, found the black-letter of Chaucer more savoury than the crabbed Gothic of Hale and Coke. In those days, too, books were not mere ornaments for a shelf: the ancients were still used like spices in conversation. A gentleman might season an argument with Virgil as readily as he seasoned his soup with mace. In Parliament and in courts they called Statius, Juvenal, and the rest to witness, as if the Muses were still living neighbours. Their reign has waned in our time; yet in George’s London they were not yet wholly turned out of doors. A man might still ask, over a dish of oysters and a bottle, whether Melpomene’s name ran in three syllables or four, and feel himself the wiser for it.

It had been told already how, in the long leisure of his youth—at home, and in that harsher leisure of captivity in a French fort by Monongahela—George had courted the tragic Muse. He had done it as most young men do: with immodest hopes. No youth aims first at an epigram. He must storm Olympus. It is only later, when the blood has learned its limits, that he will content himself with translating Horace into decent measures, like a man who, after once dreaming of feeding an army, is proud to keep a household well.

So, when he came to London, the theatre drew him as kitchens draw a hungry traveller: not merely for the eating, but for the heat, the talk, the bustle, the noises of utensils and voices, the very smell of it all. He attended performances at both houses; he haunted the theatrical coffee-houses; he listened to the critics as a young cook listens to old hands arguing over a sauce.

At the Bedford between plays, at the Cecil after them, he might be seen among the wits and actors. The tough old Macklin was there, biting like a peppercorn. Foote flitted and snapped, frolicsome as a fish in a pan. Hippisley laughed. Garrick—small of stature, large of spirit—came and went with that quick, charged presence which made even his silences audible. Around them clinked glasses, scraped chairs, rattled dice-boxes; punch was compounded with solemn care—lemons cut, sugar crushed, rum measured, water and spice married till the steam rose scented above the table; and the whole room had its own acoustic weather: the thud of tankards, the crackle of wit, the low drone of argument, now and then split by a burst of laughter like a sudden gull-cry over a river.

George’s modesty, his ready talk, and—no doubt—his reputation for money, made him welcome. Actors would drink a bowl with him; critics would sup at his expense with a hearty civility. He delighted, too, in the sense of tasting something half forbidden; for his mother approved plays but by halves, and he had the relish which comes when a dish is spiced with disobedience. He gave more than one handsome entertainment to players, and it was whispered that one or two celebrated geniuses had condescended to borrow from him—genius, like fire, consuming whatever fuel lies nearest.

All this while he was polishing his tragedy—his masterpiece, as he called it in the honest vanity of youth. He sought advice, and received the sort of applause that is easily given when negus is warm and the company benevolent. Mr. Spencer of the Temple—new acquaintance and already friendly—gave a breakfast at his chambers in Fig Tree Court, and invited a handful of gentlemen to hear Mr. Warrington read.

Breakfast in those chambers had its own proper ritual. The air carried the smell of toasted bread, and the slight bitterness of tea newly scalded; there was butter that had not been too long out of the cool, and marmalade whose orange peel still held the sharpness of the fruit. The cups chimed upon saucers; a spoon stirred and rang; a fire hissed faintly; outside, the Temple had its customary murmur—footsteps on stone, distant coach-wheels, the river’s presence felt more than heard. Against that domestic soundscape George set his louder world of convent-bells, war-horns, and slaughter.

Even Dr. Johnson was there—big, brown-coated, near-sighted, formidable; a man who could swallow tea and opinions with equal heat. He was good enough to say the piece showed talent. It offended the unities—certainly; but others had offended them, and Mr. Warrington might sin in company. There was something, Johnson said, that reminded him of Coriolanus and Othello.

“And two very good things too, sir!” George pleaded, eager as any cook whose dish is accused of tasting of a great predecessor’s.

“Well, well,” Johnson returned, not unkindly; “your catastrophe is terrible, just, and being in part true, is not the less awful.”

Then George began in earnest, and the first act opened before the breakfast-table.

His hero, Gaspar Carpezan, appears before a convent on the Rhine, which the Lutherans besiege. There is an armistice. The convent’s bell strikes noon—ding, ding, dong—its sound written so plainly in the author’s voice that the gentlemen at table might have sworn they heard iron on iron. No succours arrive. The gates open. In comes Carpezan, clad in full steel, with the great hammer of battle over his shoulder, trumpets blowing, flags displayed.

“No rudeness, my men!” cries Carpezan. “The wine is yours, and the larder and cellar are good. The church plate shall be melted. Any of the garrison who will take service with me shall have good pay. No insult to the religious ladies! I have promised safe-conduct; and he who lays a finger on them—hangs! Mind that, Provost Marshal!”

The Provost Marshal, a huge fellow in a red doublet, nods like an ox.

“We shall see more of that executioner,” Mr. Spencer murmured, leaning over his cup.

“A very agreeable acquaintance, I am sure,” said Johnson, wagging his head; “I shall be delighted to meet him again. This scene of mercenaries and camp-followers is novel and stirring, Mr. Warrington. The Colonel has gone into the convent? Let us hear what he does there.”

The Abbess appears—high-born, violent, sharp-tongued, with old ladies at her side. She has heard of Carpezan’s former violences: that hammer has smashed many images; pounds of plate have been melted down by the sacrilegious plunderer. She detests him, and tells him so with a fury of words that, for a moment, shakes even the conqueror. George read this scene with relish, letting the Abbess’s contempt crack like a whip.

But Carpezan recovers his ground. “Pray, madam,” he says, “how many ladies are there in your convent, for whom my people shall provide conveyance?”

The Abbess, troubled and angry, answers, “Besides myself, the noble sisters of Saint Mary’s House are twenty—twenty-three.”

She had been going to say twenty-four. That hesitation was a small sound in the room, but it rang like a dropped knife.

“Ha! why this stop?” asks Captain Ulric, one of Carpezan’s gayest officers, a man whose levity seems made to mock the solemn walls.

Carpezan draws a letter. “I require from you,” he says sternly, “the body of the noble lady Sybilla of Hoya. Her brother was my favourite captain, slain by my side in the Milanese. By his death she becomes heiress of his lands. A greedy uncle, they say, brought her hither and immured her. The damsel shall herself pronounce her fate—whether to remain a cloistered sister, or to return to home and liberty as Baroness of—”

The Abbess denies it. “There is no Lady Sybil in this house. The Sister Agnes was a nun professed. What was her wealth reverts to the Order.”

“Give me straightway the body of the Lady Sybil of Hoya!” roars Carpezan. “If not, I make a signal to my Reiters and give you and your convent up to war.”

Captain Ulric, peering under veils with ribald curiosity, begins some jest about choosing a plump smiling maid—like—like—when the Abbess cuts him down with a cry of “Silence!” and declares, with haughty composure, that Sister Agnes died three days ago and was buried.

Carpezan is struck as if the Abbess had hit him. The chaplain—ghastly, trembling—confirms it.

But Carpezan has in his armour a letter from Sister Agnes herself, saying she was to be buried alive in an oubliette—kept on water and bread, or left to starve. Rage takes him. He seizes the Abbess. Ulric throttles the chaplain. Carpezan blows his horn; the sound, as George read it, seemed to widen the chambers. In rush the Lanzknechts. Crash, bang! They batter doors and walls. Flames, screams, slaughter. And then Carpezan himself staggers in, bearing a fainting woman on his shoulder—Sybilla.

A little sister with red lips—one of the veiled attendants—has shown them the way to the dungeon. Betrayal comes, in this first act, from within the convent’s own kitchen of secrets.

“The convent is suppressed with a vengeance,” George said, lifting his eyes from the page. “We end our first act with the burning of the place, the roars of the soldiery, and the outcries of the nuns. They had best go change their dresses, for they will be court ladies in the next act.”

This pleased the company; they began at once to cast the play as if it already stood behind a curtain. Mrs. Pritchard would not like to be Abbess and vanish after the first act. Miss Pritchard might make a pretty Sybilla; Miss Gates the attendant nun. Garrick scarce tall enough for Carpezan—though when excited he always seemed a grenadier. Woodward would make a good Ulric. The breakfast-table became a little stage, with names placed as neatly as dishes.

Act the second: Carpezan has married Sybilla. He has enriched himself in war, is ennobled, and lives on the Danube in splendour. George’s voice slowed here; the noise of battle withdrew, and the household sounds of a great house replaced it—doors, servants, the clink of plate, the rustle of silks. Yet for all the state, the Baron is not happy. His rough soldier-manners chafe against his high-born bride. She taunts him with his low birth, his vulgar companions, whom he still loves to see about him, old comrades with hands scarred by pike and rope. There are moments, George read, when the man wishes he had never fished this lovely quarrelsome vixen from her dungeon. The act is chiefly domestic war—words like blows—until horns blow and news comes that the young King of Bohemia and Hungary is hunting that way.

Act the third shifts to Prague. The King invites Carpezan and his wife, promising preferment: from Baron to Count, from Colonel to General-in-Chief. Sybilla shines at court, the most brilliant of ladies. The King’s admiration is no longer hidden. Even in George’s reading, one could hear, beneath the words, the altered soundscape of Prague—music, laughter, the careful hush around power, the thin applause which is a kind of currency.

Johnson stirred. “Oh, stay—I have it—I know your story now,” he said. “’Tis in Meteranus, in the Theatrum Universum. I read it in Oxford as a boy—Carpezanus—Carpzoff—”

“That is the fourth act,” George answered, and went on.

In the fourth act the King’s attentions to Sybilla grow marked. Carpezan struggles against jealousy, refusing long to yield to it, until his wife’s guilt is put beyond doubt. Then comes the true, dreadful matter: the executioner who follows Carpezan’s regiment is commanded to slay Sybilla in her own palace. George read that closing scene with a cold steadiness that made the air of the chambers feel thinner: a side-room, moonlight through an oriel window, the hush after violence. And under the window the King comes with his lute and plays the song that had been their signal—an air heard earlier in festivity, now returned like a taste remembered at the worst moment, sweet and sickening together.

The song—written in an ancient manner, and repeated in the piece—Johnson, still awake then, pronounced a happy imitation of Waller; and he allowed that its gay repetition at the moment of guilt and murder deepened the gloom.

“But what comes afterwards?” Johnson asked. “In the Theatrum, Carpezan is taken into favour again by Count Mansfield, and doubtless murders other folks on the reformed side.”

George had departed from the printed history. His fifth act returned to the grand sweep of armies and fate. King Louis—terror-stricken by the bloody end of his intrigue—receives word that Solyman invades Hungary. Two noblemen tell how, in council, the injured Carpezan burst in, broke his sword, flung it at the King’s feet, and threw down a glove—daring him to wear it, swearing he would one day claim it. Then Carpezan fled, and rumor says he has joined the Turk, assumed the turban, and now stands in the Sultan’s camp, whose white tents gleam across the river.

The King prepares for battle at Mohacz. He keeps with him an aged, faithful knight, Master of the Horse, and confesses repentance, esteem for his injured Queen, and resolve to meet the day as a man.

“What is this field called?” the King asks.

“Mohacz, my liege,” says the old warrior, with a brave prophecy that before sunset Mohacz shall see a battle nobly won.

Trumpets and alarms sound—cymbals, barbaric music, the cry of Janissaries. The stage shifts to the Turkish camp. There walks the Grand Vizier, conqueror of Rhodes, dark and stern. And there too is Carpezan, in Eastern habit, with the glove in his cap like a poison flower worn for remembrance. He advises the Turks where Louis is weakest; how to meet the Hungarian cavalry’s tremendous shock and draw them toward a morass. He begs command in front, near the place where the King will engage.

“’Tis well,” says the Vizier. “Our invincible Emperor surveys the battle from yonder tower. At day’s end he will know how to reward your valour.”

Signal-guns. Trumpets. Captains retire, vowing death to the infidel and fidelity to the Sultan. The fight begins: Christians and Turks clash and skirmish; troops advance and retreat; alarms continue. George’s voice quickened; he made a sort of percussion with his consonants, as if beating a drum. Carpezan rages over the field, hammer smashing, calling for King Louis. He is about to kill a warrior who faces him when he recognises Ulric, his former captain. For a moment the renegade softens; memory breaks through like the smell of old bread in a new kitchen.

“Fly,” Carpezan bids him. “Think of Carpezan.”

Ulric begs him to return; it is impossible. They fight. Ulric will have it, and goes down under the hammer. Carpezan bends, melted at seeing his young friend wounded—when King Louis appears, plumes torn, sword hacked, shield battered with a thousand blows received and given. The guilty monarch would turn away. Carpezan is on him.

“An equal fight!” he roars. “A traitor against a traitor! Stand, King Louis! False King, false knight, false friend—by this glove in my helmet, I challenge you!”

He tears the glove out and flings it at the King. They set to. The monarch falls under the terrible arm of the man he injured, dying with a few broken words of repentance. Carpezan leans on his murderous mace and speaks a heartbroken soliloquy over the corpse.

Turkish warriors gather. The day is theirs. The Grand Vizier stands with Janissaries, whose bows and swords are tired of drinking death. He surveys the renegade.

“Christian renegade,” says the Vizier, “Allah has given us a great victory. The Christian King is slain by you.”

“Peace to his soul!” gasps Ulric, dying on the field. “He died like a good knight.”

“In this day’s battle,” the Vizier continues, “no man hath comported himself more bravely than you. You are made Bassa of Transylvania. Advance bowmen—Fire!”

At that word Mr. Fountain, even while George read, pricked up his head as if he had heard a cook say “roast” when he meant “boil.” But the scene rolled on. An arrow quivers in Carpezan’s breast.

“Bassa of Transylvania,” says the Vizier, “you were a traitor to your King, who lies murdered by your hand. You contributed more than any soldier to this day’s victory. ’Tis thus my sublime Emperor meetly rewards you. Sound trumpets! We march for Vienna to-night!”

The curtain falls in George’s manuscript as Carpezan crawls to Ulric, kisses his hands, and gasps, “Forgive me, Ulric!”

When George ended, he turned to Johnson, his face more pale than when he began. “What say you, sir?” he asked modestly. “Is there any chance for me?”

But the greatest critic in the room was scarce to be had; Johnson had been asleep for some time, and now frankly owned he had lost the latter part of the play.

The little auditory hummed and stirred, relieved as men are when a storm has passed. Yet they allowed—truly enough—that George had read the last acts uncommonly well, and they paid him compliments on matter and manner; perhaps, too, they were in good humour because the business had come to an end. Mr. Spencer’s servant handed about negus—wine warmed, lemon and spice rising in a fragrant steam. The Templars sipped, and began their grave talk, as if they were judges at a tasting, pronouncing on what should be altered for a finer flavour.

Mr. Fountain objected that the Vizier should not say “Fire!” when he bids archers kill Carpezan, since one does not fire a bow. A note was taken, as carefully as a receipt is written down.

Mr. Figtree, sentimental, regretted that Ulric could not be saved and married to a comic heroine.

“Nay, sir,” said Johnson, waking to stern historical appetite, “there was utter annihilation of the Hungarian army at Mohacz, and Ulric must take his knock with the rest. He could only be saved by flight, and you would not have a hero run away. Pronounce sentence of death against Captain Ulric, but kill him with the honours of war.”

Messrs. Essex and Tanfield, meanwhile, wondered to each other who this queer-looking pert was—this man who contradicted everybody between sips—and proposed, after the fatigues of tragedy, a boat up the river and a little fresh air, as if to wash their ears clean of battle-cries and bring them back to the kinder sounds of oars in water and wind among trees.

Gumbo’s lamentation began the instant the tidings were out—that Mr. Harry had gone a-volunteering, and gone without him. The poor fellow flung himself upon his grief with all the force of his lungs, as though sorrow were a bellows to be worked for other people’s comfort. He ran straightway to Mr. Lambert’s lodgings, for wherever that dusky youth was, there the maid-servants were sure to be found; and where the women were, he knew there would be pity, a hand to his sleeve, a corner of apron offered, a word that softened the blow.

The kitchen at Dean Street received him as a kind of chapel. There were tears, there were howls, there were sympathetic sniffings; and then, because the heart will not beat long on emptiness, there was victualling. Gumbo, who could grieve with a noble sincerity and eat with a noble perseverance, fortified Nature with beer drawn cool from the cellar and cold meat taken in thick, confident slices. The smell of malt rose like a warm fog; the fat of yesterday’s joint held the savour of pepper and char; knives tapped on trenchers; the spits in imagination still turned. If he told lies (as he did), if he was idle (as he was), if he was greedy (past denial), still the maids cried with him and called him brother; Europe, at least in that house, was not squeamish about Africa, and took the colour of a man’s skin for no more than the colour of the pot that holds good broth.

Hetty found him at one of his great bursts—roaring that Master Harry had gone a “volumteer,” and had not taken him. He would have saved Master Harry’s life any day; would have been cut into “twenty thousand hundred pieces” for him—so he swore between sobs and swallows. Hetty, who had laughed once upon a time at such stage-tears, did not laugh now. She slipped him half-a-crown with a hand that trembled, and even her pert tongue, which used to crack its little jokes like a cook snapping beans, grew gentle and shy.

Indeed, the whole house beheld a marvel: Hetty Lambert transformed. She moved about as if afraid of making a noise in a sick-room. She was humble to mamma; thankful to John and Betty for the smallest service at table; patient to Polly when the comb pulled at her hair; long-suffering when Charley from school stamped upon her toes or tumbled her workbox. In papa’s company she was silent—silent, and pale. If Mr. Lambert had commanded her to roast the leg of mutton, or walk to church arm-in-arm with Gumbo, she would have curtseyed and said, “Yes, if you please, dear papa!”

Roast the leg of mutton! She could scarce endure the smell of it when it came in, brown and crackling, the fat hissing as it met the hot dish, rosemary bruised under the knife, gravy steaming and sweet with onion; for what sort of meal, she asked herself, were the poor volunteers having with cannon-balls flying about their heads? Church! At the prayer in time of war, her knees knocked together upon the hassock; the very hush of the pew seemed full of distant drums. When the parson read, “Thou shalt do no murder,” from the communion-rail, she ducked her head as if the words were aimed at her, and fancied the holy man’s eyes were upon her secret.

She thought of travellers by land and water. She ran to the newspaper with a sickness rising in her throat—sickness not from any kitchen-smell now, but from ink and dread. She watched papa when he came home from the Ordnance Office—watched his face as if it were a dish-lid that might lift and show either comfort or ruin beneath. Is he well? Is he a General yet? Is he wounded, taken? Or—oh, hideous picture—are both his legs shot away, like that pensioner they had seen in Chelsea Garden t’other day? She made herself vows as rapidly as a cook ties up herbs. She would go on wooden legs all her life if his could but bring him safe home; she ought never to rise from her knees until he was returned.

“Haven’t you heard of people, Theo,” she said, “whose hair has grown grey in a single night? I shouldn’t wonder if mine did—shouldn’t wonder in the least.” And she peered in the looking-glass, searching for that sudden winter in her own curls.

“Hetty dear, you used not to be so nervous when papa was away in Minorca,” Theo answered.

“Ah, Theo! one may very well see that George is not with the army, but safe at home,” cried Hetty; at which the elder sister blushed, and looked away, pensive as a woman who hears her own heart named aloud. For if Mr. George had been in the army—why, that would have been another pair of boots.

And yet, while the household trembled and prayed and made little domestic rites of fear—bread cut, candles watched, newspapers unfolded—Harry Warrington, for the present, was as safe as any officer of the Life Guards at Regent’s Park Barracks.

His first taste of war might be called successful; it was certainly not glorious. The British Lion cannot always find a tiger that will stand to be torn. Sometimes he goes prowling for a worthy foe and finds only a goose; sometimes, bellowing for a single tiger, he spies six. If he fights six tigers, you may call him an ass; if he retreats, you may call him prudent. Harry’s first feat was of this kind—more smoke than steel, more marching than fighting, more burnt tar than spilt blood.

On the 1st of June, he and about thirteen thousand others went aboard at the Isle of Wight; and on the 5th, at daybreak, the fleet stood into the Bay of Cancale in Brittany. From the crowded decks the gentlemen volunteers had leisure to gaze at the French coast—green slopes, hedgerows deep with leaf, a few cattle like pale toys in the distance, a little stir of dragoons who, catching sight of our ships, trotted off as if the very salt air were British. A small fort with two guns ventured to fire at the Commander-in-Chief and the Commodore while they reconnoitred in a cutter; the insolence of those two little mouths of iron made an absurd, sharp music over the water—like a kitchen-pan struck in anger.

By two o’clock the fleet anchored, and signals flew. Grenadier companies from eleven regiments were ordered into flat-bottomed boats to assemble round the Commodore’s ship, the Essex. Mr. Howe, hoisting his broad pennant on the Success frigate, went in as near shore as he dared, the other frigates following to cover the landing. With Lord George Sackville and General Dury in command, the volunteers, the grenadiers, and three battalions of Guards pulled in.

But the French, who should by all the rules of romance have stayed to receive their enemies, ran. The frigates soon silenced the little fort; the troops assaulted it; the whole garrison was taken—being, in truth, one old gentleman who had fired his two guns gallantly and received a ball in the leg for his pains. “If every Frenchman had acted like me,” said he to his conquerors, “you would not have landed at Cancale at all.” There was a kind of homely greatness in the speech—as if some village elder had salted his honour and set it by for hard times.

The detachment took possession of Cancale, and lay on their arms all night. Harry’s comrades rallied him for his eagerness to be upon the war-path, and to bring home French scalps like a story-book savage. Yet no man fell under his tomahawk; the only blood spilt that day was of a French gentleman riding with his servant, surprised by volunteer Lord Downe in front with a company of Kingsley’s. My Lord offered quarter; the gentleman refused it; and he, the servant, and both horses were shot. Thus did pride make a quicker meal of death than any kitchen could serve.

Next day the whole force landed and advanced towards St. Malo. The villages emptied as the troops came; doors shut, dogs silent, hens left in the road with nobody to call them home. The lanes were so narrow in places that the men marched single file between high leafy hedges; had there been an enemy in earnest, a handful of peasants might have picked them off at leisure from behind green coverts. But no enemy stirred. At nightfall they reached St. Malo and were saluted with artillery fire that did little in the darkness except add a harsh clangour to the sea-wind. Under that cover, the British fired ships, wooden buildings, pitch and tar magazines in the harbour; and the blaze rose with a roar and a bitter perfume—rosin and pine, tar oozing and catching, a sweetness of burnt wood turned acrid—until the whole night seemed a vast cookery gone mad, flames licking masts as if they were spits.

It was all done with scarcely an attempt by the French to molest the force. Though it was asserted there was a considerable French strength in the town, they would not come out; and so the Duke of Marlborough and Lord George Sackville, judging it not their business to force a nest that would not fly, marched back to Cancale and got aboard again.

Exactly four weeks after leaving England, Harry found himself at Portsmouth once more. He wrote to his brother George; and George, receiving the letter, ran with it straight to Dean Street, where the Lambert family sat at breakfast with the comfortable clink of cups and the steady domestic sound of knives upon bread.

“Glorious news, ladies!” George cried, bursting in. “Our champion has come back. He has undergone all sorts of dangers, but has survived them all. He has seen dragons—upon my word, he says so.”

“Dragons! What do you mean, Mr. Warrington?” asked Hetty, half starting up, as if the word itself were cannon-fire.

“But not killed any—he says so, as you shall hear.” And George opened the letter and read, tasting his brother’s spelling and soldier’s brag as if it were some rough wine shipped home from sea.

“‘DEAREST BROTHER,—I think you will be glad to hear that I am returned, without any commission as yet; without any wounds or glory; but,—at any rate, alive and harty. On board our ship, we were almost as crowded as poor Mr. Holwell and his friends in their Black Hole at Calicutta. We had rough weather, and some of the gentlemen volunteers, who prefer smooth water, grumbled not a little. My gentlemen’s stomachs are dainty; and after Braund’s cookery and White’s kick-shaws, they don’t like plain sailor’s rum and bisket. But I, who have been at sea before, took my rations and can of flip very contentedly: being determined to put a good face on everything before our fine English macaronis, and show that a Virginia gentleman is as good as the best of ’em. I wish, for the honour of old Virginia, that I had more to brag about. But all I can say in truth is, that we have been to France and come back again. Why, I don’t think even your tragick pen could make anything of such a campaign as ours has been. We landed on the 6 at Cancalle Bay, we saw a few dragons on a hill…’”

“There!” George broke off, laughing. “Did I not tell you there were dragons?”

“Mercy! What can he mean by dragons?” Hetty cried.

“Immense, long-tailed monsters, with steel scales on their backs, who vomit fire, and gobble up a virgin a day,” said papa. “Haven’t you read about them in The Seven Champions? Seeing St. George’s flag, I suppose, they slunk off.”

“I have read of ’em,” said the solemn little boy from the Chartreux. “They like to eat women. One was going to eat Andromeda, you know, papa; and Jason killed another, who was guarding the apple-tree.”

George went on: “‘…A few dragons on a hill,’ who rode away from us without engaging. We slept under canvass. We marched to St. Malo, and burned ever so many privateers there. And we went on board shipp again, without ever crossing swords with an enemy or meeting any except a few poor devils whom the troops plundered. Better luck next time! This hasn’t been very much nor particular glorious: but I have liked it for my part. I have smelt powder, besides a good deal of rosn and pitch we burned. I’ve seen the enemy; have sleppt under canvass, and been dredful crowdid and sick at sea. I like it. My best compliments to dear Aunt Lambert, and tell Miss Hetty I wasn’t very much fritened when I saw the French horse.—Your most affectionate brother, H. E. WARRINGTON.’”

One might have thought Miss Hetty’s conscience would have been soothed by the plain words—alive and hearty. It was not so. Relief did not come as a clean draught of water, but as a broth clouded with fear: warming, yet still full of floating specks. The war had put a new flavour into her blood, and she could not taste anything without tasting it.

Mr. Lambert, in the course of his duties, went to Portsmouth and the Isle of Wight; and George accompanied him. They found Harry wonderfully altered by his little campaign: the air and the movement and the rough fare had scoured the languor out of him as salt scours a pan. He was brisk, sun-touched, eager to learn, cheerful in camp like a boy turned loose into a hard but wholesome school. Under canvas, in glorious weather, he took to his new duties with a hunger that was not for food alone, but for action; and George, pacing the streets of the warlike town arm-in-arm with him, was amused to see this once listless coffee-house lounger now quickened and made sharp-edged by drums, marching, and the clean insistence of open air.

The nation too was in high spirits. This expedition had been no epic; yet London spoke of St. Malo as if Troy had been taken. We were said to have humbled the proud Gaul. We should have vanquished him, it was cried, had he dared to appear. Such bragging is not the monopoly of any time; every people has its trumpet, and every trumpet plays loudest when it is far from the smoke. Captured treasures were sent home and exhibited. More laurels were demanded. The army, like a table once set and found agreeable, was called for again: another course, another dish of glory.

With the new expedition sailed a volunteer so distinguished that all other amateur warriors must give place: the sailor Prince, His Royal Highness Prince Edward. He was conveyed aboard the Essex in the ship’s twelve-oared barge, the standard of England flying in the bow; the Admiral followed, and then the captains in seniority—a pageant of rank over the salt water, oars dipping with a steady, disciplined splash that made a music pleasant to hear, not like the grinding and hammering noises of a later age, but clean and measured, as if the sea itself were being stroked into obedience.

Away went the fleet. Harry, in high health and spirits, waved his hat to his friends cheering on the shore. His commission must come. George thought there could be no difficulty: there was money enough to buy an ensigncy if need be; but to win it without purchase—by gallantry and good conduct—would be best. The colonel reported well of him; men and officers liked him; there was promise in the young fellow’s bearing.

And then, ten days after the sailing, London rang with famous news. On the 7th and 8th of August, his Majesty’s troops had landed in the Bay des Marais, two leagues west of Cherbourg, in the face of a large body of the enemy. Awed by British valour, that large body vanished—so the story ran, and so stories always run when told far from the place where men actually sweat and bleed. Cherbourg surrendered at discretion; English colours flew upon three outlying forts. Seven-and-twenty ships were burned in the harbours; brass cannon in prodigious number were taken; iron guns destroyed; the basin (about which the French had bragged) demolished; the two piers at the harbour’s mouth ruined. London’s bells and London’s tongues were never tired.

Just as Mr. Howe’s guns arrived from Cherbourg, Mr. Wolfe’s colours taken at Louisbourg came too. The colours went from Kensington to St. Paul’s under escort—life-guards, horse-grenadiers, standards, kettle-drums, trumpets; and at the very minute they were received at the West Gate by the Dean and Chapter, the Tower and Park guns saluted—bang, bong, bung—till the very air shook with it. One could almost believe the city lived upon noise as upon bread, and that the loudness of its rejoicing was taken for the measure of its virtue; yet those who loved quieter sounds—kettle simmering, rain on a window, the steady chew of a contented household—might have thought such thunder a poor substitute for peace.

Next day came the procession of Cherbourg cannon and mortars—great pieces with carvings and flaunting emblems, lilies and crowns and mottoes. Here was the Téméraire, the Malfaisant, the Vainqueur (the Vainqueur indeed! a pretty conqueror of Britons!), and many more, trailed through the streets while people shouted till their throats were raw. In Dean Street, Mrs. Lambert and Hetty, in their tender ignorance, were half persuaded that Harry had taken every one of the guns himself—dragging them from batteries, scattering artillerymen like crumbs from a board. His name rose in their estimation as bread rises under a warm cloth.

Madame de Bernstein asked about him. Lady Maria begged her cousin George to see her and, if possible, bring news of his brother. George, who had been the head of the family a couple of months since, found himself deposed and of scarce any account in Miss Hetty’s eyes. Wit and learning and tragedies—what were these to victories and brass cannon? George bore his deposition with meekness. Fifteen thousand Britons! Why should they not march and take Paris? Nothing more probable, thought some of the ladies; and they embraced and congratulated one another, their cheeks glowing red as if lit from within by the same candles of joy that shone in their eyes. For once they almost longed Sir Miles and Lady Warrington were in town, that they might call and ask, “Well, what say you now? Has not your nephew taken twenty-one fine brass cannon, flung a hundred and twenty iron guns into the water, seized seven-and-twenty ships, and destroyed the basin and the two piers?”

But after fair weather comes cloud. Appetite grows by what it feeds on; and our commanders, thinking they had not feasted enough upon the plunder of St. Malo, went back. After a brief time at Portsmouth and the Wight, the conquerors of Cherbourg returned to that coast. They landed in the Bay of St. Lunar, marched towards St. Malo intending to destroy it this time; but the harbour of St. Lunar was found insecure, the fleet moved up to St. Cas to keep communication, and then—the British Lion found that St. Malo, which he had thought to swallow at a mouthful, was guarded by a French army brought up by the Governor of Brittany. The coup-de-main was impossible. The leaders marched back towards their ships lying in the Bay of St. Cas.

Hide, blushing glory, hide St. Cas’s day.

As the troops marched down to embark, they became aware of an army following—sent from Brest. Two-thirds of our troops, and all the artillery, were already aboard when the French came down upon the remainder. Four companies of the First Regiment of Guards and the grenadier companies faced about upon the beach, to wait the enemy while the boats carried off the rest.

As the French descended from the heights that ring the bay, our Guards and grenadiers marched out to attack them—leaving a strong position they had held, a great dyke raised on the shore behind which they might have made a stout defence. Then it was eleven hundred against six, nay ten times their number; and after a while the little line broke and ran for the boats—a sauve qui peut. Seven hundred out of the eleven hundred were killed, drowned, or taken. The General himself was killed. And—ah!—where were the volunteers?

A man of peace might confess that he thinks less of the engaged troops than of the people they leave behind. Jack the Guardsman and La Tulipe of the Royal Bretagne are face to face striving to knock each other’s brains out; that is their trade, as bears fight bears, as lions rend lions. But the girl of Tower Hill who hung about Jack’s neck before he marched away; the lass at Quimper who gave La Tulipe his brûle-gueule and tobacco-box before his noir trajet—what have those tender hearts done that they should pay so dear?

What a state must Miss Hetty Lambert be in, when she hears of the disaster at St. Cas and the slaughter of the grenadier companies! What doubt gnaws at George Warrington; what grief and helpless commiseration fills Martin Lambert as he looks into his child’s face and reads her piteous story there! Howe, brave Commodore, rowing in his barge under enemy fire, has rescued scores of our flying men. More are drowned; hundreds are prisoners, or shot upon the beach. Among these—where is our Virginian?

Great Powers! will the vanity of men—of Frenchmen above all—never tire? A rear-guard cut off upon a strip of sand; a handful of brave fellows hunted down by ten thousand, and because Fortune, who always snaps at the hindmost, took her usual toll, the gentlemen at Paris must needs blaze powder at the Invalides and make their old stone walls clap and thunder, as if cannon-bursts could translate slaughter into glory.

I had once a mind to draw—true to the life—an honest picture of London in her own triumphs: the polished guns dragged in show by sunburnt tars; the horse-grenadiers prancing, their cuirasses ringing; the mob roaring, cheering, and filching handkerchiefs with equal fervour; our friends in some Fleet Street balcony craning forward, blessing the spectacle of British success. But since the French have been so vulgar as to mimic the Tower’s fireworks with their own, setting up St. Cas against our St. Malo, I scorn the stale comparison. I say Nolo, not Malo; and I am content—content, at least—if Harry Warrington has come back from one expedition and t’other with a whole skin.

He did come back. The sea air had tanned him to the hue of well-browned crust; the salt had stiffened the seams of his gaiters, and left, in the folds of his coat and hair, that sharp, honest smell of brine and tar which clings to a man longer than praise or blame. A ball had whistled close by his side-curl and spared it; the ocean had taken his stockings for its own a dozen times over, but had not swallowed his body. He had, it is true, shown the lapels of his coat to the enemy—those reverses which coats, like men, are made to wear—yet for as short a time as possible, withdrawing out of their sight as quick as might be.

They were at table when he told it: the Lambert parlour full of the soft domestic stir that goes on even while men speak of death. In the pauses of his narrative one heard the small music of life—china set down, a spoon clicking the rim of a bowl, the kettle’s low murmur like a contented creature on the hob; from the street beyond the window, a cart-wheel’s creak and the distant call of a seller crying his wares. Such sounds, homely and unconsidered, seemed to argue against the roar of cannon as if peace were the older language and war a brutal dialect that could never quite master a hearth.
