“I can tell you,” said Harry, speaking with that plain exactness which belongs to men who have looked on a thing and do not embroider it, “we all had to run for it; and when our line broke, it was he who could get to the boats who was most lucky. The French horse and foot pursued us down to the sea, and were mingled among us, cutting our men down, and bayoneting them on the ground. Poor Armytage was shot in advance of me, and fell; and I took him up and staggered through the surf to a boat. It was lucky that the sailors in our boat weren’t afraid; for the shot were whistling about their ears, breaking the blades of their oars, and riddling their flag with shot; but the officer in command was as cool as if he had been drinking a bowl of punch at Portsmouth, which we had one on landing, I can promise you.”

At the word punch, Mrs. Lambert’s hand, which had been dividing a little triangle of candied peel for the syllabub, paused as though memory itself had tasted the thing: rum warmed with lemon and sugar, nutmeg grated fine as brown dust; the sort of bowl that, in happier hours, makes a company bold and merry. Yet Harry’s voice did not brighten; it was merely that soldier’s habit of fastening upon the familiar—upon a bowl on a table—when the mind has too much blood and shouting in it.

“Poor Sir John was less lucky than me,” he continued. “He never lived to reach the ship, and the service has lost a fine soldier, and Miss Howe a true gentleman to her husband. There must be these casualties, you see; and his brother gets the promotion—the baronetcy.”

“It is of the poor lady I am thinking,” says Miss Hetty Lambert—haply it is to her, and for her judgement, the volunteer chiefly tells his story—“and the King. Why did the King encourage Sir John Armytage to go? A gentleman could not refuse a command from such a quarter. And now the poor gentleman is dead! Oh, what a state his Majesty must be in!”

“I have no doubt his Majesty will be in a deep state of grief,” says papa, wagging his head; and there was in the old General’s voice that dry crackle which in a well-governed room is as audible as a snapped twig.

“Now you are laughing! Do you mean, sir, that when a gentleman dies in his service, almost at his feet, the King of England won’t feel for him?” Hetty asks, her colour rising quick as if some pepper had been put on her tongue. “If I thought that, I vow I would be for the Pretender!”

“The sauce-box would make a pretty little head for Temple Bar,” says the General, who could see her meaning behind her words, and knew well enough what tumult of remorse, consternation, and gratitude beat under the bodice that had driven Harry into danger and now thanked Heaven he came back. “No,” says he, “my dear. Were kings to weep for every soldier, what a life you would make for them! I think better of his Majesty than to suppose him so weak; and, if Miss Hester Lambert got her Pretender, I doubt whether she would be any the happier. That family was never famous for too much feeling.”

“But if the King sent Harry—I mean Sir John Armytage—actually to the war in which he lost his life, oughtn’t his Majesty to repent very much?” asks the young lady, catching herself, too late, on the name that mattered.

“If Harry had fallen, no doubt the court would have gone into mourning: as it is, gentlemen and ladies were in coloured clothes yesterday,” remarks the General.

“Why should we not make bonfires for a defeat, and put on sackcloth and ashes after a victory?” asks George Warrington, who sat opposite his brother, watching him with that quiet, elder-brother measure which is half pride and half rebuke. “I protest I don’t want to thank Heaven for helping us to burn the ships at Cherbourg.”

“Yes you do, George! Not that I have a right to speak, and you ain’t ever so much cleverer. But when your country wins you’re glad—I know I am. When I run away before Frenchmen I’m ashamed—I can’t help it, though I done it,” says Harry, and there was no swagger in the confession, only that grave honesty which is, in its way, courage. “It don’t seem to me right somehow that Englishmen should have to do it,” he added, very low.

George smiled; yet he did not choose to ask what, on the other hand, was the Frenchman’s opinion. Outside, the street’s noises went on: a hammer tapping, a dog barking, the faint chiming of a bell. How strange that men can lay waste a coast and then come home to listen to such small music, as though Providence had meant the world for kettles and conversations rather than cannon.

“’Tis a bad business,” continued Harry, “but ’tis lucky ’twas no worse. The story about the French is, that their Governor, the Duke of Aiguillon, was rather what you call a moistened chicken. Our whole retreat might have been cut off, only, to be sure, we ourselves were in a mighty hurry to move. The French local militia behaved famous, I am happy to say; and there was ever so many gentlemen volunteers with ’em, who showed, as they ought to do, in the front. They say the Chevalier of Tour d’Auvergne engaged in spite of the Duke of Aiguillon’s orders. Officers told us, who came off with a list of our prisoners and wounded to General Bligh and Lord Howe. He is a lord now, since the news came of his brother’s death to home, George. He is a brave fellow, whether lord or commoner.”

“And his sister, who was to have married poor Sir John Armytage, think what her state must be!” sighs Miss Hetty, who has grown of late so sentimental, and takes sorrow as some ladies take spices—eagerly, as if the stronger flavour made life truer.

“And his mother!” cries Mrs. Lambert. “Have you seen her ladyship’s address in the papers to the electors of Nottingham? ‘Lord Howe being now absent upon the publick service, and Lieutenant-Colonel Howe with his regiment at Louisbourg, it rests upon me to beg the favour of your votes and interests that Lieutenant-Colonel Howe may supply the place of his late brother as your representative in Parliament.’ Isn’t this a gallant woman?”

“A Laconic woman,” says George.

“How can sons help being brave who have been nursed by such a mother as that?” asks the General.

The two young men looked at each other.

“If one of us were to fall in defence of his country, we have a mother in Sparta who would think and write so too,” says George.

“If Sparta is anywhere Virginia way, I reckon we have,” remarks Mr. Harry, with that half-smile of his which does not quite know how to sit upon his face. “And to think that we should both of us have met the enemy, and both of us been whipped by him, brother!” he adds, pensively.

Hetty looks at him and cannot help seeing him only as he was—tottering through the water towards the boats, a comrade bleeding on his shoulder, the enemy pressing, the shot snapping and whining like angry wasps round his head. And it was she who drove him into the danger! Her words provoked him. He never rebukes her now he is returned. Except when asked, he scarcely speaks about his adventures at all. He is very grave and courteous with Hetty; with the rest of the family especially frank and tender. But those taunts of hers wounded him. “Little hand!” his looks and demeanour seem to say, “thou shouldst not have been lifted against me! It is ill to scorn any one, much more one who has been so devoted to you and all yours. I may not be over quick of wit, but in as far as the heart goes, I am the equal of the best, and the best of my heart your family has had.”

Harry was wrong—wrong in the judgement he had made of her steadiness, and wrong in the debt he thought her owing him; and yet his magnanimous endurance of the wrong served him to regain in Miss Hetty’s esteem that place which he had lost during the previous months’ inglorious idleness. The respect which the fair pay to the brave she gave him. She was no longer pert in her answers, or sarcastic in her observations regarding his conduct. In a word, she was a humiliated, an altered, an improved Miss Hetty.

And all the world seemed to change towards Harry, as he towards the world. He was no longer sulky and indolent: he no more desponded about himself, or defied his neighbours. The colonel of his regiment reported his behaviour as exemplary, and recommended him for one of the commissions vacated by the casualties during the expedition. Unlucky as its termination was, it at least was fortunate to him.

His brother-volunteers, when they came back to St. James’s Street, reported highly of his behaviour. These volunteers and their actions were the theme of everybody’s praise. Had he been a general commanding, and slain in the moment of victory, Sir John Armytage could scarce have had more sympathy than that which the nation showed him. The papers teemed with letters about him; and men of wit and sensibility vied with each other in composing epitaphs in his honour. The fate of his affianced bride was bewailed. She was, as we have said, the sister of the brave Commodore who had just returned from this unfortunate expedition, and succeeded to the title of his elder brother—an officer as gallant as himself—who had just fallen in America.

My Lord Howe was heard to speak in special praise of Mr. Warrington; and so Harry had a handsome share of the fashion and favour which the town now bestowed on the volunteers. Doubtless there were thousands of men employed who were as good as they; but the English ever love their gentlemen, and love that they should distinguish themselves; and these volunteers were voted Paladins and heroes by common accord. As our young noblemen will, they accepted their popularity very affably. White’s and Almack’s illuminated when they returned; St. James’s embraced its young knights.

Harry was restored to full favour amongst them. Their hands were held out eagerly to him again. Even his relations congratulated him; and there came a letter from Castlewood, whither Aunt Bernstein had by this time betaken herself, containing praises of his valour, and a pretty little bank-bill, as a token of his affectionate aunt’s approbation. This was under my Lord Castlewood’s frank, who sent his regards to both his kinsmen, and an offer of the hospitality of his country-house, if they were minded to come to him.

And besides this, there came to him a private letter through the post—not very well spelt, but in a handwriting which Harry smiled to see again—in which his affectionate cousin, Maria Esmond, told him she always loved to hear his praises (which were in everybody’s mouth now), and sympathised in his good or evil fortune; and that, whatever occurred to him, she begged to keep a little place in his heart. Parson Sampson, she wrote, had preached a beautiful sermon about the horrors of war, and the noble actions of men who volunteered to face battle and danger in the service of their country. Indeed, the chaplain wrote himself, presently, a letter full of enthusiasm, in which he saluted Mr. Harry as his friend, his benefactor, his glorious hero.

Even Sir Miles Warrington despatched a basket of game from Norfolk: and one bird (shot sitting), with love to my cousin, had a string and paper round the leg, and was sent as the first victim of young Miles’s fowling-piece. When the hamper was opened in Southampton Row, the room filled at once with the green, woodland smell of feathers and cold earth; and Mrs. Lambert, ever mistress of the house’s small ceremonies, began at once to contrive how it should be roasted so the skin might crackle and the flesh stay juicy—how a pinch of salt, rubbed in with a firm hand, and a little butter slipped under the breast, could turn even a dead creature into comfort for the living. Such is the way of households: they season grief with supper, and keep memory alive by feeding it.

And presently, with joy beaming in his countenance, Mr. Lambert came to visit his young friends at their lodgings, and announced that Mr. Henry Warrington was forthwith to be gazetted as Ensign in the Second Battalion of Kingsley’s, the 20th Regiment, which had been engaged in the campaign, and which now at this time was formed into a separate regiment, the 67th. Its colonel was not with his regiment during its expedition to Brittany. He was away at Cape Breton, and was engaged in capturing those guns at Louisbourg, of which the arrival in England had caused such exultation.

In that great menagerie in the Regent’s Park—where London keeps its captives in cages and calls the place instruction—I stood one damp afternoon with my ear turned as much to the tanks as to my own thoughts. The aquarium has its own weather: a cool breath smelling of wet slate, river-weed, and that faint metallic tang you catch when a cook draws a knife along a fish’s backbone. The place is never silent. Water is a talker. It keeps up a continual hush and swash against glass, and every bubble that rises snaps like a tiny bead of glass between the teeth. Against that soft, sane music—so different from the city’s hammering wheels and shrieked hawkers—one may feel the mind unclench.

A broad fish, brown as baked crust on one side and pale as milk on the other, slid through the green light with a grace that would have made a dancing-master jealous. He turned his glistening dark back, then showed the clean white of his breast; his fins, fanning, were as neat as a cook’s wrist when she skims a broth. And this admirable motion-master, this smooth curving creature, turned out—when I read his little label—to be no prince of the sea at all, but our old homely acquaintance the flounder.

Why, we have all swallowed him at Greenwich, soused in his bath with herbs and wine, and never once suspected the beauty that lived in him. We know him only as a dish—water-souchy, with parsley and a sting of lemon, the liquor pale and fragrant, the fish tender enough to part under the spoon; we praise the cook, and forget the creature. Yet here, in his right element, he was a marvel. Take him out, lay him on boards, and he becomes a grotesque thing, flapping, disgraced, his very shape an accusation against the unfeeling air; he gasps his last as a man does when the world has stolen his proper language from him, and he is left only with the harsh syllables of strangers.

There is a proverb about fish out of water. I dare say I am not the first naturalist to discover it. But looking at that flounder, sleek in his native green, I could not help thinking of Harry Warrington, who had been floundering—poor fellow—for many a month, knocked about on dry land, made ridiculous by circumstances, and half stifled by them. Now, by a touch upon his shoulder—no more than the tap of an epaulet—he had found his true element. Health and spirits came back to him as flavour returns to a sauce the moment you put the right herb into the pot.

He delighted in soldiering, as if the very smell of pipeclay and leather, the brassy reek of powder, the hot iron breath of cannon, were a nourishment his blood had long been wanting. He went into the new trade with that hungry, eager quickness with which a born cook learns a kitchen: not merely tasting, but mastering—learning where everything lies, how the day is paced, what must be done first and what last, and which little negligence will spoil the whole. Had I the art of my friend Lorrequer, I would carry you into camp, and show you the other Harry in his proper colours: on march and parade; at mess when the beef is carved and the claret passed; under tents where the canvas keeps out rain no better than a poor lid keeps in steam; in the bustle of orders, the clink of accoutrements, the many-voiced life of a regiment. But I have no such skill, and can only bid you imagine him—Mr. Harry Warrington—in his new red coat and yellow facings, happy to bear the King’s colours, and pleased to learn and do the duties of his calling.

George, who had always honoured his brother’s better qualities even while they vexed him, was proud and thankful in his heart to see Harry so restored. He wrote to their mother in Virginia with a warmth of praise which Harry’s own modesty would never have allowed him to repeat. He told her how Harry had won his first step by his own gallantry; and George added that he wished her leave to share with her the expense of buying a higher rank for him. He could not bear, he said, that Harry should suffer in purse from a mistake which had not been of Harry’s making. While George had been believed dead, Harry had naturally thought himself heir, and had lived with an expenditure he never would have ventured on had he known he was but younger son. George called it only fair that he should contribute liberally now—almost as a thank-offering for his own return to life—to any plan for Harry’s advantage.

Then George, having set his brother’s affairs in order upon paper, came to that part which pressed nearest his own heart. He reminded his mother how the best friends the brothers had found in England were Mr. and Mrs. Lambert—Mrs. Lambert an old schoolfellow of Madam Esmond’s. Where blood relations had been worldly and unfeeling, these friends had been steadfast. The General was respected in the army and beloved by all who knew him; and Mrs. Lambert’s tenderness towards Madam Esmond’s sons had been like a mother’s. Now, George wrote, he had formed an attachment for the elder Miss Lambert—Miss Theodora—on which he believed the happiness of his life depended, and he implored his mother’s approval. He had not yet made formal offers; but he owned that he had done little to disguise his sentiments, and that the young lady, and her parents too, seemed favourable. He dwelt—like a man who has found his very bread after famine—on the girl’s goodness: she had been so admirable and exemplary a daughter to her own mother that he was sure she would do her duty by his. In short, Mr. Warrington painted her as perfection, and declared, with the entire solemnity of a man who has at last put a name to his hunger, that to win or lose her would be to be happy or wretched.

Why do I not produce this letter?—some tender reader may ask, for I have said I possess the Warrington papers. Because there is a kind of theft that is committed not with hands but with eyes and ears. It is cruel to babble the secrets of a young man’s love; to overhear his incoherent vows, to pin down with cold ink the wild, hot raptures that were meant to vanish into the air between two people only. Shall we count sighs as if they were coins? bottle tears as if they were cordial? Love—when it is real—is sacred. Wherever one sees it (and sometimes, Heaven knows, one may in this world) shooting suddenly out of two pairs of eyes; or looking sadly even from one pair; or dropping from a mother to the baby in her lap; or shining from a father as he watches his girl whirl round the room with the captain; or warming the old man’s gaze when the bonne vieille comes in—wherever that signal burns, let us salute it and pass on.

While Harry’s love had led him to the smell of powder, and to rush upon dragoons with a relish as if danger were spice, George had been engaged in an amusement far more peaceful to his nature. He was courting.

There are courtships which are carried on like campaigns, with loud trumpets and banners; and there are those which go on as quietly as a well-managed household meal—daily, necessary, full of small attentions that make the difference between mere sustenance and comfort. George’s belonged to the latter. He found pretexts as a clever cook finds uses for every scrap: a note to send that did not seem to ask for an answer, yet got one; a book to lend; a quotation from a favourite poet to copy out; flowers out of Covent Garden chosen not by show, but by scent and meaning—violets still cool from the morning, jonquils sharp as a fresh-peeled lemon, roses heavy and bruising their own perfume. In summer there were schemes without end: Ranelagh, Hampstead, Vauxhall, Marylebone Gardens; and always Gumbo and Sady—his negro servants—trotting between Southampton Row and Dean Street, carrying parcels and little messages as dutifully as errand-boys run between kitchen and pantry.

George wanted his famous tragedy copied out fair for the stage, and who could write such an Italian hand as Miss Theo? The pages passed to and fro, and with them went little notes—thanks, questions, admiration—always something. He walked to St. James’s Church and, by good luck, found himself singing from the same Prayer-book as she; and he never heard a word of the sermon, so loud were his own thoughts. He made himself prodigiously agreeable to all her relations—to the little brother and sister at school; to the elder at college; to Miss Hetty, with whom he fenced in bright passages of wit; and to mamma, who, Martin Lambert says, was half in love with him herself. For if fathers are sometimes sulky at the approach of a destined son-in-law, mothers are apt to become sentimental, and to taste their own youth again, as one tastes a dish long absent from the table and finds it stirs a whole buried season.

Here in my hands, indeed, is a packet marked in George’s neat writing: “T’s letters, 1758-9.” Shall we open it? No. Those words were whispered for one ear. Years later, when they were husband and wife, he might read them with sweet pangs as one smells, in an old chest, the faint ghost of lavender and remembers a room that is gone. But to spread them before strangers would be sacrilege. Take it on trust that the young lady’s letters were modest and pure, the gentleman’s respectful and tender.

In these last months, George Warrington had made up his mind that he had found the woman of women. She might not be the most beautiful—there was Cousin Flora, there were Coelia and Ardelia and a hundred more with brighter faces—but Theo’s sweet countenance pleased him beyond all. She might not be the most clever; yet her voice was the dearest to his ear, and—what is the strangest alchemy of love?—in her company he felt himself cleverer than ever before. Words came to him; fine thoughts; wit; generosity; a noble ease. And as for the young lady—thank Heaven I never thought so ill of women as to suppose them just—we may be sure she endowed her young hero with every excellence in the calendar, not excepting those he had never shown to anyone else.

When George’s letter reached Virginia, it set a little stir going round Madam Esmond’s fireside. So he was in love and wished to marry! It seemed natural enough; and, to a mother, there is comfort in seeing a son’s passion take a lawful road, and keep him out of the snares that lie for young men in town and camp. If he was to unite himself with a well-bred Christian young woman, Madam saw no harm.

“I knew they would be setting their caps at him,” says Mountain.

“They fancy his wealth is as great as his estate. He does not say whether the young lady has money. I fear otherwise.”

“People would set their caps at him here, I dare say,” Madam Esmond answered, grimly turning her eyes upon her dependant, “and try and catch Mr. Esmond Warrington for their own daughters, who are no richer than Miss Lambert may be.”

“I suppose your ladyship means me!” cries Mountain. “My Fanny is poor, as you say; and ’tis kind of you to remind me of her poverty!”

“I said people would set their caps at him. If the cap fits you, tant pis! as my papa used to say.”

“You think, madam, I am scheming to keep George for my daughter? I thank you, on my word! A good opinion you seem to have of us after the years we have lived together!”

“My dear Mountain, I know you much better than to suppose you could ever fancy your daughter would be a suitable match for a gentleman of Mr. Esmond’s rank and station,” says Madam, with a stately severity.

“Fanny Parker was as good as Molly Benson at school, and Mr. Mountain’s daughter is as good as Mr. Lambert’s!” Mrs. Mountain cries.

“Then you did think of marrying her to my son! I shall write to Mr. Esmond Warrington, and say how sorry I am that you should be disappointed!” cries the mistress of Castlewood.

And, for our parts, we may suppose Mrs. Mountain was disappointed and had entertained ambitious views for her girl; else why flare so angrily at the bare notion of George’s marriage?

Madam Esmond wrote back to her son that she was pleased with the brotherly love he showed; that it was right, indeed, to compensate Harry in some measure, since Harry’s expectations had led him into a costlier way of living than he would have adopted had he known his true place. Concerning the purchase of promotion, she would gladly halve the expense with George, thanking God to think Harry’s courage had won him his first step. George’s money spent thus, she added, was much more satisfactory than certain other extravagances to which she would not advert.

The extravagance she would not name was the ransom paid to the French captain’s family—an act George had done from his own stubborn honour, and to which his mother would never consent. She had a determined spirit of her own, which her son inherited; and what she called pride and obstinacy in him, she likely called firmness in herself. People a hundred years ago, I dare say, resembled their grandchildren: loving their own way mightily, and thinking it a virtue.

After paying his own ransom, his brother’s debts, and now half the price of Harry’s promotion, George saw that no small portion of his private patrimony would be swallowed up. Yet he made the sacrifice with a perfectly good heart. His mother’s letters were always urging him to remember who his grandfather was, and to support the dignity of the family accordingly. She sent him commissions for purchases in England; and though she had yet sent him but trifling remittances, she wrote so constantly of the exalted rank of the Esmonds, so peremptorily advised him to appear in the first society, to frequent the Court where his ancestors had moved, and to live always in a manner worthy of his name, that George never doubted her money would come when his ran short. He obeyed her injunctions in his style of life as dutifully as he obeyed her orders when she asked for goods.

In the papers of this period I find bills enough: for entertainments and genteel suppers where the meats were no doubt handsomely served; for court suits and lace; for liveries for his negro servants and chairmen; horse-dealers’ receipts, and so forth. Thus I am led to believe that the elder of our Virginians lived, after a while, at considerable expense. He was not wild like Harry; there was no talk of gambling or racehorses against Mr. George. But his table was liberal, his equipages handsome, his purse seemed always full; the estate to which he was heir was known to be immense.

I mention these things because they may have influenced the conduct of George and his friends in the very affair about which he had been writing. The young heir of Virginia travelled for pleasure and improvement; the queen-mother at home wrote daily, bidding him act as became his lofty station. There could be no doubt, from her letters, that she desired he should live magnificently. He was perpetually making purchases at her order. She had lately written for twelve new sets of waggon harness, and an organ that should play fourteen specified psalm-tunes; and these articles George dutifully ordered, as a son obeys even when he does not quite see the sense. She had not paid as yet, and might not pay to-day or to-morrow; but eventually, of course, she would—so George believed. And he never thought of troubling his friends with such calculations, or of discussing with them his mother’s domestic economy.

They, on their side, took it for granted that he was in competence and ease; and Mr. and Mrs. Lambert, without being mercenary, were no doubt pleased to see an attachment growing between their daughter and a young gentleman of such good principles, talents, family, and expectations.

There was honesty in all Mr. Esmond Warrington’s words and acts; and in his behaviour to the world a certain grandeur and simplicity which showed him to be a true gentleman. Somewhat cold, even haughty, towards strangers—especially towards the great—he was never supercilious. Towards women he was perfectly courteous; and with those he loved he could be kind, lively, tender—warm as a hearth when the day has been raw.

No wonder that one young woman we know of came to think him the best man in all the world—alas! not even excepting papa. A great love felt by a man towards a woman makes him better, as regards her, than all other men. George himself used to marvel at his own eloquence when he talked with the fair creature whose heart had become all his.

But we will not listen again at the keyhole. Soft words do not bear being written down. If you are sentimentally inclined—sir, or madam—lay the book aside and remember your own. You may be ever so old now; but you remember. It may be dead and buried; yet in a moment it springs up, looks, smiles, whispers as of old, clings to your arm, and drops its fresh tears upon your heart. Here is the vase, but the roses are gone; here is the shore, and yonder the ship was moored; but the anchors are up, and it has sailed away.

Et cetera.

This, however, is mere sentimentality; and as regards George and Theo is neither here nor there. What I mean to say is that the young lady’s family were perfectly satisfied with the state of affairs between her and Mr. Warrington; and though he had not yet asked the decisive question, everybody else knew what the answer would be when it came.

Mamma perhaps thought the question a long time coming.

“Psha! my dear,” says the General. “There is time enough in all conscience. Theo is not much more than seventeen; George, if I mistake not, is under forty; and, besides, he must have time to write to Virginia and ask mamma.”

“But suppose she refuses?”

“That will be a bad day for old and young,” says the General. “Let us rather say—suppose she consents, my love? I can’t fancy anybody in the world refusing Theo anything she has set her heart on,” adds the father; “and I am sure ’tis bent upon this match.”

So they waited with an anxiety that sat at table with them and went upstairs at night; they listened for every knock, as a house listens for a long-expected cart upon the road. And they trembled lest French privateers should take the packet-ship that carried, across all that loud and perilous water, the precious letter from Madam Esmond.

Colonel Wolfe, whom Harry now served under, came back from America a few weeks after our Virginian had taken his place in the regiment. He had been lieutenant-colonel of Kingsley’s, and, after Cape Breton, had his reward in a second battalion. Harry went to him with honest respect; for already London began to listen when Wolfe spoke, and to look when he entered a room. The town had grown hungry for victories, and for a captain to feed that hunger. Certain great names had lately proved but thin fare in the field; and the nation, like a company kept too long from table, turned its eyes towards the one man who seemed to promise a full, hot serving of glory.

Wolfe and General Lambert were both detained in London by business; so their friendly commerce renewed itself, and no one was more rejoiced than Lambert at his young friend’s good fortune. Harry, when he could steal an hour from duty, never tired of hearing Wolfe tell the story of last year’s campaigns. Wolfe spoke as freely as a man carving at his own board—no secret hoarding of the best morsel, no false seasoning for effect; whatever lay in his mind he set down plainly, with that heroic simplicity which makes bravery seem almost domestic. Some of the powdered gentlemen at St. James’s, accustomed to talk that was all garnish and no meat, might lift a sneer at his openness; but among our little circle his words found ears that loved honest sound—Lambert’s deep, measured assent, Harry’s quick breath now and again, the faint scrape of a chair as a listener leaned in. Even the room’s noises—coal settling in the grate, a footman passing with the soft clink of glass—seemed to fall into a kind of respectful hush when the young soldier, glowing with his own vision, spoke of war as if it were a crusade.

He had, too, the romance of a boy in him. Poetry and music pleased him; he would quote plays with the relish of a man tasting a dish he loves and cannot keep from praising. On the last day of his life, they say, he would rather have written Gray’s Elegy than have won a battle; and we may be sure that with such a taste he and George Warrington found easy fellowship. They were both lovers, both accepted, both in that warm, unreasonable weather when every common thing—an errand, a letter, a shared walk—takes on an air of destiny. Their sentimental talk would be worth setting down, if we had it truly. In one of his later letters Warrington writes, speaking of Wolfe:

“I had the honour of knowing the famous General Wolfe, and seeing much of him during his last stay in London. We had a subject of conversation then which was of unfailing interest to both of us, and I could not but admire Mr. Wolfe’s simplicity, his frankness, and a sort of glorious bravery which characterised him. He was much in love, and he wanted heaps and heaps of laurels to take to his mistress. ‘If it be a sin to covet honour,’ he used to say with Harry the Fifth (he was passionately fond of plays and poetry), ‘I am the most offending soul alive.’ Surely on his last day he had a feast which was enough to satisfy the greediest appetite for glory. He hungered after it. He seemed to me not merely like a soldier going resolutely to do his duty, but rather like a knight in quest of dragons and giants. My own country has furnished of late a chief of a very different order, and quite an opposite genius. I scarce know which to admire most. The Briton’s chivalrous ardour, or the more than Roman constancy of our great Virginian.”

As Lambert’s duties kept him in London, his family remained with him, content enough in their quiet corner of Southampton Row, where Bedford Gardens, when the season was kind, offered a little country to the eye—trees that held birdsong as if it were a possession, and flower-beds that, at dusk, breathed out damp earth and crushed green. George, too, appeared satisfied with this rural calm set inside the city’s clatter; he made his pilgrimage to Castlewood and passed a few days there, sleeping in the chamber of which he had so often heard his grandfather speak, the very room where Colonel Esmond had slept as a boy. He was received civilly by such of the family as were at home; the ladies were gracious, Lady Maria especially so, and the whole house was entertained when George and Parson Sampson read aloud the tragedy to them.

Sampson, who had the zeal of a man who finds his own youth again in another’s promise, praised it with a fervour that would not be denied; and it was through the chaplain’s pushing, more than through Mr. Johnson’s patronage after all, that Mr. Warrington’s piece ever came upon the stage. Mr. Johnson did press the play upon Mr. Garrick for Drury Lane; but Garrick had made his arrangement with Mr. Home, and so Carpezan went to Mr. Rich at Covent Garden and was accepted.

On the night of the first performance George gave an elegant entertainment to his friends at the Bedford Head in Covent Garden—an inn where roasted meats, hot from the spit, sent their rich steam into the passages, and the air was laced with wine, lemon-peel, and the faint sour of beer. From that table they went in a body to the theatre, leaving George behind with one or two companions; he stayed at the coffee-house like a general before a battle, receiving messengers from the front. Friends came and went with tidings—now hopeful, now doubtful—each report bringing with it the roar of the house as if the sound itself had travelled down the street and shaken the panes.

Barry played Carpezan; Shuter, the old nobleman; Reddish, it need scarcely be said, made an excellent Ulric. The King of Bohemia was a young actor from Dublin, Mr. Geoghegan—Hagan, as he called himself on the stage—who looked and performed the part to admiration. Mrs. Woffington, as the heroine, seemed too old in the first act; there were whispers about it, the sort of whispers that run through an audience like a draft under a door. But her murder in the fourth act—about which great doubts had been expressed—went off with terror and delight. Miss Wayn sang the ballad—supposed to be sung by the king’s page—just at the moment of the unhappy wife’s execution. The song’s sweetness, set against the scene’s cruelty, made the pit shiver; and all agreed that Barry was terrible and pathetic as Carpezan, most of all in the execution scene. The grace and elegance of young Hagan won general applause.

Mr. Rich had put the piece upon the stage with elegance; though some were doubtful whether, in the march of Janissaries at the last, he was correct in introducing a favourite elephant that had figured in various pantomimes. One of Mr. Warrington’s black servants marched beside it in Turkish habit, a splash of colour amid the painted barbaric splendour; the other sat in the footman’s gallery and wept and applauded uproariously at the proper moments. There is a kind of theatre-noise—hand on hand like hail, feet stamping, laughter bursting and then strangling itself—that can make the heart feel as if it were being beaten in a mortar. George, in his coffee-house exile, heard it only as a rumour, and each time the sound rose, he tasted it like a draught he could not see: bitter when it seemed uncertain, sweet when the messengers smiled.

The execution of Sybilla was the turning-point. Her head once off, George’s friends breathed more freely, and one messenger after another came to him to announce complete success. Mr. Barry, amid general applause, announced the play for repetition, and declared it to be the work of a young gentleman of Virginia, his first attempt in dramatic style.

We should like to have sat in the box where all our friends were gathered and watched Theo’s fluttering anxiety while the piece hung in doubt, to have seen the blush rise and the light kindle in her eyes when the victory was assured. Harry, during that trouble in the fourth act, was deadly pale—whiter, Mrs. Lambert said, than Barry with all his chalk. But when the curtain fell, if Briareus could have clapped, he could scarcely have made more noise than Harry. Wolfe and General Lambert huzzaed like schoolboys turned loose; Mrs. Lambert cried, as was her happy fashion. Hetty, practical in her own fierce way, asked: “Why do you cry, mamma? You don’t want any of them alive again; you know it serves them all right.” Yet even she was delighted—almost as much as little Charley from the Charterhouse, who had leave for that evening from Dr. Crusius, and as Miss Lucy, brought from her boarding-school on purpose to see the great occasion. My Lord Castlewood and Lady Maria were present, and his lordship went from his box to compliment Mr. Barry and the actors upon the stage. Parson Sampson, invaluable in the pit, led the applause, having, it was believed, instructed Gumbo beforehand to keep an eye upon him from the gallery and do as he did.

There was supper that night—many suppers—and London did what it always does when it is pleased: it ate and drank to prove the pleasure real. Mr. Gumbo gave an entertainment to several gentlemen of the shoulder-knot who had supported his master’s masterpiece; Harry gave a supper at the Star and Garter in Pall Mall to ten officers of his new regiment, who had come up expressly to back Carpezan. And finally George received the three principal actors, the family party from the side-box, Mr. Johnson and his ingenious friend Mr. Reynolds the painter, my Lord Castlewood and Lady Maria, and one or two more.

The supper-room had that particular smell of late festivity—meat cooling, candles guttering, citrus crushed into punch, and the faint burnt sweetness where sugar has been carelessly scorched at the edge of a bowl. Glass rang; chairs scraped; laughter came in gusts. When the toasts began, Lady Maria gaily gave “The King of Hungary” for hers, meaning the actor who had played the King. He had eloquence and fire, and excellent manners off the stage as well as on it; and, having already swallowed enough wine and punch to set his blood singing louder than the company, he protested that he had suffered death that night and hoped to die a hundred times more on the same field; but dead or living, he vowed he knew whose humble servant he should ever be. Ah, if he had but a true crown instead of his tinsel diadem, with what joy would he lay it at her ladyship’s feet! Neither my lord nor Mr. Esmond relished this exceeding gallantry; they attributed much of it, no doubt rightly, to the drink. Theo and her sister, new to the world, were a little frightened by the young man’s energy; but Lady Maria, practised in society’s noises—the false thunder of compliments, the mercenary softness of vows—took it in good part.

At a late hour coaches were called; the gentlemen attended the ladies down. After the ladies’ departure some returned to the supper-room again, as men will, to finish what they began and to begin anew what they should end. The end of it was that Carpezan had to be carried away in a chair; that the King of Hungary woke with a cruel headache; and that the Poet—who remembered making a great number of speeches—was quite astounded when half a dozen guests appeared at his house next day, whom he had invited overnight to come and sup once more.

When George put Mrs. Lambert and her daughters into their coach after the play, all the ladies were flurried, delighted, excited; and you may be sure he was with them the next day, turning the event over and over like a cherished flavour that lingers and will not be lost—this moment in the fourth act, that roar after the song, the look on Barry’s face, the sudden hush before the stroke, the wave of sound as the house surrendered. Mrs. Lambert had heard that actresses were dangerous company for young men; she hoped George would have a care and not frequent the greenroom too much.

George smiled and said he had a preventive against all greenroom temptations and was not in the least afraid; and as he spoke he looked in Theo’s face as if those clear eyes were the amulet that would keep him safe.

“Why should he be afraid, mamma?” asked the maiden simply. She had no notion of guile. To her, the world’s voices—applause, praise, a lover’s vow—still sounded like what they pretended to be.

“No, my darling, I don’t think he need be afraid,” said the mother, and kissed her.

“You don’t suppose Mr. George would fall in love with that painted old creature who performed the chief part?” cried Miss Hetty, with a toss of her head. “She must be old enough to be his mother.”

“Pray, do you suppose that at our age nobody can care for us, or that we have no hearts left?” asked mamma sharply. “I believe—or I may say I hope and trust—your father thinks otherwise. He is, I imagine, perfectly satisfied, miss. He does not sneer at age, whatever little girls out of the schoolroom may do. And they had much better be back there, and they had much better remember what the fifth commandment is—that they had, Hetty!”

“I didn’t think I was breaking it by saying that an actress was as old as George’s mother,” pleaded Hetty.

“George’s mother is as old as I am, miss!—at least she was when we were at school. And Fanny Parker—Mrs. Mountain who now is—was seven months older, and we were in the French class together; and I have no idea that our age is to be made the subject of remarks and ridicule by our children, and I will thank you to spare it, if you please! Do you consider your mother too old, George?”

“I am glad my mother is of your age, Aunt Lambert,” said George, with the most sentimental gravity.

Strange infatuation of passion! singular perversity of reason! There is a time—before marriage, often—when a man is actually fond of his mother-in-law. At this time the good General vowed, with some reason, that he was jealous. Mrs. Lambert made more of George than of any person in the family. She dressed Theo to the utmost advantage when he was expected; she was always caressing her, always appealing to her when he spoke. It was, “Don’t you think he looks well?”—“Don’t you think he looks pale, Theo, to-day?”—“Don’t you think he has been sitting up too much over his books at night?” If he had a cold, she would have liked to make him gruel herself and see his feet in hot water. She sent him little receipts for his health, penned with the care of a housewife whose love expresses itself in barley and lemon and proper measure. When he was away, she never stopped talking about him to her daughter; and Miss Theo, no doubt, found the subject agreeable.

When George came, Mrs. Lambert was always wanted for some moment in another part of the house and would bid Theo take care of him till she returned. Why, before she reappeared, you could hear her outside the door talking to her youngest children, to servants in the upper regions, making little harmless noises of household management that served as a curtain. When she came back, was not Mr. George always at a decent distance from Miss Theo—except, to be sure, on that one day when she happened to drop her scissors and he naturally stooped to pick them up? Why was she blushing? Are not youthful cheeks made to blush, and roses to bloom in spring? Mamma never noted blushes; she only began some artless talk and sat down to her work-table brimful of happiness.

At last there came a letter from Virginia in Madam Esmond’s neat, well-known hand, and George trembled and blushed before he broke the seal. It answered his letter respecting Harry’s commission and his own attachment to Miss Lambert. Of his intentions regarding Harry, Madam Esmond fully approved. As for his marriage, she was not against early unions. She would take his picture of Miss Lambert with the allowance that must be made for lovers’ portraits, and hoped, for his sake, that the young lady was all he described her. With money, as she gathered from his letter, Miss Lambert did not appear to be provided at all; which was a pity, as though wealthy in land, the family had little ready cash. However, by Heaven’s blessing there was plenty at home for children and children’s children; and the wives of her sons should share all she had. When she heard more at length from Mr. and Mrs. Lambert, she would reply more fully. She did not pretend she had not once held greater hopes for her son, who by name and prospects might aspire to the first lady in the land; but as Heaven had willed his choice should fall upon her old friend’s daughter, she acquiesced and would welcome George’s wife as her own child.

The letter was brought by Mr. Van den Bosch of Albany, who had lately bought a very large estate in Virginia and was bound for England to place his granddaughter at a boarding-school. Madam Esmond—no mercenary woman, she said—did not urge attentions to Mr. Van den Bosch merely because the young lady was heiress of a great fortune. Their properties lay close together; and could Harry find in the young lady those qualities of person and mind suitable for a companion for life, Madam Esmond would have the satisfaction of seeing both her children near her in declining years. She ended by sending affectionate compliments to Mrs. Lambert, from whom she begged to hear further, and her blessing to the young lady who was to be her daughter-in-law.

The letter was not cordial; the writer seemed but half satisfied. Yet such as it was, her consent was formally announced. How eagerly George ran away to Soho with the long-desired news burning in his pocket! Mrs. Lambert, reading his face before he spoke, took her daughter’s hand and kissed it with uncommon warmth when he said he had received letters from home. Then, with a break in his voice and a tremor he could not command, George turned to Mr. Lambert.

“Madam Esmond’s letter, sir, is in reply to one of mine, in which I acquainted her that I had formed an attachment in England, for which I asked my mother’s approval. She gives her consent, I am grateful to say, and I have to pray my dear friends to be equally kind to me.”

“God bless thee, my dear boy!” cried the good General, laying a hand on the young man’s head. “I am glad to have thee for a son, George. There, there, don’t go down on your knees, young folks! George may, to be sure, and thank God for giving him the best little wife in all England. Yes, my dear, except when you were ill, you never caused me a heartache—and happy is the man, I say, who wins thee!”

No doubt the young people knelt, as was the fashion; and we may be perfectly certain Mrs. Lambert kissed both and bedewed her pocket-handkerchief plentifully. Hetty was not present at this sentimental scene; and when she heard of it she spoke with asperity and a laugh not pleasant.

“Is this all the news you have to give me? Why, I have known it these months past. Do you think I have no eyes to see, and no ears to hear, indeed?”

Yet in private she was gentler. She flung herself upon her sister’s neck, embraced her passionately, vowed that never, never would Theo find any one to love her as her sister did. With Theo she became mild and humble. She could not always abstain from jest and satire with George; but he was too happy to heed much, and too generous not to see the jealousy beneath her sharpness.

When all parties came to read Madam Esmond’s letter carefully, they found it, in truth, vague. It promised only that she would receive the young people in her house; there was no proposal for a settlement. The General shook his head. He had not thought to examine the words so closely until some days after the engagement; now, reading them, he found small encouragement there.

“Bah!” said George. “I shall have three hundred pounds for my tragedy. I can easily write a play a year; and if the worst comes to the worst, we can live on that.”

“On that and your patrimony,” said Theo’s father.

George had to explain, with some hesitation, that what with paying bills for his mother, and Harry’s commission and debts, and his own ransom—his patrimony proper was well-nigh spent.

Mr. Lambert’s face grew graver at this; but he saw his girl’s eyes turn upon him with such tender alarm that he took her into his arms and vowed that, let the worst come to the worst, his darling should not be balked of her wish.

As for returning to Virginia, George frankly owned he liked the notion little—going back to be entirely dependent on his mother. He gave the General some idea of his home life and spoke plainly of how little slavery suited his taste. No: why should he not stay in England, write more tragedies, study for the bar, gain a place—perhaps? Why indeed? He began straightway to form a plan for another play. From time to time he brought portions of it to Miss Theo and her sister. Hetty yawned over the work; Theo declared it more beautiful even than the last, which was perfection.

Their engagement was made known to their families, and Sir Miles Warrington received a ceremonious letter from his nephew. For a while Sir Miles saw no particular objection—though, to be sure, considering the name and prospects, Mr. Warrington might have looked higher. The truth was Sir Miles imagined Madam Esmond had made a considerable settlement on her son and that his circumstances were more than easy. But when he heard George was entirely dependent upon his mother, and that his own small patrimony was dissipated, as Harry’s had been before, Sir Miles’s indignation knew no bounds. He could not find words enough for his horror at the want of principle in these unhappy young men. He thought it his duty to speak his mind and wrote his opinion to his sister in Virginia.

As for General and Mrs. Lambert, who passed for respectable persons, was it to be borne that such people should inveigle a penniless young man into marriage with their penniless daughter? Sir Miles fully explained his views to Madam Esmond; he gave George but half a finger when his nephew called; he did not even invite him to partake of the famous family small-beer. Toward Harry he somewhat unbent; Harry had done his duty in the campaign and was mentioned with praise in high quarters. He had sown his wild oats—he at least seemed to endeavour to amend. But George, in Sir Miles’s view, was a prodigal fast careering to ruin; and his name was mentioned in the family with a groan. Lady Warrington prayed for him as for a dangerous reprobate. And all the while George walked the town unconscious that he occasioned so much wrath and so much devotion.

He took little Miley to the play and brought him home again; he sent tickets to his aunt and cousins which they could not refuse without making the breach too marked. So they took the tickets, and when country constituents came to town they asked him for more—taking care, however, to give the very worst motives to his intimacy with the theatre, and to suppose he and the actresses were upon terms of disgraceful familiarity. When an august personage went to the theatre and expressed approbation of Mr. Warrington’s drama to Sir Miles at a levee in Saville House, Sir Miles modified his opinion of the piece and spoke henceforth more respectfully of it. Meanwhile George, careless of uncles and aunts and cousins, lived in the bright din of his own success—the applause still ringing in memory like a sea in a shell—and in the quieter, truer music of Theo’s voice when she spoke his name as if it were a word that could not be translated into any other tongue.

Our tender hearts are averse to all ideas and descriptions of parting; and if the reader be of the same gentle constitution, he will pardon that I pass lightly over Harry Warrington’s leave-taking. A man may fasten his cloak, tighten his sword-belt, take the last look at a familiar threshold, and yet have no words fit to carry the weight of that moment. Were not thousands in the same plight? Had not Mr. Wolfe, with his thin cheeks and bright, feverish eye, his mother to kiss—his brave father having quitted life while the son was away upon the glorious Louisbourg business—and a sweetheart to clasp in a farewell embrace? Had not stout Admiral Holmes, before he sailed westward with his squadron—The Somerset, The Terrible, The Northumberland, The Royal William, The Trident, The Diana, The Seahorse; his own flag hoisted on board The Dublin—to take leave of Mrs. Holmes and the young ladies? Was Admiral Saunders, who followed the day after, exempt from that same human ache?

The ships go down the river with all a town’s noise attending them: bells clanging as if to drive back sorrow with brass, and cannon thundering as if a louder report could drown the softer sound men fear most—the hush that comes after a door is shut. Then away go the vessels, ploughing into the tumbling waste; and on shore, black-eyed Susans—wives, mothers, sweethearts, sisters—watch a shape of masts and canvas dwindle into the sunset. It dwindles into the West. The night falls darkling over the ocean. They are gone; but their hearts are at home yet awhile.

In silence, with a heart inexpressibly softened, how each man thinks of those he has left. What a chorus of pitiful prayer rises up to the Father, at sea and on shore, on that parting night: at home, by the vacant bedside where the wife kneels and sobs; round the fire where a mother draws the children close and teaches their lips to form supplications; or on deck, where the seafarer lifts his face to the stars, and hears below him the deep, hoarse, living voice of the water as the ship cleaves through the roaring midnight. To-morrow the sun rises upon our common life again; the kettle will sing its thin domestic note; the bread will be cut; duty will call as steadily as hunger; and we commence our daily task of toil.

George accompanies his brother and stays a while with him at Portsmouth whilst they are waiting for a wind. He shakes Mr. Wolfe’s hand, looks at the General’s pale face for the last time, and sees the vessels depart amid clangour from shore and harbour. The very air seems full of harsh metal and splitting sound: the public music of departure, which sets the nerves jangling, and makes a man long for the gentler noises of home—the tick of a clock, the crackle of coals, the murmur of familiar voices speaking in the old phrases that belong to a family as surely as its plate and linen.

Next day George is back at his home, and at that business which is sure one of the most selfish and absorbing of the world’s occupations, to which almost every man who is thirty years old has served ere this his apprenticeship. He has a pang as he looks into the lodgings and at the little room Harry used to occupy, and sees half-burned papers still in the grate—black curls of ash, like the dead leaves of a thought. A few minutes later he is on his way to Dean Street again; and there, in the dimness—where the fire burns fitfully and makes now a warm island of light, now a darkness in which whispers seem louder than speech—he bends to the ear of the clinging sweetheart.

She is very happy—oh, so happy!—at his return. She is ashamed of being so, and that shame itself is part of her tenderness. Is it not heartless to be glad when poor Hetty is so melancholy? Poor little Hetty! Indeed, it is selfish to be cheerful when she is in such a sad way. It makes one wretched to see her; the girl’s very silence has a sound in it, as when a room goes still after music.

“Don’t, sir! Well, I ought to be wretched, and it’s very, very wicked of me if I’m not,” says Theo; and one can understand her soft-hearted repentance. What she means by “Don’t,” who can tell? I have said the room was dark and the fire burned fitfully; and “Don’t” is no doubt uttered in one of the dark fits, when the world seems made only of a pulse of flame and a breath against a cheek.

Enter servants with supper and lights. The bright candles at once change the air of the chamber; the family arrives; conversation becomes general, and the table gives every one a task that is also a comfort. The cloth is spread; plates and knives make their small clinks; steam rises with homely fragrance; the loaf is broken and handed; and the act of eating—so plain, so necessary—seems for a while to tether wandering hearts.

The destination of the fleet is known everywhere now. The force on board is sufficient to beat all the French in Canada; and, under such an officer as Wolfe, to repair the blunders and disasters of previous campaigns. “He looked dreadfully ill, indeed,” says one; and another answers, “But he has a great soul in a feeble body.” The ministers, the country, hope the utmost from him; and hope, too, has its own tone—half trumpet, half prayer.

After supper, according to custom, Mr. Lambert assembles his modest household, of whom George Warrington may be said quite to form a part. The chairs are drawn; the fire is mended; and the room settles into that quiet which is not emptiness but a kind of listening. As he prays for all travellers by land and water, Theo and her sister are kneeling together. There are words in a family’s own cadence—Scripture read with a particular inflection, petitions spoken in a voice that has uttered them for years—that carry more comfort than any grander or more fashionable eloquence. And so, as the ship speeds farther and farther into the West, the fond thoughts pursue it. The night passes; the sun rises; the tea is made; the streets resume their rumour; and a day or two more, and everybody is at his books or his usual work.

As for George Warrington, that celebrated dramatist is busy about another composition. When the tragedy of Carpezan had run some thirty or two-score nights, other persons of genius took possession of the theatre. There may have been those who wondered how the town could be so fickle as ever to tire of such a masterpiece—who could not bear to see the actors in other habits, speaking other men’s verses; but George, of a sceptical turn of mind, took the fate of his tragedy very philosophically, and pocketed the proceeds with quiet satisfaction. From Mr. Dodsley, the bookseller, he had the usual complement of a hundred pounds; from the manager of the theatre two hundred or more; and such praises from critics and friends, that he sat down to prepare another piece, with which he hoped to achieve even greater successes than by his first performance.

Over these studies, and the other charming business which occupies him, months pass away. Happy business! Happiest time of youth and life, when love is first spoken and returned; when the dearest eyes are daily shining welcome, and the fondest lips never tire of whispering their sweet secrets; when the parting look that accompanies “Good night!” gives delightful warning of to-morrow; when the heart is so overflowing with happiness that it has to spare for all the world; when the day closes with glad prayers and opens with joyful hopes; when doubt seems cowardice, misfortune impossible, poverty only a sweet trial of constancy.

Theo’s elders, thankfully remembering their own prime, sit softly by and witness this pretty comedy performed by their young people. The house itself seems to conspire with their content: the stairs creak in familiar places; the grate draws and sings; the rain on the panes makes a gentle hiss; and the street beyond has its London undertone—wheels, distant cries, the vendor’s call—held at bay by the thick domestic walls. And in one of his later letters, dutifully written to his wife during a temporary absence from home, George Warrington records how he had been to look up at the windows of the dear old house in Dean Street, and wondered who was sitting in the chamber where he and Theo had been so happy.

Meanwhile we can learn how the time passes, and our friends are engaged, by some extracts from George’s letters to his brother.

“From the old window opposite Bedford Gardens, this 20th August 1759.

“Why are you gone back to rugged rocks, bleak shores, burning summers, nipping winters at home, when you might have been cropping ever so many laurels in Germany? Kingsley’s are coming back as covered with ’em as Jack-a-Green on May-day. Our six regiments did wonders; and our horse would have done, if my Lord George Sackville only had let them. But when Prince Ferdinand said ‘Charge!’ his lordship could not hear, or could not translate the German word for ‘Forward;’ and so we only beat the French, without utterly annihilating them, as we might, had Lord Granby or Mr. Warrington had the command. My lord is come back to town and is shouting for a Court-Martial. He held his head high enough in prosperity: in misfortune he shows such a constancy of arrogance that one almost admires him. He looks as if he rather envied poor Mr. Byng, and the not shooting him were a manque d’égards towards him.

“The Duke has had notice to get himself in readiness for departing from this world of grandeurs and victories, and downfalls and disappointments. An attack of palsy has visited his Royal Highness; and pallida mors has just peeped in at his door, as it were, and said, ‘I will call again.’ Tyrant as he was, this prince has been noble in disgrace; and no king has ever had a truer servant than ours has found in his son. Why do I like the losing side always, and am I disposed to revolt against the winners? Your famous Mr. P----, your chief’s patron and discoverer, I have been to hear in the House of Commons twice or thrice. I revolt against his magniloquence. I wish some little David would topple over that swelling giant. His thoughts and his language are always attitudinising. I like Barry’s manner best, though the other is the more awful actor.

“Pocahontas gets on apace. Barry likes his part of Captain Smith; and, though he will have him wear a red coat and blue facings and an epaulet, I have a fancy to dress him exactly like one of the pictures of Queen Elizabeth’s gentlemen at Hampton Court: with a ruff and a square beard and square shoes. ‘And Pocahontas—would you like her to be tattooed?’ asks Uncle Lambert. Hagan’s part as the warrior who is in love with her, and, seeing her partiality for the captain, nobly rescues him from death, I trust will prove a hit. A strange fish is this Hagan: his mouth full of stage-plays and rant, but good, honest, and brave, if I don’t err. He is angry at having been cast lately for Sir O’Brallaghan, in Mr. Macklin’s new farce of Love à-la-mode. He says that he does not keer to disgreece his tongue with imiteetions of that rascal brogue. As if there was any call for imiteetions, when he has such an admirable twang of his own!

“Shall I tell you? Shall I hide the circumstance? Shall I hurt your feelings? Shall I set you in a rage of jealousy, and cause you to ask for leave to return to Europe? Know, then, that though Carpezan is long since dead, cousin Maria is for ever coming to the playhouse. Tom Spencer has spied her out night after night in the gallery, and she comes on the nights when Hagan performs. Quick, Burroughs, Mr. Warrington’s boots and portmanteau! Order a chaise and four for Portsmouth immediately! The letter which I burned one morning when we were at breakfast (I may let the cat out of the bag, now puss has such a prodigious way to run) was from cousin M., hinting that she wished me to tell no tales about her: but I can’t help just whispering to you that Maria at this moment is busy consoling herself as fast as possible. Shall I spoil sport? Shall I tell her brother? Is the affair any business of mine? What have the Esmonds done for you and me but win our money at cards? Yet I like our noble cousin. It seems to me he would be good if he could—or rather, he would have been once. He has been set on a wrong way of life, from which ’tis now probably too late to rescue him.

“O beati agricolae! Our Virginia was dull, but let us thank Heaven we were bred there. We were made little slaves, but not slaves to wickedness, gambling, bad male and female company. It was not until my poor Harry left home that he fell among thieves. I mean thieves en grand, such as waylaid him and stripped him on English highroads. I consider you none the worse because you were the unlucky one, and had to deliver your purse up. And now you are going to retrieve, and make a good name for yourself; and kill more ‘French dragons,’ and become a great commander. And our mother will talk of her son the Captain, the Colonel, the General, and have his picture painted with all his stars and epaulets, when poor I shall be but a dawdling poetaster—or, if we may hope for the best, a snug placeman, with a little box at Richmond or Kew, and a half-score of little picaninnies, that will come and bob curtseys at the garden-gate when their uncle the General rides up on his great charger, with his aide-de-camp’s pockets filled with gingerbread for the nephews and nieces. ’Tis for you to brandish the sword of Mars. As for me, I look forward to a quiet life: a quiet little home; a quiet little library full of books; and a little Some one, dulce ridentem, dulce loquentem, on t’other side of the fire, as I scribble away at my papers. I am so pleased with this prospect, so utterly contented and happy, that I feel afraid as I think of it, lest it should escape me; and, even to my dearest Hal, am shy of speaking of my happiness. What is ambition to me, with this certainty? What do I care for wars, with this beatific peace smiling near?

“Our mother’s friend, Mynheer Van den Bosch, has been away on a tour to discover his family in Holland, and, strange to say, has found one. Miss (who was intended by maternal solicitude to be a wife for your worship) has had six months at Kensington School, and is coming out with a hundred pretty accomplishments, which are to complete her a perfect fine lady. Her papa brought her to make a curtsey in Dean Street, and a mighty elegant curtsey she made. Though she is scarce seventeen, no dowager of sixty can be more at her ease. She conversed with Aunt Lambert on an equal footing; she treated the girls as chits—to Hetty’s wrath and Theo’s amusement. She talked politics with the General, and the last routs, dresses, operas, fashions, scandal, with such perfect ease that, but for a blunder or two, you might have fancied Miss Lydia was born in Mayfair. At the Court end of the town she will live, she says; and has no patience with her father, who has a lodging in Monument Yard. For those who love a brown beauty, a prettier little mignonne creature cannot be seen. But my taste, you know, dearest brother, and—”

Here follows a page of raptures and quotations of verse, which, out of regard for the reader and the writer’s memory, I decline to reprint. Gentlemen and ladies of a certain age may remember the time when they indulged in these rapturous follies on their own accounts; when the praises of the charmer were for ever warbling from their lips or trickling from their pens; when the flowers of life were in full bloom, and all the birds of spring were singing. The twigs are now bare perhaps, and the leaves have fallen; but for all that, shall we not remember the vernal time? As for you, young people whose May—or April, is it?—has not commenced yet, you need not be detained over other folks’ love-rhapsodies; depend upon it, when your spring-season arrives, kindly Nature will warm all your flowers into bloom, and rouse your glad bosoms to pour out their full song.

George Warrington had said in his letter—half laughing at it, half leaning on it like a man who puts his hand to a railing he pretends not to need—that though my Lord Castlewood had once played very sharply with Harry, he and George still met as cousins should, with a smoothness that, in London, can pass for affection. If George wanted a frank, an introduction where a door was guarded by lace and precedent, a seat to hear the thunder of a debate from the red benches, Castlewood was ever ready—so long as the helping of another man’s fortunes did not so much as scratch his own. He could be pleasant; he could be brilliant; he could even be serviceable. He had that gift, so ruinous in the end, of seeming to mean precisely what the listener most wished to hear.

Now he went further, and promised—promised with a gravity that made the promise taste substantial—to do what he could with those in power for Mr. George Warrington. George, daily less inclined to turn his face westward, seized on the offer as a hungry man seizes on bread.

For it was not only sentiment that tethered him to England. London’s life—its talk, its theatres, its books, its perpetual clatter of coaches and bells, its nightly blaze of candles and cards—pleased him infinitely more than the broad, languid stretches of plantation day. A planter’s ease might have suited him, could he have taken it with independence; but in Virginia he was, as he thought, the first and worst-treated of his mother’s subjects. He could already feel, like a strap across his shoulders, the old maternal governance tightening; he could already hear the plantation’s thick, monotonous soundscape—the drones of overseers, the creak of wagons, the same phrases repeated until they ceased to be words and became commands. And he dreaded, more than for himself, for the young bride he meant to bring there: the narrowing of her world to a routine, the petty subordination, the jealousies, the bickerings that would begin at breakfast and sour the day, the certainty of differences of opinion at every household decision, as inevitable as the noon heat. Better freedom and poverty in England, with a hope—however faint—of distinction, than that slow domestic siege.

So Castlewood’s patronage, though it came from a hand not famously clean, was eagerly accepted. My lord had not provided well for his own brother, it is true; and his own position, peer as he was, had more bitterness in it than splendour. But we believe what we wish to believe; and George chose to put weight on the promise, as if it were coin.

Unlike the Warringtons, who had received George’s engagement to Miss Lambert with varying degrees of chill and complaint, Lord Castlewood behaved as if the match were an excellent joke told at a good table. He waited upon her parents; he praised George to them with a cousinly warmth; he praised the young lady to George with a gallantry that was almost respectful; and he made himself so prodigiously agreeable in their company that these charitable folk forgot—no, rather, they were persuaded to mistrust—the bad repute of the man. It must be a wicked and scandalous world, they thought, to speak ill of one who could be so lively without insolence, so witty without cruelty, so attentive without appetite.

He said, indeed, that he was improved in their society, as every man must be who came into it; and for the time he stayed in that quiet house, it was as if he left his worldliness with his cloak in the hall, and only took it up again when he stepped into his chair and the street’s coarse roar met him. There are such little harbours, even for the wildest sailors—some domestic haven where the noises soften, where the very crackle of the fire and the clink of a spoon in a teacup rebuke the brazen shout of the gaming table. In such a haven Castlewood looked, if not wholly new, at least less battered.

Nor did the Lambert elders think the worse of him because he openly proclaimed his admiration for Miss Theo. It was genuine enough; he did not pretend it was deep.

“It don’t affect my sleep,” he said coolly; “and I am not going to break my heart because Miss Lambert prefers somebody else. Only I wish, when I was a young man, madam, I had had the good fortune to meet with somebody so innocent and good as your daughter. I might have been kept out of a deal of harm’s way; but innocent and good young women did not fall into mine—or they would have made me better than I am.”

“Sure, my lord, it is not too late!” Mrs. Lambert answered, very softly—soft as a spoon laid down on a saucer, as if loudness might jar the fragile possibility she was offering him.

Castlewood started back, misunderstanding the direction of her pity.

“Not too late, madam?” he asked.

She blushed, and steadied herself with the little domestic dignity of a mother among her own curtains. “It is too late to court my dear daughter, my lord; but not too late to repent. We read, ’tis never too late to do that. If others have been received at the eleventh hour, is there any reason why you should give up hope?”

“Perhaps I know my own heart better than you,” he said, with a plaintive humour that made his despair almost graceful. “I can speak French and German very well; and why? because I was taught both in the nursery. A man who learns them late can never get the practice of them on his tongue. And so ’tis with goodness: I can’t learn it at my age. I can only see others practise it, and admire them. When I am on—on the side opposite to Lazarus, will Miss Theo give me a drop of water? Don’t frown! I know I shall be there, Mrs. Lambert. Some folks are doomed so; and I think some of our family are amongst these. Some people are vacillating, and one hardly knows which way the scale will turn. Whereas some are predestined angels, and fly Heavenwards naturally, and do what they will.”

“Oh, my lord, and why should you not be of the predestined? Whilst there is a day left—whilst there is an hour—there is hope!” cried the fond matron, with that physician’s persistence good women have when they take a sinner for a patient.

“I know what is passing in your mind—nay, I read your prayers in your looks,” Lord Castlewood said, and his voice lowered, as though even words had to be kept from making too much noise in that decent room. “But how can they avail? You don’t know all, my good lady. You don’t know what a life ours is of the world; how early it began; how selfish Nature, and then necessity and education, have made us. It is Fate holds the reins of the chariot, and we can’t escape our doom. I know better: I see better people: I go my own way. My own? No, not mine—Fate’s: and it is not altogether without pity for us, since it allows us, from time to time, to see such people as you.”

And he took her hand, looked full in her face, and bowed with a melancholy grace. Every word might be true, and yet the truth itself might be part of the man’s indulgence—like tears that refresh a libertine as wine refreshes a drunkard. Mrs. Lambert, who heard sincerity in any tone not openly coarse, knew little of what was passing behind his fine phrases (how should she?), and so prayed for him with a gentle obstinacy. He was much better—yes, much better than the world said. He was interesting. There were hopes—why should there not be the most precious hopes for him still?

It remains to be seen which of the two judged him rightly. Meanwhile, even if the gentleman’s estimate of himself was correct, the lady’s tenderness could do him no harm. Such kind-souled doctors watch a perilous case with a zeal that is almost personal; and when the patient recovers, their interest slips away to the next bed in the ward.

But while the malady was under treatment, Mrs. Lambert could not see too much of her “sick man.” An intimacy sprang up between my Lord Castlewood and the Lamberts. It is not impossible that a worldly view or two slid, like a mouse into a pantry, even into good Mrs. Lambert’s spiritual plans; for who knows into what guarded Eden worldliness will not creep? Her son was about to take orders. My Lord Castlewood, who feared that his chaplain Mr. Sampson’s careless life and heterodox talk might lead him to resign, hinted that in such a case the modest cure would be vacant, and might suit a young divine of good principles and good manners—content with a small stipend and a small but friendly congregation.

So the acquaintance settled into habit. The ladies of Castlewood, always on their best behaviour, came more than once to curtsey in Mrs. Lambert’s drawing-room. They were civil to the parents and the young ladies; and my Lady Castlewood’s card assemblies were open to Mrs. Lambert and her household. There was play, certainly—everybody played: his Majesty, bishops, peers and peeresses. But nobody need play who did not like; and surely nobody need have scruples, when such august and venerable personages daily abetted the practice. More than once Mrs. Lambert appeared at her ladyship’s routs, grateful for her welcome, and pleased—honestly pleased, as a mother is when her daughters are admired—at the murmur of approbation the girls excited in that bright, dangerous crowd: a soft sea of voices, fans whispering like dry leaves, cards snapping, chairs scraping, a noise that could intoxicate as readily as wine.

Mention has been made of an American family, Dutch by extraction, who came to England strongly recommended by Madam Esmond, their Virginian neighbour, to her sons in Europe. Mrs. Lambert, match-maker by instinct as other people are cooks by instinct, read Madam Esmond’s intentions as clearly as if they had been written in large letters across the paper. But George was already engaged; and Harry—poor Hetty’s flame—was away on service, which circumstance Hetty’s mother perhaps did not wholly regret.

She told George, laughingly, that he ought to obey his mamma’s injunctions, break off his engagement with Theo, and make up to Miss Lydia, who was ten times—ten times! a hundred times!—as rich as her poor girl, and certainly much handsomer.
