“Yes, indeed,” said George, “that I own: she is handsomer, and she is richer, and perhaps even cleverer.” Mrs. Lambert liked those praises only by halves. “But say she is all these? So is Mr. Johnson much cleverer than I am; so is Mr. Hagan the actor much taller and handsomer; so is Sir James Lowther much richer: yet pray, ma’am, do you suppose I am going to be jealous of any one of these three, or think my Theo would jilt me for their sakes? Why should I not allow that Miss Lydia is handsomer then? and richer, and clever too, and lively, and well bred, if you insist on it, and an angel if you will have it so? Theo is not afraid: art thou, child?”

“No, George,” Theo answered; and the honest look of her eyes—clear as water in a clean glass—would have shamed any jealousy. And if, after this, mamma took occasion to leave the room for a minute to fetch her scissors, or her thimble, or a bootjack and slippers, or the cross and ball on the top of St. Paul’s, or a pocket-handkerchief forgotten in the parlour—if Mrs. Lambert departed on any errand, natural or preposterous—I shall not be surprised that, upon returning, she found George in near proximity to Theo, who had a heightened colour, and whose hand George was just dropping. I shall not pretend to know what they had been doing. Have you, madam? Have you no remembrance of what used to happen when Mr. Grundy came a-courting? Are you, who were not in the room, going to cry fie? Then fie upon you, Mrs. Grundy.

Harry being away, and Theo and George irrevocably engaged, Madam Esmond’s little plans could not bite. Why should not Mrs. Lambert have plans of her own? If a rich, handsome, beautiful little wife should fall into Jack Lambert’s Oxford path, why should she not be gathered up? So thought mamma, who was always thinking of marrying and giving in marriage; and she prattled to General Lambert, who, as usual, called her a goose for her pains. Beauty and riches, she argued, are no objection. Madam Esmond desired the family should be entertained. It was not Mrs. Lambert’s fault Harry was gone to Canada. Would the General wish him to come back, leave the army and his reputation, perhaps—yes, and come to England and marry this American and break poor Hetty’s heart—would her father wish that? Let us spare further argument, and not be so rude as to hint that Mr. Lambert had some reason when he called his fond wife by the name of that absurd splay-footed bird sacrificed at St. Michael’s.

In those days, court and city drew their distinctions as sharply as a knife draws them through crust. Mr. Van den Bosch, when he first came to London, scarcely associated with any but city folk. He lodged near his agent, and his pleasures were the sober pleasures of trade: an airing to Islington or Highgate; a promenade in the Artillery Ground in Bunhill Fields; Sunday at the Baptist meeting-house in Finsbury Fields. And yet—because even the most pious household has its little contraband delights—they went on the sly once or twice to see Mr. Garrick, or that rogue Mr. Foote at the Little Theatre. A Lord Mayor’s feast was a treat to the old gentleman; and to dance with a young mercer at Hampstead Assembly gave the utmost delight to the young lady.

When George first went to wait upon his mother’s friends, he found our old acquaintance, Mr. Draper of the Temple, sedulous in attentions to Miss Lydia; and the lawyer—who was married—told George to look out, as the young lady had a plumb to her fortune. Mr. Drabshaw, a young Quaker, nephew to Mr. Trail, Madam Esmond’s Bristol agent, was also in constant attendance upon the girl, and in dreadful suspicion when Mr. Warrington appeared.

Wishing to do honour to his mother’s neighbours, George invited them to an entertainment at his own apartments; and who should so naturally meet them there as his friends from Soho? Not one of them could deny little Miss Lydia’s beauty. She had the foot of a fairy; the arms, neck, and flashing eyes of a little brown huntress of Diana. She had brought with her from home a plaintive accent—one of those sounds that carry a whole country in the mouth; and I, moi qui vous parle, have heard a hundred gross Cockney imitations of it, and watched as many absurd disguises, until one is tempted to think the very effort to “speak properly” is a kind of tyranny, levelling all the world’s living voices into one thin, fashionable note. Who sets up to say No, forsooth? You dear Miss Whittington, with whose h’s Fate has dealt so unkindly? You lovely Miss Nicol Jarvie, with your northern burr? You beautiful Miss Molony, with your Dame Street warble? All accents are pretty from pretty lips, and who shall set the standard up—rose, thistle, shamrock, or star and stripe? If Miss Lydia’s accent had been odious, Mr. Warrington, as a man of taste, had certainly disapproved; and her schoolmistress at Kensington had not done her duty by her pupil.

After the six months were over—during which, according to her father’s calculation, she was to learn all the accomplishments procurable at the Kensington Academy—Miss Lydia returned, nothing loth, to her grandfather and took her place in the world. At first it was a narrow world: Monument Yard, respectable dinners, city gallantries, Sabbaths of proper sound and silence. But she was a resolute little person, and resolved to enlarge her sphere; and whither she chose to lead, the obedient grandfather followed. He had been thwarted in youth, he said, and little good had come of the severity he underwent. He had thwarted his own son, who had turned out ill. As for little Lyddy, he was determined she should have as pleasant a life as possible. Did not Mr. George think he was right? It was said in Virginia—he did not know with what reason—that the young gentlemen of Castlewood had been happier if Madam Esmond had allowed them a little of their own way. George could not deny the rumour, nor would he try to alter the benevolent old man’s plans. As for the Lamperts, how could they do other than welcome the kind old merchant, so tender a parent, Madam Esmond’s good friend?

When Miss came from school, grandpapa removed from Monument Yard to an elegant house in Bloomsbury; and their city friends followed at first—merchants, worthy tradesmen with whom the old gentleman dealt, their ladies and sons and daughters, all gracious to Miss Lyddy. But it would be a long task to tell how these dropped away one by one, as crumbs are brushed from a cloth when company improves. There were no more junketings at Belsize, no more trips to Highgate, no more Saturday jaunts to Deputy Higgs’s villa at Highbury, no more country-dances at honest Mr. Lutestring’s at Hackney. Even their Sunday practice changed; and, oh abomination of abominations! Mr. Van den Bosch left Bethesda Chapel in Bunhill Row and actually took a pew in Queen Square Church.

Queen Square Church—and Mr. George Warrington lived hard by in Southampton Row. It was easy to see at whom Miss Lyddy was setting her cap. And Mr. Draper, who had once been full of her and her grandfather’s praises, now warned George, and gave him reports of Mr. Van den Bosch very different from the first.

Mr. Van den Bosch, for all his brag of Dutch parentage, came from Albany and was nobody’s son at all. He had made his money by land speculation, or by privateering (uncommonly like piracy), and by the Guinea trade. His son had married—if marriage it could be called, which was doubtful—an assigned servant; had been cut off by his father; had taken to bad courses; and had died, luckily for himself, in his own bed.

“Mr. Draper has told you bad tales about me,” said the placid old gentleman to George when they spoke of it; and his tone had the weary evenness of a man who has heard his life translated into other men’s words and knows how much is always lost or poisoned in the translation. “Very likely we are all sinners, and some evil may be truly said of all of us, with a great deal more that is untrue. Did he tell you my son was unhappy with me? I told you so too. Did he bring you wicked stories about my family? He liked it so well he wanted to marry my Lyddy to his brother. Heaven bless her! I have had a many offers for her. And you are the young gentleman I should have chose for her, and I like you none the worse because you prefer somebody else; though what you can see in your Miss, as compared to my Lyddy, begging your honour’s pardon, I am at a loss to understand.”

“There is no accounting for tastes, my good sir,” George said, putting on his most superb air, as if taste were a throne and he sat in it.

“No, sir; ’tis a wonder of nature, and daily happens,” the old man pursued, good-humoured and blunt. “When I kept store to Albany, there was one of your tiptop gentry there that might have married my dear daughter that was alive then, and with a pretty piece of money; whereby—for her father and I had quarrelled—Miss Lyddy would have been a pauper, you see. And in place of my beautiful Bella, my gentleman chooses a little homely creature, no prettier than your Miss, and without a dollar to her fortune. The more fool he, saving your presence, Mr. George.”

“Pray don’t save my presence, my good sir,” George cried, laughing. “I suppose the gentleman’s word was given to the other lady, and he had seen her first, and hence was indifferent to your charming daughter.”

“I suppose when a young fellow gives his word to perform a cursed piece of folly, he always sticks to it,” said the elder; then checked himself with a rueful shake of the head. “But Lord, Lord, what am I speaking of? I am aspeaking of twenty year ago. I was well-to-do then, but I may say Heaven has blessed my store, and I am three times as well off now. Ask my agents how much they will give for Joseph Van den Bosch’s bill at six months on New York—or at sight maybe for forty thousand pound? I warrant they will discount the paper.”

“Happy he who has the bill, sir!” said George, bowing, amused at the candour and at the merchant’s innocent vanity in the sound of his own wealth.

“Lord, Lord, how mercenary you young men are!” cried the old gentleman, simply. “Always thinking about money nowadays! Happy he who has the girl, I should say—the money ain’t the question, my dear sir, when it goes along with such a lovely young thing as that—though I humbly say it, who oughtn’t, and who am her fond silly old grandfather. We were talking about you, Lyddy darling—come, give me a kiss, my blessing! We were talking about you, and Mr. George said he wouldn’t take you with all the money your poor old grandfather can give you.”

“Nay, sir—” George began.

“Well, you are right to say nay, for I didn’t say all, that’s the truth. My Blessing will have a deal more than that trifle I spoke of, when it shall please Heaven to remove me out of this world to a better—when poor old Gappy is gone, Lyddy will be a rich little Lyddy, that she will. But she don’t wish me to go yet, does she?”

“Oh, you darling dear grandpapa!” Lydia cried, with a sweetness that sounded practised and yet was warm as breath on a cold pane.

“This young gentleman won’t have you.” Lydia gave him an arch look from her brown eyes—“Thank you, sir,” without saying it. “But at any rate he is honest, and that is more than we can say of some folks in this wicked London. Oh, Lord, Lord, how mercenary they are! Do you know that yonder, in Monument Yard, they were all at my poor little Blessing for her money? There was Tom Lutestring; there was Mr. Draper, your precious lawyer; there was actually Mr. Tubbs, of Bethesda Chapel; and they must all come buzzing like flies round the honey-pot. That is why we came out of the quarter where my brother-tradesmen live.”

“To avoid the flies,—to be sure!” said Miss Lydia, tossing up her little head.

“Where my brother-tradesmen live,” continued the old gentleman, as if he liked the honest weight of those words, though he was leaving them behind. “Else who am I to think of consorting with your grandees and fine folk? I don’t care for the fashions, Mr. George; I don’t care for plays and poetry, begging your honour’s pardon; I never went to a play in my life, but to please this little minx.”

“Oh, sir, ’twas lovely! and I cried so, didn’t I, grandpapa?” Lydia cried; and one could almost hear in her voice the theatre itself—the rising sighs, the smothered sobs, the applause like rain on a roof.

“At what, my dear?” asked Gappy, truly puzzled.

“At—at Mr. Warrington’s play, grandpapa.”

“Did you, my dear? I dare say; I dare say!” The old man chuckled, half ashamed. “It was mail day; and my letters had come in; and my ship the Lovely Lyddy had just come into Falmouth; and Captain Joyce reported how he had mercifully escaped a French privateer; and my head was so full of thanks for that escape—which saved me a deal of money, Mr. George—for the rate at which ships is underwrote this war-time is so scandalous that I often prefer to venture than to insure—that I confess I didn’t listen much to the play, sir, and only went to please this little Lyddy.”

“And you did please me, dearest Gappy!” cried the young lady, and pressed herself close to him as if the squeezing could seal the affection in place.

“Bless you! then it’s all I want. What does a man want more here below than to please his children, Mr. George? especially me, who knew what was to be unhappy when I was young, and to repent of having treated this darling’s father too hard.”

“Oh, grandpapa!” Lydia cried, and redoubled her caresses, as if to drown the old remorse before it could find words.

“Yes, I was too hard with him, dear; and that’s why I spoil my little Lydkin so!”

More kisses followed. The little creature flung her polished arms round the old man’s neck, pressed her dark red lips to his withered cheek, and beat a halo of powder from his wig with the violence of her tenderness. All the while she watched Mr. George, as much as to say—There, sir! should you not like me to do as much for you?

We confess—though do we confess all? George told Theo the tale of his interview with Lyddy and Gappy, and the old man’s news regarding his granddaughter’s wealth; but I do not think he told everything. Had he done so, Theo would scarcely have been so much interested, or so entirely amused and good-humoured, when next the two young ladies met.

Before ever Lydia Van den Bosch’s little foot had tapped out its music along the boards of our tale, there is a marriage—like a sudden clap in clear weather—that must be owned and set in its place; else Mr. Warrington’s letter, and that casual line in it touching Lady Maria Esmond, hangs in the air like steam without a pot.

Lady Maria—of ancient blood, practiced manners, and an experience the town chose to call “mature”—had, in the teeth of her kin and in the teeth of the world (or, to speak more truly, behind its back), taken for husband Mr. Geoghegan, commonly called Hagan, the young Irish actor who had lately blazed in George’s tragedy. Parson Sampson, at his little Mayfair chapel, fastened the knot privily, as if it were a ribbon on a bodice and must not be seen.

And why should a woman, because she has once loved amiss, be sentenced to starve ever after? People will forgive a man his second appetite as readily as they forgive him his first; but a lady, if she but look twice at the same dish, is cried upon as if she had stolen it. Yet the truth of such hearts—clinging hearts, ivy-hearts that must have a wall—is that when the first support is pulled away, they will wind themselves upon another. It is not philosophy; it is hunger. It is the body remembering warmth; it is the mind craving a familiar voice in the room, the kettle’s homely murmur, the chair drawn close to the hearth. We may talk as we will of constancy; but the blood keeps its own calendar, and the hand will reach out again, even after it has been burned.

Only—this time the reaching was a scandal, because the hand reached down.

Hagan, in his gilt leather armour and buckled periwig, had spoken the poet’s lines as if they were his own breath: his tones struck through the house like a bow drawn across a string; his eye shone; his bearing had that brave counterfeit of nobility which the stage can lend a man so convincingly that real lords look like extras beside him. Lady Maria, who had once yielded her heart as readily as she yielded her tears, gave herself up to him with a headlong tenderness, and he—young, flattered, half frightened at the greatness of the prize—took her too, though perhaps he would have preferred the same ladyship in a younger edition.

When the thing could no longer be hidden, and her furious relations disowned her, she did not take a fine lodging and brood in velvet; she went straight into the actor’s poor rooms at Westminster, and sat down—like some high-born bird that has missed its migration—among common sparrows and common crumbs.

General Lambert brought the news home from Whitehall, and, being a good soldier of that homely age, made a jest of it at his own table, where there was always honest noise enough—the clink of a spoon on a plate, the scrape of a chair, the rustle of a gown as mamma rose to order something, the crackle of coals—those domestic sounds that keep a household in tune. He ran on with broad waggeries, the merrier for being a trifle rude: George’s share in it; Barry’s rage when he should hear; the notion of George standing as groomsman; the first baby christened after some hero or heroine of the tragedy; dragons hired from Mr. Rich’s theatre to draw my lady’s chariot; and a christening done in Macbeth’s cauldron, if the parents had a taste for it.

Little Hetty, who had been brought up among kitchens, gardens, and plain kindnesses, broke in with her quick, right-minded heat.

“Why shouldn’t she marry him if she likes him?” she asked. “Why should he not love her because she is a little old? Mamma is a little old, and you love her none the worse. When you married my mamma, sir, you have said you were very poor; and yet you were very happy, and nobody laughed at you!”

So spoke the child, because youth measures scandal by the heart and not by the heralds’ book.

“So her family has deserted her?” Hetty went on, indignation rising in her like yeast.

George told them how wrathful they were; how Lady Castlewood had gone into mourning as though for a death; how Mr. Will swore he would have the rascal’s ears; how Madame de Bernstein—most fierce of all—flamed and stormed as if the marriage were a personal affront to the Almighty.

“It is an insult to the family,” said Hetty, with that little dignity she had, “and I can fancy how ladies of that rank must be indignant at their relative’s marriage with a person of Mr. Hagan’s condition; but to desert her is a very different matter.”

“Indeed, my dear child,” cried mamma, alarmed, “you are talking of what you don’t understand. After my Lady Maria’s conduct, no respectable person can go to see her.”

“What conduct, mamma?”

“Never mind,” mamma said quickly, with that frightened severity which hides more than it corrects. “Little girls ought not to be curious. Suffice it, miss, that I am shocked her ladyship should ever have been here; and I say again, no honest person should associate with her!”

“Then, Aunt Lambert, I must be whipped and sent to bed,” said George, with mock gravity, “for I own to you—though I did not confess sooner, seeing the affair was not mine—that I have been to see my cousin the player, and her ladyship his wife.”

And he described, with that half-laughing tenderness which made his sarcasm less bitter, the dirty lodgings in Westminster; the shabbiness of it all; the old mother living there too; the little brother whom Hagan put to school. Yet George confessed that he came away liking the fellow, almost respecting him, though the marriage was as improvident as a cook who has barely flour enough for a loaf and yet invites a regiment to supper.

General Lambert growled, “Improvident, if they marry such spendthrifts as you. Master George found his relations, and I’ll be bound he left his purse behind him.”

“No, not the purse, sir,” George said, smiling in that way of his which always seemed to warm the room. “Theo made that. But I am bound to own it came empty away. Mr. Rich is in great dudgeon. He says he hardly dares have Hagan on his stage, and is afraid of a riot—like Mr. Garrick had about the foreign dancers. This is to be a fine gentleman’s riot. The macaronis vow they will pelt Mr. Hagan, and have him cudgelled afterwards. My cousin Will, at Arthur’s, has taken his oath he will have the actor’s ears. Meanwhile, as the poor man does not play, they have cut off his salary; and without his salary, this luckless pair of lovers have no means to buy bread and cheese.”

Theo’s eyes worshipped him the more because charity sat on him as naturally as a well-cut coat. “And you took it to them, sir? It was like you, George!”

“It was your purse took it, dear Theo,” he answered.

“Mamma, I hope you will go and see them to-morrow!” Theo pleaded.

“If she doesn’t, I shall get a divorce, my dear!” cried the General, roaring with laughter; and called for kisses, and dubbed his future son-in-law a fiddlestick; and so, amid clattering plates and bright talk, the great scandal of the town was reduced, for that hour, to a family jest and a household resolution to be kind.

But in the world outside—the world that listens less to the kettle and more to the coffee-house—the marriage rang like a cracked bell.

Any man who has made an imprudent match knows the gauntlet: the frozen calls, the sermons, the pity that is only another form of scorn. And if decent people cry out because you marry the curate’s daughter, or a young barrister with nothing but his reports and his debts, what must Lady Maria Hagan’s friends have felt, and even what must Mr. Hagan’s have muttered, when a fine lady with courtly habits came to take her seat at a table where the joints were counted and the tea measured by spoonfuls?

Begin with old Mrs. Hagan. Her son, since he left Trinity College at his father’s death and made himself Romeo at Crow Street, had kept her dutifully: fire in the grate, a bit of mutton on Sundays, tea that smelt of real leaf, not of hay; a coat for the little brother; a little help for the sister gone out as companion. There is a kind of household economy which is not merely arithmetic but ritual: the same pot rinsed and set to dry; the same small loaf cut carefully so the last slice may look like the first; the same silence at night broken only by the ember’s sigh and the far-off patrol. Into such a place Lady Maria descended—bringing, with her soft hands and grand manner, needs and expectations as real to her as hunger is to a poor woman. Love, especially romantic love, never counts the chairs at the table before it invites itself to sit; never asks whether there is cream enough for two.

So there she was, taking, innocently enough, the cream off the milk, the wings of the chicken, the best half of everything where there had been barely enough before. No wonder the poor old mother-in-law grumbled. Yet her private growling was nothing beside the public howl at Kensington.

Think of the acoustic storm of it—the whispering in doorways, the titter like knives on china at Court where Lady Fanny attended; the jokes at the officers’ table; the waggeries in prints and magazines; the outraged prudes clacking like geese; the laughter of clubs, loud as a drum. Madame de Bernstein fell into fits and fled to the solitude of Tunbridge Wells—where she only saw forty people of a night at cards, and called that retirement. My lord refused to see his sister. Lady Castlewood, in mourning, went to a gracious Princess who was pleased to condole with her upon the disgrace. For three whole days the town kept the marriage on its tongue as it keeps a new sauce—tasting it, praising it, spitting it out; and then other news came—victory in Germany, doubtful accounts from America, a general officer home to take his trial, an exquisite new Italian soprano—and the town, greedy for the next dish, forgot Lady Maria in her garret, eating the hard-earned meal of the actor’s family.

George Warrington wrote to his brother of a visit paid to the newly married pair. The letter had that same interweaving of war and hearth, of distant cannon and near tea-cups, which makes a family’s life, in any century, one long braid.

“My dearest little Theo,” he said, “was eager to accompany her mamma upon this errand of charity; but I thought Aunt Lambert’s visit would be best under the circumstances, and without the attendance of her little spinster aide-de-camp. Cousin Hagan was out when we called; we found her ladyship in a loose undress, and with her hair in not the neatest papers, playing at cribbage with a neighbour from the second floor, while good Mrs. Hagan sate on the other side of the fire with a glass of punch, and the Whole Duty of Man.

“Maria—your Maria once—cried a little when she saw us; and Aunt Lambert, you may be sure, was ready with her sympathy. While she bestowed it on Lady Maria, I paid the best compliments I could invent to the old lady. When the conversation between Aunt L. and the bride began to flag, I turned to the latter, and between us we did our best to make a dreary interview pleasant.

“Our talk was about you, about Wolfe, about war; you must be engaged face to face with the Frenchmen by this time, and God send my dearest brother safe and victorious out of the battle! Be sure we follow your steps anxiously—we fancy you at Cape Breton. We have plans of Quebec, and charts of the St. Lawrence. Shall I ever forget your face of joy that day when you saw me return safe and sound from the little combat with the little Frenchman? So will my Harry, I know, return from his battle. I feel quite assured of it; elated somehow with the prospect of your certain success and safety. And I have made all here share my cheerfulness. We talk of the campaign as over, and Captain Warrington’s promotion as secure. Pray Heaven, all our hopes may be fulfilled one day ere long.

“How strange it is that you who are the mettlesome fellow (you know you are) should escape quarrels hitherto, and I, who am a peaceful youth, wishing no harm to anybody, should have battles thrust upon me! What do you think actually of my having had another affair upon my wicked hands, and with whom, think you? With no less a personage than your old enemy, our kinsman, Mr. Will.

“What or who set him to quarrel with me, I cannot think. Spencer (who acted as second for me, for matters actually have gone this length—don’t be frightened; it is all over, and nobody is a scratch the worse) thinks some one set Will on me, but who, I say? His conduct has been most singular; his behaviour quite unbearable.

“We have met pretty frequently lately at the house of good Mr. Van den Bosch, whose pretty granddaughter was consigned to both of us by our good mother. Oh, dear mother! did you know that the little thing was to be such a causa belli, and to cause swords to be drawn, and precious lives to be menaced? But so it has been.

“To show his own spirit, I suppose, or having some reasonable doubt about mine, whenever Will and I have met at Mynheer’s house—and he is for ever going there—he has shown such downright rudeness to me, that I have required more than ordinary patience to keep my temper. He has contradicted me once, twice, thrice in the presence of the family, and out of sheer spite and rage, as it appeared to me.

“Is he paying his addresses to Miss Lydia, and her father’s ships, negroes, and forty thousand pounds? I should guess so. The old gentleman is for ever talking about his money, and adores his granddaughter, and as she is a beautiful little creature, numbers of folk here are ready to adore her too. Was Will rascal enough to fancy that I would give up my Theo for a million of guineas, and negroes, and Venus to boot? Could the thought of such baseness enter into the man’s mind? I don’t know that he has accused me of stealing Van den Bosch’s spoons and tankards when we dine there, or of robbing on the highway. But for one reason or the other he has chosen to be jealous of me; and as I have parried his impertinences with little sarcastic speeches (though perfectly civil before company), perhaps I have once or twice made him angry. Our little Miss Lydia has unwittingly added fuel to the fire on more than one occasion, especially yesterday, when there was talk about your worship.

“‘Ah!’ says the heedless little thing, as we sat over our dessert, ‘’tis lucky for you, Mr. Esmond, that Captain Harry is not here.’

“‘Why, miss?’ asks he, with one of his usual conversational ornaments, and a volley of oaths.

“‘O fie!’ says she, putting up the prettiest little fingers to the prettiest little rosy ears in the world. ‘O fie, sir! to use such naughty words. ’Tis lucky the Captain is not here, because he might quarrel with you; and Mr. George is so peaceable and quiet, that he won’t. Have you heard from the Captain, Mr. George?’

“‘From Cape Breton,’ says I. ‘He is very well, thank you; that is—’ I could not finish, for I was in such a rage I scarce could contain myself.

“‘From the Captain, as you call him, Miss Lyddy,’ says Will. ‘He’ll distinguish himself as he did at Saint Cas! Ho, ho!’

“‘So I apprehend he did, sir,’ says I.

“‘Did he?’ says our dear cousin; ‘always thought he ran away; took to his legs; got a ducking, and ran away as if a bailiff was after him.’

“‘La!’ says Miss, ‘did the Captain ever have a bailiff after him?’

“‘Didn’t he? Ho, ho!’ laughs Mr. Will.

“I suppose I must have looked very savage, for Spencer, who was dining with us, trod on my foot under the table. ‘Don’t laugh so loud, cousin,’ I said, very gently; ‘you may wake good old Mr. Van den Bosch.’ The good old gentleman was asleep in his arm-chair, to which he commonly retires for a nap after dinner—one of those deep, satisfied sleeps a man takes when his cellar is full and his table well served.

“‘Oh, indeed, cousin,’ says Will; and he turns and winks at a friend of his, Captain Deuceace, whom Will has introduced into this simple family as a man of the highest fashion. ‘Don’t be afraid, miss,’ says Mr. Will, ‘nor my cousin needn’t be.’

“‘Oh, what a comfort!’ cries Miss Lyddy. ‘Keep quite quiet, gentlemen, and don’t quarrel, and come up to me when I send to say the tea is ready.’ And with this she makes a sweet little curtsey, and disappears—leaving behind her, like a spice-trail, the faint promise of Bohea and buttered bread.

“‘Hang it, Jack, pass the bottle, and don’t wake the old gentleman!’ continues Mr. Will. ‘Won’t you help yourself, cousin?’—being particularly facetious in the tone of that word.

“‘I am going to help myself,’ I said; ‘but I am not going to drink the glass; and I’ll tell you what I am going to do with it, if you will be quite quiet, cousin.’ (Desperate kicks from Spencer all this time.)

“‘And what the deuce do I care what you are going to do with it?’ asks Will, looking rather white.

“‘I am going to fling it into your face, cousin,’ says I—and did so, very rapidly.

“‘By Jove, and no mistake!’ cries Mr. Deuceace; and as he and William roared out an oath together, good old Van den Bosch woke up, and, taking the pocket-handkerchief off his face, asked what was the matter.

“I remarked it was only a glass of wine gone the wrong way; and the old man said, ‘Well, well, there is more where that came from! Let the butler bring you what you please, young gentlemen!’ and he sank back in his great chair, and began to sleep again—money and meat lulling him better than any sermon.

“‘From the back of Montagu House Gardens there is a beautiful view of Hampstead at six o’clock in the morning; and the statue of the King on St. George’s Church is reckoned elegant, cousin!’ says I.

“‘D— the statue!’ begins Will; but I said, ‘Don’t, cousin! or you will wake up the old gentleman. Had we not best go upstairs to Miss Lyddy’s tea-table?’

“We arranged a little meeting for the next morning; and a coroner might have been sitting upon one or other, or both, of our bodies this afternoon; but, would you believe it? just as our engagement was about to take place, we were interrupted by three of Sir John Fielding’s men, and carried to Bow Street, and ignominiously bound over to keep the peace.”

The small rupture betwixt George and his cousin did what a drawn sword commonly does in families—it kept the scabbard shut afterward. George’s visits to Bloomsbury grew fewer, for Mr. Will, now that both parties were bound over to keep the peace, redoubled his assiduities with a triumph so insolent that George had need to clench his fingers behind his back, and think of anything rather than the supple movement of his cane.

And Lydia—artless Lydia—received her friends with that queer innocence which is a sharper instrument than malice. Six weeks since she had been frantic with jealousy at George’s supposed preference for another; now she took every occasion, before witnesses, to praise Miss Theo with a candour that stung like salt laid on a cut.

“Miss Theo is so quiet, so gentle,” Lyddy would say, smoothing her words as one smooths icing on a cake, till it shines. “You are just the husband for her, dear Mr. George. How fortunate that horrible quarrel was prevented! The constables came just in time. It was quite ridiculous to hear Mr. Esmond cursing and swearing—so angry at being disappointed of his duel! But their arrival saved your valuable life; and I am sure Miss Theo ought to bless them forever.”

Then, with that soft smile which carried no heat in it, no kitchen warmth, only the cool of a pantry stone, she would add, “You won’t stay and meet Mr. Esmond at dinner to-day? You don’t like being in his company? He can’t do you any harm; and I am sure you will do him none.”

Such speeches, dropped by a little girl among gentlemen and ladies, like white flour dusted in the wrong place, were not likely to make Mr. Warrington hanker after Bloomsbury company. He kept his own counsel about the rencontre with Will; he would not trouble the kind folk in Dean Street with it. But when at length the ladies heard, there was a stir as in a household when the spit has caught fire.

“You were actually going to take a fellow-creature’s life,” cried Theo—Theo whose whole being had a tender domestic exactitude, who could order a room, a meal, a day, with the same careful conscience—“and you came to see us and said not a word! Oh, George, it was shocking!”

“My dear,” pleaded George, “he had insulted me and my brother. Could I let him call us both cowards, and sit by and say, Thank you?”

The General sat grave as a carved saint, his mouth tight, his eye troubled.

“You know you think it a wicked and un-Christian practice, papa,” Theo pressed him, “and have often said you wished gentlemen would have the courage to refuse.”

“To refuse? Yes,” said Mr. Lambert, glumly, as if the very word sat ill on his tongue.

“It must require a prodigious strength of mind to refuse,” put in Jack Lambert, looking as gloomy as his father; “and I think if any man were to call me a coward, I should be apt to forget my orders.”

“You see brother Jack is with me!” cried George, catching at the one crumb of comfort.

“I must not be against you, Mr. Warrington,” said Jack Lambert.

“Mr. Warrington!” George turned scarlet, as if a ladle of boiling gravy had been dashed in his face.

“Would you, a clergyman, have George break the Commandments and commit murder, John?” Theo cried, aghast.

“I am a soldier’s son, sister,” the young divine answered, dryly. “Besides, Mr. Warrington has committed no murder at all. We must soon be hearing from Canada, father. The great question of the supremacy of the two races must be tried there ere long!”

He turned his back as he spoke. George eyed him with wonder, as one listens to a familiar voice suddenly speaking in an unfamiliar dialect. Hetty, grown pale at this original outburst, was drawn out of the room by her sister on some artful errand. George sprang up and followed the retreating girls to the door, then came back with his temper pricked raw.

“Great powers, gentlemen!” he cried. “I believe, on my honour, you are giving me the credit of shirking this affair with Mr. Esmond!”

The clergyman and his father looked at one another. George’s blood rose.

“A man’s nearest and dearest are always the first to insult him,” he said, flashing out.

“You mean to say, ‘Not guilty?’ God bless thee, my boy!” cried the General; and the old man’s voice broke as a kettle whistles when it first begins to boil. He rubbed his hand across his eyes, blushed like a schoolboy, and wrung George’s hand with all his might. “I told thee so, Jack.”

“Not guilty of what, in Heaven’s name?” asked George.

“Nay,” said the General, “Mr. Jack here brought the story. Let him tell it. I believe ’tis a —— lie, with all my heart.” And having uttered the wicked word, the General fairly walked out, as if to rid the room of it.

The Rev. J. Lambert looked uncommonly foolish.

“And what is this—this d——d lie, sir, that somebody has been telling of me?” asked George, grinning at him with anger and incredulity together.

“To question the courage of any man is always an offence to him,” Mr. Lambert said, soberly; “and I rejoice that yours has been belied.”

“Who told the falsehood, sir, which you repeated?” bawled George. “I insist on the man’s name!”

“You forget you are bound over to keep the peace,” said Jack.

“Curse the peace, sir! We can go and fight in Holland. Tell me the man’s name, I say!”

“Fair and softly, Mr. Warrington!” cried the young parson, colouring. “My hearing is perfectly good. It was not a man who told me the story which—I confess—I imparted to my father.”

“What?” George’s mind leapt, as a flame catches on spilled brandy. “Was it that artful, wicked little vixen in Bloomsbury Square?”

“Vixen is not the word to apply to any young lady, George Warrington!” cried Lambert, fired at last. “Much less to the charming Miss Lydia. She artful—the most innocent of Heaven’s creatures! She wicked—that angel! With unfeigned delight that the quarrel should be over—with devout gratitude to think that blood consanguineous should not be shed—she spoke in terms of the highest praise of you for declining this quarrel, and of the deepest sympathy with you for taking the painful but only method of averting it.”

“What method?” demanded George, stamping.

“Why, of laying an information, to be sure!” said Mr. Jack.

At that George broke forth into language too violent for repetition here—words that smelt of sulphur and hot iron, and were highly uncomplimentary to Miss Lydia.

“Don’t utter such words, sir!” cried the parson, who now took his turn to be angry. “Do not insult, in my hearing, the most charming, the most innocent of her sex! If she has been mistaken in her information regarding you, and doubted your willingness to commit what, after all, is a crime—for a crime homicide is, and of the most awful description—you, sir, have no right to blacken that angel’s character with foul words; and, innocent yourself, should respect the most innocent, as she is the most lovely of women! Oh, George, are you to be my brother?”

“I hope to have that honour,” answered George, smiling, for at last he began to taste what dish Jack was praising so rapturously.

“What, then—what—though ’tis too much bliss to be hoped for by sinful man—what, if she should one day be your sister? Who could see her charms without being subjugated by them? I own that I am a slave. I own that those Latin Sapphics in the September number of the Gentleman’s Magazine, beginning Lydicae quondam cecinit venustae (with an English version by my friend Hickson of Corpus), were mine. I have told my mother what hath passed between us, and Mrs. Lambert also thinks that the most lovely of her sex has deigned to look favourably on me. I have composed a letter—she another. She proposes to wait on Miss Lydia’s grandpapa this very day, and to bring me the answer, which shall make me the happiest or the most wretched of men!

“It was in the unrestrained intercourse of family conversation that I chanced to impart to my father the sentiments which my dear girl had uttered. Perhaps I spoke slightingly of your courage—which I don’t doubt—by Heaven, I don’t doubt: it may be, she has erred, too, regarding you. It may be that the fiend jealousy has been gnawing at my bosom, and—horrible suspicion!—that I thought my sister’s lover found too much favour with her—I would have all my own. Ah, dear George, who knows his faults? I am as one distracted with passion. Confound it, sir! What right have you to laugh at me? I would have you to know that risu inepto—”

“What, have you two boys made it up?” cried the General, entering at this moment, in the midst of a roar of laughter from George.

“I was giving my opinion to Mr. Warrington upon laughter, and upon his laughter in particular,” said Jack Lambert, in a fume.

“George is bound over to keep the peace, Jack! Thou canst not fight him for two years; and between now and then, let us trust you will have made up your quarrel. Here is dinner, boys! We will drink absent friends, and an end to the war, and no fighting out of the profession!”

The dinner came in with its homely music: the scrape of trenchers, the clink of glasses, the quick footfall of service that is itself a kind of domestic song. The General liked a table that sounded alive—noisy enough to drown the thin, anxious noises of the mind. Yet George’s appetite was all edge and impatience; the roast might have been leather for all the comfort it gave him. He pleaded an engagement and ran away early; and Jack must have followed speedily, for when George, after brief business at his own lodgings, came to Mr. Van den Bosch’s door in Bloomsbury Square, he found the young parson already parleying with a servant there.

“His master and mistress have left town yesterday,” said the man.

“Poor Jack!” George said, when they had moved aside a little, the street sounding around them with wheels and cries as the tide sounds around a rock. “And you had the decisive letter in your pocket?”

“Well, yes,” Jack owned, with the air of one who carries a hot dish only to have it dashed from his hands. “And my mother has ordered a chair, and was coming to wait on Miss Lyddy,” he whispered piteously.

George had a note too in his pocket for the young lady, which he had not cared to mention to Jack. His “brief business” at home had been to write a smart note to Miss Lyddy, sharp as vinegar, with a message for the gentleman who had brought her that funny story of his giving information about the duel. But the family being absent, George did not choose to leave it; paper in an empty house is like food set out for rats.

“If cousin Will has been the slander-bearer,” thought George, “I will go and make him recant.” Aloud he asked with false calm, “Will the family soon be back?”

“They are gone to visit the quality,” replied the servant, with the importance of a man who knows where the great kitchens are. “Here is the address on this paper.” And George read, in Miss Lydia’s own hand, as neat as a cook’s label tied to a jar:

“The box from Madam Hocquet’s to be sent by the Farnham Flying Coach; addressed to Miss Van den Bosch, at the Right Honourable the Earl of Castlewood’s, Castlewood, Hants.”

“Where?” cried poor Jack, aghast.

“His lordship and their ladyships have been here often,” the servant said. “The families is quite intimate.”

It was strange; for in their talk Lydia had owned but to one single visit from Lady Castlewood. And the man added, “And they must be a-going to stay there some time, for Miss have took a power of boxes and gowns with her!”

So the young men walked away, each with his letter crumpled in his pocket—love and anger both folded into useless creases.

“What was that remark you made?” asked George, at some broken exclamation of Jack’s. “I think you said—”

“Distraction! I am beside myself, George! I—I scarce know what I am saying,” groaned the clergyman, as if the air itself had turned thin in his lungs. “She is gone to Hampshire, and Mr. Esmond is gone with her!”

“Othello could not have spoken better,” said George, with a harsh laugh; “and she has a pretty scoundrel in her company! Ha—here is your mother’s chair!”

Indeed at this moment poor Aunt Lambert came swinging down Great Russell Street, preceded by her footman; the chair’s poles creaked, the bearers’ steps fell in a steady thud, like a pulse you cannot stop.

“’Tis no use going farther, Aunt Lambert!” cried George. “Our little bird has flown.”

“What little bird?”

“The bird Jack wished to pair with—the Lyddy bird, aunt. Why, Jack, I protest you are swearing again! This morning ’twas the Sixth Commandment you wanted to break; and now—”

“Confound it! leave me alone, Mr. Warrington, do you hear?” growled Jack, savage; and away he strode, far out of reach of his mother’s bearers and her anxious questions.

“What is the matter, George?” asked the lady, leaning forward in her chair, her voice small against the street’s din—hawkers, wheels, hammers far off, all the city’s constant grinding, as if London itself were a mill that never ceased.

George, ill-pleased with brother Jack’s behaviour all day, answered with cruel lightness: “Brother Jack has not a fine temper, Aunt Lambert. He informs you all that I am a coward, and remonstrates with me for being angry. He finds his mistress gone to the country, and he bawls, and stamps, and swears. O fie! Oh, Aunt Lambert, beware of jealousy! Did the General ever make you jealous?”

“You will make me very angry if you speak to me in this way,” said poor Aunt Lambert.

“I am respectfully dumb. I make my bow. I withdraw,” said George, with a low bow; and he turned towards Holborn.

His soul was wrath within him, and it sought a place to spend itself, as a cook seeks a place to set down a pan that burns his hands. Had he met cousin Will that night, it had gone ill with his sureties. He sought Will at all his haunts—at Arthur’s, at his own house. At last, at Castlewood’s London lodging, Lady Castlewood’s servants told him they believed Mr. Esmond had gone to join the family in Hampshire.

George wrote at once to his cousin:

“My dear, kind cousin William,” he said, “you know I am bound over, and would not quarrel with any one, much less with a dear, truth-telling, affectionate kinsman, whom my brother insulted by caning. But if you can find any one who says that I prevented a meeting the other day by giving information, will you tell your informant that I think it is not I but somebody else is the coward? And I write to Mr. Van den Bosch by the same post, to inform him and Miss Lyddy that I find some rascal has been telling them lies to my discredit, and to beg them to have a care of such persons.”

These neat letters despatched, he dressed himself, showed himself at the play, and took supper cheerfully at the Bedford—forcing cheer as one forces a sauce to thicken, stirring and stirring though the ingredients will not come together. Around him the town made its accustomed music: fiddles in a gallery, laughter in a room, the clatter of plates and the slap of cards—sounds that, for some men, are a shield; for others, only a louder reminder of what they cannot quiet.

In a few days, on his breakfast-table, lay a letter franked “Castlewood,” and written by that nobleman.

“Dear Cousin,” my lord wrote, “there has been so much annoyance in our family of late, that I am sure ’tis time our quarrels should cease. Two days since my brother William brought me a very angry letter, signed G. Warrington, and at the same time, to my great grief and pain, acquainted me with a quarrel that had taken place between you, in which, to say the least, your conduct was violent. ’Tis an ill use to put good wine to—that to which you applied good Mr. Van den Bosch’s. Sure, before an old man, young ones should be more respectful. I do not deny that Wm.’s language and behaviour are often irritating. I know he has often tried my temper, and that within the 24 hours.

“Ah! why should we not all live happily together? You know, cousin, I have ever professed a sincere regard for you—that I am a sincere admirer of the admirable young lady to whom you are engaged, and to whom I offer my most cordial compliments and remembrances. I would live in harmony with all my family where ’tis possible—the more because I hope to introduce to it a Countess of Castlewood.

“At my mature age, ’tis not uncommon for a man to choose a young wife. My Lydia (you will divine that I am happy in being able to call mine the elegant Miss Van den Bosch) will naturally survive me. After soothing my declining years, I shall not be jealous if at their close she should select some happy man to succeed me; though I shall envy him the possession of so much perfection and beauty. Though of a noble Dutch family, her rank, the dear girl declares, is not equal to mine, which she confesses that she is pleased to share. I, on the other hand, shall not be sorry to see descendants to my house, and to have it, through my Lady Castlewood’s means, restored to something of the splendour which it knew before two or three improvident predecessors impaired it. My Lydia, who is by my side, sends you and the charming Lambert family her warmest remembrances.

“The marriage will take place very speedily here. May I hope to see you at church? My brother will not be present to quarrel with you. When I and dear Lydia announced the match to him yesterday, he took the intelligence in bad part, uttered language that I know he will one day regret, and is at present on a visit to some neighbours. The Dowager Lady Castlewood retains the house at Kensington; we having our own establishment, where you will ever be welcomed, dear cousin, by your affectionate humble servant,

“CASTLEWOOD.”

And so, as one reads a recipe only to find the chief ingredient substituted without warning, George learned in a few lines what all his senses had been slow to believe: the white favours were not for Jack Lambert, nor for George’s own vexed imaginings, but for an earl with an old house and a hungry need to mend it.

From the London Magazine of November 1759:

“Saturday, October 13th, married, at his seat, Castlewood, Hants, the Right Honourable Eugene, Earl of Castlewood, to the beautiful Miss Van den Bosch, of Virginia. 70,000 pounds.”

Looking across the fire, towards the chair that has been my familiar harbour these many years, and towards her who has sat there—my partner in every common day and every uncommon tremor—I find myself, as middle-aged gentlemen will, repeating the same question because the answer still warms me: whether any two young people were ever more rash, more penniless, more foolishly resolved than we were when we married in the year the old King died.

Miles, my son, who has taken such prodigious leaps in the heat of fox-hunting that he seems to fly rather than ride, says that afterwards he surveys the gaps and rivers he crossed so safely with mere horror, and wonders at his own headlong madness. Yet no man in our two counties follows hounds more eagerly than he. Scent and cry are his politics; he wants no other. He has broken a collar-bone, and has had a hundred tumbles, each one a stab to his mother’s heart. And I—who am accounted a sober Justice, a scribbler of verses, a man to speak at Quarter Sessions—have been pitched over old Sultana’s head at four miles an hour, because the mare slipped on a stone while we were both dreaming along a park road, I thinking, perhaps, of a line that would not scan, or of a speech that would not end. His recklessness is the delight of his life, as my marriage has been the blessing of mine; and I never recall our imprudence but to thank Heaven for it.

Do not imagine I set up my worship as an example. I do not go preaching to all young folk, “Marry upon twopence a year!” or our vestry would look black enough at me. Yet my wife—who can tie knots in a household as neatly as any vicar ties them at the altar—is known to be a desperate match-maker; and when Hodge and Susan come into my justice-room with their timid talk of allowance and wages, we bid them spend their half-crown a week at home, add a little contribution of our own, and send for the parson. There are economies that starve a hearth, and economies that feed it. My lady has always known the difference, though she will laugh at me and say the difference is only whether I am the one to pay.

When I put questions to my dear oracle, I know beforehand what she will answer; which is, no doubt, why I consult her so often. I have but to wear a particular expression, and my Diana takes her reflection from it as quickly as the kettle takes heat from the fire. Suppose I say, “My dear, don’t you think the moon was made of cream cheese to-night?” She will answer, “Well, papa, it did look very like cream cheese indeed—there’s nobody like you for droll similes.” And, truth to tell, there are nights when the great pale disc hangs over our orchard like a round from some dairy in Norfolk: white as curd newly lifted, with a faint bluish rind, as if it had lain on clean linen in a cool pantry; and the owls make their soft questions, and the distant brook keeps time in its own tongue, and one may fancy the heavens themselves have a larder.

Or suppose I say, “My love, Mr. Pitt’s speech was very fine, but I don’t think he is equal to what I remember of his father.” “Nobody was equal to my Lord Chatham,” says my wife at once; and then one of the girls cries out, “Why, I have often heard our papa say Lord Chatham was a charlatan!” upon which mamma—who has a small armoury of phrases, each sharpened by long use—says, “How like she is to her Aunt Hetty!” The child laughs; the fire cracks; the old clock speaks its steady syllables in the corner; and all the while, under those English words we toss so lightly, there are other older sounds we do not hear—phrases my grandmother would have known, country turns of speech, scraps of dialect, half a prayer, half a curse, now gone out like an extinguished candle. The girls will never miss them, for you cannot mourn what you have never tasted.

As for Miles, Tros Tyriusve is all one to him. He reads only the sporting announcements in the Norwich paper. So long as there is good scent, he does not care about the state of the country. The music that governs his heart is not the voice of Parliament, but the whole living choir of a hunting morning: the horn cutting the mist like bright steel; the hounds’ deep-throated argument rolling over the fallows; the thud of hooves on turf; and—when modern times bring their coarse intrusions—the distant hammer of some new road-mender’s cart, the iron-shod din that startles even the rooks. Give Miles a clear wind and no wagons clattering, and he is content.

I believe the rascal has never read my poems—much more my tragedies. I mentioned Pocahontas to him the other day, and the dunce thought she was a river in Virginia. My Latin verses? How should he understand them when I know he can’t construe Corderius? Why, this very notebook lies publicly on the little table by my corner of the fireside, and any one may read it who will take the trouble of lifting my spectacles off the cover: but Miles never does. I insert loose pages with caricatures of Miles; jokes against him; little malices a father allows himself because he loves. He neither knows nor heeds them.

Only once, in place of a neat drawing of mine in China ink, representing Miles asleep after dinner—an after-dinner sleep so deep it seemed he had been basted and set to rest like a joint left too long before the hearth, and which my friend Bunbury would not have disowned—I found a rude picture of myself going over Sultana’s head, entitled, “The Squire on Horseback, or Fish out of Water.” And the fellow roared with laughter, and all the girls tittered, when I came upon the page! My wife said she never was in such a fright as when I went to my book; but I can bear a jest against myself, and have heard many—though strange to say, for one who has lived among some of the chief wits of the age, I never heard a good one in my life. Never mind, Miles. Though thou art not a wit, I love thee none the worse; there never was any love lost between two wits in a family.

And though thou hast no great beauty, thy mother thinks thee as handsome as Apollo—or as His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, who was born in the very same year with thee. Indeed, she always maintained that Coates’s picture of the Prince was very like her eldest boy, and she has the print in her dressing-room to this very day.

[Note, in a female hand: “My son is not a spendthrift, nor a breaker of women’s hearts, as some gentlemen are; but that he was exceeding like H.R.H. when they were both babies is most certain, the Duchess of Aneaster having herself remarked him in St. James’s Park, where Gumbo and my poor Molly used often to take him for an airing. Th. W.”]

In that same year, with what different prospects, my Lord Esmond—Lord Castlewood’s son—likewise appeared to adorn the world. My Lord C. and his humble servant had already come to a coolness at that time, and Heaven knows my honest Miles’s godmother, at his entrance into life, brought no gold pap-boats to his christening. Matters have mended since, laus Deo—laus Deo indeed!—for I suspect neither Miles nor his father would ever have been able to do much for themselves by their own wits.

Castlewood House has quite another face now from that venerable one it wore in my youth, when it seemed covered with the wrinkles of time—the scars of old wars, the cracks and blemishes years had scored into its hoary features. I best love to remember it in its old shape, as I saw it when young Mr. George Warrington went down at the owner’s invitation to be present at his lordship’s marriage with Miss Lydia Van den Bosch—“an American lady of noble family of Holland,” as the county paper announced her. Then the towers stood as Warrington’s grandfather the Colonel (the Marquis, as Madam Esmond would fain have called her father) had seen them. The woods—thinned, to be sure—were there, and perhaps the self-same rooks that had cawed over them threescore years before. His picture hung in the hall which might have been his, had he not preferred love and gratitude to wealth and worldly honour.

And I, Egomet Ipse who set this down, walking those long corridors, those smooth dew-spangled terraces, those cool darkling avenues where the leaves whispered in their own old dialect, felt for a while as if I were one of Mr. Walpole’s cavaliers with ruff and rapier, buff-coat and gorget; as if an Old Pretender, or a Jesuit emissary in disguise, might step from behind any tall trunk, or glide from any antique carved cupboard within. The place had a sound, too—an inhabited hush: the soft complaint of boards that had borne generations; the hollow answer of a stair; the far clink of kitchen iron; the rookery’s rough parliament in the trees. In such a house the past does not merely show itself; it speaks, though you cannot always translate its tongue.

I had the strangest, saddest, pleasantest old-world fancies as I walked: I imagined tragedies, intrigues, serenades, escaladoes; Oliver’s Roundheads battering the towers; bluff Hal’s Beefeaters pricking over the plain before the castle. I was then courting a certain young lady—madam, your ladyship’s eyes had no need of spectacles then, and on the brow above them there was never a wrinkle nor a silver hair—and I remember I wrote a ream of romantic description, under my Lord Castlewood’s franks, to the lady who never tired of reading my letters. She says I only send her three lines now when I am away in London or elsewhere. ’Tis that I may not fatigue your old eyes, my dear.

Mr. Warrington thought himself authorised to order a genteel new suit for my lord’s marriage, and with Monsieur Gumbo in attendance made his appearance at Castlewood a few days before the ceremony. I may mention that it had been found expedient to send my faithful Sady home on board a Virginia ship. A great inflammation attacking throat and lungs, fatal in very many cases in that year of Wolfe’s expedition, had seized and well-nigh killed my poor lad; and his native air was pronounced the best cure. We parted with an abundance of tears. Gumbo shed as many when his master went to Quebec; but he had attractions in this country, and none for the military life, so remained attached to my service.

We found Castlewood full of friends, relations, and visitors. Lady Fanny was there upon compulsion, a sulky bridesmaid. Some virgins of the neighbourhood attended the young Countess. A bishop’s widow herself, the Baroness Beatrix brought down a holy brother-in-law of the bench from London to tie the holy knot between Eugene Earl of Castlewood and Lydia Van den Bosch, spinster; and for some time before and after the nuptials the old house in Hampshire wore an air of gaiety to which it had long been unaccustomed.

The country families came gladly to pay their compliments. The lady’s wealth was everybody’s subject, and no doubt did not diminish in the telling. Those naughty stories rife in town, spread by disappointed suitors, took time to travel into Hampshire; and when they arrived, the country was disposed to treat Lord Castlewood’s wife with civility, and not inclined to be too curious about her behaviour in London. Suppose she had jilted this man and laughed at the other? It was her money they were anxious about, and she was no more mercenary than they.

The Hampshire folks were determined it was a great benefit to the country to have Castlewood House open once more, with beer in the cellars, horses in the stables, and spits turning before the kitchen fires. And indeed there is a kind of peace that comes of a well-governed kitchen: the steady chop of herbs on a board, the sigh of a joint as it meets the heat, the measured clatter of pewter, the yeasty breath of ale, the whole domestic orchestra playing without discord. The new lady took her place with great dignity; and it was certain she had uncommon accomplishments and wit. Was it not printed in the marriage advertisements that her ladyship brought her noble husband seventy thousand pounds? On a beaucoup d’esprit with seventy thousand pounds. The Hampshire people said it was but a small portion of her wealth. When the grandfather should fall, ever so many plums would be found on that old tree.

That quiet old man—keen as a knife at a carver’s board—began quickly to put the dilapidated Castlewood accounts in order, which long neglect, poverty, and improvidence had hurried towards ruin. The business of his life now, and for some time henceforth, was to advance, improve, mend my lord’s finances; to screw rents up where practicable; to pare establishment expenses down. He could somehow look to every yard of worsted lace on the footmen’s coats, and every pound of beef that went to their dinner. A watchful old eye noted every flagon of beer fetched from the buttery, and marked that no waste occurred in the larder. One might fancy him tasting the household with his mind, as a careful cook tastes a pot—knowing, by the least excess or thinness, where a hand has been careless. The people were fewer, but more regularly paid; the liveries were not so ragged, and yet the tailor had no need to dun. The gardeners and grooms grumbled, though their wages were no longer overdue: but the horses fattened on less corn, and fruit and vegetables were ever so much more plentiful—so narrowly did my lady’s old grandfather keep watch over the whole from his lonely little chamber in the turret.

These improvements, though told here in a paragraph, were the affairs of months and years at Castlewood; where, with thrift, order, and judicious outlay (though upon some pressing occasions my lord might say he had none), the estate and household grew in prosperity. That it was flourishing and economical, no one could deny—not even the dowager lady and her two children, who now seldom entered within Castlewood gates, my lady considering them enemies; for who, indeed, would like a stepmother-in-law? The little reigning Countess gave the dowager battle, and routed her utterly and speedily. Though educated in the colonies and ignorant of polite life in her early years, Countess Lydia had a power of language and a strength of will that all acknowledged who quarrelled with her.

And here again was a lesson of tongues: for power is not only in gold, nor in a title, but in the words you choose and the accent you dare to keep. Lydia could strike with a phrase as neatly as a cook splits a fowl at the joint; and the dowager and my Lady Fanny were no match for the young American. They fled before her to their jointure house in Kensington, and no wonder their absence was not regretted by my lord, who was in the habit of regretting no one whose back was turned.

Could cousin Warrington—whose hand his lordship pressed so affectionately at coming and parting, with whom cousin Eugene was so gay, frank, and pleasant when together—expect or hope that his lordship would grieve at his departure, his death, any misfortune that might befall him, or any soul alive? Cousin Warrington knew better.

Always of a sceptical turn, Mr. W. took a grim delight in watching the peculiarities of his neighbours, and could like this one even though he had no courage and no heart. Courage? Heart? What are these to you and me in the world? A man may have private virtues as he may have half a million in the funds. What we du monde expect is that he should be lively, agreeable, keep a decent figure, and pay his way.

Colonel Esmond Warrington’s grandfather—whose history and dwelling-place Mr. W. took an extraordinary interest in—might once have been owner of this house of Castlewood, and of the titles belonging to its possessor. Mr. Warrington often looked at the Colonel’s grave picture as it still hung in the saloon, a copy or replica of which he fondly remembered in Virginia. “He must have been a little touched here,” my lord would say, tapping his own tall, placid forehead. There are certain actions, simple and common with some men, which others cannot understand, and so deny as lies or deride as madness.

“I do you the justice to think, cousin,” says Mr. Warrington to his lordship, “that you would not give up any advantage for any friend in the world.”

“Eh! I am selfish. But am I more selfish than the rest of the world?” asks my lord, with a French shrug and a pinch out of his box.

Once, in their walks in the fields, his lordship happening to wear a fine scarlet coat, a cow ran towards him; and the ordinarily languid nobleman sprang over a stile with the agility of a schoolboy. He did not conceal his tremor, nor his natural want of courage. “I dare say you respect me no more than I respect myself, George,” he would say in his candid way; and then begin a very pleasant, sardonical discourse upon the fall of man, and our faults and shortcomings; and wonder why Heaven had not made us all brave and tall and handsome and rich.

As for Mr. Warrington—who very likely loved to be king of his company, as some do—he could not help liking this kinsman: so witty, graceful, polished, high-placed in the world, and so utterly his inferior. Like the animal in Mr. Sterne’s famous book, “Do not beat me,” his lordship’s look seemed to say; “but, if you will, you may.” No man—save a bully and coward himself—deals hardly with a creature so spiritless.

In all the old tales, at every christening and wedding, somebody is left out in the cold, and goes away nursing a grievance as if it were a coal meant to be kept alive. So it was at Castlewood when the match was made between my lord and the colonial heiress. Cousin Will, who had long counted the girl as his own prize—won, as he swore, by hazard of life and limb—took the news like a man struck across the mouth. He stormed from the house, calling down ruin on all heads, and proclaimed he would never cross the threshold again.

No one, least of all Will himself, put faith in those grand departures. Castlewood had too good a kitchen to make exile long. The house breathed roast and broth, cider and warm spice; the very chimneys seemed to send after him a ribbon of smoke as a lure. After two days’ sulk he came back, not humbled, but hungry; and in token of revenge he sat down to his father’s board, ate his fill, drank with the others, and with every mouthful seemed to swear he was swallowing the insult whole.

At the feast he raised his glass to the bride with a loud enough compliment, and under the rim of the bumper murmured perdition. In chapel, when her father gave her away and my lord vowed to love, honour, and cherish, Will made responses as if each “Amen” were a smothered curse. He was not the only malcontent. Mr. Warrington heard it at the time and afterwards till his ears ached with it: abuse of my lady and of her grandfather poured from many mouths, each speaker eager to prove he had been wronged first.

The City friends of the old gentleman cried out upon the treachery of the little American; the lawyer, who had once displayed a list of her properties as if he were laying out joints on a butcher’s block—estates, moneys, slaves, ships, expectations—now swore the whole inventory was a cheat; there was no such place as New York or Virginia; or, if there were, Van den Bosch owned no land there; there was no Guinea trade; the negroes were a bundle of black falsehoods; the old planter had salted his tale like a ham to make it keep. A Dissenting minister mourned over his stray lamb—if lamb was the name for a creature so quick-eyed and wilful. Poor Jack Lambert, the orthodox young divine, confessed to his mamma that he still kept a lock of her black hair; he kissed it, he wept upon it, and addressed it in a language that would have made his surplice start from shame. As for William Esmond, he called on Acheron and all the heathen rivers to bear witness that out of the pit itself there never crawled such an artful young devil as Miss Lydia. She was Cerberus in a petticoat; and the brother who had stolen her from him was a swindling rascal who had cajoled him with fair words and filched his prize.

“Why,” said Mr. Warrington, when Will poured out this torrent to him, “if she is the she-devil you paint, you are the better for losing her. If she means to poison her husband, as you vow, you should thank the gods you’re not the man. You cannot be better revenged on Castlewood than by letting him keep her all to himself.”

Will admitted the argument might look pretty on paper, but persisted—perhaps not unjustly—that his brother was none the less a scoundrel for cheating him of the fortune he had expected, and for which he had risked his skin.

George Warrington, who had never been able to understand what had driven cousin Will into so perilous a point of honour, pressed him; and Will, with the utmost candour, explained how the little Cerbera had contrived the meeting between them in Tottenham Court Fields—how she had pricked them both with her tongue, calling George a coward for sneering at Will, and Will a poltroon for letting taunts go unanswered; how she had flung Braddock’s expedition at George as a taunt, and boasted Will up by insulting him.

“Deuce take me,” Will said, “I never was more surprised, cousin, than when you stood your ground so coolly there. Me and my second would have laid a wager you’d never come!”

George laughed. “It was lucky for me the constables came up,” he said, “or you would have slipped your sword through me in another minute. Didn’t you see how awkward I was? And you turned white and shook with anger!”

“Yes, curse me,” Will said, colouring now till the red ran up to his forehead, “that’s my way when I’m in a rage. I was confoundedly angry with you. But now ’tis my brother I hate—and that little devil of a Countess. A countess! A pretty countess indeed!”

He discharged another broadside of oaths, and George watched, as he often did, with a kind of dry amusement, the man choking on his own fury and yet too cowardly to bite where he most wished.

“You should moderate your expressions, cousin,” George said, “regarding the dear Countess and my lord your brother. Of you they always speak most tenderly. Her ladyship has told me everything.”

“What everything?” Will cried, suddenly paling.

“As much as women ever tell. She owned she thought you had been a little épris with her. What woman can help liking a man who has admired her?”

“Why, she hates you, and says you were wild about her!” Will retorted, half incredulous, half eager to find George caught.

“Spretae injuria formae, cousin.”

“For me—what’s for me?” Will demanded.

“I never cared for her,” George said; “and hence, perhaps, she does not love me. Don’t you remember the case of the wife of the Captain of the Guard?”

“Which Guard?” Will asked, honestly puzzled.

“My Lord Potiphar,” George answered.

“Lord who?” Will cried. “My Lord Falmouth is Captain of the Yeomen of the Guard, and my Lord Berkeley of the Pensioners. My Lord Hobart had ’em before. Suppose you haven’t been long enough in England to know who’s who, cousin!”

George explained he meant the Captain of the Guard to the King of Egypt, and the wife who persecuted Joseph for not returning her affection. Will said Egypt was a confounded long way off; and if my lord what-d’ye-call’s wife lied, it was like women, who were the same everywhere, he supposed.

When Mr. Warrington paid his first bridal visit to Castlewood, the little Countess herself gave him her version of the quarrel. It differed in some points from Will’s plain-spoken narrative; but George, who had heard both, would not pretend to choose which was the more authentic. She professed herself grieved, even wounded, that she had been deceived in her brother-in-law. Court and town, she feared, had injured those high principles which all the Esmonds were born with; Will’s words were not to be trusted; a loose life and pecuniary difficulties had blunted his honour and perhaps impaired his chivalrous courage.

“Which we Esmonds, cousin,” she said, tossing her head till the light caught her bright eyes, “which we Esmonds must always possess—leastways you and me, and my lord, and my cousin Harry have it, I know!” She drew herself up as if the very syllables of that name were a coronet. “Oh, cousin George! and must I confess I was led to doubt of yours? Without courage a man of ancient and noble family like ours isn’t worthy to be called a man. I shall try, as a Christian lady, and the head of one of the first families in this kingdom and the whole world, to forgive my brother William for speaking ill of a member of our family—though a younger branch and by the female side—and making me for a moment doubt of you.”

“I, my dear lady!” George cried.

“Which he said you said of me,” she continued, her words running like a brook over stones, “and I hope you didn’t, and heartily pray you didn’t; and I can afford to despise ’em. And he paid me his court—that’s a fact; and so have others, and that I’m used to. And he might have prospered better than he did perhaps, for I did not know my dear lord then, nor come to vally his great and eminent qualities as I do out of the fulness of this grateful heart now!—but, oh! I found William was deficient in courage. And no man as wants that can ever have the esteem of Lydia, Countess of Castlewood, no more he can!”

She snapped her little fingers, as if to flick a crumb of him from her glove.

“He said ’twas you that wanted spirit, cousin, and angered me by telling me you was always abusing of me. But I forgive you, George, that I do! And when I tell you it was he was afraid—the mean skunk!—and actually sent for them constables to prevent the match between you and he, you won’t wonder I wouldn’t vally a feller like that—no, not that much!” Again the fingers snapped. “Noblesse oblige; and a man of our family who hasn’t got courage, I don’t care not this pinch of snuff for him—there, now, I don’t! Look at our ancestors, George, round these walls! Haven’t the Esmonds always fought for their country and king? Is there one of us that, when the moment arrives, ain’t ready to show he’s an Esmond and a nobleman? If my eldest son was to show the white feather—‘My Lord Esmond!’ I would say to him, for that’s the second title in our family, ‘I disown your lordship!’”

As she spoke, she looked round at the portraits by Lely and Kneller that glimmered upon the walls of the Castlewood drawing-room—faces whose mouths were set as if they still commanded men, whose eyes, though painted, seemed to listen for drum and trumpet. Even in that quiet room you could hear the house’s winter sound: the fire’s steady eating of logs, the faint crack in the wainscot as the frost worked outside, the hush of thick carpets drinking footsteps, and far off, from the courtyard, the occasional ring of a bit or stamp of a horse, like punctuation to her speech.

Over that room, and over the whole house, domain, and village, the new Countess began very speedily to rule with an unlimited sway. It was astonishing how quickly she learned the ways of command. If she did not adopt the established English methods of precedence, she invented regulations for herself, published them, and made others obey. She had been bred a Dissenter and at first made a blunder or two in the Established service—not knowing when to turn eastward, for instance, a movement not practised, I believe, in other reformed churches besides the English. But between Warrington’s first bridal visit and his second, my lady had become quite perfect; she sailed into chapel upon her cousin’s arm, her two footmen bearing her great Prayer-book behind her, as demurely as that ancient devotee in Mr. Hogarth’s “Morning,” and as if she had lived all her life with a chaplain at her elbow. She patronised the new chaplain, the service, and the church itself, as though she had never in her own country heard a Ranter thunder in a barn. The neighbouring families—grave baronets and their wives, squires of twenty descents who rode over to pay their respects—were made to know their distance and give her the pas.

She procured an old book of heraldry, and engaged a surprising old maiden lady from Winton, learned in genealogies and politeness, from whom she gleaned court etiquette as it had been known in Queen Anne’s time. Soon my lady jabbered of gules and sables, bends and saltires—not always with correctness, but with an extraordinary volubility and perseverance. She made little progresses to neighbouring towns in her gilt coach-and-six, or to the village in her chair, and asserted a quasi-regal right to homage from tenants and other clodpoles. She lectured the parson upon divinity; the bailiff upon farming; and in the stillroom would have had the housekeeper believe she had been born among pickles and preserves.

Here, at least, my lady’s genius was at home, for she loved to put her small hands to the empire of jars and kettles. She inspected the shelves where quinces lay like little suns in syrup, where damsons bled purple into glass, where walnuts, green as unripe secrets, were steeped for cordials; she would sniff at a vinegar, tap a pot of potted beef, and declare it wanted pepper or bay. The stillroom, with its warm breath of mace and clove, its beeswax and dried herbs, received her like a chapel of domestic worship.
