She gave directions how to salt a side of bacon so the fat should turn pearl and not rancid; how to scald a chine of pork before smoking; how to boil sugar to the feather, and when to lift it so it would not grain; how to blanch almonds, how to steep orange peel till the bitterness was tamed. The old housekeeper, who had made my lord and the dowager wary in former days, now found herself astonished into obedience by a mistress who could scold and praise in one breath, and who listened with her whole sharp body, as if a recipe were a campaign-plan.

As for physic, Madam Esmond in Virginia had not been more resolute about pills and draughts than Miss Lydia, the earl’s new bride. And if the household’s peace depended in part upon quiet sounds—the soft scurry of servants, the muffled closing of doors, the distant clink of plate that told of order—my lady altered the music of the place. Under her, the great London footmen who used to quarrel over cards and grumble as they swilled endless beer, now stepped nimbly when they heard her call; even their footsteps changed, less thudding, more careful, as if the very floors had learned fear. The house’s acoustics became a kind of discipline: a bell rung sharply; a voice that could cut through passages; the hush after a rebuke, in which you might hear the coals settle in the grate like a sigh.

She would have taught the great London fellows to jump behind the carriage too, only it was too high for her little ladyship to mount. She gave the village gossips instructions how to nurse and tend their children long before she had one herself. And she was brisk with her own people. Dinah, her black attendant, complained to Gumbo (who carried complaints, as servants do, from ear to ear) that her ladyship pinched her great ears and pulled at her woolly pate upon offence given.

Old age, in particular, had small sanctity with my lady. Once the settlements were made in her behalf, she treated the ancient Van den Bosch and his large periwig with scarcely more ceremony than Dinah. All trembled before her. Even old Lockwood, who had been gate-porter for half a century, and whose wits wandered as winter birds do, tried to rally them when she came into his lodge to open his window, inspect his wood-closet, and turn his old dogs out of doors.

Lockwood bared his bald head to her new authority, glanced piteously toward his niece, and shook in his chair. The lodge had its own poor homely smells—damp wood, old leather, a dog’s coat dried too near the fire—and its own small sounds, comforting to the old man: the scrape of a paw, the creak of his chair, the wind worrying the latch. My lady’s entrance was like a new instrument introduced into that little orchestra—too bright, too sharp, drowning the rest.

Gumbo, dressing his master for dinner, spoke of Elisha, of whom he had heard the chaplain read that morning—“and his bald head, and de boys who call um names, and de bars eat em up, and serve um right,” said Gumbo, grinning, as he tied a cravat. But my lady, speaking to her cousin of the porter, dismissed him with a wave.

“Pooh, pooh! Stupid old man!” she cried. “Past his work, he and his dirty old dogs! They are as old and ugly as those old fish in the pond!”

She meant the two ancient carp that had lived for centuries in the garden pond, according to tradition; their backs were coated with a hideous grey mould, and they moved slowly under the ice like legends that refused to die.

“Lockwood must pack off,” my lady continued. “The workhouse is the place for him; and I shall have a smart, good-looking, tall fellow in the lodge that will do credit to our livery.”

“He was my grandfather’s man,” Mr. Warrington said, “and served him in the wars of Queen Anne.”

On which my lady, petulant as a child tired of a story, cried, “O Lord! Queen Anne’s dead, I suppose, and we ain’t a-going into mourning for her.”

This question was brought to the family table. The dinner that day had the solid winter comforts of an old English house: a haunch that sent up a rich steam when carved, potatoes mealy and hot, cabbage softened with butter, sauces dark and shining, and a pudding that smelt of suet, lemon, and brandy. The clink of knives on plates, the murmur of servants at the sideboard, the crackle of the fire, were part of the argument, as if the house itself took a side.

My lady announced, between mouthfuls, her intention of getting rid of Lockwood.

“I am told,” Mr. Van den Bosch remarked demurely, “that by the laws poor servants and poor folks of all kinds are admirably provided for in their old age here in England. I’m sure I wish we had such an asylum for our folks at home, and that we were eased of the expense of keeping our old hands.”

“If a man can’t work he ought to go!” cried her ladyship.

“Yes, indeed, and that’s a fact!” said grandpapa.

“What! an old servant?” asked my lord.

“Mr. Van den Bosch possibly was independent of servants when he was young,” Mr. Warrington observed.

“Greased my own boots, opened my own shutters, sanded and watered my own—”

“Sugar, sir?” my lord asked, with languid politeness.

“No; floor, son-in-law!” the old man said, laughing; “though there is such tricks in grocery stores, saving your ladyship’s presence.”

“La, pa! what should I know about stores and groceries?” cried her ladyship, tossing her head.

“He! Remember stealing the sugar, and what came on it, my dear ladyship?” grandpapa chuckled.

“At any rate,” my lady persisted, “a handsome, well-grown man in our livery will look better than that shrivelled old porter creature!”

“No livery is so becoming as old age, madam,” Mr. Warrington said, “and no lace as handsome as silver hairs. What will the county say if you banish old Lockwood?”

“Oh! if you plead for him, sir, I suppose he must stay. Hadn’t I better order a couch for him out of my drawing-room, and send him some of the best wine from the cellar?”

“Indeed your ladyship couldn’t do better,” Mr. Warrington replied, very gravely.

And my lord, yawning, said, “Cousin George is perfectly right, my dear. To turn away such an old servant as Lockwood would have an ill look.”

“You see those mouldy old carps are, after all, a curiosity and attract visitors,” continued Mr. Warrington, still with that same gravity. “Your ladyship must allow this old wretch to remain. It won’t be for long. And you may then engage the tall porter. It is very hard on us, Mr. Van den Bosch, that we are obliged to keep our old negroes when they are past work. I shall sell that rascal Gumbo in eight or ten years.”

“Don’t tink you will, master!” Gumbo said, grinning broadly, his teeth flashing in the candlelight.

“Hold your tongue, sir! He doesn’t know English ways, you see,” Mr. Warrington went on, “and perhaps thinks an old servant has a claim on his master’s kindness.”

The next day, to Warrington’s surprise, my lady did indeed send a basket of good wine to Lockwood, and a cushion for his chair. The bottles clinked softly as they were carried over the gravel; that small music—glass against glass—went into the lodge like an unlikely benediction.

“I thought of what you said yesterday, at night when I went to bed,” she told George. “And guess you know the world better than I do, cousin; and that it’s best to keep the old man, as you say.”

So ended the affair of the porter’s lodge, Mr. Warrington marvelling inwardly at this strange little creature out of the West—naïve and simple in one breath, hard-hearted in the next, with a sudden capacity to mimic English mercies when she saw their use. She could adopt a phrase, a posture, an entire tone, as one might borrow a dish’s name from a foreign tongue—pronouncing it with confidence, yet not tasting all that lived in it.

“You tell me to respect old people,” she said to him another time. “Why? I don’t see nothin’ to respect in the old people I know. They ain’t so funny, and I’m sure they ain’t so handsome. Look at grandfather; look at Aunt Bernstein. They say she was a beauty once! That picture painted from her! I don’t believe it, nohow. No one shall tell me I shall ever be as bad as that! When they come to that, people oughtn’t to live. No, that they oughtn’t.”

At Christmas Aunt Bernstein came to pay her nephew and niece a visit, travelling in company with Mr. Warrington. They went at their leisure in the Baroness’s own landau. The old lady was in particular good health and spirits; the air was fresh without cruelty, and the roads rang pleasantly beneath the wheels. The hedges were bare; the fields had that winter look of rest after labour; and in the pauses of the journey, when the horses’ breath steamed and the postilion’s horn sounded from a distance like a remembered tune, Aunt Beatrice told a hundred stories of Castlewood and the old days.

Though often lethargic and not seldom out of temper, the old lady would light up at times; her conversation became wonderfully lively; her wit and malice flashed; and her memory supplied a hundred anecdotes of a bygone age and society. It is a hard condition of beauty that the possessor should not even have the long enjoyment of it, but must resign it—at most—a forty years’ lease. As she prattled of former lovers and admirers, her auditor knowing more of her past than she supposed, George would look into her face and try, from the ruins, to rebuild an image of her beauty in its prime. It was like standing in a vast abandoned house and imagining it in its season—courts where grass now grew, towers broken, doors ajar, gilt saloons tarnished, tapestries torn and cobwebbed; and yet, in the mind, chandeliers kindling, music rising, laughter running through galleries. Once there had been feasts and balls there; the clatter of fans, the rustle of silks, the bright shocks of applause. Now the same mouth that once gave orders to a roomful of men pursed itself over small irritations; the same eyes that once summoned attention narrowed in complaint. The untranslatability of it—the impossibility of carrying back into the present the exact flavour of what had been—sat in George’s mind like a word remembered from a childhood dialect that no longer had speakers.

When Aunt Bernstein came to Castlewood, her relatives—more on account of her own force of character, imperiousness, and sarcastic wit, than from any desire to possess her money—were accustomed to pay her much deference, which she accepted as her due. She expected the same from the new Countess, whom she meant to greet with especial good humour. The match had been of her making.

“As you, you silly creature, would not have the heiress,” she told George, “I was determined she should not go out of the family,” and she laughed as she spoke of the little schemes by which she had brought the matter about. She had given the girl a coronet and her nephew a hundred thousand pounds; of course she should be welcome to both.

She was delighted with the little Countess’s courage and spirit in routing the Dowager and Lady Fanny. Almost always pleased with pretty people at first sight, Madame Bernstein rattled on about Lydia’s bright eyes and lovely little figure. The marriage was altogether desirable. The old man, Van den Bosch, was an obstacle, to be sure, and his talk and appearance somewhat too homely.

“But he will be got rid of,” the Baroness said, with a shrug, as though she were speaking of a dish that had stood too long and must be removed. “He is old, and in delicate health. He will want to go to America—or perhaps farther.”

“The child has great fire and liveliness,” she continued, “and a Cherokee manner which is not without its charm. Your brother had it—so have you, Master George! Nous la formerons, cette petite. Eugene wants character and vigour, but he is a finished gentleman; and between us we shall make the little savage perfectly presentable.”

So they discoursed on the second afternoon as they journeyed toward Castlewood. The first night they lay at the King’s Arms at Bagshot, where the Baroness was received with profound respect; and thence drove post to Hexton, where she had written to have my lord’s horses in waiting. But the Castlewood horses were not forthcoming at the inn; for a couple of hours they waited, with the sound of stable-boys calling and boots on straw, and the wind fussing at shutters like an impatient servant. At last they were obliged to proceed with their Bagshot horses to Castlewood, the landau rolling on through the winter dusk, and the old lady’s voice, now sharp with recollection, now softened by fatigue, filling the carriage as steadily as the scent of the fur rugs and the faint lingering perfume from her gloves.

Our Castlewood kinsfolk kept us to the turn of the year; and when at last we had been a fortnight away—an age, as any absurd and infatuated young man will reckon time—my feet carried me back to my enchantress as surely as a hungry fellow finds the door of a kitchen by smell alone.

Madame de Bernstein, for her part, wore no sorrow at quitting her father’s house. Indeed she loosened, as it were, the strings of her tongue the moment the coach-wheels had fairly begun to sing upon the road and the wind, taking us in flank, changed the very note of the world. What had passed in that private audience where she and her niece had fought their battle-royal she never told; yet the proof of it was plain enough. She spoke no more of “forming” cette petite; and when she named the young Countess, it was with a nervous little laugh, sharp as a spoon on a china cup, and without the old sourness. Her nephew Eugene, she said, was plainly marked out to be henpecked as long as he lived—she could see it as one sees salt in a clear broth. A little order in the house would do all the good possible. The little old vulgar American gentleman—so she chose to call Mr. Van den Bosch—seemed shrewd, and might serve advantageously as steward, keeping accounts as neat as a row of spice-jars.

As for the Countess’s mother, Madame had heard a story—one of those stories that are flung like kitchen slops from one alley of talk into another—that the woman was a convict, shipped out from England, where no doubt she had beaten hemp in most of the gaols. “But,” says my aunt, with that worldly mercy which can be cruel and kind in one breath, “this need not be cried by the town-crier. And after all, with certain people, what matters birth? The young woman will be honest now for her own sake; she is shrewd enough, and will learn English presently; and the name she has a right to is big enough to carry her into any society.” A grocer, a smuggler, a slave-dealer—what mattered Mr. Van den Bosch’s pursuit? The Countess of Castlewood, says she, could afford to be anybody’s daughter; and once Eugene produced her, it was our duty to stand by her.

Mr. Warrington, who was always hoping to make kindness do the work which pride had neglected, ventured to think that the same tie which bound my aunt so strongly to her nephew might dispose her to some affection toward her niece; and he spoke of my visit to Mr. Hagan and his wife, praying her favour for them. But Madame was flint there. She begged that Lady Maria’s name might never again be mentioned; and, as though that very prohibition had set the wheel going, she talked for two hours afterwards of nobody else. She related a string of anecdotes—sharp, salted, and not fit, as books say, for virginibus puerisque—which I will not set down. This only I will say: if that poor creature sinned, she did not sin alone in our family; and if she repented, others might do well to follow her example.

Hagan, it is known, after he quitted the stage, led an exemplary life; and in the pulpit had an elegance and eloquence which showed how well he understood the cadence and music of speech. His lady adopted extreme views and was much esteemed in the sect she joined; and when I saw her last she spoke to me of enjoying a peculiar spiritual illumination, which I suspected then to be lit by the too free use of liquor. Yet I remember—as one remembers the honest taste of bread in a lean season—how she and her husband were good to me and mine when sympathy was needful and many a Pharisee turned away.

I have told already how easy it was to rise and fall in my fickle aunt’s favour; how each of us brothers in turn was embraced and neglected. My season of glory came after the success of my play. I was introduced to the town-wits; held my place among them tolerably; was pronounced pretty well bred by the macaronis and people of fashion; and might have run a career in that bright, noisy world had my purse been longer, had I chosen such a life, had I not loved at that time a pair of kind eyes better than all the painted beauties of Ranelagh, and the brightest orbs of the Gunnings or Chudleighs.

Because I was fond of your mother—will it be believed, children?—my tastes were called low by my genteel family, and deplored as though I had taken to eating with my fingers in public. So it was; and I know that my godly Lady Warrington and my worldly Madame Bernstein put their elderly heads together and lamented my way of life.

“Why, with his name, he might marry anybody,” says meek Religion, which had ever one eye on Heaven and one on the main chance.

“I meddle with no man’s affairs, and admire genius,” says my uncle; “but it is a pity you consort with those poets and authors and that sort of people, and that, when you might have had a lovely creature with a hundred thousand pounds, you let her slip and make up to a country girl without a penny-piece.”

“But if I had promised her, uncle?” says I.

“Promise, promise! These things are matters of arrangement and prudence, and demand a careful look-out. When you first committed yourself with little Miss Lambert, you had not seen the lovely American lady whom your mother wished you to marry—as a good mother naturally would. And your duty to your mother, nephew—your duty to the Fifth Commandment—would have warranted your breaking with Miss L. and fulfilling your excellent mother’s intentions regarding Miss—What was the Countess’s Dutch name? Never mind. A name is nothing; but a plumb, Master George, is something to look at! Why, I have my dear little Miley at dancing-school with Miss Barwell, Nabob Barwell’s daughter; and I don’t disguise my wish that the children may contract an attachment which may endure through their lives! I tell the Nabob so. We went from the House of Commons one dancing-day and saw them. ’Twas beautiful to see the young things walking a minuet together! It brought tears into my eyes, for I have a feeling heart, George, and I love my boy!”

“But if I prefer Miss Lambert, uncle, with twopence to her fortune, to the Countess, with her hundred thousand pounds?”

“Why then, sir, you have a singular taste—that’s all,” says the old gentleman; and he turned on his heel and left me, as a cook leaves a customer who insists on sugar in his gravy.

I could understand his vexation at my not seeing the world as he saw it. Nor did my Aunt Bernstein relish my engagement, nor the family with whom I passed so much time. Their simple ways wearied her; perhaps even offended her nice nostril. She no more liked their company than a certain person—who is not so black as he is painted—likes holy water. The old lady chafed at my perpetual attendance by my sweetheart’s lap. Having risen in her favour, I began to fall again; and once more Harry was the favourite, and his brother—Heaven knows—felt no jealousy. He was now our family hero.

From the seat of war where he was engaged he sent brief letters—plain fare, not seasoned with fine phrases; and at first Madame cared little for them or the writer, the facts not being, to her mind, amusing enough. Yet a plain letter can carry more life than a gilded one, as brown bread can hold the whole field in it.

We had early learned in London of the action on the glorious first of August at Minden, where Wolfe’s old regiment was one of the British six that helped to achieve victory on that famous day. At the same hour the young General lay in his bed within sight of Quebec, stricken with fever, and perhaps with rage and disappointment at the check his troops had just received.

In June the fleet that carried Wolfe and his army had entered the St. Lawrence; and on the last day of the month they landed on the Island of Orleans, opposite the great cliff of Quebec that rises like a wall out of the river mist. After the great action in which his General fell, my dear brother—who had accompanied the chief—wrote me one of his simple letters describing his modest share in that glorious day. He added little to what the town already had by a hundred pens, save only this: from the testimony of a brother aide-de-camp who stood by Wolfe’s side, the General spoke not a word after receiving his death-wound; so that the famous phrase put into the dying hero’s mouth is no more authentic than one of those set speeches of Livy or Thucydides which scholars love because nobody living can contradict them.

From his position on the Island—the great channel running between it and the northern shore—the General watched for a chance to strike, hungry as a man on campaign who hears, far off, the clatter of mess-tins and smells some other regiment’s stew. Above the city and below it he landed—now here, now there—bent on attacking wherever he saw an opening. It seems now a prodigious fault in the Marquis of Montcalm to accept a battle on equal terms; for Wolfe had no artillery, and when we made our famous escalade of the heights and stood on the Plains of Abraham, we were nearer the city, certainly, yet as far as ever from being within it.

The match played between those brave chiefs and their two gallant little armies from July until Wolfe won the crowning hazard in September was as eager a game as ever men played—stakes being provinces, and the counters human lives. On the first night after the landing, as Harry narrates it, the sport began. At midnight the French sent a flaming squadron of fireships down upon the British vessels discharging stores at Orleans. Our seamen, taking the matter as if it were a fair, towed the fireships clear and grounded them on shore, where they burned out with a roar and crackle that must have made the whole river-bank seem a smithy. When the French commander learned our ships had entered the river, he marched to Beauport in advance of the city and there took a strong position.

When our stores and hospitals were established, Wolfe crossed from his island to the left shore and drew nearer to his enemy. The ships were behind him in the river, but the whole country in front was in arms. Indians in the forest seized our advanced parties as they strove to clear it and murdered them with horrible tortures; and the French, for all their polish and prayers, were as savage as their red allies in that business. The Montmorenci River rushed between Wolfe and the enemy: a loud, unceasing voice in the landscape, as though the land itself counselled delay. He could neither attack the entrenchments nor the city behind them.

Bent on finding some other assailable point, the General skirted the left shore beyond Quebec. Everywhere it was guarded. Having run the gauntlet of batteries up and down the river, he returned to his post at Montmorenci.

On the right of the French position, across the Montmorenci—fordable at low tide—stood an enemy redoubt. He would have that. Perhaps, to defend it, Montcalm would be forced out from his lines, and a battle brought on. Wolfe resolved to play those odds. He would fetch over the body of his army from the Island of Orleans and attack from the St. Lawrence; and he timed his assault so that, at shallow water, his lieutenants Murray and Townshend might cross the Montmorenci. Thus, on the last day of July, he played his desperate game.

First he and General Monckton, his second in command—setting out from Point Levi—crossed the St. Lawrence from their respective stations, and were received with a storm of shot and artillery as they rowed for shore. No sooner were the troops landed than they rushed at the French redoubt without order, were shot down before it in great numbers, and were obliged to fall back. At the preconcerted signal, the troops on the other side of the Montmorenci advanced across the river in perfect order. The enemy even evacuated the redoubt and fell back to their lines; but from those lines the assailants were met with so severe a fire that to make an impression was hopeless, and the General had to retreat.

The battle of Montmorenci—Harry and I have fought it again many a time over our wine, the clink of glasses keeping time with the remembered volleys—formed the dismal burden of Wolfe’s first despatch that reached England and plunged us all into gloom. What more might one expect of a commander so rash? What disasters might one not foretell? Was ever scheme so wild—to bring three great bodies of men across broad rivers under murderous batteries merely on the chance of inducing an enemy, strongly entrenched, to quit his strength and come out to fight? It was the talk of the town. Grave people shook their heads over their dishes, and prophesied fresh ruin with their mouths full.

The General, who took to his bed after this failure, shuddering with fever, was to live barely six weeks longer—and die immortal.

How is it—by what, and whom—that Greatness is achieved? Is it Merit—is it Madness that is patron? Is it Frolic or Fortune? Is it Fate that awards successes and defeats? How did the French gain Canada from the savage, and we from the French; and after which of the conquests was the right time to sing Te Deum? We are always for dragging Heaven into our quarrels, and making the gods intervene whatever the knot may be. Does Broughton, after pummelling Slack, lift up a black eye to Jove and thank him for victory? And if ten thousand boxers are to be heard, why not one? And if Broughton is to be grateful, what is Slack to be?

Wolfe wrote from his headquarters at Montmorenci Falls on the 2nd of September—letters so noble in cadence and plainness that you know my dear scribe was not his author nor secretary:

“By the list of disabled officers (many of whom are of rank) you may perceive, sir, that the army is much weakened. By the nature of this river the most formidable part of the armament is deprived of the power of acting, yet we have almost the whole force of Canada to oppose. In this situation there is such a choice of difficulties, that I own myself at a loss how to determine. The affairs of Great Britain, I know, require the most vigorous measures; but then the courage of a handful of brave men should be exerted only where there is some hope of a favourable event. The admiral and I have examined the town with a view to a general assault: and he would readily join in this or any other measure for the public service; but I cannot propose to him an undertaking of so dangerous a nature, and promising so little success.... I found myself so ill, and am still so weak, that I begged the general officers to consult together for the public utility. They are of opinion that they should try by conveying up a corps of 4000 or 5000 men (which is nearly the whole strength of the army, after the points of Levi and Orleans are put in a proper state of defence) to draw the enemy from their present position, and bring them to an action. I have acquiesced in their proposal, and we are preparing to put it into execution.”

On the 14th of October following the Rodney cutter brought this melancholy intelligence to England: the attack had failed; the chief was sick; the army dwindling; the threatened city so strong that assault seemed almost impossible; the only chance to fight Montcalm on terms less disadvantageous than storming entrenchments, and, if possible, to draw him from his position. Would the French chief, whose great military genius was known in Europe, walk into such a snare? Pale looks were seen in the City; doubt and gloom lay in coffee-houses where the cups clattered and yet the talk sank low, as though even the room’s familiar hum had lost heart.

Three days after came the famous letters announcing that wonderful consummation of fortune with which Wolfe’s wonderful career ended. If no man is to be called happy till his death, what are we to say of this one? His end was so glorious that I protest not even his mother nor his mistress ought to have deplored it—or at any rate to have wished him alive again. I know it is a hero we speak of; and yet I scarce know whether in that last act I admire the result of genius, invention, and daring, or the boldness of a gambler winning astonishing odds.

Suppose the ascent discovered half an hour sooner, and his people—surely—beaten back. Suppose Montcalm not to quit his entrenched lines to accept that strange challenge. Suppose these points—and none of them depended on Wolfe at all—what then becomes of the hero’s glory, of the great minister who found him, of the intoxicated nation that rose frantic with self-gratulation at the victory? What fate is it that shapes our ends—or those of nations? In the many hazardous games my Lord Chatham played, he won this prodigious one. And as the greedy British hand seized the Canadas, it let fall the United States out of its grasp. Wisdom after the event is easy: we marvel at one man’s rashness when the deed is done, and at another man’s fault. What generals we are upon paper! what repartees come when the talk is finished! the game over, how clearly we see how it should have been played!

Writing of an event at thirty years’ distance, it is not hard to criticise. But at the time, when first we heard of Wolfe’s deeds upon the Plains of Abraham—of the army marshalled in darkness and carried silently up the midnight river, as if the oars themselves had learned to whisper; of the rocks scaled; of the miraculous security of the enemy; of his acceptance of our challenge; of his defeat on the open plain by sheer valour—we were intoxicated in England by the news.

The whole nation rose and felt itself stronger for the victory. Not merely those engaged in the battle, but those at home who had condemned its rashness, felt themselves heroes. Friends embraced in the street when they met. Coffee-houses and public places were thronged with people eager to talk; yet it was not only the words that made the rejoicing—there was a change in the very sound of the town, as though bells and wheels and footsteps had taken on a brisker measure. Courtiers rushed to the King and to the great Minister whose will had decreed the campaign; when he showed himself, the people followed with shouts and blessings. They did not deplore the dead warrior so much as admire his euthanasia. Should James Wolfe’s friends weep and wear mourning because a chariot had come from the skies to fetch him away? Let them watch with wonder and see him departing radiant, rising above us.

To have been near him was distinction. Every soldier who fought with him became, in public talk, a hero. In our fond little circle it was a distinction to be Harry’s brother. We did not wonder but that, from his previous knowledge of the place, he had found the way up the heights which the British army took, and pointed it out to his General. Promotion, we said, must follow as a matter of course.

Why, even our Uncle Warrington wrote letters blessing Heaven and congratulating me and himself upon Harry’s share in the achievement. Our Aunt Beatrix opened her house and received company on the strength of the victory. I became a hero by resemblance to my brother. Parson Sampson preached such a sermon that his auditors—some of whom had been warned beforehand—were with difficulty restrained from huzzaing the orator, and were mobbed as they left the chapel.

“Don’t talk to me, madam, about grief,” says General Lambert to his wife, who, dear soul, was for allowing herself some small indulgence of her favourite sorrow on the day Wolfe’s remains were buried with glory at Greenwich. “If our boys could come by such deaths as James’s, you know you wouldn’t prevent them from being shot, but would scale the Abraham heights to see the thing done! Wouldst thou mind dying in the arms of victory, Charley?” he asks of the little hero from the Chartreux.

“That I wouldn’t,” says the little man; “and the doctor gave us a holiday, too.”

Our Harry’s promotion was insured after his share in the famous battle; and our aunt announced her intention of purchasing a company for him.

Had your father, young folks, possessed even the plainest country prudence,—the sort a man learns by watching his seed-corn and his servants, and by knowing when a stew has had fire enough and when it will only burn,—not only would this portion of his history never have been penned, but you yourselves would never have been born to torment him with a hundred affectionate indignities.

You would never have come storming down passages like a troop of drummers when he is craving the hush that belongs to books; never have waked him from that honest after-dinner doze which a healthy gentleman takes as naturally as he takes his glass of ale; never have mislaid his spectacles, spirited away his newspaper at the instant the ink is dry; never have ruined him with tailor’s bills, mantua-makers’ bills, tutors’ bills, and all the dear, neat, relentless accounts by which children prove their devotion. You would never have broken his nights by having the impudence to fall ill—chicken-pox, whooping-cough, scarlet fever, and the rest of the nursery’s catalogue—while your silly mother sat listening to every change in your breathing as if the house itself had grown teeth, and every sound in the dark were a warning. When Joan cannot sleep, what use, pray, is there in Darby putting on his nightcap? If the wind frets a shutter, she hears it; if a coal sighs and settles in the grate, she starts; if the tongs clink upstairs—Heaven help me—even now the mere stir of fire-irons in an upper room has power to go through me like a chill.

And now, forsooth, that you have grown past long petticoats and nursery fevers, what must that unconscionable woman contrive but to have the south rooms made over into a nursery for possible grandchildren? She would set up the Captain with a wife—make him marry early because we did! He is too fond, she says, of Brookes’s and Goosetree’s when he is in London; she has the perversity to hint that an entrée to Carlton House, though mighty fine for a young gentleman, is a perilous dish—high-seasoned, over-sauced, and served amid a clatter that leaves the palate corrupted for plain fare. She would have Miles live away from temptation, sow his wild oats out of sight, and come home to a good hearth and an honest table, and marry, as we did.

Marry! My dear creature, we had no business to marry at all! By the laws of common sense and duty I ought to have backed out of my little engagement with Miss Theo (who would have married somebody else), and taken a rich wife. Your Uncle John was a parson and could not fight; poor Charley was a boy at school; your grandfather was too old to call me to account with sword or pistol. I repeat there never was a more foolish match in the world than ours, and our relations were perfectly right in being angry with us. What are relations made for, indeed, but to be angry and find fault? When Hester marries, mind, Master George, to quarrel with her if she does not take a husband of your choosing. When George has got his living, after being senior wrangler and fellow of his college, Miss Hester, do you toss up your little nose at the young lady he shall fancy. As for you, my little Theo, I cannot part with you. You must not quit your old father; for he likes you to play Haydn to him, and peel his walnuts after dinner.

Whilst they had the blessing (forsooth!) of meeting and billing and cooing every day, the two young people—your parents—went on in a fool’s paradise, little heeding the world’s tattling and meddling. Rinaldo was as brave a warrior as ever slew Turk; but you know he loved dangling in Armida’s garden. Pray, my Lady Armida, what did you mean by flinging your spells over me in youth, so that not glory, not fashion, not the gaming-tables, not the society of men of wit in whose way I fell, could keep me long from your apron-strings, or out of reach of your dear simple prattle?

Pray, my dear, what used we to say to each other during those endless hours of meeting? I never went to sleep after dinner then. Which of us was so witty? Was it I or you? And how came it our talk was so delightful? I remember that year I did not even care to go and see my Lord Ferrers tried and hung, when all the world was running after his lordship. The King of Prussia’s capital was taken; the town rang with it as a kitchen rings when the spit is turned and the cook cries orders and the scullions answer—had the Austrians and Russians been encamped round the Tower, there could scarce have been more stir in London: yet Miss Theo and her young gentleman felt no inordinate emotion of pity or indignation. What to us was the fate of Leipzig or Berlin? The truth is, that dear old house in Dean Street was an enchanted garden of delights. I have been as idle since, but never as happy.

Shall we order the postchaise, my dear, leave the children to keep house, and drive up to London and see if the old lodgings are still to be let? You shall sit at your old place in the window, and wave a little handkerchief as I walk up the street. Say what we did was imprudent. Would we not do it over again? My good folks, if Venus had walked into the room and challenged the apple, I was so infatuated I would have given it your mother. And had she had the choice, she would have preferred her humble servant in a threadbare coat to my Lord Clive with all his diamonds.

Once, to be sure—and for a brief time in that year—I had a notion of going upon the highway in order to be caught and hanged like my Lord Ferrers; or of joining the King of Prussia and requesting some of his Majesty’s enemies to knock my brains out; or of enlisting for the India service and performing some desperate exploit which should end in my bodily destruction. Ah me! that was indeed a dreadful time. Your mother scarce dares speak of it now save in a whisper of terror; or think of it—it was such cruel pain. She was unhappy for years after on the anniversary of the day, until one of you was born upon it.

Suppose we had been parted: what had become of us? What had my lot been without her? As I think of that possibility, the whole world is a blank. I do not say were we parted now. It has pleased God to give us thirty years of union. We have reached the autumn season. Our successors are appointed and ready; and that one of us who is first called away knows the survivor will follow ere long.

But we were actually parted in our youth; and I tremble to think what might have been, had not a dearest friend brought us together.

Unknown to myself, and very likely meaning only my advantage, my relatives in England had chosen to write to Madam Esmond in Virginia, and represent what they were pleased to call the folly of the engagement I had contracted. Every one of them sang the same song; and I saw the letters, and burned the whole cursed pack years afterwards when my mother showed them to me at home in Virginia.

Aunt Bernstein was forward with her advice. A young person, with no wonderful good looks, of no family, of no money—was ever such an imprudent connexion, and ought it not for dear George’s sake to be broken off? She had several eligible matches in view for me. With my name and prospects, ’twas a shame I should throw myself away on this young lady; her sister ought to interpose—and so forth.

My Lady Warrington must write too, and in her peculiar manner. Her ladyship’s letter was garnished with Scripture texts. She dressed her worldliness out in phylacteries. She pointed out how I was living in an unworthy society of player-folks and the like people, who she could not say were absolutely without religion (Heaven forbid!), but who were deplorably worldly. She would not say an artful woman had inveigled me for her daughter, having in vain tried to captivate my younger brother. She was far from saying any harm of the young woman I had selected; but at least this was certain: Miss L. had no fortune or expectations, and her parents might naturally be anxious to compromise me. She had taken counsel, &c. &c. She had sought for guidance where it was, &c. Feeling what her duty was, she had determined to speak. Sir Miles, a man of excellent judgment in the affairs of this world (though he knew and sought a better), fully agreed with her in opinion—nay, desired her to write and entreat her sister to interfere, that the ill-advised match should not take place.

And who besides must put a little finger into the pie but the new Countess of Castlewood? She wrote a majestic letter to Madam Esmond, and stated that, having been placed by Providence at the head of the Esmond family, it was her duty to communicate with her kinswoman and warn her to break off this marriage. I believe the three women laid their heads together previously; and packet after packet they sent their warnings across the water, as steadily as a cook sends up courses when she is bent on spoiling a feast—one after another, each with its own spice of piety or prudence, each meant to overmaster the taste of love.

Then came the raw April morning. As Corydon goes to pay his usual duty to Phillis, he finds not his charmer with her dear smile ready to welcome him, but Mrs. Lambert with very red eyes, and the General as pale as death.

“Read this, George Warrington!” says he; and as his wife’s head drops between her hands, he pushes a letter before me, of which I knew the handwriting at once. I can hear now the sobs of good Aunt Lambert; and to this day the very sound of fire-irons stirring a fire in a room overhead gives me a tremor. I heard such a noise that day in the girls’ room where the sisters were together—an anxious poking and clinking, as if some hand were trying to keep a little warmth alive in a house suddenly grown cold.

Poor gentle child. Poor Theo.

“What can I do after this, George—my poor boy?” asks the General, pacing the room with desperation in his face.

I did not quite read the whole of Madam Esmond’s letter, for a kind of sickness and faintness came over me; but I fear I could say much of it now by heart. Its style was good; its actual words temperate enough; and yet they implied that Mr. and Mrs. Lambert had inveigled me into the marriage; that they knew such a union was unworthy of me; that (as Madam Esmond understood) they had desired a similar union for her younger son—given up, not unluckily for him perhaps, when it was found Mr. Henry Warrington was not the inheritor of the Virginian property. If Mr. Lambert was a man of spirit and honour, as he was represented to be, Madam Esmond scarcely supposed that, after her representations, he would persist in desiring this match. She would not lay commands upon her son, whose temper she knew; but for the sake of Miss Lambert’s own reputation and comfort, she urged that the dissolution of the engagement should come from her family, and not from the just unwillingness of Rachel Esmond Warrington of Virginia.

“God help us, George!” the General said, “and give us all strength to bear this grief, and these charges which it has pleased your mother to bring! They are hard, but they don’t matter now. What is of most importance is to spare as much sorrow as we can to my poor girl. I know you love her so well, that you will help me and her mother to make the blow as tolerable as we may to that poor gentle heart. Since she was born she has never given pain to a soul alive; and ’tis cruel that she should be made to suffer.”

And as he spoke he passed his hand across his dry eyes.

“It was my fault, Martin! It was my fault!” weeps the poor mother. “Your mother spoke us fair, and gave her promise,” said the father. “And do you think I will withdraw mine?” cried I; and protested with a thousand frantic vows—what they knew full well—that I was bound to Theo before Heaven, and that nothing should part me from her.

“She herself will demand the parting. She is a good girl—God help me!—and dutiful. She will not have her father and mother called schemers, and treated with scorn. Your mother knew not, very likely, what she was doing, but ’tis done. You may see the child, and she will tell you as much. Is Theo dressed, Molly? I brought the letter home from my office last evening after you were gone. The women have had a bad night. She knew at once by my face that there was bad news from America. She read the letter quite firmly. She said she would like to see you and say good-bye. Of course, George, you will give me your word of honour not to try and see her afterwards. As soon as my business will let me we will get away from this, but mother and I think we are best all together. ’Tis you, perhaps, had best go. But give me your word, at any rate, that you will not try and see her. We must spare her pain, sir! We must spare her pain!”

And the good man sat down in such deep anguish himself that I—who was not yet under the full press of my own grief—actually felt his and pitied it.

It could not be. The dear lips I had kissed yesterday were to speak to me only once more? We were all here together, loving one another, sitting in the room where we met every day: my drawing on the table by her little workbox; she in the chamber upstairs; she must come down presently.

Who is this that opens the door?

I see her sweet face. It was like our little Mary’s when we thought she would die of the fever. There was even a smile upon her lips. She comes up and kisses me.

“Good-bye, dear George!” she says.

Great Heaven! An old man sitting in this room—with my wife’s workbox opposite, and she but five minutes away—my eyes grow so dim and full that I can’t see the book before me. I am three-and-twenty again. I go through every stage of that agony. I once had it sitting in my own postchaise, with my wife actually by my side.

Who dared to sully her sweet love with suspicion? Who had a right to stab such a soft bosom? Don’t you see my ladies getting their knives ready, and the poor child baring it? The very language they used had its power: words chosen as carefully as herbs in a physic, and as deadly in their way; phrases in the great family dialect—Duty, Prudence, Propriety—set above the small, native speech of two young hearts. They made her feel ashamed of the name her own tenderness gave her feelings, as if love itself were some low kitchen-word not fit for a lady’s mouth.

My wife comes in now, as I write—she has been serving out tea or tobacco to some of her pensioners—and she says, “What is it makes you look so angry, papa?”

“My love,” I say, “it is the thirteenth of April.”

A pang shoots across her face, followed by a tender smile. She has undergone the martyrdom, and in the midst of the pang comes a halo of forgiveness. I can’t forgive; not until my days of dotage come, and I cease remembering anything.

“Hal will be home for Easter; he will bring two or three of his friends with him from Cambridge,” she says; and straightway she falls to devising schemes for amusing the boys. When is she ever occupied, but with plans for making others happy? She begins naming what will be wanted—fresh eggs, a chine, a ham that has been properly smoked, rolls done crisp, and a syllabub if the cream comes sweet from the dairy—and as she speaks I hear how her voice sets the house in order, like a bell that calls all things into place. Even her domestic arrangements have a music: the rattle of cups, the soft tread on boards, the small stir of a spoon against china—sounds which, in a sick heart, may be comfort, and in a frightened one, torment.

A gentleman sitting in spectacles before an old ledger, and writing down pitiful remembrances of his own condition, is a quaint and ridiculous object. My corns hurt me, I know; but I suspect my neighbour’s shoes pinch him too. I am not going to howl much over my own grief, or enlarge at any great length on this one. Many another man, I dare say, has had the light of his day suddenly put out, the joy of his life extinguished, and has been left to darkness and vague torture.

I have a book I tried to read at this time of grief—Howel’s Letters—and when I come to the part about Prince Charles in Spain, up starts the whole tragedy alive again. I went to Brighthelmstone, and there, at the inn, had a room facing the east, and saw the sun get up ever so many mornings after blank nights of wakefulness, and smoked my pipe of Virginia in his face. Even the tobacco tasted of home and exile at once: the leaf, cured across the ocean, browned and sweetened by slow heat; the first lighted draw bitter, then mellow; the room steeped in that heavy, honest scent which clings to curtains as memory clings to the mind. When I am in that place by chance now, and see the sun rising, I shake my fist at him, thinking, O orient Phoebus, what horrible grief and savage wrath have you not seen me suffer! Though my wife is mine ever so long, I say I am angry just the same. Who dared, I want to know, to make us suffer so?

I was forbidden to see her. I kept my promise, and remained away from the house—after that horrible meeting and parting. But at night I would go and look at her window, and watch the lamp burning there. I would go to the Chartreux (where I knew another boy), and call for her brother, and gorge him with cakes and half-crowns. I would meanly have her elder brother to dine, and almost kiss him when he went away. I used to breakfast at a coffee-house in Whitehall in order to see Lambert go to his office; and we would salute each other sadly, and pass on without speaking.

Why did not the women come out? They never did. They were practising on her, and persuading her to try and forget me—working upon her day by day, as one works upon a tough joint: beating it with texts, salting it with shame, hanging it up in the cold air of “what will people say,” until the very natural juices of the heart are drawn away. Oh, the weary, weary days! Oh, the maddening time! The city itself seemed to conspire: every coach-wheel on the stones, every hawker’s cry, every bell pealing for some idle entertainment, was an insult. Noise was everywhere—yet not one of those bustling sounds could drown the silence where her name used to be spoken.

At last a doctor’s chariot used to draw up before the General’s house every day. Was she ill? I fear I was rather glad she was ill. My own suffering was so infernal, that I greedily wanted her to share my pain. And would she not? What grief of mine has it not felt, that gentlest and most compassionate of hearts? What pain would it not suffer to spare mine a pang?

I sought that doctor out. I had an interview with him. I told my story, and laid bare my heart to him with an outburst of passionate sincerity which won his sympathy. My confession enabled him to understand his young patient’s malady; for which his drugs had no remedy or anodyne. I had promised not to see her, or to go to her; I had kept my promise. I had promised to leave London; I had gone away. Twice, thrice I went back and told my sufferings to him. He would take my fee now and again, and always receive me kindly, and let me speak.

Ah, how I clung to him! I suspect he must have been unhappy once in his own life; he knew so well and gently how to succour the miserable. He did not tell me how dangerously—though he did not disguise from me how gravely and seriously—my dearest girl had been ill. I told him everything: that I would marry her and brave every chance and danger; that without her I was a man utterly wrecked and ruined, and cared not what became of me. My mother had once consented, and had now chosen to withdraw her consent, when the tie between us had been, as I held, drawn so closely together as to be paramount to all filial duty.

“I think, sir, if your mother heard you, and saw Miss Lambert, she would relent,” said the doctor.

Who was my mother to hold me in bondage; to claim a right of misery over me; and to take this angel out of my arms? He could not, he said, be a message-carrier between young ladies who were pining and young lovers on whom the sweethearts’ gates were shut; but so much he would venture to say, that he had seen me, and was prescribing for me too.

Yes, he must have been unhappy once himself.

I saw him, you may be sure, on the very day when he had kept his promise to me. He said she seemed comforted by hearing news of me.

“She bears her suffering with an angelical sweetness. I prescribe Jesuit’s bark, which she takes; but I am not sure the hearing of you has not done more good than the medicine.”

The women owned afterwards they had never told the General of the doctor’s new patient. I know not what wild expressions of gratitude I poured out to the good physician for the comfort he brought me. His treatment was curing two unhappy sick persons. ’Twas but a drop of water, to be sure; but then a drop of water to a man raging in torment.

I loved the ground he trod upon; blessed the hand that took mine and had felt her pulse. I had a ring with a pretty cameo head of a Hercules on it. ’Twas too small for his finger, nor did the good old man wear such ornaments. I made him hang it to his watch-chain, in hopes that she might see it, and recognise that the token came from me.

How I fastened upon Spencer at this time (my friend of the Temple who also had an unfortunate love-match), and walked with him from my apartments to the Temple, and he back with me to Bedford Gardens, and our talk was for ever about our women! I dare say I told everybody my grief. My good landlady and Betty the housemaid pitied me.

My son Miles—who, for a wonder, has been reading in my manuscript—says, “By Jove, sir, I didn’t know you and my mother were took in this kind of way. The year I joined, I was hit very bad myself. An infernal little jilt that threw me over for Sir Craven Oaks of our regiment. I thought I should have gone crazy.” And he gives a melancholy whistle and walks away; and that poor whistle—so small a sound—brings back to me the whole old world of noises: the London cries, the chariot-wheels, the clink of irons upstairs, the doctor’s knock, and the silence under her window.

The General had to leave London presently on one of his military inspections, as the doctor casually told me; but, having given my word that I would not seek to present myself at his house, I kept it—availing myself, however, as you may be sure, of the good physician’s leave to visit him and have news of his dear patient.

His accounts of her were far from encouraging.

“She does not rally,” he said. “We must get her back to Kent again, or to the sea.”

I did not know then that the poor child had begged and prayed so piteously not to be moved, that her parents—divining, perhaps, the reason of her desire to linger in London, and feeling it might be dangerous not to humour her—had yielded to her entreaty and consented to remain in town.

At last one morning I came, pretty much as usual, and took my place in my doctor’s front parlour, whence his patients were called in their turn to his consulting-room. Here I remained, looking heedlessly over the books on the table and taking no notice of any person in the room, which speedily emptied itself of all save me and one lady who sat with her veil down. I used to stay till the last, for Osborn, the doctor’s man, knew my business, and that it was not my own illness I came for.

When the room was empty of all save me and the lady, she puts out two little hands, cries in a voice which made me start, “Don’t you know me, George?”

And the next minute I had my arms round her, and kissed her as heartily as ever I kissed in my life, and gave way to a passionate outgush of emotion the most refreshing; for my parched soul had been in rage and torture for six weeks past, and this was a glimpse of Heaven.

Who was it, children? You think it was your mother whom the doctor had brought to me?

No.

It was Hetty.

When the first shock of meeting had spent itself, the little maiden fell upon him at once, as a kitchen-wench might fall upon a careless scullion who has let the cream boil over and spoiled the whole day’s making.

“So you are come at last to ask after Theo,” cried Miss Hetty, her voice sharp as vinegar upon hot iron, “and you feel sorry your neglect has made her so ill? For six weeks she has been unwell, and you have never asked a word about her! Very kind of you, Mr. George—mighty kind!”

“Kind!” Warrington gasped, as if the word had been thrust into his ribs. “Do you call it kind to be with her every day and all day for a year, and then to be turned out without so much as a syllable?”

“My dear, you know my promise to your father,” I put in, for I had been the messenger between these fires, and felt them burning through my coat.

“Promise!” Miss Hetty cried, with a shrug that made her little shoulders rise like a cat’s when it scents a dog. “A fine promise indeed—to make my darling ill, and then, one fine day, to say ‘Good-bye, Theo,’ and walk away for ever. I suppose gentlemen make promises because they wish to keep ’em. I wouldn’t trifle with a poor child’s heart and leave her afterwards, if I were a man. Pray, sir, by what right do you take her away from all of us, and then desert her, because an old woman in America don’t approve of her? She was happy with us before you came. She loved her sister—there never was such a sister—until she saw you. And now, because your mamma thinks her young gentleman might do better, you must leave her forsooth!”

“Great powers, child!” I cried, for her reasoning flew about the room like sparks in a draught, catching wherever there was tinder. “Was it I that drew back? Am I not forbidden your house? Did not your father require, upon my honour, that I should not see her?”

“Honour!” Hetty flung the word as if it were a bone with no meat upon it. “And you are the men who pretend to be our superiors; and it is we who are to respect you and admire you! I declare, George Warrington, you ought to go back to your schoolroom in Virginia again; have your black nurse to tuck you up in bed, and ask leave from your mamma when you might walk out. Oh, George! I little thought my sister was giving her heart away to a man who hadn’t the spirit to stand by her; but, at the first difficulty, left her!”

She ran on, in that way where anger makes a child older than her years, and grief makes her younger again in the same breath.

“When Doctor Heberden said he was attending you, I determined to come and see you, and you do look very ill—which I am glad to see; and I suppose it’s your mother you are frightened of. But I shan’t tell Theo you are unwell. She hasn’t left off caring for you. She can’t walk out of a room, break her solemn engagements, and go into the world the next day as if nothing had happened! That is left for men—our superiors in courage and wisdom; and to desert an angel—yes, an angel ten thousand times too good for you; an angel who used to love me till she saw you, and who was the blessing of life and of all of us—is what you call honour? Don’t tell me, sir! I despise you all! You are our betters, are you? We are to worship and wait on you, I suppose? I don’t care about your wit, and your tragedies, and your verses; and I think they are often very stupid. I won’t set up of nights copying your manuscripts, nor watch hour after hour at a window wasting my time and neglecting everybody because I want to see your worship walk down the street with your hat cocked!”

At that, I confess, I felt each thrust. For we men take services as naturally as we take bread—break it, dip it, swallow it, and seldom ask who kneaded it, who kept the coals alive, who carried the water that made the dough.

“If you are going away—and welcome—give me back my sister, I say!” she cried. “Give me back my darling of old days, who loved every one of us till she saw you. And you leave her because your mamma thinks she can find somebody richer for you! Oh, you brave gentleman! Go and marry the person your mother chooses, and let my dear die here deserted!”

“Great heavens, Hetty!” I cried. “Is it I who wish to leave your sister? Did I not offer to keep my promise, and was it not your father who refused me, and made me promise never to try and see her again? What have I but my word and my honour?”

“Honour indeed! You keep your word to him, and you break it to her! Pretty honour! If I were a man I would soon let you know what I thought of your honour! Only I forgot—you are bound to keep the peace and mustn’t—Oh, George, George! Don’t you see the grief I am in? I am distracted, and scarce know what I say. You must not leave my darling. They don’t know it at home. They don’t think so; but I know her best of all, and she will die if you leave her. Say you won’t! Have pity upon me, Mr. Warrington, and give me my dearest back!”

Thus she ran from scorn to entreaty, from a lash to tears—like a cook, poor soul, who cannot choose whether to beat the cream harder or to cover the pan and weep, because the guest she labours for will not eat.

Was my little doctor right in what he had hinted of his patient? Was there truly no remedy but the one Hetty cried for? Have not others endured that cruel pain of being cut from a love, suffered fever after it, lain as if death were the only broth left in the pot—and yet recovered, and afterwards hobbled through life upon a changed limb? Love is selfish; it hears its own pulse louder than any other sound. And ours, being so fierce and particular to ourselves, seemed a thing no other heart had ever borne.

Yet here, in Hetty’s very pleadings, was proof of a different suffering—one which the lovers, in their triumph and tender confidences, had been blind to. Theo and I, comfortable by our own hearth of happiness, had often spoken of Hetty’s attachment as of a storm seen safely from indoors; a ship labouring at sea while we walked by a calm river-bank. We drew, perhaps, a secret security from another’s mischance. Be the truth as it may: at the time I was eager enough to share Hetty’s terrors. I chose to believe, willingly, that the life dearest to me would be sacrificed if sundered from mine. Was I wrong? Of myself I may doubt now—indeed I know my own frailty well—but of her, never.

I would have poured all this out to our doctor; but the good gentleman clapped a figurative hand upon my mouth, as if he feared the very syllables might be overheard by Fate.

“Hush,” says he, with a comical look of fright. “I must hear none of this. If two people who happen to know each other chance to meet and talk in my patient’s room, I cannot help myself; but as for match-making and love-making, I am your humble servant! What will the General do when he comes back to town? He will have me behind Montagu House as sure as I am a live doctor; and alive I wish to remain, my good sir!”

And with that, he skipped into his carriage and was gone, leaving his wheels to rattle away down the stones like dice flung upon a table, whilst I stood in the aftermath of Hetty’s storm and felt the air strangely thin.

“And you and Miss Hetty must have no meetings here again, mind you that,” he had said previously.

Oh no. Certainly not. We were gentlemen of honour: our word was our word. Besides, had I not been granted an inestimable boon—one drop of water to a man in a desert? I was so refreshed by the sight of Hetty’s honest passion, by her very reproaches, that I thought I could endure for ever so long now upon that single draught.

I walked away with her towards Soho, and never once thought—no, not once—of contriving another meeting.

But the little emissary had contrivance in her bones, as housewives have it when they must feed a family upon scant flour and still keep every mouth believing the loaf is hearty.

She asked me if I went to the Museum now to read.

“Oh yes, sometimes, my dear,” I said; “but I am too wretched for reading now; I cannot see what is on the paper. I do not care about my books. Even Pocahontas is wearisome to me. I—”

“Nonsense!” she cried, stamping her little foot, so that her shoe gave a crisp report on the pavement, a tiny gunshot in the city’s continual cannonade of carts and cries. “Why, I declare, George, you are more stupid than Harry!”

“How do you mean, my dear child?” I asked, for I was indeed stupid—love makes a man deaf to everything but its own miserable humming.

“When do you go? You go away at three o’clock. You strike across on the road to Tottenham Court. You walk through the village, and return by the Green Lane that leads back towards the new hospital. You know you do! If you walk for a week there, it can’t do you any harm. Good morning, sir! You’ll please not follow me any farther.”

And she dropped me a curtsey and walked away, her veil over her face, as if she were hiding not from me but from the noise and notice of the world.

That Green Lane—built all over with houses now—was in my time, when good old George II still sat king, a shabby rural outlet of London, dangerous enough that City folk returning from their Hampstead villas would come in parties at night, with waiters bearing lanthorns, for fear of footpads that haunted the outskirts. The very sound of the place was a kind of warning: the wind worrying the hedge, the clop of a solitary horse suddenly checked, an owl’s complaint from a tree, and then—too often—quick feet upon the soft verge and a voice that did not ask but ordered.

Hampstead and Highgate churches, each crowning its hill, filled up the background when you turned your back on London; and for one, two, three days, Mr. George Warrington had the pleasure of looking upon that landscape and walking back in the direction of the new hospital, as punctually as if Hetty’s words were a recipe and he dared not alter an ounce.

Along the lane were small houses of entertainment. At one place, where they sold cakes and beer, at the sign of the Protestant Hero, a decent woman smiled at me on the third or fourth day and curtseyed in her clean apron.

“It appears the lady don’t come, sir!” she said, with that practical pity which feeds you instead of consoling you. “Your honour had best step in, and take a can of my cool beer.”

Even in my wretchedness I noted the smell: yeasty froth, damp wood, and those warm, carraway-scented cakes that poor folk buy for a holiday, the spice doing its best to make coarse flour feel grand.

At length, as I was coming back through Tottenham Road, on the five-and-twentieth of May—O day to be marked with the whitest stone!—a little way beyond Mr. Whitefield’s Tabernacle, I saw a landau before me; and on the box-seat by the driver sat my young friend Charley, who waved his hat and called out, “George! George!”

I ran up to the carriage, my knees knocking together so that I thought I should fall under the wheel; and inside I saw Hetty, and by her—propped with a pillow—my dearest Theo.

How thin the little hand had grown since last it lay in mine! The cheeks were flushed and wasted; the eyes strangely bright; and the thrill of her voice, when she spoke a word or two, smote me with a pang in which grief and joy were so kneaded together that I could not separate them—like salt stirred into honey until neither is itself.

“I am taking her an airing to Hampstead,” said Hetty, demure as a nun who has contrived a feast beneath her cloak. “The doctor says the air will do her good.”

“I have been ill,” Theo whispered, “but I am better now, George.”

At that moment there came a great burst of music from the people in the chapel hard by. The psalm poured out as if the doors had opened on a sea of voices—men’s basses steady as a mill-wheel, women’s tones bright as larks, children piping where they could, the whole hymn riding above the street’s harsh clatter and turning it, for an instant, into accompaniment instead of assault. In a city where every trade advertises itself by hammer and bell, by hawker’s cry and coachman’s oath, that swell of sacred sound was like a clean current of water running through a guttered lane.

I held her hand in mine. Her eyes were looking into mine once more. It seemed as if we had never been parted.

I can never forget the tune of that psalm. I have heard it all through my life. My wife has touched it on her harpsichord, and her little ones have warbled it. Now you understand, young people, why I love it so: because ’twas the music played at our amoris redintegratio—our love made whole again. Because it sang hope to me at the most miserable period of my existence. Yes, the most miserable; for even that dreary confinement of Duquesne had its tendernesses and kindly associations—poor Biche, my tipsy jailor, the reveille of forest birds, and the military music of my prison—sounds that belonged to their place as naturally as bread belongs to the oven. But this misery was soundless save for my own blood in my ears—until that hymn broke upon it.

Master Charley looked down from his box-seat upon his sister and me, caught in our beatific contemplation, and upon Hetty too, listening to the music with a face suddenly softened.

“I think I should like to go and hear it,” Hetty said. “And that famous Mr. Whitfield—perhaps he is going to preach this very day! Come in with me, Charley—and George can drive for half an hour with dear Theo towards Hampstead and back.”

Charley showed no strong desire for devotional exercises and proposed that George Warrington should take Hetty in; but Hetty was not to be denied.

“I will never help you in another exercise as long as you live, sir,” cried Miss Hetty, “if you don’t come on,”—and the youth clambered down, and they entered the temple together, swallowed up by that tide of singing.

Can any moralist, bearing my previous promises in mind, excuse me for jumping into the carriage and sitting down once more by my dearest Theo?

Suppose I did break them—will he blame me much? Reverend sir, you are welcome. I broke my promise; and if you would not do as much, good friend, you are welcome to your virtue. Not that I for a moment suspect my own children will ever be so bold as to think of having hearts of their own, and bestowing them according to their liking. No, my young people: you will let papa choose for you; be hungry when he tells you; be thirsty when he orders; and settle your children’s marriages afterwards.

And now, of course, you are anxious to hear what took place when papa jumped into the landau by the side of poor little mamma, propped up by her pillows.

“I am come to your part of the story, my dear,” say I, looking over to my wife, as she plies her needles—each small prick and pull as steady as a metronome, a domestic music answering the remembered psalm.

“To what, pray?” says my lady. “You should skip all that part, and come to the grand battles, and your heroic defence of—”

“Of Fort Fiddlededee in the year 1778, when I pulled off Mr. Washington’s epaulet, gouged General Gates’s eye, cut off Charles Lee’s head, and pasted it on again!”

“Let us hear all about the fighting,” cry the boys. Even the Captain condescends to own he will listen to any military details, though only from a militia officer.

“Fair and softly, young people! Everything in its turn. I am not yet arrived at the war. I am only a young gentleman, just stepping into a landau, by the side of a young lady whom I promised to avoid. I am taking her hand—which, after a little ado, she leaves in mine. Do you remember how hot it was, the little thing; how it trembled; how it throbbed and jumped a hundred and twenty in a minute? And as we trot on towards Hampstead, I address Miss Lambert in the following terms—”

“Ah, ah, ah!” cry the girls in a chorus with mademoiselle, their French governess, who adds, “Nous écoutons maintenant. La parole est à vous, Monsieur le Chevalier!”

So there they are, all in a circle: mamma at her side of the fire, papa at his; Mademoiselle Éléonore, at whom the Captain looks rather sweetly (eyes off, Captain!); the two girls listening like—like nymphas discentes to Apollo, let us say; and John and Tummas, with their obtuse ears, bringing in the tea-trays and urns, the steam rising with that homely fragrance of boiled water meeting leaf—comfort in a scent, memory in a breath.

“Very good,” says the Squire, pulling out the manuscript and waving it before him. “We are going to tell your mother’s secrets and mine.”

“I am sure you may, papa,” cries the house-matron. “There’s nothing to be ashamed of.” And a blush rises over her kind face.

“But before I begin, young folks, permit me two or three questions.”

“Allons, toujours des questions!” says mademoiselle, with a shrug of her pretty shoulders. (Florac has recommended her to us; and I suspect the little Chevalier has himself an eye upon this pretty Mademoiselle de Blois.)

To the questions, then.

If Captain Miles Warrington had been minded to make a bulletin of every conquest, the mess-room would have been a post-office of perfumes and protestations. But Miles—who could dress a wig-curl as carefully as another man trusses a capon—only laughed, tilted his head before the glass, and said to his father with that easy insolence youth calls prudence, “Not such a fool, Squire!”

The old gentleman, who loved an argument as he loved a well-browned crust, took the jest and kneaded it, turning it from his son to the women with the same hearty hand that, at Oakhurst, had carved joints and distributed praise. Had Miss Theo—little Theo, the healthy one—run home and poured into her mother’s ear every syllable she had murmured in the shrubbery to some Joe Blake, junior? Had mademoiselle, with her ribbons and her French accent, translated aloud the whole of that scented billet slipped to her under Sir Thomas’s frank? The very mention of the letter brought color to her cheeks, as a warm kitchen brings bloom to apples.

“No, mademoiselle,” the Squire said, giving her his broadest bow, “we all have our secrets.”

And then—because husbands, like cooks, are commonly found out by their own hearth—Lady Warrington, with a little whisper that was half triumph and half tenderness, betrayed the mystery of that long-ago ride in a landau on the Hampstead Road: she had said “Yes.” That was all. As if one small word were not sometimes a whole lifetime of meaning; as if its taste were not different on every tongue, untranslatable as the scent of crushed mint when you were a child.

So, too swiftly as George Warrington thought, the carriage had galloped out and back, and in that short compass his own “Yes” had been met by another—quiet, steadfast, and spoken without flourish. Theodosia Lambert had not promised any open defiance, not the theatrical kind. She had only told him, in the simplest terms—terms that might have been spoken over a loaf put in the oven and taken out again—that she would marry no other creature breathing. Not if she lived to Methuselah. Not if a prince offered her his hand. She had given her heart away with her father’s consent—nay, at his bidding—and she could not take it back as if it were a ribbon mislaid.

And George, who had come to measure his life by the sound of her breath, believed her as he believed the beat of his own pulse. If her father relented in a day, in twenty years, or in some other world, she would keep her promise. It was as plain, and as terrible, as salt.

When the brief interview ended, Hetty—bright Hetty—saw her sister’s face composed and sweet, and she could scarcely contain herself for joy. The doctors’ bitter draughts and bark had done less, she said, than that one stolen hour. The girls went home after their act of disobedience, and George surrendered the seat he had held beside his invalid. Hetty sprang back into place, Charley climbed to his box, and later, with the solemnity of a little chap who could judge sermons by their length and their orthodoxy, declared he had heard the dullest discourse of his life. Dissenting preachers did not suit him; their cadence, perhaps, was wrong to his ear.

At the house, a domestic music met the returning party: clatter of plates in the lower regions, a maid’s shoes on the stair, the soft chiff of silk, and—more importantly—the altered note in Theo’s voice when she answered. Even her mother, who had been ice and ceremony these many weeks, embraced both daughters with an ardor that startled them—especially the sick one, whom she held as if her arms could press health back into her.

“There is nothing like a country ride,” Aunt Lambert declared, her whole person a rich syllabub of kindness—froth, sweetness, and a little sighing air. “Hampstead Road, was it? She must go again to-morrow. Bless us, my Lord Wrotham’s horses are at your orders three or four times a week. The child shall have the advantage of them!”

Of course Aunt Lambert never once spoke of the notion that Mr. Warrington might have crossed their path. Perhaps she never entertained it. Perhaps she entertained it as women sometimes entertain such things: silently, with a hand at the curtain, eyes turned away at the proper moment. There are ladies who will hang a rope-ladder for Strephon and Chloe and then go downstairs to see whether the custard is setting, as if love were no more than another household necessity—dangerous, delicious, best managed by those who know its heat. Aunt Lambert had loved truly in her time, and the memory of that old warmth made her tender toward the young. Miss Prim, it was whispered, would rather fling a stone at cooing turtles than permit any creature to be happy in its pairing. But Aunt Lambert only said to Theo, with a softness that did not invite confession, “The air has done you good. Another drive to-morrow. And another.”

When General Lambert came in for supper, his sister was ready with her refrain. “Don’t you think, Martin, the ride has done the child wonderful good? Must she not be made to go out?”

“Yes,” Lambert answered, smiling with that large, honest readiness which would have spent coin or blood to purchase his children’s comfort. “If a coach-and-six will do her good, she shall have it. And if there are no horses, I’ll drag the landau up Hampstead Hill myself.”

At table he watched Theo with a hungry father’s attention—the way a farmer watches a late-sown field for the first green. She picked at a bit of chicken with something like appetite; the sound of knife against plate, small as it was, seemed to everyone a bell of hope. He mixed her a little negus—wine warmed and sweetened, lemon cut to let its sharp oil rise, the steam carrying spice into the room. The very smell made the evening feel like Oakhurst again: home, hearth, the old domestic orchestra of voices, ladles, and laughter. For months—since that cruel day no one named—they had not had such an hour.

But Theo, though she had lied by omission for love, was too honest to keep feeding her father a false dish long. When he returned for the third or fourth time to her improved looks—asking whether it was the air, the Jesuit’s bark, the new medicine—she laid her hand on his, and her voice trembled, though her eyes were clear.

“Can’t you think, dear, what it is?”

“What is it, my child?” General Lambert asked, and the room seemed to hush itself, as if even the crackle of the coals had learned to listen.

“It is because I have seen him again, papa,” she said.

The words fell like a plate dropped on stone. Aunt Lambert and Mrs. Lambert turned pale; Theo’s own cheek whitened even as she held his gaze.
