“It was not wrong to see him,” she went on quickly, as if speed could turn truth into mercy. “It would have been wrong not to tell you.”

“Great God!” the father groaned, snatching his hand back. Grief contorted his face so dreadfully that Hetty sprang to Theo, clasping her as Theo began to sway.

“Theo knew nothing of it, sir!” Hetty cried, head high, voice tumbling. “It was my doing—all my doing!”

Theo, half fainting, clung to her sister’s neck and covered it with kisses—twenty, fifty—like a child trying to warm cold hands with breath.

“Women, women!” General Lambert burst out, fierce and wounded. “Are you playing with my honour?”

“Martin! Martin!” Aunt Lambert sobbed, her handkerchief already in that damp, hopeless ruin of hers.

“Don’t say a word to her!” Hetty cried again; and she herself staggered back toward the wall as Theo, the sick one, fainted against her shoulder.

The next morning George Warrington sat before a breakfast that had no savor—though it might have been buttered to perfection, and the coffee as fragrant as Mocha can be in London—when his door opened and his faithful black servant announced, “General Lambert.”

One look at Lambert’s face told George the night’s confession had reached him.

“Your accomplices did not confess,” General Lambert began, when they were alone, “but sided with you against their father—a proof how desirable clandestine meetings are. It was from Theo herself I heard she had seen you.”

“Accomplices, sir?” George answered, catching at the word as a man catches at a crust when the true meal is too hot to touch. “You know how fondly and dutifully your young people regard you. If they side against you in this, it must be because justice is against you. A man like you is not going to set up sic volo sic jubeo as the only law in his family.”

“Psha, George!” Lambert cried, and behind the impatience was pain. “For though we are parted—God forbid I should desire we should cease to love each other—I had your promise you would not seek to see her.”

“Nor did I go to her, sir,” George said, flushing; for though he spoke the literal truth, he felt the lie of the spirit beneath it.

“You mean she was brought to you?” Lambert demanded, agitation rising. “Is it behind Hester’s petticoat you shelter yourself? What a defence for a gentleman!”

George’s pride and shame came up together. “I won’t screen myself behind the poor child. I attempted evasion; I am ill-accustomed to dissemble. I did not infringe the letter of my agreement, but I acted against the spirit. From this moment I annul it altogether.”

“You break your word given to me!” Lambert cried.

“I recall a hasty promise made in extreme excitement,” George answered, the words rushing now, like wine poured too fast. “No man can be bound for ever by words uttered at such a time; and no man of honour or humanity would try to bind him.”

“Dishonour to me!” the General exclaimed.

“Yes, if we are to bandy the phrase like a shuttlecock!” George flung back, too young to soften what he meant. “When that word is used there can be no question of love or age. Were you my own father—and I love you better than a father, Uncle Lambert—I would not bear it. What have I done? I have seen the woman whom I consider my wife before God and man; and if she calls me I will see her again. If she comes to me, here is my home for her, and half the little I have.

“’Tis you who have no right—having made me the gift—to resume it. Because my mother taunts you unjustly, are you to visit Mrs. Esmond’s wrong upon this tender innocent creature? You profess to love your daughter, and you cannot bear a wounded pride for her sake. Better she should perish away in misery than an old woman in Virginia should say Mr. Lambert schemed to marry one of his daughters.

“Say that to satisfy what you call honour and I call selfishness, we part, we break our hearts, we rally, we try to forget, we marry elsewhere? Can any man be to her what I have been? God forbid. Can any woman be to me what she is? You may marry her to the Prince of Wales to-morrow, and it is cowardice and treason. How can we—how can you—undo promises made before Heaven? You may part us, and she will die as surely as if she were Jephthah’s daughter. Have you vowed to Heaven to compass her murder? Kill her, if you think your promise so binds you; but this I swear: I am glad you have come, so I may formally recall that hasty pledge. Call me when she will, and I will come to her!”

It was the speech of youth—hot, absolute, certain that love is a law older than any household ordinance, certain that separation meant death. Later George would watch other passions rise, flourish, and decay, and might smile, bitterly, at his own ardours; yet he would never willingly surrender the superstition that, among all creatures, Heaven had meant these two particular hearts to beat together.

General Lambert’s reply came with an effort, as if each sentence were lifted from a weight on his chest.

“We must come, then, to what I would fain have spared myself: an unfriendly separation. When I meet you, Mr. Warrington, I must know you no more. I must order— and they will not do otherwise than obey—my family and children not to recognise you when they see you, since you will not recognise, in your intercourse with me, the respect due to my age, the courtesy of gentlemen.

“I had hoped—so far from your sense of honour, and the idea I had formed of you—that in my present grief and perplexity I should find you willing to soothe and help me as far as you might; for God knows I have need of everybody’s sympathy. But instead of help you fling obstacles. Instead of a friend—Heaven pardon me—I find in you an enemy! An enemy to the peace of my home and the honour of my children. And as such I shall treat you, and know how to deal with you when you molest me!”

He waved his hand as if cutting the air between them, set his hat on his head, and was gone.

George stood confounded, as if a familiar sound in the world—the very note by which he had tuned his days—had been struck mute. The happiness of yesterday seemed not merely ended, but poisoned. Since the first separation he had not felt so exquisitely unhappy as now, with quarrel added to parting, and himself suddenly not only alone but banished.

In a year of intimacy he had come to revere and love Lambert as he had loved no man except his dear Harry. To have that face turned away in anger was like losing the sun. Yet George felt, with the stubborn certainty of a young man who would rather be right than be comforted, that in withdrawing his promise he had acted rightly: his fidelity to Theo, and hers to him, stood first. Promises had passed between them from which no parent could absolve either; and all the priests in Christendom could only witness, not undo, the contract which had been sealed without altar or ring, but with that inward assent that makes a vow.

That day he fell, half by habit and half by aimless misery, into the library of the new Museum. There, by chance, he saw Jack Lambert; and because sorrow makes any friendly face into a harbour, George seized him—almost literally—drawing him out into the gardens where the city’s noise thinned to a distant grumble, and the sparrows, at least, kept their honest, unbought music.

Jack was a prig, to speak plainly; he loved a Latin tag as a cook loves a garnish, and sometimes the garnish was all. George did not much care for him in prosperous hours. But Jack had suffered too—in his affair with the little American—and being, as he would have said, haud ignarus mali, he was ready to pity another man’s wound.

George poured out everything: the meeting with Theo, the morning’s rupture, his resolve never to part with her. Jack’s eyes brightened with the pleasure of having an argument to arrange; his tongue produced Greek and Latin as if they were spices in a pantry. By degrees it appeared—through quotations and solemn nods—that Jack leaned to George’s side. At once George thought him a man of profound sense, clung to his elbow, and bestowed a warmth of affection upon him which Jack did not often attract.

They walked up to the Lambert lodgings in Dean Street. George watched Jack go in at the dear door and remained outside, staring at the windows with a sick desire to know whether Theo lay within, what sounds moved there—whether there was weeping, or a low voice reading, or only the hush of a house holding its breath.

He took himself to a coffee-house—Jack’s Coffee-House, by name—and called for a bottle. Port came, dark as old mahogany, smelling of raisins and warmth, and he drank as if he could drown his thoughts in it. He called another bottle. The world outside had its own harsh percussion—carts, hawkers, iron on stone—and the watchman’s cry at intervals; compared to that, the clink of glass and murmur of the room seemed almost a lullaby.

Jack did not return fast enough for a desperate man. When at last he appeared, his face was a little scared. He came to George’s box, poured himself two or three bumpers from the second bottle, and began.

Theo, it seemed, had kept her room, shaken by the previous day. Jack had come home to find dinner on the table, and afterward the General, eager for speech now that Theodosia was absent, held forth on the morning’s scene at George’s lodgings. He bade Hester be silent—poor Hester, as dumb as a mouse. He told Aunt Lambert—already dissolving handkerchiefs with tears—that women were all against him, and, in a fury, called them pimps for one another. Then he wheeled round upon Jack and demanded his view.

To Lambert’s surprise, and to his wife’s and Hetty’s delight, Jack spoke on George’s side. He ruled—quoting authorities, which he could not now precisely name between sips of port—that the matter had passed out of the parents’ hands. Consent once given had put the elders out of court. Though Jack did not hold with a host of divines those sacramental views of marriage, he held the bond yet more sacredly: marriages made before the civil magistrate without priest were, before Heaven, binding and indissoluble.

“It is not merely, sir,” Jack said to his father—here he removed his hat as if repeating a sermon, “those whom I, John Lambert, priest, have joined, let no man put asunder. It is those whom God has joined let no man separate. These young people were joined, or permitted to plight themselves to each other, by your consent—you, the priest of your own family. My views are clear, and I will lay them down at length in two or three discourses which, no doubt, will satisfy you.”

Upon which, Jack reported, his father said, “I am satisfied already, my dear boy.” And Hetty, with her arch little triumph, whispered, “Jack, mother and I will make you a dozen shirts, as sure as eggs is eggs.”

While they were thus talking, Theodosia came in—very pale, much agitated—kissed her father, and sat down at his side. She took a sippet of toast—plain, domestic, the simplest food in the world, yet sometimes the most eloquent—and dipped it in her father’s negus. Jack, between his pompous phrases, could not help noticing the detail; for a household tells its truth in such small acts: whether a sick girl can swallow, whether the warmth of wine and spice can coax life into her.

“You should have been here to hear Jack’s sermon!” Hester said.

“Has he?” Theo asked faintly, too weak to care for eloquence or citations.

“He has talked three quarters of an hour by Shrewsbury clock,” the General said—though Jack protested his own watch gave him less—“and his discourse has been you, my dear,” Lambert added, playing with Theo’s hand, “you and—and Mr. Warrington—and—George, my love.”

At that, Theo moved closer, laid her head upon her father, and wept on his shoulder. Jack, determined to be classical even in tenderness, remarked that it differed from a passage he remembered in Pausanias. Lambert asked, in honest simplicity, who Pausanias might be; and Jack, smiling at his father’s ignorance, told of Ulysses taking Penelope from her father, and the father pursuing, begging his daughter to return. Ulysses offered Penelope her choice; she covered her face with her veil—sign enough.

“For want of a veil,” Jack said, “my sister has taken refuge in your waistcoat, sir.”

They laughed, even in their ache; though Mrs. Lambert declared that had such a choice been offered her, and had Penelope been a girl of spirit, she would have gone home with her father at once.

“But I am not a girl of any spirit, dear mother,” Theo murmured, still in her father’s bosom.

After more talk, they insisted Theodosia return to bed. Jack, remembering George, slipped away to bring him news. “Passion,” Jack added, with the air of diagnosing an ailment, “is full of solliciti timoris; it racks the spirits, and, if indulged—especially by women who have little philosophy—must be injurious to health. My service to you, brother.”

From grief to hope the change was so swift it made George dizzy. Happiness flooded him, warming him like spiced wine after cold rain. “Landlord—more port!” he cried; and had Jack drunk a whole binful, George would have paid for it gladly. Jack’s sympathy was generous that day; and George, in the lavish gratitude of a man saved from drowning, swore their brotherhood would be eternal, and that if he could give Jack a bishopric—by George—he should have it.

How the night ended George could not rightly say. Jack later claimed the watchman interrupted their rhapsodies by chanting verses beneath the loved one’s window. George remembered only waking the next morning with a racking headache and yet a heart singing, as if the very birds outside had changed their tune.

He did not yet know the full extent of his relief: that the conversion of his noble enemy—the angry man of the previous morning—was already quietly accomplished. It must have galled an elder pride to yield to remonstrances spoken so little dutifully as George’s. But Lambert, the true Christian gentleman, had left that quarrel wounded and mortified, and gone about his business with a heavy thoughtfulness. In the afternoon, as was sometimes his custom, he stepped into a church open for prayers.

There, on his knees—submitting his trouble to the quarter where he came, privately, for guidance and comfort—it seemed to him that his child was right in her steadfast fidelity, and that he was wrong to demand absolute submission. So Jack’s cause had been won almost before it was pleaded. The brave, gentle heart that could not hold rancour, that bled at giving pain, that shrank even from asserting authority when authority would crush those it loved, was only too glad to return to its natural pulse of affection.

Years afterward, when the great press of time had gone over our house like a tide and left odd shells and fragments in drawers, I found among the old papers a packet, neatly docketed in my mother’s hand: “From London, April, 1760. My son’s dreadful letter.” I burnt it. I would not have that bit of domestic wreckage laid up like a family relic, for inquisitive grandchildren to finger, or for some hot-headed boy of our blood to draw forth and quote when he, too, fancied rebellion a romantic dish. For the same cause I destroyed the answer she sent me in that season of tyranny and revolt, when every line we wrote seemed dipped in gall, and yet was sealed with the old wax of duty.

I was mad—mad with separation from my mistress; and, in my madness, I took it into my head (not wholly unjustly) that my mother was the prime mover of the sharpest misery that had ever cut my life. I wrote to Virginia with what I called respect—respect held between clenched teeth. I said that whatever motives had guided her, I held her answerable for the wreck of my future, which she had chosen, wilfully, to mar. She had forced a separation between me and a virtuous, innocent creature; she had cast down that poor girl’s hopes, health, and happiness; the deed was done; I would make no comment on the doer, who must answer to God; but I did not disguise that the hurt she had done me was mortal, beyond mending by her life or mine; that my allegiance to her was broken; that I never again could be to her what I had been—her dutiful, respectful son.

Madam Esmond replied with a dignity that stung more than anger. Her style was like her needlework—fine, even, and without a loose thread. She gave no reproach, no hard word; she merely told me, coldly, that she had carried our cause before that awful tribunal of God and asked for counsel, and that as a mother she would, in humility, answer for her conduct there. Could I, as a son, answer for mine, and show, when the Great Judge put the question, whether I had honoured my father and my mother?

So the heavens were invoked—as they ever are in our private quarrels, with as much heat as in public wars. In every household dispute, as in every nation’s, we drag Providence into the room, and try to make Him sign on our side. We kneel, we demand, we shriek for sentence according to law; and outside our little chamber the great world goes on: carts rumble, kettles sing, children cry for bread, dogs bark at the milkman, coaches clatter over stones. We hate; we rage; we weep; we reconcile; we pass away; another morning rises that shines on us no more.

My letter, announcing my revolt (and I confess I had a vanity in its composition, as if a smart phrase could heal a wound), I showed to Mr. Lambert in duplicate, because I would have him understand exactly how I stood with my mother, and that, whatever threats might come, I should never consider my separation from Theo other than forced. Whenever I could see her again, I would. My word to her was in secula seculorum—binding at least while I had breath. I spoke as if she were equally bound to me, and her father knew it. He might separate us, as he might put poison before her and the obedient creature would take it and die; but the separation, the death—those would be his doing, and let him answer them.

Yet Martin Lambert was tender to weakness where his children were concerned—tender beyond prudence. He had not the heart to put any of them to torture—this one least of all. We had tried to part: we could not. He had endeavoured to divide us: it was more than lay in his power. The bars were up, but the young couple—maid within, knight without—loved each other all the same. The wall was built; Pyramus and Thisbe whispered on either side. And in the midst of grief and perplexity he still had humour enough to see his own part was sorry: the lime and rough plaster began to show a crack of light; first fingers went through, then hands; presently, had the builders been stubborn, heads would have followed. In truth it was the wall’s best business to retire.

I forget the stages and the days, and it matters little for the instruction of posterity. When my descendants come to their own love-scrapes, they will find their own ladders. I did not go back to Dean Street, I think; the open air was prescribed as the most salutary physic for Miss Lambert. I bought a good horse and rode by her carriage; and the old woman at Tottenham Court grew to know us, nodding and winking with the knowing kindness of a person who has, no doubt, warmed more than one pair of young hearts with a mug and a crust at a roadside door. I can smell the place still in memory—the peat reek and damp hedge-mould, the faint sour of stale small beer, and always the London dust riding on every breath of wind.

Doctor Heberden and the country air worked a prodigious cure. Hetty attended as duenna; and sometimes, on his holiday, Master Charley mounted my horse while I climbed into the carriage. What a world of love-making Hetty had to hear, and with what exemplary patience! If we rode in a closed coach, she would, with a virtue that deserved canonising, take to gazing out of the window at fields and clouds as though hedgerows were her peculiar passion. Then there were the letters—heaps of them—running to and fro as busy as kitchen errand-boys. Gumbo’s bandy legs were for ever trotting between my quarters and Dean Street; and Mrs. Molly, Theo’s maid, was for ever bringing back answers to Bloomsbury, with her apron smelling of starch and lavender-water. When the autumn leaves began to pale, Miss Theo’s roses were in full bloom again, and the doctor pronounced her cure complete.

While love was thus being nursed back to life like a delicate broth—watched, skimmed, warmed, never suffered to boil over—other things stirred in the household pot. I finished my great tragedy of Pocahontas; and this time Mr. Garrick accepted it, Dr. Johnson having spoken not unfavourably. My friend and cousin Hagan was engaged to play Captain Smith. The engagement came none too soon for him; and I had helped him and his family with means perhaps disproportionate to my own—especially considering the feud now blazing between Madam Esmond and me. Her answer to my angry April missive reached me toward autumn: war for war, controlment for controlment. Her thunder frightened me little. Virginia was far; her claws could not reach. And my conscience—if conscience it was, or only casuistry—found interpretations for her Scripture that kept my purpose firm. I did not tell her, nor any of my kin on either side (all bitter against the marriage), how my new loves prospered. What was the use of wrangling? Better to carve the day and its sweetness, and leave railers to grumble, and seniors to advise, over their own dinners.

In that first fever of separation I had also fired off notes—sharp enough—to my Uncle Warrington, to my Aunt Madame de Bernstein, and to my Lord or Lady of Castlewood (I forget which), thanking them for the pains they had taken to prevent the dearest happiness of my life, and promising them a corresponding gratitude from their obliged relative. Business brought the jovial baronet and his family to London earlier than usual; and Madame de Bernstein was never sorry to get back to Clarges Street and her cards. I saw them. They found me perfectly well; they concluded the match was broken; and I did not undeceive them. The Baroness took courage from my cheerful face, and made sly jokes about my philosophy and prudence as a man of the world. She was, as ever, set upon finding a rich match for me; and I fear I paid many compliments in her drawing-room to a young soap-boiler’s daughter from Mile End whom the worthy Baroness wished to thrust into my arms—plump as a Christmas goose, scented like orange-flower water, and frightened of every jest as of a sudden bang of a door.

“You court her with infinite wit and esprit, my dear,” says my pleased kinswoman; “but she does not understand half you say, and the other half frightens her. This ton de persiflage is very well amongst us; but be sparing of it, my dear nephew, among these roturiers.”

At her house, too, there was another person who did not understand my persiflage much better than Miss Badge; and this was a lady who had lived through King James the Second’s reign and was alive and worldly still under King George’s. I loved her company. Her talk was like an old receipt-book, crowded with names and seasons and private flavour: the great folks of the great days came out of her mouth as if she had only just seen them at supper. But my modest muse pipes for boys and virgins. Son Miles—if he ever reads these pages—will have no taste for court scandal, or can get fresh enough from Carlton House. No, my dear wife, you need not shake your powdered locks at me: I shall not bring a blush over our nursery bread-and-butter.

Yet this piece of scandal I cannot wholly pass; my aunt told it with infinite gusto, for she hated would-be good people and sniggered at the faults of the self-styled righteous as over a pie that had burst its crust and shown what lay within. My Lady Warrington—tall and virtuous, goodness for ever on her lips and “Heaven in her eye”—had the world in her other eye, and a shrewd appetite for advancement. When my match was supposed broken off, she tried upon me the same arts she had used on my poor Harry with such ill success—and failed with me likewise. It was not the Beauty, Miss Flora (for her master was of too illustrious a kind for my poor devotion); it was Dora the Muse who was sent to languish and pity and read even my godless tragedy, applauding and consoling. Meanwhile the Beauty—will it be believed?—was paraded before my Lady Yarmouth. My severe aunt gave an entertainment to the royal favourite, presented her boy to her, and placed little Miles under that august protection; and—so Bernstein swore—sent her daughter to stay in the lady’s house which our gracious lord and master daily visited, with designs that would have ended in a countess’s coronet in the family, but for an apoplexy that struck down the schemer. I can see it: my pretty Miles in his little uniform, led forward; the good-natured old Jezebel laying her hand on his curls; the room buzzing like a hive; and outside, in the street, the ceaseless din of London—hawkers, wheels, hammering—always drowning some finer music. Men talk of art, of virtue, of taste; and yet how readily they barter all three at the first loud knock of preferment.

Thus my life sped in the pleasantest occupation; and being so happy, I could afford to grow gentle towards those who had, after all, rather spiced than spoiled my fortune by placing a brief obstacle in my way. No particular plan was formed; but Theo and I knew a day would come when we need say Farewell no more. Should it fall a year hence, ten years hence—we were ready to wait. Day after day we discussed our little schemes, with Hetty for confidante. On our drives we spied cottages that might suit young people of small means; we made childish economies with the solemnity of statesmen: a cot and a brown loaf should content us; Gumbo and Molly should wait upon us (as indeed they have done from that day to this). At twenty, who fears poverty? Our trials would only bake our attachment the firmer, as a slow oven hardens the crust. The sweet sorrow of each day’s parting made the morrow’s meeting more delicious; and when we separated we ran home to write those precious letters which young gentlemen and ladies always write under such circumstances. My wife has them still in a great tin sugar-box in her closet; I have looked once, and found some pretty. Yet I desire my heirs and executors to burn them all, unread, at our demise—specially desiring my son the Captain (to whom manuscripts are no delight) to do this duty. Those secrets carried by the penny-post, or slipped between Molly and Gumbo, were meant for us alone. Let no descendant overhear them.

We had letters, too, telling how dear Harry continued with the army as General Amherst’s aide-de-camp after the death of his own glorious general. By mid-October came news of the capitulation of Montreal and all Canada; and a brief postscript in which Hal said he would ask for leave and must go see the old lady at home, who wrote, he said, as sulky as a bear. I could guess why, though her claws could not reach me. I had written pretty fully to my brother how affairs stood with me in England.

Then, on the 25th of October, news came that his Majesty had fallen down dead at Kensington, and George III reigned over us. I fear we grieved but little. What do those care for the Atridae whose hearts are strung only to love? A modest, handsome, brave new Prince—we took the report gladly that he had every virtue; we cried huzzay with the crowd that hailed his accession; and all the while we were only two simple sweethearts whispering our little story in a corner.

Yet who can tell how great events touch even the smallest lives? Had not our little Charley at the Charterhouse once wished impiously for a new king because, on his gracious Majesty’s accession, Doctor Crusius gave the boys a holiday? Charley and I, and Hetty and Theo (for Theo was strong enough now to walk many a mile), went to hear the Heralds proclaim the new King before Savile House in Leicester Fields. A pickpocket stole a gentleman’s watch and chain close by us; he was caught and carried to Bridewell—this, too, on account of the King’s accession. Had the King not died, the gentleman would not have been in the crowd; the chain would not have been seized; the thief would not have been caught and whipped. So we are all, more or less remotely, tangled in great changes; the drumbeat at court sets even kitchen clocks to a different time.

And so it fell out with us. My Lord Wrotham was a great friend of the august family at Savile House, who knew and esteemed his many virtues. Of all living men, my Lord Wrotham most loved his neighbour and old fellow-soldier, Martin Lambert, declaring the world held few better gentlemen. And my Lord Bute, being at first all potent with the young King, was eager—so it was said at the beginning of his brief and unlucky power—to patronise merit; and through Wrotham he was strongly prejudiced in Mr. Lambert’s favour.

At this time Parson Sampson—our old friend—was occupying poor Hal’s vacant bed at my lodgings, being in truth hunted out of his own by the bailiffs. I liked to have him near: no more amusing Jack-friar ever walked in cassock. He entered into all my rhapsodies about Miss Theo; he swore he never tired of hearing me talk of her; he admired Pocahontas and Carpezan with what I believe was honest enthusiasm; and could repeat whole passages with an emphasis that Barry or cousin Hagan could scarce surpass. He was go-between for Lady Maria and such relations as had not disowned her; and, always in debt himself, was never happier than drinking a pot with friends in similar poverty, mingling tears with them as readily as ale. His knowledge of pawnbrokers’ shops was prodigious; he boasted he could raise more on an article than any gentleman of his cloth. He never paid his own debts, to be sure, but he was always ready to forgive his debtors. Poor as he was, he found means to love and help his needy little sister. A more prodigal, kindly, amiable rogue never grinned behind bars. They say I love parasites: I confess I had a great liking for Sampson, and esteemed him much better than probably much better men.

When he heard my Lord Bute was in the cabinet, Sampson vowed his lordship must give me a place worthy of my birth and merits. I would not go to his levee? The Esmonds were proud as Lucifer; and, demmy, my birth was as good as any man’s in Europe. Where were these great Scots, Sampson roared, when the Esmonds were lords of counties, warriors, Crusaders? Beggarly islanders, by George, tearing raw fish without a rag to their backs! But the times were changed; the Scots were in luck; mum’s the word. “I don’t envy him,” says Sampson, “but he shall provide for you and my dearest, noblest, heroic captain! He SHALL, by George!” And when, the month after the accession, his Majesty ordered Richard III at Drury Lane, my chaplain cursed and swore he would have me to Covent Garden to see Carpezan too.

One morning he burst into my room where I lay rather late, waving a newspaper and singing “Huzza!” with all his might—his voice loud as a street-crier, and, to my irritable ear, as jarring as a hammer on a pot.

“What is it, Sampson?” says I. “Has my brother got his promotion?”

“No, in truth; but some one else has. Huzzay! huzzay! His Majesty has appointed Major-General Martin Lambert to be Governor and Commander-in-Chief of the Island of Jamaica.”

I started up. Here was news indeed. Mr. Lambert would go to his government—and who would go with him?

The night before, I had been supping with some genteel young fellows at the Cocoa-Tree. The rascal Gumbo had had a note for me from my dear mistress, conveying the same intelligence, and had delayed to deliver it. Theo begged me to see her at the old place at midday next day without fail.

There was no little trepidation in our little council when we met. Papa had announced his acceptance and his speedy departure. He would have a frigate and take his family with him. Merciful powers—were we to be torn apart? My Theo’s old deathly paleness returned as if a hand had snuffed a candle. Aunt Lambert thought she would swoon; one of Mrs. Goodison’s girls ran up from the workroom with a bottle of salts. “Going away? Going away in a frigate, Aunt Lambert? Going to tear her away from me? Great God! I shall die!” she cried.

She was better when mamma came up from the workroom with the salts. Those women used to meet me; and knowing Theo’s delicate state, how could they keep from compassion? The house itself seemed to breathe of women’s labour—hot irons hissing, the dry rasp of scissors, the soft thud of cloth laid on the board, and through it all the murmuring of voices kept low as in a sickroom. Mrs. Goodison, who had known and worked for Miss Molly Benson as a schoolgirl, told me she remembered Miss Esmond of Virginia perfectly, and a gown she made for the young lady to be presented at her Majesty’s ball; and even when orders came for an outfit for the three ladies, she said demurely, “why, I thought I could do no harm in completing the order.”

For the General was busy with levees, waiting on ministers, making his outfit, settling affairs; and they never happened to tell him about our little walks and meetings. The world of men was all drums and appointments and official doors; the world of women, all pins and hems and bottles of salts; and between them our love tried to keep its own small music from being drowned.

I need not say in what perturbation I went home that evening after our discussion. No—at least only a very few—more walks; no more rides to dear Hampstead or beloved Islington; no more fetching and carrying of letters between Gumbo and Molly. The former blubbered so that I was touched by his fidelity and gave him a crown-piece to go to supper with the poor girl—his sweetheart, it turned out. What, you too, unhappy Gumbo, torn from the maid you love? I was ready to mingle tear for tear, as if grief were a broth we must season together, each tasting the other’s salt.

Those of us who had been bustling about that guilty business in the morning felt our shame come back threefold when we saw what it had done to him whom, of all men, we most revered. The blow fell strangely on that good man: not loud, not violent, but with a quiet that was more piteous than any outcry. The child of his heart had deceived and disobeyed him; the whole of his household—women, servants, and we who called ourselves his friends—had, as it were, drawn a net round him and pulled it tight.

If a man’s very nature be to give, to pardon, to stoop, then to wound him is like striking at something sacred and helpless; it is like troubling a sleeping infant, or rudely jarring the arm that is nursing it. We—who had done the deed—found ourselves reduced to a kind of abasement that no words can soften. I pass over the tears, the prayers, the gentle grave sentences by which he forgave; the common worship that followed, as if to bind up the rent we had made; and then the last parting, when he went away to his government, and the ship drew off from the shore and left us behind.

Theo and I stood hand in hand, dumb and burning with humiliation. She did not come to me as my wife until he was gone. Between the marriage and his departure she kept her old place—at home, by her father’s chair; sleeping still with her sister; moving about the house as one who is afraid her footfall might sound too loud. He was kind as ever—kind with that steady, unshowy kindness that makes you ashamed to be pitied by it; but the women scarcely spoke to one another. Aunt Lambert, for once, had an acid fretfulness, as though even the air offended her; and little Hetty was feverish and strange, repeating to herself, “I wish we were gone. I wish we were gone,” as if the words were a charm to hurry time.

Though I was forgiven and admitted, I went there like a thief with a pardon in his pocket. I slunk away during those last days; I saw my wife only for a minute in the street, or in the doorway with her family near. She was not mine until they were gone.

When they had embarked, we went to Winchester and Hampton for what in happier circumstances might be called our wedding. It had the shape of rejoicing, and none of the substance. We were lonely with a loneliness that had remorse in it. We spoke of our dear father—so she called him, and so did I, for he had earned the name—as if we had buried him; as if, by our undutifulness, we had helped to lay him in the grave.

I had Sampson put the marriage in the papers. My wife used afterwards to droop her head at the poor fellow, as though she saw our secret made public in his very boots and livery. I brought Mrs. Warrington back to my old lodgings in Bloomsbury, where there was room enough for our two chairs, our two plates, and that modest life which begins with a kettle and a candle and thinks itself rich.

I wrote to my mother in Virginia. I told her no particulars. I said only that Mr. Lambert being about to depart for his government, I held myself in honour bound to fulfil my promise to his dearest daughter; and that I meant to complete my studies for the Bar, and qualify myself for employment at home, in our own colony or any other. Mrs. Mountain answered for Madam Esmond—by desire, she said, of my mother, who thought that for peace’s sake my communications had best go that way.

Meanwhile I found my English kindred in a fury so formal that it was almost comic. The butler at Hill Street, when he said, “Not at home,” presented a blank tragedy of a face—one might have studied it as carefully as Mr. Garrick studies a ghost. My poor little wife was on my arm; we tripped away, laughing, when we came upon my lady in a street stoppage, sitting in her chair like a wronged goddess, her footmen and chairmen planted round her.

I took off my hat and bowed with all the humility I could enact. I asked after my dear cousins as tenderly as if we had not scandalized her house.

“I—I wonder you dare look me in the face!” Lady Warrington gasped.

“Don’t deprive me of that precious privilege,” said I. “It is the one comfort left to me.”

“Move on, Peter!” she screamed, and the chairmen started.

“Your ladyship would not impale your own husband’s flesh and blood,” I said.

She rattled up the glass of her chair as if to shut out not only my voice, but the very air that carried it. I kissed my hand, lifted my hat again, and made her a bow that, had it been a dish, might have passed for a whipped syllabub—airy, extravagant, and meant to provoke.

Not long after, walking in Hyde Park with Theo—my dearest companion, whose presence made even the winter bright—I met my little cousin Miles exercising on horseback, with a groom behind him. The boy saw us, and, like a hawk stooping, came galloping up, the groom thundering and powdering after, bawling, “Stop, Master Miles, stop!”

“I am not to speak to my cousin,” says Miles, pulling up his pony with a boy’s audacity, “but telling you to send my love to Harry is not speaking to you, is it? Is that my new cousin? I’m not told not to speak to her. I’m Miles—cousin, Sir Miles Warrington Baronet’s son—and you are very pretty!”

“Now, duee now, Master Miles,” says the groom, touching his hat to us, and the boy trotted away laughing, looking back over his shoulder to see if he had made us smile.

“You see,” I said to Theo, “how my relations have determined to treat me.”

“As if I married you for your relations!” she answered, and her eyes—full of brave joy, full of love—made me richer than any reconciliation with Hill Street could have done.

So the winter went on: brisk, pleasant in spite of all; our little rooms snug; the kettle singing on the hob like a domestic bird; and when Sampson—abashed, yet faithful—came now and then to make the punch, the smell of the lemon-peel as it twisted under the knife, and the warm bite of the spirits as they met the sugar, seemed to set a glow in the very air. Theo had a particular neatness and tenderness in such small offices: she would pare the rind thin, avoiding the bitter white; she would bruise the peel with the sugar in the bottom of the bowl until the grains shone with the oil; and then the hot water would go in, and at last the wine, and the whole would steam up with a fragrance that made our plainest evening feel like a feast.

We went at nights to the theatre when friends brought us tickets. Day by day we expected our new play of Pocahontas to rise and eclipse former tragedies; and at home there was tea, there was talk, there was that delicious sound of quiet living—the small clicks of china, the hiss from the kettle, the crackle of the coal, the far-off rumble of coaches in the street like a tide you listen to from a safe shore. There are noises in London that bruise the mind—hammering, shouting, the endless grinding of wheels—and there are noises that comfort it; and I found, in those weeks, that our happiness depended not only on what we had to eat, but on what we had to hear.

The fickle old aunt in Clarges Street, who at my first coming to town with my wife had received me with scorn, soon softened; and no sooner did she know Theo—whom she had pronounced an insignificant country-faced chit—than she fell utterly in love with her. She would have her to tea and supper every day when there was no other company.

“As for company, my dears,” she would say, “I don’t ask you. You are no longer du monde. Your marriage has put that entirely out of the question.”

So she would have had us come to amuse her and go in and out by the back-stairs, like actors slipping behind the scenes. Theo had fine-lady pride enough to be entertained rather than wounded; and I must do the Baroness’s domestics the justice to say that, had we been duke and duchess, we could not have been received with more respect. There is a courtesy in well-trained servants that sometimes keeps alive a decency which their betters forget.

Madame de Bernstein was wonderfully tickled with the story of Lady Warrington and her chair. I acted it for her; I gave her anecdotes of the pious baronet’s lady and her daughters; and the old woman, mischievous as a girl, delighted in them as in a sharp relish.

The Dowager Countess of Castlewood, established at Kensington, gave us that reception which genteel ladies extend to their poorer relatives—civil, correct, and cold as a plate that has been warmed and wiped a dozen times. We went once or twice to her drums, but after losing more money at cards and spending more in coach-hire than I chose to afford, we gave up those entertainments. In the fashionable world people are dropped daily by death, debt, and a hundred accidents, and are missed no more than a leaf missed from a tree in autumn.

Theo did not regret our exclusion. She wore once at Kensington some little ornaments left by her mother—trinkets to which the good lady had attached a value—yet to my eyes her own white neck, her fresh modest beauty, were worth more than those twinkling stones. And there were dowagers there whose wrinkled bones blazed with rubies and diamonds, which I am sure they would gladly have exchanged for Theo’s youth and sweetness, could such things be traded like jewels.

Not a soul spoke to her—except Beau Lothair, a friend of Mr. Will’s, who prowled about Bloomsbury afterwards, and even sent my wife a billet. I met him in Covent Garden and promised to break his ugly face if ever I saw it in the neighbourhood of my lodgings. Madam Theo was not molested again.

Of our relatives the only one who came to see us was poor Maria, who, with her husband Mr. Hagan, often shared our homely dinner. We had friend Spencer from the Temple, who admired our little Arcadian felicity and asked—very gently—for our compassion for his less fortunate loves. And twice or thrice the famous Doctor Johnson came in for a dish of Theo’s tea.

A dish? a pailful. “And a pail the best thing to feed him, sar!” says Mr. Gumbo indignantly; for the Doctor’s appearance was not pleasant, nor his linen particularly white. When he ate he snorted and grew red; he sputtered; he flung his meat about; he roared in contradiction; and he annoyed Theo—whom he professed to admire—by declaring, every time he saw her, “Madam, you do not love me; I see by your manner you do not love me; though I admire you, and come here for your sake. Here is my friend Mr. Reynolds that shall paint you: he has no ceruse in his paint-box as brilliant as your complexion.”

Mr. Reynolds, a most agreeable gentleman, would indeed have painted my wife; but I knew his price and did not choose to incur it. I wish now, for the sake of the children, that I had. A face is a kind of history; and we let histories slip away because we count guineas too carefully.

What vexed Theo in Dr. Johnson more than his contradictions and dirty nails was, I think, an unfavourable opinion he formed of my new tragedy. Hagan once proposed, with his actor’s zeal, that the Doctor should hear some scenes read after tea.

“Nay, sir, conversation is better,” says the Doctor. “I can read for myself, or hear you at the theatre. I had rather hear Mrs. Warrington’s artless prattle than your declamation of Mr. Warrington’s decasyllables. Tell us about your household affairs, madam—whether his Excellency your father is well—and whether you made the pudden and the butter sauce. The butter sauce was delicious!”

He loved it so well he had carried off a large quantity in the bosom of a very dingy shirt. Theo, who made butter sauce as she did everything—patiently, with attention, not letting it break, coaxing the melted butter into the flour and liquor until it turned smooth and shining—coloured up to hear it praised, and then coloured more to see where it had gone.

“You made it as though you loved me,” he persisted. “You helped me as though you loved me, though you don’t.”

“Faith, sir,” says Hagan, with spirit, “you are taking some of the present away with you in your waistcoat.”

“Sir, you are rude!” bawls the Doctor. “You are unacquainted with the first principles of politeness, which is courtesy before ladies. Having received an university education, I am surprised that you have not learned the rudiments of politeness. I respect Mrs. Warrington. I should never think of making personal remarks about her guests before her!”

“Then, sir,” cries Hagan, fierily, “why did you speak of my theatre?”

“Sir, you are saucy!” roars the Doctor.

“De te fabula,” says the actor.

“I think it is your waistcoat that is saucy. Madam, shall I make some punch in the way we make it in Ireland?” And the Doctor, puffing, purple in the face, wiped the dingy shirt with a still more dubious handkerchief and applied it to his forehead; after which he blew a sort of hyperborean whistle, as if to blow his wrath away into the street.

“It is de me, sir—though, as a young man, perhaps you need not have told me so.”

“I drop my point, sir! If you have been wrong, I am sure I am bound to ask your pardon for setting you so,” says Mr. Hagan, and made one of those fine bows which, on his stage, could melt a pit.

“Doesn’t he look like a god?” says Maria, clutching Theo’s hand; and indeed Hagan did look handsome and noble in his heat, his colour up, his hand to his breast. Chamont or Castalio could not have presented himself better.

“Let me make you some lemonade, sir,” says Theo, eager to turn quarrel into comfort. “My papa has sent us a box of fresh limes. May we send you some to the Temple?”

“Madam, if they stay in your house, they will lose their quality and turn sweet,” says the Doctor, who could never help being master, even when he meant to be kind. “Mr. Hagan, you are a young sauce-box, that’s what you are! Ho! ho! It is I have been wrong.”

And when we were alone, Maria—who lived half in her own drawing-room and half upon the stage—began bleating out speeches, her eyes swimming with admiration.

“‘Oh, my lord, my Polidore!’” she cried, and then poured forth some tender raptures from the play as if she were still under the lamps. “Thou knowest not, my Theo, what a pearl and paragon of a man my Castalio is; my Chamont, my—oh, dear me, child, what a pity it is that in your husband’s tragedy he should have to take the horrid name of Captain Smith!”

Upon that tragedy—my Pocahontas—not only my literary hopes but much of my present livelihood depended. My brother’s debts had been discharged; my mother’s drafts from home duly honoured; my own expenses paid—moderate, but not inconsiderable—and pretty nearly the whole of my patrimony was gone. And at this moment, of all moments, I must choose for my marriage! I could raise money on my inheritance—possible, but costly. My mother could not leave her eldest son without maintenance, whatever our quarrels. I had health, strength, good wits, some friends, and a certain reputation—above all, my famous tragedy, which the manager had promised to perform, and on the proceeds of which I counted for present support.

What becomes of the arithmetic of youth? How do we persuade ourselves that a hundred pounds is maintenance, and a thousand a fortune? How dared I play at hazard with Fortune at such odds? Yet I remember I succeeded in convincing my dear General, and he left home believing that his son-in-law had—at least for the present—some score of hundred pounds at command. He and his dear Molly had begun life with less, and the ravens had always fed them. The women, those sentimental souls, could almost find a pleasure in poverty; and Aunt Lambert declared it would be wicked and irreligious to doubt that provision would be made for her children. Was the righteous ever forsaken? Did the just man ever beg his bread? She knew better.

“No, no, my dears! I am not going to be afraid on that account, I warrant you! Look at me and my General!”

Theo believed what I said—and wished to believe it myself. So we began life upon a capital of Five Acts and about three hundred pounds in ready money.

As the time drew near for my tragedy’s appearance, my friends canvassed the town to gather a body of supporters for the opening night. I am ill at begging favours from the great; but when my Lord Wrotham came to London, I went with Theo on my arm to wait on him. He received us kindly out of regard for his old friend—her father—though he shook a finger at me good-naturedly, and Theo, at that, hung down her head as if she heard again the ship’s ropes creak and the water slap against the side on the day her father went away.

However, he would do his best for the General’s daughter; he hoped for a success; he had heard great things of the piece; and he engaged a number of places for himself and his friends.

This patron secured, I had no other.

“Mon cher,” says the Baroness, “at my age I should bore myself to death at a tragedy; but I will do my best, and I will certainly send my people to the boxes. Yes! Case in his best black looks like a nobleman; and Brett in one of my gowns has a faux air de moi which is quite distinguished. Put down my name for two in the front boxes. Good-bye, my dear. Bonne chance!”

The Dowager Countess presented compliments on the back of the nine of clubs; she had a card-party that night, and was quite sorry she and Fanny could not go to my tragedy.

As for my uncle and Lady Warrington, they were out of the question. After the affair of the sedan-chair I might as well have asked Queen Elizabeth to go to Drury Lane. These were all my friends—this host of aristocratic connexions about whom poor Sampson had bragged; and on the strength of whom, as the manager said, he had given Mr. Hagan his engagement.

“Where was my Lord Bute?” the manager asked snappishly, taking snuff—how different from the brisk, engaging, obsequious little man of six months ago. “Had I not promised his lordship should come? I promised Lord Bute should come!”

“Yes,” says Mr. Garrick, “and her Royal Highness the Princess of Wales, and his Majesty too.”

Poor Sampson owned that, buoyed up by vain hopes, he had promised the appearance of these august personages. The next day at rehearsal matters were worse still, and the manager was in a fury.

“Great heavens, sir!” he cries. “Into what a pretty guet-a-pens have you led me! Look at that letter, sir—read that letter!” And he thrust a sheet into my hand.

It ran:

“MY DEAR SIR,—I have seen his lordship, and conveyed to him Mr. Warrington’s request that he would honour the tragedy of Pocahontas by his presence. His lordship is a patron of the drama, and a magnificent friend of all the liberal arts; but he desires me to say that he cannot think of attending himself, much less of asking his Gracious Master to witness the performance of a play, a principal part in which is given to an actor who has made a clandestine marriage with a daughter of one of his Majesty’s nobility.—Your well-wisher, SAUNDERS MCDUFF.”

“Mr. D. Garrick, at the Theatre Royal in Drury Lane.”

The letters danced before my eyes; not from any poetry in them, but from the sudden blow they carried. Our little lodgings in Bloomsbury, our quiet kettle, Theo’s careful hands over the sauce-boat, the very limes she had spoken of for lemonade—all seemed, for a moment, to stand on the edge of some cracking ice.

That evening my poor Theo had a nice dinner waiting: a small joint well tended, bread fresh, a dish of something she had contrived out of little, the room warm with the good smells of a home that tries hard to be cheerful. I came in from rehearsal with my face as pale as if I had been ill.

I pleaded fatigue. I dared not tell her the dreadful news.

The town, truth to say, knew less of Pocahontas than we of Virginia, who keep her name as one keeps a homely song—by repetition at the hearth until it is part of the household’s very breathing. At the hint of my friends I threw out, for a kind of lure, a brief ballad touching the Indian princess, and it found its way into the magazines a few days before my tragedy ventured itself upon the boards. Sampson hailed the device with rapture.

“It is ground-bait, sir,” cried he; “you will see the fish rise in multitudes on the great day!”

He and Spencer would have it that the verses were debated with much clatter of cups and saucers at divers coffee-houses; that one set swore Mr. Mason wrote them; another, Mr. Cowper of the Temple; and there were even mighty heads wagging that named Mr. Gray. Poor Sam—who could never resist the seasoning of a tale—had, I dare say, sprinkled those rumours himself as a cook flings in salt with a knowing hand; and had any one cried “Shakspeare!” he would have sworn my Pocahontas the Bard’s best forgotten jewel.

For my own part, Captain Smith was an old acquaintance of mine—older than London, older than my marriage—dating from the days when, a boy, I sat at my grandfather’s knees in the great Virginian library, with a favourite volume open and my finger travelling line by line as though it were a map of wonders. How the room comes back with the very smell of it—the leather of bindings warmed by the sun, the faint cedar of the presses, and, from the yard beyond, the country’s honest chorus: pigeons cooing under the eaves, a pump creaking, a negro lad singing at his work, the far clink of a pail on stone. Grandfather, in his slow rich voice, made pictures for me: Smith on the Danube fighting the Turks, Smith in savage hands in our forests, Smith—bound, bleeding, yet unbroken. Ah, that terrific encounter with the three champions! I could taste my childish excitement as sharply as vinegar on the tongue. And Bonny Molgro—what a name!—we endowed him with a turban of unimaginable breadth, whiskers like brambles, a scimitar as long as a harrow-tine, and a ferocity to match. The old book’s very cadence beat like a drum in the mind: the battle-axes clanging, the shout from the rampires, the falchion’s quick flash, and then the grisly reward—three Turks’ heads in a shield for arms, and three hundred ducats yearly for pension.

Disdaining time and place, as poets are licensed to do, I had my Smith achieve like feats upon our Potomac and the banks of James River. The ground-bait verses ran thus:

“Wearied arm and broken sword
Wage in vain the desperate fight;
Round him press the countless horde,
He is but a single knight.
Hark! a cry of triumph shrill
Through the wilderness resounds,
As, with twenty bleeding wounds,
Sinks the warrior, fighting still.

“Now they heap the fatal pyre,
And the torch of death they light—
Ah! ’tis hard to die of fire!
Who will shield the captive knight?
Round the stake with fiendish cry
Wheel and dance the savage crowd,
Cold the victim’s mien and proud,
And his breast is bared to die.

“Who will shield the fearless heart?
Who avert the murderous blade?
From the throng, with sudden start,
See, there springs an Indian maid.
Quick she stands before the knight,
‘Loose the chain, unbind the ring,
I am daughter of the king,
And I claim the Indian right!’

“Dauntlessly aside she flings
Lifted axe and thirsty knife;
Fondly to his heart she clings,
And her bosom guards his life!
In the woods of Powhattan,
Still ’tis told, by Indian fires,
How a daughter of their sires
Saved the captive Englishman.”

As for the plot of my tragedy, my children may take it down from the shelf any day and read it if they have a mind; nor am I eager to read it aloud again, since Captain Miles and the parson, last Christmas, chose to fall asleep at mamma’s request, after I had got but a couple of acts fairly upon their ears. Any person moderately conversant with plays and novels can, from the above, fill in the rest to his liking: an Indian king; a loving princess; her attendant who, like her mistress, has a heart too large for the bounds of tribe or station, and must be in love with the British captain’s servant; a traitor within the English fort; a brave Indian warrior, gnawed by an unhappy passion for Pocahontas; and, above all, a medicine-man and priest—Palmer played him very well—capable of every stratagem, and bent upon the English prisoner’s torture and death. Add to these the accidents of the wilderness, the war-dances and cries (which Gumbo, from home-knowledge, mimicked with painful truth), and the arrival of the English fleet with allusions to our late victories in Canada and the determination of Britons to rule and conquer in America—and some of us, not unnaturally, believed there was matter enough for applause.

But I had already noted the ill omens. A peevish, jealous, timid management set itself, as though by instinct, to trip the piece at every step; and there was, in certain high quarters, a prejudice against it as bitter as wormwood. What wonder, then, that Pocahontas proved no victory?

I laugh to scorn the critics’ malignity who found fault with the performance—pretty judges, forsooth, who cried Carpezan a masterpiece whilst a far superior and more elaborate work earned only their sneers! I insist that Hagan acted admirably—so admirably that a certain actor and manager of the theatre might well be jealous of him—and that but for a cabal outside, the piece would have succeeded. The order had been given that the play should not succeed; so Sampson always declared. “The house swarmed with Macs, by George,” he swore, “and they should have the galleries washed with brimstone.” He would maintain, in his honest fury, that Mr. Garrick himself would not have had it succeed for the world, and was never in such a rage as during that grand scene in the second act where Smith—poor Hagan—bound to the stake, is saved by Pocahontas; for then, for a moment, the whole house did indeed thrill with applause and sympathy.

Anybody with curiosity may refer to the published tragedy—octavo, or the subsequent splendid quarto in my Collected Works—and decide whether the scene be without merit; whether the verses be not elegant; the language rich and noble. One cause of the failure, oddly enough, was my fidelity to history. I had copied at the Museum, with care, a figure of Sir Walter Raleigh in frill and beard; and (my dear Theo giving me some of her mother’s best lace) we dressed Hagan accurately after my drawing. No man could look better. Miss Pritchard as Pocahontas I dressed, too, as a Red Indian, having seen enough of that costume at home. Will it be believed? the house tittered when she first appeared. They grew used to her, however; and just at the moment when she rushed into the prisoner’s arms, and a number were actually in tears, a fellow in the pit bawled out, “Bedad! here’s the Belle Savage kissing the Saracen’s Head;” whereupon an impertinent roar of laughter broke forth, with fitful explosions during the remainder of the play.

As the wag in Mr. Sheridan’s Critic says of the morning guns, playwrights are not content with one but must fire two or three; so with this pothouse jest of the Belle Savage—those ignorant people not knowing that Pocahontas herself was the very Belle Sauvage from whom the tavern took its name. The same fellow, like a screech-owl that will not be hushed, repeated his folly till one could have thrust a cork in his mouth with pleasure; and as each new character appeared, he baptised him with some tavern sign—the English governor, with a long beard, “the Goat and Boots;” his lieutenant (Barker), broad of face, “the Bull and Mouth,” and so forth. The curtain fell at last amid a shrill storm of whistles and hisses, which especially assailed poor Hagan whenever he opened his lips.

Sampson saw Master Will in the green boxes with some pretty acquaintances, and had no doubt that the treacherous scoundrel was among the ringleaders. “I would have flung him over into the pit,” said the faithful fellow (and he was man enough to do it), “but I saw a couple of Mr. Nadab’s followers prowling about the lobby, and was obliged to sheer off.”

So the eggs we had counted on selling at market were broken, and our hopes lay shattered before us.

I had looked in from the stage before the curtain rose. The house was pretty well filled; I remarked Mr. Johnson in the front boxes, in a laced waistcoat, with Mr. Reynolds by his side—the latter could not hear, and the former could not see, so they came good-naturedly, A deux, to form an opinion of my poor tragedy. I could see Lady Maria—by the hood she wore—in the lower gallery, once more able to sit and look at her beloved actor performing a principal part. As for Theo, she fairly owned that, unless I ordered her, she would rather not be present; and I gave no such command. If things went wrong—and my mind, like a weather-wise farmer’s, already smelt the change—her suffering would have been intolerable to me. So I let her stay away.

After a light dinner at the Bedford (a thing rather taken than tasted; for when the mind is overwrought the palate, that honest counsellor, grows dull), I went to the theatre shortly before the beginning, intending to remain until defeat or victory was declared. Yet even then I could not help seeing which way fate leaned. There was something gloomy in the look of all about me, as though the very air in the passages had been breathed too often and turned sour. Miss Pritchard had the headache; the barber who brought Hagan’s wig had powdered it like a wretch; the greenroom held none but doubtful faces; and the manager—a flippant, not to say impertinent gentleman, who himself that night looked as dismal as a mute at a funeral—had the insolence to say, “For Heaven’s sake, Mr. Warrington, go and get a glass of punch at the Bedford, and don’t frighten us all here by your dismal countenance!”

“Sir,” said I, “I have a right, for five shillings, to comment upon your face, but I never gave you authority to remark upon mine.”

“Sir,” says he, in a pet, “I most heartily wish I had never seen your face at all!”

“Yours, sir,” said I, “has often amused me greatly; and when painted for Abel Drugger is exceedingly comic”—for I have ever done Mr. G. the justice to think that in low comedy he was unrivalled.

I bowed and walked off to the coffee-house; and for five years after spoke not a word to him, until he apologised at a nobleman’s house where we met. I told him I had utterly forgotten what he alluded to; on a first night author and manager are flurried alike. And I added, “After all, there is no shame in not being made for the theatre. Mr. Garrick—you were.” A compliment which seemed to please him as much as I intended.

Fidus Achates—my good Sampson—ran to me at the end of the first act: matters, he said, were going pretty well, though he confessed the titter on Miss Pritchard’s first appearance, dressed exactly as an Indian princess should be.

“I cannot help it, Sampson,” said I, filling him a bumper of good punch—hot, fragrant, with the lemon’s sharp oil pricked from its rind—“if Indians are dressed so.”

“Why,” says he, “would you have had Caractacus painted blue like an ancient Briton, or Bonduca with nothing but a cow-skin?”

And indeed it may be that this fidelity to the truth was cause of the ridicule; in which case I, for one, am not ashamed of defeat. There are tongues that cannot bear an unfamiliar word; there are ears that mock at any accent not their own. One might as well ask a London pit to take the hush of a Virginian night for music, when they have trained themselves to relish only the iron scrape and brazen blare of town.

After the second act, my aide-de-camp came with dismal news indeed. I know not how it is: before action I was nervous enough; but in disaster a certain coolness comes upon me, as if the worst, being known, left nothing more to imagine. I asked quietly, “Are things going ill?” called for my reckoning, put on my hat, and marched to the theatre as calmly as if going to dine at the Temple; Sampson at my side, pressing my elbow, kicking link-boys out of the way, and crying, “By George, Mr. Warrington, you are a man of spirit—a Trojan, sir!”

So there were men of spirit in Troy; but fate was too strong. No man can say I did not bear my misfortune with calmness. I could no more help the clamour and noise of the audience than a captain can help the howling of the storm in which his ship goes down. Yet I was determined the rushing waves and broken masts should impavidum ferient, and flatter myself I did not flinch.

“Not Regulus, my dear madam, could step into his barrel more coolly,” Sampson said afterwards to my wife.

It is unjust to say of men of the parasitic nature that they are unfaithful in misfortune. Whether I was prosperous or poor, the wild parson was equally true, and shared our crust as eagerly as he had partaken of better fortune.

I took my place on the stage, whence I could see my poor actors and a portion of the audience that condemned me. The performers gave me a wide berth, perhaps out of pity. I believe I looked as little moved as any spectator; no one would have judged, from my face, that I was the unlucky hero of the night. But when I reached home my dearest Theo looked so pale that I knew the knowledge of my disaster had travelled faster than my feet.

Spencer, Sampson, cousin Hagan, and Lady Maria were to come after the play to congratulate the author—God wot! Poor Miss Pritchard, engaged likewise, sent word that I must understand she was far too unwell to sup. My friend the gardener at Bedford House had given my wife his best flowers to deck her little table. There they stood—poor little painted standards, as it were—and the battle lost.

I had borne the defeat well enough until I saw that sweet pale face across the table and those artless trophies of welcome set up for her hero. Then my courage, which had held against the roar of the pit, gave way before the stillness of home; and my heart felt a pang as keen as any that ever smote it.

Our meal was dismal enough, and no effort of talk could quite warm it. Yet we strove, as people will stir a fire that refuses to draw. We spoke of old Mrs. Hagan’s illness—luckily very ill at this time; her disease and its incidents proved, in odd fashion, a blessing, giving us matter not our own. Then we talked of his Majesty’s approaching marriage. I remember, too, with hateful clearness, the most futile scraps of the day—a tune a carpenter whistled near me at the playhouse, just before the dreary curtain fell; the very rhythm seemed to cling like soot.

We spoke of the death of good Mr. Richardson, author of Pamela and Clarissa, whom we all admired exceedingly. And as we talked of Clarissa, Theo put her handkerchief to her eyes once or twice and said faintly, “You know, my love, mamma and I could never help crying over that dear book. Oh, my dearest, dearest mother—how I wish she could be with me now!”

Here were tears that might be owned without naming the play; for a young lady may always weep for her absent mother.

Then we mixed a gloomy bowl—Jamaica limes squeezed till their sharpness sprang into the air; sugar melted; the spirit biting, then softening as the spoon went round—and drank to the health of his Excellency the Governor. And then, for a second toast, I filled a bumper and with a smiling face drank to “our better fortune!”

It was too much. The two women flung themselves into each other’s arms and irrigated each other’s neck-handkerchiefs with tears.

“Oh, Maria! is not—is not my George good and kind?” sobbed Theo.

“Look at my Hagan—how great, how godlike he was in his part!” gasped Maria. “It was a beastly cabal that threw him over—and I could plunge this knife into Mr. Garrick’s black heart—the odious little wretch!” And she actually grasped a weapon at her side.

But she flung it down presently, rushed to her lord and master, and embraced him in the presence of us all. I am not sure whether some one else did not do likewise. We were in a strange fever of grief and tenderness; and in the very midst of calamity Love, that sly comforter, came in among us with such fond blandishments that one scarce wished the calamity away—since it drew from us a sweetness we might otherwise have grudged the world.

Two or three days afterwards—on our birthday—a letter was brought to me in my study containing these lines:

“Returning from the cruel fight
How pale and faint appears my knight!
He sees me anxious at his side;
‘Why seek, my love, your wounds to hide?
Or deem your English girl afraid
To emulate the Indian maid?’

“Be mine my husband’s grief to cheer,
In peril to be ever near;
Whate’er of ill or woe betide,
To bear it clinging at his side;
The poisoned stroke of fate to ward,
His bosom with my own to guard;
Ah! could it spare a pang to his,
It could not know a purer bliss!
’Twould gladden as it felt the smart,
And thank the hand that flung the dart!”

I do not say the verses are very good; but I liked them as well as if they were. And when I went into the writer’s drawing-room after receiving the letter, and saw her—blushing, blessing me—her face, and the sound of her sweet young voice (which I can fancy even now as I hum the lines), seemed to me more beautiful than any dream I could borrow out of Heaven.

I am an old man now, and sit with my feet towards the fire as if I had a right to warmth purchased by years; and yet, when I look back at that leap which my Theo and I took—scarce out of our teens, with the ink hardly dry upon our names—I know well enough what a decent moralist ought to do. He ought to set himself up as a scarecrow for hot-headed youth; he ought to talk solemnly of ledgers, and rent-days, and the butcher’s bill; he ought to say “mutton chops” with a face as long as Lent, and warn every girl with a pretty hand not to put it into a poor man’s.

And yet—since truth is truth though it come without a sermon—our married life disappointed all the cautious prophets. It had its sharp seasons: griefs that bit like a north wind through an ill-fitted sash; days of want when the very sound of a knock at the door made the heart jump, lest it should be a creditor’s fist instead of a friend’s. But time, by God’s mercy, rubs the edge off many a knife; and there were consolations too, so intimate and so holy that a man scarcely dares to write them down as if they were common news for any eye. To marry without a competence is dangerous, no doubt. Society, which loves its rules as cooks love their measures, calls it a crime. Yet every year thousands commit it, trusting to no grand fortune—only to health, labour, and that strange seasoning of the blood called hope. If the genteel laws were made universal, the world would leave off multiplying; the silk-stockinged would stand shivering on the bank until a gilded barge came, while the barefooted would step into the stream and wade, and somehow get across.

Who would counsel his son to take a gentle girl from comfort to debt, privation, friendlessness, sickness, the whole sour dish of res angusta domi? I look at my own wife—at that steadfast sweetness which never turned rancid—and I ask pardon for the trials I made her taste. And yet I cannot talk of poverty as if it were nothing but ashes. I have endured it, and found it oftener tolerable than the rich imagine. There are strange pleasures that come with a scanty meal: gratitude, for one; and the clear sight that visits people in a narrow room, while fine folks, stepping from their broad sunshine into our little shadow, blunder as if half blind. They would pity us for drinking small beer, as though it were poison; they would marvel that we could say grace over cold mutton—cold, indeed, but still honest meat, and not the less to be thanked for because it had slept a night.

My good General—my father-in-law—had done the same rash thing before me. He married his Molly when he was a subaltern, with a purse no better lined than mine. They had known ups and downs, and (though my wife will never confess the point) had very likely done it in those younger days without asking leave of papa and mamma. At any rate, being pleased with their own venture, they were not frightened for ours; and when I made my statements to Mr. Lambert, I believe I was anxious to deceive him and myself together. He went off to Jamaica thinking I had a couple of thousand pounds, and so could keep his darling daughter in ease for years.

In truth, when the household had been furnished with such modest bravery as young people call necessity, the good man sailed away not much richer than his son-in-law. Theo’s portion was a handful of trinkets, some lace of Aunt Lambert’s, and twenty new guineas in a purse stitched by her mother and sisters—gold that looked splendidly heavy in the hand, and yet had a way of thinning like butter on a hot pan. For my own stock, I had counted as good a debt a sum which my honoured mother never would acknowledge, to the last day when she was called to pay the last debt of all. The money I had disbursed for her, she said, had been spent upon the estate which was to be mine at her decease. What she could spare was for my poor brother, who had nothing, and who, she reminded me in many a letter, would have been sole heir of the Virginian property but for a half-hour’s accident of birth. He was now distinguishing himself in the service of king and country; his promotion must be purchased; and to purchase it was his mother’s duty—or, she should suppose, his brother’s. When I had done with bar-studies and stage-amusements, Madam Esmond sent word by Mountain more than once that I was welcome to come home and take my place in the colony; and this she said before the news of my marriage reached her.

There is no need to set down her maternal indignation when it did. After the pacification of Canada, Harry got leave and dutifully visited Virginia. He wrote describing his reception, and my mother’s splendid entertainments. Castlewood, shut since our departure for Europe, was thrown open again; the soldier of Quebec, the friend of Wolfe, was fêted with all honour. Yet, as he told it, there were quarrels enough—dismal, noisy bouts—because my brother persisted in keeping friendship with Colonel Washington of Mount Vernon, whose praises Harry never tired of singing. I can allow the gentleman many virtues; and though England was to learn bitterly what kind of constancy he possessed, I can admire as well as his warmest friends that steadfast courage and success.

If the battles between Harry and our mother were as frequent as his letters made them, I wondered why he stayed. One reason, uncharitable perhaps, suggested itself; and it was a reason I scarcely liked to speak aloud to Theo. For we had both talked, with tender smiles and sighs, of our dear little Hetty’s romantic attachment to my brother, and wondered that he had never discovered it. I supposed, as men do, that my gentleman had found some young lady at home more to his taste than our sweet Hester, and that this accounted for his long lingering in Virginia.

Presently a letter came which was not a confession, but an admission. The person was described—never named; a Being of beauty and perfection, as such beings always are in ink. My wife asked to see the letter. I could not refuse; I handed it to her with a face as doleful as if I were reading a death-warrant. She read it, and to my surprise showed no corresponding sorrow.

“I have thought of this before, my love,” I said. “I feel with you for your disappointment regarding poor Hetty.”

“Ah! poor Hetty,” says Theo, and looked down at the carpet as if there were a history written in its pattern.

“It would never have done,” I said.

“No—they would not have been happy,” she sighed, as a woman sighs who sees further than a man pretends.

“How strange he never should have found out her secret!” I continued.

She looked me full in the face with an odd expression—half amusement, half something else, like a spice you cannot name until it pricks. “Pray, what does that look mean?” I asked.

“Nothing, my dear—nothing! only I am not surprised!” says Theo, and blushed.

“What,” I cried, with a queer commotion, “can there be another?”

“I am sure I never said so, George,” she answered quickly. “But if Hetty has overcome her childish folly, ought we not all to be glad? Do you gentlemen suppose that you only are to fall in love and grow tired, indeed?”

“What!” I said, startled as if a kettle had boiled over. “Do you mean to tell me, Theo, that you ever cared for any one but me?”

“Oh, George,” she whimpered—laughing and ashamed together—“when I was at school, there was—there was one of the boys at Doctor Backhouse’s, who sate in the loft next to us; and I thought he had lovely eyes; and I was so shocked when I recognised him behind the counter at Mr. Grigg’s the mercer’s, when I went to buy a cloak for baby, and I wanted to tell you, my dear, and I didn’t know how!”

I made her describe him—coat, hair, all—and went, moved by jealousy into which a man may put a deal of ridiculous energy. And there he was: a little bandy-legged wretch in a blue camlet coat, red hair tied with a dirty ribbon, so pitiful a rival that I could not find it in me even to reproach my wife. Nor will she ever know that I looked at the fellow, until she reads this confession. If our wives saw us as we are, I thought—smelled the stale smoke in our coats, heard the vanity in our talk—would they love us as they do? Are we as mistaken in them as they in us? I look into one candid face, at least, and think it never deceived me.

As for the exact smallness of our capital when we began, I will not set it down, lest some brisk young couple take heart and fancy that love can be eaten like bread. The unfortunate tragedy brought us nothing. Since its late publication, reviewers have spoken not unfavourably of its merits; Mr. Kemble himself did me the honour to commend it. Our kind friend Lord Wrotham would have had it published by subscription, and even sent a bank-note, asking for a hundred copies for his friends. But I have always hated that manner of levying money.
