I preferred my poverty sine dote, locked up the manuscript, with my poor girl’s verses inserted on the first page, like a pressed flower laid in a book.

Why the piece gave offence at Court I never clearly knew, unless it were because an actor who had run off with an earl’s daughter played a principal part; but I was told, too, that sentiments put into the mouths of my Indian characters—declamations against ambition, against the British desire of rule—were called dangerous and unconstitutional. So whatever little hope I had of royal favour was whisked away like flour from a board when a door bangs.

What was to be done? A few months after the failure, I counted what remained of my fortune—the calculation was not long—and resolved to beat a retreat from my pretty Bloomsbury apartments. I gave warning to our good landlady, saying my wife’s health required country lodgings. We went no farther than Lambeth. Gumbo and Molly followed us faithfully; and here, though poor as might be, we were waited on by a maid and a lackey in livery, like folks of condition. Kind relatives cried out against our extravagance; indeed, are they not ever ready to find our faults for us, and publish them to the world, as if they were town-criers?

One day, returning from London where I had been to see some booksellers, I recognised our family arms and livery on a grand gilt chariot standing before a public-house near our lodgings. Loiterers had gathered round it, gazing with awe at the footmen, resplendent in sun, quaffing flaming pots of beer. I hurried home, and found my Lady Castlewood seated opposite my wife in our little room. From the window we had a bright prospect: the river covered with barges and wherries, the old towers and trees of the Archbishop’s palace and gardens beyond—sounds of water and oar, bell and distant coach, a whole city breathing in waves and clatter. In that place, the noise was not yet the later iron roar of industry, but a human din—hoofs, wheels, voices—broken by the soft slap of tide; and I often thought how much the mind leans upon such a soundscape, as a cook leans upon the steady heat of her fire.

Theo, who can describe a scene as neatly as she can whip an egg, narrated to me afterwards every turn of her ladyship’s talk.

“I have been here this ever-so-long,” says the Countess, “gossiping with cousin Theo, while you have been away at the coffee-house, I dare say, making merry with your friends, and drinking your punch and coffee. Guess she must find it rather lonely here, with nothing to do but work them little caps and hem them frocks. Never mind, dear; reckon you’ll soon have a companion who will amuse you when cousin George is away at his coffee-house! What a nice lodging you have got here, I do declare! Our new house which we have took is twenty times as big, and covered with gold from top to bottom; but I like this quite as well. Bless you being rich is no better than being poor. When we lived to Albany, and I did most all the work myself, scoured the rooms, biled the kettle, helped the wash, and all, I was just as happy as I am now. We only had one old negro to keep the store. Why don’t you sell Gumbo, cousin George? He ain’t no use here idling and dawdling about, and making love to the servant-girl. Fogh! guess they ain’t particular, these English people!”

So she rattled on, brisk as a spoon in a tin pan, until her hour came. Then she produced a fine repeating watch and said it was time to pay a call upon Her Majesty at Buckingham House. “And mind you come to us, George,” she cried, waving her little hand out of the gilt coach. “Theo and I have settled all about it.”

When the laced footmen clambered up behind and our magnificent little patroness rolled away, I said, “Here, at least, is one who is not afraid of our poverty, nor ashamed to remember her own.”

“Ashamed!” Theo said, taking up her lilliputian needlework again, the thread slipping through her fingers with that soft whisper which, in a poor room, is as companionable as any music. “To do her justice, she would make herself at home in any kitchen or palace in the world. She has given me and Molly twenty lessons in housekeeping. She says, when she was at home to Albany, she roasted, baked, swept the house, and milked the cow.” Theo pronounced cow archly in our American way, and mimicked her ladyship’s accent so divertingly that even our anxieties had to make room for laughter.

“And she has no pride,” I said. “It was good-natured of her to ask us to dine with her and my lord. When will Uncle Warrington ever think of offering us a crust again, or a glass of his famous beer?”

“Yes, it was not ill-natured to invite us,” says Theo, slily. “But, my dear, you don’t know all the conditions!” And then, still in Lady Castlewood’s tone, she told me the whole comedy. The Countess had taken out her pocket-book and named her engagements: Monday, a Duke and Duchess with several members of my lord’s house and their ladies; Tuesday, more earls, two bishops, and an ambassador. “Of course you won’t come on them days?” says her ladyship. “Now you are so poor, you know, that fine company ain’t no good for you. Lord bless you! father never dines on our company days! he don’t like it; he takes a bit of cold meat anyways.”

Theo said, laughing, she told the Countess that Mr. Warrington cared for none but the best company, and proposed she should ask us on some day when the Archbishop of Canterbury dined with her, and his Grace must give us a lift home in his coach to Lambeth. And then, Theo added, “She is economical too. ‘I thought of bringing with me some of my baby’s caps and things, which his lordship has outgrown ’em, but they may be wanted again, you know, my dear.’ So we lose that addition to our wardrobe, and Molly and I must do our best without her ladyship’s charity.”

“When people are poor, they are poor,” the Countess had said with her usual blunt honesty, “and must get on the best they can. What we shall do for that poor Maria, goodness only knows! we can’t ask her to see us as we can you, though you are so poor: but an earl’s daughter to marry a play-actor! La, my dear, it’s dreadful: his Majesty and the Princess have both spoken of it! Every other noble family in this kingdom as has ever heard of it pities us; though I have a plan for helping those poor unhappy people, and have sent down Simons, my groom of the chambers, to tell them on it.”

Her plan was that Hagan, who had kept almost all his terms at Dublin College, should return, take his degree, and enter holy orders; “when we will provide him with a chaplaincy at home, you know.” And I may mention—though it belongs to later pages—that this benevolent plan was executed some score of months after, and that I myself was enabled to be of service to Mr. Hagan, who was among the kindest and best of our friends in our own time of want. Castlewood performed his promise loyally enough—orders and a colonial appointment came in due time; Hagan distinguished himself as soldier and preacher. But not a guinea did my lord spare, in those days, for his sister or his kinsman in their trouble. I never asked him—thank Heaven—to assist me. To do him justice, no man could speak more amiably, or with a joy I believe genuine, when my days of poverty ended.

As for my Uncle Warrington, and his virtuous wife and daughters, let me do them justice too, and declare that throughout my trial their sorrow at my poverty was consistent and unvarying. I had still a few acquaintances who saw them and brought me report of their talk; and I never could hear they uttered one good word of me or my wife. They spoke of my tragedy as a crime, and of the author as a reprobate for ever reeling about Grub Street in rags. They held out no hand. My poor wife might cry in pain, but they had not twopence to bestow. They went to church half-a-dozen times in the week; subscribed to public charities; and were of that tribe known eighteen hundred years ago, which flourishes as long as men endure—thanking Heaven they are not as other folks are, and leaving the wounded to other succour.

I do not care to recall the doubts and anxieties that beset me; the plan after plan tried and failed; the way the very street-noises seemed to reproach us—the relentless rumble of carts bringing plenty to other doors, the cheerful cry of sellers in the morning, as if the city itself had provisions, and we had only appetite. I bethought me of my friend Mr. Johnson; and when I remember the eager kindness with which he received me, I am ashamed of pert speeches I once made regarding his manners.

I told him my story: the marriage; the prospects. He would not admit they were gloomy, nor that—si male nunc—they must continue so. Before me were chances (slender enough) of a place in England; the inheritance which must be mine in the course of nature, or at least would fall to the heir we expected; a small stock of money for actual necessity; a possibility—“though, to be free with you, sir,” says he—“after the performance of your tragedy, I doubt whether nature has endowed you with those peculiar qualities necessary for achieving a remarkable literary success”; and finally, submission to maternal rule and return to Virginia, where plenty and home were always ready.

“Why, sir!” he cried, “such a sum as you mention would have been a fortune to me when I began the world, and my friend Mr. Goldsmith would set up a coach-and-six on it. With youth, hope, to-day, and a couple of hundred pounds in cash—no young fellow need despair. Think, sir, you have a year at least before you, and who knows what may chance between now and then. Why, sir, your relatives here may provide for you, or you may succeed to your Virginian property, or you may come into a fortune!”

I did not come into one that year; he did. My Lord Bute gave Mr. Johnson a pension, which set all Grub Street raging against the recipient—he having himself published no very flattering opinion upon pensions and pensioners.

Nevertheless, he did not discourage my literary projects entirely, promised to procure me work from the booksellers, and faithfully performed that promise. “But,” says he, “sir, you must not appear amongst them in forma pauperis. Have you never a friend’s coach, in which we can ride to see them? You must put on your best laced hat and waistcoat; and we must appear, sir, as if we were doing them a favour.”

The stratagem answered for a visit or two; it procured me respect enough at first, for booksellers, like cooks, are apt to measure a man’s worth by the sheen on his outer coat, not by what is within. But when they found I wanted to be paid for my work, their backs refused to bend; they treated me with a familiarity I could ill stomach. I overheard one of them, who had been a footman, say, “Oh, it’s Pocahontas, is it? let him wait.” And he bade his boy deliver the message to me.

“Wait, sir?” I cried, thrusting my head into his parlour, fuming. “I’m not accustomed to waiting, but I have heard you are.” And I strode out into Pall Mall in a mighty fluster.

And yet Mr. D. was in the right. I came to him, if not to ask a favour, at least to propose a bargain; and surely it was my business to wait his convenience. In more fortunate days I asked his pardon, and the kind author of the Muse in Livery was instantly appeased.

Little Miles came into the world within a few days of that gracious Prince whose name is shouted by cannon and echoed by bells. For the royal infant there were illuminations that made the night a second noon; salutes that shook windows and ribbed the air with thunder; and a tide of people admitted, as if to a rare show, to gaze upon him lying behind his gilt railing, with noble nurses stationed like sentries at a shrine.

For our child there was no gilded gate, no courtly hush, no train of retainers. Yet there was a kind of ceremony in our narrow rooms in Church Street, Lambeth, if one has an ear for such things: the soft creak of the stair under Molly’s careful foot; Gumbo’s low humming as he made up a fire; the small domestic orchestra of spoon on earthenware, kettle-lid trembling, linen shaken out and laid smooth. The street had its own note too—the clop of carts, the call of hawkers, a baby’s cry answered by another from some neighbouring window—and, for all its poverty, it was a kinder sound than the grand noise of celebration made to flatter power. Here, in our “trou,” as my aunt named it, life went on in the honest key: the breath of coal-smoke, the damp of the river, and the warm, milky smell that filled Theo’s chamber like a promise.

Why was our boy not called George, like his father, like the young paragon at St. James’s? I had meant it so at first. But I had known, in those months, a scantness of affection from my own blood; and a little scapegrace of that same blood—one small kinsman with a brave heart—had given us what kindness could. Theo and I, agreeing without much debate, chose to set that kindness into the child’s name, as folk set a coin into a foundation-stone: not for show, but to be there, hidden and holding.

We wrote to our royal parents with due formality to announce the birth; and, with what courage we could muster, inserted it likewise in the Daily Advertiser, even naming our place—Church Street, Lambeth—as if it were a parish in a map and not a mark of our fallen fortunes. “My dear,” wrote Aunt Bernstein in reply, “how could you point out to all the world that you live in such a trou as that in which you have buried yourself? I kiss the little mamma, and send a remembrance for the child.” Her remembrance arrived very grandly: a fine silk coverlid with lace edging fit for a prince. It lay over our firstborn’s cradle like a bit of court embroidery dropped by mistake into a poor man’s house. Useful? Not much. The price of that lace, turned into honest loaves and broth-meat, would have served us better. Yet Theo’s eyes brightened, and Molly’s too; for women, who know what it is to keep a home together by the small economies of the day, have also a tender weakness for anything that makes their baby seem protected, honoured, splendid—even if only by borrowed finery.

Good Dr. Heberden came more than once to see my wife, and to make sure all went as it should. He recommended us a surgeon in the neighbourhood; but by God’s mercy Theo needed little beyond the care our landlady could supply, and Molly, and Gumbo’s patient attendance. Gumbo’s help had its own flavour and comfort. He could turn the scantest stores into something that smelled like plenty: water warmed with a twist of peel, if peel could be had; toast dried crisp at the edge of the grate; a bit of broth coaxed from bones and a few herbs, simmered till the room itself seemed to soften. The sound of it—quiet bubbling, a ladle tapping the pot—was as healing as the thing itself.

Our humble precinct was presently adorned by a blaze of wheels and gilding: Lady Castlewood’s chariot rolled to our little gate as if it had taken a wrong turning from a drawing-room. Her ladyship brought a pot of jelly, which she thought Theo might fancy; and, no doubt, it had already figured upon a banquet-table, quivering in a silver dish under chandeliers, before it was sent on to us as a charitable after-thought.

She stayed long enough to tell us of court ceremonies and the splendour attending the birth of the august heir. While she spoke, the air about her seemed to carry with it the scent of polished leather and perfume, and the faint metallic ring of her equipage outside—little sounds of wealth that make themselves heard even when one is trying to listen only to the needs of a newborn.

Mr. Johnson happened to visit me on one of those days when my lady countess’s carriage flamed up to our gate. He was struck by her magnificence, and made bows more respectful than graceful. She called me cousin with much affability, and—benign, condescending—helped to transfer her present from the silver dish into our crockery pan; for we could not afford to keep fine things merely because they were fine.

The Doctor tasted the sweetmeat and pronounced it excellent. “The great, sir,” said he, “are fortunate in every way. They can engage the most skilful practitioners of the culinary art, as they can assemble the most amiable wits round their table. If, as you think, sir, and, from the appearance of the dish, your suggestion at least is plausible, this sweetmeat may have appeared already at his lordship’s table; it has been there in good company. It has quivered under the eyes of celebrated beauties; it has been tasted by ruby lips; it has divided the attention of the distinguished company with fruits, tarts, and creams, which I make no doubt were like itself delicious.” And with that, the good Doctor absorbed a considerable portion of Lady Castlewood’s benefaction.

As for the epithet delicious, I must speak truth. Theo, after one small taste, put it away from her with a faint shiver; it clung to the tongue with that cloyed richness which, in sickness and weakness, is a burden rather than a pleasure. Molly, lifting her head with the sharp authority of a woman who has kept pantries and knows by smell what is safe, declared it mouldy. I do not know whether it was the jelly’s fault or the journey’s—or whether our poor room, with its coal air and damp, made all fine things seem a little stale. Yet the scene itself had its meaning: what the great throw away as garnish, the small must judge, accept, refuse, or make do with.

My boy had at least the privilege—so the world would say—of having an earl’s daughter for his godmother. That office was performed by his cousin, our poor Lady Maria, whose kindness to mother and infant went beyond praise. Having lost her own solitary chance for happiness of that sort, she yearned over our child with a tenderness that was painful to see, as if each soft touch were a remembrance and a renunciation together.

Captain Miles is now a mighty fine gentleman, his uniform in the Prince’s Hussars as splendid as any that ever bedizened a soldier of fashion. But he has too good a heart—let us trust—to forget, when he recalls his own infancy, that his limbs were once dressed in little garments prepared for a poor player’s child. The finery travels strange roads in this world: lace from a rich aunt; baby-linen from a humble home; a silver dish emptied into a crockery pan. So does kindness.

Sampson christened our boy in that very chapel in Southwark where our marriage had been performed. Never were the Prayer-book words read more beautifully, more impressively, than by the celebrant that day—until the end, when his voice failed him, and he and the little congregation were forced to wipe their eyes. Even the building seemed to listen: the hollow hush under the roof; the faint stir of clothes; the small cough that someone tried to swallow; then the child’s thin wail, cutting through the solemn cadence like a bird-call in a wood.

“Mr. Garrick himself, sir,” said Hagan, “could not have read those words so nobly. I am sure little innocent never entered the world accompanied by wishes and benedictions more tender and sincere.”

And now I have not told how it chanced the Captain came by his name of Miles. A couple of days before the christening—when I believe we had still meant to call our firstborn by his father’s name—there came a little patter of horse’s hoofs up to our gate, quick and eager as a child’s drumming on a table. Who should tug at the bell but young Miles, our cousin? I fear he had disobeyed his parents to make that undutiful journey; but he sat his little horse with the proud stiffness of a boy who has been given a kingdom the size of a saddle.

“You know,” says he, breathless with riding and excitement, “cousin Harry gave me my little horse; and I can’t help liking you, because you are so like Harry, and because they’re always saying things of you at home, and it’s a shame; and I have brought my whistle and coral that my godmamma Lady Suckling gave me, for your little boy; and if you’re so poor, cousin George, here’s my gold moidore, and it’s worth ever so much, and it’s no use to me, because I mayn’t spend it, you know.”

The child spoke in his own young fashion, with that plain, headlong honesty that needs no polish; and in it there was something that none of our grander relatives—so careful of names and precedence and the proper words—had given us: the unbought sound of loyalty. Even his boots contributed to the message. He was proud of them, and made them heard on our stair as he came up—a small soldier’s march in a poor house.

We took him to Theo in her room. She kissed him and thanked him; and the moidore—warm from his palm, bright as a dropped piece of sunshine—went into her purse, where it has remained from that day. The whistle and coral were laid by for the baby; the coin, with its foreign stamp and king’s head, seemed to carry more than value. It carried the boy’s defiance of the talk at home, his belief that what was said of us was “a shame,” and his desire, in the only language a child with rich relations can command, to make good the lack.

My mother, writing through her ambassador as usual, informed me of her surprise and displeasure on learning that my son had been christened Miles—a name not known, at least in the Esmond family. I did not care to tell the reason then. Names, in great houses, are treated as if they belonged to the family plate: to be kept bright, to be handed down in the approved pattern, to be counted and displayed. But there are other inheritances than the ones a herald can read. In after years, when I told Madam Esmond how my boy came by his name, I saw a tear roll down her wrinkled cheek. And afterwards I heard she had asked Gumbo many questions about the boy who had given his name to our Miles—our Miles Gloriosus of Pall Mall, Valenciennes, Almack’s, Brighton—who carried, under all his finery and public sound, that first quiet music of kindness: a child’s hoofbeats in Lambeth, a coin offered with shame-faced generosity, a name chosen not by pride but by gratitude.

When Harry and I were boys and thought it manly to be refractory, and showed our learning by dodging it, who could have foretold that I should live to become a bearleader in sober earnest, and to one of the most tractable cubs in London? My mother—when at last Fate and time brought us within one roof again—could never be persuaded to name that season plainly. She would touch it as you touch a bruise through linen: “that terrible time, my love, which I can’t bear to think of,” “those dreadful years when there was difference between us,” and then would turn the discourse, or call for the child, or bid Gumbo see whether the kettle sang. And though my pupil, a worthy and grateful man, sent me out to Jamestown, in due course, several barrels of the liquor by which his great fortune was brewed, Madam Esmond would speak of him as “your friend in England,” “your wealthy Lambeth friend,” and never once by his name; nor would she taste a drop of his beer. We brewed our own at Warrington Manor later, as becomes a house that would not have its daily bread beholden to another man’s oven; yet our good Mr. Foker never failed, in the years of our need, to ship to Ipswich every year a couple of butts of his entire—brown as walnut peel, with a head as firm as beaten whites, and a bitterness that clung to the palate like a remembered wrong. His son is now a young sprig of fashion, and has married an earl’s daughter; the father remains what he ever was—shrewd, kind, and plain in his beneficence—and it is to the luck of making his acquaintance that I owe some of the most welcome guineas that ever clinked in my hand.

It was not only the sum, though we counted every shilling as a cook counts eggs when the market is dear; it was the occupation and the hope the office gave me—governor to Master Foker—that were precious then. A man may endure a scant table if he is not made to sit idle before an empty trencher. Mr. F.’s brewery (the site has since changed) stood by Pedlar’s Acre in Lambeth, and the surgeon who attended my wife in her confinement tended the brewer’s household too. He was a Bavarian by birth, Voelker in his own tongue, but called Lance here, as if England must file every foreign name to her own measure. Many a time the Doctor would sit in my little garden with a pipe of Virginia—rich leaf, rank and comforting, smelling of earth and smoke and a far-off tidewater—while within doors Theo moved about the room with that quiet step of hers that never startled the baby. Through him, my name and story came to Mr. Foker.

The Doctor brought his patron to our house; and when Mr. Foker found I had a smattering of his language, and could sing “Prinz Eugen der edle Ritter”—a marching song my grandfather had brought home from the wars with Marlborough, the very consonants clacking like sabres—the German conceived a sudden liking for me, as if an old melody had found its way back to him through London soot. His lady put her chair and chariot at Mrs. Warrington’s service; his little daughter took a prodigious fancy to our baby (and though the Captain is as ugly a fellow now as ever wore a queue, he was beautiful as an infant; the very image of the Squire at thirty, everybody says); and his son and heir, Master Foker, being much maltreated at Westminster because of his father’s calling, the parents asked if I would take charge of him, and paid me no insufficient sum for superintending his education.

Mr. Foker was shrewd in business, and because he and his family truly interested themselves in me and mine, I laid my pecuniary affairs pretty unreservedly before him, as one lays open a pantry to a neighbour in a bad season, saying, See—this is what there is, and this is what is not. My statement, he said, increased his respect for me. He laughed at our stories of the aid my noble relatives had given—my aunt’s coverlid, my Lady Castlewood’s mouldy jelly, Lady Warrington’s contemptuous civility. But he wept outright over little Miles’s moidore; and as for Sampson and Hagan, “I wow,” says he, “dey shall have so much beer als ever dey can drink.” He sent his wife to call upon Lady Maria, and treated her with the utmost respect whenever she came to visit him. Lady Maria stayed with Mr. Foker when Hagan went to Dublin to complete his college terms; and the good brewer’s purse ministered to our friend’s wants and supplied his outfit.

When Mr. Foker came fully to know my affairs and position, he spoke of me with a kind of enthusiasm, as if my plain refusals of temptation were heroic. I have told how my mother saved money for Harry, and how the two were in my debt; but when Harry spent money he spent it fancying it to be his, and Madam Esmond never could be made to see that she dealt hardly with me—the money was paid and gone, and there was an end. Now, at the end of ’62, Harry sent over a considerable remittance to purchase his promotion, begging me at the same time to remember he was in my debt, and to draw on his agents if I had need. He did not know how great the need was, nor how my little capital had been swallowed as quietly as broth disappears from a hungry child’s spoon.

To take my brother’s money would delay his advancement; and I did not draw upon him, though I own I was tempted. Nor, knowing my dear General Lambert’s small means, did I choose to impoverish him by asking supplies. These simple acts of forbearance my worthy brewer must needs count as exalted virtue. He wrote privately to my brother in America, praising me and my wife as the most admirable of human beings; and he called upon Madame de Bernstein—who never told me of his visit indeed, but whom I perceived about this time to treat us with a singular respect and gentleness, surprising in one I could not but account selfish and worldly. In after days I asked him how he gained admission to the Baroness.

He laughed. “De Baroness!” says he. “I knew de Baron ven he vas a vallet at Munich, and I vas a brewer-apprentice.” I think our family had best not be too curious about our uncle the Baron.

Thus the part of my life which ought to have been most melancholy was made pleasant by many friends, happy accidents, and strokes of lucky fortune. The bear I led was a docile little cub, and danced to my piping readily. Better to lead him about—to hear the scrape of his pen, the thump of his schoolbooks on the table, the honest London chorus of carts and hawkers outside our window—than to hang round booksellers’ doors, or wait on the caprice of managers. My wife and I, during our exile as we may call it, spent many pleasant evenings with these kind friends. Nor were we without intellectual enjoyments: Mrs. Foker and Mrs. Warrington sang finely together, their voices twining like two scents rising from the same pot; and sometimes, when I was in the humour, I read my play of Pocahontas to this friendly audience in a manner better than Hagan’s own, Mr. Foker was pleased to say.

After that little escapade of Miles Warrington, junior, I saw nothing of him, and heard of my paternal relatives but rarely. Sir Miles was assiduous at court (as I believe he would have been at Nero’s), and I laughed one day when Mr. Foker told me he had heard on ’Change “dat dey vas going to make your uncle a Beer.”

“A beer?” says I.

“Can’t you understand de vort, ven I say it?” cries the testy old gentleman. “Vell, veil—a Lort!”

Sir Miles indeed was the obedient servant of the Minister, whoever he might be; I am surprised he did not speak English with a Scotch accent during the first favourite’s brief reign. I saw him and his wife coming from court when Mrs. Claypool was presented to her Majesty on her marriage. I had my little boy on my shoulder. My uncle and aunt stared resolutely at me from their gilt coach window. The footmen looked blank above their nosegays. Had I worn the Fairy’s cap and been invisible, my father’s brother could not have passed me with less notice.

We did not avail ourselves often of Lady Castlewood’s queer invitation—to come drink tea and sup with her ladyship when there was no other company. Old Van den Bosch, shrewd though he was in getting a fortune, was not amusing in talk, except to his daughter, who spoke of household and City matters—bulling and bearing, raising and selling stock, the price of hay, the cost of sauces and servants—with as much keenness as any broker. Nor was my Lord Castlewood often at home, nor much missed by his wife when absent, nor very much at ease in the old father’s company. The Countess told all this to my wife with her simple candour.

“Guess,” says she, “my lord and father don’t pull well together nohow. Guess my lord’s always wanting money, and father keeps the key of the box—and quite right, too. If he could have the fingering of all our money, my lord would soon make away with it, and then what’s to become of our noble family? We pay everything, my dear—except play-debts, and them we won’t have nohow. We pay cooks, horses, wine-merchants, tailors, and everybody—and lucky for them too—reckon my lord wouldn’t pay ’em! And we always take care he has a guinea in his pocket, and goes out like a real nobleman. What that man do owe to us—what he did before we come—gracious goodness only knows! Me and father does our best to make him respectable, but it’s no easy job, my dear. Law! he’d melt the plate, only father keeps the key of the strong-room; and when we go to Castlewood, my father travels with me, and papa is armed too, as well as the people.”

“Gracious heavens!” cries my wife. “Your ladyship does not mean to say you suspect your own husband of a desire to—”

“To what? Oh no, nothing, of course! And I would trust our brother Will with untold money, wouldn’t I? As much as I’d trust the cat with the cream-pan! I tell you, my dear, it’s not all pleasure being a woman of rank and fashion: and if I have bought a countess’s coronet, I have paid a good price for it—that I have!”

And so had my Lord Castlewood paid a large price to have his estate freed, his houses and stables furnished, his debts discharged. He was slave to his little wife and her father; no wonder the old man’s society was not pleasant to the poor victim, and that he gladly slunk away from his own fine house, to feast at the club when he had money, or at any board where knives rang cheerfully and no one kept the key of the cupboard against him.

To lead a bear, as I did, is no very pleasant business, to be sure. To wait in a bookseller’s anteroom until it should please his honour to finish his dinner and give me audience—hearing the clatter of plates behind the door, the loud laugh, the scraping of chairs, the soft tyranny of a man’s leisure—was sometimes hard for a man of my name and pride. But would I have exchanged my poverty for Castlewood’s ignominy? preferred his dependence to my own? At least I earned my wage, such as it was; and no man can say I ever flattered my patrons or was servile to them, or indeed was other than sulky, overbearing, and intolerable.

Now there was a certain person with whom Fate had thrown me into life-partnership, who bore her poverty with such smiling sweetness and easy grace, that niggard Fortune relented before her, like some savage ogre in a tale that softens at a child’s song. However poor she was, all who knew her saw that here was a fine lady. The little tradesmen and humble folk round about treated her with as much respect as the richest of our neighbours. She could go into a chandler’s shop and ask for a farthing’s worth of candles, and the man would hand them as if they were wax tapers for a chapel; she could order a bone for broth, and the butcher would choose it as carefully as if it were for a duke. She knew how to make a thin joint seem plentiful: how to coax savour from a scrap of bacon and an onion; how to keep the bread warm at the hearth while the water came to the simmer; how to hush the baby with the very sound of her spoon stirring in a pot. In those little domestic noises—kettle beginning its song, crust crackling as it toasted, the faint scrape of a knife on board—there was more comfort than in any trumpets of court.

“I think, my dear,” says good-natured Mrs. Foker when they rode out in the latter’s chariot, “you look like the mistress of the carriage, and I only as your maid.” Our landladies adored her; the tradesfolk executed her little orders as eagerly as if a duchess gave them. I have often thought of the lady in Comus, how through all the rout and rabble she moves serene and pure.

Several times—as often as we chose—the good-natured parents of my young bear lent us their chariot. If I must tell truth, we drove once to the Protestant Hero and had a syllabub in the garden—cream beaten to a froth with wine and lemon, a little nutmeg grated over, the scent rising as light as gossip; and the hostess would insist on calling my wife her ladyship the whole afternoon. We visited Mr. Johnson too and took tea with him (the ingenious Mr. Goldsmith was of the company); the Doctor waited upon my wife to her coach with as much ceremony as if she had been presented at court.

But our most frequent visits were to Aunt Bernstein; and I promise you I was not jealous because my aunt presently professed a wonderful liking for Theo.

This liking grew so that she would have her most days in the week, or would keep her altogether, and think Theo’s child and husband only plagues, and hate us in the most amusing way for keeping her favourite from her. Not that my wife was unworthy of any favour; but her forced absences and the constant difficulty of intercourse raised my aunt’s liking for a while into something like passion. She poured in notes like love-letters; her people were ever about our kitchen, with messages, parcels, hints, commands. If my wife did not go, she wrote heartrending appeals, and scolded me when I saw her; and once when the child was ill (it hath pleased Fate to spare our Captain to be a prodigious trouble to us, and a wholesome trial for our tempers), Madame Bernstein came three days running to Lambeth, vowed there was nothing the matter with the baby—nothing at all—and that we only pretended his illness in order to vex her.

The reigning Countess of Castlewood was as easy and affable with her old aunt as with other folk. “What air you all about, scraping and bowing to that old woman, I can’t tell, noways!” her ladyship would say. “She a fine lady! Nonsense! She ain’t no more fine than any other lady; and I guess I’m as good as any of ’em with their high heels and grand airs! She a beauty once! Take away her wig, and her rouge, and her teeth; and what becomes of your beauty, I’d like to know? Guess you’d put it all in a bandbox, and there would be nothing left but a shrivelled old woman!”

And indeed she spoke too truly. All beauty must come to that complexion at last; decay on the tree or under ground. Here was old age without reverence: grey hairs hid or painted; the world still loud about her—wheels on stones, boys crying oysters, fiddles in distant rooms—and she tottering on it, clinging with her crutch. For fourscore years she had moved on it, and eaten of the tree forbidden and permitted. She had had beauty, pleasure, flattery; but what secret rages, disappointments, defeats, humiliations—what thorns under roses, what stinging bees in fruit!

“You are not a beauty, my dear,” she would say to my wife, “and may thank your stars you are not.” (If she contradicted herself, I suppose the rest of us do likewise.) “Don’t tell me your husband is pleased with your face, and you want no one else’s admiration! We all do. Every woman would rather be beautiful than be anything else in the world—ever so rich, or ever so good, or have all the gifts of the fairies! Look at that picture—though I know ’tis a bad one, and that stupid vapouring Kneller could not paint my eyes, nor my hair, nor my complexion. What a shape I had then—and look at me now, and this wrinkled old neck! Why have we such a short time of our beauty? I remember Mademoiselle de l’Enclos at a much greater age than mine, quite fresh and well-conserved. We can’t hide our ages. They are wrote in Mr. Collins’s books for us. I was born in the last year of King James’s reign. I am not old yet. I am but seventy-six. But what a wreck, my dear: and isn’t it cruel that our time should be so short?”

Here my wife would state, softly, the incontrovertible proposition that the time of all of us is short here below.

“Ha!” cries the Baroness. “Did not Adam live near a thousand years, and was not Eve beautiful all the time? I used to perplex Mr. Tusher with that—poor creature! What have we done since, that our lives are so much lessened, I say?”

“Has your life been so happy that you would prolong it ever so much more?” asks the Baroness’s auditor. “Have you, who love wit, never read Dean Swift’s description of the deathless people in Gulliver? My papa and my husband say ’tis one of the finest and most awful sermons ever wrote. It were better not to live at all, than to live without love; and I’m sure,” says my wife, putting her handkerchief to her eyes, “should anything happen to my dearest George, I would wish to go to Heaven that moment.”

“Who loves me in Heaven? I am quite alone, child—that is why I had rather stay here,” says the Baroness, in a frightened, piteous tone. “You are kind to me, God bless your sweet face! Though I scold, and have a frightful temper, my servants will do anything to make me comfortable—get up at any hour of night, and never say a cross word. I like my cards still. Indeed, life would be a blank without ’em. Almost everything is gone except that. I can’t eat my dinner now, since I lost those last two teeth.” And she spoke it with a sort of outrage, as if the very act of eating—of biting crust, of cracking a nut, of holding a morsel in the mouth and making it yield—were a country stolen from her by time. “Everything goes away from us in old age. But I still have my cards—thank Heaven, I still have my cards!”

And here she would begin to doze, waking up if my wife stirred, imagining Theo was about to leave her. “Don’t go away. I can’t bear to be alone. I don’t want you to talk. But I like to see your face, my dear! It is much pleasanter than that horrid old Brett’s, that I have had scowling about my bedroom these ever so long years.”

“Well, Baroness! still at your cribbage?” (We may fancy a noble Countess interrupting a game between Theo and Aunt Bernstein.) “Me and my Lord Esmond have come to see you! Go and shake hands with grandaunt, Esmond! and tell her ladyship that your lordship’s a good boy!”

“My lordship’s a good boy,” says the child.

“And if he is, I guess he don’t take after his father,” shrieks out Lady Castlewood; she chose to fancy Aunt Bernstein deaf, and always bawled in her face.

“Your ladyship chose my nephew for better or for worse,” says Aunt Bernstein, now always flurried in the young Countess’s presence.

“But he is a precious deal worse than ever I thought he was. I am speaking of your Pa, Ezzy. If it wasn’t for your mother, my son, Lord knows what would become of you! We are a-going to see his little Royal Highness. Sorry to see your ladyship not looking quite so well to-day. We can’t always remain young, and law! how we do change as we grow old! Go up and kiss that lady, Ezzy. She has got a little boy too. Why, bless us! have you got the child downstairs?”

Indeed Master Miles was down below—for special reasons—sometimes accompanying his mother on her visits; and our aunt desired the mother’s company so much that she put up with the child.

“So you have got the child here? Oh, you slyboots!” says the Countess. “Guess you come after the old lady’s money! Law bless you! Don’t look so frightened. She can’t hear a single word I say. Come, Ezzy. Good-bye, aunt!” And my lady rustled out.

Did Aunt Bernstein hear her or not? Where was the wit for which the old lady had been long famous? Was that fire put out as well as the brilliancy of her eyes? With other people she was still ready enough, unsparing of sarcasm. When the Dowager of Castlewood and Lady Fanny visited her (those exalted ladies treated my wife with perfect indifference and charming good breeding), the Baroness in their society was stately, easy, even commanding. She would mischievously caress Mrs. Warrington before them; in her absence, vaunt my wife’s good breeding; say I had made a foolish match perhaps, but certainly taken a charming wife. “In a word, I praise you so to them, my dear,” says she, “that I think they would like to tear your eyes out.”

But before the little American, ’tis certain, she trembled. She was so afraid that she did not dare deny her door; and with the Countess’s back turned, did not even abuse her.

However much they might dislike her, my ladies did not tear out Theo’s eyes. Once they drove to our cottage at Lambeth, where my wife happened to be sitting at the open window holding her child on her knee, full in view. A gigantic footman strutted through our little garden and delivered their ladyships’ visiting tickets. Their hatred hurt us no more than their visit pleased us. When next we had the loan of the brewer’s carriage, Mrs. Warrington drove to Kensington, and Gumbo handed over to the giant our cards in return for those his noble mistresses had bestowed.

The Baroness had a coach, but seldom thought of giving it to us; and would let Theo, her maid, and baby start from Clarges Street in the rain, with a faint excuse that she was afraid to ask her coachman to take out the horses. Twice on her return my wife was frightened by rude fellows on the other side of Westminster Bridge; and I told my aunt plainly I should forbid Mrs. Warrington to go to her unless she could be brought home in safety; so grumbling Jehu had to drive through the darkness. He grumbled at my shillings; he did not know how few I had. Our poverty wore a decent face. My relatives never thought of relieving it, nor I of complaining before them.

I don’t know how Sampson got a windfall of guineas; but I remember he brought me six once, and they were more welcome than any money I ever had. He had been looking into Mr. Miles’s crib as the child lay asleep—breath making its small soft sound, like a moth’s wing against candlelight—and when the parson went away, I found the money in the baby’s little rosy hand. Yes: Love is best of all. I have many such benefactions registered in my heart—welcome fountains springing in desert places, kind lights in a smoky London dusk, small human mercies that made the city’s harsh clang and rattle bearable.

This worthy divine was willing enough to give as much of his company as Madame de Bernstein chose, whether for cards or theology. Having known her ladyship many years, Sampson could see—and averred to us—that she was breaking fast; and as he spoke of her increasing infirmities, and the probability of their fatal termination, Mr. S. would discourse in a feeling manner of the necessity of preparing for a future world; the vanities of this; and the hope that in another there might be happiness for all repentant sinners.

“I have been a sinner for one,” says the chaplain, bowing his head. “God knoweth, and I pray Him to pardon me. I fear, sir, your aunt, the Lady Baroness, is not in such a state of mind as will fit her very well for the change which is imminent. I am but a poor weak wretch, and no prisoner in Newgate could confess that more humbly and heartily. Once or twice of late, I have sought to speak on this matter with her ladyship, but she has received me very roughly. ‘Parson,’ says she, ‘if you come for cards, ’tis mighty well, but I will thank you to spare me your sermons.’ What can I do, sir? I have called more than once of late, and Mr. Case hath told me his lady was unable to see me.”

In fact Madame Bernstein told my wife—whom she never refused—that the poor chaplain’s tone was unendurable; and as for his theology, “Haven’t I been a Bishop’s wife?” says she. “And do I want this creature to teach me?”

Want and its sharp schooling were over for me. I had no more to measure out a week’s living as though it were flour on a board, nor to make a joint serve twice by artful carving and more artful silence. A child’s death—God forgive me the coldness of the phrase—altered the whole disposition of my worldly cards. My little kinsman, the heir, was gone; and I, who had been a younger branch with scant sap, found myself next in succession to a good estate. My uncle and his lady were not like to have more children. Sampson, in his rough fidelity, swore the woman would “commit any crime to disappoint you;” but in truth my Lady Warrington committed none. She was struck down by the blow, and those spiritual advisers to whom she now clung taught her to name her sorrow a chastisement and to bow beneath it as beneath a yoke ordained.

“Whilst your son lived,” her clergyman told her, “your heart was turned away from the better world. You desired rank and title for his advantage. You asked, and might have obtained, an earthly coronet. Of what use is it now, to one who has but a few years to pass upon earth—what in comparison with the heavenly crown?”

The accident stirred London as a kitchen stirs when fire catches grease: quick, loud, and full of savoury talk that is not always charitable. In the chapels of that eager sect to which, after her child’s death, my aunt inclined more and more, many sermons were baked up out of the same sad dough, each text bearing upon the event, each application seasoned to the taste of the hearer. I will not dispute any poor soul’s refuge. Grief drives men and women, as hunger drives them, to what will keep life in; and I have seen a starving creature comforted by a crust that another would despise.

Lady Warrington even tried, after a fashion, to be reconciled to me. A year after her loss, being in London, she signified that she would see me. I waited on her; and she gave me, in her accustomed didactic tone, a homily upon my position and hers. She marvelled at the decree of Heaven which had permitted—how dreadfully punished!—her poor child’s disobedience to her: a disobedience by which, in the world’s coarse arithmetic, I was to profit. (It appeared the little man had broken orders, and gone out with his gun unknown to his mother.) She hoped—she prayed—that should I ever succeed to the property (though the Warringtons were, thank Heaven, long-lived, except in my own father’s case, whose days had been curtailed by the excesses of a very ill-regulated youth), but should I ever succeed to the estate and honours, my present course might be altered; that I should part from my unworthy associates; that I should discontinue connexion with the horrid theatre and its licentious frequenters; that I should turn to that quarter where only peace was to be had, and to those sacred duties which she feared—she greatly feared—I had neglected. She filled her exhortation with Scripture language, which I do not care to counterfeit.

When I took my leave she gave me a packet of sermons for Mrs. Warrington, and a little book of hymns by Miss Dora—eminent in that society of which my aunt and her mother became avowed professors—who, after the dowager’s death at Bath three years since, married young Mr. Juffles, a celebrated preacher. The poor lady forgave me then, but she could not bear the sight of our boy.

We lost our second child; and then my aunt and her daughter came eagerly enough to the poor suffering mother, and even invited us to them. But my uncle was now almost every day in our house. He would sit for hours and hours looking at our boy as though he would feed his eyes upon him and be satisfied. He brought endless toys and sweetmeats—sugar-plums that crackled between small teeth, gingerbread men whose spice rose warm the moment you broke them, little boxes that smelt of varnish and new paint, and all manner of trifles that made a nursery ring like a fair. He begged that the child might call him Godpapa.

When my own grief rose—when, at times still, and after the lapse of five-and-twenty years, it strikes me as keenly as on the day we first lost our little one—I knew how to commiserate his. But my wife could pity him before she knew what it was to lose a child of her own. The mother’s anxious heart had divined, even then, the pang in the sorrow-stricken father; mine, more selfish, learned pity only from experience; and I was reconciled to my uncle by my little baby’s coffin.

The poor man sent his coach to follow the humble funeral. The very sound of the wheels, soft on the damp road, seemed an indecency beside the muffled footfall of the bearers; yet it was his way of honouring the dead and clinging to the living. Afterwards he took out little Miles, who prattled to him unceasingly, and forgot any grief he might have felt in the delight of his new black clothes and the pleasures of the airing. How the innocent talk of the child stabbed the mother’s heart! Would we ever wish that it should heal of that wound? I know her face so well that, to this day, I can tell when, sometimes, she is thinking of the loss of that little one. It is not a grief for a parting so long ago; it is a communion with a soul we love in Heaven.

We came back to our bright lodgings in Bloomsbury soon afterwards; and my young bear, whom I could no longer lead by the hand, and who had taken a prodigious friendship for Charley, went to the Chartreux School, where his friend took care that he had no more beating than was good for him, and where (in consequence of the excellence of his private tutor, no doubt) he took and kept a good place. He liked the school so much that he says, if ever he has a son, he shall be sent to that seminary.

I could no longer lead my bear for another reason too: there was other business for me. Being fully reconciled to us, I do believe for Mr. Miles’s sake, my uncle—such an obsequious supporter of Government that I wonder the Minister ever gave him anything, being perfectly sure of his vote—used his influence in behalf of his nephew and heir; and I had the honour to be gazetted as one of his Majesty’s Commissioners for licensing hackney-coaches, a post I filled, I trust, with credit, until a quarrel with the Minister (to be mentioned in its proper place) deprived me of that one. I took my degree also at the Temple, and appeared in Westminster Hall in my gown and wig; the silk gown rubbing with a dry whisper as one moved, the great hall full of its old noises—clerks calling, papers shuffling, voices rising and sinking like wind through bare branches. London’s soundscape is a kind of weather: it presses on the nerves, it colours the spirits; and I have known a man’s temper altered by nothing more than the difference between a street where carts thunder and one where you can hear your own footfall.

That year my good friend Mr. Foker, having business at Paris, I had the pleasure of accompanying him thither. I was received à bras ouverts by my dear American preserver, Monsieur de Florac, who introduced me to his noble family, and to even more of the polite society of the capital than I had leisure to frequent. For I had too much spirit to desert my kind patron Foker, whose acquaintance lay chiefly amongst the bourgeoisie, especially with Monsieur Santerre, a great brewer of Paris—a scoundrel who hath since distinguished himself in blood and not beer. Mr. Foker had need of my services as interpreter; and I was too glad he should command them, and to be able to pay back some of the kindness he had rendered to me.

Paris had its own music: the clatter of sabots in narrow streets, the cry of vendors, the chime of church bells, and—most delightful of all to a man whose memory is kept alive by his senses—the breath of food everywhere. It came out of doorways and window-cracks: warm loaves, sour wine, frying oil, garlic bruised under a knife, and the deep, brown perfume of a stew left to whisper on coals until the very onion forgets itself and becomes sauce. At market, poultry lay in heaps; fish shone like coin; herbs were tied in little damp bundles; and women, quick-tongued as sparrows, sold and bargained as if their very syllables were spices. Yet even there one heard the first stir of a louder future—more wheels, more hammering, more barracks-drill—noise that doesn’t belong to any place and yet claims every place for its own. It is a melancholy thing when a city’s old humane sounds—voices, steps, the tap of a knife on a board—are drowned by the blunt, mindless roar of power.

Our ladies, meanwhile, were residing at Mr. Foker’s new villa at Wimbledon, and were pleased to say that they were amused with the “Parisian letters” I sent to them through my distinguished friend Mr. Hume, then of the Embassy, and which subsequently have been published in a neat volume.

Whilst I was tranquilly discharging my small official duties in London, those troubles were commencing which were to end in the great separation between our colonies and the mother country. When Mr. Grenville proposed his stamp-duties, I said to my wife the bill would create a mighty discontent at home; for we were ever anxious to get as much as we could from England and pay back as little. But assuredly I never anticipated the prodigious anger which the scheme created. It was with us as with families or individuals: a pretext is given for a quarrel; the true cause lies in long bickerings and former injuries. Many foolish exactions and petty tyrannies, the habitual insolence of Englishmen towards all foreigners, all colonists, all folk who dare think their rivers as good as our Abana and Pharpar; the natural spirit of men outraged by our imperious domineering spirit—these set Britain and her colonies to quarrel. The astonishing blunders of the system adopted in England brought the quarrel to an issue which I, for one, am not going to deplore.

Had I been in Virginia instead of London, ’tis very possible I should have taken the provincial side, if out of mere opposition to that resolute mistress of Castlewood, who might have driven me into revolt as England did the colonies. Was the Stamp Act the cause of the revolution?—a tax no greater than that cheerfully paid in England. Ten years earlier, when the French were within our territory and we were imploring succour from home, would the colonies have rebelled at the payment of this tax? Do not most people consider the tax-gatherer the natural enemy? Against the British in America there were arrayed thousands and thousands of the high-spirited and brave; but there were thousands more who found their profit in the quarrel, or had private reasons for engaging in it. I protest I do not know now whether mine were selfish or patriotic, or which side was in the right, or whether both were not. I am sure we in England had nothing to do but fight the battle out; and, having lost the game, I do vow and believe that after the first natural soreness the loser felt no rancour.

What made brother Hal write home from Virginia—whence he seemed exceedingly loth to quit—such flaming patriotic letters? My kind, best brother was always led by somebody: by me when we were together (he had such an idea of my wit and wisdom that if I said the day was fine he would ponder over the observation as though it were one of the sayings of the Seven Sages), by some other wiseacre when I was away. Who inspired these letters, this boisterous patriotism, which he sent to us in London?

“He is rebelling against Madam Esmond,” said I.

“He is led by some colonial person—by that lady, perhaps,” hinted my wife.

Who “that lady” was, Hal never had told us; and indeed he besought me never to allude to the delicate subject in my letters to him: “for Madam wishes to see ’em all, and I wish to say nothing about you know what until the proper moment,” he wrote. No affection could be greater than that which his letters showed. When he heard (from the informant I have mentioned) that in the midst of my own extreme straits I had retained no more than a hundred pounds out of his aunt’s legacy, he was for mortgaging the estate he had just bought; and had more than one quarrel with his mother in my behalf, and spoke his mind with a frankness I should never have ventured to show. Until her angry recriminations (when she charged him with ingratitude, after having toiled and saved so much and so long for him), the poor fellow did not know that our mother had cut off my supplies to advance his interests; and by the time this news came to him his bargains were made, and I was fortunately quite out of want.

Every scrap of paper we ever wrote, our thrifty parent at Castlewood taped and docketed and put away, as a careful housewife ties up dried herbs and labels them for winter physic. We boys were more careless about our letters to one another— I especially, who perhaps chose rather to look down upon my younger brother’s literary performances; but my wife is not so supercilious, and hath kept no small number of Harry’s letters, as well as those of the angelic being whom we were presently to call sister.

“To think whom he has chosen, and whom he might have had! Oh, ’tis cruel!” cries my wife, when we got that notable letter in which Harry first made us acquainted with the name of his charmer.

“She was a very pretty little maid when I left home; she may be a perfect beauty now,” I remarked, reading over the longest letter Harry ever wrote on private affairs.

“But is she to compare to my Hetty?” says Mrs. Warrington.

“We agreed that Hetty and Harry were not to be happy together, my love,” say I.

Theo gives her husband a kiss. “My dear, I wish they had tried,” she says with a sigh. “I was afraid lest—lest Hetty should have led him, you see; and I think she hath the better head. But, from reading this, it appears that the new lady has taken command of poor Harry,” and she hands me the letter.

It ran thus, in my brother’s free, hearty hand—his phrases full of Virginia and of himself, as if you could hear, under the ink, the creak of porch-boards and the hush of pinewoods beyond:

“My dearest George hath been prepared by previous letters to understand how a certain lady has made a conquest of my heart, which I have given away in exchange for something infinitely more valuable, namely, her own. She is at my side as I write this letter, and if there is no bad spelling, such as you often used to laugh at, ’tis because I have my pretty dictionary at hand, which makes no faults in the longest word, nor in anything else I know of: being of opinion that she is perfection.

“As Madam Esmond saw all your letters, I writ you not to give any hint of a certain delicate matter—but now ’tis no secret, and is known to all the country. Mr. George is not the only one of our family who has made a secret marriage, and been scolded by his mother. As a dutiful younger brother I have followed his example; and now I may tell you how this mighty event came about.

“I had not been at home long before I saw my fate was accomplisht. I will not tell you how beautiful Miss Fanny Mountain had grown since I had been away in Europe. She saith, ‘You never will think so,’ and I am glad, as she is the only thing in life I would grudge to my dearest brother.

“That neither Madam Esmond nor my other mother (as Mountain is now) should have seen our mutual attachment, is a wonder—only to be accounted for by supposing that love makes other folks blind. Mine for my Fanny was increased by seeing what the treatment was she had from Madam Esmond, who indeed was very rough and haughty with her, which my love bore with a sweetness perfectly angelic (this I will say, though she will order me not to write any such nonsense). She was scarce better treated than a servant of the house—indeed our negroes can talk much more free before Madam Esmond than ever my Fanny could.

“And yet my Fanny says she doth not regret Madam’s unkindness, as without it I possibly never should have been what I am to her. Oh, dear brother! when I remember how great your goodness hath been—how, in my own want, you paid my debts, and rescued me out of prison; how you have been living in poverty which never need have occurred but for my fault; how you might have paid yourself back my just debt to you and would not, preferring my advantage to your own comfort—indeed I am lost at the thought of such goodness; and ought I not to be thankful to Heaven that hath given me such a wife and such a brother?

“When I writ to you requesting you to send me my aunt’s legacy money, for which indeed I had the most profitable and urgent occasion, I had no idea that you were yourself suffering poverty. That you, the head of our family, should condescend to be governor to a brewer’s son!—that you should have to write for booksellers (except in so far as your own genius might prompt you), never once entered my mind, until Mr. Foker’s letter came to us, and this would never have been shown—for Madam kept it secret—had it not been for the difference which sprang up between us.

“Poor Tom Diggle’s estate and negroes being for sale, owing to Tom’s losses and extravagance at play, and his father’s debts before him—Madam Esmond saw here was a great opportunity of making a provision for me, and that with six thousand pounds for the farm and stock, I should be put in possession of as pretty a property as falls to most younger sons in this country. It lies handy enough to Richmond, between Kent and Hanover Court House—the mansion nothing for elegance compared to ours at Castlewood, but the land excellent and the people extraordinary healthy.

“Here was a second opportunity, Madam Esmond said, such as never might again befall. By the sale of my commissions and her own savings I might pay more than half of the price of the property, and get the rest of the money on mortgage; though here, where money is scarce to procure, it would have been difficult and dear. At this juncture, with our new relative, Mr. Van den Bosch, bidding against us (his agent is wild that we should have bought the property over him), my aunt’s legacy most opportunely fell in. And now I am owner of a good house and negroes in my native country, shall be called, no doubt, to our House of Burgesses, and hope to see my dearest brother and family under my own roof-tree. To sit at my own fireside, to ride my own horses to my own hounds, is better than going a-soldiering, now war is over, and there are no French to fight. Indeed, Madam Esmond made a condition that I should leave the army, and live at home, when she brought me her 1750 pounds of savings. She had lost one son, she said, who chose to write play-books, and live in England—let the other stay with her at home.

“But, after the purchase of the estate was made, and my papers for selling out were sent home, my mother would have had me marry a person of her choosing, but by no means of mine. You remember Miss Betsy Pitts at Williamsburgh? She is in no wise improved by having had her face dreadfully scarred with small-pock, and though Madam Esmond saith the young lady hath every virtue, I own her virtues did not suit me. Her eyes do not look straight; she hath one leg shorter than another; and oh, brother! didst thou never remark Fanny’s ankles when we were boys? Neater I never saw at the Opera.

“Now, when ’twas agreed that I should leave the army, a certain dear girl (canst thou guess her name?) one day, when we were private, burst into tears of such happiness, that I could not but feel immensely touched by her sympathy.

“‘Ah!’ says she, ‘do you think, sir, that the idea of the son of my revered benefactress going to battle doth not inspire me with terror? Ah, Mr. Henry! do you imagine I have no heart? When Mr. George was with Braddock, do you fancy we did not pray for him? And when you were with Mr. Wolfe—oh!’

“Here the dear creature hid her eyes in her handkerchief, and had hard work to prevent her mama, who came in, from seeing that she was crying. But my dear Mountain declares that, though she might have fancied, might have prayed in secret for such a thing (she owns to that now), she never imagined it for one moment. Nor, indeed, did my good mother, who supposed that Sam Lintot, the apothecary’s lad at Richmond, was Fanny’s flame—an absurd fellow that I near kicked into James River.

“But when the commission was sold, and the estate bought, what does Fanny do but fall into a deep melancholy? I found her crying one day, in her mother’s room, where the two ladies had been at work trimming hats for my negroes.

“‘What! crying, miss?’ says I. ‘Has my mother been scolding you?’

“‘No,’ says the dear creature. ‘Madam Esmond has been kind to-day.’

“And her tears drop down on a cockade which she is sewing on to a hat for Sady, who is to be head-groom.

“‘Then, why, miss, are those dear eyes so red?’ say I.

“‘Because I have the toothache,’ she says, ‘or because—because I am a fool.’ Here she fairly bursts out. ‘Oh, Mr. Harry! oh, Mr. Warrington! You are going to leave us, and ’tis as well. You will take your place in your country, as becomes you. You will leave us poor women in our solitude and dependence. You will come to visit us from time to time. And when you are happy and honoured, and among your gay companions, you will remember your—’

“Here she could say no more, and hid her face with one hand as I, I confess, seized the other.

“‘Dearest, sweetest Miss Mountain!’ says I. ‘Oh, could I think that the parting from me has brought tears to those lovely eyes! Indeed, I fear, I should be almost happy! Let them look upon your—’

“‘Oh, sir!’ cries my charmer. ‘Oh, Mr. Warrington! consider who I am, sir, and who you are! Remember the difference between us! Release my hand, sir! What would Madam Esmond say if—if—’

“If what, I don’t know, for here our mother was in the room.

“‘What would Madam Esmond say?’ she cries out. ‘She would say that you are an ungrateful, artful, false, little—’

“‘Madam!’ says I.

“‘Yes, an ungrateful, artful, false, little wretch!’ cries out my mother. ‘For shame, miss! What would Mr. Lintot say if he saw you making eyes at the Captain? And for you, Harry, I will have you bring none of your garrison manners hither. This is a Christian family, sir, and you will please to know that my house is not intended for captains and their misses!’

“‘Misses, mother!’ says I. ‘Gracious powers, do you ever venture for to call Miss Mountain by such a name? Miss Mountain, the purest of her sex!’

“‘The purest of her sex! Can I trust my own ears?’ asks Madam, turning very pale.

“‘I mean that if a man would question her honour, I would fling him out of window,’ says I.

“‘You mean that you—your mother’s son—are actually paying honourable attention to this young person?’

“‘He would never dare to offer any other,’ cries my Fanny; ‘nor any woman but you, madam, to think so!’

“‘Oh, I didn’t know, miss!’ says mother, dropping her a fine curtsey, ‘I didn’t know the honour you were doing our family! You propose to marry with us, do you? Do I understand Captain Warrington aright, that he intends to offer me Miss Mountain as a daughter-in-law?’

“‘’Tis to be seen, madam, that I have no protector, or you would not insult me so!’ cries my poor victim.

“‘I should think the apothecary protection sufficient!’ says our mother.

“‘I don’t, mother!’ I bawl out, for I was very angry; ‘and if Lintot offers her any liberty, I’ll brain him with his own pestle!’

“‘Oh! if Lintot has withdrawn, sir, I suppose I must be silent. But I did not know of the circumstance. He came hither, as I supposed, to pay court to Miss: and we all thought the match equal, and I encouraged it.’

“‘He came because I had the toothache!’ cries my darling (and indeed she had a dreadful bad tooth. And he took it out for her, and there is no end to the suspicions and calumnies of women).

“‘What more natural than that he should marry my housekeeper’s daughter—’twas a very suitable match!’ continues Madam, taking snuff. ‘But I confess,’ she adds, going on, ‘I was not aware that you intended to jilt the apothecary for my son!’

“‘Peace, for Heaven’s sake, peace, Mr. Warrington!’ cries my angel.

“‘Pray, sir, before you fully make up your mind, had you not better look round the rest of my family?’ says Madam. ‘Dinah is a fine tall girl, and not very black; Cleopatra is promised to Ajax the blacksmith, to be sure; but then we could break the marriage, you know. If with an apothecary, why not with a blacksmith? Martha’s husband has run away, and—’

“Here, dear brother, I own I broke out a-swearing. I can’t help it; but at times, when a man is angry, it do relieve him immensely. I’m blest, but I should have gone wild, if it hadn’t been for them oaths.

“‘Curses, blasphemy, ingratitude, disobedience,’ says mother, leaning now on her tortoiseshell stick, and then waving it—something like a queen in a play. ‘These are my rewards!’ says she. ‘O Heaven, what have I done, that I should merit this awful punishment? and does it please you to visit the sins of my fathers upon me? Where do my children inherit their pride? When I was young, had I any? When my papa bade me marry, did I refuse? Did I ever think of disobeying? No, sir. My fault hath been, and I own it, that my love was centred upon you, perhaps to the neglect of your elder brother.’ (Indeed, there was some truth in what Madam said.) ‘I turned from Esau, and I clung to Jacob. And now I have my reward, I have my reward! I fixed my vain thoughts on this world, and its distinctions. To see my son advanced in worldly rank was my ambition. I toiled, and spared, that I might bring him worldly wealth. I took unjustly from my eldest son’s portion, that my younger might profit. And oh! that I should see him seducing the daughter of my own housekeeper under my own roof, and replying to my just anger with oaths and blasphemies!’”

When news reached my mother in Virginia that I had taken employment at home, she received it, I think, as a commander receives a flag of truce—coldly, as if conceding were a kind of defeat. She withdrew her supplies without a word, and I could not but read the intention in the silence: to pinch us, to make our little household feel the edge of want until I should surrender, pack up wife and child, and return across the sea into dependence under her roof and her rule.

We never, to her dying day, spoke plainly of that quarrel in money. She stopped my allowance; I made no appeal; and by shifts, by work, by the patient economies of my wife’s hands, we lived without her aid. Of any repentance on her part I heard nothing directly. Only Harry, in one of those private confidences which he had a brother’s kindness to make, let fall that she had suffered inwardly, and had owned—if not to me, at least to her own conscience—that she had been hard.

In later years, when chance and time brought us face to face again, Madam Esmond’s manner had a new gentleness in it, a studied respect, and—more marked than all—an uncommon, almost ceremonious affection towards my wife. It was as if she wished me to understand, without the humiliation of words, that she knew she had been wrong. She offered no apology. I asked none. Pride stood sentinel between us both; and I am not certain which of us kept the straighter back.

Harry being provided for—his welfare I never grudged—my mother’s savings, her hoardings and schemes, were in the end to my advantage as her heir. There was a time when a handful of guineas would have been more useful to me than the hundreds which might come when I had no need. Yet when the tide turned at last and we had ease, I could afford to remit what I might once have demanded. Remit is the word. Forgive is another thing, and rarer. Some souls, I have seen, forgive as naturally as a herb scents the hand that bruises it. In me there is too much of the old iron. I can pass over; I cannot always soften.

So I made no sign of submission in Virginia yonder; and for years we lived estranged, with only an occasional message passing between the women—some brief announcement of a child’s birth, or a formal courtesy sent at Christmas with a ribboned parcel.

Then came troubles of another sort. The first storms in America about the Stamp Act were not the only ones. In London, too, the air grew sharp. Though in our quarrel with the colonies I have been on the Tory side—as, indeed, I have commonly found myself on the losing side in most controversies—believing the Imperial Government had full right to levy taxes, yet I must needs publish a pert letter to a member of the House of Burgesses in Virginia, in which I handled freely the habitual insolence of the mother-country, and spoke sentiments disagreeable to persons in power. The consequence was prompt: I was deprived of my little place as hackney-coach licenser.

The blow fell with double weight upon my uncle, Sir Miles Warrington. No man ever loved respectability more devoutly, or feared disgrace as if it were a contagion. He had grown to an extreme affection for my wife—who could resist her?—and for my little boy. For myself he entertained a pitying contempt which always infinitely amused me. He had a natural scorn for poverty and a corresponding worship for success. Any opinion that swerved from the beaten track frightened him; truth-telling made him turn pale. Yet, in spite of the shocks I gave him, he continued to come and see Theo and the child, and even me—granting me a mournful recognition, as one gives to a doomed man. He no longer cut me, as he had done at the time of our first differences; he looked on me as a melancholy lost creature, past all worldly help. Never mind. We must cast about for a new scheme of life; and at this juncture the repayment of a debt by Harry enabled me to breathe for some months, even for years. Strange fatuity of youth! How did we dare to be so poor, and yet so little cast down?

In that season his Majesty’s royal uncle of Cumberland fell down and perished in a fit; and, oddly enough, his death occasioned a remarkable change in my fortune.

My poor Sir Miles never missed a court ceremony to which he could thrust himself. Drawing-rooms, christenings, balls, funerals—he was present at all. If ever a prince or princess was ailing, his coach was at their door. Leicester Fields, Carlton House, Gunnersbury—nothing was too far if there was a title to bow to and a hand to kiss. Nothing, therefore, could satisfy him now but to attend the stout Duke’s funeral. He stood bareheaded in the rain through the whole ceremony, caught a great cold and an inflammation of the throat; and one morning—before I had almost heard of his illness—a lawyer waits on me in Bloomsbury, bows, and salutes me by the name of Sir George Warrington.

So party and fear of the future were over. We laid the poor gentleman by the side of his little son, in the family churchyard where so many of his race repose. Little Miles and I were the chief mourners. The tenants bowed and curtseyed with a zeal that had more of prudence than grief. The dowager and her daughter withdrew to Bath presently; and I and my family took possession of the house of which I have now been master these thirty years. Be not too eager, O my son. Have but a little patience, and I too shall sleep under yonder yew-trees, and the people will be tossing up their caps for Sir Miles.

A prosperous country life is easily chronicled, because it repeats itself with the seasons. The steward’s books tell, year by year, what rents were paid and what forgiven; what wheat stood best after beans; what fields were left fallow; how the hedges were laid and the ditches scoured. The house journals note who visited, and how long; what pensioners my wife had, and how she doctored and relieved them, and how they died; what year I was sheriff; how often the hounds met near us.

But those ledgers, though exact as a cook’s scale, can never set down what truly made the place a home: the way Theo governed the kitchen like a small kingdom—quietly, inexorably, and with a tenderness that showed itself in broth and bread long before it found words. In our first years, when we were still learning the estate’s temper as a man learns a horse’s mouth, she would be in the still-room at dawn, listening for the sounds of the house as if the whole building had a pulse: the low crackle of peat; the rooster’s insistence; the soft knock of the dairy-maid; the far, watery music of the pump. There are noises that soothe and noises that harry. In London I had lived with wheels forever grinding the street, with hawkers crying as if they meant to split your skull, with the metallic clang of the city hammering at the nerves. Here the loudest violence was a cart-wheel over a stone, or the gust that set the bare branches creaking. Even the dogs’ bark had a country meaning: not rage for rage’s sake, but warning, welcome, or the simple joy of breath.

We could not afford the fine mansion in Hill Street which my predecessor had occupied; we took a smaller house in town when we must go, and yet contrived to spend more money in it. We made not half the show—fewer liveries, fewer equipages, less plate—than my uncle had been famous for; but our beer was stronger, and my wife’s charities more costly than those of the Dowager Lady Warrington. No doubt her ladyship thought there was no harm in spoiling the Philistines; for she made us pay unconscionably for the goods she left behind her in our country-house; and I submitted to most of her extortions with unutterable good-humour. What a value she imagined her potted plants in the greenhouses bore! What a price she set upon that horrible old spinet in her drawing-room!
