And the framed pieces of worsted-work performed by the accomplished Dora and the lovely Flora—had they been masterpieces of Titian or Vandyck, she could hardly have rated them higher.

Yet though we paid so generously, though we were—without boasting—far kinder to our poor than ever she had been, for a while we had the very worst reputation in the county. Old stories had been told to my discredit, and they spread like sour yeast in a warm pantry. I thought I might perhaps succeed to my uncle’s seat in Parliament as well as to his land; but I found, I knew not how, that I was voted a person of dangerous opinions. I would not bribe. I would not coerce my own tenants at the election of ’68. A gentleman came down from Whitehall with a pocket-book full of bank-notes; and I discovered that I had no chance against my competitor.

And now that we were at ease in worldly means—now that obedient tenants bowed as we went to church; that we drove to visit friends, or to the neighbouring towns, in the great family coach with the four fat horses—did we not often regret poverty and the dear little cottage at Lambeth, where Want was ever prowling at the door? I found myself, more than once, longing to be bear-leading again, and vowing that translating for booksellers was not such very hard drudgery. When we went to London we made sentimental pilgrimages to our old haunts. I dare say my wife embraced all her landladies. And we asked our friends of those times to share the comforts of our new home.

The Reverend Mr. Hagan and his lady visited us more than once. His appearance in the pulpit at B———, where he preached (as we thought) very finely, caused an awful scandal there. Sampson came too, another unlucky Levite, and was welcome as long as he would stay. Mr. Johnson talked of coming, but put us off once or twice. I suppose our house was dull. I know that I myself would be silent for days; and I fear my moodiness must often have tried the sweetest-tempered woman in the world.

I did not care for field sports. The killing of one partridge was so like the killing of another, I wondered how men could pass day after day in pursuit of that kind of slaughter. Fox-hunting stories began at four o’clock when the cloth was removed, and lasted till supper. I sat silent and listened; day after day I fell asleep. No wonder I was not popular with my company.

What confession is this? Here was the storm over, the rocks avoided, the ship in port—and the sailor not overcontent. Was Susan—whom I had been sighing for during the voyage—not the beauty I had expected to find her?

In the first place, Susan and all the family can look into her William’s logbook; and so, madam, I am not going to put my secrets down there. No, Susan, I never had secrets from thee—so far as concerns fidelity. I never cared for another woman. I have seen more beautiful—Mrs. Carter and Miss Mulso, Mrs. Thrale and Madam Kaufmann, the angelical Gunnings and her Grace of Devonshire, and a host of beauties who were not angelic by any means—and I was not dazzled. I may have led your mother a weary life and been a very Bluebeard over her, but then I had no other heads in the closet.

Only, the first pleasure of taking possession of our kingdom over, I own I began quickly to tire of the crown. When the captain wears it, his Majesty will be a very different Prince. He can ride a-hunting five days in the week and find the sport amusing. He would hear the same sermon fifty times and not yawn more than I do at the first delivery. But sweet Joan, beloved Baucis! being thy faithful husband and true lover always, thy Darby is ashamed of having been testy so often; and, being arrived at the consummation of happiness, Philemon asks pardon for falling asleep so frequently after dinner.

There came a period when, having reached the summit of felicity, I was quite tired of the prospect: I yawned in Eden and said, “Is this all? What, no lions to bite? no rain to fall? no thorns to prick you in the rose-bush when you sit down?—only Eve for ever sweet and tender, and figs for breakfast, dinner, supper, from week’s end to week’s end!”

Shall I make my confessions? Hearken! Well then—if I must make a clean breast of it—

* * * * * *

Here three pages are torn out of Sir George Warrington’s manuscript book, for which the editor is sincerely sorry.

I know the theory and practice of the Roman Church; but, bred of another persuasion, and sceptical and heterodox regarding that, I can’t help doubting the other too, and wondering whether Catholics in their confessions confess all. Do we Protestants ever do so? Does any man confess all?

Does yonder dear creature know all my life—she who has been partner of it for thirty years; who, whenever I have told her a sorrow, has been ready with the best of her gentle power to soothe it; who has watched when I did not speak, and when I was silent has been silent too, or else (with the charming hypocrisy of woman) has worn smiles and an easy face to make me fancy she felt no care, or would not disturb her lord’s secret when he seemed to wish it private?

Oh, the dear hypocrite! Have I not watched her hiding the boys’ peccadilloes from papa’s anger? Have I not known her cheat out of her housekeeping to pay off their little extravagances, and talk to me with an artless face as if she did not know that our revered captain had had dealings with the gentlemen of Duke’s Place, and our learned collegian at term’s end had pressing reasons for sporting his oak against University tradesmen? Why, from the earliest days thou wert forever concealing something from me—this one stealing jam from the cupboard; that one getting into disgrace at school; that naughty rebel (put on the caps, young folks, according to the fit) flinging an inkstand at mamma in a rage, whilst I was told gown and carpet were spoiled by accident.

We all hide from one another. We have all secrets. We are all alone. We sin by ourselves and, let us trust, repent too. Yonder dear woman would give her foot to spare mine a twinge of the gout; but when I have the fit, the pain is in my slipper. The poets end their tales at marriage or death, huzzahing for the couple till the postchaise turns the corner, or fetching the hearse and plumes and shovelling them underground. But when Mr. Random and Mr. Thomas Jones are married, is all over? Are there no quarrels at home—no Lady Bellastons abroad—no constables to outrun—no temptations to conquer, or be conquered by?

The Sirens sang after Ulysses long after his marriage, and suitors whispered in Penelope’s ear; and he and she had weary days of doubt and care. So have we all. As regards money I was put out of trouble by the inheritance; but does not Atra Cura sit behind baronets as well as equites?

My friends in London used to congratulate me on my happiness. Who would not like to be master of a good house and a good estate? But can Gumbo shut the hall-door upon blue devils, or lay them always in a red sea of claret? Does a man sleep the better who has four-and-twenty hours to doze in? Do his intellects brighten after a sermon from the dull old vicar; after ten minutes’ cackle and flattery from the village apothecary; after Sir John and Sir Thomas and their ladies, who come ten moonlight muddy miles to eat a haunch and play a rubber?

There are pleasures in precedence—room made for you at quarter-sessions; tradesmen bowing at your carriage door; my lady wife taken down the second or third to dinner. But these pleasures fade—nay, have their inconveniences. For seven years after we came to Warrington Manor, our two what they called best neighbours were my Lord Tutbury and Sir John Mudbrook. We are of an older date than the Mudbrooks; consequently my Lady Tutbury always fell to my lot at table—deaf and asleep after dinner; or if I had Lady Mudbrook, she chattered with a folly so incessant and intense that even my wife—consummate hypocrite—could scarce keep her complacency, knowing the rage with which I fumed at the other’s clatter.

I came to London; I showed my tongue to Dr. Heberden; I poured out my catalogue of complaints. “Psha, my dear Sir George!” says the unfeeling physician. “Headaches, languor, bad sleep, bad temper—” (“Not bad temper: Sir George has the sweetest temper in the world, only he is sometimes a little melancholy,” says my wife.) “—Bad sleep, bad temper,” continues the implacable doctor. “My dear lady, his inheritance has been his ruin; and a little poverty and a great deal of occupation would do him all the good in life.”

No—my brother Harry ought to have been the squire, with remainder to my son Miles, of course. Harry’s letters were full of gaiety and good spirits. His estate prospered; his negroes multiplied; his crops were large; he was a member of the House of Burgesses; he adored his wife; could he but have a child his happiness would be complete. Had Hal been master of Warrington Manor in my place, he would have been beloved through the whole country: steward at the races, gayest of jolly huntsmen, the bien venu at every mansion round about—where folk scarce cared to perform the ceremony of welcome at sight of my glum face. As for my wife, all the world liked her, and agreed in pitying her. I know not how the report got abroad, but it was generally agreed that I treated her with awful cruelty, and that for jealousy I was a perfect Bluebeard.

Ah me! It is true I have had many dark hours; that I pass days in long silence; that the talk of fools and whipper-snappers makes me rebellious and peevish; that when I feel contempt I sometimes do not know how to conceal it—or did not. I hope, as I grow older, I grow more charitable. Because I do not love bawling and galloping after a fox like the captain yonder, I am not his superior; in this respect I humbly own he is mine. He has perceptions denied me; enjoyments I cannot understand. Because I am blind, the world is not dark. I try now and listen with respect when Squire Codgers talks of the day’s run. I do my best to laugh when Captain Rattleton tells garrison stories. I step up to the harpsichord with old Miss Humby (our neighbour from Beccles) and try to listen as she warbles her ancient ditties. I play whist laboriously. Am I not trying to do the duties of life? And I have a right to be garrulous and egotistical, because I have been reading Montaigne all the morning.

I was not surprised, knowing by what influences my brother was led, to find his name among the Virginia burgesses who declared that the sole right of imposing taxes on the inhabitants of the colony is, and ever hath been, vested in the House of Burgesses, and who called upon the other colonies to pray for royal interposition in favour of the violated rights of America.

And it was now—after we had been some three years settled in our English home—that a correspondence between us and Madam Esmond began again. It was my wife who, upon some pretext such as women always know how to find, re-established relations. Mr. Miles must needs have the small-pox; he miraculously recovered, without losing any portion of his beauty; and upon his recovery the mother wrote her prettiest wheedling letter to the grandmother of the fortunate babe.

She coaxed with modest phrases and humble offerings of respect and goodwill. She narrated anecdotes of the boy’s precocious genius (what hath since happened, I wonder, to stop the growth of that gallant young officer’s brains?), and she must have sent a lock of the darling’s hair; for the old lady, in her reply, acknowledged receipt of such a present. I wonder, as it came from England, they allowed it to pass the custom-house at Williamsburg.

In return for these peace-offerings and smuggled tokens of submission came a tolerably gracious letter from my Lady of Castlewood. She inveighed against the dangerous spirit pervading the colony; she lamented to think her unhappy son was consorting with people who, she feared, would be no better than rebels and traitors. She did not wonder, considering who his friends and advisers were. How could a wife taken from an almost menial situation be expected to sympathise with persons of rank and dignity who had the honour of the Crown at heart?

If evil times were coming for the monarchy—for the folks in America appeared disinclined to pay taxes, and required everything should be done for them without cost—she remembered how, to monarchs in misfortune, the Esmonds (her father the Marquis especially) had ever been faithful. She knew not what opinions—though she might judge from my newfangled Lord Chatham—were in fashion in England. She prayed, at least, she might hear that one of her sons was not on the side of rebellion.

When we came, in after days, to look over old family papers in Virginia, we found “Letters from my daughter Lady Warrington” neatly tied up with a ribbon. My Lady Theo insisted I should not open them; and the truth, I believe, is that they were so full of praises of her husband that she thought my vanity would suffer from reading them.

When Madam began to write she gave us brief notices of Harry and his wife. “The two women,” she wrote, “still govern everything with my poor boy at Fannystown (as he chooses to call his house). They must save money there, for I hear but a shabby account of their manner of entertaining. The Mount Vernon gentleman continues to be his great friend, and he votes in the House of Burgesses very much as his guide advises him.

“Why he should be so sparing of his money I cannot understand: I heard of five negroes who went with his equipages to my Lord Bottetourt’s; only two had shoes to their feet. I had reasons to save, having sons for whom I wished to provide, but he hath no children, wherein he certainly is spared from much grief; though, no doubt, Heaven in its wisdom means our good by the trials which, through our children, it causes us to endure. His mother-in-law has been ailing.

“Ever since his marriage, my poor Henry has been the creature of these two artful women, and they rule him entirely. Nothing, my dear daughter, is more contrary to common sense and to Holy Scripture than this. Are we not told, Wives, be obedient to your husbands? Had Mr. Warrington lived, I should have endeavoured to follow up that sacred precept, holding that nothing so becomes a woman as humility and obedience.”

Our mother’s summons, so tenderly urged, might have thawed flint; and more than once we set ourselves to speak of Virginia as of a promised season,—how we would take the whole of Young Rachel’s cabin, and carry the children across as though it were but a jaunt down to Bath. Yet the household has its tyrannies more absolute than kings. The baby took a feverish turn, and the doctor, after sniffing at the air and feeling the little pulse with a face too wise for comfort, forbade the voyage; and what mother can sail while her child is left ashore? So Young Rachel went without us.

The next year my own body—always ready to mutiny when my mind begins to enjoy itself—chose to declare war by way of the gout. I was laid up, nursed, scolded, and fed with a discipline that made me feel, between pain and patience, as though I were being pickled for preservation. And then, while we still spoke of “next spring, next autumn,” came the news from Jamaica, which struck all our plans to the ground as a wind strikes the blossom.

Two years after we had made the Manor our home, our dear General returned from his government a little richer in coin, but robbed of the one treasure for which no counting-house ever kept a book. My Theo’s mother—soft-voiced, warm-handed, the gentlest friend (save one) I have ever known—had died abroad of the fever. She had not lived to see our prosperity with her own eyes; yet, as her husband said, with that grave simplicity which made his grief the more piercing, “She sees us, though we do not see her; and she thanks you, George, for having been good to her children.”

We had thought he would not long remain behind her. His love for her had been the business and holiday of his whole life; to be without her was like sitting at a table where every dish is served and yet the appetite is gone. It was pitiful to watch him among us. In Theo’s very step upon the stair, in the turn of her head when she listened, in certain little ways of smoothing a child’s sleeve or laying a napkin straight, he found the lost face again and again, as one finds a remembered tune under new fingers. What cheer we could offer, we offered. But little Hetty—under Heaven—became his chief prop. She had refused advantageous matches in the island, the General told us; and on her return to England my Lord Wrotham’s heir had thrown himself at her feet.

“I love best to stay with my father,” Hetty said. “So long as he is not tired of me, I care for no husband.”

“Nay,” we cried, when this last great match was pressed, “let the General keep house with us six months at the Manor, and you shall have him at Oakhurst for the other six!”

But Hetty declared her father could never bear Oakhurst again now that her mother was gone; and she would not be bought by a coronet and a rent-roll. The General, speaking of her with that just, quiet penetration which made his tenderness the more manly, said gravely that the child seemed to have no wish toward marriage at all—perhaps from some early disappointment of which she never spoke. We, respecting silence as one respects a closed door in a sick-room, asked no question.

By this time my brother Lambert had a college living near Winchester, and—by the same inevitable logic which provides a parsonage with a pulpit—he had a wife to fill the drawing-room and take possession of the kitchen. We professed but a moderate liking for this lady, though we made her welcome when she came. She was a woman who could not be happy unless she were proving her honesty by the pain she gave; and she took a malicious pride in calling it duty.

“My dear Sir George,” she was pleased to say, “I have often and often told our dear Theo that I wouldn’t have a pretty sister in my house to make tea for Jack when I was upstairs, and always to be at hand when I was wanted in the kitchen or nursery, and always to be dressed neat and in her best when I was very likely making pies or puddings or looking to the children. I have every confidence in Jack, of course. I should like to see him look at another woman, indeed! And so I have in Jemima—but they don’t come together in my house when I’m upstairs—that I promise you! And so I told my sister Warrington.”

“Am I to understand,” says the General, his voice very gentle and very dangerous, “that you have done my Lady Warrington the favour to warn her against her sister, my daughter Miss Hester?”

“Yes, pa, of course I have. A duty is a duty, and a woman is a woman, and a man’s a man, as I know very well. Don’t tell me! He is a man. Every man is a man, with all his sanctified airs!”

“You yourself have a married sister, with whom you were staying when my son Jack first had the happiness of making your acquaintance?” the General asked.

“Yes, of course I have a married sister; every one knows that—and I have been as good as a mother to her children, that I have!”

“And am I to gather from your conversation that your attractions proved a powerful temptation for your sister’s husband?”

“Law, General! I don’t know how you can go for to say I ever said any such a thing!” cries Mrs. Jack, growing scarlet and louder, like a kettle that will boil over because it cannot argue.

“Don’t you perceive, my dear madam,” says the General, “that it is you who have insinuated as much, not only regarding yourself, but regarding my own two daughters?”

“Never, never, never, as I’m a Christian woman! And it’s most cruel of you to say so, sir. And I do say a sister is best out of the house, that I do! And as Theo’s time is coming, I warn her, that’s all.”

“Have you discovered, my good madam, whether my poor Hetty has stolen any of the spoons? When I came to breakfast this morning, my daughter was alone, and there must have been a score of pieces of silver on the table.”

“Law, sir! who ever said a word about spoons? Did I ever accuse the poor dear? If I did, may I drop down dead at this moment on this hearth-rug! And I ain’t used to be spoke to in this way. And me and Jack have both remarked it; and I’ve done my duty, that I have.” And away she flounced, crying, as though tears could wash away what her tongue had thrown.

“And has the woman had the impudence to tell you this, my child?” the General asked, when Theo—who was a little delicate—came down to tea.

“She has told me every day since she has been here. She comes into my dressing-room to tell me. She comes into my nursery, and says, ‘Ah, I wouldn’t have a sister prowling about my nursery, that I wouldn’t.’ Ah, how pleasant it is to have amiable and well-bred relatives, say I.”

“Thy poor mother has been spared this woman,” groans the General.

“Our mother would have made her better, papa,” Theo said, and kissed him. And I saw, by the softened look that passed between them, that both were saying their prayers without words.

Yet truth must be owned: to love one’s kin is not always easy; to live with one’s neighbours is not always amusing. Jack Lambert came next day with a sulky brow and a hearty knife. His wife had served him her own version of the scene, hot and highly seasoned; and he brought it with him like a bad aftertaste. He was angry, but anger did not diminish his appetite. He preached a sermon for us—long, lumbering, and empty; and little Miles, once more in sables, sat by his grandfather, his small hand tucked into the old man’s as naturally as a fledgling finds the warm place under a wing.

We asked if the General would keep house for us while we made our Virginian journey. The housekeeper should obey Hetty as though she were mistress born; the butler’s keys should pass into the General’s keeping. Gumbo—though not, I thought, with an overgood grace—was to go with us to Virginia: for he had meanwhile tied himself to Mrs. Molly in honest matrimony, and peopled a cottage in my park with sundry tawny little Gumbos, who ran in and out like squirrels, and filled the place with a perpetual patter of bare feet and shrill laughter.

So, leaving our house under the General’s care and Hetty’s vigilant kindness, we travelled to London, then down to Bristol. Our obsequious agent there had the chance of vowing prayers for our prosperity, and of declaring—hands uplifted—that children so beautiful as ours (for we had an infant now to accompany Miles) were never carried aboard ship since Noah’s ark. The vessel’s smells—tar, damp rope, salt meat, sour beer—rose like a coarse chorus; yet between such rude odours one caught, now and then, the clean bite of sea air and the faint sweetness of biscuit, and my wife, even in that unromantic theatre, contrived to make a nursery of her corner. We made the voyage without accident.

How strange the feeling was, as we landed from our boat at Richmond! The river spoke in its broad, slow voice; the wharf creaked; the calls of negroes carried over the water; the wheels of a waiting coach grated on grit; and, behind all, the great hush of the land—so different from England’s ceaseless clatter—seemed to listen. A coach and a host of negroes were there to receive us; and hard by, a gentleman on horseback, with negroes in our livery, too. He sprang down and rushed to embrace us. It was our dearest Hal. We were charmed—no, moved beyond words—to see him. He rode with us to our mother’s door.

There she stood on the steps to welcome us; and Theo, in the very sweep of her gratitude, knelt to ask her blessing.

Harry rode in the coach as far as our mother’s house, but would not, as he said, spoil sport by entering with us. “She sees me,” he owned, “and we are pretty good friends; but Fanny and she are best apart; and there is no love lost between ’em, I can promise you. Come over to me at the Tavern, George, when thou art free. And to-morrow I shall have the honour to present her sister to Theo. ’Twas only from happening to be in town yesterday that I heard the ship was signalled, and waited to see you. I have sent a negro boy home to my wife, and she’ll be here to pay her respects to my Lady Warrington.” And with that, he jumped out and left us to meet our mother alone.

Since I had parted from her I had seen courts, and paid duty at St. James’s; yet I had seen no one more stately than the lady who received us now. The house was plain enough—wood-built, with a gallery running round, as our Virginian houses are—but she made it a palace by the manner in which she moved within it. She raised Theo from her knee, embraced her, and led her in as though she were placing a crown upon her own choosing.

Old Nathan was still major-domo; a score of black faces grinned welcome; and time had done its quiet work among them as among all tribes—children become men and women, men become grey, and new little feet appear where none were before. Some names I remembered had grown out of remembrance; some heads I had left jet-black were now powdered by nature’s snow; and little ones, born since my time, peeped from doorways with great eyes and naked soles that made no noise on the boards.

“I’m little Sip, Master George!” one cried.

“I’m Dinah, Sir George!”

“I’m Master Miles’s boy!” said a little fellow in fresh livery and boots of nature’s blacking, proud as any drum-major.

Before the day was over the whole household had contrived, under one pretence or another, to pass before us, bowing and smiling as though welcome were a duty of the place, like prayer. I know not how many repasts were served. Virginia hospitality has a rhythm like tide: it comes in, retreats, and comes in again, each time bearing new dishes upon its broad shoulder. The kitchens breathed constantly—wood-smoke, bubbling fat, pepper, boiled greens, and that deep, sweet smell which comes when ham has been long at the fire and begins to give itself up. One could hear the mortar thud with herbs, the knife on the block, the clink of pewter, the soft scuff of feet on packed earth behind the house. Even in rejoicing, a plantation is an instrument always playing: the voices of servants, the creak of hinges, the distant lowing, the domestic orchestra which, in a healthy place, keeps the mind steadier than any sermon.

In the evening my Lady Warrington had to receive all the little town’s gentry, which she did with perfect grace; and I shook hands with old acquaintances—old enemies, I was going to say; but I had come into a fortune and was no longer a naughty prodigal. Why, a drove of fatted calves was killed in my honour. My poor Hal was of the entertainment, but gloomy and crestfallen. His mother spoke to him, but as a queen to a rebellious prince: he was her son, and not yet forgiven.

We slipped away from the company and went up to the rooms assigned to me; but scarcely had we begun to speak freely when our mother appeared—taper in hand—her pale face lighted from below so that it seemed carved in wax and will.

Did I want anything? Was everything as I wished? She had peeped in at the dear children sleeping like cherubs. How she caressed them and delighted in them! How she was charmed with Miles’s little airs of command, and the baby Theo’s smiles and dimples!

“Supper is just coming on the table, Sir George. If you like our cookery better than the tavern, Henry, I beg you to stay.”

What a difference lay in the very syllables she gave to each of us! Hal’s head drooped, and he followed her down.

A clergyman begged a blessing on the meal, and with no little art and eloquence touched upon our arrival home, our safe passage across stormy waters, and the love and forgiveness awaiting us in the mansion of the Heavenly Parent when the storms of life were over. We had, it seemed, a new clergyman—quite unlike some whom I remembered in earlier days. I praised him; but Madam Esmond shook her head. She feared his principles were dangerous; she feared others had taken up those dangerous principles. Had I not seen, she asked, the paper signed at Williamsburg the year before—Lees, Randolphs, Bassets, Washingtons, and the like, and—oh, my dear!—our name too (that is, my brother’s, by what influence she did not like to say), and this unhappy Mr. Belman’s who had begged a blessing last night?

If there had been quarrels in our little society when I left home, what were those to the feuds raging now? We had sent the Stamp Act and been forced to repeal it; then tried new duties, and repealed those too—all save tea. From Boston to Charleston, tea was seized and flung aside as though it were poison. Even my mother, loyal as she was, gave up her favourite drink. My poor wife must have forgone hers too, but we had brought a quantity for our private use aboard ship, and paid four times duty for it at home; so our little pot could still sing in the mornings, and the fragrant steam—so domestic, so intimate—rose like a small act of resistance in the other direction. There is a strange power in a familiar brew: it carries memory on its scent, and the tongue, tasting what it cannot name, finds itself suddenly back in a former life. Yet even that comfort was not without its quarrel, for every cup seemed to ask: whose law is in it? whose labour? whose word counts as “right”?

For my part I never hesitated about paying duty. The home Government must have revenue, or its pretensions to authority were idle. They say the colonies were tried and tyrannised over; I say the home Government was tried and tyrannised over. ’Tis an affair of argument now, and history; we tried the question and were beat, and the matter is settled as completely as the conquest of Britain by the Normans. From conviction, I trust, I took the British side. In that brief and unfortunate war-experience of my youth, the army’s cry had been that Braddock’s expedition failed and disaster fell upon us through the remissness, selfishness, and rapacity of many of the very people we came to defend. The colonists would have everything done for them and do nothing: they bargained extortionately with their champions, failed in contracts, furnished niggardly supplies, multiplied delays until the hour for useful action was past, and so helped invite the catastrophe which need never have occurred but for their ill-will.

What shouts of joy there had been for the Minister who devised the conquest of Canada! Monsieur de Vaudreuil said justly that that conquest was the signal for the colonies’ defection; and my Lord Chatham, having done his best to win the first part, contributed more than any man in England to complete the second. The colonies were insurgent, and he applauded their resistance. How many waverers must he have heartened into revolt! It was as if a general should say to mutineers, “God save the King! My men, you have a right to mutiny!” No wonder they set up his statue here and his picture there, while hanging Ministers and Governors in effigy. At Williamsburg, some wiseacres subscribed for a portrait of my lord as a Roman orator pointing to Whitehall, and the very window whence Charles the First was beheaded—a neat allegory, and a pretty compliment to a British statesman. I hear, however, that my lord’s head was painted from a bust, and so was taken off without his knowledge.

My country is England, not America or Virginia; and I took the English side. My sympathies were with home, where I was now a squire and citizen. Yet had my lot been to plant tobacco and live by the James or Potomac, no doubt my opinions would have altered; for the same earth that feeds a man also teaches him, and every dialect has its own tyranny of meaning. When I visited my brother at his new house and plantation, I found him and his wife staunch Americans, as Theo and I were British. We had words, as who had not in those times, but without rancour; even my new sister could not bring us to that, though she tried her best in company and, I doubt not, in curtain-lectures after, like a notable housewife measuring out obedience as she measured out flour. But Hal and I trusted one another so entirely that even his duty to his wife would not make him quarrel with me. He loved me from old times, when my word was law to him. He still protested that he and every Virginian gentleman of his side were loyal to the Crown. War was not yet declared; gentlemen of different opinions still kept decent manners, as men keep the peace at table while the knives are near. At public dinners the King’s health was still ostentatiously drunk; every colony, preparing for Congress and resisting taxation, was loud in its regard for “the King our Father,” and pathetic in appeals that he would dismiss evil counsellors and listen to moderation and reason.

Up to the last, the Virginian gentry were a grave, orderly, aristocratic folk, with a strong sense of their own station. In later days, nearer home, we have heard of fraternisation and equality. Among the great people of our Old World I have never seen a gentleman stand more upon his dignity and maintain it better than Mr. Washington—no, not the King against whom he took arms. To the French gentry who joined the crusade against us and took their revenge for Canada, the American chief appeared anax andron, and they allowed his better could not be seen in Versailles. Though quarrelling with the Governor, the burgesses still kept private courtesies, exchanging dignified civilities as though a ritual of words might yet bind what policy was tearing. When my Lord Bottetourt arrived and held his court at Williamsburg in no small splendour, all the gentry waited upon him—Madam Esmond included. And when Lord Dunmore succeeded him, bringing a fine family, he too was treated with respect in private, though in public the House and Governor stood at war.

These quarrels are history; they concerned me personally only thus: our burgesses being convened for the first of March in the year after our arrival, it was agreed we should visit the capital and pay duty to his Excellency. Since Hal’s unhappy marriage Madam Esmond had not performed this duty, though once accustomed to do so; but now that her eldest son was in the colony again, she opined we must certainly wait upon the Governor. Nor were we sorry to escape our little Richmond and taste the provincial capital’s gaieties.

Madam engaged—at a great price—the best house to be had at Richmond for herself and family. Now that I was rich, her generosity took on a curious edge. More than once I had to interpose (her old servants wondering too) and beg her not to be so lavish. But she answered gently that in former days she had occasion to save, which existed no more. Harry had enough—surely—with such a wife as he had taken out of the housekeeper’s room. If she chose to be a little extravagant now, why hesitate? She had not her dearest daughter and grandchildren with her every day; she had fallen in love with all three and spoiled them as much as they could be spoiled. Besides, in old times I could not accuse her of too much extravagance; and this was almost the only allusion she made to our former pecuniary differences.

So she had the servants dressed in their best; her best wines; plate and furniture sent by sea from Castlewood at no small charge; and the very dress in which she had been married in George the Second’s reign. We flattered ourselves that our coach made the greatest figure of any except his Excellency’s. We engaged Signor Formicalo—his Excellency’s major-domo—to superintend the series of feasts given in my honour; and more fleshpots were set a-stewing in one month, the servants said, than had been known since the young gentlemen went away. The kitchens became a kind of memory-workshop, boiling up the past in broth and gravy. One might have thought Madam Esmond meant to prove, by spice and silver, that she had never diminished—only waited.

So great was Theo’s influence over my mother that she actually persuaded her, that year, to receive our sister Fanny, Hal’s wife. Fanny would have stayed upon the plantation rather than face Madam Esmond; but trusting to Theo’s promise of amnesty, she came up to town, made her curtsey, and was forgiven. And rather than be forgiven in that fashion, I own I would prefer perdition or open persecution.

“You know these, my dear?” Madam Esmond said, pointing to her fine silver sconces. “Fanny hath often cleaned them when she was with me at Castlewood. And this dress too, Fanny knows, I dare say? Her poor mother had the care of it. I always had the greatest confidence in her.”

Wrath flashed from Fanny’s eyes—quick as a struck spark—yet our mother, who had forgiven, did not perceive; forgiveness with her was a sovereign act, and sovereigns are not accustomed to notice what subjects feel.

“Oh, she was a treasure to me!” Madam resumed. “I never should have nursed my boys through their illnesses but for your mother’s admirable care. Colonel Lee, permit me to present you to my daughter, my Lady Warrington. Her ladyship is a neighbour of your relatives the Bunburys at home. Here comes his Excellency. Welcome, my lord!”

And our princess made before his lordship one of those curtseys of which she was proud; and I fancy some of the company ventured to smile.

“By George! madam,” says Mr. Lee, “since Count Borulawski, I have not seen a bow so elegant as your ladyship’s.”

“And pray, sir, who was Count Borulawski?” asks Madam.

“He was a nobleman high in favour with his Polish Majesty,” replies Mr. Lee. “May I ask you, madam, to present me to your distinguished son?”

“This is Sir George Warrington,” says my mother, pointing to me.

“Pardon me, madam. I meant Captain Warrington, who was by Mr. Wolfe’s side when he died. I had been contented to share his fate, so I had been near him.”

And the ardent Lee swaggered up to Harry, took his hand with respect, and paid him compliments which made me, at least, pardon the man his impertinence; for my dearest Hal walked gloomily through his mother’s rooms in the old uniform of the famous corps he had quitted, as though it were a garment of honour and reproach stitched together.

We had had many meetings which the stern mother could not prevent, and in which that instinctive love binding us—indestructible as blood—had its hour to speak. Entirely unlike in tastes and pursuits—his life eager exercise, field-sport, and hardy amusements; mine a dawdling over books, a languid watching of my own mind—we nevertheless had such a sympathy as almost passes the love of women. Hal confessed as much in his artless way when we went away without wives or womankind (except a few negroes left in the place) and passed a week at Castlewood together. There, with the house’s old boards creaking under familiar steps, and the night sounds of the plantation—frogs in the marsh, wind in the pines, the far-off cry of an owl—falling into their ancient places like notes in a tune, we found ourselves again in the circle of our beginnings, even while the world outside was busy breaking its own language into two hostile dialects, each calling itself loyalty and each hearing treason in the other’s words.

What crooked ordinance of Fortune is it that forever contrives to lodge me in the thinner party? Propose in any assembly to hand this realm to the Pretender of Rome, or the Grand Turk, and clap a new creed upon our necks, and the motion would likely carry—while I, by instinct as much as conscience, should be found voting No. So it went with me in Virginia. The Patriots would have me for a Tory because I would not shout with them; the Tories presently christened me a dangerous Republican because I would not rage with them. The very hinges of the time were loosened. Before a year was out I found myself longing, with a homesick hunger, for the flat fields by the Waveney and the honest, familiar noises there—the rookery at dusk, the cart-wheels in sand, the church bell—anything but the jangling, watchful din that had begun to thicken round us like summer gnats.

Yet go I could not. My mother stood almost alone, a lady with a high spirit and a small frame, and though the world might crack, she would not quit her land at such a season; and I, having any manhood, could not desert her. Besides, at his Excellency’s table, amid plentiful claret and the soft chink of glasses, it was agreed upon by those who called themselves well-affected that a man must stand by his post. The Governor, warmed by wine and company, spoke as though the very flagstaff were a sacred thing: statue signum, signifer! We Cavaliers would rally; we would not give way; we would make the rebels learn what it was to flout the Crown. Those vows were pledged and repledged, as if loyalty could be measured by the depth of a bumper.

Of all our Virginian acquaintance, my mother was the steadiest. Gentlefolks had come in numbers to Williamsburg; and a party of them, in that way which makes amusement a species of public declaration, had determined to offer her Excellency, the Governor’s lady, a ball. But news arrived of the Boston Port Bill, and, straightway, the House of Burgesses took fire with indignation, and voted protest, and decreed a solemn day of fasting and humiliation throughout the country—prayer to Heaven to avert the calamity of civil war. The invitation to my Lady Dunmore had already been given and accepted; so the gentlemen resolved, with that odd American faculty of trying to eat their cake and keep it, that the ball should go forward on the appointed night, and that sackcloth and ashes should be put on afterwards.

“A ball!” cries Madam Esmond, when the project is brought to her. “I go to a ball given by a set of rebels who are going publicly to insult his Majesty a week afterwards? I will die sooner!” And she wrote, in her own precise hand, to the stewards of the entertainment, that, considering the dangerous posture of affairs, she could not dream of appearing at their festivities.

The next time she went abroad in her chair, she was met with cheers—white and black together, as if the town had turned out for a holiday. “Huzzah, Madam!” “Heaven bless your ladyship!” They took her refusal for a patriotic act. My mother, who could endure many mistakes but not that one, put her head out between the chair-curtains and cried, with all the strength in her small lungs, “God save the King!” The people, catching the words as they might a tune, bawled “God save the King” too. In those days everybody could shout that loyalty; it was a refrain that covered contradictions, like a well-known hymn sung by a congregation that does not agree upon the sermon.

On the night of the assembly my poor Harry, being a Burgess and one of the givers of the feast, put on his old uniform red coat of Wolfe’s—soon, God knows, to be exchanged for another colour—and went off with Madam Fanny to the ball. My Lady Warrington and I, strangers in the country and English in everybody’s eyes, were permitted by my mother to attend the gathering from which she, of course, absented herself. I danced a country-dance with the lady of Mount Vernon, and found her lively, pretty, and amiable, with a quickness in her step that answered the fiddle as if she had known its voice since childhood. But when my wife afterwards praised Mrs. Washington’s grace, my mother received the commendation with a grimness that might have turned a bowl of syllabub.

Could not Sir George Warrington, she asked, have danced with my Lady Dunmore or her daughters, or with anybody but Mrs. Washington? To hear her, the Colonel of Mount Vernon must needs think himself and his wife the grandest people in the room; and she—my mother—remembered him a road-surveyor at a guinea a day! There was no measuring, she said, the pride of these provincial upstarts; and my Lord Dunmore’s partiality for that gentleman had plainly turned his head. Of Mr. Washington’s pride I know nothing; but my mother never could be brought to love him nor anything that was his.

Her displeasure did not end with the dance. Three days later, when the appointed fast and humiliation came round, and Mr. Washington attended the service performed by our new clergyman, my mother chose that same day to invite Mr. Belman to dinner, with sundry colonial authorities. It was not merely hospitality: it was a proclamation. The clergyman excused himself. Madam Esmond tossed up her head and said he might do as he liked.

She made a parade of a dinner; and indeed, in the very ordering of her table there was something of battle. The house smelt of roasting meats and rich gravies when other houses had shut their kitchens as though food itself were indecent on a day of penitence. The fire crackled; the spits turned; the cook’s knife went tap-tap-tap on the board with a steady confidence, mincing herbs and onions for sauces as if politics were nothing beside a well-managed pan. There were breads laid in folded napkins, and jellies that trembled like captured light, and a punch-bowl set out with such ceremony that one might have thought it an altar. At night she lighted her windows when the rest of the city was in darkness and gloom, so that her candles shone out like defiance.

Then, with a mischievous bravery, she begged Mr. Hardy, one of his Excellency’s aides-de-camp, to sing “God save the King.” The people outside listened, and some of them, hearing music where they expected only prayers, supposed it might be part of a religious service which Madam was celebrating. The air of the hymn floated into the street with the warm breath of the house—spiced wine, melting fat, beeswax candles, and the faint sour of wet wood from the palings. But my mother, having set her foot upon the path, would not stop at the first step. She called for “Britons, strike home!”

The simple young gentleman, fresh from Europe, began it; and at the first insolent notes, a great roar rose in the street—an angry living thing made of many throats. A large stone, flung by some rebellious hand, came whizzing through the night and plumped into the punch-bowl before me, shattering it; the sweet liquor and fruit peels and shattered glass splashed across the cloth and floor, and the smell of spilled spirits rose sharp and raw, drowning for a moment the domestic comfort of meat and candle.

My mother went to the window, nothing daunted. I see her now: her rigid little figure against the black, her head held high, her frilled arms outstretched, the stars twinkling over her like indifferent witnesses; and she sang in chorus, “Britons, strike home! strike home!” The crowd below shouted, “Silence! For shame! Go back!” but she would not go back—not she.

“Fling more stones, if you dare!” she cried.

More might indeed have come; but some gentlemen, issuing out of the Raley Tavern, interposed. “You mustn’t insult a lady,” says a voice I think I know. “Huzza, Colonel!” “Hurrah, Captain!” “God bless your honour!” the people answered, and so the enemies were pacified for the moment.

My mother, protesting the whole disturbance was over, would have had Mr. Hardy sing again; but he gave a sickly grin and said he really did not like to sing to such accompaniments. The concert ended. Yet I am bound to say that some scoundrels returned later in the night, frightened my poor wife almost out of her wits, and broke every single window in the front of our tenement. “Britons, strike home!” had been a little too much. Madam should have contented herself with “God save the King.”

All this while the town’s outward chorus of loyalty went on. Militia were drilled in the open, their muskets clicking and stamping with a harsh, regular sound that infected the ear like a fever. Bullets were cast; the very domestic hearths were turned to furnaces for war, lead melting in ladles where yesterday a cook had stirred syrup. Powder was stored; supplies were hidden; cunning plans were devised to disappoint royal ordinances. Yet “God save the King” remained the cry everywhere. And if I said to the gentlemen-patriots, “You are scheming for separation; you will bring down on yourselves the wrath of the greatest power in the world,” they answered always, “We mean no separation; we yield to no men in loyalty; we glory in the name of Britons,” and so forth, and so forth. The powder-barrels were heaped in the cellar, the train laid; and Mr. Fawkes, for all that, persisted in his dutiful petitions and meant no harm—not he!

I confess that when I spoke of the might of our country I expected she would exert it, and not attempt to overpower three millions of fellow-Britons upon their own soil with a handful of battalions, a half-dozen generals from Bond Street, and a few thousand bravos hired in Germany. As if we wished to insult the thirteen provinces as well as subdue them, we must needs loose upon them Hessians, and set the murderers out of the Indian wigwams to do our work. Was our quarrel to be fought with tali auxilio and istis defensoribus? It is easy now, we being worsted, to pore over the map of the empire wrested from us, and show where a march, an advance, a day more of darkness or light, might have put the enemy into our hands. Long Island should have exterminated Washington’s army; he should never have come out of Valley Forge except a prisoner. The South, after Camden, seemed ours, but for the meddling from New York that paralysed the exertions of the only truly capable British general who appeared in the war, and pushed him into that miserable cul-de-sac at York Town, whence he could only issue defeated and captive. Oh, for a week more, an hour more, when so much hung on time and temper!

But it was ordained by Heaven—and for the good, as we can now have no doubt, of both empires—that the great Western Republic should separate from us. And the gallant soldiers who fought on her side, their indomitable Chief above all, had the glory of facing and overcoming not only veteran troops amply provided and inured to war, but cold, hunger, wretchedness, dissension, and treason within their own camp—where all must have gone to wreck but for the pure, unquenchable flame of patriotism that burned forever in that heroic breast.

With the young Mr. Washington of my earlier days I had not much sympathy; though my brother, being more frank and affectionate than I, was his fast friend when they were equals, and in later days when the General, as I do own and think, was all mankind’s superior. Washington before the enemy was no braver than hundreds who fought with him or against him (who has not heard the repeated sneers at “Fabius,” in which his factious captains indulged?), but Washington as Chief of a nation in arms—calm in conspiracy, serene between open foe and darker enemies behind; inspiring order into hungry men in rags; stung by ingratitude and betraying no anger; ready to forgive; invincible in defeat; magnanimous in conquest; never so sublime as on the day he laid down his victorious sword and sought his noble retirement—here indeed was a character to admire and revere: a life without stain, a fame without flaw. Quando invenies parem? In a more extensive work I have planned and partly written upon this war, I trust I have done justice to his greatness; and if I recorded opinions that could offend both parties, it was because respect extorted them.

How odd, too, that the contrariety in my own temper and in my brother’s placed us, as by some perverse music, on wrong sides of the coming storm. Harry should have been the Tory, and I the Whig. Theoretically my opinions were the more liberal. My brother, especially after his marriage, became what our Indian nabobs call a Bahadoor—ceremonious, stately, exacting respect as if it were rent due on a manor.

When my Lord Dunmore talked of liberating the negroes, to induce them to join the King’s standard, Hal would have hanged the Governor and the “Black Guards” (as he called them) whom his Excellency had crimped. “If you gentlemen are fighting for freedom,” I said, “sure the negroes may fight too.” On which Harry roared, shaking his fist, “Infernal villains! if I meet any of ’em they shall die by this hand!” And my mother agreed that a negro insurrection was the most abominable and parricidal notion that had ever sprung up in her unhappy country. She, at least, was consistent: she would have black and white obedient to the powers that be; whereas Hal only could admit that freedom was the right of the latter colour.

As proof, Madam Esmond and Harry pointed to an instance in our own family: Mr. Gumbo.

I had purchased his liberty and given it him as reward for his admirable love and fidelity to me when times were hard. Returning to Virginia, he was scarcely a welcome guest among my mother’s servants. He was free and they were not: he became, as it were, a little living standard of insurrection, planted in the very midst of our kitchen and quarters. He took on airs of protection and consequence, talked big of “at home” (meaning Europe), and bragged of his doings there. He drew the household about him as naturally as a stewpot draws hands and noses on a cold evening. They would stand in doorways and by the yard, listening to his tales, the night full of crickets and distant drums from militia practice, while closer at hand the domestic sounds went on—the thud of a pestle, the scrape of a trencher, the hiss when fat met flame. He had seen the world, and like the monkey that has seen the world, he made a show of it.

Now Sady—Hal’s boy—had gone to America of his own desire, yet was not free. Hence jealousies between him and Mr. Gum; and battles, in which they practised the noble arts of boxing and butting learned at Marybone Gardens and Hockley-in-the-Hole. Nor was Sady alone in his dislike. Almost all my mother’s servants hated Gumbo for the airs he gave himself.

And I grieve to say our faithful Molly—his wife—was as jealous as any. The blacks could not pardon her for having demeaned herself, as they chose to call it, by marrying one of their own kind; she met with no respect, could exercise no authority, and came to her mistress with ceaseless complaints of idleness, knavery, lies, stealing—each tale sharper than the last, as if she were forever shaking grit out of a sack. At last she brought a story of jealousy against a certain Dinah, or Diana—who, I heartily trust, was as innocent as her namesake, the moonlight visitant of Endymion.

On the article of morality Madam Esmond was a very Draconess; the accused, in her court, were already guilty. She made charges against Mr. Gumbo; he replied with asperity. Forgetting that he was now a free gentleman, my mother ordered Gumbo to be whipped. At that, Molly flew at her ladyship—her wrath against her husband’s supposed infidelity vanishing in a flash before the notion of such indignity put upon him. There was a rebellion in our house at Castlewood, and the very domestic air seemed to take sides: the clatter of pans in the kitchen sounded like arms, the voices in the passages like mutiny.

A quarrel followed between me and my mother, for I took my man’s part. Hal and Fanny, on the contrary, sided with her; and in so far the difference did good, that it brought about some little intimacy between Madam and her younger children. This particular storm was speedily soothed; but it was plain that the standard must be removed from our house. We determined that Mr. Gumbo and his lady should return to Europe.

My wife and I would willingly have gone with them, God wot; for our boy sickened and lost his strength, and caught fever in our swampy country. But at this time she was expecting to lie in of our son Henry, and she knew too that I had promised to stay in Virginia. It was agreed that we should send the two back. When I offered that Theo should go, she said her place was with her husband; her father and Hetty at home would care for our children; and she scarce let me see a tear while she made ready the departure of her little ones.

There is a kind of silence that gathers round such work as surely as flour settles on a bakeboard: the hush around the tables where small shirts are folded and stacked; the careful tying of strings; the laying by of tiny caps; the way a mother’s hands will linger on linen as though touch could store warmth for a voyage. There are the stealthy visits to the children’s chamber while they sleep—breath sweet with milk, hair damp at the nape—while you stand in the doorway listening to their small, unconscious music. And then the parting: the barge waiting; the oars creaking; the splash and drip of water; the calls from boatmen; the shore beneath your feet suddenly too firm and too far away, as the boat slides off with what is dearest to you and cannot be recalled.

Had the Prince of Wales been bound upon that voyage he could not have been better provided. Where, sirrah, is the Tompion watch your grandmother gave you? and how did you survive the boxes of cakes the good lady stowed away in your cabin—spiced little rounds, sugared and packed so closely that the very scent of them seemed meant to keep hunger at bay like a charm?

The ship which carried away my poor Theo’s children returned with the Reverend Mr. Hagan and my Lady Maria aboard—who meekly chose to resign her rank, and was known in the colony (which was not to remain a colony very long) only as Mrs. Hagan. In the time when I stood in favour with my Lord Dunmore, a living falling vacant in Westmoreland county, his Excellency gave it to our kinsman. Hagan arrived in Virginia time enough to christen our boy Henry, and to preach sermons on the gloomy posture of affairs, which Madam Esmond pronounced prodigious fine.

My Lady Maria won my mother’s heart by a scruple of precedence. “My father, your brother, was an earl, ’tis true,” said she; “but your ladyship is a marquis’s daughter, and I never can think of taking place of you.” So fond did my mother become of her niece that she even allowed Hagan to read plays—my own humble compositions among others—and was forced to own there was merit in the tragedy of Pocahontas, which our parson delivered with uncommon energy and fire.

Hal and his wife came but rarely to Castlewood and Richmond while the chaplain and his lady were with us. Fanny was curt and rude with Maria; would giggle and laugh strangely in her company; and repeatedly reminded her of her age—to our mother’s astonishment, who often asked if there were any cause of quarrel between her niece and her daughter-in-law. I kept my own counsel; yet I could not help being touched by the meekness with which the elder lady bore these persecutions. Fanny loved to torture her in her husband’s presence—who, poor fellow, was in happy ignorance of his wife’s early history—and the other endured her agony, wincing as little as might be.

Sometimes I remonstrated with Madam Harry, asking if she were a Red Indian, that she should torture her victims so. “Have not I had torture enough in my time?” she said, and looked as though she were resolved to repay injuries. “Nay,” I answered, “you were bred in our wigwam, and I remember nothing but kindness.” “Kindness!” she cried. “No slave was ever treated as I was. The blows which wound most often are those which are never aimed. The people who hate us are not those we have injured.”

I thought then of little Fanny in our early days—silent, smiling, eager to run and do our bidding—and I grieved for my poor brother, who had taken this sly creature into his bosom.

In the years when we called ourselves the outlying rooms of Great Britain, we had a homely, half-ashamed use for America besides its tobacco and its timber: we made it a larder for our refuse, a distant shelf on which to set the jars that had burst in the heat of London. Convicts in irons, indentured men with their names sold like sacks of meal, younger sons whose debts and bawling creditors made England too tight a kitchen for them—away they went, shipped like casks, to roll and clatter on strange wharves and be broached among other people’s plantations.

We were much like those voyagers who, discovering new shores, brought over cats and pigs and English weeds, and called it civilisation; only we were apt to send, with equal care, our black sheep, to graze and breed where they might do least noise at home. I confess my own hand had been in that provisioning. We could find no fit employment in England for the worthy Hagan—husband to my kinswoman Maria—and so we were glad enough to pack him off to Virginia, and give him a colonial pulpit-cushion to thump.

He behaved there, to do him justice, as a brave honest gentleman. He did his duty thoroughly by his congregation, and to his King too; and so far my small patronage bore a better savour than I deserved. Madam Theo would always press this upon me whenever I owned my prick of conscience: that my conduct in this, as in all matters, had been guided by the highest principle of morality and honour. She could salt and preserve any action of mine till it seemed fit for a prince’s table.

Yet if we had had a living at home—if I could have chosen who should stand at our parish board, speak from our desk, pray over our bread—would I have given it to Hagan and selected him and his wife to minister among us? I fear not. I never doubted Maria’s sincere repentance; but I think, in the secret pantry of my pride, I was relieved to have her work it out in the wilderness. I say it now, owning my fault, and the stale taste it leaves on the tongue.

Twice, when I needed it most, this same Maria—whom we had sent away like a blemished vessel—helped me with her sympathy and friendship. She bore her own distresses courageously, and, with a tenderness that asked no payment, laid her hand upon other people’s griefs as one lays a cloth over rising dough. And yet I, and some of mine (not Theo), would look down upon her. For shame—shame on that pride, which can sit to a full table and still find bitterness.

Nor was my poor Lady Maria the only one of our blood whom the family was content to have out of sight among American forests and rivers. Having borrowed, stolen, cheated at home until he could cheat, borrow, and steal no more, the Honourable William Esmond, Esquire, was accommodated with a place at New York; and his noble brother and royal master heartily desired that they might see him no more.

When troubles began to thicken—first as talk, then as meetings, then as hard resolves—we heard of the fellow again, and of his doings in his new habitation. Lies and mischief went before him like advance-servants banging on doors. My Lord Dunmore told me that Mr. Will declared publicly our estate of Castlewood was only ours during his brother’s pleasure; that his father, out of consideration for Madam Esmond—his lordship’s half-sister—had given her the place for life; and that he, William, was actually in negotiation with his brother, the present Lord Castlewood, for the purchase of the reversion.

We had the deed of gift in our strongroom at Castlewood, and it was registered in due form at Williamsburg; so we were easy as to law. But intention is everything; and Hal and I promised each other that, as soon as we met Mr. William, we would wring from him a confirmation of this pretty story, if only to show the colour of his impudence in his own words.

What Madam Esmond’s feelings were, I need not particularise, for they were of a kind that made themselves heard through walls. “What! my father, the Marquis of Esmond, was a liar, and I am a cheat, am I?” cries my mother. “He will take my son’s property at my death, will he?” And she was for writing, not only to Lord Castlewood in England, but to his Majesty himself at St. James’s; and was only prevented by my assurance that Mr. Will’s lies were notorious among all his acquaintance, and that we could not expect, in our own case, that he should be so inconsistent as to tell the truth.

Presently we heard of him as one of the loudest Loyalists in New York—Captain, and then Major, of a corps of volunteers sending their addresses to the well-disposed in all the other colonies, and announcing their perfect readiness to die for the mother country. There was much fine phrasing in those papers, like froth whipped up to look substantial. Meanwhile, our own life in Virginia went on with the stubborn, daily precision of housekeeping: fires to be lit, meat to be salted, corn to be ground, children to be kept from mischief, and men to be kept from drinking themselves into speeches.

Yet the sound of the country altered, as weather alters. In Williamsburg, even the air seemed full of lids slamming—doors of taverns, shutters of meeting-rooms, the sharp crack of argument. We could not lie in a house without a whole window; and shutting the shutters of that unlucky mansion we had hired, Madam Esmond left our little capital, and my family returned to Richmond, which also was deserted by the members of the dissolved Assembly.

Captain Hal and his wife went back early to their plantation. I, not a little annoyed at the turn events were taking, divided my time between my own family and that of our Governor, who professed himself eager to have my advice and company. We differed strongly in politics, but as yet there was no personal breach. Even after the dissolution of our House of Assembly—the members adjourning to a tavern, and there holding that famous meeting where, I believe, the idea of a congress of all the colonies was first proposed—the gentlemen most resolute in opposition remained on good terms with his Excellency, ate at his board, drank his wine, and rode with him on excursions of pleasure. The world had not yet broken into open war; it was still a household that quarrelled at table, then called for a fresh dish.

The session over, the gentry went home, and meetings sprang up in their respective counties as naturally as bread rises in warm pans. Other provincial Assemblies were abruptly dissolved; and it was agreed everywhere a general congress should be held. Philadelphia, as the largest and most important city on our continent, was selected; and those celebrated conferences began—the angry preface of war.

We were still at God save the King; still sending humble petitions to the throne; still talking of rights in the language of loyalty. But words, like old recipes, change their flavour in new mouths. I remember that while this great argument was gathering like thunder beyond the Blue Ridge, I went to visit my brother Harry at Fanny’s Mount. His new plantation lay not far from ours, with the Rappahannock between, and towards the Mattaponey.

One morning he rode out on business; in the afternoon I too took horse. The day was clear, and the country had that particular hush which makes every small noise distinct: the creak of saddle-leather, the click of a bit, the long insect-hum from the grass, and, far off, the faint chopping rhythm of an axe. A groom told me master was gone towards Willis’s Ordinary. Thinking no harm, I followed.

As I came out of the wood into a clear place not far from Willis’s, the soundscape changed at once. Instead of birds and leaves, there were men’s voices, abrupt and uneven, and the harder noises of metal and wood: a ramrod clink, the thud of feet on trampled earth, the scrape of a pike being shifted in clumsy hands. There was Captain Hal on horseback, with three- or four-and-thirty countrymen about him, armed with every sort of weapon—pike, scythe, fowling-piece, musket—and Hal, with two or three likely young fellows as officers under him, putting the men through their exercise.

It was a strange sight in that open Virginian field, as if the ordinary business of planting had turned itself inside out and shown its iron bones. The scythes that should have whispered through hay were held up like lances; the same hands that kneaded maize dough and split rails now fumbled at muskets; and the air, which commonly carried the domestic music of a plantation—pestle in mortar, a kettle’s lid, a distant fiddle on a Saturday—was cut through by rough commands and the awkward chorus of obedience.

When I rode up, a queer expression passed over Hal’s face, as if I had stepped unbidden into his kitchen while he was preparing a secret dish.

“Present arms!” says he; and the little army tried to perform the salute as best they could, their motions not yet one sound, but many sounds at once—iron against iron, breath against breath. “Captain Cade, this is my brother, Sir George Warrington.”

“As a relation of yours, Colonel,” says the man addressed as captain—an individual with a weather-browned face and a grip like a vise—“the gentleman is welcome,” and he held out a hand accordingly.

“And—and a true friend to Virginia,” says Hal, reddening as he spoke it, as though he must force the words down like a strong dram.

“Yes, please God! gentlemen,” said I; whereon the regiment gave a hearty huzzay for the Colonel and his brother. Their shout rolled away over the field and was swallowed by the woods, leaving behind it a moment’s ringing emptiness, as after a church-bell.

The drill over, the officers—and the men too—were for adjourning to Willis’s and taking refreshment. One could already imagine the ordinary’s thick air, the smell of beer and tobacco, the scrape of chairs, the rising talk: how easily a day’s work of war could be folded into the old habit of eating and drinking together. But Colonel Hal said he could not drink with them that afternoon; and we trotted homewards together.

“So, Hal, the cat’s out of the bag!” said I.

He gave me a hard look. “I guess there’s wilder cats in it. It must come to this, George.” Then, lowering his voice as if the very trees might carry tales, he added, “I say, you mustn’t tell Madam.”

“Good God!” I cried. “Do you mean that with fellows such as those I saw yonder, you and your friends are going to make fight against the greatest nation and the best army in the world?”

“I guess we shall get an awful whipping,” says Hal, “and that’s the fact. But then, George,” he added, and his sweet kind smile came, as it always did when his heart was settled, “we are young, and a whipping or two may do us good. Won’t it do us good, Dolly, you old slut?” And he gave a playful touch with his whip to an old dog of all trades running by him, who accepted the correction as if it were part of the day’s sport.

I did not try to urge upon him—though I had done so in vain many times before—our British side of the question, the side which still seemed to me the best. He was accustomed to put off my reasons by saying, “All mighty well, brother: you speak as an Englishman, and have cast in your lot with your country, as I have with mine.”

To this there is no answer. When men reach that point, argument becomes only another kind of noise, and the matter must be fought out; and the strongest then calls himself right. Which had the right in the wars of the last century—the King or the Parliament? The side that was uppermost was the right, and on the whole more humane in victory than the Cavaliers would have been had they won. Nay, suppose we Tories had carried the day in America—how frightful and bloody that triumph might have been! One imagines ropes and scaffolds, noble heads laid low, the harsh music of drums outside prison doors.

A strange feeling, I own: I was on the Loyalist side, and yet wanted the Whigs to win. My brother Hal, on the other hand—who afterwards distinguished himself greatly with his regiment—never allowed a word of disrespect against the enemy whom he opposed.

“The officers of the British army,” he used to say, “are gentlemen—at least, I have not heard they are much changed since my time. There may be scoundrels and ruffians among the enemy’s troops; I dare say we could find some such among our own. Our business is to beat his Majesty’s forces, not call them names. Any rascal can do that.”

And from a name Mr. Lee gave my brother, which many of his rough horsemen did not understand, Harry was often called “Chevaleer Baird” in the Continental army. He was a knight indeed, without fear and without reproach.

As for my argument—What can such people as those you were drilling do against the British army?—Hal had his confident answer ready, spoken as plainly as if he were naming the ingredients of a dish.

“They can beat them,” says he. “Mr. George—that’s what they can do.”

“Great heavens!” I cried. “Do you mean, with your company of Wolfe’s, you would hesitate to attack five hundred such?”

“With my company of the 67th, I would go anywhere. And agreed with you, that at this present moment I know more of soldiering than they.” He turned in the saddle, and his voice took that practical tone he had when speaking of ground, distance, and cover. “But place me on that open ground where you found us, armed as you please, and half a dozen of my friends, with rifles, in the woods round about me—which would get the better? You know best, Mr. Braddock’s aide-de-camp!”

There was no arguing with such determination. “Thou knowest my way of thinking, Hal,” I said. “And having surprised you at your work, I must tell my lord what I have seen.”

“Tell him, of course. You have seen our county militia exercising. You will see as much in every colony from here to the Saint Lawrence or Georgia. As I am an old soldier, they have elected me colonel. What more natural? Come, brother—let us trot on. Dinner will be ready, and Mrs. Fan does not like me to keep it waiting.”

So we made for his house, which stood open, like all the houses of our Virginian gentlemen, where not only every friend and neighbour, but every stranger and traveller, was sure to find welcome: the very architecture of hospitality, doors wide as if the country still trusted its own peace.

Within, the day’s ordinary comfort asserted itself. One smelt the kitchen before one saw it: woodsmoke clinging sweetly to the air, the fatty promise of meat kept warm, the faint sourness of yeast at work, and that clean, sharp scent of herbs bruised under a cook’s palm. The clatter of plates and the softer, steady sounds of preparation—knife on board, spoon in pot—made a domestic music against which the earlier drilling, with its harsh clashes and shouted words, seemed both near and unbelievable, as if war were only another tune being rehearsed outside.

“So, Mrs. Fan,” said I, when we met, “I have found out what game my brother has been playing.”

“I trust the Colonel will have plenty of sport ere long,” says she, with a toss of her head—so quick, so bright, that even her defiance had the crispness of a well-fired crust.

My wife thought Harry had been hunting, and I did not care to undeceive her. The table was laid, and the household moved in its practised order, as though the world’s fate were not being argued in taverns and congresses, as though men were not learning to shoulder arms where yesterday they had shouldered sheaves. Yet what I had seen, and what Hal had told me, sat with me through the meal, like a new word in the mouth—unfamiliar, untranslatable into the old family dialect, and impossible to spit out.

When I had done with my visit to my brother, and my wife with our child were again safe under my mother’s vigilant roof at Richmond, I rode across to his Excellency at his country quarters near Williamsburg. The roads already had that charged hush which comes before storms: not silent, but listening. You could hear the frogs in the ditches and the saw of cicadas in the pines as plainly as a sermon—nature keeping her own order while men prepared to unmake theirs.

Everywhere in the colonies, as far as our couriers and newspapers could carry tidings, there were open drills, secret meetings, lists taken, powder counted, talk sharpened into purpose. Virginia had appointed her Delegates for the General Congress to sit at Philadelphia—names which, since then, have gone abroad like stamped coin. In Massachusetts, people and King’s troops stood nearly muzzle to muzzle. In Maryland and Pennsylvania we chose to believe the temper more loyal; in the Carolinas and Georgia, they said, the Crown might still reckon on a stout majority. And for our own province—how could one suppose the Old Dominion would fling off the ancient habit of allegiance? Had we not gentry proud of Cavalier blood, and old houses where the King’s health was pledged as dutifully as bread was broken?

Round the Governor the Loyalists swarmed, loud as locusts, full of those brave words that come so readily when a man’s boots are clean and his sword unblooded. At their tables the air was thick with claret and candle-grease, roast venison, pepper, and the salt edge of ham—those domestic perfumes that seem to promise stability, even while the talk at the board promises destruction. They drank his Majesty’s health again and again, the glasses clinking like little bells of certainty, and all the while they thundered that, when the time came, they would draw steel and scatter the rascally rebels like chaff.

In such company I was forced to hear my brother Harry’s name handled as if it were some tainted meat set among wholesome victuals. His wife, they said—too often with that relish men take in blaming women—had led him into these extreme opinions. He was infatuated by his friendship for the gentleman of Mount Vernon; he followed that man’s judgement in all things; he was committing himself day by day farther in a desperate course.

“This is your friend,” they cried to me; “this is the man your Excellency favoured—he that ate at your board, that had your special confidence!”

Much of it was true, and yet what they called treachery was, in those first months, very often a desperate loyalty of another kind: a longing to remain faithful, to strain every last sinew of reconciliation before the dreadful alternative—revolt and separation—became the only road left. But my companions had no palate for such distinctions. They wanted their politics like their punch: strong, sweet, and unquestioned.

They urged me to intercede. Was it yet too late? Would my influence reclaim Harry, if the Government offered him a command? They spoke, too, with a kind of patronage toward my mother and me—our loyalty, our service, should purchase forgiveness for my brother’s “benighted conduct.”

Williamsburg was all alternation: triumph in the morning, gloom by supper; fury at the rebels, then anxious waiting for aid from home; boasts that England’s power would soon crush the provinces, then whispers of doubt that slid along the table like spilled oil. I promised what I could. I wrote to Hal, though with little hope, setting forth again the arguments I had used before.

My mother wrote too.

In truth I expected less from her letter than from mine; she had a habit, in any dispute, of driving her Scripture like a stake. She cited the powers that be, threatened punishments, and—worst of all—hinted at his “subjection” to his wife, which is the one accusation sure to make an honest husband more stubborn. She did not show me what she wrote, perhaps wisely; but she did show me his answer.

To my surprise, Hal replied with texts of his own—scores of them—laid down with neatness, temper, and a kind of polish I should once have doubted him capable of. It had his cadence, but not always his hand. I learned soon enough that he had taken counsel of Mr. Belman, the New Richmond clergyman, who had declared for the Whig side and preached and printed against Hagan—our Hagan—so that, I fear, Belman carried the better of the controversy, as an able cook carries a dish by knowing when to salt and when to let the meat speak.

My own letters he did not answer.

Pressed yet again by the friends of Government, I wrote—most imprudently—that I would visit him by week’s end at Fanny’s Mount. I rode there and found only my sister.
