She received me with perfect cordiality, bright as a hearth when you come in from rain, and told me that Hal had gone far toward the Blue Mountains to look at horses and would be away—she did not know how long.

There are evasions as plain as closed shutters at noon. I understood. There was no hope.

“My dear,” I said, “as far as I can judge from the signs of the times, the train that has been laid these years must have a match put to it before long. Harry is riding away. God knows to what end.”

“The Lord prosper the righteous cause, Sir George,” she said, without wavering.

“Amen, with all my heart,” I answered. “You and he speak as Americans; I as an Englishman. Tell him from me, that when anything in the course of nature shall happen to our mother, I have enough for me and mine in England, and shall resign all our land here in Virginia to him.”

“You don’t mean that, George?” she cried; and her eyes brightened as if I had set a dish before her she had long desired.

“Well, to be sure, it is but right and fair,” she added presently. “Why should you, who are the eldest but by an hour, have everything? a palace and lands in England—the plantation here—the title—and children—and my poor Harry none? But ’tis generous all the same—leastways handsome and proper, and I didn’t expect it of you; and you don’t take after your mother in this, Sir George, that you don’t, nohow. Give my love to sister Theo!”

She offered her cheek to kiss, and I rode away with a heaviness I could not put off. With such a woman beside him—so quick in feeling, so sure in judgement—how was I to hope to convert my brother?

I went back to his Excellency, and we agreed it was time to arm in earnest. The Court and officials were agitated and excited; and, to my mind, needlessly savage in their abuse of the “wicked Whigs,” shouting Old England for ever as if volume could conjure ships across an ocean. But they were eager for the day when parties might meet hand to hand and they could ride the rebels down.

In Council his Excellency thanked me, and I engaged to raise a body of men for the Crown. Thus began the corps afterwards called the Westmoreland Defenders, of which I had the honour to be appointed Colonel.

The announcement was printed in the Government Gazette. We had no trouble filling the officer lists; gentlemen are never scarce where titles are to be had. But recruits—plain men with hoes in their hands and families at table—came in slowly, and vanished quickly, like dew when the sun comes high. Still, friend Hagan stepped forward at once to offer himself chaplain. My mother gave us our colours, and went about the country with a zeal that made her small figure seem larger than life. And the most indefatigable recruiter of all was my old tutor, little Mr. Dempster—who had been out as a boy on the Jacobite side in Scotland, and now travelled even into the Carolinas among the children of his banished comrades who had once worn Prince Charles’s white cockade, and who, in this quarrel too, showed themselves stubbornly loyal.

Meanwhile Hal’s “horse journey” carried him far beyond the Blue Mountains—on to Annapolis and Baltimore, and from Baltimore to Philadelphia, where a second General Congress was sitting. The very route of his going seemed like a thread being drawn through the colonies, stitching them into something new.

And then, as all the almanacs now record, Lexington happened. The first shots were fired in the war that would end in the independence of our native country.

We still protested loyalty to his Majesty; we still spoke of petitions and rights; yet men assembled with arms round about Boston—twenty thousand of these “loyal petitioners,” cannon among them, helped out of Government stores. Mr. Arnold began his career with boldness—daring and burglarious—forcing fort doors as if the King’s locks were mere inconveniences. Three generals from Bond Street, with reinforcements, sailed to help Mr. Gage out of his ugly place. Presently the armies were engaged, and our British generals commenced their conquest and pacification with the “glorious blunder” of Breed’s Hill, after which they fortified and waited while Congress deliberated who should command the confederated forces.

We all know on whom their choice fell.

Of the Virginian regiment that marched to join the new General-in-Chief, one was commanded by Henry Esmond Warrington, late a Captain in his Majesty’s service; and by his side rode his little wife, of whose bravery we were to hear much. I confess I was glad she had quitted Virginia; had she remained after her husband’s departure, my mother would infallibly have gone over to give her battle, and I was thankful that such a domestic civil war was spared our history.

The rush of our farmers and country-folk went northward. Virginia itself was flattered that a Virginian gentleman had been chosen for the principal command. Across the provinces the news of blood drawn at Lexington ran like fire through dry corn. Men denounced British cruelty with a passion that did not pause to weigh words. The soldier, indeed, was but doing his duty; he was met and resisted by armed men who meant to prevent him from taking what he deemed his own. But anger has its own language, and soon all men had chosen their side. Breed’s Hill grew in the imagination into a mountain visible from every colony, with Liberty, Victory, Glory blazing upon its summit. If farmers and ploughmen could stand against these dreaded troops, if doctors and lawyers could out-general famous officers, then—so men boasted—Britons might conquer the world, but their children across the Atlantic could match and conquer Britons.

For bravery and for vainglory I know not which deserves the palm. We laugh at our French neighbours for gasconade; but for steady self-esteem and indomitable confidence, who rivals Britons save their own descendants?

In our parts, the people took the people’s side. My Westmoreland Defenders—never robust in numbers—thinned further after the news of battle, and thinned worst of all because of the conduct of our Governor, which enraged no one more than his own partisans. For months in meeting after meeting, over thousands of bumpers, it had been agreed and applauded that his lordship would plant the King’s standard and summon loyal gentlemen to rally round it. I could name many a man—now a snug officer under the United States—whom I have heard hiccup out a prayer to perish under the folds of his country’s flag, or roar challenges to absent traitors with the rebel army.

But let bygones be bygones. Public history has recorded this: that his lordship—peer of Scotland, the King’s representative—who invited all lieges to join the standard, was the first to put it in his pocket and flee to his ships out of danger. He would not leave them save as a pirate at midnight to burn and destroy. We loyal gentry were left ashore, committed, exposed to greater peril because of the weakness and cruelty of him who ought to have led us.

It was early June. Orchards and gardens bloomed with their plenty; the smell of apple blossom, wet earth, and young leaves lay over the fields, mingled with kitchen smoke and the yeasty breath of bread. A week before I had been in Williamsburg, exchanging compliments with his Excellency, planning future movements, and parting with hands shaken hard and vincere aut mori—conquer or die—on our lips as if words could serve for powder.

Our small family sat in Richmond, as we did daily, talking of affairs in the north and of the quarrels between our Assembly and his Excellency, when Hagan burst into the parlour—Hagan, always as if he carried a whole bell-tower in his chest—and cried, “Have you heard the news of the Governor?”

“Has he dissolved the Assembly again, and put that scoundrel Patrick Henry in irons?” my mother demanded, her voice sharp enough to slice bread.

“No such thing. His lordship with his lady and family have left their palace privately at night. They are on board a man-of-war off York, whence my lord has sent a despatch to the Assembly, begging them to continue their sitting, and announcing that he himself had only quitted his Government House out of fear of the fury of the people.”

What was to become of sheep when the shepherd ran?

The House of Assembly sent entreaties as pathetic as any prayer: they guaranteed him safety if he would but land; they implored him to appear among them, if only to pass bills and transact necessary business. No. The man-of-war was his seat of government, and he desired his House of Commons to wait upon him there. This was planting the King’s standard with a vengeance.

He had left us. The Assembly ruled in his stead. A rabble followed the fugitive viceroy to his ships, and negroes deserted from plantations to join this other deserter. He landed here and there in darkness, seizing and burning with an alacrity that matched the most lawless of our opponents. He invited runaway negroes to his standard; he sent an ambassador to Indians begging them to join him. When he came ashore it was to burn and destroy; when people resisted, as at Norfolk and Hampton, he retreated to his ships again.

Even my mother, after that flight, was scared at the shape of affairs and doubted the speedy putting down of rebellion. The arming of negroes was, in her judgement, the most cowardly blow of all. Loyal gentry were ruined, robbed of what property they had. From Richmond and Castlewood a score of our worst hands deserted to his lordship’s fleet; some were slain; a couple were hung by the enemy for plunder and robbery committed while with that precious “army.”

Because her property was injured, and the King’s chief officer proved an imbecile, would Madam Esmond desert Royalty and Honour? Never. She was never so prodigiously dignified, so enthusiastically loyal, as after she heard of his lordship’s defection. Neighbours who thought quite otherwise listened without unkindness. Her oddities were known through the province; young men, I fear, would “smoke” her—draw her out to tell stories of her Marquis father, the splendour of her family, the old France that lived in her tongue. Yet along with the pomp, her charities were remembered; and many a “rebel,” as she called them, had a sneaking regard for the little Tory lady.

As for me—the Colonel of Westmoreland Defenders, a colonel without much of a regiment—I escaped some serious danger in consequence of disputes I was known to have had with Lord Dunmore.

After he had burned the stores at Hampton and issued his proclamation calling the negroes to his standard, I went on board his ship and took the liberty to remonstrate regarding both measures. I implored him to return to Williamsburg, where hundreds—thousands, I hoped—would be ready to defend him to the last extremity. In my remonstrance I spoke freely; or rather, I suspect my contempt showed itself in my manner as plainly as rancid butter shows itself on the tongue.

His lordship flew into a rage, declared I was a rebel like all the rest, and ordered me under arrest on board his own ship.

In my quality of militia officer—I commonly wore a red coat then, to show I bore the King’s colour—I begged for a court-martial immediately. Turning to two officers who had witnessed our altercation, I desired them to remember all that had passed. These gentlemen, no doubt, thought as I did about our chief’s behaviour; and the interview ended in my going ashore without a guard.

The story travelled, and improved in the telling, as stories do when they pass from mouth to mouth like a dish being seasoned anew at every table. Among the Whig gentry it was said I had spoken my mind manfully; no Whig, they declared, could have uttered sentiments more liberal. When riots broke out in Richmond and many Loyalists were in peril, fleeing to the ships, my mother’s house and property were never endangered, nor her family insulted. We were still in that earlier stage when reconciliation was thought possible.

“Ah! if all the Tories were like you,” a distinguished Whig once said to me, “we and the people at home should soon come together again.”

That was before the Fourth of July—before the Declaration which made reconcilement impossible.

Afterwards, when rancour thickened, motives less creditable were assigned. It was said I chose to be a Liberal Tory because I was a cunning fox and meant to keep my estate whichever way events went. And I must add that this opinion of me has obtained in high quarters at home too, where a profound regard for my own interest has been supposed to have guided my conduct during the unhappy troubles.

There were, however, two or three people in the world—since I had not told my mother how I meant to cede to my brother all my life-interest in our American property—who knew I had no mercenary motive. It was not worth undeceiving others. What is life worth, if a man must feel himself forever on the track—la piste—of calumnies?

To this day I do not quite know how it happened that my mother, that notorious Loyalist, remained for several years undisturbed at Castlewood, save that now and then a stray troop of Continentals was quartered upon her. I cannot say for certain, though I can guess shrewdly.

Madam Fanny, after a campaign before Boston, came back to Fanny’s Mount, leaving her Colonel. My modest Hal, until the end of the war, would accept no higher rank, believing he could be more useful commanding a regiment than a division. And after Fanny’s return, it was remarkable how her old asperity toward my mother seemed to melt away, and what an affection she showed for her—and for all the property. She was great friends with the Governor and with influential gentlemen of the new Assembly. Madam Esmond was harmless, they said; and for her son’s sake, who was bravely battling for his country, her errors should be lightly visited.

Thus my mother remained unharmed for years—except for heavy requisitions, which of course she had to pay—until the day when redcoats appeared about our house, and then, at last, serious evil came near enough to be heard in the night like distant drums.

What was the value of a Colonel when his regiment was no more than a name written fair upon parchment, and his commission—so proudly flourished by the Governor and Council—had been signed by men who now skulked out of sight, lodged aboard ships like rats in a bilge, venturing ashore only for a piratical swoop and a blaze? My Lord Dunmore’s black allies, whom he had summoned round him with promises and proclamations, frightened away the King’s own friends; and, worse, we heard he had sent an envoy to the southern Indians, bidding them come down in numbers to tomahawk our people into obedience.

“And these,” I said to my mother, with a chill that tasted like iron on the tongue, “are to be our allies!”

For as she and I exchanged our ominous look, memory came—sharp as vinegar in a wound—of a painted face bending over mine at Braddock’s Field, and the knife laid to my throat until Florac’s stroke knocked the savage down. We put Castlewood into as good a posture of defence as our country wit could compass: bars on doors, shutters strengthened, men set to watch, muskets cleaned and laid ready. Yet, in truth, it was not so much the Rebels we dreaded as the red men and the blacks—war loosed from its leash, running hungry through the night.

I had never seen Madam Esmond lose heart but once; and that was when she told my wife, and me, with our child beside her knee, how her own husband fell in an Indian foray more than forty years ago. The tale had scarcely ended, the embers scarcely settled into their night-red hush, when figures were seen moving before the house. The owls were calling in the trees, the frogs in the low ground kept up their constant kettle-drum; and, under that uneasy music, the soft scuff of feet on dry grass seemed as loud as marching. Nothing could persuade my mother the shapes were anything but savages. She sank upon her knees, her hands clasped as if to wring the very mercy out of Heaven.

“The Lord have mercy upon us!” she cried. “The Indians—the Indians!”

Yet the painted heroes from the South never came. Dunmore’s negro soldiers melted back to his ships, or wherever pay, rum, and plunder could be found; and the worst terror proved, for a time, to have been a phantom of the mind. Still, I own I looked at my mother’s grey head, at my wife’s brown hair, and at the golden ringlets of our little one, with a pang so keen it was almost a sickness—lest the chance of war should fling them into the hands of men to whom women and children are but spoil. And we—on our side—had summoned such instruments. I dare not set myself up as an interpreter of Providence; yet it seemed to me that the employment of Indians and German mercenaries bore its own punishment. The mercenaries, when struck, yielded; and each yielding stiffened the spirit of the Continentals. And one drunken murder—Miss McCrea, butchered by half a dozen savages—did more harm to the Royal cause than many a lost field.

When the Indian panic ebbed, my mother’s courage returned as flame returns to a lamp when the draught is stopped. But her mind, now steady, fixed itself upon another danger—the danger I ran by remaining in Virginia, and the danger my presence brought upon all who belonged to me.

“What harm can they do me,” says she, “a poor woman? If I have one son a colonel without a regiment, I have another with a couple of hundred Continentals behind him in Mr. Washington’s camp. If the Royalists come, they will let me off for your sake; if the rebels appear, I shall have Harry’s passport. I don’t wish, sir, I don’t like that your delicate wife and this dear little baby should be here, and only increase the risk of all of us! We must have them away to Boston or New York. Don’t talk about defending me! Who will think of hurting a poor, harmless, old woman? If the rebels come, I shall shelter behind Mrs. Fanny’s petticoats, and shall be much safer without you in the house than in it.”

She spoke thus partly because it was reasonable, but more because her heart was set on driving me and mine out of the storm. For herself, danger or no danger, she was rooted like an old orchard tree in the soil where her father was buried and where she had been born. She lived backwards, so to speak—fed on memory as other folk live forward on hope. She had seen the new generation, blessed it, and already begun to bid it farewell.

While we debated Boston, news came that the British had evacuated that luckless town altogether—never having ventured to attack Mr. Washington at Cambridge, though he lay there for months without powder, almost at our mercy; but waiting until he had procured ammunition and seized Dorchester Heights, which commanded the place, and so forced the whole army to retreat. That the King’s troops won Bunker’s Hill is as certain as that they beat the French at Blenheim; yet, after that day, our chiefs appeared to have caught a strange fear of assaulting entrenchments. Why hesitate from July to March to strike an enemy almost defenceless? Why the half-heartedness at Long Island, when the Continental army seemed in our hand? Why that astonishing timorousness later—of Howe before Valley Forge, when a starving, sickening force in rags could scarcely man its lines against a great, victorious, well-appointed army?

It was curious to note how the tones of partisans shifted as fortune rose and fell. When the evacuation of Boston reached us in the country, every little Whig in the neighbourhood came bowing to Madam, counselling a speedy submission. She no longer flaunted her loyalty as openly; yet she never swerved. Night and morning, in private, poor Hagan prayed for the Royal Family in our house; and on Sundays any neighbour might attend the service, where my mother acted as a very emphatic clerk, and the prayer for the High Court of Parliament under our most religious and gracious King was stoutly delivered.

The brave Hagan was a parson without a living, as I was a militia colonel without a regiment. He had continued to pray for King George in Williamsburg long after his Excellency the Governor had run away; but one Sunday he found a corporal’s guard at the church door, who told him the Committee of Safety had put another divine in his place, and he was desired to keep a quiet tongue.

He bade them “lead him before their chiefs”—for our friend loved tall words and a tragic posture—and so he was marched to the Capitol, a jeering chorus of white and coloured blackguards at the skirts of his gown. There he confronted Messrs. Henry and the new State officers—“the robbers,” as he called them, “in their den.” Of course he was ready with a prepared harangue (there are men who would not object to martyrdom so long as it be performed in a full house), but Mr. Henry was too busy to grant him that theatre. After three or four hours’ waiting in an anteroom, in company of negroes, Hagan entered with undaunted mien and began, “Sir, by what authority am I, a minister of the—”

“Mr. Hagan,” says Henry, cutting him short, “I am too busy to listen to speeches. And as for King George, he has henceforth no more authority in this country than King Nebuchadnezzar. Mind you that, and hold your tongue, if you please! Stick to King John, sir, and King Macbeth; and if you will send round your benefit-tickets, all the Assembly shall come and hear you. Did you ever see Mr. Hagan on the boards, when you was in London, General?”

And with that he turned upon General Lee—Mr. Washington’s second in command—then in Virginia on State business; and our good Hagan, reddening, near to tears with shame, was bundled out. After that, we judged his ministrations safer in the country, and removed him from his restive lambs in town.

The new government’s choice of Virginians for the highest posts bribed and flattered many leading men, who, but for the outrageous conduct of our own administration, might have remained faithful to the Crown and made head against the rebellion. Yet though Loyalists were gagged and muzzled, though the Capitol was in Whig hands, and our vaunted levies of loyal recruits were, for the most part, Falstaff’s regiments, the faithful still kept intelligences with one another, and with our neighbours. We did not rise; we ran away. In examinations before committees and justices, some frightened people put on republican airs and vowed perdition to kings and nobles. But we knew each other. According as the chances shifted—according as the master’s hand grew more or less hard—we concealed our colours, showed them, half showed them, or apostatised for the nonce and cried, “Down with King George!”

Our negroes carried tokens and messages from house to house. Plots and schemes ran under the floorboards of society like rats in the granary—silent, constant, and hard to catch. When a battle is over, the neutrals come running to the winning side and shout as loud as patriots. The runaways are not counted. Will any man tell me the ardent signers and well-wishers of the Declaration were not a minority, and that the minority did not win?

We heard that a part of the defeated Massachusetts army was about to make an important expedition southward, on which the greatest hopes were founded. I, longing for action—any movement that was not merely waiting to be seized—put myself in communication with ex-Governor Martin of North Carolina. I proposed joining him, with three or four Virginian gentlemen—officers, like myself, of that notable corps of which we only wanted privates.

We made no particular mystery of leaving Castlewood; the affairs of Congress were not going so well yet that the new government could afford to lay stress or tyranny upon doubtful persons. Gentlemen’s houses remained open; and, in our southern fashion, we visited friends for months. My wife and I, with our infant and a fitting suite of servants, took leave of Madam Esmond as if for a neighbourly stay. We went from plantation to plantation—each table spread with its own smoke and savour: bacon cured in hickory, pone hot from the hearth, peaches that burst at the bite, coffee boiled strong enough to stand a spoon—until at last we reached Wilmington, North Carolina, where we expected to stretch a hand to succours coming to meet us.

Before our arrival, the Carolinian Royalists had shown themselves in force and suffered for it. Their encounters with the Whigs were unlucky. The poor Highlanders fared no better in drawing sword for King George here than when they had drawn against him in their own country.

We reached Wilmington at the end of May, and found Admiral Parker’s squadron there, with General Clinton and five British regiments aboard, bound for a descent upon Charleston.

The General, to whom I immediately made myself known, saw that my regiment consisted of Lady Warrington, our infant (whom she was nursing), and three negro servants; and he received us with a grim welcome. But Captain Horner of the Sphinx frigate, who had served on the Jamaica station and had tasted, like the rest of the world, many kindnesses from our dear Governor there, heard that my wife was General Lambert’s daughter, and eagerly welcomed her aboard, giving up his best cabin to our service. So we were refugees too—like my Lord Dunmore—having waved our flag, pocketed it, and slipped out by the back door.

From Wilmington we bore away quickly to Charleston; and in the passage, and in our delay within the river before the assault, I came to some acquaintance with Mr. Clinton, which grew into further intimacy. It was the King’s birthday when we appeared in the river; we determined it was a glorious day for the commencement of the expedition.

It did not begin for some days; and I leave out purposely all descriptions of Penelope parting from Hector. In the first place, Hector is perfectly well (though a little gouty), and no rascal Pyrrhus has made prize of his widow. And in war, are not such partings occurring every hour? Yet I can see the gentle face still, over the bulwark, as we descended the ship’s side into the boats—the infant smiling on her arm. Old stories indeed. Captain Miles, having no natural taste for poetry, you have forgot, no doubt, Mr. Pope’s verses in which you are described parting from your heroic father; but your mother often read them to you when you were a boy, and keeps the gorget I wore that day somewhere amongst her dressing-boxes now.

My second venture at fighting was no more fortunate than my first. We came back to our ships that evening thoroughly beaten. The madcap Lee—whom Clinton had faced at Boston—met him now at Charleston; and Lee, with the gallant garrison, made a brilliant resistance. Sullivan’s Island was a nut we could not crack. The roar of our frigates, the continual cough and thunder of guns, could not pound its shell; the very air smelled of burnt powder and hot pitch, and the river carried the bitter tang of smoke as if it were a stew left too long upon the fire. The passage by which we moved to the assault was not fordable, as those officers found—Sir Henry at their head, for he was always the first to charge—who tried to wade it. Death by shot, by drowning, by catching my death of cold—these I had braved before I returned to my wife. Our frigate grounded for a time and got off with difficulty, being agreeably cannonaded by the enemy until she slid free of the bank.

A small incident in the midst of this unlucky struggle was the seed of a later intimacy between me and Sir Henry Clinton, and bound me to that gallant officer during the period in which it was my fortune to follow the war. Of his qualities as a leader there may be many opinions; I fear to say, regarding a man I respect and admire, there ought only to be one. Of his personal bearing and courage there can be none. Whether at the final charge on Breed’s Hill, or here before Sullivan’s Fort, or later at Fort Washington, when, standard in hand, he swept up and entered at the head of the stormers, Clinton was always foremost in the race of battle.

We were taking to the water from our boats, intending to force a column toward the fort through a way our own guns had rendered practicable, when a shot struck a boat alongside us—so well aimed that three-fourths of her crew were at once hors de combat, and the officer steering and the flag behind him were knocked down together. I could not help crying out, “Bravo! well aimed!” for no ninepins ever went down more helplessly than those poor fellows.

Then the General turned on me rather grimly. “Sir, the behaviour of the enemy seems to please you!”

“I am pleased, sir,” I answered, “that my countrymen yonder should fight as becomes our nation.”

We floundered on amid the same amiable attentions from small arms and great, until the water was up to our breasts and deepening at every step; then we were fain to take to our boats again and pull out of harm’s way. Sir Henry waited upon Lady Warrington on board the Sphinx after this and was very gracious, and mighty facetious regarding the humble writer of these pages, whom his Excellency always described as a rebel at heart.

May my children live to see no great revolutions—such as that now raging among our miserable French neighbours. Save a very few, the actors in those tragedies do not bear to be scanned too closely: chiefs often ranting quacks; heroes ignoble puppets; heroines anything but pure. The prize is not always to the brave. In our Revolution it fell, for once and for a wonder, to the most deserving. His triumphs were not in rare engagements where he obtained a trifling mastery, but over Congress; over hunger and disease; over lukewarm friends and smiling foes in his own camp. When the struggle was over and our chiefs began to squabble and accuse each other before the nation—what excuses were offered, what pretexts urged, what piteous pleas that fleets came too late, regiments mistook orders, cannon-balls would not fit the guns! Here was a general who beat us sometimes with no shot, no powder, no money; and he never spoke of a convention. Through all the doubt and darkness, I think only the American leader’s indomitable soul remained entirely steady.

Of course our Charleston attempt was trumpeted as a prodigious victory by the enemy, who had learnt—perhaps from their parents—to cry victory if a corporal’s guard were surprised, as loud as if a pitched battle were won. Mr. Lee rushed back to New York, trumpeting his glory, and no man received him with more eager delight than the Commander-in-Chief of the American army. It was “my dear Lee” and “my dear General” between them then; and it has always touched me to note the simple confidence with which the Commander-in-Chief regarded officers who had once served with the King. That mad, flashy braggart (and another Continental general, whose name and luck afterwards were notorious) took advantage of that modesty—advised, blustered, sneered, disobeyed—daily throwing fresh obstacles in the path over which only Mr. Washington’s endurance could have marched.

Whilst we were away in South Carolina, the famous Fourth of July had taken place; and we and the thirteen United States were parted for ever. Virginia distinguished herself too by declaring that all men are equally free; that all power is vested in the people, who have an inalienable right to alter, reform, or abolish their government at pleasure; and that the idea of an hereditary first magistrate is unnatural and absurd.

Our General presented me with this document fresh from Williamsburg as we sailed northward by the Virginia capes; and, with no little amusement, pointed out the faith to which, from the Fourth instant inclusive, I was bound. There was no help for it: I was a Virginian. My godfathers had promised and vowed in my name that all men were equally free (including, of course, the poor race of Gumbo), that monarchy is absurd, and that I had the right to alter my form of government at pleasure.

I thought of Madam Esmond and how she would look when these articles were brought her to sign; how would Hagan receive them? He demolished them in a sermon where all the logic was on his side; but the U.S. Government has not, somehow, been affected by his discourse. And when he came to the point that all men being free, therefore Gumbo and Sady and Nathan had assuredly a right to go to Congress—“Tut, tut, my good Mr. Hagan,” says my mother, “let us hear no more of this nonsense; but leave such wickedness and folly to the rebels!”

By the middle of August we were before New York, whither Mr. Howe had brought the army that had gone to Halifax after its inglorious expulsion from Boston. The American Commander-in-Chief was there, and a great battle inevitable; and I looked forward with an inexpressible doubt and anxiety, knowing that my dearest brother and his regiment formed part of the troops we must attack—and could not but overpower.

Almost the whole American force came over to fight on a small island where every officer on both sides knew they were to be beaten, and from which there seemed no chance of escape. Two frigates, out of the hundred we had, placed to command the enemy’s entrenched camp and the point of retreat across the East River, would have destroyed every bark in which he sought to fly, and compelled him to lay down his arms on shore.

He fought. His hasty levies were utterly overthrown; some of his generals, his best troops, his artillery taken; the remnant huddled into their entrenchments after their rout, the pursuers entering with them. Then the victors were called back. The enemy was pent in a corner, and could not escape.

“They are at our mercy, and are ours to-morrow,” says the gentle General.

Not a ship was set to watch them. Not a sentinel of ours could see a movement in their camp. A whole army crossed, under our eyes, in one night, to the mainland without the loss of a single man. And General Howe was suffered to remain in command after this feat, and to complete his glories of Long Island and Breed’s Hill at Philadelphia. A friend crossed in the night with news that the enemy was ferrying over; but he fell upon a German picket—who could not understand him; their commander was boozing or asleep. By morning, when the spy was brought to someone who could comprehend the American tongue, the whole Continental force had crossed the East River, and the empire over thirteen colonies had slipped away.

My opinions of our chief were by no means uncommon in the army, though perhaps wisely kept secret by those immediately under him. Am I unluckier than other men, or why are my imprudent sayings carried about more than my neighbours’? My rage that such a victory should be so used was no greater than that of scores of gentlemen. Why must my name be given up to the Commander-in-Chief as the guiltiest of grumblers? Personally, General Howe was brave, amiable, good-humoured.

“So, Sir George,” says he to me, “you find fault with me, as a military man, because there was a fog after the battle on Long Island, and your friends, the Continentals, gave me the slip! Surely we took and killed enough of them; but there is no satisfying you gentlemen amateurs!”

And he turned his back, shrugged, and spoke to another. Amateur I might be, and he the most agreeable of men; but if King George had said to him, “Never more be officer of mine,” yonder pleasant Cassio would most certainly have had his desert.

It has often seemed to me—though I speak as one who never wore epaulettes save by accident—that the rude earthworks flung up on Breed’s Hill fed the whole American war thereafter, as surely as a starter feeds the next day’s bread. Behind those clods and rails, the rebels dealt us such slaughter, and bore themselves with such steadfastness, that many a British chief, remembering the taste of that first mouthful, grew shy of forcing barricades ever after. At White Plains, when Mr. Washington’s army lay for the second time almost within our grasp, we heard later that our victorious troops were checked by a breastwork made of cornstalks and straw—poor materials, you would say, yet packed by fear and resolve into something hard as oak.

And then, as if Fate herself were a negligent steward, opportunities were set before us and left to grow cold. A whole winter lay open, when the Congress troops, dwindled and dismayed, lay hungry and ill-armed at Valley Forge; and the magnanimous Mr. Howe left them there, untouched, while his brave, full-fed, perfectly appointed army fiddled and gambled and feasted in Philadelphia. Triumphal arches went up; tournaments were held in a pleasant mockery of the Middle Ages; wreaths and garlands were offered by beautiful ladies to this clement chief, with fantastical mottoes proclaiming his immortality. Why have my ungrateful countrymen in America never raised a statue to him? They had not in all their army an officer who fought their battles better—who enabled them to retrieve their errors with such dexterity, who took care their defeats should be so little hurtful to themselves, who, when the stronger force in the course of events naturally got uppermost, showed such tenderness, patience, and complacency in helping the poor disabled opponent to his legs again.

Think of eighteen years earlier, and the fiery young warrior whom England had sent to fight her adversary on that continent. Fancy him for ever pacing the defences behind which the foe lies sheltered; sleepless by night and day; consuming in fierce longing; winding a track with a hunter’s scent that pants for battle; climbing silent precipices before dawn; watching until the heart within him is worn thin—until the enemy shows, and then, springing, grappling, dying, slaying. Think of Wolfe at Quebec; and then hearken to Howe’s fiddles, and see him smiling amongst the dancers at Philadelphia. The ear, too, keeps a ledger: a nation may be ruined as much by what it chooses to listen to as by what it chooses to see. The scrape of bows and the clink of glasses, gilded into “music,” can drown a people’s own alarms; and long after the last note, the silence returns with its bill unpaid.

A favourite scheme with our ministers at home, and with some of our generals in America, was to establish a communication between Canada and New York; by which means it was hoped New England might be cut off, overpowered in detail, and forced into submission. Burgoyne was entrusted with the conduct of the plan, and set forth from Quebec in high confidence. His march began in military state: trumpets of proclamations blew before him; he bade the colonists remember the immense power of England; and summoned the misguided rebels to lay down their arms. He brought a formidable English force, an army of German veterans not less powerful, a dreadful band of Indian warriors, and a brilliant train of artillery. It was supposed the people round his march would rally to the Royal cause and standards. The Continental force in front of him was small at first, and Washington’s army was weakened by the withdrawal of troops hurried forward to meet this Canadian invasion. A British detachment from New York was to force its way up the Hudson, sweeping away opposition on the route, and make a junction with Burgoyne at Albany. Then was the time when Washington’s weakened army should have been struck too; but a greater Power willed otherwise—nor am I, for one, even going to regret the termination of the war.

As we look over the game now, how clear seem the blunders made by the losing side! From the beginning to the end we were for ever arriving too late. Supplies and reinforcements from home—too late. Troops in difficulty—succour too late. Our fleet off York Town—too late, after Cornwallis had surrendered. A way of retreat opened to Burgoyne—but he resolved upon retreat too late. I have heard discomfited officers in after days prove infallibly how a different wind would have saved America to us; how we must have destroyed the French fleet but for a tempest; how once, twice, thrice, but for nightfall, Mr. Washington and his army were in our power. Who has not speculated, in reading history, upon the Has-been and the Might-have-been? I take my tattered map-book from its shelf and look upon the board on which the great contest was played; I wonder at the curious chances which lost it. Putting aside any idle talk about the respective bravery of the two nations, I cannot but see we had the best cards, and lost the game.

I own the sport had fascination for me, and stirred my languid blood. My brother Hal, when settled upon his plantation in Virginia, was perfectly satisfied with the sports and occupations he found there. The company of the neighbours sufficed him; he never tired of looking after his crops and his people, taking his fish, shooting ducks, hunting in his woods, or enjoying his rubber and his supper. Happy Hal in his great barn of a house, under roomy porches, dogs lying round his feet; his friends, the Virginian Will Wimbles, at free quarters in his mansion; his negroes fat, lazy, and ragged; his shrewd little wife ruling over them and over her husband, who always obeyed her implicitly when living, and was pretty speedily consoled when she died. I say happy, though his lot would have been intolerable to me—wife, friends, plantation, the town life at Richmond (which succeeded to the honour of being capital when our Province became a State). How happy he whose foot fits the shoe which fortune gives him!

My income was five times as great; my house in England as large, built of bricks and faced with freestone; my wife—would I have changed her for any other in the world? My children—well, I am contented with my Lady Warrington’s opinion about them. Yet with all these plums and peaches and rich fruits out of Plenty’s horn poured into my lap, I fear I have been but an ingrate; and Hodge, my gatekeeper—who shares his bread and scrap of bacon with a family as large as his master’s—seems to enjoy his meal as much as I do, though Mrs. Molly prepares her best dishes and sweetmeats, and Mr. Gumbo uncorks the choicest bottle from the cellar.

There are smells that do not forget us though we forget them: the slow brown of a crust in the oven; the sharp sting of a pickle barrel opened; the hush that falls in a house when a pudding is set down and all tongues pause, as if to hear the steam speak first. Yet, alas, sweetmeats have lost their savour for me, however they rejoice my young ones in the nursery, and the perfume of claret palls upon old noses. Our parson has poured out his sermons many and many a time to me, and perhaps I did not care for them much when he first broached them. Dost thou remember, honest friend?—sure he does, for he has repeated the story over the bottle as many times as his sermons almost, and my Lady Warrington pretends as if she had never heard it—I say, Joe Blake, thou rememberest full well, and with advantages, that October evening when we scrambled up an embrasure at Fort Clinton and a clubbed musket would have dashed these valuable brains out, had not Joe’s sword whipped my rebellious countryman through the gizzard.

Joe wore a red coat in those days—the uniform of the brave Sixty-third, whose leader, the bold Sill, fell pierced with many wounds beside him. He exchanged his red for black and my pulpit. His doctrines are sound, and his sermons short. We read the papers together over our wine. Not two months ago we read of our old friend Howe’s glorious deed of the first of June. We were told how the noble Rawdon, who fought with us at Fort Clinton, had joined the Duke of York; and to-day his Royal Highness is in full retreat before Pichegru; and he and my son Miles have taken Valenciennes for nothing! Ah, parson! would you not like to put on your old Sixty-third coat? (though I doubt Mrs. Blake could ever make the buttons and button-holes meet again over your big body). The boys were acting a play with my militia sword. Oh, that I were young again, Mr. Blake! that I had not the gout in my toe; and I would saddle Rosinante and ride back into the world, and feel the pulses beat again, and play a little of life’s glorious game!

The last “hit” which I saw played was gallantly won by our side; though ’tis true that even in this parti the Americans won the rubber—our people gaining only the ground they stood on, and the guns, stores, and ships which they captured and destroyed, whilst our efforts at rescue were too late to prevent the catastrophe impending over Burgoyne’s unfortunate army.

After one of those delays which always seemed to clog our plans and blunt the blows intended by our chiefs, an expedition was got under weigh from New York at the close of September ’77; that, had it but advanced a fortnight earlier, might have saved the doomed force of Burgoyne. Sed Dis aliter visum. The delay was not Sir Henry Clinton’s fault, who could not leave his city unprotected; but the winds and weather which delayed the arrival of reinforcements long awaited from England.

The fleet which brought them brought also long and fond letters from home, with the very last news of the children under the care of their good Aunt Hetty and their grandfather. The mother’s heart yearned towards the absent young ones. She made me no reproaches; but I could read her importunities in her anxious eyes, her terrors for me, and her longing for her children. Why stay longer? she seemed to say. You who have no calling to this war, or to draw sword against your countrymen—why continue to imperil your life and my happiness? I understood her appeal. We were to enter upon no immediate service of danger; I told her Sir Henry was only going to accompany the expedition for part of the way. I would return with him, the reconnaissance over; and Christmas, please Heaven, should see our family once more united in England.

A force of three thousand men—including a couple of slender regiments of American Loyalists and New York militia (with which latter my distinguished relative, Mr. Will Esmond, went as captain)—was embarked at New York; and our armament sailed up the noble Hudson, that presents finer aspects than the Rhine in Europe to my mind. Nor was any fire opened upon us from those beetling cliffs and precipitous palisades by which we sailed—the enemy, strange to say, being for once unaware of the movement we contemplated. The river spoke its own language: the slap of oars, the groan of timber, the creak of rigging, and, from the heights, now and then the lonely call of a bird. Those clean natural sounds—unbought, unadvertised—had more art in them than all the fiddling in Philadelphia.

Our first landing was on the eastern bank at a place called Verplanck’s Point, whence the Congress troops withdrew after slight resistance, their leader, the tough old Putnam, supposing our march was to be directed towards the Eastern Highlands, by which we intended to penetrate to Burgoyne. Putnam fell back to occupy these passes, a small detachment of ours being sent forward as if in pursuit, which he imagined was to be followed by the rest of our force. Meanwhile, before daylight, two thousand men without artillery were carried over to Stoney Point on the western shore opposite Verplanck’s, under a great hill called the Dunderberg by the old Dutch lords of the stream, hanging precipitous over it. A little stream at the northern base of this mountain cuts between it and the opposite height on which Fort Clinton stood—named not after our general, but after one of the two gentlemen of the same name, among the oldest and most respected of the provincial gentry of New York, and who were at this moment actually in command against Sir Henry. On the next height is Fort Montgomery; behind them rises Bear Hill; whilst at the opposite side of the magnificent stream stands Saint Antony’s Nose, a prodigious peak indeed, which the Dutch had quaintly christened.

The attacks on the two forts were almost simultaneous. Half our men were detached for the assault on Fort Montgomery, under the brave Campbell, who fell before the rampart. Sir Henry—who would never be out of danger where he could find it—personally led the remainder, and hoped, he said, that we should have better luck than before Sullivan’s Island. A path led up to the Dunderberg, so narrow as scarcely to admit three men abreast; and in utter silence our whole force scaled it, wondering at every rugged step to meet with no opposition. The enemy had not even kept watch there; nor were we descried until we were descending the height, at the base of which we easily dispersed a small force sent hurriedly to oppose us.

The firing which here took place rendered all idea of surprise impossible. The fort was before us. With such arms as the troops had in their hands they had to assault; and silently and swiftly, in the face of artillery playing upon them, the troops ascended the hill. The men had orders on no account to fire. Taking the colours of the Sixty-third and bearing them aloft, Sir Henry mounted with the stormers. The place was so steep that the men pushed each other over the wall and through the embrasures; and it was there that Lieutenant Joseph Blake—the father of a certain Joseph Clinton Blake, who looks with the eyes of affection on a certain young lady—presented himself to the living of Warrington by saving the life of the unworthy patron thereof.

About a fourth part of the garrison, as we were told, escaped out of the fort; the rest were killed or wounded, or remained our prisoners within the works. Fort Montgomery was, in like manner, stormed and taken by our people; and at night, as we looked down from the heights where the King’s standard had been just planted, we were treated to a splendid illumination in the river below.

Under Fort Montgomery, stretching over to that lofty prominence called Saint Antony’s Nose, a boom and chain had been laid with vast cost and labour, behind which several American frigates and galleys were anchored. The fort being taken, these ships attempted to get up the river in the darkness, out of reach of guns which they knew must destroy them in the morning. But the wind was unfavourable; escape proved impossible. The crews therefore took to the boats and landed, having previously set the ships on fire with all their sails set; and we beheld those magnificent pyramids of flame burning up to the heavens and reflected in the waters below, until, amid prodigious explosions, they sank and disappeared.

Even fire has its appetite; it licks pitch and tar as greedily as any kitchen blaze takes fat that drips upon the coals. The smell of burning rope and resin came down like a bitter sauce over the river air, and the crack of spars was like bones breaking. Yet, mingled with it all, there was the steady pulse of the stream itself, indifferent, carrying ash and bright embers alike, as if to remind us that Nature keeps her own tongue while men shout in theirs.

On the next day a parlementaire came in from the enemy to inquire as to the state of his troops left wounded or prisoners in our hands; and the Continental officer brought me a note which gave me a strange shock, for it showed that in the struggle of the previous evening my brother had been engaged. It was dated October 7, from Major-General George Clinton’s divisional headquarters, and stated briefly that Colonel H. Warrington, of the Virginia line, hoped that Sir George Warrington escaped unhurt in the assault of last evening, from which the Colonel himself was so fortunate as to retire without the least injury.

Never did I say my prayers more heartily and gratefully than on that night, devoutly thanking Heaven that my dearest brother was spared, and making a vow at the same time to withdraw out of the fratricidal contest into which I had entered only because Honour and Duty seemed imperatively to call me. I own I felt an inexpressible relief when I had come to the resolution to retire and betake myself to the peaceful shade of my own vines and fig-trees at home.

I longed, however, to see my brother ere I returned, and asked—and easily obtained—an errand to the camp of the American General Clinton from our own chief. The headquarters of his division were now some miles up the river; and a boat and a flag of truce quickly brought me to the point where his out-pickets received me on the shore.

My brother was very soon with me. He had only lately joined General Clinton’s division with letters from headquarters at Philadelphia; and he chanced to hear, after the attack on Fort Clinton, that I had been present during the affair. We passed a brief, delightful night together: Mr. Sady, who always followed Hal to the war, cooking a feast in honour of both his masters. War makes poor larders; yet the faithful cook contrived, as such men do, to find comfort in the very act of contriving—some salted meat made tender by long simmering, maize-cakes crisped on a hot plate, and a little sharp relish of whatever could be pickled or pounded with salt. The hut filled with the homely perfume of broth and corn, so unlike powder-smoke; and in the pauses between our talk, we could hear the river’s far-off breathing and, nearer, the low stir of a camp at rest—boots scuffing, a sentry’s cough, a kettle’s lid chattering as it cooled. In such sounds, more than in speeches, men remember what they are.

There was but one bed of straw in the hut where we had quarters; and Hal and I slept on it, side by side, as we had done when we were boys. We had a hundred things to say regarding past times and present. His kind heart gladdened when I told him of my resolve to retire to my acres and to take off the red coat which I wore: he flung his arms round it.

“Praised be God!” said he. “Oh, heavens, George! think what might have happened had we met in the affair two nights ago!” And he turned quite pale at the thought.

He eased my mind with respect to our mother. She was a bitter Tory, to be sure, but the Chief had given special injunctions regarding her safety. “And Fanny”—Hal’s wife—“watches over her, and she is as good as a company!” cried the enthusiastic husband. “Isn’t she clever? Isn’t she handsome? Isn’t she good?”—never, fortunately, waiting for any reply to these ardent queries. “And to think that I was nearly marrying Maria once! Oh, mercy, what an escape I had!” he added. “Hagan prays for the King every morning and night at Castlewood, but they bolt the doors, and nobody hears. Gracious powers! his wife is sixty if she is a day; and oh, George! the quantity she drinks is—”

But why tell the failings of our good cousin? I am pleased to think she lived to drink the health of King George long after his Old Dominion had passed for ever from his sceptre.

Morning came, when my brief mission to the camp was ended; and the truest of friends and fondest of brothers accompanied me to my boat, which lay waiting at the riverside. We exchanged an embrace at parting; and his hand held mine yet for a moment ere I stepped into the barge which bore me rapidly down the stream.

Shall I see thee once more, dearest and best companion of my youth? I thought. Amongst our cold Englishmen, can I ever hope to meet with a friend like thee? When hadst thou ever a thought that was not kindly and generous? When a wish, or a possession, but for me you would sacrifice it? How brave you are, and how modest; how gentle, and how strong; how simple, unselfish, and humble; how eager to see others’ merit; how diffident of your own!

He stood on the shore till his figure grew dim before me. There was that in my eyes which prevented me from seeing him longer.

Brilliant as Sir Henry’s success had been, it was achieved, as usual, too late; and served but as a small set-off against the disaster of Burgoyne which ensued immediately, and which our advance was utterly inadequate to relieve. More than one secret messenger was despatched to him who never reached him, and of whom we never learned the fate. Of one wretch who offered to carry intelligence to him, and whom Sir Henry despatched with a letter of his own, we heard the miserable doom. Falling in with some of the troops of General George Clinton, who happened to be in red uniform (part of the prize of a British ship’s cargo, doubtless, taken by American privateers), the spy thought he was in the English army and advanced towards the sentries. He found his mistake too late. His letter was discovered upon him, and he had to die for bearing it.

There is a cruelty in uniforms beyond their cloth: they are a lexicon men wear on their bodies, a set of meanings imposed and read at a glance. One scarlet coat can say “friend” or “enemy” according to the reader; and when the wrong word is spoken, no man may translate himself in time. In such moments, language dies on the tongue, and the body pays for the misunderstanding.

In ten days after the success at the forts occurred the great disaster at Saratoga, of which we carried the dismal particulars in the fleet which bore us home. I am afraid my wife was unable to mourn for it. She had her children, her father, her sister to revisit; and daily and nightly thanks to pay to Heaven that had brought her husband safe out of danger. The war, with all its proclamations and parades, dwindled then to what it always becomes at last: a table set again, familiar voices under a roof, the small domestic sounds returning to their rightful dominion—spoons against china, a hearth settling, bread broken, and the heart, which has been living on noise, learning once more the quiet dialect of peace.

Need I paint to you the home-coming, when the latch lifted and a whole household, long scattered like seed before a hard wind, dropped again into one warm furrow? A mother’s joy does not require ink; it sits in the eyes, shines in the quick, busy hands, and kneels down of itself in the stillest corner of a familiar room, as if the very boards were an altar. Our rooms were wide enough to hold us all—nursery, parlour, chambers above stairs, and the long passage where the sound of steps at night used to be a kind of family clock. Yet for all that space, Aunt Hetty would not remain beneath our roof.

She said it fairly: to lay down her borrowed motherhood—those elder children who had been hers in all but blood for near three years—cost her too sharp a pang; she could not yet sit at our table and be content with a second place. So she went away with her father to Bury St. Edmunds, a short ride from us, and kept house there; and in that quieter distance she spoiled her eldest nephew and niece as if it were a secret indulgence, pinching sweetmeats into their palms and letting them run riot among her own cupboards.

It was the year after our return that Mr. B—he of the Jamaica plantations—died, leaving her half his fortune; and only then did I hear how the worthy gentleman had once been very hotly enamoured of her under that island sun, and, though she refused him, showed his constancy in his will. Heaven knows how much of Aunt Hetty’s property Monsieur Miles hath already eaten, as if money were a pudding set before him: the price of his commission and its glittering outfit; the gorgeous uniforms that require more gold lace than good sense; play-debts, and those little transactions in the Minories that smell of candle-grease and cheap gin; the cost of Pall Mall taverns and petits soupers; cards—even “in moderation”—at the Cocoa-Tree. Do you think, sirrah, I do not know what human nature is, and what these enjoyments cost; and that a gentleman cannot purchase them all on the five hundred a year which I allow him? Aunt Hetty declares she has made up her mind to be an old maid.

“I made a vow never to marry till I could find a man as good as my dear father,” she said; “and I never did, Sir George. No, my dearest Theo, not half as good; and Sir George may put that in his pipe and smoke it.”

And yet, when the good General died—calm, full of years, and ready, as he said, to be gone—I think it was my wife who shed the most tears. There are griefs that make no show in the hardened, and those that overflow in the tender like milk boiling at the lip of a pan.

“I weep because I think I did not love him enough,” said the creature; whereas Hetty scarce departed from her calm—at least outwardly and before us all. She speaks of him constantly still, as though he were alive; recalls his merry sayings, his gentle, kind ways with his children; and at such times she brightens so suddenly that she looks for a moment quite a girl again. Often she sits cheerfully in church and looks up at the slab that carries his name and some of his virtues—and for once tells no lies.

I had fancied, now and then, that my brother Hal (for whom Hetty had a juvenile passion) still held some corner of her heart. Ten years ago, when he came to see us, I told him of that childish romance, half in hope—foolish match-maker that I am—that he might ask her to replace Mrs. Fanny, who had been gathered to her fathers; and regarding whom my wife, with her habit of making herself guilty for any shortness of feeling, would still reproach herself because she did not regret Fanny enough. Hal came to us plunged in grief about his loss, vowing the world did not contain such another woman. Our dear old General was alive then, and took him in and housed him as he had done in the happy early days; the women played him the very same tunes he had heard when a boy at Oakhurst—the harpsichord’s thin sweetness, the fiddle’s plaintive scrape—and each air, like a dish long absent from the table, brought back its own savour of the past. In our country rooms you could hear the house itself—wind worrying at the casement, the sober tick of the clock, the soft complaint of a kettle beginning to sing—no roaring streets, no iron wheels to bruise thought; and in that kinder soundscape memory comes easily, and grief too.

Everybody’s heart was softened by old recollections, and Harry never tired of pouring out his recitals of his wife’s virtues to Het; and then, as though to rest himself, would talk fondly of his dear Aunt Lambert, whom he loved with all his heart, and whose praises, you may be sure, were welcome to the faithful old husband, out of whose thoughts his wife’s memory was never, I think, absent for three waking minutes.

General Hal went to Paris later as an American General Officer in blue and buff—the colours that Mr. Fox and other gentlemen had brought into fashion here likewise—and he was made much of at Versailles, though he was presented by Monsieur le Marquis de Lafayette to the Most Christian King and Queen, who did not love Monsieur le Marquis. I believe a Marquise took a fancy to the Virginian General and would have married him out of hand, had he not resisted and fled back to England, to Warrington, and especially to Bury, where folks would listen to him talk about his late wife with endless patience and sympathy. As for us, who had known the poor paragon in the flesh, we were civil but not quite so enthusiastic, and sometimes rather puzzled to answer our children’s questions about Uncle Hal’s angel wife. Children, at least, insist upon particulars: whether the angel liked custards, whether she laughed, whether she ever burnt a pie. They will not be fobbed off with halos.

The two Generals and myself, and Captain Miles, and Parson Blake—who was knocked over at Monmouth the year after I left America, and came home to change his coat and take my living—used to fight the battles of the Revolution over our bottle. The claret had its own rich smell, like warm fruit and old wood; the glasses chimed; the cork, drawn, made its small report like a musket far away; and outside, in the dark, you could hear the owls and the hedgerows settling. It was a blessed thing to argue with only that honest country music for accompaniment, and not the ceaseless clatter of towns where men are driven out of their own hearing by commerce and wheels and brazen entertainments.

The parson would cry, “By Jupiter, General”—he compounded for Jupiter when he laid down his military habit—“you are the Tory, and Sir George is the Whig! He is always finding fault with our leaders, and you are for ever standing up for them; and when I prayed for the King last Sunday, I heard you following me quite loud.”

“And so I do, Blake, with all my heart; I can’t forget I wore his coat,” says Hal.

“Ah, if Wolfe had been alive for twenty years more!” says Lambert.

“Ah, sir,” cries Hal, “you should hear the General talk about him!”

“What General?” says I (to vex him).

“My General,” says Hal, standing up and filling a bumper. “His Excellency General George Washington!”

“With all my heart,” cry I; but the parson’s face puckered as though the toast soured his wine.

Hal never tired of speaking of his General; and it was upon some such evening, when the bottle had gone twice round and the candles sank low and made long hollows in men’s cheeks, that he told us how he had actually been in disgrace with this leader whom he loved so fondly. Their difference, it seems, was about Monsieur le Marquis de Lafayette—he who played so fine a part in the late history, and who hath so suddenly slipped from the stage of it.

Hal’s previous rank in our own service and his acknowledged gallantry during the war ought, as he thought, to have secured his promotion in the Continental army, where a whipper-snapper like M. de Lafayette had but to arrive and be complimented by Congress with the rank of Major-General. Hal, with the freedom of an old soldier, had expressed himself somewhat contemptuously regarding certain appointments made by Congress, where miserable intrigues and cabals were set to work by unscrupulous officers greedy of advancement. Mr. Warrington—imitating perhaps in this the example of his now illustrious friend of Mount Vernon—affected to make the war en gentilhomme: took his pay, to be sure, but spent it upon comforts and clothing for his men; and as for rank, declared it was a matter of no earthly concern, and that he would as soon serve as colonel as in any higher grade. No doubt he added hot remarks regarding certain general officers of the Congress army, their origin and the causes of their sudden lifting: notably he was angry at the marvellous leap of that young French lad—the Marquis, as they loved to call him—who, by the way, was a prodigious favourite of the Chief himself.

There were not three officers in the whole Continental force (after poor madcap Lee was taken prisoner and disgraced) who could speak the Marquis’s language; so Hal could judge the young Major-General more closely and familiarly than other gentlemen, including the Commander-in-Chief. Mr. Washington good-naturedly rated friend Hal for being jealous of the beardless commander of Auvergne; was himself not a little pleased by the filial regard and profound veneration which the enthusiastic young nobleman always showed him; and had, moreover, the very best politic reasons for treating the Marquis with friendship and favour.

Meanwhile, as it afterwards turned out, the Commander-in-Chief was most urgently pressing Colonel Warrington’s promotion upon Congress; and as if his difficulties before the enemy were not enough—he being that hard winter entrenched at Valley Forge, commanding five or six thousand men at most, almost without fire, blankets, food, or ammunition, in face of Sir William Howe’s perfectly appointed army, three times as numerous as his own—as if that were not enough to try him, he had further to encounter the cowardly distrust of Congress, and insubordination and conspiracy amongst the officers in his own camp.

During that awful winter of ’77, when one blow struck by the sluggard at the head of the British forces might have ended the war, and all was doubt, confusion, and despair in the opposite camp (save in one indomitable breast alone), my brother had an interview with the Chief which he afterwards described to me; and Hal could never speak of it without his voice thickening, as if memory were a crust he must swallow.

Mr. Washington had won no such triumph as that which the dare-devil courage of Arnold and the elegant imbecility of Burgoyne had procured for Gates and the northern army. Save in one or two minor encounters which proved his daring bravery and unceasing watchfulness, he had met defeat after defeat from an enemy in all points his superior. Congress mistrusted him. Many an officer in his own camp hated him. Those disappointed in ambition, those detected in peculation, those whose selfishness or incapacity his honest eyes had spied—were all, more or less, leagued against him. Gates was the chief toward whom the malcontents turned: Mr. Gates was the only genius fit to conduct the war; and with a vaingloriousness he afterwards generously owned, he did not refuse the homage paid him.

To show how dreadful were the troubles and anxieties with which General Washington had to contend, I may mention what at that time was called the “Conway Cabal.” A certain Irishman—a Chevalier of St. Louis, and an officer in the French service—arrived in America early in ’77 in quest of employment. He was speedily appointed brigadier, and could not be content, forsooth, without immediate promotion to major-general. Mr. C. had friends in Congress, who, as the General-in-Chief was informed, had promised him his speedy step. General Washington remonstrated, representing the injustice of promoting to the highest rank the youngest brigadier in the service; and whilst the matter was pending, he was put in possession of a letter from Conway to General Gates, complimenting him, saying that “Heaven had been determined to save America, or a weak general and bad councillors would have ruined it.” The General enclosed the note to Mr. Conway without a word; and Conway offered his resignation, which Congress refused, appointing him Inspector-General of the army with the rank of Major-General.

“And it was at this time,” says Harry—his fingers tightening round the glass as if it were a musket-stock—“when, by heavens, the glorious Chief was oppressed by troubles enough to drive ten thousand men mad—that I must interfere with my jealousies about the Frenchman! I had not said much: only some nonsense to Greene and Cadwalader about getting some frogs, against the Frenchman came to dine with us; and having a bagful of Marquises over from Paris, as we were not able to command ourselves. But I should have known the Chief’s troubles, and that he had a better head than mine, and might have had the grace to hold my tongue.

“For a while the General said nothing; but I could remark, by the coldness of his demeanour, that something had occurred to create a schism between him and me. Mrs. Washington, who had come to camp, also saw something was wrong. Women have artful ways of soothing men and finding their secrets out. I am not sure I should ever have tried to learn the cause of the General’s displeasure—for I am as proud as he is—and besides,” says Hal, “when the Chief is angry, it was not pleasant coming near him, I can promise you.” My brother was indeed subjugated by his old friend, and obeyed him and bowed before him as a boy before a schoolmaster.

“At last,” Hal resumed, “Mrs. Washington found out the mystery. ‘Speak to me after dinner, Colonel Hal,’ says she. ‘Come out to the parade-ground, before the dining-house, and I will tell you all.’ I left a half-score of general officers and brigadiers drinking round the General’s table, and found Mrs. Washington waiting for me. She told me it was the speech I had made about the box of Marquises, with which the General was offended. ‘I should not have heeded it in another,’ he had said; ‘but I never thought Harry Warrington would have joined against me.’

“I had to wait on him for the word that night, and found him alone at his table—just the scratch of his pen, the low crackle of a poor fire, and beyond the thin walls the camp’s uneasy hush: men coughing, a sentry’s foot, a far-off murmur like the sea made by wind in bare trees. ‘Can your Excellency give me five minutes’ time?’ I said, with my heart in my mouth. ‘Yes, surely, sir,’ says he, pointing to the other chair. ‘Will you please to be seated?’

“‘It used not always to be Sir and Colonel Warrington between me and your Excellency,’ I said.

“He said, calm, ‘The times are altered.’

“‘Et nos mutamur in illis,’ says I. ‘Times and people are both changed.’

“‘You had some business with me?’ he asked.

“‘Am I speaking to the Commander-in-Chief or to my old friend?’ I asked.

“He looked at me gravely. ‘Well—to both, sir,’ he said. ‘Pray sit, Harry.’

“‘If to General Washington, I tell his Excellency that I, and many officers of this army, are not well pleased to see a boy of twenty made a major-general over us, because he is a Marquis, and because he can’t speak the English language. If I speak to my old friend, I have to say that he has shown me very little of trust or friendship for the last few weeks; and that I have no desire to sit at your table, and have impertinent remarks made by others there, of the way in which his Excellency turns his back on me.’

“‘Which charge shall I take first, Harry?’ he asked, turning his chair away from the table and crossing his legs as if ready for a talk. ‘You are jealous, as I gather, about the Marquis?’

“‘Jealous, sir!’ says I. ‘An aide-de-camp of Mr. Wolfe is not jealous of a Jack-a-dandy who, five years ago, was being whipped at school!’

“‘You yourself declined higher rank than that which you hold,’ says the Chief, turning a little red.

“‘But I never bargained to have a macaroni Marquis to command me!’ I cried. ‘I will not, for one, carry the young gentleman’s orders; and since Congress and your Excellency chooses to take your generals out of the nursery, I shall humbly ask leave to resign, and retire to my plantation.’

“‘Do, Harry; that is true friendship!’ says the Chief—with a gentleness that surprised me. ‘Now that your old friend is in a difficulty, ’tis surely the best time to leave him.’

“‘Sir!’ says I.

“‘Do as so many of the rest are doing, Mr. Warrington. Et tu, Brute, as the play says. Well, well, Harry! I did not think it of you; but, at least, you are in the fashion.’

“‘You asked which charge you should take first?’ I said.

“‘Ch—the promotion of the Marquis? I recommended the appointment to Congress, no doubt; and you and other gentlemen disapprove it.’

“‘I have spoken for myself, sir,’ says I.

“‘If you take me in that tone, Colonel Warrington, I have nothing to answer!’ says the Chief, rising up very fiercely; ‘and presume that I can recommend officers for promotion without asking your previous sanction.’

“‘Being on that tone, sir,’ says I, ‘let me respectfully offer my resignation to your Excellency, founding my desire to resign upon the fact that Congress, at your Excellency’s recommendation, offers its highest commands to boys of twenty, who are scarcely even acquainted with our language.’ And I rose and made his Excellency a bow.

“‘Great heavens, Harry!’ he cries—about this Marquis’s appointment he was beaten, that was the fact, and could not reply to me—‘can’t you believe that in this critical time of our affairs, there are reasons why special favours should be shown to the first Frenchman of distinction who comes amongst us?’

“‘No doubt, sir. If your Excellency acknowledges that Monsieur de Lafayette’s merits have nothing to do with the question.’

“‘I acknowledge or deny nothing, sir!’ says the General, stamping his foot, looking as though he could be terrible if he would. ‘Am I here to be catechised by you? Stay. Hark, Harry! I speak to you as a man of the world—nay, as an old friend. This appointment humiliates you and others, you say? Be it so! Must we not bear humiliation, along with the other burdens and griefs, for the sake of our country? It is no more just perhaps that the Marquis should be set over you gentlemen, than that your Prince Ferdinand or your Prince of Wales at home should have command over veterans. But if in appointing this young nobleman we please a whole nation, and bring ourselves twenty millions of allies, will you and other gentlemen sulk because we do him honour? ’Tis easy to sneer at him (though, believe me, the Marquis has many more merits than you allow him); to my mind it were more generous, as well as more polite, of Harry Warrington to welcome this stranger for the sake of the prodigious benefit our country may draw from him—not to laugh at his peculiarities, but to aid him and help his ignorance by your experience as an old soldier. That is what I would do—that is the part I expected of thee—for it is the generous and manly one, Harry. But you choose to join my enemies, and when I am in trouble you say you will leave me. That is why I have been hurt: that is why I have been cold. I thought I might count on your friendship—and—and you can tell whether I was right or no. I relied on you as on a brother, and you come and tell me you will resign. Be it so! Being embarked in this contest, by God’s will I will see it to an end. You are not the first, Mr. Warrington, has left me on the way.’

“He spoke with such tenderness, and his face wore such unhappiness as he spoke, that remorse seized me, and pity too; and I cried out I know not what incoherent old words, and vowed that if he would say the word, I never would leave him. You never loved him, George,” says my brother, turning to me, “but I did beyond all mortal men; and though I am not clever like you, I think my instinct was right. He has a greatness not approached by other men.”

“I don’t say no, brother,” said I, “now.”

“Greatness, pooh!” says the parson, growling over his wine, as though greatness were a spice he mistrusted.

“We walked into Mrs. Washington’s tea-room arm-in-arm,” Hal resumed; “she looked up kind, and saw we were friends. ‘Is it all over, Colonel Harry?’ she whispered. ‘I know he has applied ever so often about your promotion—’

“‘I never will take it,’ says I. And that is how I came to do penance,” says Harry, “with Lafayette the next winter.” Hal could mimic the Frenchman to admiration. “‘I will go weez heem,’ says I. ‘I know the way to Quebec, and when we are not in action with Sir Guy, I can hear his Excellency the Major-General say his lesson.’ There was no fight—you know we could get no army to act in Canada—and we returned to headquarters. And what do you think disturbed the Frenchman most? The idea that people would laugh at him because his command had come to nothing. And so they did laugh at him—almost to his face too—and who could help it? If our Chief had any weak point it was this Marquis.

“After our little difference we became as great friends as before—if a man may be said to be friends with a Sovereign Prince, for as such I somehow could not help regarding the General. One night, when we had sate the company out, we talked of old times, and the jolly days of sport together both before and after Braddock’s; and that pretty duel you were near having when we were boys. He laughed about it, and said he never saw a man look more wicked and more bent on killing than you did: ‘And to do Sir George justice, I think he has hated me ever since,’ says the Chief. ‘Ah!’ he added, ‘an open enemy I can face readily enough. ’Tis the secret foe who causes the doubt and anguish! We have sat with more than one at my table to-day, to whom I am obliged to show a face of civility, whose hands I must take when offered, though I know they are stabbing my reputation and eager to pull me down from my place. You spoke but lately of being humiliated because a junior was set over you in command. What humiliation is yours compared to mine, who have to play the farce of welcome to these traitors; who have to bear the neglect of Congress, and see men who have insulted me promoted in my own army? If I consulted my own feelings as a man, would I continue in this command? You know whether my temper is naturally warm or not, and whether, as a private gentleman, I should be likely to suffer such slights and outrages as are put upon me daily; but in the advancement of the sacred cause in which we are engaged, we have to endure not only hardship and danger, but calumny and wrong, and may God give us strength to do our duty!’ And then the General showed me the papers regarding the affair of that fellow Conway, whom Congress promoted in spite of the intrigue, and down whose black throat John Cadwalader sent the best ball he ever fired in his life.

“And it was here,” said Hal, concluding, “as I looked at the Chief talking at night in the silence of the camp, and remembered how lonely he was, what an awful responsibility he carried, how spies and traitors were eating out of his dish, and an enemy lay in front of him who might at any time overpower him—that I thought, ‘Sure, this is the greatest man now in the world; and what a wretch I am to think of my jealousies and annoyances, whilst he is walking serenely under his immense cares!’”

“We talked but now of Wolfe,” said I. “Here, indeed, is a greater than Wolfe. To endure is greater than to dare; to tire out hostile fortune; to be daunted by no difficulty; to keep heart when all have lost it; to go through intrigue spotless; and to forgo even ambition when the end is gained—who can say this is not greatness, or show the other Englishman who has achieved so much?”

“I wonder, Sir George, you did not take Mr. Washington’s side, and wear the blue and buff yourself,” grumbles Parson Blake.

“You and I thought scarlet most becoming to our complexion, Joe Blake!” says I. “And my wife thinks there would not have been room for two such great men on one side.”

“Well, at any rate, you were better than that odious, swearing, crazy General Lee, who was second in command!” cries Lady Warrington. “And I am certain Mr. Washington never could write poetry and tragedies as you can! What did the General say about George’s tragedies, Harry?”

Harry burst into a roar of laughter—in which, of course, Mr. Miles must join his uncle, clapping as if at a play-bill in a noisy pit.

“Well!” says Hal, wiping his eyes, “it’s a fact that Hagan read one at my house to the General and Mrs. Washington and several more, and they all fell sound asleep!”

“He never liked my husband; that is the truth!” says Theo, tossing up her head. “And ’tis all the more magnanimous of Sir George to speak so well of him.”
